docs.title: Information System — Design Documentation
docs.text:
Design documentation for the organization's information system: people, accounts, membership over time, the groups and offices people belong to, and permissions.

Status: draft, actively being specified. Nothing here is frozen. Decisions holds what is settled and why; open questions holds what is not.

These documents are the specification. There is no schema file and no code to disagree with, so a rule that is not written down here does not exist. Every page states the design as it is now; what a page used to say, and the argument that changed it, lives in the decision log — nowhere else.

docs.title: The one idea this whole design rests on
docs.text:
A person is not a type. A person is a person.

Nothing about being a child, an adult, a counselor, a parent, or a member is a property of a human being. Each of those is either

  • an event or period — membership, guardianship, holding an office, being in a group; or
  • a derived fact — a person whose recorded birth date makes them a minor on the date being asked about, or one side of an active guardianship row.

There is one membership type, and it is ageless: no floor, no ceiling, no age-out, no child→adult transition. Age is a fact about the person, recorded once as person.birth_date, and it matters where the law says it matters — guardianship, and whatever rule an organizer writes for one event. It never matters in a membership row. No column anywhere says which bodies are for children; the control that does that job is that a named adult holds the write, and nobody joins anything by their own act.

The case that forced this: a person who was a member from September 1990 to June 2010, and again from October 2024 to the present. They were a child member, then nothing, then an adult counselor. That is one person row and two membership rows. A model with is_member or member_type on the person cannot express it.

The legacy corpus arrives as two exports — people, with the period each was a member of the organization, and events, with who attended. Because the people export states membership periods, the import writes bounded membership rows: both ends dated, data_confidence = 'low', one row per stated period, never open-ended and never inferred from attendance — an open membership satisfies is_current_member(), so an inferred one would make every 1998 roster a current member today. The import writes no sub-unit history, because the corpus names no sub-units and there are no sub-units to name; a group's roster before go-live is a thing a person types in. "Who was in Pack 12 in 1998?" has no answer, and that is a property of the design rather than a gap in the data.

Five rules the data model obeys throughout:

# Rule Consequence 1 Personhood is separate from participation person holds identity only. No member flags. 2 Participation is a period, not a boolean membership, person_group_member, guardianship, role_holder all carry valid_from / valid_to. 3 Access is granted, never implied by identity Being a parent does not by itself reach the child's data — the guardianship row's right_level does, and none is a value it is allowed to hold. 4 A group is not membership, and neither is an office There is one membership, at the unit. A person_group holds a dated roster and a role holds dated holders, and neither grants anything by being what it is. 5 Authority is one permission, allowed or denied A grant names one permission code, one scope (the unit, or exactly one item) and an effect. Allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. No levels, no "nearer wins", deny absolute.

Rule 4 has two subjects and they are kept apart on purpose. A person_group is a set of people — a lifetime, a dated roster, no authority, joinable only by somebody else's act. A role is an office: a named thing like chair or treasurer, with dated holders and no permissions inside it. An office confers nothing at all; what a chair may do is a grant written somewhere that names ROLE(chair). "Am I a paid-up member?" is one row, one status, one date, however many Thursday-evening groups the person turns up to and however many of them they run.

Why the two are never merged: a group's roster is materialized and dated, while an office is held by a rule that is re-evaluated on the date being asked about. One of them has a reconstructable past and the other does not, and a grant's reach must be readable from the grant.

Rule 5 replaced an older principle rather than inheriting it. Where this page states a boolean answer, an earlier design stated "authority does not flow down the hierarchy: a unit is covered only if it exposes its scope". That died with the hierarchy — the unit is a scope, not a row, and there is exactly one of it, so there is nothing above or below to flow between.

A safeguarding property went with the hierarchy and nothing here reproduces it. Access to a body's children used to have to be granted by that body, by the people who know them, who recruited the leader, and who can be asked. With one unit, a person.view grant at unit scope reaches every member's entire record — the widest read permission in the system. What stands between a person and that read is a named adult holding the write, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years, and a report of who holds the write. What did not go with it is the half of the rule that still has a subject: nothing is implied by who somebody is, and a deny cannot be outvoted.

docs.title: Reading order
Domain — what the organization actually is
docs.text: Document Covers glossary.md Ubiquitous language. Read this first. glossary-authorization.md The words the permission system is made of: grants, scopes, operands, expressions. domain/01-overview.md The model in plain language: actors, lifecycles, how a person's history reads. domain/02-actors.md Accounts, self-registration, unauthenticated people. domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md Historical records, matching, merging and unmerging people. domain/08-person-data.md What the system knows about a person, and why it is all one kind of data. Read it next to the identity document above — together they draw the boundary. domain/04-organization-structure.md The unit as a scope, groups, offices, and what joining one means. domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md Register → request → accept → pay → member → lapse → return. domain/06-authorization-model.md The permission model end to end. The one to read if you read only one. domain/06a-audiences-and-selectors.md Who a grant is aimed at: the expression grammar, the selector registry, and the rules that keep a tree safe. domain/07-events.md Events, registration, and how authority reaches an event. §1–§7. domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md Capacity and the waitlist, presence, cancellation, payments, the forms. §8–§13.

docs.title: Data model — the tables
docs.text: Document Covers data-model/00-conventions.md Naming, keys, temporal patterns, enums. Read before reviewing any data-model document — §6a says who enforces what. data-model/01-identity.md person — what the organization knows about a human, no status, no role, no type — what is deliberately not on it, and person_name. §1–§3. 01a account, account_credential, person_contact, person_identifier — signing in, being reached, and being named by other systems. §4–§7. 01b identity_hypothesis, person_merge, the views that exclude merged and redacted rows, the nightly checks, open issues. §8–§11. The three parts share one section numbering. data-model/09-attributes.md attribute_definition, person_attribute, attribute_option — everything about a person that is not a name, a gender or an age. data-model/02-organization.md person_group, person_group_member — named sets of people, their lifetimes, their dated rosters. There is no unit table; the unit is a scope. data-model/03-membership.md membership_type, membership_request, membership — the period, the renewal window, the sweep. data-model/04-relationships.md guardianship, and the history of its right level. data-model/05-authorization.md permission, role, role_holder, access_grant. §1–§7. 05a · 05b The grantee expression: audience, the grammar, selector_type, and the audience_operand tree. §8. 05c access_log and the resolver. §9–§10. 05d The invariants, what day one looks like, and what is open. §11–§13. The six parts share one section numbering, so a § citation names a number and this table says where it lives. 05e api_key — a caller that is nobody: what it may hold, what it may never hold, and how its calls reach the same resolver. §14–§17. data-model/06-audit-and-import.md audit_log — the data-change trail, its trigger, what is stripped before a row is written, the history query. §1–§2. 06a import_batch, the staging tables, the six stages, reversibility, idempotency, and what a source row actually evidences. §3. 06b redaction_log, the integrity checks over both trails, open issues. §4–§6. The three parts share one section numbering. data-model/07-finance.md Fees and payments. Provisional — you have not specified this yet. data-model/08-events.md event, organizers, registrations, questions, answers. §1–§7. 08a How authority reaches an event, the three queries that matter, integrity checks, open issues. §8–§11. The two parts share one section numbering.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Document Covers appendix/erd.md Entity-relationship diagrams. appendix/permission-catalog.md Every permission code, and the offices the organization starts with. appendix/removed-concepts.md Names that are not in the model, what to use instead of each, and the decision that took it. decisions/index.md Every decision, its reasoning, and the round that took it. open-questions.md What is unresolved, each with its schema impact, plus the assumption index.

docs.title: Scope boundaries
docs.text:
In scope now: identity, everything else the organization records about a person, accounts, membership over time, groups and offices, guardianship, events, and the authorization system.

Deliberately deferred — referenced so the data model does not block them, not designed: fee and payment processing beyond the provisional shape in data-model/07-finance.md, documents, reporting, notifications, and the API and UI layers. Each is listed in open-questions.md with the hooks already left for it.

Communication sits between the two lists, and the line is worth drawing rather than guessing. Its shape is decided: internal first, external channels are delivery rather than a product, anyone may send a direct message, broadcast is one ordinary scoped permission, the recipient chooses the channel, and a direct message to a minor is mirrored to that minor's guardians. Its codes are in the catalog. What is undesigned is the module — templates, opt-out granularity, retention, moderation. Notifications stay genuinely undesigned, and nothing in this design sends anything to anybody today (D-164): what is deferred is a module nobody has designed, not a promise anybody is waiting on. The renewal window made notifications dated rather than status-driven, which is a design note, not a design.

There is no health module, and none is waiting to be designed. Everything the organization knows about a person beyond a name, a gender and an age is one class of data, held in fields the organization defines while it runs — domain/08-person-data.md and data-model/09-attributes.md. Sensitivity is graded by what a grant exposes, never by which table a permission code names.

docs.title: How to change this documentation
docs.text:
You are expected to iterate. When refining:

  1. State what is. A page carries the current design and no history. When you overrule something, delete the old statement from the page and let the decision entry own the exchange. Where a reader would plausibly reach for the thing you removed, leave one line naming it, saying it is not there, and saying what to use instead — that is a guardrail, not a memory.
  2. Update the affected documents. Domain files carry the model in plain language; data-model files carry the rules and the fields they bind. No file carries SQL: a rule is written as a numbered requirement, and data-model/00-conventions.md §6a names the layer that must carry it. Where no layer can enforce a rule, the text says a convention, not a guard rather than letting a reader assume a guarantee.
  3. Record anything non-obvious that you overrule in the decision log, in the round that took it, and add it to that page's index.
  4. Move a resolved item out of open-questions.md rather than deleting it, so the reasoning survives.
  5. A name that leaves the model gets one row in the removed-concepts appendix and an entry in the log. The organization may still be using the word, so it is not deleted from its vocabulary — only from the model.

Where this documentation states an assumption you did not make, it is written as Assumption: in italics, so you can find and kill it with a search.

Decisions behind this page: D-001, D-005, D-037, D-038, D-083, D-086, D-088, D-090, D-092, D-093, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100.

docs.title: Glossary — Authorization terms
docs.text: The authorization half of the glossary: the words a grant, an audience, an expression or an audit row is written out of. Terms defined elsewhere in the glossary — person, group and office, guardianship — are not repeated here.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
Permission — The atomic unit of authority: a coded capability such as membership.request.approve or person.view. Permissions are the only things the authorization layer actually checks. Each row carries applies_to (unit, or unit_and_item — where the code may be granted at all, checked when a grant is saved, so a grant of event.create written on an event is refused rather than evaluated) and right_kind (read | write, which exists for exactly one customer: the guardianship channel). Codes are stable identifiers, never display strings, and there is no <resource>.admin wildcard and no prefix match (D-068). Specified in data-model/05 §2.

Role — An office, not a bundle: see Organization. The one sentence people get wrong — a role confers nothing, and the codes it carries are the live grants naming ROLE(x). Roles are runtime data with no exception: the organization invents them, composes them out of grants and deletes the unused ones, and no role ships (D-052, D-150).

Scope — What a grant applies to: the unit, or exactly one item (scope_type + scope_id), never a nested body and never a choice between several items. Items are registered in grant_scope_type — event, person_group, role, and document deferred — and unit is the one row that is not item-scoped. Inheritance, stated once: a grant at the unit reaches every item of every type, because nothing is left between them and there is no owner to test; a grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else (domain/06 §2).

Grant — The whole of the grants channel, and its shape is the whole definition: grantee + scope + one permission_id + effect + period, in access_grant. The grantee is a person, an audience or an API key — exactly one of the three, never two and never none (D-116); the scope is the unit or one item; the effect is allow or deny; the period is valid_from / valid_to, live on the checked date. Plus provenance — granted_by, granted_at, grant_reason, and for lent authority is_delegated with delegated_from. One code per grant, not a set and not a level, which is what makes "what exactly does this person have?" a list of rows — a key's list is the same list of the same kind — and "who else can do this?" the same list read the other way. Nothing adds a membership test to a grant — see Selector below. See domain/06 §5.

API key — api_key: one registered integration that calls this system over an API, installed in the system by a named person, and a grantee in the same sense a person is — the third kind named in Grant above (D-116). One row is one caller and holds one live secret, which rotates in place: replacing the secret moves no grant and no audit reference, and the row carries a code so a grant and an audit row name the same integration across years. valid_to is optional and absent means current, and nothing about a key is derived from whoever installed it — created_by is attribution for an act, and owner_person_id is a contact, not a channel (D-119, D-120). What a key is not: not an account, which is a way for a person to log in; not an office, which a person holds and which confers nothing; not a selector, since no expression may name one and no set contains one, EVERYONE included (D-117); and not a grantable item, because api_key is not in grant_scope_type. A key may never be granted system.admin, nor any of api_key.view, api_key.create, api_key.rotate, api_key.end — a key may not change what a key can do, and may not become everything — refused when the grant is saved, with integrity check 20 the whole net for rows that skipped the save (D-122). Specified in data-model/05e.

Caller — Whoever a permission check is answered about: a person, or a key. The word is invariant 19's subject: written about a person alone, that invariant would not have forbidden a table keyed by api_key_id and permission_code and holding a boolean, and "the integration's permissions" is the most natural such table in this system to write (D-123). A request authenticates as a person or as a key, never as both, and in both audit trails actor_person_id and api_key_id are mutually exclusive. One resolver, and one entry point per kind of caller — can(person, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at, owner_person_id) and can_key(api_key, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at) — and the second takes no person of any kind: a claimed person would make the trail's word for who acted an input (D-121). Nothing else is — this system writing to itself is not a third caller, it is an empty actor column, and it holds no grants (An empty actor column below).

An empty actor column — actor_person_id with nothing in it, in access_log or in audit_log, or an empty created_by / updated_by: read as this system acting on its own, a complete answer to "who did this" rather than a missing one. It is not a caller — a check is answered about a person or a key (see Caller above) — and this system holds no grants, is named by no grant and appears in no role_holder row; nothing in a permission check reads an empty actor column to decide an answer. Two limits keep it narrow: only where empty is legal (import_batch.created_by and api_key.created_by are required, and a grant's granted_by names a person) and only in an actor column — an absent scope_id is a check at the unit, not a writer. Where the trail has a label column, the writer's name comes from a fixed list, so a label such as system:renewal-sweep is one of the few names this system signs its own writes with and bare system is retired; the list, what it costs, and the check that reports an off-list label are stated once in 00-conventions §7a (D-125).

Allow / deny, and the decision rule — Allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. That is the whole of precedence, and everything else in the model is elaboration (domain/06 §7). A deny is absolute: it is checked before anything else, at any scope, so no item is local enough to override a suspension. A deny is legal at the unit as well as on an item, and is never conditioned on membership in either direction. - inside an expression is not a deny and the two are not interchangeable: subtracting a set narrows one grant's reach, while a deny defeats every grant that applies to the grantee it names, written anywhere by anyone — "she must not have this, whatever else she is given" is only ever a deny. Absolute over the grantee it names, and over no other: a deny on a person leaves a key standing, and a deny on a key leaves the person who installed it standing (D-118). The hygiene rule that comes with it is a report, not a constraint: a live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow is dead weight, and a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason.

Channel — There are three, and one absolute deny in front of them: grants, guardianship, and resource ownership. Guardianship is reached when the person the act is about is not the person performing it, which nobody has to remember, because the shape of the call decides — not the permission's name, since a parent editing their child's address is an ordinary person.contact.edit and a name-based rule would have skipped it (D-079). Corollary, and the part people get wrong: the guardianship channel can only say yes. When there is no guardianship, or the right is too low, it says nothing and the person's grants are still tried — otherwise a parent who is also the event registrar would be blocked from the roster by their own view over their child. Prohibitions are not made here; they are explicit denies. Roles and groups are not channels: they are sets that grants point at, and a key is not a fourth one. Two of these three cannot fire for a key at all, because ownership compares a person's id against a row and guardianship needs a party to a guardianship row — neither is refused by a new rule, each is simply unreachable, so a key's authority is its grants, in full and only. A check answered for a key records unit_grant or item_grant exactly as one for a person does: what the trail adds is who, not how (D-118).

Audience — The organization's word is permission group; the table is audience; both mean one thing. An audience is an expression over named sets of people, stored as a tree of binary rows and aimed at by a grant (D-101). Author in sets, evaluate per person: a check asks about one person, so the resolver compiles the expression down to a predicate and never materializes a set. The named sets are the whole vocabulary — GROUP(x) (a dated roster), ROLE(x) (an office), AUDIENCE(code) (another saved expression), PERSON(x) (one person, and the only way to write a set somebody typed by hand: PERSON(a) + PERSON(b)) — plus EVERYONE, MEMBERS, the two age operands OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n), and the five event operands. The operators are + - *; the age operands are ordinary named operands composed by those three, so MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19) is an ordinary term. GUARDIANS is not in that list, in either spelling: guardianship is a channel and not a set, so a kept list of contact adults is a GROUP(x) (D-113). No audience ships. A grant is aimed at an expression, and the operands are writable anywhere: an audience is a name worth a row only when something is going to name it, and a one-operand audience almost never is (D-153). A count of the operands belongs only in the registry table itself (data-model/05 §8). Fail closed in every direction: an operand that does not resolve is the empty set, and an expression that cannot be evaluated reaches nobody. The direction is the half people get backwards: a failed operand on the + or * side narrows the set and a failed operand on the - side widens it, so EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with a dead x is fail-closed and locks out everybody, in one step, which is not a safe state. An audience carrying a leaf that does not resolve is listed for its owner, and no save is refused because a leaf is broken. A missing value on the person being asked about is not a failure at all — a person with no birth date is simply not in OLDER(18), exactly as a person with no membership row is not in MEMBERS. Because a grant's reach is not visible in the row that grants it, whoever edits a grant or an audience is shown the expanded set of people — for a specific item — rather than a name (domain/06 §6.2).

Selector — One operand of an audience expression: a named operand, which means a row in the seeded registry selector_type (code, takes_argument, binds_to_item, argument_type). The parser reads its reserved words from that table, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the save path checks arity against it. A row is not removable out from under a rule: since D-109 a named thing a rule may still name is retired as deprecated or hidden, both of which keep resolving, and only disabled changes the answer — see Deprecated / hidden / disabled. What is required of an operand is that it be named, in the registry and not merely in a sentence — and that holds of prose too: every selector name that appears in these documents must be a selector_type row, which is what a count you read rather than one you rely on looks like. The registry is a closed language: every row ships with the platform, the table is organization-read-only, and a new operand is a decision entry plus a seed row, never a row somebody types into a screen. That closure is the line that keeps D-060's refusal of a rule engine true: OLDER(13) is a row, and AGE >= 13 is not one and cannot be, because the language has no >= anywhere to put it. Eligibility stays capability: the system applies no gate on its own; a person may write one with the vocabulary that ships, and membership is never implicit: it is a term the writer puts in, so requiring it is MEMBERS * ROLE(x), waiving it for a whole office is ROLE(x) alone, and waiving it for one named person is MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y). A grant naming ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently and forever, and nothing enforces the term — a convention, not a guard (see The permissions tab). The only grants this system writes for itself are the twelve beside an event, they name ORGANIZERS rather than a ROLE(...), and they carry no MEMBERS on purpose (D-151). Why: the resolver applies no membership test of its own at any scope, so the term is either written into the expression or it is nowhere (D-100).

Operand The set, on the checked date Argument EVERYONE Any person, including those with no account and no membership none MEMBERS Holds a membership live on the checked date none OLDER(n) / YOUNGER(n) n or older / strictly under n, both read from the birth date on the checked date — so this set gains and loses people at midnight with no write, and can(..., on date) for a past date answers for that past date. A person with no birth date is in neither of them, which is an ordinary answer and not a resolution failure — as a person with no membership row is not in MEMBERS a whole number of years — the registry's first argument that is not an entity, and therefore nothing for a merge to repoint ROLE(x) / bare x Holders of that office (role_holder) a role name GROUP(x) / bare x Members of that group (person_group_member) a group name AUDIENCE(code) The value of another saved audience's expression an audience code PERSON(x) One named person — a set of one, which is a set, so it is an ordinary row of the registry like every other operand. Summed, it is also the hand-typed set: PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) a person ATTENDED / PLACED / CONFIRMED / ON_WAITLIST / ORGANIZERS The four attendance tiers and the organizer roster optional event

Refused, and worth naming because a reader reaches for them: PRESENT(e) — a predicate over the check-in box would revoke a leader's access to their own camp photos whenever somebody forgot to tick it; WHITELISTED — no stored state to evaluate (EV-6). Both are refusals rather than type errors, and neither is seeded (D-107).

A hand-written set is a sum of PERSON leaves. It inherits the properties a named set needs: belonging to this one expression, invisible in the group browser, dying with the audience, and editable one name at a time — (GROUP(kitchen) + PERSON(honza)) - PERSON(a) - PERSON(b). What has no spelling is a date on a name: a sum of leaves carries no valid_from / valid_to, so a time-windowed exception is a second grant with its own period, and a reviewer asking what does this person have? must find two grants rather than one audience. Since every hand-named person is a selector_arg_id, and that column deliberately has no foreign key, a merge must repoint the leaves that name the absorbed person (shape 3).

Names are one namespace across role, person_group and audience.code, and every selector_type.code is a reserved name — a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system. No single constraint spans three tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts the write path exists (D-081). What is stored is always kind + id, so a rename never rewrites a grant. Bare names do not resolve to audiences: AUDIENCE(veterans) is written out (D-103). And nothing a stored expression can name is ever deleted while a rule may name it — a selector_type row, a role, a person_group, an audience is given a state instead of a DELETE — because the namespace has to be stable against renames, deletions and quiet retirements alike, all three of which rewrite what a rule means without anybody editing the rule.

Operand, operator, and the canonical form — An expression is built from + union, - difference, * intersection, with brackets. * and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; brackets override — arithmetic-shaped on purpose, with one deliberate departure: - does not sit beneath *, because the first expression anybody writes in this language, MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS, is meant the left-to-right way. The canonical stored rendering prints every bracket, always — (MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS — the editor rewriting what is typed into that form before it saves, so that a grant read two years from now means what its author meant and a later change of precedence changes nothing already stored. Storage is a binary tree, one row per node (operator + left_id + right_id) or leaf (selector_kind + selector_arg_id), with audience_id denormalized onto every row; one parent per node, never a DAG, because a shared node would let one edit silently widen every grant using it. The tree is stored exactly as its author wrote it — one row per node, left to right, no rebalancing. Cycles are refused at the save by a reachability walk over the reference closure, not just the cheap parent-chain one, because a forest of trees pointing at each other does cycle. That walk is the only structural guard: an expansion is bounded by acyclicity alone — no bound on height, no bound on breadth, and deliberately no cap on the read path, because a cap there would become the thing that decides who a grant reaches. So "a check costs a bounded amount" is not a property of this system, and what is accepted instead is a stated size: a few hundred people, a few dozen registrants on a typical event, a big camp on the order of two hundred (D-112), with the two rules that must survive any growth being a check compiles its expression to a predicate and never materializes the set and a listing is paginated. Nothing lists the widest or deepest audiences — the permissions tab lists only what is broken and what looks odd — and that is a convention and not a guard either way. See F-21.

AUDIENCE(code) — The operand that names another saved audience's expression, evaluated live. It is what makes a rule namable: GROUP() and ROLE() name rosters, so without it the advice "name the composite once and aim grants at it" had nothing to name, and it is the only arm whose argument is a decision about access rather than a roster — "the same people that grant may see the fee ledger, plus the accountant". A reference names a code (optional, unique-where-set) and may not point at an audience with none; an audience may not be ended or deleted while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from a live grant, names it, because "ended" would otherwise be a way to silently empty an operand and an empty operand behind a - makes the result wider; naming an audience requires reading it and grants no read of it to the people inside it. What to do instead of deleting one: retire it as deprecated or hidden, both of which still resolve, and use disabled only when emptying it is the intent — see Deprecated / hidden / disabled. What it costs: editing a referenced audience is a retrospective edit to every grant naming it, which is why saving such an edit shows which grants name it, at what depth, and the set it resolves to before it commits. The record of whom a grant reached is the expression, the preview is logged as a rendering on a date, and a history of inner expressions is not kept; so "who could see this child's data in 2024?" is reconstructable when the grant pointed at a group, whose membership rows are dated, and is not owed when it pointed at a nested audience (D-110). Recomputation for a past date stays possible and is never promised.

Three shapes a set can arrive in: a roster somebody maintains, a saved expression evaluated live, and one person written into the expression itself.

GROUP(x) AUDIENCE(x) PERSON(x) What it is A dated roster somebody maintains A saved expression, evaluated live One person, typed into this expression Who changes who is in it person_group.member.manage audience.update on that audience whoever may edit this audience Exists outside a grant? Yes No No "Was she in it on 1 June 2024?" Answerable Not past the audit window Not past the audit window — the leaf is a row of the tree, and the tree's past is an audit payload Sensitive as ⚠ company 🔒🔒 authority 🔒

Bound operand — The argument-less form of an operand that means relative to the item being checked: PLACED on the event under check, not PLACED(1204). The form exists to kill a specific flaw — one grant per event with the event's own id typed into it is a thing you do 400 times and forget on the 401st — and two rules keep it safe, both enforced when the grant is saved, with the operand named in the refusal: a bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant (at the unit there is nothing to bind it to) and only on a matching item type (PLACED on a group grant is refused, because that item is not an event — selector_type.argument_type checked against grant_scope_type). The consequence: the set a grant reaches is per-item, so the editor's preview is computed for an item and says so on screen. A Compiled expression holds no item precisely because the item arrives as a parameter, so the item is bound at resolution, not at compilation — and nothing resolved while checking one item (a bound operand's set, a preview's expansion) may ever be served for another. Anything that does cache a resolution, including a roster cache or an expansion keyed per (audience, item), is keyed by the item or is wrong on the 401st event. selector_type.binds_to_item is true exactly for the five event operands — ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST, ORGANIZERS — which cannot be evaluated without the event the grant sits on, and is false for everything else. A bound operand never meant the subject of the item and never will; there is no third binding kind.

admin — A word to avoid: readers bring three different meanings to it and only one of them exists here. There is no grant level (access_level, permission_level are not in this schema, and a grant does not rank) and no per-resource wildcard (person.admin, event.admin are not codes and nothing matches a prefix). What survives of "can do everything": system.admin — the only wildcard permission, seeded applies_to = unit, so it can never arrive through an item grant — and roles and audiences, the bundles the organization composes, where "someone who can do everything about events" is written out as a couple of dozen grant rows rather than implied by a resolver rule.

What protects a vocabulary — Its table, and not a flag on its rows. Three tables ship rows and no screen adds one or removes one: permission, grant_scope_type and selector_type, plus the two effects and both permission enums. What refuses an addition or a deletion is that the write path does not exist — no permission.create and no permission.delete code is in the catalog, permission.edit reaches a code's labels and never its code, and a selector_type row typed into a screen would be a word no resolver arm evaluates (D-152). Organization-named things are protected the other way: a role, a group or an audience is never deleted once a rule may name it, only retired as deprecated, hidden or disabled — see Deprecated / hidden / disabled. A per-row "the platform shipped this" boolean is not a sensitivity mark and not a category either: applies_to and right_kind grade what a code does, and the catalog's 🔒 marks grade what it exposes (D-086).

What is seeded — Three vocabularies, two effects and two enums: the permission codes, the grant_scope_type rows, the selector_type rows, allow and deny, and both permission enums (applies_to, right_kind). They arrive with the code because the code has to agree with them — a grant naming a code that does not exist is a save-time refusal, and an operand no migration seeded is a word that fails to parse. Membership ships one row (member in membership_type, kept as a table so a second kind is a data change rather than a migration). Nothing else ships: no role, no audience, no grant, no group — a seeded group would be an invented one, and day one is one account holding system.admin at the unit, from which the first office, the first audience and the first grant are ordinary writes (D-150). "Every event's answers go to its organizers" is not a shipped row either: the act that creates the event writes twelve item-scope allows beside the event, one per code whose applies_to admits an event, each aimed at the bound operand ORGANIZERS (D-151). Roles, groups and their rosters are runtime data in every other case (D-052).

Effective permission — The union of everything a person may do right now, computed from live grants whose expressions contain them on the checked date, plus ownership and guardianship. Never a table, always derived, so it cannot drift out of sync with the grants that produce it: a check resolves against live rows every time, and the only things that may be kept are a Compiled expression, The request memo and The batch reads. The historical question points at no table either, because the record of whom a grant reached is the expression, not a snapshot of people; a materialized effective_permission table would have to arrive on its own merits, when the stated size says it must, and be named for what it is (F-7).

Compiled expression — The only thing in this system that may be cached across requests, and it is not an answer. Parse the stored tree once, resolve operand kinds once, emit the parameterized predicate once — keyed by the expression's root plus ruleset_version, and holding no person and no item, because both of those arrive as parameters. Nothing in it depends on whom or where it is being asked about, so the only writes that can stale one are a change to the words and a change to the seeded vocabulary they are written in: ruleset_version's entire bump set is audience_operand and selector_type. A named roster may also be cached across requests — ROLE(x) over role_holder, GROUP(x) over person_group_member, keyed by the name — on two conditions: the key is the thing the write touches, so invalidation is local to the row that changed and never global, and the cache holds the dated rows, or the set with its validity ranges, never the set as of today, so the checked date is still applied at check time and a period ending at midnight needs no job to be seen. An answer may never be stored: invariant 19, TIME-BOMB — no row, table or field may map a caller, or a caller-and-code, or a caller-and-item, to a permission answer, a caller being a person or a key. api_key.last_used_at is not such a row — it says an event happened, and nothing reads it to decide an answer now (D-114, D-123). Half of that guard is structural — the schema has nowhere to put one — and the residue is honest: anyone who wants a cache back must arrive with a decision entry carrying a per-person invalidation handle and a stated list of watched tables derived from the operand registry rather than from a list of ideas; until then it is a convention, not a guard.

The request memo — In-process only, and confined to one request. One indexed read fetches the checked caller's live grant rows; every code, item and date that request asks about is evaluated against them in memory, and a named operand that recurs — ROLE(leader), GROUP(cubs) — is resolved once per request instead of once per check. The deprecated | hidden | disabled flag is read the same way: once per request, memoized for that request, consulted live rather than compiled in. Lifetime is the request, so it has no invalidation policy and no staleness window at all (D-114).

The batch reads — can_many(person, codes[], item?) and which_of(people[], code, item) — the entry points a screen's affordances and a list's people are answered from: one resolution, one pass. The cost that made a cache look necessary was never one check, it was the N+1 across a screen. The per-item preview and the permissions tab are written against these, not against a loop of single checks, and they therefore do their work on open; at the size stated above that is affordable, and it is recorded as a dependency, not a measurement (F-15).

Deprecated / hidden / disabled — The three states a named thing gets instead of being deleted, and the rule that keeps them three different things: only disabled changes an answer. Nothing a stored expression can name — a selector_type row, a role, a person_group, an audience — is ever deleted while a rule may name it (D-109):

State Still resolves? Offered when writing a rule? Flagged? deprecated yes, unchanged no — not addable, not introducible by an edit yes, highlighted in the editor wherever it appears hidden yes, unchanged no no — not obsolete, just not everybody's business disabled no — the empty set no yes, and this is the only state that changes an answer

The invariant that stops deprecated drifting into disabled: deprecating or hiding what an expression names must not change the set the expression resolves to. Disabling is the loudest switch in the module — it stops every rule naming that thing, in every scope, at once, and re-enabling restores all of them without anybody editing a grant — so disabling and re-enabling are audited writes that print the rules they touch, resolved before and after. The flag takes effect now because resolution consults it live, once per request and memoized for that request: a state is not compiled in to the compiled form, which is why the flag left ruleset_version's bump set while still meaning now. The check worth writing: if a flag ever is compiled into a cached form, "deprecating and hiding must not change the answer" keeps holding while "disabling takes effect now" silently stops being true. Its upside is the answer to "how do I turn off that whole naming without editing forty grants?" One exception, and it is the only way left to make a broken leaf: PERSON(x) names a person, and redaction can require the row to actually go — erasure wins. A person is not a selector, and no convenience owed to an expression author survives a former member's right to be deleted.

The permissions tab — One place on the permissions page that lists rules worth a writer's attention, and it has exactly two sections. Broken — a live rule whose expression names a deprecated, hidden or disabled thing, or fails to resolve at all; its dominant cause is a redacted person. Unusual — a rule that resolves correctly and merely looks odd (a grant naming ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS), kept out of Broken on purpose: Broken says something happened to your rule behind your back, Unusual says your rule means what you wrote. The two sections make different claims about the writer and must not be merged. It is a convention, not a guard in a strong sense: nothing it lists is blocked, and nothing is refused because it is listed — what it buys is that a report has to be remembered and a tab is where the person already is. What is on that page is the tab and nothing else.

Delegation — Temporarily granting someone your authority (a leader going on leave). Modeled as an ordinary grant with its provenance set: is_delegated, delegated_from naming who it came from, grant_reason, and a mandatory valid_to. Because a grant is one permission code, "do not lend more than you hold" is a set-membership test. A deny cannot be lent and cannot be lent around, and system.admin is never delegated. Lending is said on the grant, not on the role (an assumption; see the index in open-questions.md).

Decisions behind this page: D-052, D-060, D-068, D-079, D-081, D-086, D-100, D-101, D-103, D-107, D-109, D-110, D-112, D-113, D-114, D-116, D-117, D-118, D-119, D-120, D-121, D-122, D-123, D-125.

docs.title: Glossary — Ubiquitous Language
docs.text: Terms used consistently across every document in this folder. Where everyday language is ambiguous, the definition here wins and the schema follows it. Each entry says what a term means in the system as designed today; how a term came to mean that is in the decision log.

docs.title: The three-way split that everything else depends on
docs.text:
These three words are frequently conflated in real organizations. This design keeps them strictly apart, because conflating them is the single most common source of unfixable data models in this domain.

Term Definition Table Person A human being the organization knows about, now or ever. Exists independent of whether they have ever logged in, paid, or applied. person Account A set of login credentials attached to a person. Optional — a person imported from a 1994 paper roster has no account. account Member Not a noun in this system. A person is "a member" at a moment in time if they hold a qualifying membership. It is always a question with a date attached. membership

A fourth, related distinction:

Term Definition Table User Avoid entirely. When you mean the account, say account; when you mean the human, say person. Most systems use "user" for the wrong one and it never gets fixed. —

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Person — A human. Stores given name, family name, birth date, and gender. Nothing else: no member status, no child/adult flag, no group, no office, and no deceased flag — the organization does not record death. What the organization records about the human is not on this table at all: it is descriptive data, reached by the same permission as the rest of the person record, because none of it is a different kind of object. Specified in data-model/01 §2.

Account — Credentials and login state for a person. A person may have zero or more accounts over their lifetime (a childhood account abandoned in 2010, a new one created in 2024), but at most one live one — closed rows aside. Accounts are never shared between people, not even between a parent and child.

Account activation gate — The rule that an account may not reach active while an unresolved identity hypothesis names its person. A sign-up that strong-matches an existing person — exact legacy member number, or exact birth date together with a normalized name, never the fuzzy band — raises a hypothesis. Its own rows are created and stay pending_verification: nothing is merged, nothing is linked, nothing is activated. The contact point the person typed survives as the credential it was offered as, and identity_reviewer decides it with person.merge. The holding message confirms nothing, since a sign-up form that can answer "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle over a roster of children; and a hypothesis that is blocking an account gets an age check that somebody reads, because a stalled queue is not a data-quality problem but a specific person who cannot log in (D-089). "I have a new e-mail address" is not this case and is not routed through it: account_credential holds many credentials for one account.

Contact point — A single email address, phone number, or postal address belonging to a person, one row per point in person_contact rather than a column, so that a person can have five email addresses, or a new kind invented later, without a migration. Each has a type, a purpose, and a verification timestamp. A postal address is a contact point of type postal: two people at one address are related by a query, not by a table, and a shared address grants nothing to anybody.

Identity hypothesis — A proposed but unconfirmed link between two person rows that may actually be the same human. Created during legacy import, by the nightly matcher, when someone registers claiming a historical identity, or by a sign-up that strong-matches a person who already exists. Confirming one triggers a merge; while one is unresolved it also holds the account of any person it names out of active — see account activation gate.

Merge — The act of declaring two person rows to be one human, and collapsing them. Never a delete: the absorbed row survives as a tombstone pointing at the survivor, so that historical foreign keys keep resolving. Always a human's decision (person.merge), including at the highest score — and refused outright when the chosen survivor turns out, on resolution, to be the person being absorbed.

Merge chain — What forms when a survivor is itself later absorbed. The pointer is not rewritten forward: A→B→C stays a chain and resolve_person() walks it to the live row. Chains persist because reversing a merge would otherwise be a reconstruction of facts nobody recorded. Two rules come with the chain, neither on the read: a cycle is impossible because the merge is refused, never because a hop limit gave up; and a chain longer than three hops is reported, which is a statement about the matcher's queue, not about the row.

Unmerge — Reversing a merge a human approved. The tombstone comes off, rows created before the merge go back to the revived person, and rows created inside the window are flagged for a human rather than split by a rule — every access_grant from that window flagged, not guessed. The merge is reversible; the merged window is not: what two people did while they were one row stays one row's history, because the record cannot separate who did it. No permission of its own — undoing an identity correction is the same act as making one, so it is person.merge.

Membership export — One of the two files the legacy corpus actually is, and neither of them is a roster. A row says: a person, a birth date, and the period they were a member of the unit. A people batch turns it into person rows and bounded membership rows — both ends dated, data_confidence = 'low', batch id set — and no fee obligation of any kind. It names no group either, so it answers neither "who was in the Thursday group in 2011" nor "were they a child or a rover", and nothing is created in person_group from it: a corpus that names no groups means every roster row is typed by a person, which is also the only way one can be true.

Attendance export — The other file: events, and which people came. It becomes event rows with no owner — there is no column for an imported event to have (D-102) — with one event_registration per attendee at attending and was_present = true, and no not_attending rows, because an absence row would say the system asked someone who was never asked. Attendance never becomes a membership, and it never becomes a group roster either: attendance is read through the ATTENDED and PLACED selectors, and no rows are written into person_group_member from it.

docs.title: Personal data
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person once you subtract what they are called and counted as. The module is domain/08-person-data.md, the tables are data-model/09-attributes.md.

Descriptive data — Everything the system holds about a person other than their name, their gender and their age: one class of data, with no privileged corner inside it. Allergies, medication, insurance numbers, languages, measurements, clothing sizes, dietary habits, a grandparent's phone manner — the same kind of fact, held in fields rather than files, none of it a different kind of object from any other, and all of it reached by the permission that already reads the person. The term exists to rule a category out: there is no sensitive sub-record with its own codes. Why: a sub-record of its own was declined on the merits, and its cost — one read rule over the whole record — is stated in D-083. It is the reason person.view is graded in the catalog's top tier.

Attribute definition — One thing the organization has decided to collect: a code, a label, a description of what belongs in the field, a value type, and whether several values may be current at once. The type draws the form and raises the warning; it never refuses a save a human insists on — 2019 recorded as the year of a checkup is a truer record than an empty field behind a validation error. Creating, renaming, merging or retiring a definition is attribute.define; recording a value against one needs nothing beyond person.edit.

Person attribute — The value one person currently has for one code. Overwritten in place: the row is the organization's present belief, and the sequence of earlier beliefs lives in the audit trail, values included, for 24 months — logged on the same terms as a contact point or a note, because a list of person fields whose values must not be logged would be a privileged corner, and would leave nothing behind for an overwritten value. What guards the trail is who may read it, not what it omits — and it omits, on a clock: those logged values are emptied 24 months after they were written (see payload reduction), so the trail is the record of what changed, who did it and when for the life of the system and the record of the values for two years. The honest name for the whole stack is therefore no long history, not merely no temporal columns: the value lives in one overwritten row, the copy of it depends on a write path remembering to log, and the copy ages out. If a case ever needs the long version, the fix is temporal columns on the value — D-085 reversed — and not a longer trail. No valid_from / valid_to, deliberately (data-model/09 §3).

Retired code — A definition taken out of data entry and left alone everywhere else: readable, reportable, revivable, its values untouched. Deleting a label must never delete the facts filed under it, or the badly-named label is never retired and the vocabulary accretes instead of being curated. Redaction is the opposite operation: retiring keeps the values, erasing a person deletes them, immediately and whatever their age. The other thing that removes stored values is payload reduction, below, and the distinction is that redaction answers to a person and is absolute, while reduction answers to a calendar and is bounded.

Payload reduction — Emptying the old_values / new_values out of an audit row 24 months after it was written, leaving everything else standing: actor, on-behalf-of, operation, table, record id, changed fields, transaction, session, channel. The trail goes on answering who changed this row, when, and were they allowed to for the life of the system, and stops answering and to what after two years; twelve months is the floor the window may be set to. Not redaction, which is a named person's erasure, immediate and absolute, and reaches payloads of any age; not an import revert, which deletes the rows a batch created. Reduction is the one case in this design that deliberately unwrites later than the write, so its failure mode is not running at all — hence a scheduled job with a check that reports any row past its window still carrying a payload (D-088).

The two clocks — The accounting skeleton (membership, fee_obligation, payment, and the anonymised person row an erasure leaves behind) has no clock at all, justified as the organization's own history. Assumption: that this indefinite retention of rows about a named person has a legal basis — organizational history plus accounting obligations, against a redacted person row that keeps the skeleton non-identifying — is unverified, and a decision log is not the document that grants it. The audit trail runs the opposite direction: rows forever, payloads for 24 months. Erasure sits outside both, immediate and absolute. access_log is a third thing and neither clock: its rows are deleted 24 months after they are written, by a scheduled job, because what was read stops being answerable and no skeleton of it is kept — the two trails now differ in kind and not only in length (D-145). Three exceptions to "nothing is hard-deleted", then: a staging truncate, the delete an erasure has to make, and this trail ending on a calendar (data-model/00 §4).

Curation — Keeping the vocabulary meaning one thing: merging near-duplicates, retiring codes nobody uses, and writing the description that stops one code meaning four things to four people. It is attribute.define plus somebody who reads what they are given — the permission is the curator, there being no proposal stage and no queue between a save and the record (D-141), which is also why curation has no age signal any more: what notices a rotting vocabulary is a report, not a waiting list. The documents treat it as a job rather than an outcome — an open vocabulary left unwatched decays into allergy, Allergy, alergie and allergies (2), after which the layer still stores everything and answers nothing.

Not to be confused with identity, which stays structured in its own tables: a fact keeps a table of its own when there is a rule about it that an open layer physically cannot hold — one primary postal contact, one current name, a birth number that may not repeat. The boundary is that test, not sensitivity (domain/08 §1).

docs.title: Organization
docs.text:
The unit — There is exactly one, and it is the organization. It is a scope, not a row: no table, no id, no parent, no type, no name history, no path. In grant_scope_type its code is unit — the one row there with is_item_scoped = false — and a grant written at the unit carries no scope_id. Say the unit: not "the root unit", not "the organization unit", not "org"; there is no second unit for the word root to distinguish this one from, and a name that implies a second one is how a hierarchy creeps back into a sentence. Membership, a role, and a grant at non-item scope are all held at the unit, and a grant at it reaches every item of every type. There are no unit kinds either: pack, troop and section name nothing in the model, and where these documents need a set of people they say group (D-097). What one unit costs — there is no body between a person and a unit-scope read, and no per-unit report — is stated in domain/04 §1.

Group — A person_group: a named set of people with explicitly stated, dated members and a lifetime of its own. A name, a description, valid_from / valid_to and the audit columns; its roster is person_group_member(person, valid_from, valid_to, who wrote it, note), dated rows that may not overlap counted over all rows, half-open. Company, not a body: the Thursday group, the kitchen crew, this year's camp staff — in the organization's own words "a temporary set of members that do e.g. events together". What a group is not: no parent and no children, no type and no vocabulary of types, no code, no path, no nesting rules, no rename history, no split or merger edge, no leadership of its own, no roles, and no fee. Being in a group authorizes nothing — person_group.member.manage writes a roster and nothing else; participation is not authority, and tidier storage does not promote it (D-098). A group is an item (registered in grant_scope_type), so "these two may work this group's roster" is a grant on one group. Its two dated facts are different facts: the group's own period says it existed, the member rows say who was in it, and "who was in schuzka2026-1 on 14 March 2026" is a point-in-time read over the roster — which is why the rows are dated, and why that answer survives the audit trail's payload expiry. A group is not an audience: a group states its members and an audience picks them (Audience). Nobody writes themselves onto a roster — person_group.member.manage has no self-scoped variant and none will be added, and no group is seeded. Moving a person between groups closes one dated row and opens another. Specified in domain/04 §2 and §3.

Office (a role) and role_holder — An office is a small, visible set of holders — the leaders, the finance people, IT — where a group is company. The difference decides who may edit the membership: role.assign / role.unassign are 🔒🔒, the most sensitive family in the catalog, while writing a group's roster is person_group.member.manage at ⚠. role keeps code, name, description, sort_order; role_holder(role, person, valid_from, valid_to, granted_by, note) is the holder row and names exactly one person — one grantee per row, always, because F-12 is closed and the answer is no. A role confers nothing: the codes an office carries are the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x), which is what makes "what may a treasurer do?" a query over rows a person wrote (D-100). An office is held at the unit, always; a role is an item, so a grant can be written on one. Nothing forces a holder row to end — the report is the control (D-071), and an empty office is not a reportable vacancy: absence of rows has no start date, and no office is marked elective in the first place (F-18, closed by D-136)

docs.title: Membership
docs.text:
Membership — The period during which a person is a member of the unit. Holds valid_from, valid_to (null = open/current), and a status in an approval workflow. A person accumulates multiple memberships over time; they never overwrite one another. "Everyone in the organization" is one query against membership. There is exactly one kind of it and it is ageless: membership does not distinguish children from adults, has no age ceiling, and does not end because a person got older. Being a counselor or a leader is an office held through role_holder, never a membership type.

Membership type — A table kept for the future, currently holding one row: member. It survives as a table rather than collapsing into a constant so that a second kind of membership (a supporting or honorary one) would be a data change rather than a migration. The fee is flat and per person, so the type does not affect pricing either.

Membership request — A person's application to become a member of the unit. Separate from the membership itself, because a request has its own lifecycle (submitted, under review, rejected, withdrawn) and can be rejected without ever producing a membership. Nothing gates a request except identity and payment — there is no checklist to satisfy. Which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, never a preference on the request.

Lapse — A membership ending because the yearly fee was not paid or the person withdrew. Distinct from termination for cause, which requires a reason to be written. A lapsed person is not a member and holds no member permissions, though a renewal window lets them rejoin without re-applying.

Renewal window — The fixed period after a membership expires during which payment restores it without re-applying, and — importantly — opens the new period at the expiry date, so the record shows continuous coverage and the person is not misclassified as a returning member. Tracked as dates, not a status: during the window the person is simply expired.

Returning member — A person whose new membership follows a gap. The system detects this rather than treating them as new: 1990–2010, gap, 2024–present.

Imported membership — An imported membership is bounded at both ends, always. A membership is never inferred from attendance (D-093).

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
Guardianship — A period during which one person is responsible for another. Directional: guardian → dependent. Carries relationship kind (parent, legal_guardian, foster_parent, step_parent, grandparent, sibling, other) and an end date that a person sets. Not a birthday: the system takes no position on majority, and no job ends one (D-069).

Party to a guardianship — The guardian and the subject, both. They, and not staff, run the arrangement: either may end it, a guardian may add another guardian, and no request has to go through the organization (D-073). Staff hold the same powers and are a route, never the route. A guardianship is a relationship between two people who are both principals on the row, and that is why they run it.

Guardian's right — One of exactly three values on the guardianship row: none, view, or write. Nothing more granular exists (D-074). A right is measured against permission.right_kind (read | write): none covers nothing, view covers read codes, write covers both. A guardian is a channel, not a set and not a grant: a guardian's act is checked under the ordinary code for the thing being touched, so this is one vocabulary and not a second authorization model. Being a guardian still grants nothing by itself; none is a real value and the common starting point for anything the guardian did not assert themselves.

How the channel answers: a check looks for a live guardianship row linking the person asking to the person the action is about, and reads right_level off it — a lookup over a relationship, not a set anything resolves; the channel returns an allow or says nothing at all. The history of that value is guardianship_permission (right_level, valid_from, valid_to, changed_reason, changed_by) — no grantee, no permission code, no audience. A guardian is neither a grantee nor an operand, and write means any action about this child, which is wider than any expression could assemble and narrower in the direction that matters: it reaches no item that is not about the child. There is no guardian-shaped permission code anywhere in the catalog and none scoped to "my ward", so nothing has to be granted for a guardian to act as a guardian (D-113). The system computes no guardian list from these rows; "send these six children's parents the newsletter" is a person_group somebody maintains, aimed at through GROUP(x).

What the short vocabulary gives up is recorded in the catalog: it is not possible to say "read everything except the medical record." Why: the case that sentence was invented for — a parent keeping access to everything about their child except the medical file, by court order — was declined on the merits, because there is no medical record inside the person record to be excepted from: everything other than name, gender and age is descriptive data of one class (D-083). So the right level is none, view or write, applied to the record whole, and what was given up is not a half-built feature but an arrangement the organization decided not to want.

A key is a grantee, and never an operand. Where a guardian holds a channel and no grant, an integration holds grants and belongs to no set, EVERYONE included — and it is not an account, which is a way for a person to log in (API key, D-116, D-117).

Acting on behalf — Performing an operation as another person, under that guardianship row's right level (view to read it, write to change it). Every such operation records both the acting person and the subject person (data-model/04 §5).

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: The authorization vocabulary — permission, scope, grant, allow and deny, channel, audience, selector, the expression grammar, the compilation, a key and the caller a check is answered about, what an empty actor column in a trail says, and the states a named thing gets instead of deletion — is defined on its own page: glossary-authorization.md.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event — A dated occasion that people register for: a camp, a trip, a hike, a jamboree. It has a start and an end, an optional capacity, an optional fee, and a set of organizers. It has no status column — visibility is the permission model, and cancellation is a recorded fact rather than a state. Nothing owns an event: there is no event.org_unit_id and no can_event(); the people connected to an event are named by selectors that bind to it (Bound operand), and an event is addressed by being the item of an item-scope grant, which is the only way anything reaches it (D-064, D-102).

A weekly meeting is not an event. Forty meetings a year are not forty events, so there is no recurrence, no series and no occurrence table. What the meeting has is a group to be in — a dated roster, not a calendar of evenings. "Was Jan at the meeting on 14 March?" is answerable by nobody: a group says who is in it between two dates, not who walked in on a given evening.

Organizer — Someone running an event. A roster entry on the event (event_organizer) with an optional label ('lead', 'cook', 'driver') and an order — not an access_grant, and analogous only to being a member of a group. Authority to act on the event arrives from the grants written by the act that creates the event: one item-scope allow per code whose applies_to admits an event — twelve beside every event, event.answer.view among them — each aimed at the bound operand ORGANIZERS (D-151). An event created without them has organizers who can do nothing, which is why the events with an incomplete organizer bundle report exists (08a §10 check 2) (D-062).

Registration — One person's answer about one event: attending, or not_attending. "Unanswered" is not a value — it is the absence of a registration row, so "who has not replied yet?" is the eligible set minus the registered set.

Eligibility — Who may register. This is capability, not a rule engine: event.register_self is an ordinary permission, allowed by a live allow grant and blocked by any live deny, granted either on the unit or on the event itself; opening a camp to members is one access_grant naming an audience whose expression contains MEMBERS; an age-restricted camp is a camp opened to a group (D-060).

Waitlist — What happens when a full event gets a self-service registration: the person is written down and ordered, never refused. Organizers may exceed capacity outright, and the overrun is reported rather than prevented — the leader who knows there are two spare tents is trusted (D-065).

Presence — Whether someone actually turned up, marked by an organizer after the fact. Three-valued: NULL (no register taken), true, false. For a camp this is the record of who was in the organization's care, and it cannot be reconstructed from registrations. Not the same as registration — a no-show is a registration with was_present = false. Because it is NULL until somebody marks it, there is no PRESENT selector: a selector that meant "came" would silently mean "was not marked absent" on every event nobody took a register for.

The four attendance tiers — Four argument-less selectors that bind to the event a grant is scoped to, so a sentence written once reads correctly on every event it is copied to. From widest to narrowest:

Selector Who it reaches, on the bound event ATTENDED anyone whose response is attending — asked, said yes, whether or not there was room PLACED those attending who were not waitlisted — the set the capacity actually let through CONFIRMED PLACED and is_confirmed — somebody has since looked at each of them ON_WAITLIST written down, ordered, not yet placed — waiting, not attending ORGANIZERS the event's organizer roster — the set an event's own twelve grants are aimed at

They are not one set with flags: ATTENDED is wider than PLACED precisely because a full event says yes to more people than it can seat, and CONFIRMED is narrower than PLACED because a seat is not a headcount. WHITELISTED is not one of these, and is not a selector at all — see EV-6.

docs.title: Money
docs.text:
Payment request — A liability rendered payable: an amount, a recipient account, a start, and an optional expiry. The request, not the payment, is the entity the finance module is built around, because it is the only thing that connects "we expect money" to "money arrived". It is not an invoice; the organization may also owe people invoices, which is still open (D-075).

Variable symbol — The number a payer types into their bank, and the number the bank reports back against the money. Unique across every symbol ever issued, not merely across live ones, and taken from a sequence — never derived from a birth date, a member number, or anything else a stranger could guess. Anyone can type eleven digits into a payment form; guessing a symbol puts a stranger's money into a child's financial record.

A QR code is a rendering, not data. It encodes the symbol, the amount and the recipient that already exist. Nothing stores it and nothing invalidates it.

There is no card gateway. The organization collects, but by bank API rather than checkout: no card tokens, no disputes, no chargebacks, no processor reconciliation, and no pending or failed payment status — a bank transfer the bank has reported does not later fail. A refund is a second payment going the other way, never a reversal of the first.

Unmatched money — A transfer whose symbol resolves to nothing live: mistyped, belonging to a cancelled event, already settled, or the wrong amount. It waits for a person. It is never auto-applied by payer identity — a parent with two children pays one amount is the normal case, not the edge case, and the fallback would be wrong on the common path (D-076).

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
Direct message — One person to one person. Everyone can send one; there is no permission for it.

Broadcast — The only messaging permission, and an ordinary scoped one: a grant like any other. Held at the unit, message.broadcast reaches everyone; the narrower reading is a grant naming a group, reaching that roster. There is no global broadcast flag: a permission that has to be granted is one that can be given to some people and refused to others, whereas the flag would be all-or-nothing and would leave a section leader choosing between an organization-wide power and typing the same sentence twelve times. Whether broadcast should ever be grantable on an item is messaging's open question, not the model's (D-077).

Delivery channel — Email, push, or in-app, chosen by the recipient, not the sender. The sender chooses who; the recipient chooses how it arrives. This is why the system is the medium rather than a mail relay: a bounced email is a failed delivery on one channel, not a lost message.

Age is not a sender concept — and it is not a recipient concept either. Nothing restricts who may address a child; what stops a private message to a child from being unnoticed is mirroring, and no check in the resolver ever looks at an age.

Mirroring — A copy of a direct message addressed to a minor, delivered to that minor's guardians whose right is view or write — the three-value right of the guardianship channel, not a level — fixed to that set at the moment of sending. Visibility, not approval: nobody has to agree before the message is sent. A guardian at none receives nothing, because none is the organization having already decided that this party sees nothing about the child — and a minor whose guardians are all none is the same shape as a minor with no guardian at all, so it is reported together with it (D-082).

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Temporal row — Any row with valid_from / valid_to. valid_to IS NULL means "still true". All permission checks and history queries filter on these. The full pattern is specified in data-model/00-conventions.md.

Point-in-time query — A question of the form "who/what was true on date D?" — "Who was in the group schuzka2026-1 on 1 June 1998?", "Was this person a member when they attended camp?" These are first-class requirements, not an afterthought, because there are four decades of history to preserve. The answer depends on which named set the question is about, and there are only two kinds to be about: a group answers it from its dated roster, and an audience cannot answer it at all — its expression is evaluated live, and its one past is the audit trail. That includes a name typed straight into the expression: a PERSON(x) leaf carries no dates of its own, so "was she in this audience on 1 June 2024?" is a recomputation over audit payloads that expire after 24 months (D-088).

As-of vs audit time — Two different times, both needed. As-of is the date the fact was true about the world (a membership that ran 1990–2010). Audit time is when the row was written in the system. A membership backdated during a 2026 data-entry session has as-of 1990–2010 and audit time 2026. Do not conflate them.

docs.title: Roles in conversation (informal terms — not names in the model)
docs.text:
The words you and the organization will naturally use, and what they map to:

Informal term What it is in the model "child member" a person with an open membership whose birth_date makes them a minor — age is a fact about the person, not a kind of membership "counselor" / "leader" an office held through role_holder — never a membership type, and conferring nothing by itself: authority comes from the grants that name ROLE(counselors) "parent" / "caretaker" party to an active guardianship row "leader of the Thursday group" there is no such thing: an office is held for the unit and has no scope column, so this is a member of that group, plus whatever a grant aimed at them or at it allows "in the Thursday group" an open person_group_member row in that person_group — company, not authority "ex-member" person with a membership whose valid_to has passed "lapsed but can still renew" valid_to passed, within the renewal window "registered but not a member" person with an account and no open membership — they may sign in and see their own data, but hold no member permissions "they're allowed to attend" a live allow grant naming event.register_self, aimed at them or at a set they belong to (a grant aimed at an integration is the third kind of grantee and answers for that integration alone, never for a person attending), and no live deny anywhere naming them — not a level, and nothing inherited from a unit that owns the event "open to everyone" a grant whose expression is the operand EVERYONE — or MEMBERS, if membership is wanted. There is no shipped audience behind either word (D-153): an audience is a name somebody writes when they have a reason to reuse one, and a bare name in an expression is not a reference to an audience at all — audiences are named only as AUDIENCE(code) "the treasurer" role_holder of treasurer, held for the unit — there is no narrower place to hold it, and holding it answers no permission question on its own "put me in the Thursday group" a person_group_member row somebody else writes under person_group.member.manage, which has no self-scoped variant — there is no self-service path and no permission with which to build one "the kitchen crew" a person_group if the answer is a list of people somebody keeps up by hand, dated and quotable years later; an audience if the answer is a sentence recomputed each time it is asked. "Whom did this grant reach on 1 June 2024?" is answerable for the first and not the second "the permission group for the kitchen crew" one or the other of the row above; an expression names a group through GROUP(code) and another audience through AUDIENCE(code) "the old Pack 12 came back" there are no units to bring back. The closest thing left is a group whose name repeats a dead one, and that is only a reused label: groups have no code, no succession and no rename history "the organizers" the event's own event_organizer roster, reached as ORGANIZERS on a grant scoped to that event — an appointment on the thing being run
