Decisions behind this page: D-060, D-062, D-064, D-065, D-069, D-071, D-073, D-074, D-075, D-076, D-077, D-082, D-083, D-085, D-088, D-089, D-093, D-097, D-098, D-100, D-102, D-113, D-116, D-117.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
Everything still unresolved — fourteen questions, each with its schema impact, what changes once you answer, ordered roughly by how much they block. Thirteen of the seventeen questions that were on this page were answered by round 20, every 🟡 among them, and that round also took the last three of § J — what remained of the section round 18 raised by writing down who enforces each invariant. The round also left one behind it: F-34, raised by the answer it gave to AT-2 rather than found on this page: deleting the attribute proposal stage turned out to delete a schedule nobody had written down. It is filed under § F with the questions it resembles, not in a section of its own — a question a ruling raised is an ordinary open question once it exists. § J is therefore gone, emptied by being answered rather than by being reversed, which is the first time this register has closed a section that way.

Marked: 🔴 blocking something else · 🟡 important · 🟢 can be deferred.

A question that has been answered is not kept here. Its entry is deleted; what remains is one row in § R. Resolved naming the question, the decision that settled it and what the answer cost, and the reasoning lives in that decision entry. Nothing is silently dropped: a row in § R carries a short anchor, so a link written years ago against F-7 still lands somewhere true.

What the five survivors are, since that is short enough to say here: A-4's remainder is the organizational calendar, E-3 is how this organisation reads its own civil code, and F-9 and F-11 both turn on what a membership type is for. F-34 is the odd one: nothing in the schema waits on it — it asks who does a job and when, which no ruling can decide alone because the answer is a person's name and a date. Not one of the five is 🟡.

The section letters are names, not a sequence. Sections B, C and D held only closed questions and are gone; § J joined them in round 20, emptied by answering it, and § G (events) and § Ga (attributes) went the same way when their seven questions were answered. The modules they framed are unaffected — both are designed, and § H still links them. The ids those sections held — B-2, C-5, D-9, EV-2, AT-4 — are still how § R means them, and E-6 is still the question it was when it was filed.

§ I lists every assumption the documentation is standing on; § How to answer says which of these is worth answering next.

docs.title: A. Blocking the core design
A-4 (remainder) 🟢 The organizational calendar
docs.text:
Answered. The fee expires on 1 January (D-047) and the renewal window is 60 days (D-048).

What is left is not a question but a discipline. Both values live in membership_type as columns — expiry_month, expiry_day, renewal_grace_days — so either can be moved by an UPDATE. The one way to lose that property is a scheduled job or a front end that contains the literal 60 or 1. Worth one line in code review: do these values come from the row?

See: data-model/03 §1, domain/05 §6

docs.title: E. Guardianship
E-3 🟢 Guardian acting for an adult child
docs.text:
Question. Can a parent register their adult child for an event, with the child's consent?

Recommendation. An explicit consent-based delegation, not a guardianship — the legal basis differs and access_grant.is_delegated already supports it.

Note. Now that grants can target audiences (D-042), the event-wide version of this question — "register everyone in this group" — is answered without touching guardianship at all. What remains is the individual case.

docs.title: F. Authorization
F-9 🟢 Should membership_type stay a table with one row?
docs.text:
Question. D-037 kept membership_type as a table with a single seeded member row, on the principle that vocabularies are rows and not enums — at the cost of an FK that always holds one value.

Impact. A deliberate trade, not an oversight. Worth confirming it is the trade you want, since it is the one place the design pays a structural cost for a hypothetical future.

See: data-model/03 §1

docs.title: F-11 🟢 Does the identity reviewer need to read the person record to settle a claim?
docs.text:
Question. D-089 routes a colliding sign-up to identity_reviewer and resolves it with person.merge. The office an organization writes for this job — the catalog's §11 is an example of writing one — holds person.merge, import.view and import.apply, and not person.view. Nothing ships a reviewer, so what used to be a fact about the seed is now a choice somebody writes: as written, a reviewer decides "is this the same child?" from match signals, names and dates, without opening either record.

Why this is a question now and was not one before. Merging already needed a human, but the alternative to merging was doing nothing: a wrong call left two rows side by side, visible in the nightly duplicate report, correctable next quarter. The activation gate changed the stakes. A reviewer who rejects a hypothesis lets an account go live; one who confirms it joins two lives, including a login, into one row. Both directions now have a person waiting on the far side of the answer, which is a different job from tidying a queue, and a job the permission set does not obviously cover.

Positions. - Leave it — the signals are the decision, and a reviewer who needs to read both records is a reviewer who is about to merge on a hunch anyway. Cheapest, and consistent with "identity is what the match says, adjudicated by a person". - Grant person.view to identity_reviewer — settles it, and quietly makes an identity role one of the roles that can read a child's whole record, which is a bigger thing than the role's name suggests and is exactly what the catalog's top tier is reserved for. - A narrower read the catalog does not have yet — the resolver code that would expose only the two candidate rows and their signals, which would be a new code and therefore a decision entry, not an edit to this file. It is not proposed here, and would need arguing.

Recommendation. Leave it, and watch the queue rather than the design. If reviewers start resolving hypotheses at a suspiciously high confirmation rate without asking for context, that is the sign the signals are not enough — and the honest response is a person.view grant discussed as a top-tier membership, not a new code invented at a desk.

Needed. Nothing before implementation. Revisit when the first real import has produced a real queue.

docs.title: F-34 🟢 Who writes the vocabulary the first import needs, and who holds attribute.define afterwards?
docs.text:
Question. Round 20 deleted the attribute proposal stage: a definition is live at the save of whoever holds attribute.define, and the legacy import refuses at apply time on a mapped column naming a code that is not already defined and live (D-141, data-model/09 §7). So the several hundred definitions the first real batch needs have to be authored before the batch that looks like it produces them. Who writes them, over what period, and who holds the code once the import is done?

Why this is a question now and was not one before. proposed was the answer while it existed: the import could write codes nobody had read and the queue was where the reading happened. It was a bad answer — a third status no decision had granted, with a check whose whole job was to age it out — but it carried a schedule inside it, and deleting the status deleted the schedule with it. This is the one place in the round where deleting a mechanism removed the answer to a question nobody had written down, and the round noticed only afterward.

Impact. None on the schema — no column turns on this, and no invariant is stated about it. It is a sequencing risk on the single most fragile operation in the corpus. Day one does not block, and since round 21 that is true in the plainest possible way: day one is that one account, holding system.admin, which satisfies every code including this one, so the first definitions are writable before anything else exists. What is undecided is the work and the handover, and the round narrowed this question to the handover: who reads the column map, whose job it is to write several hundred codes and their value vocabularies before a batch is scheduled, and who holds attribute.define after the person who set the system up stops being the person using it — because one holder is not curation, and the queue that used to make an uncurated vocabulary visible is gone (data-model/09 §8 is what notices rot now, and it can only fire on codes that exist).

Positions. - The map and the vocabulary are one artefact, written in one sitting. This is what domain/03 §7 already assumes: whoever authors the column→code map authors the codes, and having held the permission while reading the list is the endorsement the old status was invented to express. Cheapest, and it makes the import a two-part job done by one person. - A definitions file imported before the person batch. Turns the vocabulary into a second import format — real design work that does not exist in these pages, and it would need its own refusals. Not proposed here. - Distribute attribute.define first and let the curators write it together. The honest answer to "one holder is not curation", and it is a decision about who may decide what the organization knows about people, which is exactly the kind of thing this catalog refuses to decide in passing.

Recommendation. Take the first position and write it down as a plan rather than a ruling: the import is scheduled after the vocabulary exists, the map is reviewed top to bottom by the person who wrote it, and attribute.define is named to a person — not to an office, since an office confers nothing (D-100) — before the first batch is attempted. The wrong answer is a new status or a new queue, which is the thing this round just spent an entry deleting.

Needed. Nothing before implementation. Needed before the first real import is scheduled: a named holder of attribute.define, and the codes the map names committed somewhere a second pair of eyes can read them.

See: D-141, AT-2 (the question this one replaces), domain/03 §7, permission-catalog §12.

docs.title: H. Not yet designed
docs.text:
Each of these is referenced by the schema and has hooks left for it. Two rows carry a ✅ because the area needed no new module: events was designed in round 5, and the medical record was answered out of existence in round 7 — what a reader who says "the medical record" is pointing at is the attribute vocabulary of data-model/09, one class of person data with no privileged subset (D-083).

Area Hooks already in place Notes Events ✅ Designed — domain/07, data-model/08 Fifteen questions answered, and the three that were still open — EV-2, EV-4 and EV-6 — were answered in round 20. Nothing about events is open on this page. Fees and payments data-model/07-finance.md — architecture settled, policy open Five open questions — discounts, invoices, the accounting export, jurisdiction, and the variable symbol — which is the whole of it, and the sentence used to read nine open questions without naming one of them while the module page kept a twelve-item list of its own that nothing here could see. Round 22 closed the rest of that list by answering it: the fee is koruna (D-155), it buys membership and nothing else (D-156), there are no waivers (D-157), a refund happens at the bank (D-158), no proration rule (D-160), one live price (D-161). Round 6 had already closed the architectural ones: money arrives by bank API, is requested by variable symbol + QR code, there is no card gateway, and unmatched money queues (D-075, D-076). The five are still not registered here, which is now a stated choice on the module page rather than an accident of this page's construction. Documents access_grant.scope_type = 'document'; the evidence-reference hook belonged to the removed requirement tables Needs: storage, versions, retention, consent-driven access. Consents No dependent.consent.* any more — a guardian at write may give and manage consents (D-074) Needs: template, per-activity consent, expiry, revocation, who may consent. No longer connected to a membership requirement (D-044). is_legal_decision_maker on the guardianship row is the existing hook for "who may sign" — and it is now the only place that distinction lives, since the right level cannot express it. Health records ✅ Designed — as domain/08 and data-model/09 There was no medical record to design. D-083 ruled that everything about a person except name, gender and age is one class of data, held as fields in a vocabulary the organization defines at runtime (D-084). Reading is person.view, writing is person.edit, and only the vocabulary needs a code of its own. What is left undesigned is policy around one class rather than a second module: what happens to the history of a value once the audit payloads expire. The other half of that sentence is now answered — whether attribute.define is a sufficient gate for a vocabulary free to invent a "health" category tomorrow, which round 20 settled by deciding there is no second gate: a definition is live at the save of whoever holds the code (D-141), and the widening is a stated property of that code rather than a queue in front of it. The trail side of the same worry is AT-4. Communication message.send_direct, message.broadcast (scoped) — shape decided, detail undesigned Shape decided by D-077: internal first, external channels are delivery; everyone may send direct; broadcast is one scoped permission; the recipient picks the channel. Needs: templates, opt-out granularity, retention, moderation. The rule against contacting minors directly was declined as a sender restriction and replaced by mirroring — see MSG-1. Reporting report.* permissions sketched The historical queries in domain/05 are the starting set. Query 10 (members per year, as far back as the records reach) is the acceptance test. API and UI api_key and its four codes: who may call in is designed (05e, D-116); the resolver's at parameter exists partly for this The caller is designed; the wire is not. What a request looks like, how a secret is presented and carried, and how a session survives a login are API-layer work, and D-072 is the standing division — what is decided is only what may be stored: a hash, and nothing else. The UI side of the same decision is one permissions page answering a second question (§15's tabs). Calls going out were answered in round 20 without being designed: an outbound call is a person's act or this system's job, never a third kind of actor (F-27, D-146). Beside it, three things are settled rather than open — this system's own writers are an empty actor column read as the system acting on its own and named by a fixed label list (D-125), a lockout is a report plus a written procedure rather than a mechanism (D-126), and everything a caller sends over the wire is API work, not schema work. Notifications — Nothing in this design notifies anybody today, and that is a ruling rather than a gap (D-164, generalizing D-137): a report is a tab somebody opens and the audit trail is the control. The one person the authority model does point at survives this untouched, because D-126's break-glass actor is a procedure needing somebody, not a message needing a recipient. What this row still describes is an undesigned module, and its one dated shape is worth keeping if it is ever built — the renewal window makes it dated rather than status-driven, a job over in_renewal_window() rather than a watcher on a status column. Nothing waits on it: no rule in the register reads a send, because nothing is sent. Payment gateway — Answered, so this row is now narrower than it was. The organization collects via bank API, not a card gateway (D-075): no webhooks, no disputes, no processor reconciliation. What remains undesigned is the statement import itself — file formats, the idempotency key, and what happens to an account the bank revises. Multi-language — Answered for the attribute vocabulary by D-149: one language, no translation columns. The same reasoning covers the other words the database holds — nothing else on it was asked about separately — because a row holding two labels has to be asked which of the two the record is. The example this row was written with has itself gone: there is no unit left whose name could be translated (D-097).

docs.title: K. Filed by a module page
docs.text:
Nine questions, every one of them raised by round 22, each verified on the page that holds it and deliberately not asked there. They are on this register rather than left in a decision page because they are the defect they came from. A module page had been keeping an open-issue section for sixteen rounds which this register could not see and no reader reached: data-model/07 §5 called itself "the whole of this document, essentially", filed nothing here, and this page's finance row reported "nine open questions" without naming one. A question that is not on a register is not an open question; it is a sentence on a page. These nine are the repair, and the finding that required it is told properly in round 22.

None of the nine blocks anything, and none was answered this round — they are written here in the words the page that holds them uses, so that answering one starts from the place that has to change rather than from a summary of it. Two of the nine ask whether a column should exist at all (K-4, K-6); the rest ask for a rule, a list, or a name.

docs.title: K-1 🟢 Must a member row sit inside its group's own period?
docs.text: Found in data-model/02 §8, which says the containment is "nowhere ruled", and mirrored in the register, whose row for it gives the save-time check as none — containment is assumed and the backstop as 02 §6 check 2. What changes when it is answered: either a refusal at the save, or the report stays the whole control and the register's row says so on purpose rather than by omission.

docs.title: K-2 🟢 Is an ended group hidden from pickers, and may it be reopened?
docs.text: Also 02 §8. It collides with §1's rule that a returning name is a new group: if an ended group may be reopened, "the same name twice" stops being one rule and becomes two. What changes: nothing in a table; one sentence about what a picker lists, which is the sort of answer this repository has been happiest to receive.

docs.title: K-3 🟢 Where is a claimed continuity between two groups recorded?
docs.text: 02 §8 again. D-098 refused group-to-group edges, and the one rule this corpus had about continuity belonged to units: D-096 ruled a reused number a new unit unless someone records the continuity, and D-097 removed the units. What changes: either a self-reference on person_group, which is a decision to reopen that refusal, or the words "the same troop, 1998" stay outside the database, which is survivable and should be written down as chosen.

docs.title: K-4 🟢 Is person.gender needed at all, and if so with what value set?
docs.text: Verbatim from 01b §11. It is on a page about erasure, which is why it matters: a column kept for a form nobody remembers filling is a column the organization has to justify keeping. What changes: a column, its value set, and its place in the redaction rules.

docs.title: K-5 🟢 Does the organization have, or will it have, a national SSO identity provider?
docs.text: Also 01b §11. What changes: how much of account_credential is ever built. It is the difference between this system holding password hashes and holding one external identifier, which is why it is filed even though its answer is a sentence.

docs.title: K-6 🟢 Should person.notes exist at all?
docs.text: Argued on the page that holds it: 01-identity's What is deliberately not on this table. It is the last free text about a person kept outside the attribute vocabulary, it is logged with its contents, and it is deliberately not on the redactor's list — which makes it the one column where "may contain a diagnosis" is a property of the design rather than of careless typing. What changes: a column, or the attribute vocabulary gaining the one job this column was doing.

docs.title: K-7 🟢 Which tables does the audit obligation actually cover?
docs.text: 06b §6, which asks for confirmation rather than derivation — §2.1 already obligates every business table, so what is outstanding is somebody reading the list and saying yes. What changes: nothing, if the list is right, which is the cheapest question on this page and the one nobody volunteers for.

docs.title: K-8 🟢 Who reads the queue of money that cannot be matched, and how often?
docs.text: data-model/07 says unmatched money waits for a person, and D-076 decided that waiting is better than guessing. What changes: nothing in the schema — a name and a rhythm, which is the shape of question F-34 is on this page for.

docs.title: K-9 🟢 May staff create an account for a child, or only for an adult?
docs.text: domain/02 §7, and the one question round 22 touched without closing it: D-166 ruled that no consent step and no age gate lives on an account, which settles what the account is not and says nothing about who may open one. What changes: nothing structural — and that is the reason it is worth answering, since a permission with no default is decided by whoever writes the grant.

docs.title: R. Resolved — moved to the decision log
docs.text:
Kept here so a reader of this file knows the question was asked and where the answer lives, rather than finding it silently deleted.

Was Question Settled by In one line A-1 The organizational structure D-035 One root; all sub-units nest arbitrarily beneath it. Reversed in round 10: there are no sub-units at all, and the unit is a scope rather than a row (D-097). A-1 The unit type vocabulary D-054 Not seeded — org_unit_type is runtime data; only the root type ships. Deleted with the table (D-097). B-1 How much legacy data, in what shape? D-056 Large, with legacy member numbers — exact matches, so review is a work queue. Fully answered in round 8: thousands of roster rows, no payment data at all, so every historical row is a participation (D-090). Round 10 moved the noun: the participation table is gone, so an attendance row with no dates imports as a dated person_group_member row or nothing at all (D-097, D-098). D-9 Is household load-bearing at all? D-057 No — removed entirely. Addresses are temporal person_contact rows. F-1 Which permissions and roles does the organization need? D-055 The catalog stays large and granular; it is a menu, not a checklist. — Eligibility for an event — a separate rule engine? D-060 No — eligibility is capability. event.register_self at contribute, via audiences. — Is unanswered a stored attendance value? D-059 No — absence of a row. Two stored values: attending, not_attending. — Is a weekly meeting an event? D-058 No. Round 10 moved the answer: a Thursday group is a person_group with a dated roster, and unit_participation is deleted (D-097). Still no recurrence, no series table, no occurrence table, and no row that says who attended a given evening. — One owning unit per event, or several? D-058 Exactly one. Reversed in round 10b: nothing owns an event — event.org_unit_id is deleted and the people connected to it are named by selectors that bind to it (D-102). — Are organizers a grant or a roster? D-062 A roster on the event — labelled and ordered. Grants stay separate. — Do unit roles reach the unit's own events? D-063 Yes — an event is an artifact of its unit, not a child. Reversed in round 10b: the artifact rule and can_event() are deleted, and nothing reaches an event from a unit (D-102). D-031's finding survives as the safeguarding property stated in the authorization ERD. — Does an event have a status (draft, published)? D-064 No status column. Visibility is the permission model; cancellation is a fact. — What happens when a full event gets another registration? D-065 Waitlisted for self-service; admitted for organizers; the overrun reported. — Does paying confirm a place? D-066 Yes when the event has a fee; most events are free and confirm immediately. — Do organizers record who actually came? D-067 Yes — was_present, three-valued. It is the "who was in our care" record. — May an event form collect medical detail? D-061 Effectively yes: answers are read by that event's organizers, and no event permission reaches the health record, so the form is the only route for a camp leader to learn an allergy at all. A recorded widening, restated after D-074 removed the namespace the original wording relied on. A-2 Permissions conditioned on membership status D-039 Yes, enforced by the resolver, with guardianship and ownership carved out. Round 10 deleted the gate (D-100): membership is now a term a grant's expression may name, not a precondition the resolver checks. A-3 Activate on payment or on approval? D-040 On payment; the fee expires yearly and a dated renewal window replaces a grace status. A-4 Background checks D-043 None are recorded in this system. A-4 The expiry date D-047 1 January; the organizational year runs with the calendar. A-4 The renewal window length D-048 60 days, stored as a parameter rather than compiled in. C-1 May the root read into its sub-units? D-049 No. scope_exposure is the only crossing; no reporting channel is built. Formally closed in round 9, and D-094 gave it a mirror: imported events belong to the root, so a unit's own event list contains history it did not run. Round 10 dissolved the question: there is no sub-unit to read into and scope_exposure is deleted (D-097). C-3 Is a reused unit number the same unit? D-096 A new unit, unless someone records continuity as successor_of. A code is a typed label, not an identity. Moot with the table (D-097). C-4 Does appointing someone create a role assignment? D-091, restated by D-098, D-100, D-101 No. Round 10 redrew the line the answer drew: the union-of-three-arms became an expression language (+ - *), a group became a hand-stated dated roster, and an audience became the rule. Appointing still creates nothing, and there are no positions left to appoint. Rule-filled roles went to F-12, which round 10 closed no. C-5 What creates the units the import's rows point at? D-092, D-093, D-094 Nothing, because the rows name no units. People arrive as bounded memberships, events as root-owned events with registrations. The historical record has no sub-units in it. C-6 Should allows_minors refuse a minor's position as it refuses their participation? D-095 Neither: units carry no restrictions and the flag is removed. The control is that nobody joins a unit or takes a position themself — a counselor writes the row. Positions went in round 10 (D-100); the control is now person_group.member.manage. D-6 How may the membership gate be waived? D-051 A person-level system.gate_exempt permission, in addition to the role flag. Both are deleted (D-100). What survives is the reason: a sweep must not lock out the one person who can repair it. D-7 The root participation row at renewal D-050 Extended across the renewed period; one row, no gap. Retired with the table (D-097). C-1 (largely) Organization-wide operational roles without downward inheritance D-035 The problem dissolves: the root owns the registry and the fees. What remains is a reporting question — see C-1. One unit now, so the shape is gone entirely (D-097). C-2 May units be reparented retroactively? D-036 Not at all — a unit that moves is a new unit. Moot with the units (D-097). D-1 Fee per person or per household? D-037 Per person, flat, yearly. D-2 One open membership, or several of different types? D-037, D-041 One type, so one open membership, enforced person-wide. The participation half of D-041 is moot (D-097). D-3 Age-out timing D-038 Retired — there is no age-out. D-4 Child → adult transition D-038 Retired — there are no membership categories to transition between. D-5 Membership type vocabulary D-037 One type, member; counselor is a position, not a type. E-1 Default rights when a guardianship is created D-046 write for a self-registered child's guardian; view for staff-created and imported rows; chosen at creation when recorded manually. D-074 turned the answer from a code bundle into one level, which is why the decision still stands on its original wording. F-2 Polymorphic scope_id vs a grantable_item supertable your answer, round 6 Polymorphic — scope_type plus scope_id, as currently designed. — The bulk scope-exposure tool D-045 Removed once audiences existed to cover the case it was for. — What a membership request must contain D-044 Identity and the fee. The whole requirement mechanism is gone. — Whether grants may target groups D-042 Yes — built-in rule-evaluated audiences plus admin-managed named groups. E-2 What happens to guardianship at majority? D-069 Nothing — no job, no queue, no computed date. A person ends the row. (Reverses D-024.) F-3 Must a high-authority role assignment have an end date? D-071 No. The membership gate plus a human review report; the earlier "yes" recommendation is withdrawn. Both halves moved: the gate is deleted (D-100) and the report became a tab (D-109). F-4 Should person.admin subsume merge and redact? D-068 Moot — there are no per-resource admin permissions. The choice moved into reviewable role contents. (Reverses D-007.) — Should every resource expose an admin permission? D-068 No. Sixteen codes and the resolver's prefix match are gone; roles are the bundle. EV-1 Does an event need an age ceiling? D-070 No. The grant is the rule; a future ceiling would be a built-in audience, not a column. EV-5 Should event.manage_participants split? this round Yes — event.presence.mark at contribute, one level below the roster. Round 10 note: the split stands; the level does not (D-099). D-8 Should unit_participation reference the membership? D-097 Retired with the table. The refusal is still live reasoning: participation had to survive without a membership, which is why person_group_member is keyed on a person. See data-model/03 §9. F-12 May a role be held by a rule, as an audience is? D-100 No. An office is held by a named person and confers nothing; a group is company; a grant is what reaches a set. The office record stays the one dated, human-readable answer. — Is there more than one unit, and does anything belong to it? D-097 No. org_unit and friends, unit_participation, scope_exposure and the traversal functions are deleted; the unit is a scope, not a row. Two-way door: no. — What is a group? D-098 person_group: named, dated, states its members, has a lifetime, grants nothing by itself. A group is company; a selector picks people; a grant is what reaches them. — What does a grant do, and how much? D-099 Allows or denies one permission at one scope, for a period. Allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies. No levels, no rank integer, no locality. — Is a role a bundle of permissions, and is membership a precondition? D-100 Neither. role_assignment → role_holder; role_permission, positions and the membership gate are deleted; the test moved into the expression (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)). Posture: default-on → opt-in. — How is an audience stored? D-101 As an expression tree over named sets — + - *, brackets, fully-bracketed canonical form, cycles refused at save, the language seeded as selector_type. Semantic equality given up (see F-14). — Who owns an event, and whom does a grant about it reach? D-102 Nobody owns it. event.org_unit_id, can_event() and the artifact rule are deleted; four attendance tiers and ORGANIZERS bind to the item, and the answer-view grant is a seeded template instantiated per event. — May a rule be reused by name? D-103 Yes: AUDIENCE(code), referenced by code, one namespace with roles and groups, cycles refused across audiences at save, and an audience named by a live grant may not be ended. Its past reach is not reconstructable (see F-17). Amended in the same round: the same refusal now extends to a group named by a live grant — see assumption 63. F-19 A permission code is a row, prose names codes, and nothing checks the two D-104 The class is real — four instances in ten rounds, in two different registries. The naming grammar is now three rules (action-final; a middle segment names stored state; no grade words, no prefix) with system.admin the single named exception. The event QR capability never existed: invented in prose, deleted in prose, no decision entry at either end. The check adopted is a hand-run diff report — a convention, not a guard. **(Round 18 made it executable, and made it a gate: scripts/check-registries.py reads the six registries out of the pages that hold them, exits non-zero on a finding nobody has read, and keeps what it was told to keep in scripts/registry-baseline.txt, one reason per line — D-127.) E-6 A guardian may appoint a guardian — notify anyone? D-137 Attribution is enough: no notification, no queue, no addressee. The act is a write, the write is audited, and the trail is the control. The recommendation on the page named a "safeguarding contact" and no such office exists — safeguarding_officer is a worked example the catalog marks as not shipping, and D-132 deletes the seed. What it costs: nothing tells anyone that a third adult gained authority over a child. The answer to who added them is excellent, and the answer to did anybody think about it is the person who did it, alone, at the moment they did it. F-8 Retention policy for access_log D-145 Confirmed, and stricter than the proposal: rows are deleted at 24 months, not emptied. audit_log keeps the opposite shape — rows for life, payloads emptied — so D-088's two clocks now differ in kind as well as in length. This is the third named exception to 00 §4's "nothing is hard-deleted"; the job that does it gets a sixth actor label, system:log-reduction, and the age-out gets a check of its own. Assumption 50 is retired by this row. F-27 The integration that this system calls D-146 Nothing is designed, and no third kind of actor will be invented when something is. An outbound call is either a person acting — the actor column holds them and their permission is checked — or this system acting on its own: an empty column and a label from the fixed list (D-125). Refused: an api_key as the actor of an outbound write, because a secret must not carry the accountability of an act. EV-2 Retention of event_answer D-140 No expiry for registrations or answers. Neither ends with its event and neither ends on a clock; "answers end with the event" is deleted as a policy. Erasure reaches answers and empties them: event_answer.value is set to empty and the row survives. The asymmetry this question was built on — the same fact kept forever as an attribute and quietly discarded as an answer — is closed by making the two rules agree. EV-4 was_present as a safeguarding record D-147 Neither. Presence is a column of a registration and inherits its retention — just settled, indefinitely — and the codes that already reach the roster. This system keeps no safeguarding register: no background checks (D-043), no medical record (D-083). A column with a clock and a permission of its own would have been the first wall of an archive this design has refused four times. EV-6 WHITELISTED — the word people reach for D-148 Refused, in writing, where the tiers are listed. No is_whitelisted, no fifth tier, no operand, no reserved name: anyone adding is_whitelisted is reimplementing grants badly. The need is real and is met by rows that already exist — an invitation is a grant aimed at a person, and a person who never registered is described by the absence of a row. The refusal already existed four times over; what was missing was the sentence, and it was missing in domain/07a §9. AT-1 Should an event question bind to an attribute code? D-139 Yes — bound to the code, never to a value row. The form prefills from the stored value as a suggestion the answerer confirms or edits, and submitting it performs a write-back: a new person_attribute value dated today, recorded as written by the answering person. The condition that fenced this binding off — 00 §4's "safe only while nothing references an attribute row" — is not detonated, because the binding names a definition, which is never deleted and is retired instead. A reference to a person_attribute row id stays exactly as forbidden as that paragraph says. AT-2 Who curates the vocabulary, and how long may a proposal sit? D-141 There is no proposal. A definition is live at the save of whoever holds attribute.define; proposed, proposed_by, proposed_at, the curation queue and the check that aged them out are all deleted — proposed was a third status no decision had granted (D-084 says live or retired). A value may not invent a code: an import column that maps to nothing is an error at apply time, not a proposal waiting for a curator. The permission is the curator — a role would confer nothing (D-100). The mechanism is settled; the schedule it used to carry is not, and that is F-34. AT-3 Do attribute labels need translation? D-149 No. One language, the one the organization writes in: no label_cs/label_en pair, no translation table, no locale column. A row holding two labels has to be asked which of the two the record is, and whichever answer is chosen demotes the other to a translation of it. The form is for the conversation and the vocabulary is for the record; only one of them has to be stable enough to query. AT-4 Is one permission enough to guard a trail that holds person data? D-138 audit.view is the whole gate — one permission, no per-entry filter, now decided rather than merely unbuilt: 06 §2.3 records the per-entry check as considered and left unimplemented. A history screen over the trail is a person-data surface, granted rarely and marked. A per-entry check would have made what an officer can read about 2019 depend on an expression changed last week — and that legibility is the whole reason the trail exists. F-28 Is the displayed name a copy to keep in step, or a field to delete? D-142 The copy stays and the drift is reported. The register's none was wrong in the understating direction: 01b §10 already counts persons whose given_name/family_name differ from the open person_name row — the very check this question offered as "cheap to write". What closed was the admission, not the check, and it is the mirror image of round 19's phantom row: none is as much a claim about a page as a citation is (D-129). F-32 A delegation the delegator has lost — reported, or invisible? D-143 At grant time only, and the delegation stands — to its own valid_to, or to a revocation. No use-time re-check, no report, nothing cascades, which is what the data model already said (05 §6: "nothing about the person who lent it is re-validated when a check runs") while domain/06 §9 promised the opposite and the register recorded the rule as enforced twice. Two bounds survive: a delegation must expire (integrity check 11), and system.admin cannot be delegated at all. F-33 Does a code's right_kind have to match the code, or is it a note? D-144 A note: required, agreeing with nothing, checked by nothing — and kept required, because a code whose declared kind reads oddly is worth noticing while reading, and that is the column's whole job. The register row claiming the save enforces the match is withdrawn, not repaired (D-129): no page states such a rule, and no page claims to. A right_kind can contradict its code forever, and only a reader will notice.

docs.title: I. Assumption index
docs.text:
Every Assumption: the documentation is standing on, so they can be reviewed as a group. Confirming one promotes it to a numbered decision: the row keeps its number, gains a †, and says which decision carries it now. A row whose subject was deleted keeps its number too, struck, with the decision that deleted it — the numbers are stable identifiers, so an earlier round's citation of "assumption 61" still resolves.

The fate of a superseded assumption is one clause here and a decision entry elsewhere; the argument is in the entry, and this index is a register, not a second copy of it.

# Assumption Where 1 PostgreSQL 14+ with btree_gist data-model/00 2 No automatic merging (D-004) † domain/03 3 ~~Minors need guardian consent for an account~~ — falsified, and it was load-bearing: an account carries no minimum age and no consent step, and account.guardian_consent_at is deleted rather than left empty (D-166). A minor may register unattended and nothing in the model objects, because an account is a login and authority over a child lives on the guardianship row. What the assumption was afraid of moves to the legal review as its fourth policy — whether a child may hold an account with no guardian's answer recorded anywhere domain/02 4 A self-registered child's parent gets a write right over the child (D-046, as amended by D-074) † data-model/04 5 ~~Locality orders allows only~~; deny is absolute (D-032) † — half of this row is deleted: locality went with the levels (D-099), and the surviving half is now the whole decision rule: allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies domain/06 6 Membership activates on payment (D-040) † domain/05 7 The fee is per person and yearly (D-037) † domain/05 8 Renewal opens a new row, not an extended valid_to (D-016) † domain/05 ~~9~~ ~~Guardianship reviewed at majority, not auto-expired~~ — superseded: neither, the system takes no position (D-069) data-model/04 10 Display name uses preferred_name if set data-model/01 11 Merge chains are allowed, because reversing a merge has to stay possible (D-087) † data-model/01 12 Only confirmed payments count toward a balance data-model/07 ~~13~~ ~~No sub-unit types are seeded; nesting is permissive by default~~ (D-054) — deleted, not reversed: org_unit_type and org_unit_type_rule went with the hierarchy (D-097), so there is nothing left to seed and no nesting to be permissive about. A-1's closure is the decision of record data-model/02 14 membership_type is seeded with exactly one row (D-037) † data-model/03 15 person.gender is needed for reporting data-model/01 16 Imported rosters end at the organizational year end (D-028) † — the row stated the shape and not the date, and the date was answerable from two pages away: D-169 settles that the last day is 31 December and the stored valid_to is 1 January of the following year, because every period here is half-open data-model/06 17 All business tables are audited data-model/06 18 ~~Currency is EUR~~ † corrected: the currency is koruna (D-155), and the correction was already implied by the module's own money path — D-075's variable symbol and QR route is a Czech one. All four currency columns read CZK, and a second currency is refused rather than deferred data-model/07 19 access_log is not human-annotatable data-model/05 ~~20~~ ~~Each permission has an admin sibling~~ — superseded: no per-resource wildcard codes (D-068) throughout 21 No downward inheritance; ~~exposures are written by the unit~~ (D-031) † — deprived of its subject, not weakened (D-097): the rule was always about a hierarchy that no longer exists, and what survives is the ordinary reading of a scope — a grant reaches its scope and nothing beside it domain/06 §2 22 The person record holds no deceased flag (D-034) † data-model/01 ~~23~~ ~~Positions are multi-holder unless max_holders says otherwise~~ (D-033) — deleted by D-100 with position, position_assignment, is_leadership and max_holders. The vacancy question it answered is now unanswered by construction; see F-18, which D-136 answered by deciding not to record it domain/04 24 Membership is ageless — no category, no min_age, no max_age (D-038) † data-model/03 25 A grant targets a person or an audience, never both (D-042) † data-model/05 26 ~~Built-in audiences are rules evaluated by the resolver, not stored lists~~ (D-042) † — reversed twice, and the second reversal is the one to keep. An audience stores an expression and nothing else: a hand-written set is PERSON(x) leaves inside it — rows of the tree, not rows of a roster, with no dates of their own (D-101 then D-105, which deleted the LIST leaf round 10 put back). D-042's half about rules is therefore true again, for a new reason: the words are what is stored, and the words can happen to name people. The two audiences this row used to count are gone (D-153), and so is the count they were inside: data-model/05d §12 now says what ships and names no audience among it. data-model/05 ~~27~~ ~~Belonging to a sub-unit is participation, not membership~~ (D-041) † — deleted with the sub-units (D-097). The distinction it drew is now drawn between a group (company) and a grant (authority), by D-098 data-model/02 ~~28~~ ~~Roles require a current membership unless requires_membership = false~~ (D-039) † — the gate is deleted (D-100); membership is now a term a writer puts in a grant expression, and the posture is opt-in data-model/05 ~~29~~ ~~There is no bulk exposure tool and no bulk: reason marker~~ (D-045) † — moot twice over: scope_exposure itself is deleted (D-097), so there is no tool to build and nothing to mark data-model/05 30 No background checks are recorded anywhere (D-043) † throughout 31 access_grant.scope_id is polymorphic, with no foreign key (F-2) † data-model/05 32 The organizational calendar is 1 January plus a 60-day window (D-047, D-048) † data-model/03 ~~33~~ ~~The root reads into a sub-unit only through scope_exposure~~ (D-049) † — there is no sub-unit and no exposure (D-097). C-1's closure is the record; the safeguarding property it protected ("a child's records are reachable only through a guardianship row") was never carried by this mechanism and is untouched domain/06 ~~34~~ ~~A renewal extends the root participation row rather than closing it~~ (D-050) † — the row is deleted (D-097). The reasoning survives where the row did not: data-model/03 §9 keeps it, because the renewal rule in §3 still rests on it. See D-7 data-model/03 ~~35~~ ~~The membership gate is waived by a person-level permission, not only a role flag~~ (D-051) † — the gate and system.gate_exempt are both deleted (D-100). What survives is the reason: a sweep must not lock out the one person who can repair it, which is now an argument about the seeded grants carrying MEMBERS. See D-6 data-model/05 36 The permission catalog is deliberately comprehensive and granular (D-055) † appendix/permission-catalog.md 37 The legacy corpus is large and carries legacy member numbers (D-056) † domain/03 38 There is no household table; addresses are temporal person_contact rows (D-057) † data-model/04 39 ~~An event belongs to exactly one unit~~; a weekly meeting is not an event (D-058) † — first half deleted by D-102 (event.org_unit_id is gone; nothing owns an event), second half intact but no longer named "participation": a Thursday group is a group now (D-097, D-098), and no row says who attended a given evening data-model/08 40 "Unanswered" is the absence of a registration row (D-059) † data-model/08 41 Eligibility is capability — there is no rule engine (D-060) † domain/07 42 Event answers are read by that event's organizers (D-061) † — still true, and no longer a resolver clause: it is one grant row per event (event.answer.view, scoped to the event, aimed at ORGANIZERS), which D-102 calls out as the deliberate move from prose to data. Round 21 found the two words doing different work: it is not a seeded template instantiated per event, it is a row the create writes — one of twelve (D-151). An event created without its grant has organizers who can read nothing, and now there is an author to name in that report data-model/08 43 Organizers are a roster on the event, not grants (D-062) † data-model/08 ~~44~~ ~~An event is an artifact of its unit, so unit roles reach it~~ (D-063) † — deleted by D-102, along with can_event(). Nothing reaches an event from a unit any more; authority arrives through a grant scoped to the event itself, and the sentence "an event is an artifact, not a child" is withdrawn rather than restated domain/07 45 There is no event status; visibility is the permission model (D-064) † data-model/08 46 Capacity is a waitlist threshold organizers may exceed (D-065) † data-model/08 47 Payment confirms a place; free events confirm immediately (D-066) † data-model/08 48 Presence is a three-valued fact, not a boolean (D-067) † data-model/08 49 Keeping named membership and fee rows indefinitely after an erasure request has a legal basis (D-088) — unverified, and commissioning the review is the organization's job data-model/00 50 Retired by D-145, and retired wrongly as worded. access_log did take the same 24 months as the audit payloads — but not the same treatment: its rows are deleted, while audit rows live on and only their payloads are emptied. The number was right and the shape was not, and the shape is the part a data subject is asking about data-model/05 51 Audience membership is recomputed at check time and never stored, so "who could read this in 2023" may be unanswerable once the audit payloads expire (D-091, restated for D-098/D-101) † — the half of this that used to be true of roles is no longer at risk: an office is a dated role_holder row and a group is a dated roster, both stored, and F-12 closed on exactly that ground. What remains exposed is the expression, and it is now a question with a number: F-17 data-model/05 52 The historical record contains no sub-unit participation, because the corpus names no units (D-092) † — now true for a second, stronger reason: even if the corpus had named them there would be nowhere to put the answer (D-097). The finding about the source is what matters and is unchanged data-model/06 53 An imported membership carries no fee obligation, and its outstanding_balance is NULL rather than zero (D-093) † data-model/07 54 A bare name in an expression resolves to a role or a group only, never to an audience — and the one-namespace rule across role, person_group and audience.code, with every selector_type.code reserved, is carried by the write path with no constraint spanning three tables (D-101, D-103) † data-model/05 55 Delegation is a set-membership test, and role.is_delegatable does not exist — the model has no column that says an office may delegate (still no decision on the test itself — but D-143 has fixed when it is applied: at grant time, once, and domain/06's promised second application is deleted rather than built) domain/06 56 Finding which grants name an audience, and at what depth, is cheap enough to show before saving an edit to a referenced audience (D-103) — stated as an assumption in the decision itself and measured by nobody F-16 57 A grant's scope is the unit or exactly one item (D-102) † — and the half this row drew from it is wrong, which is the most useful thing about it: it read "one item per grant" as though a template were the cheap way to say twelve rows, and D-151 found the seed page and the event page disagreeing about the row count with an integrity check written against the second reading. There is no template; there are twelve rows per event, written by the create. data-model/08 58 ~~The PERSON(x) appearing in D-100's and D-101's worked expressions is shorthand for a second grant row, not a missing seeded operand~~ (D-101's registry amendment, class in D-104) † — the opposite: it was seeded, as the thirteenth selector_type row, and one of the twelve that remained once D-105 deleted LIST. This row recorded the wrong answer, and the error is the point: the registry was checked against nothing. Two decision entries wrote the registry while the seeded table was copied from the evaluator's arm list, so MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) did not parse for a whole round, and the repair already circulating read PERSON(y) as LIST — which subtracts everybody on the list, and is now impossible to write. The instance is told in the catalog's open issues and in F-5; the rule it produced is that an operand's registry row and its seed are one fact, not two. D-101, F-5 59 Two expressions with one meaning are two audiences: nothing computes semantic equality, and nothing will (D-101) † F-14 60 An audience preview is per-item and lazy, and no screen expands a set for more than one item at a time (consequence of D-102's per-item reached set) — unmeasured at real event sizes, and round 14 added a dependency without changing the assumption. Nothing pre-pays a preview any more: with no answer cache to warm, the preview computes on open, so its affordability rests on the request memo and on can_many existing — two things these documents can name and cannot enforce (D-114, F-15). F-15 61 ~~A cache key is (person, permission, item), and a stale allow is the failure that matters because deny is absolute~~ (D-102, D-099) † — round 14 deleted this row's subject rather than settling it: there is no cache, so there is no key, no TTL and no stale allow (D-114; D-111 was the answer it had been waiting for). Two halves outlive the object they were written about, and both are about meaning rather than storage: the item belongs to whatever a permission predicate is bound to — a compilation carries the item as a parameter and holds no item, so nothing resolved while checking one item may be served for another; the checked date belongs inside the answer, which is why any computed roster holds dated rows and never "today's set". D-114, data-model/05 §10 62 A person_group_member row lies inside its group's own period — assumed in §2 of data-model/02, reported by integrity check 2 as "a list to read rather than a breach", and ruled nowhere. Raised by the page's own author as an assumption these documents are standing on data-model/02 §8 63 ~~A group may be ended while a live grant or a live expression names it~~ (D-103, amended in the round after the audience row) † — refused at save, in both directions, and on the - side rather than the allow side: a live grant on an ended group is safe where it allows and widens a deny where it subtracts, so an ended operand is a way to silently empty a set that was narrowing something. ROLE(x) needs no such rule and the difference is the finding — an office has no role.retire and cannot be emptied quietly, while a group is emptied in one field. The rule itself is data-model/02 §3. D-103, data-model/02 §8 64 An operand's set moves when somebody writes — twelve rounds of invalidation lists were built on this and none of them said it out loud † — falsified by design by D-107: OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) move at midnight, for one person, with no row to change and no event to subscribe to. Round 14 closed the gap that acceptance was papering over (D-114): with resolution live and no answer stored, a birthday moves the answer at the instant it happens, so the ruling that a calendar drift is fine has nothing left to accept. The write case was never safe either — the lists could never say which writes, and the boundary D-111 drew left out membership, whose membership.terminate is the corpus's most safeguarding-shaped write. The corrected form is not "sets move on writes" but "sets move whenever anything they can read changes": the read path, not a list. F-6, D-114 B-2 May a merge be reversed? D-087 B-3 Erasure: what is kept, and for how long? D-088 B-4 What may a sign-up do when it collides with a live account? D-089 E-4 Does a guardianship know about membership — does a lapse or a renewal touch right_level? D-115 E-5 Who administers a guardianship row? D-073 E-7 Can a guardian see the profile but not the medical record? D-083 F-4a Should the catalog be generated from the seed, or the seed from the catalog? D-072 F-5 Which primitive facts can the expression language still not state? D-113 F-6 How long may a cached permission answer be reused, and what invalidates it? D-114 F-7 A nightly rebuild of cached answers, or a materialized effective-permission table? D-111 F-13 Is a rule that resolves correctly but looks odd a warning at save? D-109 F-14 May two expressions be tested for reaching the same people? D-105 F-15 Is the per-item audience preview affordable? D-112 F-16 Is listing the grants that name an audience affordable? D-112 F-17 Whom did a grant reach in May, when a nested audience has changed since? D-110 F-20 Should WHITELISTED be seeded once a whitelist feature exists? D-113 F-21 Who reads the report about what an expression names and what it costs? D-109 F-22 May the editor fold and flatten an expression for display? D-105 F-23 Is a resolved audience stored as the record of whom a grant reached? D-110 F-25 What is this system's own name when it writes to itself? D-125 F-26 When nobody who can hold system.admin can sign in, what happens? D-126 F-10 Which invariants the ORM cannot express, and who writes those? D-130

| EV-3 | What happens to outstanding payment requests when an event is cancelled? | D-076 | Cancelling voids the event's outstanding payment requests, recording why, and money already received becomes a queue item — answered in the finance module rather than here, by D-076. | | H-0 | What is the medical record, which five files cited and none defined? | D-083 | Found while starting the health-records module, and it changed what that module is: the referent was not missing, the category was. Everything about a person except name, gender and age is one class of data, held as fields — D-083, with the shape of the layer in D-084 and the boundary in D-085. The three options this entry offered are recorded nowhere else, which is right: they were the shape of the question, not of the answer. | | MSG-1 | May a volunteer message a minor directly? | D-082 | Yes — mirror it to the minor's guardians, tell the sender, block nothing (D-082). Raised by D-077, which declined the restriction rather than forgetting it; three details were settled with it, because "mirror it to the guardians" does not by itself say who the guardians are to this message. | | F-29 | What can a report see about a trail whose payload has expired? | D-133 | Nothing, and the design now says so on the page that states the rule rather than leaving the reader to assume a trail with this much prose beside it checks itself. The premise did not survive being written down: the payload window was never what blocked the first check — api_key.valid_to, api_key.revoked_at and audit_log.occurred_at are all accounting skeleton, and a report over them would work in year thirty (06b §5). So the answer is not "cannot" but "will not", and what the design gives up is stated: nobody will ever be able to demonstrate that no write was audited against a key that had already ended. The question's other half was not a rule at all — the register row minted beside it asserted that which audit views a holder may open follows the payload window, citing 06 §2, and no page in the corpus says any such thing; 06 §2.3 says close to the opposite, that a per-entry check inside the history view was considered and left unimplemented, which is AT-4's subject and already registered there. Under D-129 a register row is a claim about a page, so the row is withdrawn rather than repaired. Costs: one paragraph in 06b §5, one 00a row deleted, one none that no longer reads as temporary. | | F-30 | Five polymorphic columns, and the orphans that are the design working | D-134 | Four get a scan; the audit row never will. field_conflict.entity_id is scanned outright — a conflict naming a row that is not there is a broken import, and the sentence saying so had never been written. access_log's three are scanned with the legal-absence rule beside them, because a target that is gone because a person was erased on purpose is not an integrity failure. audit_log.record_id is the deliberate exception and the interesting half of the answer: an audit row that outlives the row it described is what a redaction looks like afterwards (D-088), so a check counting those orphans as breaches would report the erasure path's own correct output as a failure — worse than no check, because the first false alarm teaches people to ignore the real one. Costs: a new check beside check 2 in 05d §11; 00 §9 and erd-b corrected, both of which still said there were exactly two reference-less keys; and 00a's row re-pointed at the page that owns the rule instead of at an appendix. The question's own arithmetic was wrong when it was filed: its positions offered to "scan the two a person can cause" and then named four columns. | | F-31 | The two modules with no check list of their own | D-135 | Yes — three checks each. 07-finance is asked to recompute the balance from §3's definition, to count a payment whose allocations do not account for its amount, and to find money nobody ever asked for; 06a-import is asked whether an imported membership is bounded at both ends, whether one occasion became one event, and whether a batch can account for what it did. The import page turns out to have had the strongest of the three in it already and never knew: an unbounded imported membership satisfies is_current_member(), so that row is the one place in the whole register where a data defect reaches the permission gate. Costs: a section on each page, three new 00a rows for rules both pages had stated and never registered, one dangling citation repaired (§3.1 had been citing "check 1 in §5" in a page with no §5), and 00a's What the register cannot say losing the structural excuse it had been giving for its own blanks. | | F-18 | Does a role record elected versus appointed, and what does an election write? | D-136 | It records neither, and a role holds only the people. An election is run outside this system — nominations, a ballot, a quorum, minutes — and what arrives is the outcome: one role_holder row, two dates, note for whoever wants the reason beside the fact (domain/04 §6, 05 §4). granted_by is not the answer to "was she elected?" and never claimed to be: it names whoever wrote the row, which for an election is a secretary. The refusals and their reasons: a flag would make the distinction queryable and guard nothing, and a field that looks like a control where no control is wanted is worse than the absence, because someone comes to rely on it; an election table would describe a process this system does not run, on D-043's ground; and the distinction has nowhere to bite, because an office confers nothing by being held. The cost, said plainly: nothing here will ever refuse to appoint someone to an office the bylaws reserve for a vote. Also worth recording: two of this question's load-bearing facts had already gone while it sat open — role.max_term_months is deleted, and role.is_system is deleted too — ruled by D-132, gone from the schema since D-152, which took the other three with it. |

docs.title: How to answer
docs.text:
Nothing here blocks anything. No question on this page is marked 🔴, and none has been since round 4: the model is settled enough that most answers here change data rather than structure, which is what makes them worth a moment rather than a decision meeting. Fourteen questions are left and every one of them is 🟢 — round 20 answered thirteen, and all six 🟡 on the page went with them, and round 22 added § K without closing one. Four of the five are left for a reason, not for a lack of priority: A-4's remainder is the organizational calendar, E-3 is a reading of this country's civil code, and F-9 and F-11 are one question seen twice — what a membership type is for. The fifth is F-34, and it is new: round 20 raised it by answering AT-2, and it is 🟢 for one reason only — the first real import is not next week. None of those five closes on a ruling alone, and F-34 least of all, because its answer is a person's name and a date rather than a rule.

§ K is the opposite kind of debt, and that is why it was worth filing nine questions at once. Six of its nine close on a ruling alone — K-1, K-2, K-3, K-4, K-6 and K-9 each need one sentence from somebody who knows the organization. K-5 and K-7 need a fact rather than a decision — whether an identity provider exists, and whether a list is right — and K-8 needs a name and a rhythm, which is the same shape F-34 has and the reason neither is answerable by a ruling.

What this repository owes instead is two things, and neither of them is a question.

  1. ~~Round 21, which is a sweep and not a decision.~~ Ran, on 2026-10-31, as round 21. D-132 was ruled two rounds ago and is now applied: the seeded roles, the seeded audiences, the seeded event.answer.view grant, the worked-example offices presented as seed and all four is_system columns — the two D-132 named plus permission.is_system and selector_type.is_system, which went on the argument that a column reading "a migration wrote this" protects nothing (D-150 … D-154). Round 20 deliberately kept it out, so that thirteen answers and a twenty-five-page sweep would not land together; the sweep was roughly that size and the estimate is replaced in the round page by a count from the diff. Two of round 20's entries — D-141 and D-143 — were written so that the sweep had to read them, and it did. Nothing in this list is owed any more; the fourteen questions above are the whole debt, and the legal review below it.
  2. The legal review, which is not a question this register can answer and which now has four policies in front of it instead of three: named membership and fee rows kept indefinitely, audit payloads emptied at 24 months, access_log rows deleted outright at 24 months (D-145), and — new since round 22 — whether a child may hold an account with no guardian's consent recorded anywhere (D-166, which deleted the column that would have recorded it and left the jurisdictional question with the review that can answer it). Two of the four are this system's own clocks; the other two are the ones a data subject asks about, and the fourth is the only one this design answers by not holding a record at all. Assumption 49 is its subject — and since D-093 the indefinitely-kept population includes thousands of imported people who never used the system, which is the same judgement at a scale the review has not yet been shown.

Everything else can be answered as we go.

What happened to the questions that are not here is in the decision log, not here. § R is the register — the question, the decision that owns the answer, what the answer cost — and the reasoning is in the entry each row links to. Four rounds are worth reading for what their entries do not say: rounds 7 and 8 settled identity and history without changing a table, round 9 settled the organization and produced two lessons larger than its decisions, round 10 redesigned the model instead of answering anything, and round 13 closed questions by removing the machinery that raised them. Each of those pages now says so at the top.

docs.title: Appendix — ERD: authorization
docs.text:
The authorization model as one diagram, the tables behind it, and the expression tree an audience is stored as.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: erd.md holds §1–§4, the diagrams of the people — identity and attributes, the unit's groups and offices, membership, guardianship; erd-a-authorization.md holds §5–§5b, the whole authorization answer, its tables and the audience expression tree; erd-b-inventory.md holds §6–§8, the temporal pattern, the table inventory and the foreign key summary.

   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

       item of every type; a personal deny beats an audience allow, because this step has
       already returned (D-013). Revoking is ending that row's period, never a rank of its own.
    1  a live ALLOW at the unit ── reaches every item of every type: there is no tier
       between the unit and an item (D-097), and no owner of an item to ask (D-102).
    2  a live ALLOW on this exact item ── exact scope type and id. Nothing precedes it:
       one resolver, and no special case for events inside it (D-102).
    3  OWNERSHIP ── the checked person is the actor. Their own row, their own data.
    4  GUARDIANSHIP ── entered by SHAPE (the subject is not the actor), never by a code's
       name; answers with an ALLOW only, when `right_level` covers `permission.right_kind`
       — none covers nothing, view covers `read`, write covers both (D-074, D-079, D-099).

   against a row, and a key is not a person — so neither channel is refused by a rule of its
   own, neither is reachable (D-118). can_key therefore takes no owner and no person of any
   kind: that parameter would be the impersonation hole, because a claimed person is exactly
   that — claimed (D-121).
   The allow steps are ALTERNATIVES producing one boolean: their order decides which channel
   the audit names, never what the answer is. There is **no locality rule**: locality could
   only ever order allows against each other, and a boolean has nothing to order (D-099).
   Step 0 is not an ordering either — it is a check that runs before every other.

Key points:

  • One table grants. access_grant is the only place authority is written, plus the one table over a single person, guardianship_permission (§4, step 4 above). role_holder, person_group_member and every operand of an audience decide only whom a grant reaches — being in a set is worth exactly what the grant aimed at that set says (D-005, restated for roles by D-100). role_holder carries no scope columns, no level and no resolver channel; what it shares with access_grant is only the temporal shape every dated row has.
  • There is no wildcard permission. A check for X.y needs an exact grant of X.y, or system.admin (D-068). "Can do everything about events" is a role some grants name, each grant naming one of the thirteen event.* codes. Why admin is never ambiguous here: a grant carries no level, so the word appears in exactly one place — the code system.admin — D-099.
  • Deny is absolute. A live deny beats every live allow, with no tie-break, and the only thing that removes one is a person ending its period (D-013, D-099). That is why valid_to earns its keep on a deny row, and why a live deny matching no live allow is a reported shape rather than a harmless row — a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction outlives its reason. Why the ranking went: D-013 let a newer act outrank a denial, so a stale deny was one late revocation away from winning anyway. Deleting the ordering deleted the hatch.
  • The membership gate is opt-in, written in the expression. MEMBERS is an operand evaluated live on the checked date, so MEMBERS * ROLE(x) gates an office and ROLE(x) alone does not, and the "except this one person" case is written inside the same expression (D-100). The failure mode is a grant written ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS, authorizing a lapsed member silently and forever, failing closed-looking so nobody notices — the control is the Unusual section of the tab on the permissions page, which lists exactly that shape and refuses nothing, plus the writer's own habit that a grant template carries MEMBERS — no grant arrives already carrying it, and the only grants this system writes by itself, the twelve beside an event, must not (D-109, F-13). Ownership and guardianship are not gated and never were.
  • The guardianship channel is entered by shape, not by permission name (D-079): the check is about someone other than the actor, and the channel answers with allows only. A sufficient right_level returns true; no row, none, or too low a level returns nothing at all and the actor's own grants are tried. A prohibition is therefore a deny grant, never a low level. What the channel compares a permission against is now permission.right_kind — a column D-099 added and names as having exactly one customer, this channel.
  • There is no downward crossing, because there is no down. With one unit there is no outside it for authority to leak toward, so D-031 was not weakened, it was deprived of its subject (D-097). A grant at the unit therefore reaches every item of every type, and system.admin with it. What is lost and reproduced nowhere is the safeguarding property: access to a body's children had to be granted by that body — by the people who recruited its leader and can be asked. What remains is a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years, and a report of who holds the write, minus the part where the adult was somebody the body chose.
  • A grantee may be an audience, or a key. access_grant.person_id, audience_id and api_key_id carry exactly one value between them — never two, never none (D-116). An audience is an expression over named sets (D-101): every operand is evaluated live and nothing is stored as a roster, a hand-written set is written PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) like any other set (D-105), and two sets are composed with an operand rather than an edge between them. Author in sets, evaluate per person: a check compiles the expression to a predicate and never materializes a set, and an operand that does not resolve is the empty set (D-106). That is one of the two rules the stated scale names as surviving any growth — the other is that a listing is paginated — and it is why the system gets slow before it gets wrong (D-112). Why "fail closed" is the wrong shorthand here: a failed operand on + or * narrows the set and a failed operand on - widens it, so EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with a dead x is fail-closed and lockout-everybody in one step. The failure stays fail-closed and stops being silent: an audience carrying a leaf that resolves to nothing is listed on the tab on the permissions page (D-109), and no save is refused for it. One thing can still produce such a leaf: a redacted person. Nothing else a rule names is deleted any more, and the empty set a disabled operand yields is somebody's deliberate act, not a failure. A person with no birth date is not such a failure either: that operand resolves perfectly well, and they are simply not in the set.
  • A key is the third grantee, and it holds no expression. The seeded selector_type registry keeps its thirteen rows and none of them names a key, so there is nothing to compile for one and no set it could join — EVERYONE is every person, so a key is not even in the widest operand (D-117). What that keeps is this diagram's largest machinery unchanged: a grant naming a key is read as written, ruleset_version keeps the two tables that bump it, and api_key_id is a real foreign key, so the reference-less polymorphic keys stay the two they were. What it costs is that "grant this to the integrations" is not one sentence: twelve integrations need twelve grants, and the thirteenth is a write somebody performs.
  • Nothing owns an event (D-102). The people connected to an event are named by operands that bind to it — ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ATTENDED, ON_WAITLIST — each a set the item itself defines. An operand is a set, not a grant, which is why D-062's "an event_organizer row grants nothing" is the whole story: the row appoints, the operand resolves. The consequence worth remembering: a bound operand is illegal at the unit, so "every event's answers go to its organizers" is twelve item-scope allows written beside the event row by the act that creates the event, one set per event, in one transaction — and an event whose creation died partway through has nobody who can read its answers, which is what the events with an incomplete organizer bundle report is for — it counts every event, not only staffed ones, and names which of the twelve are absent. That failure has an author: one create, named in the trail, rather than a configuration step nobody took (D-151).
  • scope_id is polymorphic (no FK) so a new grantable item type is a config row, not a migration. Accepted cost, with four mandatory mitigations — the same trade-off and the same four mitigations hold for the second reference-less key, audience_operand.selector_arg_id (D-011, D-101).

See ../data-model/05-authorization.md and ../domain/06-authorization-model.md.

docs.text:
erDiagram

    API_KEY {
        integer id PK

        date valid_from
        date valid_to
