        uuid owner_person_id FK
        uuid created_by FK
        timestamp revoked_at
        uuid revoked_by FK
        string revoke_reason
    }
    PERSON_GROUP {
        uuid id PK
        string name
    }
    PERSON {
        uuid id PK
        string public_id
    }
    EVENT {
        uuid id PK
        string title
    }
    PERSON ||--o{ ROLE_HOLDER : "holds an office"
    PERSON ||--o{ ROLE_HOLDER : "appointed the holder"
    ROLE ||--o{ ROLE_HOLDER : "is held"
    PERSON ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is granted to"
    PERSON ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "delegated by"
    AUDIENCE ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is granted to"
    API_KEY ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is granted to"
    PERMISSION ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "is its one code"
    GRANT_SCOPE_TYPE ||--o{ ACCESS_GRANT : "types the scope"

Key point: access_grant is a pentagon of references and grants exactly one thing — a grantee (person or audience or key), a scope, one permission, an effect, a period (D-099). Uniqueness follows the shape: at most one live allow per grantee, scope and permission — and because a unique index does not constrain a row whose grantee column is NULL, that one rule is three unique indexes, one counted over the rows naming a person, one over the rows naming an audience, one over the rows naming a key (D-116). Denies sit deliberately outside all three so a deny can sit beside an allow on the same item — that pair is the only way to say "this person has the unit's events, except this one". A person, a set and a key are three grantees, so the same code on the same item may live once for each of them, and no row there is another one's duplicate.

No line leaves scope_id, and that is the diagram telling the truth. The edge that exists runs to grant_scope_type, the seeded registry (unit — the only row with is_item_scoped = false, event, person_group, role, document deferred) which is what states which table the unresolved id belongs to. The id itself is ⇒ polymorphic: no foreign key, validated by the registry plus a nightly orphan scan per type (D-011, §8). A unit grant carries no scope_id at all, which is the entire schema-level content of "the unit is a scope, not a row".

A role is not a permission bundle. An office carries no codes of its own: what a treasurer has is the live grant rows whose audience names that office as ROLE(x), so "what may a treasurer do?" is a query over rows a screen can show (D-100). role_holder is a dated holder row — person, role, period, who granted it, note — and names one person, never a rule: an office that cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023" is not an office record (F-12). role itself has no period: it is a definition, valid always, and the period lives on the holder row (D-053). The second arrow into person is granted_by, and it is drawn to a person because the column records who appointed — a fact carried on the appointment, readable five years later by whoever has to ask. The act of appointing is what audit_log holds, with its actor taken from the request context rather than from the row (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2); the two are not one column's job, and every other actor column here (access_grant.granted_by, person_group_member.added_by) points the same way for the same reason. The first actor column in this appendix that does not point at a person is on a trail, not in this diagram: access_log.api_key_id and audit_log.api_key_id name the registered caller a request authenticated as, mutually exclusive with each trail's actor_person_id — a request is made by a person or by a key, never by both at once, so there is no actor column to disagree about and on_behalf is never set on a row whose actor is a key (D-121). A trail row naming neither is not a missing arrow: the empty column is this system acting on its own and a complete answer to who did this, and where the trail has a label column the writer's name comes from a fixed list rather than from free text (../data-model/00-conventions.md §7a, D-125).

Names are one namespace. role.code, person_group.name and a set audience.code are unique together, case- and separator-folded, and every selector_type.code is reserved — so a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than discovered later as an expression whose meaning moved. No constraint spans three tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts the write path still does (D-101, D-103, D-081). What is stored is always kind + id, so a rename never rewrites a grant.

docs.title: 5b. The audience expression
docs.text:
The rows of one audience's expression tree. The audience is the tree; audience_operand holds its nodes and leaves, one row each.

erDiagram
    AUDIENCE {
        integer id PK
        string code
        string name
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND {
        integer id PK
        integer audience_id FK
        integer parent_id FK
        string operator
        integer left_id FK
        integer right_id FK
        string selector_kind FK
        integer selector_arg_id
    }
    SELECTOR_TYPE {
        string code PK
        string name
        boolean takes_argument
        boolean binds_to_item
        string argument_type
    }
    ROLE {
        integer id PK
        string code
    }
    PERSON_GROUP {
        uuid id PK
        string name
    }
    PERSON {
        uuid id PK
    }
    EVENT {
        uuid id PK
        string title
    }
    AUDIENCE ||--o{ AUDIENCE_OPERAND : "has its tree"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND ||--o{ AUDIENCE_OPERAND : "has a child"
    SELECTOR_TYPE ||--o{ AUDIENCE_OPERAND : "types the leaf"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| ROLE : "ROLE(x) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| PERSON_GROUP : "GROUP(x) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| AUDIENCE : "AUDIENCE(code) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| PERSON : "PERSON(x) - no FK"
    AUDIENCE_OPERAND }o--o| EVENT : "ORGANIZERS(x) - no FK"

Five of these lines are ⇒ in the notation above, and not one of them is a foreign key. A leaf's selector_arg_id is one integer column pointing at role, person_group, audience, person or event depending on selector_kind — the same polymorphism, the same four mandatory mitigations and the same nightly orphan scan as access_grant.scope_id, the same trade-off accepted for both keys (D-011, D-101). Drawing it as five real edges would be the lie; drawing it as no edges at all would hide the fan. The registry is what resolves the ambiguity, and it is a real edge: selector_type says whether the code takes an argument, whether the argument-less form binds to the item being checked, and what type the argument is — the parser reads its reserved words from that table, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the save path checks arity against it (D-101). It is seeded and organization-read-only — the whole table is written only by migrations and no screen edits it: "the language becomes data" has never meant the language is extensible at runtime, and a seeded code with no shipped evaluator arm is a deployment bug that surfaces as an empty set — which is why the registry holds no row waiting to be implemented.

argument_type has six values and five of them are tables. OLDER and YOUNGER (D-107) take an integer — a whole number of years — so selector_arg_id holds 18 for OLDER(18), and this is the first operand argument in the registry that names no row. The five drawn edges are still exactly five, and the count this appendix keeps is unchanged for the right reason rather than by luck: a scalar sitting in selector_arg_id is not a reference, so there is nothing to repoint when a person is merged, nothing for a cascade to find, nothing for the orphan scan to walk, and the binding check that compares argument_type against a grant's item type simply does not apply to an operand that binds to no item. There are still exactly two reference-less polymorphic keys in what this part draws — access_grant.scope_id and audience_operand.selector_arg_id — and 18 is not one of them, because the check is about references. The shared inventory in §8 keeps the design's whole count, which is seven: the other five sit on the two trails and on a merge conflict, none of which is drawn here. The two operands read person.birth_date as of the date being checked, which is why they are a registry row and nothing more: they are ordinary named operands, composed by + - * like every other, and the set they name changes with no write at all.

No leaf resolves to anything but people, and that is why there is no GRANTS(…). An operand resolves to a set of people, because a set of people is what a grantee that is a set is — the two grantees that are not sets, one named person and one registered key, name a single bearer and are reached without this tree at all (D-117); a set of grants is a filter over the grant list, and "these twenty rows, now also for that office" is something an editor does while finding the rows to act on, not something a stored grantee could ever be evaluated against. The bulk operation stays an affordance over the list, and the registry refuses the kind rather than leaving it unimplemented (D-101).

One row is one node or one leaf, never both. A node carries operator (+ union, * intersection, - difference) with left_id and right_id, which are not interchangeable because - is not commutative; a leaf carries selector_kind and, where the registry says so, selector_arg_id. parent_id lives on the child, so a node belongs to exactly one expression and a sharing table is refused — editing a shared node would silently widen every grant using it. audience_id is denormalized onto every row so the read path fetches one audience's rows in one indexed read and assembles the tree in memory; it never walks a parent chain (D-101). OLDER and YOUNGER are two seeded rows of that registry and nothing more: the operator enum is + - *, an attribute adds no node kind and no column, so (MEMBERS * OLDER(18)) - YOUNGER(6) is stored with the shapes that already existed — a * node with a MEMBERS leaf and an OLDER leaf, under a - node whose right operand is a YOUNGER leaf (D-107).

AUDIENCE(code) is the leaf that points back into this diagram (D-103): it names another saved audience by its code, which is why code exists and is optional, and why an unnamed audience is simply not composable. The AUDIENCE leaves are the reference edges, so "does this cycle", "how deep", "which grants name this audience" and "may I end it" are all one indexed query over selector_kind = 'AUDIENCE' rows. Why a saved expression can still cycle when every one of them is a tree: one tree cannot, but a forest of trees pointing at each other can. The save-time reachability walk therefore goes inside this tree and across every AUDIENCE(x) leaf, and it is the only structural guard there is — no cap on expression depth survives (D-105). The walk looks for cycles and nothing else: the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it, with no depth bound and no rebalancing, and nothing bounds what an expression may cost — affordable at the stated size of a few hundred people and a few dozen registrants per event, with a named trigger to reopen the question (D-112). Depth and width stay a convention, not a guard (D-081): there is no report of the widest and deepest audiences, and what the permissions page shows is the tab listing rules that name something deprecated, hidden or disabled or fail to resolve — silent about how wide any of them is (D-109). The protection that keeps the dangerous case out is that an audience named by a live grant may not be ended or deleted while that grant lives: under -, an emptied operand makes the answer wider.

A hand-written set is an expression like any other (D-105), written as PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) in the same tree as every GROUP(x) and MEMBERS leaf. What that gives up is written as lost, not as managed: no per-person dates — a person is in the audience or not, and a June-to-August exception is a second grant with its own period, which is what D-099's shape is for — and no record of who added a person beyond who last saved the tree. Why a name in an expression was never merged into GROUP(x): a group's members are the organization's record and are true with no grant pointing at them, while a name written into an expression is meaningless outside the expression it completes (D-098). Naming people inside a grant must not make them group members, and (GROUP(kitchen) + PERSON(honza)) - PERSON(a) says the whole thing: the same set as any list spelling, one fewer kind of thing in the model, and no chance of the permission table becoming the system's roster.

PERSON(x) is drawn as the person argument edge, and the edge has exactly one occupant. PERSON is one of the thirteen seeded selector_type rows — the seeded registry, not an evaluator's arm list, is the record of what the language accepts (D-107, D-104, D-113). A guardian is not a second occupant. Guardianship is a level over a child — none, view or write read off the guardianship row (D-074) — and not a set the expression language resolves, so an operand aimed at guardians would offer, one code at a time, a subset of what those people already hold (D-113). What the registry row adds over the storage fact — selector_arg_id may hold a person id (D-011) — is one fact of meaning: an expression may name a single human who is on nobody's roster. Since a hand-written set is a sum of these (D-105), the edge is load-bearing: every hand-named person in the system is a selector_arg_id with deliberately no foreign key. PERSON is the one argument kind the repoint duty still reaches (D-109): retiring an office, a group or an audience is one write to that row and no expression is edited, because nothing a rule names is deleted — it goes deprecated, hidden or disabled, and only disabled changes the answer. A person is not in that protected set, because D-088 lets a redaction require the row to actually go and erasure wins. So a merge repoints the PERSON leaves naming the absorbed person, a redaction leaves the rest resolving to the empty set, and a redacted person is the only remaining way to produce a broken leaf — shown on the permissions tab rather than in a report nobody opens, with the nightly orphan scan as backstop rather than mechanism. PERSON, ROLE, GROUP and AUDIENCE are the four codes whose argument names a person, an office, a group or another audience. The fifth drawn edge, to event, belongs to the item-bound codes — ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ATTENDED, ON_WAITLIST — whose argument is optional exactly because the item being checked usually supplies it (D-102).

See ../data-model/05a-audience-and-grammar.md §8 and ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.

docs.title: Appendix — ERD: the temporal pattern, the table inventory, the foreign keys
docs.text:
How a dated row is written so that an answer survives the thing it describes, then one entry per entity in the whole system, and every reference between them.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: erd.md holds §1–§4, the diagrams of the people — identity and attributes, the unit's groups and offices, membership, guardianship; erd-a-authorization.md holds §5–§5b, the whole authorization answer, its tables and the audience expression tree; erd-b-inventory.md holds §6–§8, the temporal pattern, the table inventory and the foreign key summary.

docs.title: 6. Temporal pattern, illustrated
docs.text:
Every [T] table above uses the same shape. The returning-member case shows why:

flowchart TB
    P["person 100 — Jan Novák"]
    M1["membership #1 · member<br/>1990-09-01 → 2010-06-30 · terminated"]
    GAP["14-year gap<br/>no rows; visible as data, not inferred"]
    M2["membership #2 · member<br/>2024-10-01 → open"]
    G1["person_group_member · oddílová rada<br/>1996-09-01 → 2004-06-30"]
    G2["person_group_member · registre 2025<br/>2024-10-01 → 2025-12-31"]
    RH["role_holder · treasurers<br/>2025-01-01 → open"]
    AU["audience · MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)<br/>an expression, evaluated live"]
    AG["access_grant · payment.record<br/>allow, at the unit<br/>2025-01-01 → open"]
    GA["guardianship → child A<br/>2015-03-01 → open<br/>right_level: write"]
    GB["guardianship → child B<br/>2018-07-01 → open<br/>right_level: view"]
    P --> M1
    M1 --> GAP --> M2
    P --> G1
    P --> G2
    P --> RH
    P --> GA
    P --> GB
    RH -.->|"named by code inside"| AU
    AU -.->|"aimed at by"| AG
    RH ==>|"the office reaches them only<br/>through that grant"| AG

Note the two membership rows have the same type. They differ only in period and end reason: this person was a member twice, and a membership carries no age — the type is a fee and renewal parameter, not a kind of person (D-038).

Where the first row came from is not drawn. A 1990s roster row states a period of membership, and since D-093 one reviewed batch may turn that stated period into membership #1 itself: both ends dated, data_confidence low, the batch id on it, no fee_obligation and a balance that stays absent rather than zero, because the corpus carries no money in it (D-090). Two shapes remain forbidden, and they are the two the ban was ever really about: an open-ended imported membership, and one inferred from an attendance row. A closed period gates nothing in the present; an open one hands authority to whoever signs up under that name tomorrow. A people batch writes the membership and nothing else — a membership has no twin row beside it (D-097) — and the group rows are written by somebody who knows the group exists (../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §7).

Questions this shape supports, none of which a flag on the person row could answer:

  • Was this person a member on 1998-06-01?
  • How many years of membership, excluding the gap?
  • Which groups were they in during 2003? — person_group_member answers it, because those rows are dated rather than derived from a rule that could change its mind.
  • Who held the office of treasurers in 2023? — the same shape of answer, one role_holder row, which is why F-12 is answered no: an office is held by a named person.
  • Would that grant have reached them on that date? — holder row, expression and grant are all evaluated as of the same at, and none of the three may be stored as a materialized list (D-101).
  • How old were they when they joined the second time? — answered from person.birth_date, which the membership rows never copy.
  • Who are the returning members — more than one membership with a gap between?

Every one of them is answered as of a date, and an as-of date must be applied to every join in the answer, not only to the first one — a period joined without it leaks the present into the past. That is what the [T] marking on the tables above exists to make visible.

docs.title: 7. Table inventory
docs.text:
One entry per entity: what it is, what it references, how many may exist, and whether it is temporal. ⇒ marks a polymorphic reference with no foreign key. Entries that exist only to join two other entities say so. A table that no longer exists is not here: this is the inventory of what the schema is now, and every gone name has its row in removed-concepts.md.

Read the [T] column as a decision, not a default. A no is normally a lookup table, a definition, or an append-only trail — the kinds of thing that have no period to carry. Exactly one no in this inventory is a choice about a person's data rather than a lack of one: person_attribute, and the reason is written out under its own block below and in §1a.

Identity

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] person The human being. Holds identity only — no status, no role, no membership Nothing, except itself: merged_into_person_id ⇒ self One per human, effectively; a merged row survives as a tombstone and is never deleted. The pointer is never rewritten forward when the survivor is itself absorbed, so chains persist and resolve_person() walks them (D-087) no person_name One name a person has had, and when person Many per person; one current row per name_type yes account The ability to log in. Optional, and independent of membership person Zero or many per person over a lifetime; at most one live row no account_credential One authentication method's secret or external handle account — deliberately not person Many per account; one current row per external issuer and reference pair yes person_contact An email, phone or postal address, as a dated row rather than a column person Many per person; one current primary per type and purpose yes person_identifier An identifier issued outside the system person; identifier_scheme for its scheme Many per person; (scheme, value) unique among current rows yes identifier_scheme The vocabulary of identifier schemes Nothing Lookup table, one row per scheme no identity_hypothesis A proposal that two person rows are the same human person twice; the reviewer is a person At most one live hypothesis per pair; a rejected pair may be re-proposed no person_merge The record that one row was absorbed into another, and how to undo it person twice; identity_hypothesis, optional One per merge performed; a reversal is recorded on the same row no field_conflict One value a merge could not decide between two candidates — raised for either half of the record, an identity field or a descriptive value (§1a) person_merge; ⇒ (entity_table, entity_id) — polymorphic by nature Many per merge no

Personal attributes — everything known about a person other than name, gender and age (§1a)

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] attribute_definition One thing the organization collects about people: the code, its label, its type, and whether several values may be current at once Nothing One code per normalized spelling — Allergy and allergy are one row; statuses live and retired only — a definition is live at its save (D-141) — and retiring keeps the row and its values no attribute_option One allowed value of a one_of definition attribute_definition One row per code per definition; a retired option is never re-meaning, because values stored against it are historical facts no person_attribute The value one person currently has for one code person, attribute_definition, and attribute_option when the type is one_of One current row per person and code; more only where the definition sets allow_multiple, which no constraint can check (it reads another table) no — deliberately

That last no is the decision, and it is the reason this row spells it out. Values are overwritten in place and audit_log — carrying the values themselves, for 24 months — is the only history. This is the one place in the schema where "what did we believe in 2019?" is answered from the trail rather than from business data, and the answer reaches two years back and no further (D-088): the honest description of this trade is no long history, not merely no temporal columns, and the trail carrying it is discipline rather than guarantee (D-081). Why this is written out on one row of an inventory: if a case ever needs the long version, the fix is temporal values on this table, not a longer trail — a decision worth one entry, and the argument for it is in D-085 and ../data-model/09-attributes.md §3. The two vocabulary tables carry status instead of periods, which is what lets a code be retired without touching a fact; only redacting a person erases values, and a redacted person still holding attribute rows, or still having their values readable in the trail, means the redaction did not happen (../data-model/09-attributes.md §8).

Groups and offices — what the organization module holds now (§2), plus the two office tables it shares with authorization, drawn in §5a and specified in ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3 and §4

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] person_group A named set of people with a lifetime — a crew, a registration team, everyone who ever ran the camp. Confers nothing: authority arrives only through a grant aimed at the group Nothing. Its name is unique together with role.code and a set audience's code, which no constraint can express, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts the write path still does One row per name. Ended by valid_to, never deleted while member rows exist, and ending it is refused while a live grant — or a live audience reachable from one — names it, because EVERYONE - GROUP(x) with an emptied group denies everybody yes person_group_member Join entity: this person was in this group for that period. Written by a person, never derived from a rule person_group; person — person, not membership, so a 1998 roster row does not have to invent a membership in order to be true; and person as the one who added them Many per group at once; no overlapping periods for one person in one group, over all rows including ended ones, which a hand-written exclusion constraint enforces and the write path only explains (../data-model/02-organization.md §2) yes role An office — treasurers, registrar, counselors are the names this corpus uses when it needs one, and none of them is a row the platform writes. A definition, valid always; the period lives on the holder row. It carries no permissions and confers nothing: the codes an office holds are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x) Nothing. Its code joins the same one namespace as group names, and every reserved selector_type.code is refused against it One row per code; deleting one is refused while holder rows exist, so an office cannot be emptied in one save no role_holder Who holds an office for what period — one named person, never a rule: an office record that cannot answer "who held this in 2023" is not one (F-12) role; person twice — the holder, and the person who appointed them At most one open row per person and role; no overlap over all rows; nothing forces a row to end, and the standing report is the control (D-071) yes

Membership

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] membership_type The fee and renewal parameters. One row, member, kept as a table so the vocabulary can grow Nothing Exactly one row today (D-037) yes membership One period of membership, with its own ending person, membership_type; itself via renewed_from_membership_id Many per person over a lifetime; one open at a time, ever yes membership_request An application. Two person references on purpose: the subject and the submitter person twice, membership_type, and membership twice (what it produced, what it renews). It names no group and no unit beyond the unit itself: which set a new member lands in is a later write on that set, not a term of the application (D-098) At most one open request per person no

Relationships

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] guardianship One adult's responsibility for one dependent, carrying one right_level person twice — never the same person twice One current row per pair; unlimited past rows; a dependent may have any number of guardians at once yes guardianship_permission The temporal history of that row's right level — one value with three choices, changed over time (D-074) guardianship Exactly one open row per guardianship; its value is what guardianship.right_level copies yes

Authorization — the tables are drawn in §5a and the expression in §5b

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] permission One coded capability — the only thing a check asks for, and a grant names exactly one Nothing One row per code; the code never changes. applies_to says whether the code may be granted at the unit or also on an item, checked when the grant is saved; right_kind exists for exactly one customer, the guardianship channel (D-099) no grant_scope_type The registry of things a grant may be written on, and the table its id lives in. unit is its only non-item row — which is where the unit now lives Nothing One row per scope kind: unit, event, person_group, role, and document deferred. Adding a grantable thing is a row here rather than a migration. api_key is deliberately absent: a key is a grantee and never a thing a permission is granted on, so "rotate the accounting key and no other" is not a writable grant at this scale, and the debt is recorded rather than hidden (D-122) no access_grant The only table that grants. A grantee, a scope, one permission, an effect, a period Exactly one grantee of three kinds: person, audience or api_key — never two, never none (D-116); grant_scope_type and ⇒ scope_id, absent exactly at unit; permission; person as grantor, delegator and revoker — always a person, including on a grant whose grantee is a key At most one live allow per grantee, scope and permission, counted once per grantee kind so the one rule is three partial unique indexes — denies sit outside all three on purpose, because allow-beside-deny is the only way to say "the unit's events, except this one"; a delegation must carry an end date, and a grant naming a key is never a delegation and so carries no mandatory expiry (D-116, D-120) yes audience A set of people a grant may name — an expression over named sets, stored as a tree (D-101) Its own operand rows; code is optional and is the only thing another audience may name (D-103); an operand is one named row of the registry, never a stored roster (D-105) One row per audience; the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it and its height is bounded by nothing — the save-time cycle walks are the only structural guard, and nothing bounds what resolving one costs, which D-112 accepts at the stated size rather than leaves unaddressed (D-081); an audience a live grant names is never deleted — it is flagged deprecated, hidden or disabled, the first two changing no answer and the third resolving to the empty set on purpose, as an audited write that prints the rules it touches (D-109) — a flag is a state, not part of a compilation, so resolution reads it live, once per request, and disabled means now rather than next time the rules are compiled (D-114); an ended audience reaches nobody, so ending one is refused while a live grant names it yes audience_operand Join entity: one row of one audience's expression tree — a node (operator, left_id, right_id) or a leaf (selector_kind, ⇒ selector_arg_id), never both audience, denormalized onto every row so one audience's tree is one indexed fetch; itself, parent_id on the child; selector_type; and ⇒ a role, person_group, audience, person or event with no foreign key — D-011's accepted trade-off, extended by D-101 One row per node or leaf; a node never belongs to another audience than its parent's; the forest is acyclic, checked on save no selector_type The registry of operands the language has: the reserved word, whether it takes an argument, whether its argument-less form binds to the item being checked, and what type the argument names Nothing Thirteen seeded rows — the thirteen operands of the language, including PERSON, which is what lets an expression name a single human (D-105), and including OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n), the two whose argument_type is a whole number of years rather than a table and whose set moves with no write at all, because they read person.birth_date on the date being checked (D-107). Six argument_type values, five of them tables; the operators are + - *. The whole table is written only by migrations and organization-read-only, and every row both seeded and shipped — a code with no evaluator arm is a deployment bug, not a held feature (D-104) no api_key A caller that is nobody: one registered integration, installed by a named person, holding one live secret that is shown once and kept only as a hash. Not an account (a way for a person to log in), not an office (held by a person, confers nothing), not a selector (no expression can name one) — and so a grantee in exactly the sense a person is (D-116) person as owner_person_id — a contact, not a channel, never read to decide an answer; person as created_by, required, because attribution for an act is not a dependency of the authority; person as revoker. Grants name it from access_grant.api_key_id, a real foreign key and not a third reference-less key (§8) One row per integration; code and secret_hash each unique among live rows — the second a lookup before it is a constraint; valid_to optional, absent meaning current, and nothing forces a key to end: the report is the control (D-120). Rotating replaces the hash in place, so there is no window in which both secrets work and no history of past ones (D-119). Nothing at all is derived from created_by, and no key is ever inside an expression — the registry keeps its thirteen rows and none of them names a key (D-117) yes access_log The audit trail — who did what, by what authority, with what result person as actor and as subject, or api_key as actor instead of a person — the two are never both set; ⇒ authorization_ref_id naming access_grant or guardianship_permission — the enum holds exactly those two channels, so an older row reading role or system names a channel this model cannot read, which is deliberate (D-100); ⇒ entity_id Append-only to the application; rows are deleted at 24 months by a scheduled job, which is the third exception to "nothing is hard-deleted" and the opposite shape to audit_log, whose rows live forever with emptied payloads (D-145, against D-088) no

role and role_holder are inventoried under Groups and offices above, where the module keeps them; both are drawn in the authorization diagram, because that is where a reader meets what they do — which is nothing at all, on their own.

Audit and import

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] audit_log The row-level trail of changes to business tables, before and after values included until the payload window passes ⇒ (table_name, record_id) — polymorphic; person as actor, and on whose behalf, or api_key as actor instead of a person — the two actor columns are mutually exclusive and on_behalf_of is never set on a row whose actor is a key (D-121); a row naming neither is this system acting on its own, a complete answer to who did this, and the trail's own actor_label then says which writer it was, from a fixed list rather than from free text (../data-model/00-conventions.md §7a, D-125) One row per change; the row is never deleted, but a scheduled payload reduction empties the values 24 months after writing (D-088) no redaction_log That a redaction happened to a person, by whom, and to what person; the person who requested and the person who performed it One per redaction performed no import_batch One arrival of historical data, where it stands, which half of the corpus it carries (people or events), and the raw-column→code map a person read before it applied person as creator, applier and reverting party One per batch; the map lives here as one object rather than per staged row, because it is one artefact a human reads top to bottom and the codes it names arrive live (D-090, D-092); staging rows may be truncated once applied no staging_import A raw source row, verbatim, with its file and line import_batch One per source row per batch no staging_import_row That row parsed, plus what the parse could not decide, and what it eventually created staging_import; person as resolver; and what it created — person and, on a people batch, the membership whose both ends the source stated (D-093: a stated period may be imported, an open-ended one may not and one inferred from attendance may not), and on an events batch the event and the event_registration One per staged row no

Finance (provisional)

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] fee_schedule What may be charged, for what kind of period membership_type, optional — absent means it applies to any type. A schedule is organization-wide by construction: there is no unit row to attach one to (D-097) As the organization defines yes fee_obligation What one person owes for exactly one thing person (who it is for), fee_schedule, and exactly one of membership, membership_request, event_registration Many per person; the target is never two and never none. An imported membership creates none, and its outstanding_balance is NULL rather than zero, because zero would be a claim the export does not support (D-093) no payment Money that arrived person as payer — deliberately not the person the fee is for One per recorded receipt no payment_allocation Join entity: this payment counted towards this obligation, by how much payment, fee_obligation A given payment is allocated to a given obligation at most once no payment_request The ask, carrying the variable symbol that ties a bank transfer back to it fee_obligation — the amount is copied, never recomputed Several per obligation over time; at most one live; the symbol is unique over every symbol ever issued no bank_transaction One incoming transfer as the bank reported it payment_request when matched — absent means it is in the queue; import_batch Unique per bank reference within an account; immutable once imported no

Events

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] event A dated occasion people register for. Owned by nobody fee_schedule, optional, when it costs money. It belongs to no unit and nobody: the people connected to an event are named by operands that bind to it (ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ATTENDED, ON_WAITLIST), so there is no owner for a check to ask (D-102). created_by is attribution, not ownership, as D-005 says. The act that creates an event also writes its authority: twelve item-scope allows beside the event row, in the same transaction, one per event.* code whose applies_to admits an event — all thirteen except event.create, which is applies_to = unit — each aimed at an audience whose expression is the bare operand ORGANIZERS (D-151) One row per occasion, and twelve grants beside it; no recurrence, no series no event_organizer Who is running an event, with a label and an order — an appointment, not a grant (D-062) event, person Many per event; the list is the domain answer to "who runs this", and it is the one cascade delete in this design (§8) no event_registration One person's answer about one event, plus whether they turned up event, person — person, never membership, so a 1998 camp roster does not smuggle its people into MEMBERS today One per person per event; unanswered is the absence of a row (D-059); was_present is three-valued and is deliberately the basis of no selector no event_question One thing this event asks, of attendees, organizers or both event; and optionally attribute_definition by code, which is what lets a question prefill from a stored fact and write a fresh value back — the binding never names a value row (D-139) As many as the event asks; defined per event, never shared yes event_answer What one person said to one question, stored as a row and not as JSON event_question; person — who answered, for a child the child, not the registration row and not whoever submitted on their behalf One row per question per answerer; no expiry — it outlives its event, and erasure empties the value and keeps the row (D-140) no

Reference vocabularies — grant_scope_type, selector_type, identifier_scheme, permission. Four, and one fewer than this page used to list: reason_code is deleted by D-128, because a reason is what a person writes, not a row to maintain. Each is named by a value held elsewhere rather than pointing at anything, and each exists so that a vocabulary is data the organization can see rather than a list inside the application. attribute_definition is the same kind of thing in spirit and a different shape in fact — it has a curation lifecycle, a child table, and rows pointing back at it — so it is inventoried above rather than here.

event carries no [T] — it has no valid_from / valid_to, because an event is a dated occasion rather than a period-tracked record. Its lifecycle is starts_at / ends_at / cancelled_at, and it has no status column at all (D-064). event_registration likewise stores no period: a person is attending, or they are not, and "unanswered" is the absence of a row (D-059).

[T] = temporal, carries valid_from / valid_to. A no says it does not; where the reason for not is a decision about someone's data rather than the nature of the table, the row says so — which in this inventory is person_attribute, and nowhere else.

docs.title: 8. Foreign key summary
docs.text:
Columns with no FK, and why:

Column Why no FK access_grant.scope_id Polymorphic by design. Validated by grant_scope_type + orphan checks. It is absent exactly when the scope type is unit, and that absence is the schema-level form of "the unit is a scope, not a row" (D-097). audience_operand.selector_arg_id The second one, and newer: one integer pointing at a role, a person_group, an audience, a person or an event depending on selector_kind, resolved by selector_type.argument_type and caught by the same nightly orphan scan. D-101 carried D-011's trade-off across deliberately, mitigations included — the registry is the only thing that says which table an id belongs to, so an unmapped kind is the empty set, not an error. It also sometimes holds no reference at all: OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) store a whole number of years here (D-107), and that does not make a third key — 18 points at nothing, so the orphan scan has nothing to walk, a merge has nothing to repoint, and this row is still describing one column that sometimes carries a reference and sometimes carries a scalar. access_log.scope_id Same shape as the grant's; absent for a check at the unit. Followed by 05d §11 check 23, with exactly one legal absence available to it: of the kinds this column can name, only an event is ever removed, and only by the import's revert. access_log.authorization_ref_id Points at one of two tables, access_grant or guardianship_permission, and nothing else; a historical row whose channel reads role keeps the word and loses the reference, which is the honest state of a value whose table is gone (D-100). Followed by the same check and excepted by nothing, because neither target is ever deleted: a set id that does not resolve is the only unacceptable answer. A row whose channel is outside the enum names no table at all, so the scan reports it beside the findings rather than as one. access_log.entity_id Polymorphic target of the audited action. Followed by the same check, with its exception written there: an absence is legal only where the table named is one this design removes and the trail shows the removal — a person_attribute row for an erasure, a person, membership or event row for a revert. Whether this column is ever written naming a person_attribute row is stated nowhere, so the erasure arm may have nothing to fire on. field_conflict.entity_id Polymorphic; recorded alongside entity_table. Followed by the same check, and its finding is the dangerous one of the four: a conflict row naming nothing is an import that recorded an undecided field against a row which is not there, and the decision a person later takes inherits that. Revert accounts for the ones whose entity_table is person or membership and left an entry naming the row; the rest are broken. audit_log.record_id Polymorphic; recorded alongside table_name. Not followed, deliberately (D-134): an audit row outliving the row it described is what an erasure and a revert look like afterwards, and 06b §5's check 6 locates the payloads it exists to test through exactly this reference. A count here would report the two paths this design trusts as integrity failures.

There are seven reference-less keys, and the class matters more than the count. access_grant.scope_id and audience_operand.selector_arg_id are ids with no constraint behind them, and each carries the same four things that make that survivable: a registry saying which table an id belongs to, a save-path check against that registry, an orphan scan the scheduler owns, and an explicit rule that a failure resolves to the empty set (../data-model/00-conventions.md §9). The other five are the same class of column and they do not all get the same answer, which is what F-30 asked and D-134 settled: four are followed by 05d §11 check 23, and audit_log.record_id is followed by nothing on purpose, because an id in a trail is written in order to outlive the row it names and the redaction check reads that reference in order to run at all. What the six followed columns share is the registry and the scan; what none of the seven gets is a constraint, because no foreign key can name one of several tables. A scalar is not one of the seven: OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) write a whole number of years into audience_operand.selector_arg_id, and there is no table that number should have named, so there is no registry lookup to miss, no orphan for the scan to find and nothing for a merge to repoint. The count is about references, and 18 is not one (D-107). A candidate arrived with api_key and is not one either: access_grant.api_key_id names exactly one table, always, so it carries an ordinary foreign key and needs none of the four things above — no registry saying which table it means, no save-path check against that registry, no orphan for the scan, no rule about what an unreadable kind resolves to. Becoming the third grantee cost a column with a constraint, not a column without one (D-116).

access_grant has no grantee column — that is the one mutual-exclusion case rather than a missing-FK case: exactly one of person_id / audience_id / api_key_id is set, never two, never none. All three columns are nullable, so nothing but the rule says whom a grant means; a grant naming none is meaningless and one naming two is ambiguous about whom in the audience it speaks for. The three are not three spellings of one thing: a person and a key are read exactly as written, and only an audience is an expression evaluated as of the date being checked (D-116, D-117). audience_operand carries the same shape of rule one table down — operator with left_id/right_id, or selector_kind with selector_arg_id where the registry says the code takes an argument — and for the same reason: a row satisfying neither is a node in no tree, and an expression containing one resolves to nobody.

Every other column ending in _id has a real foreign key with ON DELETE RESTRICT — the newest of them api_key's owner_person_id, created_by and revoked_by, and the api_key_id carried by access_grant, access_log and audit_log — with one exception: event_organizer.event_id is the single ON DELETE CASCADE in the design — an appointment is nothing once the occasion it appointed somebody to is gone, and the guards in ../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §8 are what make that delete safe to allow at all. Two operands whose argument is an integer add no key and no cascade, because there is no row for either to be a child of — still one cascading column, still event_organizer.event_id. Everything else that merely looks like a child restricts: a registration, an answer, a member row, a holder row, a grant. The general rule, and this one exception, are written down once in ../data-model/00-conventions.md §9 — nothing cascades in front of a 40-year trail.

docs.title: Appendix — Entity Relationship Diagrams
docs.text:
This appendix describes relationships — what points at what, how many, and whether the link is temporal. Field-level definitions live in the data-model documents, each in the one that owns the entity, and are deliberately not repeated here.

The schema these diagrams draw is governed by ../data-model/00-conventions.md. The appendix is split by subject area so each part stays readable; the areas connect through person, which appears in all of them.

Notation: → is a foreign key pointing at the referenced table. ⇒ is a polymorphic reference (no database-level foreign key). Temporal tables are marked [T].

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: erd.md holds §1–§4, the diagrams of the people — identity and attributes, the unit's groups and offices, membership, guardianship; erd-a-authorization.md holds §5–§5b, the whole authorization answer, its tables and the audience expression tree; erd-b-inventory.md holds §6–§8, the temporal pattern, the table inventory and the foreign key summary.

docs.title: 1a. Personal attributes — everything that is not a name, a gender or an age
docs.text:
erDiagram
    ATTRIBUTE_DEFINITION {
        string code PK
        string label
        string description
        string value_type
        string value_unit
        integer sort_order
        boolean allow_multiple
        string status
        datetime retired_at
    }
    ATTRIBUTE_OPTION {
        string definition_code FK
        string code
        string label
        integer sort_order
        string status
    }
    PERSON_ATTRIBUTE {
        uuid person_id FK
        string attribute_definition_code FK
        string value_option_code FK
        string value
        string recorded_note
        string source
        datetime created_at
    }
    PERSON ||--o{ PERSON_ATTRIBUTE : has
    ATTRIBUTE_DEFINITION ||--o{ ATTRIBUTE_OPTION : offers
    ATTRIBUTE_DEFINITION ||--o{ PERSON_ATTRIBUTE : defines
    PERSON_ATTRIBUTE }o--o| ATTRIBUTE_OPTION : selects

Key point: these three tables are the whole of what the system knows about a person beyond name, gender and age. There is no health table beside them and no privileged corner inside them: personal data is one class of data, graded by what a grant exposes rather than by which table it reads (D-083), and what the organization collects is named by a vocabulary the organization maintains itself (D-084). Reading is person.view, writing is person.edit, and only the vocabulary needs a code of its own (attribute.define). Fields and rules: ../data-model/09-attributes.md.

None of the three is [T], and the no beside them in §7 is a decision, not an omission. A person_attribute row is the current belief, overwritten in place, and audit_log holds the sequence of beliefs, values included for as long as the payload window lasts — 24 months, after which the row is reduced and the values are gone (D-088) — which is why the trail is guarded as person data is (the permission catalog §8). This corpus gives periods to things that are true over an interval — a membership, an address, an office held, a guardian's authority — and a descriptive value is not one of those: it is a statement made now about whatever it is about, with a timestamp on the assertion. A valid_from here would ask a volunteer when an allergy began, which is a question the organization is not competent to record and has no rule that could use (D-085). The cost is named rather than left out: the history of a value lives in the one control D-081 calls the corpus's weakest, and §7 lists it as the accepted risk. It is also a deliberate departure from guardianship two sections below, which keeps its current value and its history in business tables — because authority is asked "what was it on that date?" as a routine part of answering whether an act was permitted, and an allergy list is not.

The two vocabulary tables are non-temporal for a smaller reason of their own: a code leaves service by status, not by a period, so a value recorded against a retired option keeps meaning what it meant on the day it was chosen. Retiring therefore never touches a fact — only redacting a person erases one (../domain/08-person-data.md).

docs.title: 2. Organization
docs.text:
There is no organization-structure diagram, because there is no organization structure. There is one unit, it is the organization, and it is a scope and not a row: grant_scope_type carries a code unit with is_item_scoped = false, and a grant written at it has no scope_id (D-097). What this section draws is the one set-shaped thing the module holds: the group — a set of people, not a body — beside the roster that belongs to it.

erDiagram
    PERSON_GROUP {
        uuid id PK
        uuid public_id
        string name
        string description
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
    }
    PERSON_GROUP_MEMBER {
        uuid group_id FK
        uuid person_id FK
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
        uuid added_by FK
        string note
    }
    PERSON ||--o{ PERSON_GROUP_MEMBER : "is in"
    PERSON_GROUP ||--o{ PERSON_GROUP_MEMBER : has

Key point: a group is a named set of people with a lifetime, and that is the whole of it — no parent, no type, no code, no path, no nesting rule, no rename history, no split or merger edge, no leadership, no roles, no fee (D-098). The member row is dated, so the roster answers "who was in schuzka2026-1 on 14 March 2026" from its own rows rather than from the audit trail, whose payloads expire after 24 months (D-088). No two rows for one person and one group overlap, counted over all rows and half-open, so a person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is two rows and never one row edited in place.

Membership of a group confers nothing. A set is not a grant; a group member is reached only because some grant's expression says GROUP(x) (D-005). The group is an item in grant_scope_type, so a grant may be written on one — that edge is in §5a, not here, because access_grant owns it and not this module. The box is deliberately alone beside its roster: name is unique across role and person_group together, but no constraint spans two tables, so that is a write-path rule and not a drawn edge (D-101).

There is no unit table in any diagram in this appendix. The unit appears once, as the unit row of grant_scope_type (§5a) — a lookup row naming a scope, not a body, and there is nothing nested under it (D-097). What a reader might expect a unit to do is done by these instead: belonging to the unit is membership (§3), belonging to a set of people is person_group_member (above), an elected leader is a role_holder row, and do not place a child where nobody is responsible is person_group.member.manage held by a named adult, because nothing on a group says who it is for (D-095, D-100, D-098).

See ../data-model/02-organization.md and ../domain/04-organization-structure.md; the scope itself is ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §2.

docs.title: 3. Membership
docs.text:
erDiagram
    MEMBERSHIP_TYPE {
        string code PK
        integer duration_months
        integer expiry_month
        integer expiry_day
        integer renewal_grace_days
    }
    MEMBERSHIP {
        uuid person_id FK
        string membership_type_id FK
        string status
        datetime valid_from
        datetime valid_to
        uuid renewed_from_membership_id FK
        decimal outstanding_balance
    }
    MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST {
        uuid person_id FK
        uuid submitted_by_person_id FK
        string status
        uuid membership_id FK
        uuid previous_membership_id FK
    }
    PERSON ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : has
    MEMBERSHIP_TYPE ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : defines
    MEMBERSHIP ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP : renews
    PERSON ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST : subject
    PERSON ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST : submits
    MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST }o--o| MEMBERSHIP : produces
    MEMBERSHIP ||--o{ MEMBERSHIP_REQUEST : precedes

Four points that matter:

  • membership_request has two person references: person_id (the child, who would become a member) and submitted_by_person_id (the parent, who applied). Collapsing them makes the audit trail false.
  • A request asks for membership of the unit and names no body. No edge leaves this diagram for a group: which group a new member lands in is a write on the group — one person_group_member row, §2 — and not a preference on the application (D-097, D-098). Where an applicant would have said which group they had in mind, the row has the free-text notes it already carries.
  • Belonging lives in two shapes, and neither is a membership. person_group_member (§2) is a group's dated roster and is keyed on person, never on membership: an imported roster row or a 1998 camper has no membership row to point at, and inferring an open-ended one would sweep that person into MEMBERS today (D-098). A membership is membership of the unit, and it owes no second row to anything. Field rules: ../data-model/03-membership.md.
  • membership_type exists, with exactly one row, kept as a table so the vocabulary can grow, and it carries fee and renewal parameters. Why the row exists at all: membership is ageless (D-038), and age is read from person.birth_date where it matters — which is guardianship, entered by the shape of a request — so age is nobody's eligibility check and a membership type never was one.

docs.title: 4. Guardianship
docs.text:
erDiagram
    GUARDIANSHIP {
        uuid guardian_person_id FK
        uuid dependent_person_id FK
        string relationship
        string right_level
        datetime valid_from
        datetime valid_to
        boolean is_primary_contact
        boolean is_legal_decision_maker
    }
    GUARDIANSHIP_PERMISSION {
        uuid guardianship_id FK
        string right_level
        string changed_reason
        uuid changed_by FK
        datetime valid_from
        datetime valid_to
    }
    PERSON ||--o{ GUARDIANSHIP : guardian
    PERSON ||--o{ GUARDIANSHIP : dependent
    GUARDIANSHIP ||--o{ GUARDIANSHIP_PERMISSION : records
    PERSON ||--o{ GUARDIANSHIP_PERMISSION : changes

Key point: guardianship is a general graph — one guardian → many dependents, many guardians → one dependent, and a person may be both. Authority is per guardianship row, and since D-074 that row carries one value — none, view or write — so a parent may write one child's records and only read another's. See ../data-model/04-relationships.md.

docs.title: Appendix — Permission Catalog: the codes
docs.text:
Every code the system ships, grouped by the thing it acts on — people, accounts, membership, the unit, groups and roles and audiences, guardianship, the permission system itself, audit and system, events, and the keys that call from outside — each with the grant that carries it.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: permission-catalog.md holds §1, the conventions; permission-catalog-a-codes.md holds §2–§8b, the codes; permission-catalog-b-roles-and-open-issues.md holds §9–§12, the namespaces that are not here, the deferred ones, the worked examples of writing an office, and what is open.

docs.title: 2. People and identity
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants person.view — ⚠⚠ See person records — all of them, including every descriptive value person.create — Add a person record person.edit — ⚠ Change person details, including descriptive values person.contact.view — ⚠ See contact points person.contact.edit — ⚠ Change contact points person.merge — 🔒 Confirm identity matches and merge people — and reverse a merge, and resolve a sign-up collision; there is no separate code for any of the three person.redact — 🔒 Perform a GDPR-style erasure attribute.define — Curate the vocabulary of descriptive data — create, rename, merge or retire a code

Why person.merge and person.redact are not part of person.edit: both have privacy consequences far beyond editing a record, and the merged window cannot be reversed — the union of two people's permissions is real from the moment the merge commits, whatever is discovered afterwards. Reversing a merge is a supported operation, and it is the same code, because undoing an identity correction is the same act as making one (D-087).

Three operations, one code.

  • Unmerging a merge a human approved: person.merge. Same named human, same queue, same rows. A person.unmerge code would grade undoing a mistake as safer than making one.
  • Resolving a sign-up collision — working the claim a colliding registration files: person.merge. Resolving it is confirming or rejecting an identity_hypothesis, which is what person.merge already means (../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §4).
  • Linking a colliding sign-up to the person it matched: nothing, deliberately. There is no account.link and no account_claim table (§3). An automatic link once the e-mail verifies is D-004 under another name, and its failure mode is one human's descriptive data becoming another human's record.

What that means for a bundle. There is no wildcard to carve an exception out of. Since D-100 deleted role_permission, an office holding all of person.* is the live grant rows naming ROLE(x) — one row per code, dated, attributable — so a bundle that mixes the dangerous two with routine editing is visible in a role editor instead of hidden in a resolver rule. §11 carries the rule that follows: no worked-example office mixes person.merge or person.redact with routine person.edit, and one that does should be named for what it is.

No person.background_check.*. The organization has no background checks handled by this system, so there is nothing to view and nothing to record (D-043). If that changes, the permission pair and a dated record with an expires_at are the natural shape, and they belong here next to person.* — a clearance is a fact about a person, not about their membership.

docs.title: Descriptive data
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is one class of data, in fields the organization defines while it runs (../domain/08-person-data.md, ../data-model/09-attributes.md, D-083, D-084). The catalog's whole involvement in that is one code added and none removed:

  • Read: person.view. Write: person.edit. That is the entire access story. No code gates descriptive data separately, because there is nothing left for one to gate: a code separating, say, the allergy list from the rest of the record would reinstate the privileged subset D-083 refused on the merits. There is therefore no health.* or medical.* namespace and no per-field access rule — category on a definition groups a form and grants nothing. If a narrower tier is ever genuinely needed, the route is a decision entry about a second grant scope over a defined set of data, not a code with a suggestive name.
  • attribute.define is the one code, and it is the narrow one (D-084): it creates, renames, merges and retires a definition — deciding what the organization collects, which is what makes the data queryable. Recording a value against a definition that does not exist is refused, and it creates nothing: a value may not invent a code, so the vocabulary grows only by a save from a person holding this code, and it is live at that save (D-141) — the permission is the curator, there being no queue left to hold a proposal and no office that would confer the reading of one (D-100). Its sensitivity column stays empty because it reads nobody's data — the vocabulary is rows about codes, and the values underneath it are reached through person.view like anything else.
  • person.view carries ⚠⚠ because the marker grades what a grant exposes, and this one exposes everything known about a child — an allergy list, an insurance number, a note about who the child actually lives with.

person.redact reaches the layer too, and in the opposite direction from retiring a definition: retiring one keeps the values, redacting a person erases theirs — in the audit trail as well as in the row, since a trail that still reads out an erased value has preserved it rather than missed it (../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

docs.title: 3. Accounts
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants account.view — ⚠ See account records account.create — Create an account for someone account.suspend — ⚠ Suspend an account account.close — ⚠ Close an account account.credential.reset — 🔒 Issue a credential reset

account.suspend is not membership.suspend. Suspending a login does not remove someone from the organization; the two are separate lifecycles and separate permissions.

Nothing in this namespace links an account to a person it already belongs to, and the absence is decided, not overlooked. A sign-up that strong-matches an existing person raises an identity_hypothesis and brings nothing into the world that a human has not approved — nothing merged, nothing linked, nothing activated; the account sits at pending_verification until a reviewer decides, and deciding is person.merge (§2, D-089). So there is no account.link code and no claim object for one to act on: the second live account those would manage is exactly what the rule forbids, and the case they would have been asked to solve most often is already handled underneath permissions — account_credential holds many credentials for one account, so a member with a new e-mail address is adding a credential to the login they have, not acquiring a second one.

docs.title: 4. Membership
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants membership.view — ⚠ See membership records membership.request.create — Submit an application membership.request.review — ⚠ Read and work an application membership.request.approve — ⛔ Approve or reject an application membership.activate — Activate a membership membership.lapse — ⛔ Lapse a membership (administrative, non-payment) membership.suspend — ⛔ Temporarily suspend a membership membership.terminate — ⛔ End a membership for cause / expel membership.backdate — ⚠ Enter or correct historical membership periods

Where the two roster questions are answered. "Who is in the organization?" is membership.view — one query over membership, with no depth in it, because there is one unit. "Who is in this group?" and "write that group's roster" are person_group.view and person_group.member.manage (§5a, D-098). There is nothing in between to transfer a member across either: moving a person from one group to another is person_group.member.manage — close one dated row, open another — and it does not touch their membership at all (../data-model/02-organization.md §4).

membership.terminate is the most consequential non-system permission in the catalog. A lapse is administrative; a termination is a decision about a person's standing in a youth organization, frequently with safeguarding and reputational consequences. It should be held by very few people, and it must not be implied by membership.lapse. Grant it explicitly, per person — which since D-099 is the only thing a grant can be: one code, one effect.

person_group.member.manage has no self-scoped variant and none will be added (D-095, whose reasoning D-098 transfers intact). Every grant of it means "over this group's roster" or "over every group's roster", never "over my own row" — so "nobody writes themselves into a group" is not a check the write performs, it is the shape of the thing being granted: there is no smaller grant to make yourself. The same holds for role.assign (§7): nobody appoints themselves, and D-095 was explicit that no code should exist that could express either act.

This is also where the safeguarding control lives. No column anywhere says which sets are for children, so nothing refuses to place a minor in one. What is left is that this code is held by named adults at the unit, that the write is audited like any business-table write with its recorded values emptied after 24 months (D-088), and that there is a report of who holds it (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §3). What it gives up is worth naming: nobody collectively chooses the named adult, because there is no body to choose (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §1). A group has no fee, so unlike a membership there is no gate in front of it besides this permission (../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md §1).

Nothing about a code says whether it requires a paid-up holder, so this table has nothing to hide and nothing to warn about. Where a grantee is a set, the grantee's expression performs the membership test: it says MEMBERS * ROLE(x) when the fee is meant to matter and omits it when it is not, evaluated live on the checked date (§11, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.1), which is where the gate went when D-100 deleted it along with the code that waived it. The two grantees that are not sets carry no such test: a grant written to one named person, or to one registered key (§8b, D-116), has no expression to evaluate, so the fee is nobody's question there and the grantee's own standing is the whole of what was chosen.

docs.title: 5. Organization and positions
docs.text:
Nothing is granted here, because nothing described is left. The six org_unit.* codes went with the unit hierarchy (D-097) and the two position.* codes went with positions (D-100). Where each act is performed now is in removed-concepts.md, which is where a name from an older draft is looked up. The heading stays so a reader arriving from an old bookmark finds the reason and not an empty space.

Two rulings outlived the codes they were written about, and they are why role.assign carries 🔒🔒.

  • Nobody appoints themselves. An appointment was made to a person by somebody else, was never self-scoped, and came with eligibility rules about the office rather than the appointment. Those columns are deleted with the table and none of them has a self-service form in the new model either: role.assign has no self-scoped grant (§7).
  • An appointment writes one row, and nothing derives authority from it. The sentence existed to stop a leadership slot silently reaching people through a group's filling rule, which stopped covering the person on the day the assignment closed (D-091). Filling rules and positions are both gone, so the derivation is gone rather than relocated: a holder row is written by a named person under role.assign, and the only thing that turns it into authority is a grant naming ROLE(x) (D-101).

What is genuinely lost is elected-versus-appointed as stored data (D-100), and it stays lost by decision: D-136 closed F-18 with the ruling that a role holds only the people who hold it. The distinction survives only as offices the organization invents — elected_council beside appointed_it — or not at all (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §6).

docs.title: 5a. Groups, roles and audiences
docs.text:
Three small tables and their codes: a group (person_group, dated member rows, a lifetime) is company (D-098); a role (role, role_holder) is an office, and confers nothing (D-100); an audience is an expression over named sets, and is what a grant aims at (D-101). Writing a group's roster and writing an office's holder list are different codes on purpose — that difference is the whole reason there are two tables — and the office codes are in §7.

Code Namespace Sens. Grants person_group.view — ⚠ See which groups exist, their lifetimes, and who is in them — a roster is a list of people, which is what ⚠ grades person_group.create — Create a group: a name, a description, a lifetime. applies_to = unit person_group.edit — Change a group's name or description. A rename rewrites no grant (§5) person_group.end — Set the group's valid_to. It ends a set, not anyone's standing — hence no ⛔, deliberately person_group.member.manage — ⚠ Add, move or end a member. Never self-scoped (§4); applies_to = unit_and_item audience.view — See the expressions a grant can be aimed at, and the people each one resolves to audience.manage — ⚠ Create an audience; change its expression — which is the whole of it: a hand-named person is a PERSON(x) leaf inside that expression, so there is no second object to edit (D-105)

There is no code for crossing between units, because there are no units to cross. May the center read what happens inside a body it does not run? is not a question this model declines to answer; it cannot be asked, and ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §2 is where that is worked through. The names — scope.expose, scope.exposure.review, scope_exposure — are in removed-concepts.md, with the rule they enforced.

person_group.member.manage is a ⚠ next to a 🔒🔒 two rows away, and the gap is the design. D-100 refuses to merge person_group and role into one table with a kind column precisely because one membership table gives a single code that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into SYSTEM_ADMINS. Same columns, different codes, and GROUP(x) / ROLE(x) distinct in the grant text so the difference is visible to whoever reads the grant. A group additionally authorizes nothing by existing: no parent, no type, no leadership, no roles of its own, no fee — a member of a group can do nothing, which is D-005 one level down (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §2).

A group and a role are both items, which is what makes "these two may work this roster" a grant. Both are registered in grant_scope_type, so the code above can be held at the unit — reaching every group, existing and future, because nothing stands between a unit grant and an item after D-097 — or written on one group, reaching that roster only (../data-model/02-organization.md §3). Reaching the second requires the first: a grant on an item is written by someone who holds the code at the unit, or holds a grant on that item.

A live grant whose group has ended is a listed oddity rather than a failure: it applies to nobody, which is the safe direction, and the report of such rows is where the stale one surfaces (../data-model/02-organization.md §6).

audience.manage is the permission that creates a grant target, and it is wider than it was. Whoever holds it can assemble a set of people which a later access_grant may then address (D-042) — authority over who could be granted, one step removed from granting. Whether it belongs to a dedicated office or to whoever runs things is open (§12).

One code over a whole expression, and the hazard moved with it. An audience is a tree of + - *, composition happens in the grant (GROUP(kitchen) + ROLE(troop_staff)), and a tree cannot cycle, so widening is always a named act in a row somebody wrote. The silent version was audience_include: "add the kitchen crew to everything the troop-staff group is used for" widened every grant aimed at anything including it, through an edge nobody could see the shape of. It went with its depth cap, its transitive walk and its write-time cycle check in D-101. What did not get smaller: EVERYONE is a legal operand, so nothing in this table distinguishes "add these five people" from "this grant reaches the whole organization", and no separate code was invented to do it. That stays an open question, not an answer (§12), and until it is answered the only control is the one D-091 named and D-102 sharpened: the editor shows the people a grant reaches, expanded, computed for an item, rather than the expression's name (../domain/06a-audiences-and-selectors.md §6.2).

The display is itself a read over people, and this catalog does not grade that yet. Showing a resolved set means enumerating which humans an expression currently covers — which is what audience.view is for, on a row carrying no sensitivity mark. Listing the holders of "everyone except the counselors in schuzka2026-1" is not the same kind of act as listing the kitchen crew, and the grading was written before the two could be one query (§12).

docs.title: 6. Guardianship
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants guardianship.view — ⚠⚠ See guardianship relationships guardianship.create — ⚠⚠ Record a guardianship guardianship.end — ⚠⚠ End a guardianship guardianship.assign — ⚠⚠ Add another guardian over the same dependent guardianship.change_right — 🔒 Change a guardianship's right_level

These are the only codes in the catalog that a private individual holds over their own household without being granted them. D-073 makes the parties to a guardianship principals on the row: a guardian may end it, add another guardian, and change its level; the adult subject may end it over themselves. Staff hold the same codes and are an route, never the route.

A guardian's rights are one value with three choices, never a list of codes. guardianship.change_right sets right_level, and there is nothing else to grant: the per-capability dependent.* namespace such a grant would have drawn from was refused on the merits (D-074).

What the three choices are compared against is a column, not a ladder: permission.right_kind ∈ read | write, where none covers nothing, view covers the read codes, and write covers both. That is the column's only customer in the whole system (§1), and it is why a code added to this catalog has to be typed read or write at all: the column is required, because a nullable one whose null-ness silently means something would let a permission arrive with a guardian's answer already decided by nobody. Nothing else could have used this comparison — since D-099 a grant carries no level to compare a code against.

Required, agreeing with nothing, checked by nothing: right_kind is a note, and it stays required. Nothing in the schema or the write path asks whether a code typed read really is one, and no report counts the codes where the two disagree — so a right_kind can contradict its code forever, and only a reader will notice (D-144). That is what the column is for. A code whose declared kind reads oddly next to its name is worth noticing while reading a catalog, which is what this page is; the alternative was a validation rule that would have had to hold, somewhere, a second list of which codes are reads — a copy of this column in prose, and the one defect this corpus keeps hitting is a copy that drifted. Every marking in the tables below is therefore an author's statement, filled in because the column cannot be left empty.

docs.title: 7. Permissions administration
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants role.view system See the offices that exist and who has held them, over what period (role_holder) role.create system 🔒🔒 Create an office: a code, a name, a description. It carries no permission — see the note below role.edit system 🔒🔒 Change an office's name or description role.delete system 🔒🔒 Delete an office. Only possible if it was never held role.assign system 🔒🔒 Write a role_holder row — make someone a holder. applies_to = unit_and_item: on one role, this is "manage the counselors roster" role.unassign system 🔒 Close a role_holder row — set its valid_to permission.view system See the permission catalog permission.edit system 🔒🔒 Change the permission catalog access_grant.create — ⚠ Create a grant — the act that turns a code into someone's authority access_grant.revoke — ⚠ End a grant early, or write a deny system.admin system 🔒🔒 Everything. Single top-level capability, applies_to = unit. Never grantable to a registered key (§8b)

A role confers nothing, and that is the sentence to read before this table. The codes an office carries are the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) (D-100, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §4). What role.create and role.edit touch is a name, a description, an order — an office is a set with a label, and a set is not a grant (D-005). What role.view shows is the holder register, the one question this part of the catalog answers: who was treasurer in 2023?

role.assign is the permission to escalate privilege. Whoever holds it can write themselves a holder row in an office that grants them system.admin. It must be held by very few people and every holder row must be logged, and the holders counted in a report somebody opens. Note that system.admin is deliberately a single top-level permission rather than a per-resource one — concentrating the most dangerous capability and keeping its holders on one list that is read is safer than scattering equivalents of it. role.assign has no self-scoped form and none will be added (§4, D-095): the reason it is not a check the write performs is that there is no smaller grant to make yourself.
