Roles are runtime data, and these six permissions are how the organization administers them. role.create names a new office; role.edit renames one; role.delete removes one created by mistake; the reach of any of them is written by access_grant.create down the table. §11 is therefore a set of worked examples to be edited, not a fixed vocabulary. Whether an office's authority is conditional on a paid-up holder is not configuration either: it is in the text of each grant, which says MEMBERS * ROLE(x) when the fee is meant to matter.

There is no role.retire, and a role cannot be switched off (D-053). A role is a definition and is valid always; the period lives on the holder row. Ending a role's use means closing holder rows, which is role.unassign — one person at a time, or a loop over the holders. The shape is deliberate: what ends is someone's authority, a fact about a person and not about a definition. Nothing here expires on its own. No dormant authority quietly lapses when a holder's fee runs out, so the report of holder rows that never end (D-071, whose posture transfers from assignments to holder rows) is carrying all of the weight.

The bulk privilege change is a grant, not a role edit. A role carries no permissions, so role.edit changes a label; what escalates everyone holding x, immediately, without touching a holder row and without notifying anybody, is saving a grant aimed at ROLE(x). That is access_grant.create with an expression in it, and it is exactly why role.* stays 🔒🔒 while the composition of grants is the least-graded write in the catalog (§12). Escalating one person and escalating an office are different powers, and neither is implied by the other.

role.delete only works on an office that has never been held. No delete may leave a role_holder pointing at a role that is gone: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3 states the guard and the order it refuses in. One guard, and it is referential integrity — role_holder.role_id references role.id, a migration-level constraint — and that is what makes this permission not self-policing rather than unprotected: a constraint refuses a delete that arrives from an import, from a manual fix, or from a second client as surely as from the screens. A per-row "do not delete this" flag beside it was offered and deleted, because such a flag is a property of the row being deleted and no index can see it — it would have been a check inside the transaction that deletes, where a model-layer guard is a friendlier message, not the refusal (D-152). A role that has been held is left in place, so the answer to "what office did this person hold in 2019?" survives — which is precisely when someone asks it. What remains deletable is an office created by mistake and never held, which is what deleting an office was always for.

Nothing waives the membership test, because nothing imposes it. The resolver asks no membership question of a grant, so there is no exemption for a person to hold: the test is the expression the grant was written with — MEMBERS * ROLE(x) where the fee must hold, ROLE(x) where it need not, and (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) + PERSON(y) when one named person is to survive their own lapse (§11, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.1). The waiver code, the role flag that waived a whole office, and the resolver function that read them are in removed-concepts.md.

access_grant.create says you may write grant rows, and since D-163 it no longer says what they may say. What bounds a grantor is the shape of the grant — one code, applies_to refusing it on an item it does not fit, a scope that is the item the grant names or the unit, MEMBERS as the writer's own act — and now the granter too: a row may name only a permission its writer holds, at a scope reaching what they write. This page said the opposite for five rounds and said it as candour ("nothing here pretends otherwise"), and the sentence it drew the conclusion from — that the test an authority may not exceed its holder's is written only for delegations (../domain/06-authorization-model.md §9) — was true the whole time and simply incomplete: delegation was the one place the test had been written, not the only place it applied. So system.admin can no longer be handed out by a holder of access_grant.create who does not hold it, which is what §12 called the sharpest hole in this file and what closed it. The one write the ceiling does not read is the bundle an event create writes — twelve rows naming nobody the writer chose (D-170) — and it is named here because an appendix that lists a rule's exceptions beside the rule is the only kind of appendix worth reading.

docs.title: 8. Audit and system
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants audit.view — ⚠⚠ Read the audit log — including the before/after values it carries, which are person data like any other audit.export — ⚠⚠ Export audit records import.view — ⚠ See import batches import.stage — Stage an import import.apply — 🔒 Apply a staged import import.revert — 🔒 Revert an applied import report.view — ⚠ Run standard reports report.export — ⚠⚠ Export report data

audit.view is graded ⚠⚠ because the trail is a second copy of the person record. audit_log carries the before and after images of what changed, descriptive values included, on the same terms as a person_contact row or a note change. So reading the trail over a scope is reading person data over that scope, and reading more than person.view shows: the current row is the organization's present belief, the trail is every belief it has held. Nothing filters which fields that applies to — a rule naming the person fields whose values may not be logged would be a privileged subset of the record, which is what D-083 refused, and it would hollow out D-085, whose justification for overwriting a value in place is that the trail holds the sequence. What protects the trail is the guard on it — scope, this mark, and who holds it — exactly as the guard on person.view protects the record. Why: the mark follows what a grant exposes, not the table a code names — D-086.

And this one code is the whole gate, with no per-entry filter behind it — now decided rather than merely unbuilt. 06 §2.3 records the per-entry check as considered and left unimplemented, and D-138 is the decision that says so: what an officer can read about 2019 does not depend on an expression changed last week, which is the legibility the trail exists to provide. The widening above is therefore a stated property of one grant and not a bug waiting for a filter — which is also what makes ⚠⚠ and the question of who holds this code the whole of the control.

The contents expire, which bounds that exposure without removing it. A row lives for the life of the system; its old_values/new_values are emptied 24 months after they were written, by a scheduled job this corpus calls payload reduction — a third operation on the trail, distinct from redaction (a person's erasure, immediate and absolute, whatever the age of the row) and from an import revert (D-088). "Every belief it has held" is therefore true only of values less than two years old; about anything older the trail answers who touched this row, when, and were they allowed to and not and to what. It puts a horizon under the risk rather than making it impossible. AT-4 stays open, because a window on the payload is an argument about how long a bad grant can do harm, not an answer to whether one permission should guard the trail.

Payload reduction needs no code here, and saying so is the check that it was considered. Nobody performs it interactively: it is scheduled, and the guard on it is a check that reports a row past the window still carrying a payload (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2.2). A permission for it would imply a person choosing not to run it.

The excluded-keys list has one job: values that must never be logged at all. Credential secrets, tokens, session material. Personal data is not on it, because personal data is protected by who may read the table, not by a list of its names.

Erasure reaches the payload. A redaction that rewrote the business tables while the erased values stayed readable in the trail is a failed redaction, not a partial one (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2, ../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

audit.export sits at ⚠⚠ for a reason unrelated to what it reads. An export carries the payload outside every mechanism this catalog governs: scope stops at the file, revoking the grant does not recall the copy, and a later redaction cannot reach it. It is graded by where the data goes, not by what the code is allowed to see.

One permission is the guard, and that is now decided rather than open: audit.view is the whole gate, with no per-entry filter behind it (D-138, answering AT-4 (../open-questions.md)). The grading above is what the decision rests on: the trail is read with the guard of person data, and the widening that comes with one code over a second copy of the record is written here as a property rather than left to be discovered. What the decision spends is exactly what it names: a history screen over the trail is a person-data surface, so ⚠⚠ and the question of who holds this code are the whole of the control, and a grant to a wider audience widens reading about every year at once.

docs.title: 8a. Events
docs.text:
An event is an item like any other (D-102). Nothing owns an event — there is no owner column and no unit-authority shortcut — so a grant at the unit reaches every event because there is no tier between the unit and the item and no owner to test, and every event check goes through the ordinary resolver and nothing else. Registration is eligibility: a live allow of event.register_self is the rule for who may sign up, and there is no separate eligibility mechanism (D-060). And there is no door code. Nothing in this catalog grants a gate-crashing capability, and none was ever registered here or on any other page (§12, D-104); arriving people are recorded by whoever holds event.presence.mark, with a clipboard if necessary, and D-075 keeps the only QR code in this system attached to a payment, where it is a rendering and not a row.

Code Namespace Sens. Grants event.view — See an event event.create — Create an event. Held at the unit — nothing owns an event, so there is no one to create one for event.edit — Change an event's details, dates, capacity event.cancel — ⚠ Cancel an event — keeps registrations, notifies nobody by itself event.organizer.manage — ⚠ Add or remove organizers — a roster write, which aims ORGANIZERS at more people and so widens every grant pointed at that set event.register_self — Register yourself — this is the eligibility rule event.register_other — ⚠ Register someone else (a minor, a walk-in) event.manage_participants — ⚠ Manage the roster — add or remove registrations, work the waitlist, promote event.presence.mark — ⚠ Mark who turned up — nothing else, and never a set anyone is granted over (§1) event.answer.view — ⚠⚠ Read registrant answers (tent, dietary, …) — the note below, and one of the twelve grants written beside every event event.question.manage — ⚠ Define what the event asks event.grant_access — 🔒 Grant access to an event. What distinguishes it from access_grant.create is the scope alone — and it is one of the twelve grants written beside every event, so whoever runs an event may hand out access to that event and to nothing else, without holding access_grant.create at the unit (§12) event.delete — 🔒 Delete an event — only possible with no registrations

Where each of these may be granted, and what kind of right it is (§1) — nothing else rides on top:

Code applies_to right_kind event.create unit write event.view, event.answer.view unit_and_item read every other event.* code unit_and_item write

At the unit a code reaches every event; on one event it reaches that event; nothing rides on top of either. The read rows are read because a guardian's view is meant to reach them (§6) — which is the only reason the column exists. Why: a grant allows or denies one permission and carries no level — D-099.

The five sets bound to an event are grantees, not codes. ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST and ORGANIZERS name the people connected to the item a grant is written on, and they belong to the audience language, not to this catalog: an operand is a set, and a set is not a grant (D-062 survives untouched — an event_organizer row grants nothing). Two refusals come with them and both land when the grant is saved: a bound (argument-less) operand is legal only on an item-scope grant, and only where selector_type.argument_type matches the item — PLACED on a group grant is refused because that item is not an event. And PRESENT(<event>) is refused outright (§1). A grantee is not always one of these sets, and the other two kinds are named rather than implied: a grant written to one named person, or to one registered key (§8b), has no operand in it and no set behind it, because no selector names a key and a key is in nobody's set — including the set of every person (D-117). The definitions, and the reason PLACED rather than ATTENDED is the capacity set, are in ../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §8.

event.presence.mark is split off event.manage_participants on purpose. Marking presence is a task handed to whoever is at the door with a clipboard; managing the roster is a task for the event's leadership. One permission covering both forces the organization to hand the clipboard-holder the ability to delete a child from the camp roster. Splitting it costs two rows and makes the ordinary delegation ordinary, and the distinction is written as the only thing a grant can say: one code, so granting event.presence.mark on an event cannot smuggle in event.manage_participants. Why: it follows membership.lapse versus membership.terminate — one routine, one consequential (D-022) — and adding a row is free because the catalog is a menu, not a fixed set (D-055). EV-5 asked whether the split was needed; the split is the answer, and the rung it originally came with is D-099's.

event.register_self is the whole of D-060. Opening an event to the membership is one row: an access_grant scoped to that event, of event.register_self, aimed at MEMBERS. One row is the point — nobody is enumerated, so nobody is left out when the roster changes, and nothing has to be re-run when someone joins. The row says exactly one thing, which is the eligibility, and says nothing about anyone else's task.

An age-restricted camp is a narrower expression instead — MEMBERS * GROUP(camp_2026_junior) aimed at the same one code, or the same subtraction pattern read the other way. There is no age rule on the event and there will not be one — an open event with an age ceiling is accepted as a risk, on the grounds that a registration-time condition the capability model does not know about is the first rule-engine rule (D-070). If it ever needs closing, the shape is a new selector in the selector_type registry, not a column (../domain/07-events.md §4) — and note that GROUP(...) is a set somebody maintains, so "who is eligible" stays a roster with a person's name on every row rather than a predicate the resolver evaluates.

event.cancel is separated from event.edit deliberately. Cancelling is the most consequential thing anyone does to an event: it affects every registrant, it usually involves money, and it is a decision rather than an edit. It does not notify anyone — that is the communication module's job, and conflating the two makes "who cancelled this, and when?" harder to answer than it should be.

event.delete is on this list and nothing else has an equivalent, because events are the one thing in this data model that can be deleted. A draft event with no registrations is a mistake to be cleaned up; anything else is cancelled, not deleted (D-064). No event with even one registration row may be deleted — Guard 2 in ../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §8 is the rule, and cancelling is what to do instead. The obligation is not the permission's to carry: event.delete decides who may ask, and only a migration-level constraint — event_registration.event_id referencing event.id with no cascade — refuses the same delete when it arrives from an import or a hand-written fix instead of a screen. Enforcing this in the model layer alone would leave the record of who was coming deletable by everything except the intended route.

event.answer.view is where D-061 lives, and it lives there as a grant. "Answers are read by that event's organizers" is said where permissions are said: an item-scope allow of event.answer.view, scoped to the event, aimed at an audience whose expression is the bare operand ORGANIZERS (D-102). And it is one of twelve. The act that creates an event writes the event's authority beside the event row, in the same transaction as the event: one item-scope allow per code, aimed at ORGANIZERS, for every catalog code whose applies_to admits an event — every event.* code except event.create, which is applies_to = unit because nothing owns an event, so twelve grants beside every event (D-151). The set is derived, not hand-picked, and that is the whole of its maintenance cost being zero: a code added to event.* is in the next event's bundle without anyone remembering a list, and a curated list would have owed somebody the omission forever. Because a bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant, none of this can be one row covering every event: it is twelve rows per event, and the import owes the same twelve beside every event it writes (../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §8). All twelve are written without MEMBERS, and must not be "corrected" — an organizer appointed for one weekend is not required to hold a current membership, and a MEMBERS on those rows would take an organizer's read of their own event's answers away the night their fee lapsed (D-062). What is open is the safety net rather than the rule: an event whose twelve writes were not one transaction has no organizer who can read its answers, and "these twelve rows exist together" is a report — events with an incomplete organizer bundle, naming which of the twelve are absent — that no layer of this project can express as a constraint (shape 3). That failure now has an author, which is what the check is for: it reads as a bug report about one create, not as a missing migration.

Whoever runs an event reads that event's answers with no additional gate. Holding an office grants nothing (§7), and leadership is not guardianship: guardianship authority belongs to the guardians (§9) and is not reachable by leading an event. Why: D-061 names this a widening and records it as one — the parent tells the people who are present, per event. The catalog's registered spelling is event.answer.view, singular, and §12 says what it means for a code to be a row rather than prose (F-19).

The form is the fallback for a fact the organization has not recorded, not the ceiling on what an organizer may know. Descriptive data exists (../domain/08-person-data.md), and a leader holding person.view over that unit reads a recorded allergy there. Why: D-061 was written when the form was the only readable route to such a fact — the narrowing is D-085's, and the decision it narrows stands.

This code is graded ⚠⚠ because the answers are person data. A tent size and an adrenaline-pen answer live in the same payload, and D-083 refuses a class of data more delicate than the rest, so the payload is graded as what it exposes rather than as the logistics category it is filed under — the same rule §8 applies to audit.view (D-086). The grading narrows nothing: organizers still read with no additional gate; what the mark changes is what a reviewer notices before ticking the box on a grant that reaches thirty volunteers.

Only preference-level detail belongs on a form, and that is guidance on a label, not a guard. No layer enforces it and none can: nothing distinguishes "vegetarian" from "carries an adrenaline pen" to a database (../data-model/08-events.md §7). It rests entirely on whoever writes the form.

docs.title: 8b. Keys — a caller that is nobody
docs.text:
A registered key is the third thing a permission is held by. An integration that calls this system over its API is one row in api_key, installed by a named person, holding one secret that is shown once and kept only as a hash — and it is a grantee, in the same sense a person is, reached through the same single grant channel and no other (D-116). It is not an account, which is a way for a person to log in, and it is not a selector: no expression names a key, so a key holds the grants that name it and nothing besides (D-117). The table itself, what its secret may and may not do, and the resolver entry point a call is checked through are in ../data-model/05e-keys-and-callers.md; what the catalog owes is four rows, typed.

Code Namespace Sens. Grants api_key.view — Which keys exist, what each of them is granted, and when each was last used api_key.create — 🔒 Register a key — mints its secret and shows it once, and never again api_key.rotate — 🔒 Replace a live key's secret, showing the new one once — no window in which both secrets work api_key.end — 🔒 Set a key's valid_to, or revoke it now with a reason

Where each of these may be granted, and what kind of right it is (§1) — nothing else rides on top:

Code applies_to right_kind api_key.view unit read api_key.create, api_key.rotate, api_key.end unit write

The marking changes no answer, and is filled in because the column is required. right_kind has one customer, the guardianship channel (§6), and that channel asks about one child's record — while these four codes live at the unit (../data-model/05-authorization.md §2). api_key.view is read because it is the read of a list, and the three writes are write because each lets its bearer install or unmake a caller. api_key.view carries no sensitivity mark, on the precedent of role.view and permission.view two sections away: reading the register of integrations exposes nobody's personal data, and the secret the row holds never leaves the row — not on this screen, not in an export, not in a log line. Why the mark follows what a grant exposes and not the table a code names: D-086.

None of these four is system.*, and that is a difference rather than a spelling. The system namespace holds the codes that administer this system's own machinery — the catalog, the offices, the grant rows (§7) — and it is the one place where the rule that permission.resource equals the code's first segment is waived: in a system. code those two disagree on purpose (../data-model/05-authorization.md §2). These four act on a table that exists, exactly as event.* and person_group.* do, so the first segment already is the resource and a prefix would be a second, drifting copy of a name the code carries. And a prefix would buy nothing, because a namespace routes nothing: the resolver stopped branching on the prefix, and D-124 deleted the last reading under which one routed something. The unit-only reach is carried by applies_to above, where the save checks it; what a reader needs is the 🔒. The precedent is in §7 and is stronger than anything here: access_grant.create, the act that turns a code into somebody's authority, carries no namespace at all.

What a key may never be granted is five named codes, not a set derived by rule: system.admin and the four above. The grant is refused when it is saved (../data-model/05-authorization.md §6), and integrity check 20 is the entire net, because no database rule spans permission and access_grant (D-122). One sentence covers both halves — a key may not change what a key can do, and may not become everything. A bearer secret holding everything is the whole organization in a request header; a key holding api_key.create mints its own replacements, so rotating a stolen key means looking for the rows a thief installed rather than the rows a person installed. Like check 17's .admin assertion this is an equality against named rows, and not *.api_key and not "any code about keys": an allow-list is where a wildcard comes back to life, which is exactly why the refused set is spelled out code by code.

No office holds any of the four on day one, and none should: whoever holds system.admin already satisfies every one of these checks, because system.admin satisfies every code (D-124). The capability to install a permanent outside authority is the capability to escalate, and the 🔒 on the three writes is that sentence — it arrives through access_grant.create like every other code, so there is no second route to it and nothing holds it quietly: an office has one of these four because a named person wrote that row, or it has none. The fourth thing a new resource owes this catalog, a row in grant_scope_type, is declined for a key on purpose (D-122): a key is not a grantable item, so none of these codes can be written on one and "rotate the accounting key and no other" is not writable — anyone who may issue a key may issue any key. That is accepted at this scale, and it is recorded here as an unpaid debt rather than as a design feature.

A key's authority is its grants, in full and only. Two of the three channels of authority compare a person against a row — ownership and guardianship — and for a key neither is refused by a fresh rule so much as unreachable, because there is no person for either to compare (D-118). The consequence worth reading twice: a deny written against the person who installed a key does not touch the key. Deny is absolute, but it defeats the allows of the grantee it names, and these are two grantees. What covers that is a list rather than a guard: the Unusual section of the tab on the permissions page lists live keys beside people, with what each holds, when it was last used and whether its contact still has an account, so a review reads one grant list and not two (D-109, D-120). A grant to a key is never a delegation, on the reasoning that already refuses it for an audience: lending is one person's act towards another, and there is no person here to lend (D-116).

§1's naming rules hold here with no exception taken: every last segment is an act, and the first segment names stored state — a table that now exists. rotate is a last segment this corpus has deleted before, as event.qr.rotate in removed-concepts.md — a code that never existed in any registry and was deleted for being prose only (D-104). These rows are not its revival. The lesson of that deletion is a name must have a row behind it, and here the row exists before the prose does (D-122).

docs.title: Appendix — Permission Catalog: absent namespaces, worked-example offices, open issues
docs.text:
What the catalog deliberately does not have, what arrives with the unbuilt modules, what an installation actually has on its first day, how an office is written when somebody writes one, and what is not settled.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: permission-catalog.md holds §1, the conventions; permission-catalog-a-codes.md holds §2–§8b, the codes; permission-catalog-b-roles-and-open-issues.md holds §9–§12, the namespaces that are not here, the deferred ones, the worked examples of writing an office, and what is open.

docs.title: 9. There is no dependent.* namespace
docs.text:
A guardian has no permission codes. Their rights are one value on the guardianship row — none, view or write (D-074, §6) — and the eighteen codes that used to sit in this namespace, dependent.profile.view, dependent.medical.admin and their siblings, are indexed with the other dead names in removed-concepts. Nothing here may be reinstated by pattern-matching one of those names: there is no set left for a name to stand for. If the finer split turns out to matter in operation, it is a new decision argued from the current documents — one grant scope over a defined set of data — and not a restoration.

What cannot be expressed was declined, not left unbuilt. A court order giving one parent access to everything about their child except the medical file cannot be expressed: view is one value over the whole of a child's record, so a grandmother granted roster visibility gets the fee history with it. There is also no medical record to be shut out of — everything other than name, gender and age is one class of data reached by person.view and governed by the guardian's level whole (../domain/08-person-data.md). Why: the story was put to the organization and refused on the merits — "medical data is not different in any way" — which is D-083, and it is why E-7 closed as a dissolved question rather than an answered one. Read the inexpressibility as settled, not as pending work: reopening it means producing the case that was declined, not finding a code to restore.

What still holds:

  • A guardian's authority is per guardianship row. The channel is entered by whose record the act touches and answers only about that row (D-079), so a guardian cannot do organization-wide things and cannot reach a different dependent's records. What write means is this row's dependent, both kinds: it covers the write codes and the read ones, where view covers only read and none covers nothing — compared against permission.right_kind, not against a level (§6).
  • A deny still reaches the channel. A live deny beats every allow that applies, at any scope and in any channel (D-032, D-099), so "this guardian, nothing" remains expressible: a deny at the unit aimed at the person, PERSON(x). There is no narrow deny — no operand names one child's guardians to aim one at, because the channel resolves no sets and the name an expression can carry here is the person's (D-113). What was lost is the narrowness, not the refusal.
  • A guardianship at none grants literally nothing, so being a guardian grants nothing by itself — the safeguarding property the eighteen codes were written for, held without any of them.
  • An event's answers are not guardian data. They are read through event.answer.view, a permission on the grant side, carried by one of the twelve grants the act that creates the event writes beside it and aimed at ORGANIZERS (§8a), and leadership is not guardianship (D-061).

See ../data-model/04-relationships.md §2 for the value, its defaults by source, and the three-value ordering it is a range of — none < view < write, which is D-074's own ordering over one column and not the access-level ladder D-099 deleted. Nothing in this catalog is a range of anything.

docs.title: 10. Deferred namespaces
docs.text:
Placeholders for features you have not specified. Listed so the naming convention is established before anyone invents an inconsistent one.

Resource Permission Notes document document.view, document.create, document.edit, document.delete, document.grant_access document is already a row of grant_scope_type, marked deferred — the item exists in the registry before the module does, which is what the polymorphic scope_id is for (D-011). The code is the one this catalog's own §1 rule pays for: document.grant_access sits beside access_grant.create exactly as event.grant_access does, and §12 asks the question once for both. fee fee.view, fee.create No ⛔ and no 🔒, and the reason is a deletion rather than a decision about sensitivity: fee.waive went because there are no hardship waivers (D-157) and fee.refund went because a refund is a transfer the bank makes and a payment row records, not an act authorized on a screen (D-158). What is left is reading a fee and writing one, which needs no sensitivity mark and never did. payment payment.view, payment.record, payment.reverse report report.finance.view, report.membership.view, report.safeguarding.view ⚠⚠ report.safeguarding.view consent consent.template.edit, consent.record.view message message.send_direct, message.broadcast Decided in shape, undesigned in detail (D-077). Everyone may send direct; broadcast is an ordinary scoped permission. The unit is one scope (D-097), so held at the unit broadcast reaches everyone; the narrower audience — this body, not the unit — is a grant on a person_group, reaching that roster, which D-099 makes available. Which of the two messaging means, and whether message.broadcast should be applies_to = unit_and_item, is messaging's decision, not this catalog's (§12). Recipient chooses the channel, which is not a permission at all. A direct message to a minor is mirrored to that minor's guardians and the sender is told it will be — no permission, no age branch in the resolver (D-082) partner (namespace) For external organizations, if the model expands.

What each new resource owes the authorization module is four things — all cheap, all required, and no level table among them (D-099): codes (two or more lowercase segments, first segment = resource), each with a right_kind — read or write, required, because that column is a guardian's answer and not a hint (§6) — each with an applies_to, checked on save (§1); and a row in grant_scope_type if its records are things a grant can be written on, which is what makes a document or a group an item at all.

docs.title: 11. Roles — worked examples of writing one
docs.text: Examples of an act, not a list of rows. The heading says "roles" and most of what follows is grants, because an office has no contents: the codes an office carries are the live grants whose expression names it, one row per code, each with its own scope and its own period (D-100). MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers) on fee.create is one such row, and it — not the office — is what lets a treasurer issue a fee. A role is two things: a name a grant can be aimed at, and the register that answers who held this in 2023 (role_holder, which is why F-12 closes with no — a holder row names one person). Offices are runtime data: the organization creates them, names them, writes and closes their holders, and deletes the never-held ones (§7). Reach is not runtime data — it is administered through access_grant.create and access_grant.revoke, so it is reviewed in access_grant, not in a role editor (§7).

docs.title: What an installation has
docs.text:
Counting only the tables this section is about: no office and no grant. Nothing about an organization's authority arrives built. Day one is one account and one ordinary access_grant row giving it system.admin at the unit — one row, one audit row beside it, and nothing in the model that can tell it apart from a grant written a year later (D-150). Everything else that ships is vocabulary: the permission rows of this catalog, the selector_type operands (§1), the grant_scope_type rows that make an event or a group or a role an item, the two effects and the two enums (§12). None of that is authority, and the sentence is repeated here because this section is where a reader looks for it.

What an installation has Table Written by What it grants one grant of system.admin at the unit, naming one account access_grant the installation, as an ordinary grant row with an ordinary audit row beside it Everything — the one wildcard, applies_to = unit, so never reachable on an item (§1, §7). This is the entire configuration of a new installation twelve item-scope allows beside every event, aimed at an audience whose expression is the bare operand ORGANIZERS access_grant the act that creates the event, in the same transaction as the event row (D-151) That event's organizers run that event. The twelve are §8a's event.* codes except event.create, whose applies_to is unit — so event.answer.view is one of twelve grants written beside every event, not a lone answer-read grant, and one of the other eleven is event.grant_access (§8a)

Why a role and not a group, when D-098's own definition of a group is "a temporary set of members that do events together" and counselors are neither temporary nor event-shaped: the table decides which code protects the set, and every safeguarding convention in this area hangs from that answer being unchangeable by an ordinary grant — role.* is 🔒🔒, person_group.member.manage is ⚠ (§5a). That argument is about which of two tables a permanent population lives in, and it stands untouched; what it never needed was for the platform to write the row. counselors is the name the corpus uses when it needs an office, and it is now openly one (D-154). What refuses a deletion of any office that has been held is the foreign key from role_holder, a migration-level constraint, and it protects every office the organization ever writes at least as well as it would have protected a shipped one (§7, D-152).

Nothing names ROLE(counselors) until somebody writes the grant, and that is the design rather than an omission. Being a counselor confers nothing until someone writes the grant (D-005). What that leaves open is not a permission but a number, and it is the price D-100 names for moving the gate into the expression: the reach of the counselor office is only as correct as the roster, so the import reconciliation of D-090 counts people marked as counselors in the legacy corpus against role_holder rows written. An import that misses three hundred counselors fails closed — nobody's access breaks — which is exactly why nobody notices. And on a first run there is no such office, so that reconciliation has nothing to reconcile and reports nothing — a report whose subject arrives later, not a report that is broken.

Who may make someone a counselor, over just that one office. role.assign writes a role_holder row and is applies_to = unit_and_item (§7), so holding it at the unit lets you fill every office in the organization, which is what 🔒🔒 is for, while a grant of it on the item counselors says these two may manage the counselor roster and nothing else. That is D-098's move read symmetrically, and it is why role is a row of grant_scope_type.

The twelve grants beside an event are written without MEMBERS, and must not be "corrected." An organizer appointed for one weekend is not required to hold a current membership — D-062's appointment model assumes exactly that — so a MEMBERS on those rows would take an organizer's read of their own event's answers away the night their fee lapsed. They are also the only grants this system writes by itself, and that is worth stating beside one of D-100's three controls, which counted on a shortcut that does not exist here: it was that any grant template carries MEMBERS, so the path of least repetition is the safe path, and there is no repetition to take — every grant an office holds will have been written by hand, and the one automated write path in the system produces twelve rows that must not carry it (05 §6). Nor can those twelve be one row covering every event — a bound operand cannot sit on a unit-scope grant — which is why the act that creates an event writes them beside it (§8a).

docs.title: The worked-example offices
docs.text:
None of the following ships, and nothing below is a row the platform writes. These are the names the rest of the corpus uses whenever it needs an office to talk about, written out the way an office has to be written by the person writing it: one role.create for the name — which confers nothing on its own — and then one grant per code, all aimed at one expression, all at the unit, because there is nowhere else for a code about people to be aimed (§1), each with its own period, and then a role.assign for whoever holds it. Do not read a row as a requirement, and do not expect the list to survive contact with the organization.

Office The grant rows that are its reach Grantee expression Why that expression system_admin system.admin — one row, and it is enough ROLE(system_admin) no MEMBERS, deliberately: the 1 January case below registrar person.view ⚠⚠, person.create, person.edit ⚠, person.contact.view ⚠, person.contact.edit ⚠, account.view ⚠, account.create, account.suspend ⚠, account.close ⚠, account.credential.reset 🔒, membership.view ⚠, membership.request.create, membership.request.review ⚠, membership.activate, membership.backdate ⚠, import.view ⚠, import.stage, import.apply 🔒, import.revert 🔒 — nineteen rows MEMBERS * ROLE(registrar) staff working the organization's own records; the office stops when the fee lapses membership_approver membership.request.review ⚠, membership.request.approve ⛔ MEMBERS * ROLE(membership_approver) as above treasurer fee.view, fee.create, payment.view, payment.record, payment.reverse, report.finance.view MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurer) as above, and one list shorter than it was: the treasurer waives nothing and refunds nothing here (D-157, D-158) safeguarding_officer membership.view ⚠, report.safeguarding.view ⚠⚠, membership.terminate ⛔ MEMBERS * ROLE(safeguarding_officer) whoever finds the problem and whoever ends a membership over it are the same person, and nobody else leaders the thirteen event.* codes (§8a), membership.view ⚠, person_group.view ⚠, report.membership.view ⚠ — sixteen rows ROLE(leaders) volunteers, so no MEMBERS (property 4): the office must survive a lapsed fee, and it reaches every event, not one body's events audience_admin audience.view, audience.manage ⚠ MEMBERS * ROLE(audience_admin) §5a, including the naming rule this office is subject to identity_reviewer person.merge 🔒, import.view ⚠, import.apply 🔒 MEMBERS * ROLE(identity_reviewer) and no person.view — property 5 auditor audit.view ⚠⚠, audit.export ⚠⚠, report.view ⚠ — read-only, no writes ROLE(auditor) no MEMBERS: an auditor who forgets to pay must not lose the read (property 4)

An office's reach carries two kinds of period, and both are worth knowing before you set either. The office is held for a period (role_holder.valid_from/valid_to) and each of its grants has a period of its own, so an office's reach is an intersection of up to twenty dates, and the question when does this person stop being able to do that? has more than one right answer. Nothing forces either kind of row to end — the posture of D-071 applies to both, and the control is the report.

Three of these offices name codes this catalog has not registered, and one office is made entirely of them. The treasurer's eight rows are fee.*, payment.* and report.finance.view, and all three of those namespaces are §10 placeholders — so that office cannot be written today, and its row count is a wish rather than a migration. safeguarding_officer and leaders each name one deferred report code among otherwise live rows, which is the milder form of the same thing. The counts above therefore say what an office would hold once finance ships; the live half of each list is what a person could write today. Nothing in the schema stops a grant row naming a code that does not exist, so this paragraph is F-19 one section further along: the catalog names the office, the office names the code, and no row agrees.

Read event.* above as a count, not as a wildcard. Since D-068 there is no resolver rule that makes person.* mean anything; the notation means "every person. code listed in §2", and a real office has an explicit grant row for each — which since D-100 is the only place such a list exists at all. Three consequences for whoever writes these:

  1. registrar omits person.merge and person.redact by not having those rows, and the exclusion is exactly that literal: two rows nobody inserted, visible in access_grant with a date and an author, reviewable like any other row. identity_reviewer is the office that does hold person.merge — the whole of identity correction: merging, reversing a merge, and deciding a sign-up collision (§2) — listed beside registrar so the difference between the two is legible. An office that bundles a resource including its 🔒 codes should be named for that, since nothing else records the choice: person.redact is irreversible, and person.merge is undoable but unions permissions the moment it runs (D-087), which is why 🔒 and not a word like irreversible is what a reviewer should read.
  2. leaders holding event.* means thirteen explicit rows (§8a), and a fourteenth added later is not in the office until someone writes it. Integrity check 18 surfaces an orphaned permission — one no live grant names — and it does not surface "this office arguably should have had it." That is the cost D-068 accepts. access_grant is the only place an office's list exists, so the question should this office have that code? has no page that answers it: check 18 answers only does any live grant name this code?
  3. auditor is an office that reads the whole person record, and does it without person.view. audit.view is graded ⚠⚠ in §8 precisely because the payload is a second copy of the record, so this row grants a ⚠⚠ read over what the system believed about a child and when it believed it. That read has a floor: payloads older than 24 months are emptied (D-088), so what is exposed reaches back two years and no further, while the who-did-what-to-which-row part reaches back for the life of the system. That bounds this row's exposure and does not soften its grading. Nothing here forbids it — it is a plausible office — but the row must not be described to anyone as "just the logs", and it is scoped and dated for the same reason the ⚠⚠ rows above it are.

docs.title: How the gate is written
docs.text:
MEMBERS is an operand, evaluated live on the checked date, so whether an office survives its holder's lapse is a property of the expression written on the grant (§7, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §6.1). Three things a writer says with it:

Expression What the writer is saying MEMBERS * ROLE(x) this office is for people who are members right now ROLE(x) written without MEMBERS; a lapse in the fee ledger does not stop this office (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) + PERSON(y) one named person is the exception, and the exception is visible to everyone who reads the grant

A second grant aimed at PERSON(y) is the other way to write the third row, leaving the gated expression alone; D-100 keeps both legal and calls the second arguably clearer for a permanent exception, because it keeps the exception off the expression everyone else reads. Why: there is nothing to waive and no column to set — the test is not a resolver clause any more, so the fee either appears in the expression or it does not. What used to carry it — a role flag exempting a whole office, a person-level permission exempting one named person, and the resolver clause that asked the question of every grant (D-039, D-100) — is in removed-concepts.md.

There is no default, in either direction, and that is the ruling. Which offices are written without the term is decided per office, by whoever writes the grant (D-165); the Unusual section below lists every ROLE(…) operand with no MEMBERS, not a marked subset, and a grant written without the term needs no reason field: grant_reason is already an optional column on the row (05 §6), and it stays optional. §12 carries the ruling and its edges.

The posture is opt-in, so name the new failure rather than bury it. An expression written ROLE(treasurers) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently, for as long as the grant lives: forgetting MEMBERS is now possible, and waiving it is a deliberate act in the text. Three controls, none of which is the resolver:

  • The tab on the permissions page, in its Unusual section: live grants that name a ROLE(…) operand and contain no MEMBERS. An office held by a non-member is the case worth a human eye, and this population is narrow enough to actually be read — system_admin, leaders and auditor are on it here, and all three are on it because someone chose them, which is the whole point. It is a section of a tab rather than a report, because a report has to be remembered and the writer is already standing on that page; and it says unusual, never broken, because such a grant resolves exactly as written (F-13, D-109).
  • Any grant template carries MEMBERS, so the path of least repetition is the safe path. This control has nothing to work on and must not be trusted with anything: no grant arrives carrying MEMBERS, because the only grants this system writes by itself are the twelve beside an event, and those must not carry it (§11, §8a). Every office grant in existence has been written by hand, so the safe path is not the short one. Recorded in §12.
  • Import completeness. The counselor office is only as correct as the roster behind it: a grant aimed at ROLE(counselors) says nothing about anyone the import left out. The duty is stated above, and a short import fails closed.

One of these offices is not a preference, and it is the one to copy carefully. system_admin is written ROLE(system_admin), with no MEMBERS, because on 1 January the expiry sweep of D-040 lapses every membership in the organization including the administrator's, and a gated administrator loses the ability to repair the system on the day it breaks. That is a property of the system, not a policy choice — and it is now an expression rather than a flag, which means it can be got wrong. The loud mistake is the opposite one: writing MEMBERS * ROLE(system_admin) "for consistency" reproduces the lockout, silently, with no error message. Whether any office exists to be written this way on day one is a different question, and the answer is no: day one is one account and one grant naming that account, not an office, so there is nothing to gate, nothing to forget MEMBERS on, and the January risk arrives with the first office somebody writes (What an installation has, §12).

Eight properties worth noting:

  1. membership_approver is separate from registrar. Deciding who becomes a member is a different act from processing records. If your organization wants one person to do both, hold both offices — which now literally means two holder rows and two sets of grant rows — but keep them separately attributable, because that separation is the only thing the office names buy.
  2. safeguarding_officer holds membership.terminate. The permission to end someone's membership sits with the person responsible for safeguarding, not with whoever chases fees. This is deliberate. There is no person.background_check.* for it to hold: the organization records no background checks (D-043). What it also does not have here is person.view: three rows, and the ⚠⚠ one is the report rather than the record. If working a case needs the record, that is a fourth grant row — scoped, dated, attributable, and visible to anyone who asks what this office can read, which is the review §2 moved to when it graded person.view ⚠⚠.
  3. No office is a guardian. The guardianship channel is only consulted when the subject of the act is someone else, and it only finds a guardianship row (D-074). Leadership is not guardianship, so no office hands anyone a guardian's right over a child — not the right to act for that child, and not the row that decides what the family may see. What an office can do, and does openly, is read the child's record. With no privileged subset inside the person record, a leader granted person.view reads the whole of a member's descriptive data, allergy list included (D-083, ../domain/08-person-data.md) — and one such grant reaches every member in the organization, because there is no narrower scope than the unit for a code about people (§1, D-097). Nothing about leading anything grants it: no channel opens on its own, and the row that would is explicit, scoped, dated and readable in access_grant. That is also why §2 grades that code ⚠⚠: the safeguarding review is the question which grants were given this one?, which is a question the catalog can answer. Do not re-derive it as a list of codes to keep out of offices — the rule is about the channel, and there is no code left to quarantine.
  4. system_admin, leaders and auditor are the three example offices written without MEMBERS. The instinct behind them is one sentence — staff-like offices working on the organization's own records hold a membership; volunteer-facing offices need not — and it is a writing habit, the judgment of whoever writes each grant, not a default the design carries in either direction and not a resolver clause (D-165). The failure it prevents is specific: the volunteer whose own fee is unpaid still runs the Thursday meeting, and must not lose their roster the night it lapses. That volunteer's office appears in the Unusual section of the tab on the permissions page — grants naming a ROLE(…) operand with no MEMBERS — which is how the organization notices, and the resolver is still not how it punishes. See ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §4.
  5. identity_reviewer decides identity questions about children without a read over the person record. The office carries three rows — person.merge, import.view, import.apply — and person.view is not among them: the reviewer works from the candidate pair, the match_signals recorded against it, and the names and dates those signals compare. That is deliberate as it stands — the question being decided is whether two rows are one human, and the descriptive values underneath are not evidence about that — and it is the same shape as auditor reading the trail without holding person.view. What round 8 changed is the pressure on it. This is now also the office a blocked sign-up lands on (D-089): an account held out of active by an unresolved hypothesis, with the review queue's age check naming it because the stalled item is a person who cannot log in — a listing read by whoever works the queue, since nothing in this design sends anything (D-164). If reviewers begin asking for context they cannot see, that is the finding to act on, and the two honest answers are a scoped, dated person.view on this office, or a review screen that shows more of the signals. Reaching instead for an organization-wide person.view would put the catalog's largest ⚠⚠ read in the office with the most write authority over identity. Tracked as F-11, where none of the three positions is yet recorded as taken.
  6. No office in this set holds person_group.member.manage, and the omission is now ruled rather than open — the blank is the answer, named as one by D-167 so no later round repairs it. What D-095 decided has not moved: joining a set is somebody else's act, the write is never self-scoped, and this code is the only thing standing between a person and a group's roster (§5a). As written, leaders may see a roster and cannot write one — and because the answer behind D-095 was "they will be assigned to the unit by the counselors" while counselors is an office somebody writes rather than one that arrives (What an installation has), until an organization writes that office and gives it this code, the only person who may write a roster is the one account holding system.admin at the unit — one ordinary access_grant row, satisfying this code the way it satisfies every code (§7). It is recorded here instead of added to the table on purpose: which volunteer office may put a child on a group's roster is the organization's decision, and an appendix that quietly hands it to leaders would be making a safeguarding choice on someone else's behalf (§12).
  7. attribute.define is held by nothing here, and an office is the wrong shape for the answer. open-questions AT-2 points at this section as the place the question gets answered, and the honest answer for a volunteer organization is one or two people rather than an office: a grant aimed at PERSON(x) (§1) is the form that fits, with a date on it, and an office would only be a way of making one person's job look like a policy — a role confers nothing a grant does not already confer (D-100). What changed under this property is the shape of the risk, and it got sharper rather than softer. There is no proposal stage left, so nothing arrives in a queue to be noticed later (D-141): an office that holds no attribute.define is an office that cannot name a new thing at all, because a value recorded against a code nobody has defined is refused rather than filed. §12 states what that costs.
  8. An office name is load-bearing, because names are one namespace. A bare name in an expression resolves against role and person_group together, so an office called leaders and a group called leaders cannot both exist, and the collision is caught on the write path rather than by a constraint (there is no constraint spanning two tables) (D-101, D-081). Every selector_type.code is reserved on top of that, so an office called MEMBERS is refused when it is saved rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system. audience_admin is therefore a name with a second duty: as well as saying who may edit audiences (§5a), it occupies a name no group may take — and note that it grants nothing over person_group at all, so whoever manages audiences and whoever manages groups may be, and here are, different people.

docs.title: 12. Open issues
docs.text:
• The catalog's disposition is settled; its contents are not. It stays comprehensive and granular (D-055), so there is no "prune this down" review to do. What remains is additive: each unbuilt module brings its own permissions as it is specified, and unused rows cost nothing.
  • Which offices' grants carry MEMBERS: per office, by whoever writes the grant, no default either way — not into the expression and not out of it — and that is the ruling. Which offices are written without the term is decided per office, by whoever writes the grant (D-165): no office can inherit an entitlement by being written from a template, and no office can inherit a lockout that way either. No screen adds the term and no screen strips it. The answer is written into a grant's expression, and the control D-100 nominated for it exists — as a section of a page, not a report: the Unusual section of the tab on the permissions page lists live grants naming a ROLE(…) operand whose expression contains no MEMBERS (§11) — every one of them, not the offices somebody marks sensitive, because a list filtered by which grants should carry the term would encode exactly the default this ruling declines to set. And a grant written without the term needs no reason field: grant_reason is already an optional column on the row (05 §6) and it stays optional, because requiring one would turn the absence of a default into a small approval process. The list's width — every such grant rather than a marked subset — and the day-one clause below are this round's reading of the ruling, not the ruling's own words. Nothing is refused and nothing is warned when such a grant is saved. Why: that test fires on the intended case as often as on the mistake, and a prompt that cries wolf teaches the writer to route around it, so F-13 closed on the weaker half on purpose (D-109). Day one's grant carries no MEMBERS term at all — it names a person, and a grant aimed at one person has no expression to carry one, and a grant that has no expression to carry one cannot be read as having declined one — so the lockout D-051 was written against is answered by D-150, not by an exemption. What is still owed is the thing F-13 itself nominates: whether those MEMBERS-less office grants turn out to be mistakes or choices.
  • What a holder of access_grant.create may write now has a bound, and the bound is the writer. A write to access_grant may name only a permission that the person writing it holds, at a scope that reaches what they are writing — the granter's ceiling (D-163), stated where the model states write-path refusals, as check 7 of the seven in 05 §6. access_grant.create has always said you may write grant rows; that it never said what they may say was this file's sharpest hole, and the answer is none of the three options this page offered — no second code for the system. namespace, no two-person rule, no verdict of trail-and-judgment. Why: the level ladder was still doing this one job — a grant could not carry a rank above its writer's own — and D-099 deleted it without replacing that ceiling; the bound that came back is the check the resolver already performs, pointed at the granter at save time, so a writer predicts may I grant this? from the question they already ask. Three consequences, each stated with the rule on 05 §6: a right held only through a delegation does not raise the ceiling — lending is not holding — and delegation still works, because the delegator writes the row and holds the right directly; the ceiling stops escalation and not spread: a person who holds person.view at the unit may hand it to twenty people, since they hold it, and no report covers that distribution and none was called for. The entry a reader will find nearest to the claim, the wide half of check 7 in 05d §11, is about something else — a grant that widened because a set under a - stopped resolving, which is an expression changing shape under a row nobody edited; and granted_by is now the precondition of a security rule rather than bookkeeping, because the ceiling reads a named person and D-125 guarantees every grant row names one. Day one is untouched: the account of D-150 holds system.admin at the unit, which satisfies every code, so the origin of authority is exempt by construction rather than by a special case.
  • event.grant_access has a subject, and the subject is every event. What distinguishes it from access_grant.create is the scope alone (§8a), and the reading this file left open is the one that stands: it is a scoped front door onto the same table, and it arrives in the bundle of twelve that the act creating an event writes beside it, so whoever runs an event hands access to that event out without holding access_grant.create at the unit and without asking anybody (D-151). The two codes authorize the same write to the same table, and what differs is which code the person was given — the resolver matches one code exactly, the item-facing screens check event.grant_access and the general permission screens check access_grant.create. That is two codes for one write, said here rather than dressed up as an invariant. What makes it survivable is that they come through different doors: one is in every event's bundle and leaves when the event's grants end, the other is a unit-scope decision about who may operate the permission system. And the ceiling is structural either way — the scope an organizer may write is the event they run, and applies_to = unit refuses system.admin on an item at the save, so the wildcard cannot be handed out from an event (§1, §7).
  • A deny that matches no allow is invisible, and D-099 asks for a report nobody has written. The new integrity report is "a live deny matching no live allow is dead weight" (§9 restates it). It is not the same question as integrity check 18's — that one asks which permissions no grant names, this one asks which grants do nothing — and it is easy to under-build: a deny aimed at a set that currently resolves nobody looks identical to a deny that is working. Open only as a report with no owner; the semantics are settled.
  • A leaf that names nothing is still the empty set, and it is also a line on a page. EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with a dead x subtracts nobody and therefore still denies everybody, and nothing is refused at save because a leaf is broken (D-106). What makes the two cases tellable apart is the listing: an audience carrying a leaf that does not resolve is listed, for the audience's owner, in a second column of the page F-21 already asks for — and it is the thing that separates the two rows this bullet is about: a deny over a set that is genuinely empty, and a deny whose operand has quietly stopped resolving. The direction is the fact worth carrying, not a volume: a failed operand on the + or * side narrows the set, and a failed operand on the - side widens it, so - is not the noisy operator, it is the only one whose failed operand can grant — and a check that "fails closed" on that side is fail-closed and lockout-everybody in the same step. And one thing is not a failure at all: a person with no birth date is not a broken OLDER(18). The operand resolves perfectly well, to the set of people who are that age on the date being checked, and that person is simply not in it, exactly as a person with no membership row is not in MEMBERS. A missing value on the person being asked about never reaches the report, which is the distinction the page has to preserve or it pages about every incomplete import in the legacy corpus. The page is a query with an owner, not a guard (D-081's phrase, applied to it by D-106): no save depends on it, and the catalog mints no code for reading it.
  • audience.manage is one code over an expression, and the largest act it covers is still unmarked. Composition is the expression now (D-101): an inclusion is an ordinary + beside a leaf, and the leaf that should worry everyone is EVERYONE. There is no smaller act to grant either — may tick names on this audience without may rewrite the rule is not a shape any code could cover, because D-105 deleted the list those names sat on; if the need is ever real it is a new question about the editor. The shape of the concern is one edit long: whoever can edit one expression can widen every live grant aimed at it, including by writing EVERYONE, which is legal, reachable, and resolves to non-members and the public — and the reach is now transitive, because D-103 lets one audience be named inside another, so editing a widely-named audience widens every grant aimed at every audience that names it. Either composition is documented as plainly inside audience.manage — accepting exactly that consequence — or it gets a code of its own; no code was invented here to fill the gap. The interim control is the editor showing the expanded set and the affected grants before the save, which is a user-interface requirement carried in ../domain/06a-audiences-and-selectors.md §6.2, not a permission.
  • Nothing bounds what a permission check costs. There is no depth bound: audience.selector_depth_limit is gone, and with it the save-time refusal that made "a check costs a bounded amount" true; the two cycle walks — inside the tree, and across audiences through every AUDIENCE(x) leaf — are the only structural guard there is (D-105). An expansion that never terminates is still refused, because acyclicity is what the deletion left intact; what a terminating expansion costs is bounded by nothing, and that is accepted, because the size is stated: a few hundred people in the organization, a few dozen registrants on a typical event, a big camp on the order of two hundred — a size stated rather than measured, with the trigger written down beside it that a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event, reopens the question (D-112). What exists for looking at any of this is the tab on the permissions page, which lists rules that name something deprecated, hidden or disabled, or that fail to resolve, and says nothing about how wide any of them is (D-109); there is no standing report of the widest and deepest audiences, and the registry diff that would catch a prose code naming no row is run by hand — D-081's convention, not a guard. No number makes an audience too wide and nothing in the language caps one. The two rules that must outlive any growth are already written — a check compiles its expression to a predicate and never materializes the set, and a listing is paginated — so this module gets slow before it gets wrong. The catalog mints nothing against it: no code governs expansion, and none could — whoever can write EVERYONE into an expression already holds audience.manage (§5a).
  • A grant's reach moves with the calendar, and there is no write to mark the moment. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are ordinary named operands composed by the same three operators as every other (§1), and they are the first whose membership changes with no write at all (D-107): a person turns eighteen, joins the set, and no row was touched — which is exactly why age bands, with the per-person expiry dates they would need, are not in this design. Nothing is invalidated, because nothing that depends on a person is stored: a check resolves, a request memoizes, and the only cached thing is a compilation of an expression root plus ruleset_version — bumped by writes to audience_operand and selector_type, the two tables whose rows change what an expression means, and holding no person and no item (D-114). A birthday, a period reaching its own valid_to, a registration write and a membership termination each move the answer at the instant they happen. What follows is open, and it is only the cost: nothing bounds such a check, because the bound this system had was a depth bound and D-105 deleted it, so an age-bearing expression is one more set to expand and it is bounded by nothing; that is F-21, and the catalog mints nothing against it: no code, no column, no number, no threshold. Whom a derived set reached is not a finding here. The preview a writer looked at is a workbench, never a record, and the record is the expression (D-110): the audit row says this person wrote these words, about this item, on this date, and what the preview printed beside it is logged as a rendering on a date, never as a statement of who was in it. Ask whom a grant reached in May and the model evaluates those words against the data of May: there is no list to read back, and these documents do not promise the answer. What that costs is named here rather than found sideways — an edit to a shared audience is a retrospective edit to every rule that names it — and the control is the editor printing the resolved set before such an edit saves. Why: this rests on a premise the organization supplied — that the people writing the rules know what they are doing — written down in D-107 with its two limits, and it is affordable only because nothing a rule names is deleted, so the words keep resolving (D-109).
  • audience.view carries no sensitivity mark, and the thing it shows is a list of people. A grant aimed at a name resolves through dated holder rows, group rosters and MEMBERS, and an expression containing EVERYONE resolves to the whole organization and beyond it. Whether reading a resolved expression needs a grade of its own — or whether person.view already covers it and the display is the leak to watch — is unsettled (§5a).
  • D-100 wrote its 1 January rule about an office, and on day one there is no office for it to fail in. The entry assumed an administrative office exists and is written without MEMBERS, so the expiry sweep of D-040 cannot lock the administrator out. Day one cannot be locked out, because it has no office: the one grant names one account rather than an expression, so there is no MEMBERS in it to add and none to forget, and the person who set the system up is still holding everything on 1 January (D-150). What moved is where the mistake can be made: it is now whoever first writes MEMBERS * ROLE(system_admin) "for consistency" (§11), and every office grant that will ever exist has been written by hand, since no grant arrives from anywhere carrying anything (§11). The January reason survives as a property of day one rather than as a rule about offices, and that is now the ruling and not a reading: the design states no default for MEMBERS in either direction (D-165).
  • Whether report.* should be per-report permissions or one report.view with row-level filtering.
  • Whether the organization has offices this catalog does not anticipate (a chaplain, a quartermaster, a camp chief). This is answerable by the organization itself rather than by a change to the data model and a migration — one role row and some grants — which is the point of roles being runtime data. Since D-098 the same is true of a set of people who simply do things together, and the two are told apart by which table they are in and therefore by which code protects them (§5a).
  • Which audiences the organization needs, and who may create a person_group — audience_admin is proposed, and it is an office rather than a unit leader's extra code now that there are no units (D-042, F-5). There are no kinds of audience — one expression language over named sets, no built-in versus named split and no filling rules (D-091, D-101) — so this is genuinely two questions: which selector_type operands the language has, which is thirteen and §1 prints the names, and who may create a group, which is person_group.create (§5a). Neither question is "which audiences ship", because none do. The two named audiences went and nothing replaces them: everything either one carried is written as an operand where the grant is written — EVERYONE for "every person", MEMBERS for "everyone holding a membership live on the checked date" — and an audience earns its row when somebody intends to name it (AUDIENCE(x)) (D-153). No operand names a person's guardians: the channel carries a level over a child, not a set (D-113), which closes the last part of F-5; and WHITELISTED, the one name with no stored state behind it, is refused rather than pending (D-148) and so is not a gap in the registry — no operand may be added for it, and nothing reserves its name.
  • Which office may put a person on a group's roster is not named, and the blank is the answer. D-167 rules that this stays unnamed on purpose, so that no later round repairs it as a hole: person_group.member.manage is the whole of the right to place a person in a set — one code, applies_to = unit_and_item, never self-scoped, and the only thing between a person and a roster (§5a, §11 property 6) — and on day one the only grantee that may write a roster is the one account holding system.admin at the unit. The catalog's side is settled; which volunteer office holds the code is the organization's decision to record as role rows and grant rows, for the reason §11 property 6 carries: an appendix that quietly hands it to leaders would be making a safeguarding choice on someone else's behalf. The cost sits in day one rather than in the schema — the first roster anybody builds is built by the account that must not be used day to day — and the relief is one role row and a grant, not a migration (D-154, D-100).
  • message.broadcast has one scope, and messaging has not ruled on what that means. There is one unit scope (D-097), so a broadcaster held there reaches everyone (D-077), and the narrower audience has to be a grant aimed at a person_group, which is a different shape of decision (who may create the group, and whether it is the broadcast grant or the group roster that carries the ⚠). §10 records it as messaging's call; the catalog has not silently re-specified it either way, including whether the code should become applies_to = unit_and_item.
  • membership.manage does not exist, and five places in these documents used it as their example. D-099 quotes the organization's own observation — "on an event, membership.manage, or event.create, make no sense" — the domain model and the authorization module each restate that sentence as the reason applies_to exists, and the events page carries a refusal row naming the code. This catalog has never registered it — membership acts are membership.activate, .lapse, .suspend, .terminate, .backdate and the request pair (§4) — and no code is minted here to make an example true: a refusal that names nothing refuses nothing, which is the class of bug D-097's unit_leaders correction exists to warn about. The five places now name membership.terminate, which is the exact fit and a registered code — a fact about a person at the unit that no event owns — found by the registry diff rather than by a reader (D-127); the organization's quoted words are left as they were spoken. Had the other branch been taken, the code would owe what every registered code owes: a right_kind, an applies_to, a ⛔ mark, and a row in §4. This was one instance of the gap D-104 closes as F-19: a code is a row that ships, this catalog is prose about rows, and the check adopted is a two-way report over the shipped registries, run by hand. D-104 supplied the grammar and the report; it did not re-point these five sentences, and that repair still belongs to whoever owns each of those pages.
  • The registered spelling of a code is this catalog's, and prose is prose. event.answer.view is singular — the code in §8a, one of the twelve grants §11 says are written beside every event, and no other spelling (../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §8 records how that was settled, and the catalog is the arbiter). The case that did not settle quietly is the finding worth carrying: a door-scanning capability was argued over at length and exists nowhere — not in this catalog, not in the events module, not in the ERD, not in the decision log — so nothing ever refused it, because since D-072 these documents are the specification and a permission legally exists only as a row in the shipped permission registry; the question that ends any such argument is which shipped row carries this? (D-104). What survives of it is §1's three rules, the two-way registry report D-104 adopts, and a presence story that is event.presence.mark and nothing more (§8a, D-067). If door scanning is ever wanted it arrives as an open question and then a decision entry naming the permission, the artifact that rotates and who may reprint it — not as a code beside a paragraph about a door.
  • attribute.define is in the catalog and in no office §11 works through, and that gap is now the whole of the open half. The permission and its rules are settled (§2), and so is the second half of what AT-2 asked: there is no proposal, so there is no age for a proposal to reach (D-141). Who holds the code is what remains — tracked as AT-2 in ../open-questions.md, and §11 property 7 records the shape the answer should take (a dated grant aimed at one person, not an office). The risk of leaving it unheld changed kind and got worse. While a proposal stage existed, an office without the permission was a slow leak: values arrived against invented codes, sat in a queue, and the vocabulary rotted while still storing everything. Now a value recorded against a code nobody has defined is refused at the write: an office that cannot name a new thing writes it into person.notes or does not write it at all, which is the exact failure the whole attribute layer exists to prevent, arriving as a wall rather than as a leak. The checks that notice a vocabulary rotting are in ../data-model/09-attributes.md §8, and none of them can fire on codes nobody was able to create. The import half is answered, and only that half: every code the legacy batch's column→code map names must already be defined and live when the batch applies, and an unmapped column stops the batch — so the vocabulary is authored before the import that looks like it produces it, and day one does not arrive with several hundred codes nobody has read (D-141, D-090, ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §7). Who writes those first few hundred definitions, and when, is a question this round raised rather than answered (F-34). Settled, so that nobody reopens them from the shape of this page. A grant carries one code, and there is neither a level nor a "nearest scope wins" ordering to pair with it (D-099); the unit is a scope and never a row (D-097); nothing owns an event (D-102); leadership is an office, not a position (D-100); PERSON(x) is in the selector language and LIST is not, and data-model/05a §8 is where the operand registry is written out in full, thirteen rows, each one either a rule about people or a row that takes an argument; presence is not a set anyone may be granted over (§1 carries the argument); a code's last segment is an action (§1, D-104).
