Every one of those is one entry in decisions/index.md, findable by number, and each entry names what enforces the rule now — which is the discipline D-081 states. What is open is the list above this paragraph, and nothing else in this file.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Appendix — Permission Catalog
docs.text:
Every permission code, its namespace, and the grant that carries it.

This is the proposed catalog. Its rows are the permission vocabulary, which arrives with the code; who holds any one of them is a grant row, and day one is one account holding system.admin and no other grant (../data-model/05d-invariants-and-seed.md §12, D-150).

What a row here is. A capability, and nothing more. There is no level paired with a code — D-099 deleted the ladder that paired them — so whoever grants it says how far it reaches, for how long, and to whom — in one row, whose grantee is one person, one registered key, or a set written as an expression (§1). And §1's two naming shapes are rules now, not descriptions of the rows below: the last segment names the action, a middle segment names something the schema stores, no grade words and no prefix — with system.admin named as the single exception (D-104).

Deliberately comprehensive and granular, and staying that way (D-055). This is a menu, not a checklist. Administrators assign people only the permissions they actually need; that is only possible if the capabilities exist as separate rows to assign. Further permissions arrive with the modules not yet specified — documents and communication. Events were on that list and are no longer: §8a carries their thirteen codes (§10).

This is the opposite disposition from roles, and the asymmetry is deliberate. Roles are runtime data the organization invents (D-052); permissions are capabilities the code implements. You cannot assign a power the data model cannot express, so a comprehensive permission catalog costs only rows — while a comprehensive role list would be a specification pretending to be data.

Codes are still stable identifiers: adding one is free, renaming one is a migration (§1). What is not yet settled is the exact contents — tracked in §12.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: permission-catalog.md holds §1, the conventions; permission-catalog-a-codes.md holds §2–§8b, the codes; permission-catalog-b-roles-and-open-issues.md holds §9–§12, the namespaces that are not here, the deferred ones, the worked examples of writing an office, and what is open.

docs.title: 1. Conventions
Code shape
docs.text:
<resource>.<action>               e.g.  person.edit
<resource>.<subresource>.<action> e.g.  event.answer.view

resource is always the first segment and matches permission.resource. Codes are stable identifiers — the display_name may change, the code may not. Renaming a code is a breaking change requiring a migration that rewrites every access_grant row naming it. Before D-100 the same migration also rewrote role_permission rows; that table is deleted, and a grant is now the only place a code is written down — which makes the rule smaller, not weaker.

Those two shapes are rules for adding a code, and since D-104 they are written here as rules rather than as a description of what is already in the tables below. As a description they arbitrated nothing: both readings of one disputed name fitted them exactly, and that dispute ended with the capability deleted rather than either spelling chosen (§12). Three rules, and the moment they cost nothing is the moment a code is added:

  1. The last segment names the action. Read the code on its own and ask what does this let me do? event.grant_access answers it; a noun-final code states an object instead. Since D-099 a grant permits exactly one thing, so a grant of an object would need a second sentence to say what it permits — and a second sentence is where a permission's real scope always hides.
  2. A middle segment names something the schema stores. answer is event_answer, presence is a column of event_registration, and contact, credential, member, participant and request are rows. A permission may not be built out of an artifact the database does not keep, because a grant has to be checkable against stored state and there is none to check against: the payment's QR code is exactly that artifact, and D-075 already ruled it a rendering of three stored facts rather than data. No code in this catalog spells qr, and none may (§12).
  3. No grade words, and no prefix. Not admin, all or everything, and not any code whose meaning is "every sibling under this prefix" — D-068 deleted sixteen of them and computed the wrong answer for the one it chose to exempt, dependent.admin — which D-074 then deleted too, for having no set left to stand for (the table further below). D-104 restates that decision as a rule about codes that have not been written yet, which is the only form of it that can still prevent anything.

One exception, named because a rule with an unnamed exception is a rumour: system.admin. Its last segment is not an action, and it stays. It survives because its meaning is defined by the resolver — checked outright, applies_to = unit, never reachable through an item grant (§7) — rather than read off its name, and because D-068 exempted it in so many words rather than by omission. It is the only code in this system allowed to be a noun, and the exemption sets no precedent: <resource>.admin is precisely what rule 3 refuses and precisely what was deleted.

The three rules were run against the sixty-six live codes the tables below held when D-104 ran them, and corrected nothing — sixty-five satisfy both tests, and the sixty-sixth is system.admin. Four codes have arrived since that count — the api_key.* rows of §8b — and they satisfy the three rules rather than testing them (D-122). That null result is the reason this section changed voice rather than its contents: a convention that is followed and not stated fails exactly once, on the first thing nobody thought to compare, and the thing this round failed on had never existed anywhere but in prose (§12). Nothing in the schema will ever notice a code drifting from its row — the check D-104 adopts is a person remembering to run a report over the seeded registries in both directions, which this repository can only ever do by hand (F-19).

This file is the only list of grantable codes, and both directions are decisions. A code minted while a decision is being propagated, and a code that simply stops appearing here, are the same mistake: a migration nobody decided. A decision entry that wants a code adds one to the table of the resource it acts on, in the same round; a decision entry that removes one leaves a row in removed-concepts.md.

docs.title: What a grant is
docs.text:
A grant is five things: a grantee (one person, one audience expression, or one registered key) + a scope (the unit, or exactly one item) + one permission code + effect ∈ allow, deny + a period. The answer it feeds:

allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. (D-099)

That is the whole of the precedence rule, and it is why nothing in this catalog carries a rank beside a code. Four things a rank used to promise, and what does each of them now:

  • Bundle several codes under one word — one grant row per code, and the bundle is a role or an audience (D-068), which is what roles are the bundle already said.
  • Grade one act at two strengths — two codes, with permission.right_kind ∈ read | write saying which side each sits on (§6).
  • Decide whether a grant is enough for the code being checked — nothing to decide: a grant names exactly one code and the answer is yes or no.
  • Order two grants that both apply — two allows produce one answer. Deny is absolute and is asked first (effect = deny on a grant row), which is D-032's surviving half and the whole of it.

So there is no word manage standing over a set of codes, and "what does manage give me on this event?" has no lookup to answer it; "what exactly does this person have?" is answered by reading their grant rows. The rank integer that ladder rested on is gone (D-012), along with the table that mapped levels onto codes — and the bug that table's guard existed for, 'admin' < 'contribute' comparing alphabetically and inverting the model, cannot occur where there are no levels, which is a better fix than the guard was.

Two columns moved onto permission itself, and only one of them is comfortable.

  • right_kind ∈ read | write survives only so that D-074's guardianship channel has something to compare a permission against now that the ladder is gone: none covers nothing, view covers read codes, write covers both. Nothing else in the system compares it. It is a column whose only job is one other mechanism, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it later (§6).
  • applies_to ∈ unit | unit_and_item is where a code may be granted at all, and it is checked when the grant is saved, not at check time: an item scope is refused for codes like event.create (an event cannot be created twice, so a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question) and membership.terminate (a membership is a fact about a person at the unit, not something an event owns). The example D-099 gives for the second half is membership.manage, and this catalog has never carried a code of that name — §12 records that rather than minting it. The system namespace is unit-only the same way, which is who enforces now for the old rule that system.admin can never arrive through an item grant (D-081).

Scope is two things, not a ladder. A grant at the unit — the organization, of which there is one, and which is a scope and never a row (D-097) — reaches every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. There is no tier between them and no relation on the item to test: no owner, no parent, no covering body.

docs.title: A grantee is a person, a key, or a set
docs.text:
A grant names exactly one grantee, and two of the three kinds are a single reference rather than an expression: one person, or one registered key (§8b, D-116) — each read exactly as written, with no set behind it and nothing to evaluate. The third kind is a set, and a set is always written as an expression, in the selector language of D-101: the leaves EVERYONE, MEMBERS, OLDER(n), YOUNGER(n), PERSON(person), ROLE(name), GROUP(name), AUDIENCE(name), and the five event-bound sets ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST, ORGANIZERS — each written with its argument spelled out, or bound to the item being checked (D-102) — combined with + union, - difference, * intersection, and brackets. * and - bind tighter than +, * and - bind equally with each other, left to right, and the stored form brackets every bracket anyway (../domain/06a-audiences-and-selectors.md §6.2), so (MEMBERS * OLDER(18)) - YOUNGER(6) is printed exactly as it is stored and nobody has to hold a precedence table to read a grant row.

Those leaves are the registry, not a sample of it, and the registry itself is the seeded selector_type rows: ../data-model/05d-invariants-and-seed.md §12 states them and counts them, once. The names are repeated here so a grant row can be read where it is written; a second page printing the count would only be a second thing to go stale.

A leaf outside that registry does not parse. Three things the language therefore does not have:

  • No comparison operator. There is no >=, no <, no bare AGE, so AGE >= 18 is not an expression and cannot become one: an operand must be a named row of selector_type, and there is nowhere in the grammar to put an operator between two things that are not sets. That clause — not any claim about what counts as a set — is what keeps eligibility rule engines out (D-060, as amended by D-107). It is not because an attribute differs in kind from a set: OLDER(18) is the set of people who are eighteen on the date checked exactly as MEMBERS is the set of people who pass is_current_member, and every operand in the registry is a test with a set behind it.
  • No hand-written set. A list of people typed into a rule is not a leaf and has no table of its own: it is a sum, PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) (D-105). Anything dated and shared is a person_group instead — a roster with a lifetime and an owner, rather than a second list the permission system keeps.
  • No guardian set. A guardian's authority is right_level ∈ none | view | write over a child (§6, D-074), entered by the shape of the request; the channel resolves no sets, so GUARDIANS is not a selector in either spelling and no expression names one child's guardians (D-113).

Two leaves move with the calendar. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) read person.birth_date as of the date the check is made, so a person joins or leaves one of those sets with no write of any kind — and a check asked about a past date answers for that past date. Exactly these two, and no others: the other dated operands, ROLE, GROUP and AUDIENCE, move when somebody makes a write with a date on it. Nothing is stored about the answer, so there is nothing to invalidate; a check resolves against live rows, and a birthday moves an age set at the instant it happens, with no job standing between the two (D-114). What that costs this catalog is one sentence it used to be able to write — this is cheap because it is cached. What it says instead is what a check actually reads: one indexed read of the checked person's grant rows per request, plus two batch reads for the shapes that need them, can_many(person, codes[], item?) for a screen's affordances and which_of(people[], code, item) for a list's people. No table changes when a person turns eighteen, so there is no row to expire — which is the property age bands would not have had, and why bands are not in this design.

The record is the expression. The editor's preview is a workbench: an audit row logs the words, and a preview is logged as a rendering on a date, never as a statement of who was in it (D-110, §12).

So event.answer.view on an event is aimed at ORGANIZERS, an open camp is opened by MEMBERS, a gated office is MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers), and the exemption for one named person is (MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)) + PERSON(jan) — a second grant aimed at that person is the other way to write the same thing, and it keeps the exception off the expression everyone else reads.

Three refusals belong next to the language, because each is a temptation this catalog creates. None of them is refused on a type argument: a selector may be a hard-coded computation in the resolver, because MEMBERS is one, and an operand may read a column against a date, because OLDER(n) does. Nothing is kept out of the registry for what it is, so every refusal here is an argument about consequences.

  • PRESENT(<event>) is not seeded, on the argument that always carried it: was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register, so an operand over it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos — a leader's access to their own camp — because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. Presence stays a three-valued safeguarding signal (D-067), and nowhere in this file is it a set anyone may be granted over. Nothing in the grammar would stop anybody adding it, which is exactly why the consequence has to be the thing that says no.
  • WHITELISTED is not seeded because there is nothing stored to evaluate (F-20): an operand with no argument, nothing bound to the checked item and no column behind it is a word pointing at a state this system does not keep. The feature it was wanted for arrives as grants anyway, and the events question it was handed to is now answered: refused, with no column, no fifth presence tier and no reserved name (D-148, F-20).
  • A bare name is one namespace across roles and groups (D-101), which makes §11's office names a load-bearing vocabulary and makes every selector code a reserved name: an office called MEMBERS is refused when it is saved, and so is one called OLDER or YOUNGER. It is the parser that refuses them, not a review, which is what keeps OLDER(18) from ever meaning an office with that name.

docs.title: There is no wildcard, except system.admin
docs.text:
Every capability in this catalog is narrow and explicit. A check for X.y is satisfied by an exact grant of X.y — or by system.admin, which is checked outright and is the only permission in the system that means everything.

A check for 'X.y' is satisfied by: an exact grant of 'X.y', OR 'system.admin'.

There are no per-resource admin permissions. The earlier convention that every resource should expose an <resource>.admin subsuming its narrower codes — a prefix match computed in the resolver — was reversed by D-068, which also deleted the resolver branch that implemented it.

"Someone who can do everything about events" is a role, not a permission — the organization composes it from the thirteen event.* codes. That is the division D-052 already drew: the code implements capabilities, the organization groups them. A per-resource admin was the code guessing at a bundle on the organization's behalf. Since D-100 the composition is literal: a role confers nothing, so the bundle is thirteen live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) — thirteen rows you can read, which is what D-068 was reaching for.

The cost, because it is real. A new narrow permission is not automatically covered by the offices that should imply it; someone must write the grant row. Integrity check 18 is the safety net the wildcard used to be — it lists permissions no live grant names, which is what a missed bundle looks like now that no role carries a permission list of its own. It fails closed: a capability goes unheld and somebody says so, rather than a capability going unmeant and nobody saying so.

docs.title: Two things named "admin", which are not the same thing
docs.text:
Two meanings survive in this catalog, and they are not the same one:

  • system.admin is the one wildcard permission: everything, carried by a grant at the unit and never on an item (applies_to = unit). It is the only code in this system allowed to end in a noun — exempted by name in words by D-068 and named as an exception by D-104, because its meaning is defined by the resolver rather than read off the name. It is not a precedent (§1).
  • .admin is not an action in this catalog. §1's first naming rule is that the last segment names an action (D-104), and admin is a grade word rather than an act: no code here pairs read against admin, and the rule refuses the spelling in codes that have not been written yet. What a bundle of codes is for, a role does (§1).

Every other thing that spelled admin — a grant level, a per-resource wildcard, a shorthand over a guardian's capabilities — is gone and is indexed in removed-concepts. Two of those deletions are worth reading together before reinstating anything that spells the word: D-068 refused a wildcard per resource but deliberately kept one stored shorthand, and D-074 withdrew that exemption when the set it stood for went away — the reasoning about wildcards never changed, the thing it was a value of did.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Namespace Resolved against Channel (absent) access_grant — aimed at a person, at an audience expression, or at a registered key — and ownership 1, 3 system access_grant at the unit only — applies_to = unit, so never on an item 1

Two namespaces, because only two things are dispatched by a name — and the four api_key.* codes of §8b are ordinary codes in the row above, not a third one: their first segment already names a stored table, so a prefix would be a second, drifting copy of a name the code carries. The channel numbers are the three in ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §1: grants, guardianship, ownership. Every code in this catalog — system.admin included — arrives through the one grant channel, because an office confers nothing by being held (D-100) and there is no second route to a code. What keeps a system code out of an item grant is applies_to, checked when the grant is saved (D-081), not the shape of a channel that could carry it: system.admin must never reach a single event, a group or an office.

There is no dependent namespace (§9, D-074): a guardian's rights are one value on the guardianship row, and the guardianship.* codes of §6 administer that row from the grant side — a resource namespace like any other, not the guardianship channel.

Which leaves the guardianship channel with no prefix to dispatch on, which has to be said rather than left implied. It routes on a fact about the request instead of a fact about the name: the channel is consulted whenever the person the action is about differs from the person performing it. That holds the invariant the prefix was standing in for — no caller chooses a channel, because a caller who chooses one is the same authorization rule written twice, once correctly — and it holds it more widely: under a prefix rule, a guardian asking to change their child's address with a person.contact.edit code did not route through guardianship at all, because the code did not carry the right prefix. Nobody chooses; the shape of the request selects.

The guardianship.* codes are additionally satisfiable by being a party to the row, and not only by a grant (D-073).

docs.title: Sensitivity marker
docs.text:
The Sens. column flags permissions that need extra care:

Mark Meaning ⚠ Granting it exposes personal data ⚠⚠ Granting it exposes children's personal data — or the same about an adult, where the code reads a whole person record rather than one field of it. Since D-083 there is no separate health data class to name: the mark grades what a grant exposes, not which field the code points at 🔒 Granting it confers authority over the permission system itself 🔒🔒 The escalating half of that family: granting it changes what other people can do, not merely what the holder can do. role.* is marked this way in D-100, which names it "the most sensitive code family in the catalog" ⛔ Granting it can end someone's membership or standing

These marks should drive UI warnings, and they are what the reports in ../data-model/05d-invariants-and-seed.md are read with — a mark is on the screen somebody opens, because nothing in this design sends anything to anybody (D-164). A mark grades what a grant exposes, not the table a code names (D-086), and the two families a reader is most likely to place wrongly are placed by it: person_group.member.manage takes ⚠ because a roster is a list of people, and role.* keeps 🔒🔒 because writing a holder row writes who may hold everything else.

docs.title: Removed Concepts
docs.text:
A lookup for names that are not in the model. Every spec page states the design as it is now and carries no history, so this is the one page where a dead name is written down — with what it was, why it went, and the decision that took it. The argument is in the decision log; the row here is only an index to it.

Read it when a word from an older draft, another system, or a conversation does not appear anywhere in these pages. The organization may still use the word — a removal from the model is not a removal from its vocabulary.

Name What it was Why it went Use instead Decision account.guardian_consent_at the moment a guardian consented to a child's account — a column on the login, with no age threshold defined anywhere in the corpus to compare it against an account is a login, and nothing about a child is decided on it: no minimum age, no consent step, no branch in the sign-up path. A column that looks like a gate where no gate is wanted is worse than the absence, because somebody comes to rely on it the guardianship row (data-model/04 §2) if the organization ever wants a guardian's answer written down; the jurisdictional half is the legal review's fourth policy D-166 audience_include, include_depth_limit a stored edge putting one permission group inside another, and the cap on how deep those edges could nest arms became operands and + composes inside one grant, so membership of a set is now written where it is used GROUP(x) + GROUP(y), or name the composite once as a saved audience D-101 audience_member the audience's own hand-typed list of people, with per-person dates and an adder a hand-written set is a sum of PERSON() leaves like any other set, and the list was a second roster the permission system owned PERSON(a) + PERSON(b); for anything dated and shared, a person_group D-105 everyone, all_members the two audiences the platform shipped: one whose whole expression was EVERYONE, one whose whole expression was MEMBERS, each named so a grant could point at it, each marked not editable by a screen a name over a one-operand expression is worth a row only if somebody is going to name it, and naming is one row a person writes when they have a reason; the editor refusals that guarded them guarded a category that does not need a flag — an expression is not a member list, and there is no audience_member table to add somebody to the operand written directly in the grant's expression: EVERYONE, MEMBERS; a named audience is one someone writes, and AUDIENCE(x) is what makes a name worth having D-153 dependent.*, guardianship_permission eighteen per-capability codes on a guardian: a read and an act spelling over each of eight resources — profile, contact, membership, event, fee, medical, achievement, document — plus dependent.admin over the lot, each its own row one right per guardianship row, compared against permission.right_kind; the granular split was declined, not left unbuilt right_level ∈ none / view / write on guardianship D-074 background_check, person.background_check.*, and with them the identity_hypothesis.proposed_by value background_match the system's record of whether an adult had been checked, and the name the nightly batch matcher's row went by while that record existed outside the system's remit: it records the appointment, not the vetting behind it nothing in the model; the organization keeps that outside D-043 can_event() a wrapper around can() that called it twice and added an event-shaped clause: the holder of a unit-level event permission reached every event nothing owns an event, so there was no unit authority to extend; docs.title: The codes that left the catalog
docs.text:
A code is a stable identifier, so one leaving the catalog silently is a migration nobody decided. The tables in the catalog hold only codes that can be granted today; these were granted, and here is where their act is performed now.

Code The act Where the act is now Decision ~~org_unit.view~~ the list of units, and the "which units exist" report Nowhere. The unit is a scope, not a row: there is no list to read D-097 ~~org_unit.create~~ creating a unit Nowhere, and nothing needs creating — the unit arrives as a code in grant_scope_type, not as data D-097 ~~org_unit.edit~~, ~~org_unit.rename~~ renaming what a body is called person_group.edit, and it is cheap: a grant and an expression store kind + id, never a name, so a rename rewrites nothing D-097, D-101 ~~org_unit.restructure~~ splitting, merging and succeeding a unit Nowhere, and the loss is stated once in D-097: a group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them unless somebody writes one D-097 ~~org_unit.close~~ ending a unit person_group.end — which ends a set, and is graded accordingly D-097 ~~position.view~~, ~~position.assign~~ seeing a body's slots; appointing somebody into one role.view and role.assign (catalog §7). An elected leader is a holder of a role, and the audience rule that used to read unit_leaders is ROLE(leaders) D-100 ~~unit_participation.view~~, ~~unit_participation.manage~~ seeing and writing one sub-unit's participants membership.view for the organization (one query, no depth), person_group.view and person_group.member.manage for a group. D-095's discipline transfers intact: never self-scoped, the write is somebody else's act, the report is the control D-097, D-098 ~~membership.transfer~~ moving a member between units person_group.member.manage — close one dated row, open another — and it does not touch the membership at all. Obsolete twice over: D-041 moved unit belonging into a participation row, and D-097 deleted that D-041, D-097 ~~guardianship.permission.grant~~ granting a guardian individual capability codes there was no namespace to grant from: a guardian's rights are one value with three choices guardianship.change_right

Two habits this page is meant to prevent. Naming a removed thing in a spec page, which is what put the history back into the pages this appendix exists to keep clean; and re-adding one quietly, which is why every row ends in a decision — a concept comes back by a decision entry, or it does not come back.

Decisions behind this page: D-001, D-037, D-038, D-040, D-041, D-043, D-044, D-050, D-057, D-063, D-068, D-074, D-083, D-095, D-096, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-104, D-105, D-113, D-114, D-150, D-151, D-152, D-153, D-154.

docs.title: Data Model Conventions
docs.text:
Read this before reading any other document in this folder. Every entity in this system is described using the patterns here, and the patterns are load-bearing — deviating from them in one table creates bugs that only appear across decades of history.

What this file is, since D-072. It used to be the preamble to a set of CREATE TABLE statements. Those statements are gone — the schema is the ORM's job — and what remains is the part that was never about SQL: the rules about time, identity, deletion and rank that a generated schema will happily violate without noticing. Nothing here is a suggestion. A convention in this folder is a bug that has already happened somewhere, written down.

docs.title: 1. Target platform
docs.text:
Assumption: PostgreSQL 14+, reached through an ORM.

The design relies on four things from the platform, and it is worth being exact about which four, because an ORM hides the list:

  • Range types with an overlap operator (daterange, tstzrange, &&) — for the "no overlapping periods" invariants that the whole temporal model depends on.
  • Exclusion constraints (EXCLUDE USING gist, with btree_gist) — the only way to state "no two open rows may overlap" that survives every possible writer.
  • A structured column type (jsonb) — for match signals, audit diffs, event answers and other semi-structured payloads whose shape is per-row by design.
  • Recursive queries — for the unit hierarchy. Note that this one is only for structure: no authorization path may walk the hierarchy (../domain/06-authorization-model.md).

Native enum types are avoided — see §5.

What the ORM changes, and what it must not be allowed to change: see §6a. Read it before generating the first migration. The short version is that most ORMs cannot emit an exclusion constraint, and the fallback they offer — validation in the model layer — is precisely the mechanism this document has always warned against. Hand-written migrations for those tables are not a deviation from "use the ORM", they are the condition on which it is safe.

If the target turns out not to be PostgreSQL, exclusion constraints become triggers plus periodic consistency reports. That is a materially weaker guarantee and it must be recorded as an accepted decision, not discovered as an outage. Tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: 2. Naming
docs.text:
Object Convention Example Table snake_case, singular person, membership_request Column snake_case valid_from, person_id Primary key id always the same name, so joins read uniformly Foreign key <referenced_table_singular>_id person_id → person.id Boolean is_ / has_ / requires_ prefix is_delegated, binds_to_item Timestamp <verb>_at created_at, verified_at Date/period valid_from / valid_to never start_date/end_date Junction table <a>_<b> in alphabetical order guardianship_permission, not permission_guardianship. (The example here was audience_member for ten rounds, which was a better illustration because its two halves are further apart alphabetically; the table is deleted by D-105, and a naming convention should not be taught with a table that does not exist.) Lookup table singular of the vocabulary it is selector_type, grant_scope_type Index names the table and what it answers "the open rows for one person", not idx_3

Singular table names are not aesthetic. membership reads correctly in a sentence about one row, which is how most of this system's rules are written; plural table names produce code that says memberships[0].membership_id and reviewers stop reading it.

There is no deleted_at column. Deletion is handled by temporal closure and tombstones, never by a soft-delete flag — see §4.

Naming survives the move to an ORM; it is the one section of this file that the ORM will follow without being told, provided someone wrote these rules into the ORM's own conventions.

docs.title: 3. Primary keys
docs.text:
Every table has a surrogate id. No natural keys as primary keys, ever.

Rationale specific to this project: natural keys here are things like names, old member numbers, and email addresses — all of which change, repeat, and get corrected. A name is not unique (and was less so in 1994). An email address is reused by providers and reassigned between people. A legacy member number may be absent, or duplicated across two source systems. A natural key that turns out to be wrong is a key that must be rewritten, and a rewritten primary key rewrites every historical reference beside it.

The surrogate key is a 64-bit integer, not 32-bit, because this system accumulates rows for decades and because access_grant.scope_id must never run out of room or recycle.

Exception, and it is a security requirement: person.public_id — a separate UUID column, used for every external exposure.

Rationale: access_grant.scope_id is a bare bigint with no foreign key, and ids appear in URLs and exports. Sequential ids leak record counts and — more seriously — let someone enumerate /person/1001, /person/1002 and discover members. Expose public_id in all external interfaces; keep id internal. An ORM that marshals entities by primary key has, by default, published the internal counter.

docs.title: 4. Deletion policy
docs.text:
Nothing is hard-deleted. There is no deleted_at and no delete for business data. Three exceptions are named below — a staging truncate, one delete that erasure has to make, and one trail that ends on a clock — and each is narrow enough to prove the rule rather than erode it. **Two of the three reach no business row anyone would miss — a staging table between two batches, and a trail of reads — and the one that does reach a person's values does it for the only reason that has ever justified deleting anything: they asked.

Situation Mechanism A period ended Set valid_to A person left the organization Close their membership; the person row remains A grant revoked Set access_grant.valid_to; keep the row Two people merged Tombstone: set merged_into_person_id; row remains A group ended Set person_group.valid_to; its member rows remain An access_log row passes 24 months Deleted, by a scheduled job — the third exception below. The only rows in this design that age out, and the only ones that ever did GDPR-style erasure requested Redact field values; do not delete rows — see §8. One table is deleted rather than redacted; the exception below names it and why

This is not nostalgia. Historical foreign keys — "who attended this camp in 2003" — must resolve forever. A hard delete breaks the audit trail and, in a youth organization, the safeguarding record.

The first exception: staging tables (staging_import*) may be truncated after a batch is applied, subject to the project's retention policy.

The second exception is not convenience and it should be read as a decision, not an oversight. Redacting a person deletes their person_attribute rows (§8 item 2). Everywhere else in this file, erasure means overwriting a value and keeping the row, because the row is what old references point at. A descriptive value is the one thing that has no row worth keeping: the row is the value — there is no period that closed, no assignment that ended, no id another table cites. Blanking the value instead would leave the shape of a person's erased life behind as a permanent record of it: which codes they had, how many of each, and the dates they were first recorded. Retiring the code is not the answer either, and D-084 is explicit that retirement must never destroy values — retirement is an act about the vocabulary, erasure is an act about the person, and the two point in opposite directions on purpose (09-attributes.md §6). This exception is safe only while nothing references an attribute row, and nothing still does. The candidate this paragraph named arrived in round 20: an event question may now be bound to a stored value (D-139), and it was designed around this rule rather than discovering it. The binding names a definition, never a value row — event_question.bound_attribute_code points at attribute_definition.code, which is never deleted and is retired instead, and so outlives the person whose values sit under it. That is what keeps the delete invisible: there is no edge for §9 to walk. A reference from any table to a person_attribute row id remains forbidden by this paragraph, and would have to be argued for against it, not merely written.

The third exception is a trail, and it is the newest. D-145 confirms what 05c §9 had only proposed: an access_log row older than 24 months is deleted, by a scheduled job, because that is what the organization decided its access trail is worth. It is an exception in the shape this section wants: no business row is touched, no table holding a person's record is in its scope, it moves only forward from a row's own write, and it is one named job — system:log-reduction in §7a, with a check counting the rows that should have gone and are still there. audit_log is not in its scope and keeps the opposite shape (D-088): rows for the life of the system, payloads emptied. Read "append-only" in this corpus as no application writes or removes these rows, which is what it always protected — not as a promise that a row survives its own retention window. What the two trails answer differs after the window, and nothing pretends otherwise: what was changed is answerable forever, what was read stops being answerable at two years.

This rule is now carried entirely by discipline, and that is worth saying out loud. A ON DELETE RESTRICT default, a revoke of DELETE from the application role, an ORM whose delete method nobody has ever called — those were enforcement. What remains is an instruction to whoever configures the ORM: deleting business rows is not a feature this system has. Do not wire a "remove" button to an ORM delete call. The audit log will not save you, because it records changes to rows that still exist.

docs.title: 5. Enumerations
docs.text:
Status vocabularies are text with an allowed-value list, not the database's native enum type.

Why, given that native enums are more compact:

  • Adding a value to a native enum is easy; removing or reordering one is painful, and over a 40-year lifespan a status vocabulary will be revised.
  • Native enum ordering is baked in, and the order of states here is meaningful — and it is not the order the type would infer (see below).
  • An allowed-value list is visible in schema introspection and in every migration tool, which makes review and diffing straightforward.

The rule, in the words D-072 left behind when it took the CREATE TABLE and CHECK syntax out: the vocabulary lives with the entity, the values are closed, and the vocabulary is reviewable without reading application code.

docs.title: Critical rule: status strings are ordered, and the order is not alphabetical
docs.text:
Several status columns have a meaningful progression, and code must compare by rank, never by string. Read this as a rule about the next ordered column you add: the vocabulary it was written for — revoked, view, contribute, manage, admin, ranked inside the strings — is gone, because D-099 made a grant name one permission code whose effect is allow or deny. The mistake generalizes and the vocabulary did not. Comparing strings ranked admin below contribute — full control including granting access, under read and add — with no error, no failed test and no log line (D-012).

And the survivor is the dangerous shape, not the safe one. One ordered vocabulary is left: a guardian's right over a child is none, view, or write (D-074). Those three words happen to sort alphabetically in exactly the intended order — none < view < write — so a string comparison here passes every test you can write today, and breaks silently the first time somebody adds a fourth value in the middle of the scale. The old bug at least announced itself on the first comparison; this one is a trap set for whoever extends the list. So:

  • Never compare the right to itself as a string. Ask whether the permission being checked is a read or a write (permission.right_kind, D-099) and whether the guardian's right covers that kind. The comparison is against a column on the permission, not between two words.
  • One comparison, one column. There is no master scale that a guardian's right is a slice of, and adding a second way to rank rights is how a guardian ends up able to do more than the adult who holds the grant.

When adding any new ordered vocabulary, ask the same two questions this section has always asked: is it data with a stored rank, or is it this rule wearing a name — and if it is data, does a string comparison of it happen to look correct?

docs.title: 6. The temporal pattern
docs.text:
The pattern behind every period in this system.

entity
  id
  the thing the period is about        e.g. person_id
  valid_from    DATE        NOT NULL
  valid_to      DATE        NULL       -- NULL = still true
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL

docs.title: The four rules
docs.text:
1. valid_to IS NULL means "still true". Not a far-future sentinel date. A sentinel like '9999-12-31' looks convenient and breaks every "is open" check, every range query, and every index on open rows. Do not use one.
  2. Periods are half-open [valid_from, valid_to). A membership ending 2010-06-30 and another starting 2010-06-30 do not overlap. Closed intervals make adjacent periods collide, and you will spend a day debugging it. This rule is invisible in a schema and cannot be inferred from column names; it must be written in whatever the ORM uses to express such a thing, and tested.
  3. Overlap is prevented below the application, not inside it. An import script, a manual data fix, a future API, and a bulk edit all bypass model-layer validation. The invariant must hold for writers that were never written. → §6a.
  4. created_at is audit time, not world time. It is distinct from valid_from — a membership backdated to 1990 during a 2026 import has valid_from = 1990-09-01 and created_at = 2026-…. Never conflate them, and never derive one from the other. A system that sets valid_from from the clock cannot import its own history.

docs.title: Why days, not timestamps
docs.text:
DATE granularity is correct for most periods here: memberships, guardianships, unit assignments, fees and exposures start and end on days. Timestamps invite timezone-dependent boundary bugs on questions like "was this person a member on 1 June?".

Where sub-day precision genuinely matters — session validity, a delegation in force during one meeting — the same pattern uses timestamps. Both patterns exist in this system; each entity states which one it uses, because a comparison between the two is where the boundary bugs live.

docs.title: Indexing the pattern
docs.text:
Two access paths carry the load and both must exist when the schema is generated:

  • One entity's periods, newest first — the history view.
  • The open periods for one entity — restricted to rows with no valid_to. This is the index that matters. "Currently active" is the overwhelmingly common question, it stays small because open rows are a small fraction of history, and it is the one an ORM will not create on its own, because it is not an index on a column combination the model declares — it is an index with a condition. If your migrations do not contain a filtered index, nobody thought about this.

docs.title: 6a. Who enforces an invariant now
docs.text:
This section exists because the constraints live in migrations now, which moved a responsibility — and a moved responsibility that nobody names is a responsibility nobody holds.

Every data-model document in this folder states its rules as prose: "no two open rows may overlap", "at most one primary contact", "a revoked grant must name who revoked it". Prose does not reject a row. Three layers could do it, and they are not equivalent:

Layer Survives an import? Survives a manual fix? Survives a second client? Model-layer validation in the ORM No No No Migration-level database constraint Yes Yes Yes Nightly consistency report Yes, eventually Yes, eventually Yes, eventually

The rule for this system, stated once and applied everywhere: an invariant that is a correctness property of the data belongs in the database, emitted by a migration, even when the ORM cannot generate it and the migration must be written by hand. Model-layer validation is a usability feature — it produces a good error message before a round trip — and it is not an invariant. The nightly report is a safety net for the invariants that were never expressible as a constraint at all, and each document's "Invariants to verify" section is exactly that list.

Three consequences that are easy to get wrong:

  1. The overlap invariants need hand-written migrations on PostgreSQL. Most ORMs cannot emit an exclusion constraint over a range built from two columns. Writing those twenty-odd lines once, per temporal table, is cheaper than the alternative — which is duplicate open rows discovered in 2031 by someone who cannot tell which one was ever real.
  2. Uniqueness that depends on a condition needs a partial unique index. "One open request per person and type", "one primary contact among current rows", "one live allow per grantee, scope and permission" are all this shape. A unique constraint over the unconditioned columns is not the same rule and is usually wrong in the direction of too strict — it forbids the second closed row, which history requires. The predicate is the rule, not a comment on it: three indexes differing only in a predicate are three rules, and copying one and editing the table names is how a wrong one ships.
  3. Uniqueness decided by data cannot live in an index at all. identifier_scheme.is_unique says per scheme whether a value may repeat (01a-accounts-and-contacts.md §7); no index can consult a row of a different table. This one is genuinely application-level plus a report, and it is documented as such rather than being pretended away. The earlier version of that document had the opposite bug — an index that applied to every scheme, ignoring the flag and making school_id unrepeatable in fact. The report this consequence promises is 01b §10's duplicate-identifier count, which D-130 added: the paragraph had promised it since it was written and no page contained it.
  4. Which of the three layers, for which rule, is answered once — in 00a, not here. Four shapes, one layer each: a temporal exclusion is a hand-written constraint, a conditioned uniqueness is a partial index, a rule that reads another table is the write path with a named report beneath it, and a value that may never change has nothing automatic behind it and says so. Where a register row and the page it cites disagree, the page is wrong (D-129), because the register holds nothing but the three facts a page is allowed to leave implicit — and a fourth copy of a rule is the thing this corpus keeps getting wrong.

And the honest cost, stated in D-072's own terms: some rules now have no enforcement anywhere automatic can reach. They are written as invariants to verify and they will catch drift only if someone runs them. A prohibition nobody runs is a convention, not a guard — and this repository has no build step to run one, so the check that could be automated is a script run by hand (D-127). What changed in round 18 is that running it is now part of finishing a round rather than a habit someone either has or does not, and that its findings are kept in a file, so the difference between "checked" and "read once and accepted" is something a reader can look up.

docs.title: 7. Standard columns
docs.text:
Every business table carries:

Column Kind Purpose id 64-bit surrogate key Set by the database, never by the caller created_at timestamp, required Audit time of insert created_by person, optional Who inserted. Absent for the writers that have no row of their own — the sweeps, payload reduction, migrations — and an empty one of these is read as this system acting on its own (§7a, D-125). An import batch is not one of them: import_batch.created_by is required there (06a §3), so the page that carries imports already names a person. A row an integration wrote is not one of them either: the audit trail names the key there, and no person is inferred from it (D-121). updated_at timestamp, optional Audit time of last change updated_by person, optional Who last changed it import_batch_id import batch, optional Set on imported rows — the only way to undo a bad import

Temporal entities additionally carry valid_from / valid_to.

Entities that record a decision about a person (terminations, rejections, rejections of identity hypotheses) additionally carry a reason:

Column Kind <verb>_reason text, required where the act needs a why — a value somebody types, not a row of a table (D-128) <verb>_reason_note text, for the long explanation a reason field is too short for

Reason codes are a lookup table, not free text. "Why was this membership terminated?" must be reportable and comparable across years. Free text is not. The note exists so the code does not have to carry the nuance, and a decision with a code and no note is fine while the reverse is not.

updated_at and updated_by were maintained by a database trigger. With the schema generated, nothing maintains them unless someone says so — and an ORM that sets them only on the paths the application happens to take gives you an audit trail that is silently incomplete. Either maintain them at the database level or accept that updated_at means "last changed through the app". Do not leave it undecided; an audit column nobody thinks about is worse than no audit column, because people rely on it.

api_key.created_by is required, and it is the one column of this shape in the authorization module that is never blank. Installing a permanent outside authority is the most sensitive write that module offers, and a key nobody is answerable for is exactly what this file's posture refuses. The line above about jobs does not reach it, because no job installs a key: a person installs a key, and a key never installs one — api_key.create is among the codes a key may never be granted (05e-keys-and-callers.md §15, D-122). Required is not inherited: the column says who performed the install and nothing else, and a key outlives that person with its authority untouched (D-120).

docs.title: 7a. What an empty actor column means
docs.text:
Stated here once, because four pages used to state it their own way and round 16 proved they would drift. D-125.

An actor column left empty is read as this system acting on its own, and that is a complete answer to "who did this". Not a missing answer and not a forensic gap. It applies to access_log.actor_person_id (05c §9), to audit_log.actor_person_id (06 §2), and to the standard created_by and updated_by above. Since round 16 a machine that calls in from outside is not in this reading: it is a row, in api_key_id, and an empty actor column now means the writers that have no row — the sweeps, the reductions, the migrations.

Two limits, because a rule about actors stated as a rule about NULLs gets misread everywhere.

  • Only where empty is legal. import_batch.created_by is required (06a §3), api_key.created_by is required (D-116), and a grant's granted_by names a person. Those rows have no empty to interpret.
  • Only in an actor column. An absent scope_id is a check at the unit; an absent authorization_ref_id is no grant involved; an absent subject_person_id is an action about nobody's record. None of them is the system.

And where the trail has a label column, the label comes from this list. It is the one place a writer's name is written down, so a row nobody recognizes has something to be compared against — the vocabulary is what turns "the system" from a shrug into a claim.

The label Who wrote the row What it was doing there system:renewal-sweep the 1 January renewal sweep Expiring memberships whose window closed — and nothing else; a guardianship's valid_to is never set by a job (04 §1) system:payload-reduction payload reduction Emptying old_values and new_values once a row passes the payload window (D-088) system:log-reduction the access trail's age-out Deleting access_log rows once they pass their 24 months (D-145). Added in round 20 and not cosmetic: a job that removes rows has to be nameable, and an empty actor column that could equally be the renewal sweep or a migration is not an answer to who deleted my access history. Not to be confused with system:payload-reduction above, which empties columns of the other trail and deletes nothing system:bank-pull the bank statement fetch The bank_transaction and payment rows that answer a variable symbol (D-075). For the run with nobody in the room — a fetch someone performs from a screen names that person instead, and whether anyone ever performs it this way is not decided here; what is decided is whose rows they are when nobody does migration:<id> a named migration Any structural change, and any one-off correction — a fix that is not in a migration is a fix nobody can attribute import_batch:<id> a run of the import pipeline Not anonymous and never was: import_batch.created_by names the person who uploaded the file

Bare system is not one of them. It means "one of the above, and I am not saying which", which is the drift the vocabulary exists to stop (D-125). A writer that is not on the list joins the list on this page before it writes, and 06b §5 reports any row whose label is not here.

What this costs, and what it does not do. Nothing in the database refuses an off-list label: this is a documented vocabulary, not a table, so the enforcement is a report and a review. A row written by a one-off script that guessed at a label from this list will therefore look legitimate, which is the honest downside of choosing no column over a system_writer registry (D-125 refused that registry, and refused a secretless kind of api_key). And the empty column carries attribution only. Nothing in a permission check reads one, which is the same rule that already forbids reading a key's last_used_at to decide an answer (check 22) — so this is not the nullable-whose-absence-silently-means-something that §2 of the authorization model warns about, because its meaning is written down in one place instead of inferred in four.

docs.title: 8. Personal data and erasure
docs.text:
This system holds data about children, which raises the stakes on every decision here.

Requirements the design must satisfy:

  1. A deletion request must not destroy the audit trail. Implement as redaction: set person.redacted_at, overwrite names and contact points with a redaction marker, and keep the row and its ids so historical references still resolve. The person is no longer identifiable; the record that someone was in Troop 12 in 2003 survives.
  2. Redaction must cascade. It reaches contact points, identifiers, and free-text notes that may contain personal data — and it deletes every person_attribute row belonging to the person (09-attributes.md §6). That is the one place in this system where erasure deletes rather than overwrites, and §4 says why it is the only row that can be handled that way. A redacted person with attribute values attached is a redaction that did not happen. A redaction_log records what was redacted and when. It also reaches an event's answers, and there it overwrites rather than deletes: an event_answer row belonging to a redacted person has its value emptied and the row remains (D-140). The two shapes are one decision, not an inconsistency: a descriptive value has no row worth keeping because the row is the value, while an answer is a fact that a question was answered on a dated occasion, and that fact belongs partly to the event. event_registration is not in either shape: whether a person came is organizational history under item 3, and this is stated because D-147 declined to make it a record class of its own.
  3. Some data must not be redacted, and the reason is now stated rather than left unopposed — membership periods, unit participations, fee obligations, payments and position assignments are organizational history rather than personal data, and removing them would falsify records that the organization is often obliged to keep. Until D-088 this item was a carve-out nobody had had to defend; it is now the permanent half of a pair of clocks, and those rows carry no retention period at all. That is what gives redaction_log.retained_reason a judgement worth recording instead of a formality (06-audit-and-import.md §4). What the decision did not do is supply a legal basis, and the difference should not be blurred: what stands here is an assumption pending review — organizational history plus accounting obligations, leaning on a person row that the erasure in item 1 has made non-identifying — recorded as an assumption and not as settled law. The uncertainty about that half reaches nothing on this side: the erasure in items 1 and 2 is immediate and absolute, and would be if the retained half were cut to a single year tomorrow.
  4. Whatever keeps its own retention policy must be able to see person.redacted_at, and erasure reaching it is a rule that store has to implement. There is no separate health or safeguarding store for such a rule to live in: a diagnosis is an attribute value now, with the same access, protection and retention as a shoe size (D-083, 09-attributes.md). The store this system does have is audit_log, and this item is worth keeping precisely because it is easy to wave through: its retention has half an answer — the rows are kept for the life of the system and their payloads are emptied 24 months after they are written (D-088; 06-audit-and-import.md §6 keeps the legal half that remains) — and a redaction that stops at the business tables while the trail keeps the erased values is a redaction that failed in the one place a regulator looks. The window is a ceiling on how long a value may sit there, never a waiting period: erasure reaches the same two columns on request, at any age of the row, and does so immediately. That is the distinction the two separate checks in that document's §5 are for — one fires when a person's erasure did not happen, the other when the clock's work did not happen — and it is the reason this section describing erasure does not make a store honour it; the checks are what notices.
  5. Sensitive attributes should not be over-collected. person.gender is included because Scouting-type organizations typically must report it; if yours does not, remove the field rather than keeping it "just in case". The same test now applies per code, since most of what is collected is decided at runtime: a code nobody can justify is retired (09-attributes.md §2), and retirement — which stops the collecting without destroying what was already recorded — is the mechanism. Erasing what was recorded is item 2, and only item 2.
  6. Redaction is invisible in listings and visible in the database. A redacted person must not appear where people are listed, and must still resolve wherever an old record points at them (01b-merges-views-and-checks.md §9). These two requirements are one rule with two halves and the first version of that document had only one of them.
  7. The trail is a second copy of the person record and has to be guarded like one. For a person's descriptive data the trail holds the value — the before and after image, exactly as it does for a contact point or a note — because D-085 chose overwrite-in-place on the strength of the trail being the history there is, and a trail that records a value existed without recording which one answers neither of the two questions an audit entry is built for (who said this and what did they say). The consequence is therefore about the log rather than about the shape of a row: an audit entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it carries, which is a requirement on a permission's sensitivity mark and not on anything the schema can express — see 05c-access-log-and-resolver.md §9, which argues against copying data into a less-guarded place and describes this table better than it knows: the trail is such a copy, holding the whole person record in its payloads while historically being graded below it. Nothing here makes that guard true; the catalog does, or does not (appendix/permission-catalog-a-codes.md §8). The mechanism that implements erasure against this table is in 06-audit-and-import.md §2.2 and its §4, and 09-attributes.md §6 is where the trade is stated next to the values. The same section carries the fact that this copy expires: the values this item names are emptied out of payloads 24 months after they were written (D-088), which shortens the exposure this item is complaining about and settles nothing about the guard it demands — so the sentence opening this item, the trail is a second copy of the person record, is true for two years and untrue afterwards, and the mark on the permission has to be right for the years in which it is true. The clock makes erasure neither cheaper nor slower. Items 1 and 2 act on those same columns on request, at any age of a row, and the row's scheduled emptying satisfies nobody's erasure request.

Legal review is required before implementing §8. This section describes the technical mechanism, not the compliance policy. Tracked in ../open-questions.md.

What the review is handed has changed shape, which is worth saying so nobody reads this note as unchanged. It used to be asked "how long may this trail keep personal data, and which fields count as personal data". The corpus now puts a concrete policy in front of it instead of a blank: rows forever and payloads for a bounded window on one side (item 4), an accounting skeleton with no clock at all on the other (item 3), and no graded category of field anywhere for it to deliberate over, because D-083 deleted that idea. What is asked is narrower and harder: on what basis does the retained half survive indefinitely. That is the assumption item 3 names, and nothing in this section makes it lawful.

The key-name list is a credential filter, and reading it as the personal-data filter is the mistake to avoid. It once carried a list of sensitive key names — notes, custody_arrangement, and the rest — and stripped any image holding one, which presupposed a sensitive subset of the person record: a list of names is a way of pointing at some fields and not others. D-083 removed the subset, and what is left of the list is a set of arbitrary fields — one that fails on the first value stored under a name nobody predicted, in an attribute layer whose whole purpose is that nobody can enumerate its names. So the list keeps exactly one class of value out of the trail: the values that must never be logged at all — credentials, tokens, the secret half of an integration — the only values where being in a log is itself the harm. Everything else, notes, the reason fields and an attribute value included, is logged in the clear and protected by who may read the log (item 7), because the answer to who may read a child's address was never a list of field names. Read the list as a credential filter and it is a working mechanism; read it as the personal-data filter, notice that allergy is not in it, and conclude the payload is covered. 09-attributes.md §6 carries the same warning next to the values themselves.

Two things that used to do this work are gone, and they failed in different directions. Redaction of the audit payload was a trigger stripping listed keys out of the before/after images; there is no trigger, so both halves of that job — credential stripping, and the scrub items 2 and 7 require when a person is erased — are application behaviour. Forgetting the first writes a secret into a table designed to be read later by auditors; forgetting the second leaves an erased person's values in the trail with a redaction_log row next to them saying they are gone. (Inside that trigger was a list of keys to scrub unconditionally, and nothing ever read it: a dead list of forbidden fields is not a protection.) The other is the listing view that excludes redacted rows, which is §6a's problem in general. Neither failure is loud, and both are written down because a compliance property resting on a code review is the kind of thing an organization discovers from a regulator.

docs.title: 9. Referential integrity rules
docs.text:
Rule Rationale References restrict, with one deliberate exception A person cannot be removed while memberships reference them, and nothing but the exception below cascades. The exception is event_organizer.event_id — deleting an event removes its organizer rows, the single ON DELETE CASCADE in this design (08-events.md §3 explains why it is safe there and nowhere else). Cascade delete is refused everywhere else It is the enemy of a 40-year audit trail, and ORM relation configs default to it. Check every one, and read the exception above before you "fix" the one row that is allowed to cascade. Optional references document why they are optional An optional reference is usually a design decision worth recording, and it is invisible in the schema. There are seven reference-less keys: six are followed by a scan, and one is followed by nothing on purpose Two were followed before this round — access_grant.scope_id and audience_operand.selector_arg_id, by 05d §11 check 2. Four more are followed now: access_log.scope_id, access_log.authorization_ref_id, access_log.entity_id and field_conflict.entity_id, by 05d §11 check 23, which also carries the exception access_log's three need — some missing targets are legal, because two paths hard-delete business rows and a trail row may not be rewritten to follow them. audit_log.record_id is the seventh and is scanned by nothing, deliberately: an audit row outliving the row it described is what the erasure path and the revert path look like afterwards, and it is the reference the redaction check reads in order to run at all (D-129 is what found that the old count was the count of the ones somebody looked at; F-30 is settled by D-134) Circular references are broken with an optional column, not a deferred constraint membership_request ↔ membership is the one instance; the two-step insert is documented where it lives.

The polymorphic access_grant.scope_id deserves its warning again now that the schema is generated: an ORM will want to make this a real relation, and making it one is a design change. It points at the unit, or at exactly one item — an event, a person_group, a role, or the deferred document — depending on the sibling scope_type column (D-097 deleted the unit family from that list, so "a unit" and "an organization" are now the same answer rather than two of them). No foreign key can express that, and every query that joins it must filter on scope_type first. If the ORM maps it as a relation to one table, the others become silent wrong answers rather than errors.

docs.title: 10. Migration discipline
docs.text:
• Every migration is reversible, or explicitly marked irreversible with a rationale. A migration that drops a column holding historical data is irreversible by definition.
  • Never rewrite a historical row's meaning. Adding a column is fine; changing what an existing value means is a data migration that needs its own review, and it is the kind of change that makes old audit entries lie.
  • Backfills are separate from schema changes, in their own migration, so a failed backfill does not roll back a schema change and vice versa.
  • Seed data for vocabularies (permission, grant_scope_type and selector_type — the last of these being the language an audience expression is written in, D-101) lives in migrations, not in application startup code, so the vocabulary is versioned with the data it describes. Application-startup seeding produces environments that disagree about what event.answer.view reaches. It is also the reason selector_type is read-only to an organization: an operand added at runtime is a word no resolver knows, and the empty set is a quiet way to say so.
  • Two documents are the source of truth for what a migration must achieve: each data-model file's Rules block for the constraints, and its Invariants to verify block for the reports. A migration that implements neither set completely has generated a schema, not a design.

docs.title: 11. Where each subject is described
docs.text:
Not "where the DDL lives" — that question stopped meaning anything at D-072. Each document below states the fields, rules, invariants and open issues for its part of the model.

Document Entities 01-identity.md person, person_name, account, account_credential, person_contact, person_identifier, identity_hypothesis, person_merge 02-organization.md person_group, person_group_member — and nothing else, because there is no unit table: the unit is a scope (D-097) 03-membership.md membership, membership_type, membership_request 04-relationships.md guardianship (carrying the guardian's current right_level), guardianship_permission (the history of that value) 05-authorization.md permission, role, role_holder, access_grant, audience, audience_operand, selector_type, grant_scope_type, access_log, api_key (a caller that is not a person: 05e-keys-and-callers.md §14–§17) — and no member table for an audience, because a hand-named person is a PERSON(x) leaf in the expression (D-105) 06-audit-and-import.md audit_log, field_conflict, redaction_log, import_batch, staging_import* 07-finance.md fee_schedule, fee_obligation, payment_request, payment, bank_transaction — provisional on policy 08-events.md event, event_organizer, event_registration, event_question, event_answer 09-attributes.md attribute_definition, attribute_option, person_attribute — everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age (D-083, D-084). It is last in this table because it is last in every other document's account of a person: it references person and nothing references it

Each document presents its entities in dependency order: one appears only after everything it references. That ordering was needed to make a schema file execute; it is kept because it is also the order in which the model is understandable.

Messaging is not in this table. message and message_recipient are decided at D-077 and not yet designed; they will need their own document. The absence is tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — 00a. Who enforces each invariant
docs.text:
One row for every rule this schema states, saying what carries it, what would notice a breach, and what a breach looks like. Written so that the answer to "is that rule guarded?" is one lookup instead of twenty pages.

← 00-conventions | 01-identity

This page does not restate any rule. It links to the page that owns each one, because a restated rule is a second copy of it, and the defect this corpus keeps hitting is a copy that drifted — the story the catalog's §12 tells about a seeded table copied from an evaluator's arm list, and the reason D-127 diffs documents against their own registries rather than against a list. What is here is the three facts a rule's own page is allowed to leave implicit — which layer carries it, which report would see a breach, and what a breach looks like — and the register is where a blank in those two columns is visible instead of being a sentence on page 412 that nobody re-reads.

The four shapes, and the layer each is assigned (D-130):

Shape What it is The layer that carries it Why not another layer 1 No two rows overlap in time A hand-written PostgreSQL exclusion constraint, emitted by a migration The ORM cannot generate one, and an application check is bypassed by the import, the bulk edit and the fix at 2am (00 §6's rule 3) 2 Unique, but only among rows meeting a condition A partial unique index, emitted by a migration The unconditioned constraint is a different and usually wrong rule — it forbids the second closed row, which history requires 3 The answer reads another table, a resolver, or a graph The write path, inside the transaction that writes No constraint spans two tables. The layer named in this register is always the write path; what varies is whether a report was named beneath it 4 A value that may never change once set Nothing automatic. The rule, the referrer listing, and the review There is no offending row to catch — only a rewritten history — and 00 §10's rule against rewriting a historical row's meaning is the prose that stands behind it

How to read the two right-hand columns. Backstop names the report that would list a breach, by the page and number where that report is written. none in bold is not an omission of this page and not a slur on the rule: it means the corpus names no such report anywhere, which is the finding. Five rows are in that state and all five are shape-3 rows, whose only enforcement is a line of code. The five are not one kind of blank, and the kinds are worth naming because they fail differently. Two are rulings: D-133 decided that a rule about an ended key gets no report, and D-143 decided the same about a delegation outliving the permission behind it — in both cases the absence was chosen, and said on the page that owns the rule rather than only here. One is a promise with an address: D-130's identifier row names the section the report will be added to, so that none is dated rather than permanent. Two are blanks this page is not allowed to fill by inventing a check nobody asked for. The count came down from eleven — seven after round 19, five after round 20 — and none of the six losses was a re-reading. Two pages were given the check sections they lacked (D-135). Two rows here turned out to describe a rule no page states at all, so they are gone rather than repaired (D-133, D-144) — which is the half of this page's history it should be embarrassed by. And one none was simply false in the other direction: the displayed-name row said no report existed while the report had been sitting in 01b §10 since the page that owns the check was written (D-142). That is the reason this column is worth the trouble it costs: a citation can be checked and a claim of absence cannot, so a blank is as much a claim about the corpus as a link is, and it can be wrong while looking humble. Breach is what the bad data looks like afterwards, because a shape-1 breach and a shape-2 breach both read as "two rows" and only one of them is a duplicate.

Nine numbered checks, on three pages, are assertions about the code rather than reports over data — the six TIME-BOMB checks of 05d §11 (15, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 22), 02 §6 check 4, and 08a §10 checks 1 and 9. They are cited below as save-refusal, never as a report: they verify that a guard still exists, never that the data is clean. Filing one as a backstop would overstate coverage in exactly the direction that matters.

docs.title: 1. No two rows overlap in time
docs.text:
Four rules. All four are a hand-written exclusion constraint over a range built from valid_from and valid_to, half-open, so that a row ending 2010-06-30 and one starting 2010-06-30 do not collide.

A report beneath a real constraint is a courtesy, not a control — the constraint cannot be breached quietly — so a none in this table or the next is only a finding where the layer is the write path.

docs.title: 4. A value that may never change once set
docs.text:
This shape is not empty. It was described as empty on the strength of one deleted instance; four live ones were already in these pages, and the test that separates them from a column nobody would think to rename is the same test that made the two named candidates worth naming: a rename rewrites what references it, and nothing leaves a row in the wrong state for a report to find. Eight rows are below and seven of them are members, counted off the table rather than carried down: the audience row is the eighth and is the correction, not a member. The seventh arrived in round 20 without anyone looking for it — a decision about event forms made a vocabulary code referenced, and the shape grew by whatever the corpus references, which is the one property of this shape that does not need a checker.

docs.title: What the register cannot say
docs.text:
• It cannot say whether a write path still contains its rule. Every shape-3 row above rests on code this repository does not contain. Where a numbered check exists for such a rule, it is a save-refusal: it re-asks whether the guard is there, and it is the only thing standing between a removed line of code and a silent rule.
  • It cannot reach a rule stated only once, in prose, on the page it governs. That is what the inventory behind this page was for, and what it found in the way of absences is in the open questions, each one naming the page it is missing from.
  • It cannot rank the nones. It used to be able to say at least where they clustered, and the answer was two pages: 07-finance.md and 06a-import.md had no "Invariants to verify" section, so every rule they stated was unassigned by construction rather than by oversight. That structural excuse is gone (D-135) and both pages now carry their own list, which leaves this column holding only rules that were read in the round that found them and left unguarded on purpose or on the table's own limits. Ranking those is still not something a register can do without inventing a severity, which is the thing it refuses to do.
  • It is not a substitute for the constraint. A row here saying migration is not the migration. 00 §6a is the rule about what must be emitted below the application; this page is the evidence that the rule was applied to every row and told where it was not.

See also 00-conventions §6a, 05d §11, the registry diff, the decisions D-130 and D-131, and the four this page's blanks produced in the next round: D-133, D-134, D-135 and D-136.

docs.title: Data Model — Identity: the central claim, person, and name history
docs.text:
person — what the organization knows about a human, on which there is no status, no role and no type — the columns deliberately left off it, and the name history in person_name. How that human signs in and is reached is 01a; how two rows become one person is 01b.

Every pattern referenced here is defined in 00-conventions.md.
