Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 01-identity.md holds §1–§3 (the central claim, person, person_name), 01a §4–§7 (account, account_credential, person_contact, person_identifier), and 01b §8–§11 (identity_hypothesis, person_merge, the views, the integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 1. The central claim
docs.text:
person   ── what the organization knows about a human. No status. No role. No type.
account  ── how that human logs in. Optional. Zero or more over a lifetime.

There is no is_member, member_type, is_child, is_adult, unit_id, or role on person. Each of those is either a period in another table or a derived fact. This is the single most important property of the schema and the one most likely to be undone by a well-meaning future change.

docs.title: 2. person
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only public_id external identifier, required Unique. Generated when the row is created. This is what URLs and exports carry given_name text, required Names are also stored as temporal rows in person_name (§3). These two columns are the current, canonical form, denormalised for display and search; history and legal-name variants live in person_name family_name text, required As above birth_date date, optional Nullable because legacy records frequently lack it. Never required — a 1994 roster with no birth date must still import birth_date_precision text, optional One of: exact, month, year, unknown. Because an imported birth date of 1990-01-01 often means "year 1990, month and day unknown". Storing the precision prevents false matches on a guessed day and prevents "happy 1 January birthday" emails gender text, optional One of: male, female, other, unknown. Included because youth organizations typically must report it. Remove if yours does not need it — do not collect what you cannot justify preferred_name text, optional What the person is actually called. Distinct from given_name so that the organization's records stay legally correct while the person is addressed correctly — "Alexandra" recorded, "Lex" displayed record_origin text, required One of: self_registered, staff_created, legacy_import. Default self_registered data_confidence text, required One of: high, medium, low. Default high. low for imported rows: it drives whether a merge may absorb this row, and whether the UI warns before displaying it as fact merged_into_person_id reference to person, optional Tombstone. When set, this row is absorbed and queries must follow the pointer. Never deleted (§8) merged_at timestamp, audit time, optional redacted_at timestamp, audit time, optional Set when a GDPR-style erasure was performed. Names and contacts are overwritten and the person's person_attribute rows are deleted; the row and its id survive so historical references still resolve (00-conventions §8) notes text, optional Free text about a person, and the only such text that lives outside the attribute vocabulary — see What is deliberately not on this table below. May contain anything, including a diagnosis sitting under a column nobody would call medical. It is logged with its contents, like every other field on this row, and it is deliberately not on the redactor's list — a column named as an exception is the field-name rule D-083 removed, and the protection is the guard on the trail (00-conventions §8 item 7). Whether the column should exist at all is argued below created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows. Its link to import_batch can only be made once that table exists

Rules

  • There is deliberately no deceased flag. The organization does not record whether a person has died. A membership simply ends; the reason for the ending lives in the generic reason fields (membership.termination_reason, membership.ended_note) like any other ending — text somebody types, not a row of a table (D-128), and the organization's own vocabulary for such reasons is theirs to define. Do not add is_deceased or deceased_at back: it is not data the organization keeps.
  • public_id is unique.
  • A person may not be merged into themselves — merged_into_person_id may never name this same row, nor any row that resolves to it. The one-hop case is the degenerate form of the cycle banned in §8, not a separate rule beside it.
  • merged_into_person_id and merged_at are set together or both left null. A pointer with no date, or a date with no pointer, cannot be explained to anyone.
  • A birth_date_precision may be recorded without a birth_date only when it says unknown. Every other precision claims something about a date that is not there.

Indexes

  • Person search by name, with both names compared case-insensitively.
  • Persons by birth_date, restricted to rows that have one.
  • Persons that have not been merged — a partial index, because every ordinary listing must exclude merged rows and it has to stay cheap.
  • Persons that have not been redacted — same reason.
  • Lookup by public_id.

docs.title: Notes on specific choices
docs.text:
birth_date_precision. Without it, a legacy import that only knows the year produces 1990-01-01, which then matches every other year-only record born in 1990 on the same invented day, and sends birthday greetings on 1 January. Cheap column, prevents a whole class of matching noise.

public_id alongside id. External references use public_id. Sequential internal ids appear in access_grant.scope_id and in URLs; exposing them would let anyone enumerate member records. See 00-conventions.md.

merged_into_person_id and redacted_at are both on person rather than in side tables. They are read on every query (every listing must exclude merged and redacted rows from ordinary views), so they need to be cheap. They are also the reason the two partial indexes above exist.

docs.title: What is deliberately not on this table
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is a descriptive value in person_attribute, and this table carries no column for any of it — no allergy, no medication, no insurance number, no shoe size, no preferred contact language, no diagnosis (09-attributes.md, D-083). That is not a gap waiting for the next module. An earlier design did put the medical facts on a shelf of their own, behind codes of their own, and the answer that produced D-083 refused the shelf: a drug dosage and a clothing size are the same kind of object — recorded by the organization, wrong in three years, unenumerable in advance — and a permission that reads a person reads the whole record whatever the shelf is called (domain/08-person-data.md).

given_name/family_name/preferred_name, gender and birth_date are the only descriptive facts that are columns here, and they are the last the model will accept. The test for keeping one is not sensitivity — notes sits in the field table above and is a worse exposure than most of what moved out. The test is whether a rule exists that an open layer physically cannot hold. "One current name per person", "exactly one primary postal contact among the open rows", "a school id may repeat, a birth number may not" — each is a constraint over a known set of columns, and a key/value layer has no known set of columns, which is the whole of what it is for. Folding person_name, person_contact or person_identifier into the attribute layer would have relocated four working constraints into application code and been called uniformity (shape 3). Identity is closed because it was enumerated years ago and has not changed; description is open because nobody can enumerate it (D-085).

The rule cuts both ways, and review is where it is applied. A fact with no such rule behind it does not earn a column here, however reasonable it looks — that is the sentence that keeps is_deceased's cousins out. And a table already in this document does not lose its columns because the new layer looks tidier — that is the sentence that keeps a well-meaning unification of "everything about a person" from quietly turning four enforced rules into four hopes.

One consequence names itself. person.notes is the last free text about a person kept outside the vocabulary, and it is the column a reviewer should ask about: a sentence typed there is invisible to to any report on a code, and to the screen a first aider reads at 23:00, while the same sentence recorded as a value against a code is visible to both — and recording it that way is now one act by one person rather than a request waiting for somebody with time, since a definition is live at the save of whoever holds attribute.define and there is no queue left to wait in (D-141, 09-attributes.md §2). Whether the column should exist at all is open and already argued (06-audit-and-import.md §6); what is settled is that it carries no protection the attribute layer does not carry, and less readability.

docs.title: The answer to "who is a member?" is never on this table
docs.text:
To be unambiguous, the two facts:

  • Currently a member — the person has a membership whose valid_to is absent and whose status is active.
  • Was a member on 1998-06-01 — the person has a membership whose period contains that date: valid_from on or before it, and valid_to either absent or after it. Its status is one of active, completed, lapsed, terminated.

Note the second fact includes closed statuses — "was a member in 1998" is true regardless of how the membership later ended. Getting this wrong is why "years of membership" reports are usually wrong.

docs.title: 3. person_name — name history
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required name_type text, required One of: legal, preferred, maiden, former, alias, imported given_name text, required family_name text, required middle_name text, optional valid_from date, optional Optional because an imported name often arrives with no start date at all valid_to date, optional NULL = current for this name_type source text, optional self, staff, legacy_import import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional

Rules

  • valid_to is either absent, or valid_from is absent, or valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • One current name per person and name_type: at most one row with valid_to absent. Two pages cite this as one of the constraints that keeps the attribute layer honest, and until D-129 this table stated only the ordering rule. A partial unique index, and §2's denormalised copy of it is reported, not constrained.

Indexes

  • A person's names.
  • Fuzzy search across all historical names — both names lowercased, family name first, and usable for prefix matching. This is what legacy matching reads.

Why name history is a table. Three concrete cases:

  1. A member married and changed their family name. The 1998 roster has the maiden name; the 2026 registration has the married name. Legacy matching must find the link, and the historical record must keep the name it actually had.
  2. An imported name has a typo (Novak for Novák). Correcting it must not destroy the imported form, because that is what the paper says and someone will ask.
  3. A person goes by a different name than their legal one. Both must be storable, and which is used where must be deterministic.

person.given_name/family_name are the denormalised current values and are what the UI displays. person_name is the source of truth for matching and for historical queries. This is a deliberate denormalization — the alternative is joining on every list view — and it must be updated in the same transaction whenever the canonical name changes.

Assumption: display should use person.preferred_name ?? person.given_name. If the organization requires legal names on official documents, that rule lives in the document layer, not here.

docs.title: Data Model — Identity: accounts, credentials, contact points, identifiers
docs.text:
account and account_credential — how a human logs in, and by what — then person_contact and person_identifier: where they can be reached, and what other systems call them by. The human these rows all belong to is §2.

Every pattern referenced here is defined in 00-conventions.md.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 01-identity.md holds §1–§3 (the central claim, person, person_name), 01a §4–§7 (account, account_credential, person_contact, person_identifier), and 01b §8–§11 (identity_hypothesis, person_merge, the views, the integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 4. account
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required Not unique. Uniqueness applies only to live accounts, under Rules username text, optional status text, required One of: pending_verification, active, suspended, closed. Default pending_verification verified_at timestamp, audit time, optional created_by_staff boolean, required Default false last_login_at timestamp, audit time, optional failed_login_count integer, required Default 0 locked_until timestamp, audit time, optional status_reason text, optional Why suspended or closed, in the words of whoever did it (D-128) status_note text, optional The human explanation created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • At most one live account per person: unique over person_id across the rows whose status is pending_verification, active or suspended. Closed rows are not covered, so a person may accumulate as many closed accounts as their history contains.
  • username is unique compared case-insensitively, over the rows that have one and are not closed. A closed account releases its username for someone else to take. It covers live rows only, not all rows.
  • An account may not reach active while verified_at is absent.
  • An account may not reach active while an unresolved identity_hypothesis names its person — a hypothesis sitting in proposed or needs_review, on either side of the pair. This is the second gate on the same transition and D-089 is why it is here. It is written as a gate on a status rather than as a rule against creating the row, because the row has to exist for the claim to be attached to anything, and because the queue a claim lands in already exists (§8) with its signals, its ordering and its reviewer. See the collision flow below for what that buys and what it costs.

Indexes

  • A person's accounts.

Why person_id is not unique. The partial unique index expresses the real rule: one live account per person, while permitting closed historical accounts. A plain UNIQUE (person_id) would make it impossible to close an old account and open a new one — which is exactly the returning-member case at the account level.

An account is a login, and nothing about a child is decided here. account keeps the columns that describe authentication and no others: there is no minimum age for one, no consent step, and no branch in the sign-up path that a minor's sign-up takes and an adult's does (D-166). What a new account can reach is nothing until somebody writes a row about its person — a grant, a guardianship, a membership — which is what every new account is anyway, not a defence built for this case. If the organization wants a guardian's answer on record, it goes on the guardianship relationship, where an adult's authority over a child is already written, dated, revocable and carrying its own right_level (04 §2); no column returns here for it.

A colliding sign-up files a claim and brings nothing into the world that a human has not approved. This is the case the second gate above exists for (D-089): someone arrives at the sign-up form through a door the system did not know they had, and their details strong-match a person who already exists. The tempting answer was the convenient one — verify the e-mail, see that the signals are strong, link the two accounts — and it is D-004 wearing a different coat: a false-positive link is one human's descriptive data becoming another human's record, and a merge is the hard part to undo even with §9's reversal. The other tempting answer was the permissive one — let the second live account stand — which drops the uniqueness rule above and splits one person's consents, payments and attributes across two ids until somebody happens to notice, in exactly the records where nobody notices. So the system refuses, files the claim, and waits.

What actually happens, in the order it happens. The sign-up's rows are created as any sign-up creates them and stay pending_verification; an identity_hypothesis is raised naming the two person rows, with proposed_by of person because that is what happened — a person asserted this is them — and its match_signals carrying which of them matched; the gate holds the account where it is; the person at the form sees a holding message. Nothing is merged, nothing is linked, nothing is activated. The address they typed is not thrown away: it stays on the pending account as the credential it was offered as, the identifier awaiting verification, rather than being echoed back to a browser and lost — which matters because the reviewer's second possible answer is "this is a different person", and that answer should leave the applicant finishing the sign-up they started rather than starting it again.

The trigger is a strong match, and the threshold is the whole rule. A hypothesis is raised at sign-up on an exact legacy member number, or an exact birth date together with a normalized name match — the top of the band ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md §4 already weights, and nothing below it. The soft band must not raise one. Blocking a stranger's registration on a fuzzy score is the failure this rule would most deserve to have caused, and the two sides of that trade are not symmetric: the cost of letting a true duplicate through is bounded, reviewable, and caught by the nightly matcher anyway, while the cost of stopping a new member is a child who cannot sign up to a camp on the day the form closes.

The holding message confirms nothing, and this is a security requirement rather than a tone choice. It says the request was received and will be checked. It says nothing about whether the name, the birth date or the member number matched anything at all, because a sign-up form that answers "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle over a roster, and this system's roster is children (05-authorization.md is the document that spends its length on why that distinction is worth a resolver). The same form that legitimately helps a returning member find their account is the form that lets anyone with a birth date enumerate who is enrolled. So the message is identical whether the match was exact, partial, or absent, and it stays identical whether or not an account exists to be found.

Resolving the claim is not a new permission and not a new queue. A reviewer confirms or rejects the hypothesis, which is person.merge and already sits with identity_reviewer; confirming it merges the two person rows under §9's rules, rejecting it lifts the gate and the account activates. No new code is involved on either side, for the same reason §9 gives for reversal needing none: undoing and correcting an identity are one act by one named human.

Confirming the claim closes the placeholder account; it does not move it. This is the part of the flow that looks obvious and is wrong, so the wrong version is written out first: the sign-up's person row is absorbed, the sign-up's account still points at it, so repoint account.person_id at the survivor and the applicant keeps the login they were building. That write is refused by §4's own rule — one live account per person, unique over the pending, active and suspended rows — for the common case where the survivor already has an account; and in the case where it is not refused it quietly makes a login older than the person's own, carrying a verification and a credential history that belong to an act the survivor never performed. The rule is instead, in this order:

  1. Close the placeholder account — status becomes closed, with the reason naming the hypothesis that closed it. Closed rows are outside the uniqueness rule (§4), which is exactly why closing works where repointing does not, and the row survives as the record that someone applied.
  2. Move the credential, not the account. The typed address was verified as far as it ever was, and throwing it away punishes the one person in this flow who did the right thing. It is added to the survivor's live account as an account_credential row (§5) — credentials are many-per-account already, which is why this is an addition rather than an exception. Where that account has no live account to receive it, the survivor is given one, carrying the moved credential and the placeholder's verified_at: the address was verified, and making somebody click a second link to prove a claim a reviewer has already confirmed is bureaucracy with a security costume.
  3. A credential of the same type already live on the survivor's account is not overwritten. Two password rows do not both become current; the arriving one is left unverified and a field_conflict (§10's queue) is raised for the person to sort out, because this is the one branch where the system cannot tell whether it is looking at the same address typed twice or at two different claims to one mailbox.
  4. One audit entry names both accounts, both persons and the hypothesis, and it is written by the same transaction that closes the row. Not two entries, and not the merge's own entry doing double duty: the merge says two people became one, and this says a login changed hands, which is the question whoever reverses the merge (§9) will actually be asking.

What this costs is the applicant's session, and it is worth naming. Someone mid-sign-up whose claim is confirmed does not continue in the account they were filling in; they log in to the one they already had. That is one extra login against the alternative of an account that belongs to two people's history at once, and the holding message (§4 above) is where they are told it. Two costs come with it and both are stated rather than absorbed. A genuinely new person who happens to match now waits for a human, so the blocking condition carries an age check shaped like field_conflict's thirty days below — a number on a report somebody opens, because nothing in this design tells anybody that a queue has stalled (D-164). A stalled identity queue stopped being a data-quality problem the moment it could hold a login, and the person it is holding has no way to say so except by telephoning someone. And the reviewer deciding it is deliberately half-blind — the office that holds the merge holds no read over the person record, so it decides from signals and names, which is the correct conservative shape and also the thing to revisit if reviewers start asking for context they cannot see. No platform ships that office: some organization writes it, aims person.merge at ROLE(x) and leaves person.view out of the grant, and the conservatism is in the grant it chose rather than in a row the design brought with it (05d §12).

The everyday case is not this case, and naming it stops the rule being oversold. "I have a new e-mail address" has never been a second account and is not one now: account_credential (§5) holds many credentials for one account, so a new address is an addition to the login a person already has and runs past nothing here. The collision case is narrower than signing up twice — it is a person arriving through a door the system did not know they had.

A suspended account does not suspend a membership. They are independent lifecycles. The schema enforces this by simply not linking them.

docs.title: 5. account_credential
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id account_id reference to account, required credential_type text, required One of: password, passkey, totp, oauth, staff_link. Multiple methods per account. oauth supports a national Scout identity provider; staff_link supports a one-time link issued to a member who cannot self-serve secret_hash text, optional Password/OTP hash. Absent for passkey and oauth external_ref text, optional OAuth subject id, or WebAuthn credential id external_issuer text, optional OAuth issuer valid_from timestamp, audit time, required Default: now valid_to timestamp, audit time, optional NULL = current last_used_at timestamp, audit time, optional revoked_reason text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • A password, totp or staff_link credential must carry a secret_hash. A passkey or oauth credential must carry both external_ref and external_issuer. A credential with nothing to check against cannot exist.
  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.
  • One current credential per (external_issuer, external_ref) pair among oauth rows that are still current. It covers open rows only — an expired credential does not hold its external identity back.

Indexes

  • An account's current credentials — the open half of the period only.
  • The oauth uniqueness above, which is itself a lookup: given an issuer and a subject id, which account is this.

Why credentials are not columns on account. Adding passkeys, an organizational SSO, or a one-time-link flow later must not require restructuring account and migrating every existing password. Keeping secret_hash off the account table also means the common "show me the user" query never touches credential material.

valid_to on a credential is how password history and revocation are expressed. A revoked credential stays as a row, so "was this account ever accessed with a credential that has since been revoked?" is answerable.

docs.title: 6. person_contact
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required contact_type text, required One of: email, phone, postal, website, messaging purpose text, required One of: login, membership, emergency, billing, guardian, general value text, required Normalised per type: emails lowercased, phones E.164, postal as structured JSON value_detail free-form jsonb, optional For postal addresses: {street, city, postal_code, country}. Avoids six optional fields that only apply to one contact_type label text, optional home, work, school — display only is_primary boolean, required Default false verified_at timestamp, audit time, optional verified_by text, optional One of: self, staff, bounce_check, import valid_from date, required Default: today valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Addresses change; history is required source text, optional self, staff, legacy_import import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.
  • At most one current primary per (person, contact_type, purpose). It covers open rows only: a superseded primary does not block the new one.

Indexes

  • A person's contact points.
  • A person's current contact points by type and purpose — open rows only.
  • Email lookup on value lowercased, over current email rows only.
  • Phone lookup on value as stored, over current phone rows only.

purpose is the column that makes this operationally useful. It lets the permission system distinguish "a unit leader may see emergency contacts for camp" from "only billing staff may see payment email addresses". Without purpose, every contact is equally sensitive and the only safe choice is to hide all of them.

The partial unique index on the primary contact enforces "one primary email per person per purpose" without preventing a person from having four non-primary addresses. Note this index is what makes the merge conflict in §8 possible — resolving two is_primary rows is a review step, not a rule.

The email index is functional — it indexes value lowercased because email matching in the legacy importer must be case-insensitive, and a plain index cannot serve that.

docs.title: 7. person_identifier
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required scheme text, required national_scout_id, legacy_member_no, legacy_member_no_oldsystem, government_id, school_id, insurance_no. Validated against identifier_scheme below value text, required issued_at date, optional valid_to date, optional IDs expire or are superseded verified_at timestamp, audit time, optional source text, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

identifier_scheme — the vocabulary of schemes.

Fields

Field Kind Notes code text, required The value person_identifier.scheme holds name text, required is_unique boolean, required Default true. True: a value may appear on only one person (national id, member number). False: values legitimately repeat (school id across schools) description text, optional

Rules

  • Uniqueness is per scheme, and identifier_scheme.is_unique decides it. For a scheme flagged unique, (scheme, value) is unique over the identifiers that are still current — those with no valid_to. A superseded number may be reused; a current one may not be shared. The rule covers open rows only.
  • For a scheme flagged not-unique there is no such rule, and that is the point of the flag. school_id repeats by design: the same school issues the same number to many children, and each of them is a different person who genuinely carries it. is_unique = false means one value may appear on any number of people, and means it at enforcement time, not as a note in a description column.
  • Corrected here, and worth reading as a lesson. The rule as first written applied to every scheme and never read the flag; the flag and the rule were the same idea stated twice, once enforced and once decorative. The effect was that school_id could not in fact repeat — the second child at that school with the same number would have been rejected as a duplicate identifier, at import time, by a constraint whose own table said it should not exist. A column that no rule reads is not documentation, it is a promise. This is the same failure D-072 warns about from the other side: a rule nobody runs is a convention, and a flag nothing consults is decoration. Both read correctly on the page.

Indexes

  • A person's identifiers.
  • The uniqueness lookup above.

This table is the highest-value asset in the legacy import. If the old system issued member numbers, an exact (scheme='legacy_member_no', value=…) match is the strongest identity signal available — strong enough to short-circuit a fuzzy name comparison. See ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md.

Why not put these on person as columns. A person may have zero identifiers (most self-registered children), one, or several; schemes appear and disappear over decades; and national_scout_id must be unique while school_id must not. Columns would mean a schema change per scheme and a nullable-unique mess.

docs.title: Data Model — Identity: identity hypotheses, merges, views, checks
docs.text:
identity_hypothesis and person_merge — two rows becoming one person: the signals a proposal carries, the conflicts a merge could not decide, and what a reversal can and cannot undo. Then the views that encode "exclude merged and redacted" and "as of a date" so application code cannot forget them, the checks that run nightly, and what is still open.

Every pattern referenced here is defined in 00-conventions.md.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 01-identity.md holds §1–§3 (the central claim, person, person_name), 01a §4–§7 (account, account_credential, person_contact, person_identifier), and 01b §8–§11 (identity_hypothesis, person_merge, the views, the integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 8. identity_hypothesis and person_merge
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_a_id reference to person, required The lower of the two ids — canonical ordering, so that (a,b) and (b,a) cannot both exist person_b_id reference to person, required confidence number between 0 and 1, required Inclusive of both ends match_signals jsonb, required A list of signals, each with a name, a weight and whether it matched — [{signal: 'birth_date_exact', weight: 0.4, matched: true}, {signal: 'name_normalised', weight: 0.3, matched: true}, …]. Stored so a human reviewer can see WHY the matcher proposed this status text, required One of: proposed, needs_review, confirmed, rejected, superseded. Default proposed proposed_by text, required One of: import_job, match_job, person, staff. match_job is the nightly batch matcher, as opposed to a person suggesting a match by hand proposed_by_person_id reference to person, optional Set when a person proposed it proposed_at timestamp, audit time Default: now reviewed_by reference to person, optional reviewed_at timestamp, audit time, optional review_note text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • person_a_id names a lower person id than person_b_id, and the two are never the same person.
  • A hypothesis cannot be confirmed or rejected without a reviewed_at.
  • One live hypothesis per pair: unique over (person_a_id, person_b_id) while the status is proposed, needs_review or confirmed. A rejected or superseded hypothesis does not block a new one, so the pair can be re-proposed later.

Indexes

  • The review queue: status, then confidence highest first, restricted to the rows still waiting — proposed and needs_review.

person_merge — the record that one person row was absorbed into another.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id surviving_person_id reference to person, required merged_person_id reference to person, required The absorbed row. It keeps its id; person.merged_into_person_id points here hypothesis_id reference to identity hypothesis, optional The hypothesis this merge came from, when one did merged_at timestamp, audit time Default: now merged_by reference to person, required reason text, optional reversed_at timestamp, audit time, optional reversed_by reference to person, optional reversal_note text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • A person may not be merged into themselves: surviving_person_id and merged_person_id are never the same person.
  • A merge is refused when the chosen survivor resolves — by walking the chain — to the person being absorbed. That includes the one-hop case just stated and the case that actually happens: absorbing B into A when A has already been absorbed into B. D-087 puts this check on the merge and not on the read, and the placement is the substance of the rule: a cycle refused on the way in cannot be reached, whereas a step limit on resolve_person() achieves nothing except deciding which of two wrong answers to return — the tombstone, or wherever the walk happened to stop. There is no schema object that spans two rows of a walk, so this is a rule about an operation; the cycle check in §10 is a canary for it having leaked, not the guard.

Indexes

  • Merges by surviving person, and merges by merged person — both directions get asked.
  • Merges by merged person that have not been reversed — the "who is this person now" query.

The canonical ordering (person_a_id before person_b_id) is not cosmetic. Without it the matcher can create both (100, 847) and (847, 100), and a reviewer will confirm one while the other sits in the queue forever — or worse, confirm both. The ordering rule plus the partial unique index makes the pair identity unambiguous.

match_signals as JSONB rather than columns, because the signal set will evolve as the matcher improves, and because these are write-once-read-for-review, never queried analytically.

person_merge is append-only — reversed_at is set, rows are never deleted. An unmerge does not remove the merge record; it records that it was undone, so the history of the mistake is visible. See ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md.

Reversing a merge is a required operation, not an accommodation. Those three columns exist because someone asked for the capability, and D-087 is where it was asked for; §9 explains that this is the reason chains were kept rather than the other way round. Two consequences sit under it, and both are easy to lose later.

  • Reversal needs no permission of its own. Unmerging is the same act as merging — an identity correction made by a named human — so it is person.merge, which identity_reviewer already holds. A separate code would grade undoing a mistake as safer than making one, which is precisely backwards: the mistake is the thing that needed the guard.
  • A merge can be undone; the merged period cannot. The reversal procedure lifts the tombstone and returns the rows created before the merge, but the rows created inside the window are flagged for a human rather than guessed at — and every access_grant from that window is flagged, not redistributed, because the authority exercised in there really was exercised by somebody the record can no longer separate. That asymmetry is the honest core of the feature: the row is restorable, the interval is not. Anyone who reads reversed_at as "as if it never happened" is reading the wrong column for that claim, which is why the reversal record is kept rather than deleted.

docs.title: Merge conflicts
docs.text:
field_conflict — one field the merge could not decide.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id merge_id reference to person merge, required entity_table text, required person, person_contact, membership, … entity_id surrogate id, required The row in entity_table. No reference — with the table named per row it would point at any table in the schema field_name text, required surviving_value text, optional merged_value text, optional resolution text, optional One of: kept_surviving, took_merged, manual, unresolved resolved_value text, optional resolved_by reference to person, optional resolved_at timestamp, audit time, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Indexes

  • A merge's conflicts by resolution.
  • A merge's conflicts that are still unresolved — the reportable set.

Every field the merge could not resolve automatically lands here as unresolved. A merge with unresolved conflicts must be visible in an operational report — otherwise these rows accumulate silently and the data is quietly wrong.

Conflict cases worth naming, because each needs a human decision and none has a safe rule:

Case Why it cannot be automatic Two is_primary emails of the same purpose Which one does the person actually use? Two different birth_date values One is a typo; guessing produces a wrong legal record. Two overlapping memberships May be legitimate, or may mean the merge is wrong. Two different current names One may be a maiden name, or they may be different people. Two accounts, both active Which one is in use?

docs.title: 9. Views
docs.text:
Convenience views that encode the "always exclude merged and redacted" and "point in time" rules, so that application code cannot forget them.

v_person — the person rows most queries actually want: a person who is neither merged away nor redacted. Both exclusions, not one. They are different reasons and they must not be collapsed: a merged row is a duplicate that points at the real answer, while a redacted row is a person who was erased, whose names and contacts no longer exist. Neither belongs in a list of people, and a listing that shows one and hides the other is worse than either, because it teaches the reader that the redacted child is a data-entry error.

Nothing else carries this rule. There is no view definition anywhere in this repository (§1 of D-072), so this page is the only place the rule lives and it has to be right. D-080 records the time it was not: the view excluded merged rows while §1 and §2 required both of them, and the prose lost.

What is deliberately not excluded anywhere: the row itself. A redacted person is still a row with a still-working id, so historical references keep resolving (§2's redacted_at). Anything that must reach a merged or redacted row — audit, as-of reconstruction, resolve_person — queries person directly and says so. v_person is the view for "people", and people is not what an audit trail is asking for.

resolve_person(id) — turns a possibly-merged id into the survivor. These steps run in this order, and the order is the rule:

  1. Begin at the person row carrying the given id.
  2. If that row has no merged_into_person_id, stop; this id is the answer.
  3. Otherwise move to the row its merged_into_person_id names and repeat from step 2.

v_person_display — one row per person v_person admits, carrying id, public_id, a display given name (preferred_name where present, given_name otherwise), family_name, a display name formed by putting the two together with a space, birth_date, birth_date_precision and redacted_at.

What v_person_display does not carry, and why that is a rule rather than an omission. It is a display row — the columns needed to name a person in a list — and it carries no descriptive values. It cannot: a view is a fixed list of columns and the attribute layer is the part of a person with no fixed list, which is §2's test arriving from the other side. Naming the boundary matters because the failure mode is silent. Anything asked about a person, rather than about what they are called, reads person and person_attribute together under the one person.view that reaches both (09-attributes.md §4) — the allergy list a first aider asks for, the record a guardian opens, the form a leader fills in. A screen built on v_person_display alone answers those questions with a name and a birth date, shows no empty field where an allergy should be, and looks entirely healthy while doing it (domain/08-person-data.md §3). The view stays narrow for the reason it exists — every picker and roster in the system reads it and none of them needs the record — and the obligation sits on the caller: do not answer a question about a person out of a view that only knows how to print one.

resolve_person follows every hop because merges chain: A absorbed into B, later B absorbed into C. A single-level pointer lookup would return B, whose row is itself tombstoned. Every place that accepts a person id from outside must call this. Getting it wrong means a historical record links to a tombstone and the UI shows a blank name — or the wrong one.

Chains are a decision, not an assumption. They stay because reversing a merge is a required operation rather than a convenience — someone asked for it as a requirement (§8), and D-087 is that request. The shape of the trade follows from it: with chains kept, a reversal is a replay; with flattening, it is a rebuild. Flattening is therefore closed off, not merely slower, and "flattening is faster" buys nothing except the death of a feature somebody named.

Two rules keep a permanent chain safe.

  • A cycle cannot be created, and the place it cannot be created is the merge, not the read (§8's rule). A read-side hop limit is not a weaker version of this guard; it is a different and worse thing, because it always returns an answer.
  • Chain length is a signal, not an error. Resolution has no hop limit — a bound would silently hand back a tombstoned id, which is the single failure this function exists to prevent, and the argument for following every hop above is the argument for having no bound. Instead a chain longer than three hops is reported, because four merges in a row on one line of people does not mean the data is odd: it means the matcher is producing duplicates faster than a human can settle them, which is a statement about the queue and not about the row. Check 3 in §10 is written for exactly this: a survivor that has itself been absorbed is what a chain looks like when it works, so only the depth of a chain means anything.

"Every place that accepts a person id from outside must call this" is a rule about application code, which application code can forget, and D-072 took away the database-level ways of catching the forgetting. Check 4 in §10 is the net under it — live rows that reference a tombstoned person, the only form of this failure that is still visible after the fact.

docs.title: 10. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Checks that should run nightly, and that somebody reads the same morning. These encode invariants that no per-column rule above can express. A result here is a report a person opens; no check in this section sends anything to anybody (D-164), and where a bullet below says a finding belongs in the report rather than in a log, what it means is that the finding must not wait for a reader to stumble on it.

Invariants to verify

  • A person with more than one live account. Count account rows per person whose status is pending_verification, active or suspended; anything above one is a breach of the rule in §4, and the point of the check is to confirm that rule really does exclude the pending-plus-active combination.
  • Two current identifiers where the scheme forbids it. Count person_identifier rows per (scheme, value) among the current ones, for every scheme whose is_unique is true; non-zero is a breach of the rule in 01a §7, which no index can carry because the answer lives in another table's column. 00 §6a promised this report in the sentence that explained why, and D-130 is the round that wrote it down somewhere.
  • A person whose displayed name is not their current one. Count persons whose given_name/family_name differ from the person_name row with no valid_to for the same name_type; the copy is what every list view shows, and it is an obligation on the writing transaction that nothing enforces. This bullet is the answer to what F-28 asked, and the answer is: the copy stays, and this is the report that keeps it honest (D-142). Delete the copy and read the name from the history was the other option, and it was refused because the name a reader must be able to print for somebody who has never been opened as a record — a roster printed at a door, a label, a search hit — should not depend on walking a history table for the open row. The view that would replace the copy is the same query; the copy is its materialised half, and a drift check is the price of materialising anything, paid in the open. What this bullet had never carried was the admission that it existed — the invariant register said for two rounds that no report counted this drift, in a column where a claim of absence is as checkable as a citation (D-129), and the register now names this bullet as that rule's backstop.
  • A tombstoned person with no merge record. Count persons whose merge pointer is set but who do not appear as the merged person of any un-reversed person_merge row; non-zero means a pointer was written without the record that explains it, which is the case the append-only table in §8 exists to make impossible.
  • A merge chain longer than three hops. Walk each tombstone's pointer and count the hops to the survivor; report the chains over three. This is a report about a queue, not a finding about a row. How many survivors have themselves been absorbed means nothing: with chains kept D-087, a person absorbed twice has a survivor who was absorbed, by construction, so that count is the normal shape of the data and its expected value is not zero. What carries information is the depth: four merges in a row on one line of people means the matcher is producing duplicates faster than a human can settle them. It is read alongside the review queue's age, never on its own, and it asks for no urgency — there is nothing wrong to fix on the row, and a finding whose only possible answer is "work faster" only teaches a reader to skip the findings that aren't.
  • A live row that references a tombstoned person. Count rows in any table that names a person which point at a person whose merge pointer is set, where the referring row is itself live. This is the only net under §9's rule that every entry point calls resolve_person(), and it exists because D-072 took the database-level ones away. Getting that call wrong is invisible at the moment it happens — a blank name in a list, at worst the wrong name — and permanent afterwards, because the row is written and referenced by whatever came after it. This one belongs in the report, not in a log: the gap is not reconstructable later, and unlike a missing audit entry it misattributes a person rather than merely forgetting them.
  • A cycle in the merge graph. Walk the pointers and look for a row reachable from itself. There should never be a single row here: §8 refuses a merge whose chosen survivor resolves to the person being absorbed, so a non-zero count is not untidy data, it is that rule having failed, and it is the one merge finding that should stop work rather than fill a report — resolve_person() does not terminate on a cycle, and every screen and every resolver hop that touches the affected people goes with it.
  • An account held below active by an unresolved hypothesis for more than 30 days. Count accounts whose status is not active or closed, whose person is named by a hypothesis still in proposed or needs_review, where that hypothesis is older than 30 days — the same shape as the conflict-age check below, for the same reason. It belongs in the report, not in a log, and the reason is worth keeping in the check's own text: a stalled identity queue stopped being a data-quality problem the day it acquired the power to hold a login. Behind each row is a specific person who cannot sign up — often to a camp whose form closes this week — and no channel by which to tell anyone except a telephone call.
  • Unresolved merge conflicts older than 30 days. Count field_conflict rows resolved to unresolved and created more than 30 days ago; non-zero means the review queue is being ignored and the data is quietly wrong.
  • Redacted people still referenced by a live account. Count account rows that are not closed and belong to a person with redacted_at set; non-zero means an erasure left a working login behind.
  • Imported people with no membership period. Count people whose record_origin is legacy_import and who have no membership row at all. What makes this a check rather than a census is the ratio: a batch in which nobody has a period is a batch whose rows simply said nothing, and a batch whose stated-coverage figure disagrees with the periods written is a partially applied one. A row that created a membership its export did not state is a different finding, and lives in 06-audit-and-import.md §5. A check whose trigger condition is normal for the whole corpus is not a check. This row is really a claim about what an import is allowed to conclude, and it has had to pass that test twice. Once when a roster-only row was the ordinary condition of the entire legacy corpus, so the check reported all of it as a failed batch — which is why D-090 turned it to no participation row. Once when the people export turned out to state membership periods, so the import writes bounded membership rows for precisely those people and nobody else (D-093). The reading in between is void on its own terms: the participation table it named is deleted (D-097). What survived both reversals is the test, which is why the row is read as a ratio and not as a count.
  • A redacted person with descriptive values still attached. Stated where the rows are, as check 5 of 09-attributes.md §8 — attribute rows belonging to a redacted person, and attribute values still present in audit_log. It is named here because the redaction checks above are the same erasure guarantee read from the identity side, and a half-finished erasure does not announce which table it stopped in. Of everything on either list, that is the one that must not wait for the next time a reader looks.

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
• Erasure policy specifics: what must be redacted vs. retained. The retention shape is decided; what is open is whether it has a basis. The shape is (D-088) — so what is left is the question a decision log cannot settle, namely whether indefinite retention of named membership and fee rows has a basis. See 00-conventions.md and 06-audit-and-import.md §6.
  • Whether person.gender is needed at all; if so, what value set.
  • Whether the organization has (or will have) a national SSO identity provider — this determines how much of account_credential is actually used.

Both questions this page grew up around are settled and closed in the register: whether merge chains stay (they do, and the two rules a permanent chain needs are written where they are obeyed — the cycle refusal in §8, the length report in §10), and whether a person may hold two live accounts at once (no — and the case that made that question hard is answered by a gate rather than an exception, so a colliding sign-up files a claim and activates nothing instead of becoming a second account). See B-2 and B-4.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Groups
docs.text:
person_group and person_group_member: named sets of people with dated members, and a group as an item a grant can be written on.

The unit has no table on this page, because it is a scope: grant_scope_type carries a code unit with is_item_scoped = false, and there is exactly one of it (D-097). Membership of the unit is in 03-membership.md; roles and role_holder are in 05-authorization.md §3–§4. A reader who came from an old report and is looking for one of the tables that used to be on this page will find §5; every one of those names is also indexed in ../appendix/removed-concepts.md.

Domain rationale: ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

docs.title: 1. person_group
docs.text:
A group is a named set of people with a lifetime. It is not a body: no parent, no type, no code, no path, no permissions of its own. The full argument for each absence is in ../domain/04-organization-structure.md §2, and the absence table below is the same list stated as columns.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only; never exposed. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system, and unique. name text, required The one the organization uses in speech and in an expression as GROUP(name). Carries no identity — see the naming rules below. description text, optional What the group is for, for whoever finds it in a list two years from now. valid_from date, required When the group began. valid_to date, optional NULL = open. An ended group is never deleted: its member rows still answer the historical question (§4). Setting it is refused while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names the group (§3). created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns (00-conventions §7). An empty created_by is read as this system acting on its own by §7a — and this table has no routine case of one: the import owes it no rows (§1) and the seed ships none (§7), so an empty one here is a migration or a one-off correction, which is the shape §7a's list is written to name.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from. Either end may be absent on valid_to, and no comparison is attempted when it is.
  • name is unique across person_group, role and audience together, compared after folding case, whitespace and separators on write. Bare COUNSELORS resolves against roles and groups at once, so one namespace is what makes an expression mean one thing (D-101); audience.code is in the same namespace, since a name that resolves two ways is a silent grant (D-103). Note the asymmetry: audience.code is optional and unique-where-set, so an unnamed audience is simply not composable, while a group's name is required — a group that cannot be named cannot be talked about either. No constraint spans three tables, so the write path carries this rule and integrity checks 3 and 4 in §6 cover both halves of it — the split D-081 requires, stated here rather than assumed.
  • Every selector_type.code is a reserved name. A group called MEMBERS is refused when it is saved, not discovered later as an expression whose meaning moved (D-101). The reserved list is read from the registry rather than duplicated, which is one of the jobs that makes selector_type real data and not a tidying.
  • There is no import_batch_id on either table in this document, and that is a fact rather than an omission. The corpus names no groups (D-092) and the import owes no group rows (D-097), so no row here can ever have been produced by the batch. A column that is always NULL, on the one table whose whole content is a human decision, would advertise a capability the module does not have.

Columns a body would have had, and are not here. Each absence is a decision rather than an omission, so the list is worth keeping next to the table:

Not present Why it is absent parent_group_id, path, depth, any nesting rule the hierarchy itself (D-097) group_type_id, and any vocabulary of group kinds org_unit_type, and D-054's argument about not guessing words code D-096's method says a label carries no identity, so a second label would only create a second way to be wrong (§1's naming rules) status (proposed/active/closed), closed_reason_code a group has a period. Two states, valid_to NULL or not, and no status that can disagree with it data_confidence the rows are typed by a person (§4); there is nothing uncertain about how they arrived name history rows a rename edits name, and the previous name is gone — the cost §1's naming rules state any split / merger / successor_of edge D-098 refuses group-to-group edges outright: a split is one group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them join_reason_code, leave_reason_code, is_primary, role_in_unit the same list, on the member table (§2) allows_minors, or any flag about who may belong D-095, and nothing on a group replaces it (../domain/04-organization-structure.md §3) fee_*, dues_* membership at the unit is the only thing that costs money any role, office or leadership column D-098: nothing on a group says who leads it; an office is a role and its holder a role_holder row (05-authorization.md §4, D-100)

Naming, and the rule that a name does not carry. A name that comes back after a decade is a new person_group row, unless somebody records the continuity (D-096, whose method is that continuity is asserted, never matched). The default is stated because an unstated one gets implemented by whoever writes the matching screen, and that screen matches on name. Where the assertion would be recorded is not decided: no group column carries it, so the enforceable half of the rule is the default and the rest is prose. The domain page states the cost: ../domain/04-organization-structure.md §4. What is settled is that a rename is cheap and safe: a grant and an expression store kind + id, never a name, so renaming a group never rewrites a grant (D-101).

person_group is registered in grant_scope_type — which is what makes a group an item, and is §3.

docs.title: 2. person_group_member
docs.text:
The roster, as dated rows. One row per person per membership period. Joining, leaving and coming back are all periods on the same pair, which is what lets the roster answer a question about the past without asking the audit trail — whose payloads expire after two years (D-088) and which must not become the history of record for anything (D-098).

Fields

Field Kind Notes group_id reference to person_group, required person_id reference to person, required Never a membership, never a user account: a person (D-009's rule, transferred to the table that outlived unit_participation). valid_from date, required The first day the person is in the group. valid_to date, optional NULL = still in the group. The day the person is no longer in it, half-open — see the overlap rule. added_by reference to person, required Who wrote it. Required, not optional: no row in this table is allowed to be unattributed, because the permission that writes it is the module's only safeguard (§4). note text, optional Why, in the organization's words. Free text, deliberately — see below for what it is not. created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • No two rows for the same (group_id, person_id) may cover the same date. The rule counts every row, open and closed alike — there is no status to scope it by, and scoping it to the open rows would be a different and weaker rule. Periods are half-open, so a row ending on a day and a row beginning on that same day do not collide (D-002). Consequences, both wanted: a person who left in 2020 and returned in 2024 is two rows, and a hand-edited single row that hides the gap is refused by the shape of the data rather than by a rule nobody remembered to write.
  • A person may be in any number of groups at the same time. No cross-group rule of any kind, and no is_primary deciding which roster to show first.
  • group_id and person_id are never edited on an existing row. Close the row and open a new one (§4).
  • A member row whose period lies outside its group's period is reported, not refused. The two periods are two facts and D-098 keeps both without ruling that one contains the other, so containment is assumed here and nowhere decided. Status: assumption — see integrity check 2, and §8.

Who enforces the overlap rule. D-081 makes a rule name its enforcement, so the answer is specific. The migration layer, by the standing rule of 00-conventions.md §6a: a correctness property of the data belongs in the database, even when the ORM cannot generate it and the migration must be written by hand. Application validation still belongs on the write path, because it produces the error message a volunteer can read — but it is a usability feature and not the invariant. Underneath, integrity check 1 is the nightly net.

And this is shape 1, and its layer is assigned: the overlap invariant needs an exclusion constraint over a range built from two columns; no ORM emits one, so the register names a hand-written migration as the layer that carries it. Three specific traps on the way to writing this one by hand:

  • Shape 1 is usually worded "no two open rows overlap", and this rule is not that rule. Copying the shape as worded — a constraint scoped to rows with no valid_to — would permit a closed row and an open row for the same person and group to overlap, which is exactly the pair that makes "who was in this group in 2019?" have two answers. It is the same mistake §6a warns about from the other side: a conditioned constraint over unconditioned columns is a different rule. This one must be written over all rows.
  • valid_to is NULL for an open row, and the corpus refuses a sentinel date (03-membership.md §3), so the range cannot be built from the columns as they stand; it has to be built from an expression that supplies an upper bound. That is a second reason a generated schema will not have this constraint, and the reason the hand-written version is the deliverable rather than the annotation.
  • Half-open is part of the rule, not an implementation detail. A closed-open range ([from, to)) makes a leaving day and a joining day coexist, which is what §4's transfer relies on. An inclusive range refuses every transfer that happens on a single day and would be quietly loosened by whoever hits it.

Until that migration exists, this is a convention, not a guard — the phrase 00-conventions.md §6a reserves for exactly this case. It is stated here rather than softened because the alternative is a document that implies a database refuses overlapping rows when nothing yet does.

docs.title: 3. A group is an item: a grant can be written on one
docs.text:
person_group has a row in grant_scope_type, so a group is a thing a grant may be written on — which is how "these two people may work this group's roster" is said without inventing a scope (D-098). The scope types now are unit (not item-scoped, the organization itself), event, person_group, role, and document (deferred). role joins as an item for the same reason and by the same move (D-100).

Shape of grant on a group Reaches Written by at the unit, person_group.member.manage every group, existing and future — nothing stands between a unit-scope grant and an item after D-097 access_grant.create at the unit on one group, person_group.member.manage that roster only a holder of the code at the unit, or of a grant on that group either of the above, effect = deny defeats every allow that applies to that person, including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else the same — denies are legal at the unit and on an item (D-099)

person_group.member.manage is therefore applies_to = unit_and_item on the permission row (D-099): the two arms above are what that value is for. There is no self-scoped variant and none will be added — nobody writes themselves onto a roster (D-095, transferred intact in D-098).

The same group is also a leaf in an expression. GROUP(name) names this table's set, and the set is the member rows live on the date being checked (D-101; storage of the expression tree is not this page's subject). Three consequences worth stating next to the table they touch:

  • Membership confers nothing. The group is a set; a set is not a grant, and reaching a person through GROUP(x) happens only because some grant's expression says so (D-005).
  • An operand that does not resolve is the empty set. A deleted group id, an orphaned argument, a broken expression: it reaches nobody, and the answer is denial. Fail closed in every direction, as the resolver's rules already require. GROUP(nonexistent) is not an error at check time and must never become a permissive default.
  • The polymorphic id has no foreign key, exactly as access_grant.scope_id accepted it (D-011), and the compensating orphan check is specified once in 05d-invariants-and-seed.md §11. This page does not re-state it.

Ending a group is refused at save while something live names it, and the reason is the subtraction, not the grant. D-103 rules it for audiences — an audience may not be ended or deleted while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from a live grant, names it — and extends the same refusal to person_group in the round after, on identical reasoning. The reverse lookup is the audience arm's own query, one index: audience_operand rows whose selector_kind = 'GROUP', together with the grants whose scope is the group. Why a refusal, and not the report this page first wrote: an empty set is not neutral. A grant that merely has an ended group as its scope reaches nobody and is dead weight on the allow side, of the kind D-099 already reports for denies that deny nothing; named inside an expression the same emptiness points the other way, because EVERYONE - GROUP(x) with an empty GROUP(x) denies everybody. One field set on one group's row would then silently widen a deny that somebody else wrote, inside a grant the person who ended the group may never open. The refusal has two arms and the second is the one people forget, because it is not about ending anything: saving a new grant whose expression contains GROUP(x) for a group that is already ended is refused by the same rule, since the writer is pointing a live grant at an empty set, and EVERYONE - GROUP(x) is the same mistake arriving from the other end. A rule written only around the end-date field would leave that grant savable and this page's own report populated with something that looked allowed. The write path refuses both saves and integrity check 5 in §6 is the net beneath it — the split D-081 asks for, since a refusal that no code implements enforces nothing.

ROLE(x) needs no equivalent rule, and the difference is the shape of the set, not the idea of naming one. An office cannot be emptied quietly: there is no role.retire, no status column, and deleting a role is already refused while holder rows exist, so ending an office means ending role_holder rows one at a time, on a screen that shows each person. A group has a lifetime, and valid_to is one field that empties a set in one save. That is why the refusal names groups and audiences and not roles (D-103, whose own exception row states the point: the hazard is a property of the shape).

A group's set is stable across items, and that is worth one sentence of contrast. GROUP(x) means the same people whoever is being checked, so the grant editor's expansion of a group grant is per grant; the operands that bind to the item (PLACED, ORGANIZERS, …) mean different people on different events and must be previewed per item (D-102). The presence operand is not among them: PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is refused, because a column that is NULL until somebody takes a register would revoke a child's access to their own photos because a volunteer forgot a tick box.

A deny that matches no live allow is dead weight and is reported — the check is specified in 05d-invariants-and-seed.md §11 and applies to group-scope denies as to any other, because a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason (D-099).

docs.title: 4. Joins, leaves and transfers: close one row, open another
docs.text:
Every change to a roster is a period ending and a period beginning. Nothing on a member row is edited to move a person anywhere. This is the discipline 03-membership.md states for a membership, restated here because this is the table it is exercised on:

Never rewrite a member row to point at a different person or a different group. Close it and open a new one. Rewriting destroys the answer to "where was this child in 2003?" — and unlike most tempting edits, this one leaves no bad row behind, only a history that quietly stopped being true.

Change The write Rows afterwards Someone joins insert one row, valid_from = the day, added_by = the writer 1 Someone leaves set valid_to on the open row — the only in-place edit this table permits, and only on the row that is open 1 They come back later insert a second row. Never reopen the first, never extend it 2 They move from group A to group B on 1 June close A's row with valid_to = 1 June, open B's row with valid_from = 1 June 2, one in each group A group splits in two create the two groups, insert member rows for whoever is in each, move whatever grants name the old one, and only then end it — valid_to is refused while a live grant or expression names the group (§3). No edge connects them — see §1's absence table old group closed, two open A name comes back years later a new person_group row (§1) 2 groups, same name, no relation

Half-open is what makes the transfer row land on one day. A row ending on 1 June and a row beginning on 1 June do not overlap, so a handover has no gap and no double-count, and no one has to invent a midnight.

A row is written by a person, and that is the whole of how the roster gets populated. The import owes no member rows, and nothing is inferred from attendance, from an event, or from anything else the schema holds (D-092, D-097). The gate is person_group.member.manage, at the unit or on one group (§3), the write is audited, and the row names who wrote it — which is D-095's answer to do not place a child where nobody is responsible for them.

No reason field, and no role label, on purpose. No join_reason_code / leave_reason_code, so there is no transfer, promotion, reorganisation, unit_closed vocabulary to maintain, get wrong, or pretend is a safeguard — the eighteen-ticks-without-a-receipt shape D-095 refused. And no label saying what a member is, because such a label becomes an authorization check the moment somebody asks "can they edit the roster?". The note column is where any of that reasoning goes, as prose, unread by the resolver (D-098).

A grant that needs one more person does not get it by editing a roster. The temptation is real, because a group is the thing with a roster editor. It is refused because a group's rows are true when no grant points at them (D-098): editing one to move one grant's reach edits a roster that other grants read, and invents a group nobody talks about. The alternative is in the expression, where D-105 put it — write PERSON(honza) in the expression that needed them, where it is visible, dated by the grant that carries it, and meaningless outside it (D-101).

docs.title: 5. What this page held before round 10
docs.text:
What was here was a different module. Until round 10 this page described the organization's structure: units nested in units, typed, with nesting rules deciding what a unit of one type may contain; name rows carrying rename history; split, merger and succession edges; a roster per unit; positions people were appointed into; and scope_exposure rows letting one unit reach into another. D-097 deleted the hierarchy, D-098 took its smallest body and made it a person_group, and D-100 deleted the positions. What that machinery was for is done now by things that are not structure: belonging to the organization is a membership (03-membership.md), a set of people is §1–§2, an elected leader is a role_holder row (05-authorization.md §4), and do not place a child where nobody is responsible for them is person_group.member.manage held by a named adult (§4).

Every one of those names has a row in ../appendix/removed-concepts.md, with what went beside it, why, and what enforces whatever survived: the org_unit family with its type rules, name rows and relationship edges; unit_participation with its join and leave reason vocabularies; position and position_assignment with their occupancy columns; scope_exposure and the scope.expose codes; and the unit_ancestors() / unit_descendants() traversal. Integrity checks 1–10 of the old §9 went with their subjects, which D-097 records along with the job of the one check whose whole duty was asserting that a migration had emitted a guarantee rather than that any row was clean — a pattern that survives as check 4 below. Nothing survived as data except the rosters, which became person_group_member (§2); membership of the unit is the membership row, and it owes no second row to anything (03-membership.md §5).

docs.title: 6. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. Two member rows for the same person and group covering the same date (§2). Counts overlapping pairs over all rows, half-open, so it agrees with the constraint it is the net beneath. §2 names the migration as the enforcing layer, as shape 1 assigns it; this report is what notices if that migration was never written, which is the job the register names this check for.
  2. A member row lying outside its group's own period (§2). A list to read rather than a breach: the two periods are two facts and containment is assumed here, not ruled (Status: assumption — §8). A large count means people are editing old rows instead of opening new ones.
  3. A group name that collides — with another group, with a role, with a set audience.code, or with a reserved selector_type.code (§1). Reports the collisions the write path should have refused; a non-zero count means a path exists that bypasses it, which in a system with an import, a data fix and a second client is a question of when.
  4. The cross-table name rule is still carried by the write path (§1). Not a data report: an automated test that attempts to save a duplicate name, and a second that attempts MEMBERS, and expects both refusals. No constraint can hold this rule, so if the code loses it, nothing else notices: this is an assertion that a guarantee still exists rather than that the data looks fine, which is why it is numbered here rather than left to the test suite's own memory.
  5. A live grant whose scope is a group that has ended, or a live expression with a GROUP(x) leaf on one. A save-time refusal, and a report that watches whether the refusal is still there. D-103 refuses the end date at save while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from a live grant, names the group; §3 states the rule, the query behind it, and why an empty operand on the - side is dangerous rather than merely inert. What the report still earns is D-081's half of the arrangement — the refusal is application code, and application code loses things. Two causes put a row on this list and both are now regressions: either the write path stopped refusing the end, which means fixing the code and then the rows; or the grant was written onto a group that was already ended — a direction the rule needed saying twice, because a constraint on ending alone would leave this report full of behaviour that looked permitted (D-103 refuses both). That second cause is why the question about hiding ended groups from pickers (§8) is not cosmetic. Read the leaves sitting inside a subtraction first: EVERYONE - GROUP(ended) denies everybody, where the same ended group as a plain scope denies nobody.
  6. An open group with no open member rows for a long period. A data-quality list: often legitimate (a project group between seasons), sometimes a group that ended and nobody set valid_to. Nothing should reject it; somebody should be able to see it.

Checks 1 and 4 fail on different things and must not be read alike. Check 1 finds bad rows; check 4 finds a missing guarantee while every row is still clean. Only check 4 belongs in CI.

docs.title: 7. Seed data
docs.text:
No group is seeded, and that is the decision rather than a gap. The seed ships zero person_group rows. The corpus names no groups, so there is nothing to import and nothing to infer (D-092); a seeded group would be an invented one, which is the exact error D-054 recorded about the unit vocabulary — a wrong vocabulary in seed data is harder to dislodge than an absent one. Groups are runtime data, exactly as role is (D-052): the organization creates them, names them in its own words, and ends them.

The one set people expect to find here is a role, and it is not on this page. The office this design keeps using as its example, counselors, belongs in the role table and not this one: a permanent, organization-wide population is the opposite of what a group is (D-100). That was a decision about which table, never about who writes the row — no role ships, so this one is written by the organization like every other (D-150, D-154). What an event's organizers may do is not here either, and it is not a shipped row: the act that creates the event writes one item-scope allow per event code aimed at ORGANIZERS, twelve beside every event (D-151; D-102 owns the sets they are aimed at, and §3 explains why a group is an item).

Nothing about the unit is seeded on this page. The unit arrives as a code in grant_scope_type, a lookup row in the authorization module, so there is no root row to create and no type to give it. Nothing is seeded that could contradict the runtime behaviour, which is the property D-054 was protecting above.

docs.title: 8. Open issues
docs.text:
• Where a claimed group continuity is recorded. §1 states the default (a returning name is a new group) and D-096's method says the continuity is asserted, never matched — but no row on this page can hold the assertion, and D-098 refuses group-to-group edges.
