  • Whether a member row must lie inside its group's period. Assumed in §2, reported in §6 check 2, and nowhere ruled. A one-sentence decision either way; left open rather than decided by a document.
  • Whether an ended group is hidden from pickers, and whether it may be reopened. An ended group has a behaviour; person_group has a period and no rule about which screens read it. Reopening an ended group by clearing valid_to would also collide with §1's rule that a returning name is a new group, so the two questions are one question.

The questions this page once wondered about, open and settled alike, are registered in ../open-questions.md; a settled one is listed there with the decision that settled it.

docs.title: Data Model — Membership
docs.text:
membership_type, membership, and membership_request.

Belonging to the organization is a membership; belonging to a group is person_group_member, specified in the groups module. Nothing is in between: there is no per-unit participation row, because the unit is a scope and not a table (D-097). §5 is the pointer left where that table used to be specified, and where the write obligation it carried now sits on groups.

Domain rationale: ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: 1. membership_type — one row, kept as a table
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes code text, required 'member' — and nothing else, for now. name text, required description text, optional duration_months integer, required, defaults to 12 12: the fee is yearly. Kept as a column rather than a constant so a type with a different term could be added as a row, with no migration. expiry_month, expiry_day integers, required, both defaulting to 1 When the fee expires (D-047): 1 January. The organizational year runs with the calendar, so "a member this year" means what a reader expects, and the sweep, the campaign and the reports all land on a boundary nobody has to look up. These are columns, not a constant in a scheduled job, for the reason given for the renewal window below: the date is a parameter the organization may move, and moving it must not require a code change. Every lapse date, the yearly sweep and the renewal worklist derive from these two values. renewal_grace_days integer, required, defaults to 60 The renewal window after valid_to, during which a payment restores the membership without re-applying and backdates the new period to the expiry date. Dates, not a status: the person is expired throughout (D-040). 60 days (D-048). Read it from here; never hardcode 60 in a job or a front end (D-048). The requirement attached to that answer was precisely that the value stays tunable. is_self_registerable boolean, required, defaults to true requires_approval boolean, required, defaults to true sort_order integer rank, required, defaults to 0 valid_from, valid_to period (from/to, open-ended allowed); both ends optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • code is unique over all rows.
  • expiry_month is between 1 and 12; expiry_day is between 1 and 31.
  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from. Either end may be absent, and no comparison is attempted when one is.

docs.title: Why this table still exists with one row
docs.text:
There is exactly one membership (D-037). Everyone who is a member holds membership_type = 'member', the fee is flat and per person, and being a counselor or a leader is a role, never a type (D-100).

The table survives rather than collapsing into a constant for two reasons:

  1. Consistency with the design's own principle. Vocabularies are rows, not enums — the same argument that keeps the seeded registries as tables (grant_scope_type, selector_type). A second kind of membership (a supporting or honorary one) would then be a data change.
  2. A place for the organizational calendar to live. The term, the expiry date and the renewal window are genuinely type-dependent parameters even when there is one type — and they are the parameters most likely to be tuned. Putting them in a row rather than in code is what makes "it should not be hard to modify" (D-048) true by construction rather than by discipline.

The cost is honest and small: an FK that currently always holds one value. Recorded here rather than hidden.

docs.title: What is deliberately not on this table
docs.text:
The type says nothing about who may join, and nothing about what they pay. No age floor, ceiling, or automatic age-out: membership is ageless and age is a fact about the person (D-038). No requirement a request can be held up by: nothing gates a request but identity and payment (D-044), and the system records no background checks at all (D-043). No flag saying whether two memberships may overlap — the person-scoped overlap constraint of §3 decides that, and decides it the same way for every type. No fee reference: the fee is flat and per person, so a schedule attaches to the obligation instead (07-finance.md §2). And the grace is a window read from renewal_grace_days, never a status a member enters (D-040).

Why: a vocabulary row that also carries eligibility rules is a second place the admission policy can drift out of agreement with itself — D-037. The names of the columns that carried those rules are indexed in removed-concepts.md.

docs.title: 2. membership_request
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system; unique. person_id reference to person, required The subject: the person who would become a member. For a minor's application this is the child, not the parent. submitted_by_person_id reference to person, optional Who actually submitted it. Equals person_id for self-application; differs when a guardian (or staff) applies on behalf. This is the act-on-behalf record. requested_membership_type_id reference to membership_type, required status text, required, defaults to draft One of draft, submitted, under_review, approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired. submitted_at timestamp, optional decided_at timestamp, optional decided_by reference to person, optional rejection_reason text, optional Free text, written by whoever rejects (D-128) rejection_note text, optional membership_id reference to membership, optional Set on approval. The reference is added only once membership exists (§3): this is the design's circular pair, broken with an optional column and not a deferred constraint, which is what 00 §9 requires (D-129). previous_membership_id reference to membership, optional Links a renewal or re-application to the prior membership. This is how a returning member's chain is expressed. expires_at timestamp, optional An unreviewed request eventually goes stale. Needed so the review queue does not accumulate abandoned drafts forever. notes text, optional source text, optional self, guardian, staff or import. created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • A request in approved or rejected has both decided_at and decided_by. There is no decision without a decider and a time.
  • Any request that is not draft has a submitted_at.
  • An approved request points at a membership. The one allowance is a request decided at a time still in the future, which is how the request and the membership are inserted in two steps inside one transaction; the link is not optional once that transaction is over.
  • At most one open request per person per membership type. Open means draft, submitted or under_review. Decided requests — approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired — are outside the rule, which is what lets a person apply again after being turned down.

Indexes

  • On person_id with submitted_at descending: one person's applications, newest first.
  • A partial index over the review queue only — rows in submitted or under_review, which is the whole queue and nothing else.
  • On submitted_by_person_id, covering only the rows where that optional column is actually set.

person_id vs submitted_by_person_id is the most important pair in this table. The subject is the child; the submitter is the parent. Collapsing them into one column — which is what most systems do — makes it impossible to answer "who applied for this child?" and falsely attributes the parent's action to the child. See ../domain/02-actors.md.

Why requests are a separate table from memberships. A rejected request produces no membership and must not pollute member listings; a person may submit several over time; and review data (who decided, why) has no meaning on a membership. See ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

A request asks for membership of the organization, and names no body beneath it (D-098) — because there is no body beneath it to name (D-097). The want behind a which group? field is real: a reviewer would like to know where the applicant expects to turn up. It is served by the free-text notes the row already has, which is what such a field always was — a sentence addressed to whoever reads the request, carrying no authority. Placing the person is a separate act and a separate row — one person_group_member row, written by a person holding person_group.member.manage — and an approved request with no group beside it is a complete, ordinary outcome. Which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request.

A rejection requires a reason (ck_request_rejection_reason is the rule's name): no rejected request may be written without one. Two columns of the same row, so a migration can state it directly as a check on the row — and it belongs there rather than only in the model layer, because the two paths that most need catching, an import and a hand-corrected row, never reach a model-layer guard. "Why was this application turned down?" is asked months later, sometimes by the family. A rejection with no recorded reason is an answerable question made unanswerable.

previous_membership_id is what makes the returning-member chain explicit rather than inferred from date arithmetic.

docs.title: 3. membership
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system; unique. person_id reference to person, required membership_type_id reference to membership_type, required status text, required One of pending_payment, active, suspended, lapsed, terminated, completed. No default — the state is always chosen deliberately. completed has exactly one writer: the legacy import marks every closed period it inserts completed, because none of the six means a source stated this and nobody here decided, and completed is the second-worst of the two readings available (D-162); low in the column below is what makes it survivable. valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = open / current. Never NULL on an imported row — both ends are what makes an imported membership safe, and check 1 of 06-audit-and-import.md §5 counts the rows that broke it (D-093). joined_via_request_id reference to membership_request, optional renewed_from_membership_id self-reference to membership (the previous one), optional Forms the renewal chain. See domain/05 §6. outstanding_balance money amount, optional Denormalised from fee_obligation/payment. 07-finance.md §3 recommends dropping this column in favour of v_fee_obligation_balance — a wrong balance suspends the wrong child. Kept here only until that decision is taken. NULL on every imported row, and since D-093 put memberships back into the import that is load-bearing rather than incidental: the export carries no payment data, and a zero would be a claim — settled — that the export does not support. There is no fee_obligation underneath these rows either, which is what makes the NULL unambiguous rather than merely uncomputed (07-finance.md §2, D-090). termination_reason text, optional Free text, written by whoever terminates (D-128) termination_note text, optional ended_by reference to person, optional ended_at timestamp, optional data_confidence text, required, defaults to high One of high, medium, low. import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows. notes text, optional created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • A terminated membership has both a termination_reason and an ended_at.
  • A membership may not be renewed from itself: renewed_from_membership_id never points at its own row.
  • THE critical rule — one person, one membership, full stop. Two rows for the same person may not cover the same date while either of them is pending_payment, active or suspended. Periods are half-open, so one ending on a day and another beginning on that day do not collide. Statuses outside those three are outside the rule entirely, and the rule reaches every person regardless of membership type — the type is not part of it, and that omission is deliberate, as the next section explains.

Indexes

  • ix_membership_current — per person, over rows that are open and active. The membership gate reads through this, and it is the index a far-future sentinel date would defeat — see Why valid_to IS NULL and not a sentinel below.
  • On valid_to over active rows that have one. This drives the renewal worklist: who expires soon, who is in their renewal window.
  • On (status, valid_to) over active and pending_payment rows — the states anyone is actually queried in.
  • On person_id with valid_from descending, and a period index per person: one person's membership history, and the range scan the overlap rule and every point-in-time question use.

docs.title: One person, one open membership
docs.text:
The uniqueness rule is scoped to the person, not to the type (D-037): with one membership type, the case an honorary member who is also an active member cannot arise, so "one person, one open membership" is an enforceable invariant rather than a convention. It is conditional uniqueness — one open row per person — which is the shape 00-conventions.md §6a says a migration must emit by hand: a unique constraint over all rows is a different rule and the wrong one, because it forbids the second closed membership that the person's history requires.

This is what makes is_current_member() a question about one row, one status, one date rather than one that has to reconcile concurrent memberships. It is worth saying who reads it: MEMBERS is evaluated live on the checked date, and it evaluates to exactly this predicate (§6, D-100). The constraint is what makes that evaluation cheap and unambiguous.

docs.title: renewed_from_membership_id and the renewal window
docs.text:
When a person pays inside the renewal window (D-040), the new membership's valid_from is set to the previous row's valid_to, not to the payment date. Two consequences worth stating:

  • The history shows continuous coverage — no gap, no spurious "returning member".
  • The person is nevertheless expired during the window (D-040). The two facts are compatible because the window is a date range, not a status: they were not a member while it was open, and the record of that period is filled in retrospectively once they pay. Nothing needs backdating in the audit sense, because the new row's as-of start is the expiry date and its audit time is the payment date — the two-times distinction in 00-conventions.md.

A payment after the window opens the new membership at the payment date, and the gap is real.

docs.title: The exclusion constraint and status transitions
docs.text:
The overlap rule covers only pending_payment, active, suspended. A terminated/lapsed/completed row is excluded, so a new membership can be created with a valid_from inside an old one's period without violating the constraint. This is deliberate — a returning member's new membership may legitimately overlap the tail of a lapsed one if the dates were entered imprecisely. Historical imports rely on this.

Consequence: the constraint does not prevent two active memberships with overlapping periods if one was inserted while in another status and then transitioned. A status update re-evaluates the constraint (PostgreSQL does check exclusion constraints on UPDATE), so this is safe — but the transition from lapsed back to active can therefore fail with a constraint violation. That is correct behaviour: it means the person has two overlapping claims to membership and someone must resolve it. Handle it as a business error, not a crash.

Which layer carries all of that: the migration. A status transition that re-checks the overlap is only a violation if the constraint is in the database, and no ORM emits an exclusion over a period assembled from valid_from and valid_to scoped to three statuses — the migration writes it, as 00-conventions.md §6a requires. The same check performed in the model layer returns a friendlier message a moment earlier and guarantees nothing: a batch that imports the legacy people export writes memberships by the thousand (D-090, D-093), and a hand-corrected row never passes through the model layer either. Both meet the constraint in the database; neither would ever meet a model-layer check.

docs.title: Why valid_to IS NULL and not a sentinel
docs.text: Repeated from the conventions because it is the mistake most likely to be made here. A '9999-12-31' sentinel breaks IS NULL checks, makes daterange spans enormous, and defeats the ix_membership_current partial index. Use NULL.

docs.title: renewed_from_membership_id
docs.text:
Renewal opens a new row (Shape A in ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md). The self-reference makes the chain explicit:

membership 501  member  1990-09-01 → 1991-06-30   completed
     ↑ renewed_from
membership 502  member  1991-09-01 → 1992-06-30   completed
     ↑ renewed_from
membership 503  member  1992-09-01 → 1993-06-30   completed
(The type is member on every row — there is only one type, and the person's age is not part of it: §1, D-037, D-038.)

"Why does this person have 15 membership rows?" is then answerable by following the chain rather than by reasoning about dates. And a gap — a missing link — is visible as data.

docs.title: Current-membership queries
docs.text:
Five questions the membership table has to answer, each with the exact rule that decides it. The wording of each is load-bearing; the differences between them are the design.

  • Is this person a member right now? is_current_member(person) — true when they have a membership whose status is active and whose period covers today: valid_from on or before today, valid_to absent or after today. No grace coalescing: a lapsed membership is lapsed, and the renewal window (domain/05 §6) is a date range for rejoining, not a state in which the person is a member. This predicate is what the MEMBERS selector evaluates on the checked date (§6) — the resolver asks the expression instead of asking this of a person directly, which changes the predicate's callers and not its meaning.
  • Was this person a member on a given past date? was_member_on(person, date) — true when a membership of theirs covers that date, on the same half-open terms, and its status is anything except pending_payment. Note the asymmetry with the question above: now demands active, then admits every terminal status, because how a membership ended does not change that it existed.
  • When does the organizational year containing a date expire? membership_expiry_date(as_of) — expiry_month and expiry_day read off the member row, applied to the year of as_of. Always derived from those two columns and never from a constant (D-047).
  • May this person renew without re-applying? in_renewal_window(person, as_of) — true when they have a membership of theirs that has ended (valid_to set) with valid_to on or before as_of, and valid_to plus that type's renewal_grace_days still after as_of; in other words the window is [expiry, expiry + grace), half-open like every other period here. No status is consulted — this is arithmetic on dates alone. D-040: expired, but inside the window. This is the distinction a grace_period_days membership status would have blurred: they are not a member, and they may rejoin cheaply. 60 days, read from the row (D-048). Not a member during the window: this answers "may they rejoin cheaply?", never "do they have access?".
  • How long has this person been a member? membership_years(person) — the sum of the lengths of their memberships, with today standing in for an open valid_to and any pending_payment row left out, expressed in years of 365.25 days.

membership_years sums the periods rather than subtracting the first join date from today. The difference is the 14-year gap in the returning-member case, and getting it wrong mislabels a returning member as having 36 years of service.

Age is never asked of a membership. The question is this person currently a child or an adult? has no answer on this table, because membership is ageless (D-038); it is a fact about the person, and the views ask it there:

Is this person a minor? is_minor(person, as_of) — true when person.birth_date is recorded and as_of falls before their eighteenth birthday. A person with no recorded birth date is not a minor by this test; nothing guesses one. A fact about the person, never about their membership.

This matters for guardianship and safeguarding, which are where age legitimately bears — not for whether someone may be a member.

docs.title: 4. What a membership request must contain
docs.text:
Identity and the fee — nothing to verify (D-044). A request is a person, a submitted timestamp, a reviewer, a decision and a payment. The membership_request table in §2 is complete as it stands, and no checklist table sits beside it.

Guardian consent is not a membership requirement. It belongs to the guardianship layer, where it is a relationship fact rather than an item on a form — 04-relationships.md.

If a requirement ever appears — a form, an interview, a document — it arrives as a table added deliberately, with the requirement that made it necessary recorded as a decision.

Why: the general-purpose mechanism was deleted rather than kept as empty infrastructure, so a future requirement is a decision rather than a reuse of a shelf that is no longer there — D-044.

docs.title: 5. unit_participation — deleted by D-097
docs.text:
Deleted by D-097. There is one unit, it is the organization, and it is a scope rather than a row — so there is no body below it to belong to, and no table to record belonging in. Everything the table carried goes with it: the sub-unit rosters, the root participation row every membership owed, the transfers between units, the display label and primary flag those rows carried, the vocabulary of reasons a row was opened or closed, and the confidence value an import stamped on them. removed-concepts.md indexes their names.

What the reasoning was, and what survives the table. Belonging below the organization is participation, not a species of membership (D-041). An earlier name for that table had asserted otherwise, and the distinction settled the questions the name raised — which membership was which, and whether a fee was owed twice. The distinction is alive one level down: membership of a group confers nothing and owes nothing, because participation is not authority and being stored in a tidier table does not quietly promote it (D-098, restating D-005). The key says the same thing: person_group_member is keyed on person_id, never membership_id, because a person may belong somewhere with no membership behind them, and a row about 1998 must not become unrepresentable because the record of 1998 status is thin or absent.

Where each question goes now (D-098) — two shapes, and no depth parameter on either:

Question Read Who is in the organization on date D? membership — one query over the period and status of §3 Who is in group G on date D? person_group_member — a point-in-time read over the dated rows, 02-organization.md §1

What the pair used to buy was one query shape for both rows of that table, and that is what is given up. What is given back is the redundancy: two tables kept in step only by an obligation on every writer, and a report watching for the writers who forgot.

docs.title: The write obligation is retired, and so is the check that watched it
docs.text:
No write owes a second row to anything (D-097). The rule this section carried was that no write may change a membership's period, or open or close one, without making the matching change to that person's root-unit participation row in the same transaction — two rows holding one fact — and integrity check 1b was the report that found whoever skipped it. Nothing enforces either of them now, because there is nothing left to enforce: the second row is deleted, so this is not a rule running without a guard but a redundancy removed, and membership is the single record and cannot disagree with a copy of itself. Obligation and check retire together rather than being restated somewhere else, which is what D-081 asks for: said plainly, not left as a silence.

Why this is written down instead of quietly dropped: the pairing was reversed twice inside three rounds — a correction, the reversal of that correction, then the deletion of the arm both readings were arguing about — and what every one of them got right is the framing rather than the conclusion. The obligation was never about one batch: import, renewal, extension and hand-corrected row each owed the paired write exactly as much, and the answer moved twice only because nobody had read the input file (D-092, D-093). Read the input before saying what an import owes.

A renewal opens a row that starts where the old one ended. The sweep sets the expiring row's valid_to to the expiry date, and a payment inside the window opens the new membership with valid_from set to exactly that date (§3, and ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md §6), so the record reads as continuous coverage while the person was expired throughout the window. The deleted root row bought its version of that look by being extended rather than closed and reopened (D-050); what was accepted along with it is worth stating once, because it is the same answer today — a roster answers who was in this body when, and a child who was there across a lapse has exactly one answer to that, while membership remains the authority on payment. With the second row gone, both answers come from membership alone.

docs.title: Moving between groups closes one row and opens another
docs.text:
Moving a person from one group to another is two writes — closing one person_group_member row and opening another — never an edit of the group on the existing row (D-098). Close-and-open is what preserves "where was this child in 2003?"; an in-place update destroys it, and the whole temporal design exists to answer that question. Nothing about the person's membership, their fee, or their standing as a member changes, because moving was never a membership event.

Who enforces it now. The close-and-open pair is the write path's, behind person_group.member.manage, audited and naming who wrote the row; the invariant underneath it — no two rows for one person and one group overlap, counted over all rows and not only the open ones, half-open so a row ending on a day and one beginning that day do not collide — is shape 1, which a hand-written migration emits and the ORM will not. A person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is therefore two rows, never one row edited in place: the edit destroys the answer to "were they in the group in 2019?". The groups module owns both, and this document does not re-specify them — 02-organization.md §1–§2 and ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

What was given up, named as a loss. A group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them unless somebody writes one: org_unit_relationship's split_from / merged_into / successor_of are deleted, so restructuring has stopped being a recorded event (D-097's third loss). The bulk reorganisation transfer goes with it — close and open across every member of a body, as one named procedure with a dry run, carrying a reason saying why. There is no reorganisation to perform in one statement now, and the lineage it recorded is a thing a person would have to write down on purpose. The roster's own columns went too: a vocabulary of reasons for opening and closing a row, a primary-group flag saying which of a person's groups to show first, a display label, and an import-confidence value with nothing left to import into — the corpus names no groups either, so every group member row is typed by a person, which is also the only way one can be true (D-092). D-098 gives up the lot, on the instruction that a group needs no special features; their names are indexed in removed-concepts.md.

docs.title: 6. Membership and the authorization system
docs.text:
The resolver does not ask whether you are a member. The grant does (D-100). This is the single largest coupling between these two modules, so it is stated in full rather than in a footnote. MEMBERS is a selector operand, evaluated live on the checked date, and the question must this person be a current member to hold this? is answered by whether the expression says so:

What the writer means What the writer writes This office is for members only MEMBERS * ROLE(x) This office is for whoever holds it, member or not ROLE(x) …and this one named person too MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y)

Who enforces the rule: whoever writes the grant, by putting MEMBERS in the expression or leaving it out — and the expression is a row that can be read. A waiver for one person is + PERSON(y) in the same grant, which PERSON being a seeded selector makes ordinary (data-model/05 §8); where the exemption should outlive the office and carry its own dates, it is a second grant aimed at the person instead (D-105).

And that is the ruling, not an assumption standing in for one: per office, by whoever writes the grant, no default either way — not into the expression and not out of it (D-165). No screen fills the term in and no screen strips it, and a grant written without the term needs no reason field — grant_reason is an optional column and stays optional. Day one's grant carries no MEMBERS term at all: it names one person, and a grant aimed at one person has no expression to carry one, and a grant with no expression to carry one cannot be read as having declined one — so the lockout D-051 was written against is answered by D-150 and not by an exemption.

Guardianship and ownership were never gated. A parent's authority comes from a legal relationship, so an unpaid fee must not stop a parent acting for their child; and a lapse must not lock a person out of the very screen they renew on. Both are channels, and a channel is not something a grant gates. The third case — appointed counselors and local leaders the organization needs present regardless of their own fee status — is the only one that was ever a waiver of a gate, and it is now simply the second row of that table: write the office without MEMBERS.

The posture is opt-in, so the new failure is named rather than buried. The gate used to be default-on, so forgetting it was impossible; now a grant written ROLE(TREASURERS) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently, forever. Three controls, none of which is the resolver:

  • A standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand whose expression does not contain MEMBERS — check 1 of §7. An office held by a non-member is the case worth a human eye, and the report is narrow enough to actually be read.
  • The grants this system writes for itself are named, and their missing MEMBERS is deliberate. Creating an event writes twelve item-scope allows beside the event row, all aimed at the bare operand ORGANIZERS, none carrying MEMBERS — an organizer appointed for one weekend is not required to be a paying member (D-151). They name no ROLE(...), so the report above never sees them; every grant that does arrive through a screen is fair game for it.
  • Import completeness. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS is only as correct as the counselor roster: the gate used to fall out of membership alone, so an import that misses 300 counselors silently un-gates them. It fails closed — nothing breaks, which is exactly why nobody notices — and the import reconciliation report of D-090 must count people marked as counselors in the corpus against role_holder rows written.

What still costs, unchanged by the move:

  • A membership transition invalidates nothing, because nothing is stored to invalidate. A check resolves against the live rows and MEMBERS is evaluated on the checked date, so a lapse or a termination is visible the moment it is written; there is no answer kept anywhere that could go stale, and the yearly expiry sweep keeps every other thing it had to do (D-114, §11's invariant 19).

Why this is spelled out instead of left unsaid: the coupling this page once demanded here was real, the cache policy written three rounds later left membership off its list, and membership.terminate is exactly the ⛔ action a concerned guardian waits for. An invariant with nowhere to be violated closes that class of miss better than a louder requirement — which is what D-114 records. - A lapse silently removes access — from exactly those grants whose expression names MEMBERS, and from none of the others. "Why can't I see this?" now has an answer that is a date and a line of grant text.

The "leaver with access" report is two reports. D-071's posture transfers intact to role_holder: nothing forces a holder row to end, and the control is the report. Checks 1 and 2 of §7 are that control — one for grants that gate nothing, one for offices held by people who are not members.

Dormant authority is a real hazard. A membership that lapses and is renewed a year later resurrects every still-open role_holder row the person accumulated in the interim, including ones a human had quietly decided not to reinstate — and where the grant behind that role was written without MEMBERS, it was not dormant at all in the meantime, it was live. Closing the holder row at the same time as the membership is the honest fix; the reports find the ones that were missed. A role holder row should not outlive the membership that justified it.

A role is held at the unit and nowhere else. role_holder carries no scope columns, because D-097 left one scope; there is no body to hold an office of. The table, the ROLE(x) selector and the codes an office carries belong to 05-authorization.md §3 role and §4 role_holder.

docs.title: 7. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify. Six checks, numbered from 1. The retired numbers are listed after them, so that a citation of an old number — the decision log cites several — lands on an explanation rather than on a gap.

  • 1. Live grants that gate nothing. Counts live grants whose audience expression names a ROLE(...) operand and does not contain MEMBERS — D-100's standing report, restated here because this is the module whose data it reads. Enforced by no layer, and no layer can: whether an office is written with MEMBERS is a choice made in the grant text, so the controls are this report and the import count of §6 (§6 also names the twelve grants an event creation writes; this report never sees them, because they aim at ORGANIZERS and name no ROLE(...)). A non-zero count is not a fault — it is the list of offices worth a human eye, and it is narrow enough to actually be read.
  • 2. Non-members holding an office. Counts open role_holder rows whose holder is_current_member() says is not a member (§3). Enforced by nothing, deliberately: D-071's posture transfers to role_holder, so no constraint and no sweep ends a holder row and this report is the control. Read it with check 1, which says whether that role's grants are gated: on a gated role this is dormant authority that springs back to life at the next renewal, and on an ungated one it is access that is live today (§6).
  • 3. Approved requests that never produced a membership. Counts requests that are approved, carry no membership_id, and were decided more than seven days ago. Non-zero is an approval that went nowhere. Enforced by the §2 requirement that an approved request points at a membership once the deciding transaction is over — a deferred reference rather than a suggestion, and one a migration can state on the row.
  • 4. Memberships expiring soon. Counts active memberships ending within the next 90 days — the renewal campaign worklist (domain/05 §6), not a fault. Run by whoever runs the campaign; nothing here guards it, because there is nothing to guard.
  • 5. Renewal chains with a broken link. Counts memberships whose renewed_from_membership_id names a row that does not exist. Non-zero means the chain is followed into nothing. Enforced by the ordinary foreign key on that column, which any migration emits; the check survives as the assertion that the key is there, which is the form 00-conventions.md §6a prescribes for a constraint this project's ORM does not generate on its own.
  • 6. Renewals inside the window whose new period does not start at the previous expiry date. Counts renewals whose valid_from differs from the previous membership's valid_to and begins less than 91 days after it. The renewal rule (D-040) backdates the new period, so a mismatch means either a genuine post-window rejoin or a bug. Enforced by nothing: both answers are legal data, so only a report separates them, and only a reader decides which one it is looking at.

Checks 1 and 2 are read together, and neither alone is the control — one is a report about grant text and the other a report about people, and the risk only appears across both: an office held by somebody who is not a member is dormant authority when its grants say MEMBERS, and live access today when they do not (§6).

Check 4 is operational (a worklist for the renewal campaign). The rest are data-quality checks for cases no constraint rejects at the write.

Two checks this module deliberately does not hold. The one D-099 asks for — a live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow, and so denies nothing — is a report over grants, not over memberships, and belongs to 05d-invariants-and-seed.md §11. The no-overlap invariant over person_group_member belongs to the groups module, 02-organization.md §6. Naming both here is to stop either being written twice and drifting.

Retired with unit_participation (§5), listed so that a citation of an old number lands somewhere:

Old Was Where it went 1 participation rows with no membership at that time Deleted with the table (D-097). What survives is a habit rather than a query: every imported row satisfied this predicate by design, so the report's floor was thousands of findings that were correct — the shape to avoid before writing any "row without its obvious partner row" report here 1b the root participation row disagreeing with the membership it mirrored Deleted with the redundancy it watched (§5). There is no second row, so there is nothing to disagree and no writer left to name 2 ⚠ participants in units that do not allow minors Withdrawn by D-095. Who enforces the rule now: person_group.member.manage, held at the unit — which reaches every group — or granted on one group as an item, audited and naming who wrote the row (D-098). What is lost is unchanged and unrecoverable: no column says which groups take children, so the system can neither answer the question nor report on it

docs.title: 8. Seed data
docs.text:
The organization starts with a single membership type — member, named and described in plain words, open for a person to register themselves for, and left to requires_approval at its default of true. The term and the calendar parameters on that row are §1's, not constants anywhere else.

One row, and that is the whole vocabulary (D-037). The fee is flat and per person, so there is nothing to vary by type; being a counselor or a leader is a role, not a type (D-100); and membership is ageless, so there are no age limits to seed (D-038).

Nothing else is seeded here, and the office this design keeps naming as its example is not seeded either. counselors would be a row of the authorization module and not of this one, and no role ships at all: day one is one account holding system.admin at the unit, and the first office is a write like any other (05d-invariants-and-seed.md §12, D-150, D-154). D-100 settled which table a permanent, organization-wide population belongs in; it never asked anybody to write the row. A role is a set that confers nothing until a grant names it: no more than a membership type has ever conferred.

All three are settled, and all three are §1's columns — 12 months, 1 January, 60 days (D-047, D-048). None is a placeholder: the term is what the yearly lapse sweep (07-finance.md §4) and the period a renewal opens both read, and a term of the wrong length produces a membership that ends on a date nobody chose. None of the four is a constant, so tuning any of them is an UPDATE, not a release — which is the whole difference between a settled value and a hard-coded one.

The one rule about these four values: read them from the row. A scheduled job, a front end or a report that contains the literal 60 or 1 has quietly reverted a parameter to a constant, and the organization will discover it the first time it changes its mind.

No requirement is seeded, because no requirement exists (D-044): consent of any kind lives in the guardianship layer where it is a relationship fact, background checks are not recorded at all (D-043), and a reference, a form or a photograph has never been a condition of joining.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether 60 days is the right renewal window for an organization whose renewal campaign is a handful of people. The mechanism is settled and the value is a column read from the row (§1, §8); only a year of real lapses answers the value.
  • Whether outstanding_balance should exist as a denormalised column or be computed (§3) — depends on the finance design in 07-finance.md.
  • Which offices are written without MEMBERS is ruled, and what it rules is that nothing defaults. The membership gate left the resolver for the grant text (§6, D-100), so somebody decides, per office, that a lapsed member may still hold it — and nothing in the model records who decided it or why, only whether the expression contains the word. The standing report of §7 check 1 is the control over the outcome, not over the choice. What was an assumption is now the ruling: per office, by whoever writes the grant, no default either way — not into the expression and not out of it — so no office inherits an entitlement from a template and none inherits a lockout, and a grant written without the term needs no reason field, grant_reason staying the optional column it is (D-165). Day one's grant carries no MEMBERS term at all — it names one person, and a grant aimed at a person has no expression to carry one — so the lockout D-051 was written against is answered by D-150 and not by an exemption. Two clauses here are this round's reading of the ruling rather than the ruling's own words: that the report of §7 check 1 lists every such grant rather than the offices somebody marks sensitive, and that a grant with no expression to carry the term cannot be read as having declined one.
  • Whether a group is ever allowed to state an age rule of its own is answered: it is not, and the age rule is a report. A group carries no eligibility and D-098 refuses it one, so nothing says children only about a group today; the answer is a report over person_group_member and is_minor(), which is a question about the data rather than a rule in the model — and that is the ruling now rather than the gap: age is reported and never enforced, so no column, no check and no gate is owed to it, and enforcement is declined rather than deferred (D-168). What it is enforced by is whoever reads the report; what it costs is that nothing stands between a roster and a mistake.

Settled, and stated where the rule lives rather than here. Whether a person may hold several open memberships, when a membership activates, whether permissions follow membership state, the age questions, the grace period and the requirement mechanism are settled and stated — in §1, §3, §4 and §6. Whether the legacy import may create a membership is D-093 and 06a §3.1. Two of those answers have a consequence worth keeping in view, because both are easy to undo: the roster is keyed on a person and never on a membership, so belonging survives where no membership record survives (§5), and a renewal inside the window opens its row at the previous expiry date, which is what makes a lapse invisible in the coverage and still visible in the money (§3).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Relationships
docs.text:
guardianship, and the single right level that travels with it.

Domain rationale: ../domain/02-actors.md.

This document describes requirements. It contains no DDL (D-072); the ORM decides how each rule is enforced.

docs.title: 1. guardianship
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id internal identifier Never appears in a URL or an external reference guardian_person_id reference to person, required One side of the relationship dependent_person_id reference to person, required The other side. Must not equal the guardian relationship enum: parent / legal_guardian / foster_parent / step_parent / grandparent / sibling / other, required sibling and other exist because the organization will meet cases that do not fit, and forcing them into parent corrupts the data. A 19-year-old legal guardian of a 12-year-old sibling is real right_level enum: none / view / write The whole of the guardian's authority (D-074). Current value, denormalised for the read that happens on every authorization check; history in guardianship_permission (§2) valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Set by a person — a party to the row (§1 "Guardianship ends"), or a staff member asked to record it. Never by a job: the system takes no position on majority (D-069) is_primary_contact boolean, required, default false Who the organization calls in an emergency. Independent of right_level — a grandparent with no system access at all can still be the emergency contact. See ../domain/02-actors.md §6 is_legal_decision_maker boolean, required, default false Distinguishes who may make legal decisions — consent for medical treatment, travel — from who provides day-to-day care. Often different people lives_with boolean, optional Deliberately optional: false means guardianship without cohabitation (shared custody, a guardian in another city), which is a different fact from unknown. Relevant to contact routing, never to authority custody_arrangement free text A description, not a computable fact, and kept that way on purpose (§7) source enum: self / staff / import / court_order Decides the starting right_level (§2 defaults, D-046) verified_at timestamp, optional verified_by reference to person, optional evidence_reference free text Where the proof of guardianship is filed. For legal guardianship this matters: the organization must be able to show that it checked ended_reason text, optional Free text (D-128) ended_note free text created_at, updated_at timestamps created_by, updated_by reference to person import_batch_id reference to import batch Legacy rows only

Rules

  • A person may not be a guardian of themselves: the two person references must differ.
  • valid_to, when present, must be after valid_from.
  • At most one current guardianship per (guardian, dependent) pair. Their periods may not overlap, over all rows and not only the open ones — a hand-written exclusion constraint, like the three in 00a §1, and §6 check 7 is the net beneath it. Past ones are unlimited and expected: a court order lapses and is renewed.
  • A dependent may have any number of simultaneous guardians, each with its own row and its own right_level.
  • is_primary_contact is not unique per dependent. A child can have two primary contacts.

Indexes

  • Lookups in both directions by person and valid_to — "who is this person's guardian" and "who does this person guard" are equally common.
  • A partial index on current rows only, and a second on current rows that are primary contacts: the emergency-contact lookup must not scan history.

docs.title: The relation is a general graph, not a two-level hierarchy
docs.text:
The requirements permit:

  • One guardian → many dependents. Multiple rows with the same guardian. This is "one parent can manage multiple children".
  • Many guardians → one dependent. Both parents, brothers' grandparents, a legal guardian plus a step-parent. Nothing assumes a child has exactly two guardians.
  • A person being both. Person A is guardian of B and dependent of C. Costs nothing to allow, and avoids a rewrite when a member reaches majority and becomes guardian to a younger sibling.

You specified the first two explicitly. The third is free.

docs.title: Per-dependent authority
docs.text:
Authority is per guardianship row, never per person. A parent can hold write for one child and view for another — a realistic shared-custody arrangement, and one the model must represent without inventing a second parent identity.

Authority sits on the row, not on the person, and it is one of three values, not a set of capability codes (D-074). §2 states what that grain costs.

docs.title: Guardianship ends — and who is allowed to end it
docs.text:
valid_to is set when:

  • a party to the row ends it. The guardian, or the adult who is the subject of it (D-073);
  • a court order changes the arrangement, which staff record;
  • the guardian dies — and note the organization does not record death (D-034), so this too arrives as a person ending a row, with whatever reason the organization uses.

Staff may always do it when asked. Staff may never be the only way it happens.

The parties are principals, not third parties with a grant. A guardianship row is not the guardian's record, and it is not the subject's record. It is a record of a relationship between them, and both hold it — which is why neither of them needs a grant to act on the row. Who may end it is answered locally, a paragraph above: a party to the row, or staff acting on a request, with staff never the only way it can happen.

It is not the ownership channel, and the distinction is worth keeping. Ownership is your own record. Ending a guardianship over yourself is not editing your own record; it is dissolving a relationship you are one half of. Mechanically this is the guardianship channel gaining a direction: it already asks "may guardian G act on D's records?", and it now also answers "may a party act on the guardianship row itself?", for exactly three acts — ending it, adding another guardian, and changing the right level. The resolver still has four channels (D-010, and the channels' dispatch changed in D-079).

The three acts a party may take, and no others:

Act Guardian Subject (adult) Staff End the row ✅ ✅ ✅ Add another guardian over the same dependent ✅ ❌ ✅ Change right_level downward ✅ ✅ ✅ Change right_level upward ✅ ❌ ✅ Edit the dependent's records per right_level own record per role

Read the last row against the first four, because an implementation will get this backwards. The four acts above are not gated by right_level: a guardian whose right is view, or even none, may still end the guardianship, and a person who has never been a guardian at all may not. The level ranks what you may do to the child's records, which is the fifth row and nothing else — it is not a general competence over the relationship, and reading it as one would mean that lowering someone's access to a medical file also locked them out of leaving the arrangement. The party direction follows the same rule as the record direction: it can only say yes (D-079). Being a party grants the act; not being one leaves the actor's own guardianship.* role permissions to be tried, which is how staff in the table above get their ✅s. An explicit deny still runs first and beats both.

The asymmetry, stated plainly. A guardian may appoint a guardian: the act is one code — guardianship.assign, which the catalog marks ⚠⚠, second only to reading a person — and anyone holding it over a child gives a second person that same authority, with no approval from the organization and no second signature anywhere. The ordinary case is a mother adding the father. The design does not prevent the non-ordinary case; it attributes it instead — who added whom, when, from which account, is audited, and that is the whole of the control. Nothing notifies anybody. There is no office to notify and nothing in this design that would receive a notification at all, and the notice-to-a-"safeguarding-contact" option this page once recommended was refused rather than left un-built: a control whose recipient is a row somebody must remember to create is off by default and silent about being off, which is worse than a trail that is on whether or not anyone configured it (D-137). That is a deterrent and an evidence trail, not a wall, and the cost is the one that decision states plainly: nothing will ever tell a parent, a second guardian, or an officer that a third adult was given authority over a child — the answer to who added them is excellent, and the answer to did anyone think about it is the person who did it, alone, at the moment they did it. See E-6.

The system does not notice birthdays in this connection. No job, no review queue, no computed candidate date (D-069, reversing D-024 and closing E-2).

Why not, including why the gentler version was also refused. The legal reasoning is unchanged and still correct: in many jurisdictions a parent's authority over health and school records does not end at 18, and in some it ends at a different age, so any computed date is a claim the system cannot support. What D-069 adds is that a review queue makes the same claim more quietly. A queue asserts this arrangement is now suspect, in every case, for every family, including the ones where the adult child actively wants their parent to keep handling the paperwork. Deferring a decision is not declining to make one, and the queue was a decision.

D-069 refused, D-073 supplies. Read as one decision in two halves: a legal relationship between two people ends when one of those people says so, and the organization's job is to be told rather than to permit it. Without D-073, D-069 was a refusal with no alternative; the exit it assumed had no door.

What is lost, precisely: a prompt, not a record. valid_from/valid_to mean "who is listed as my guardian, and since when?" is a query with a complete answer including the date each ended. What replaces the prompt is the report in §6, run by a person on purpose.

docs.title: is_primary_contact vs is_legal_decision_maker
docs.text:
Two distinct questions that a single "is primary parent" flag conflates:

Question Column Who do we phone at 2am when the child is injured at camp? is_primary_contact Who may sign the consent form for that treatment? is_legal_decision_maker

They are often different people, and conflating them means either the wrong person is called or an invalid consent is accepted. Both are separate flags rather than one is_primary, because a child can have two primary contacts and one decision maker.

docs.title: 2. The guardian's right: none, view, or write
docs.text:
A guardian either cannot see the child's records, can see them, or can change them. That is the entire vocabulary (D-074).

guardianship_permission survives as the history of that value, not as a capability list. One row per change, exactly one row open at a time, so "what was this guardian allowed to see in March 2024?" stays answerable — the same current-value-plus-temporal-history shape that person uses for names.

Field Kind Notes guardianship_id reference to guardianship, required Scoped to the row, never to the (guardian, dependent) pair right_level enum: none / view / write, required The value being recorded valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Ending this row without ending the guardianship changes the right; a new row starts it again changed_reason free text e.g. default for self-registered guardianship, court order 2026-03-14, guardian request changed_by reference to person, optional NULL when the default was applied by the application at creation. 00-conventions §7a is what that empty means — a complete answer, not a person nobody remembered

Rules

  • Exactly one row per guardianship may be open at a time.
  • Every change is a row; the value on guardianship.right_level is always the open row's value. If the two disagree, the row is authoritative and the copy is wrong.
  • Scoping to the guardianship row and not to the person pair is deliberate (D-020): when a guardianship ends and a new one begins — a renewed court order, a lapse and re-establishment — the rights must not silently carry over. A new relationship is a new row and a new, deliberate level.

docs.title: Three values, two kinds, and no scale
docs.text:
Three values are compared against a column, not against a ladder. permission.right_kind ∈ read | write is the whole mechanism: none covers nothing, view covers the codes marked read, write covers both (05-authorization.md §1). There is nothing to order and no rank to keep in step, because three values against two kinds is a lookup, not a scale, and that column has no other customer in the system.

A guardian is not a staff member, and what says so is the shape of the request, not a rank. The guardianship channel is entered only when the check is about somebody other than the actor (D-079), so the widest guardian right in the system reaches the child's record and cannot reach a roster, a fee schedule or another family — not because its rank was too low, but because those checks are not about the child and the channel is never asked.

docs.title: What the collapse gives up, written down rather than discovered later
docs.text:
A guardianship carries one value where it once carried a set of capability codes, and every dependent.* code is deleted (D-074). The consequence is stated rather than softened: it is not possible to say "read everything except the medical record." The arrangement those codes existed for — a court order restricting one parent's access to the health facts about a child while their other access continues — cannot be represented, and E-7 records it as refused by deleting the premise: there is no medical record inside the person record to be excepted from, because everything other than a name, a gender and an age is descriptive data of one class (D-083). So view reads the record whole: a grandmother granted visibility and nothing else sees the fee history and the health facts alike.

What still holds:

  • write is not manage, and since D-099 there is no manage to be short of: the ceiling on a guardian is the channel, which answers only for checks about this child. A guardian cannot do organization-wide things because those checks are not about the child, not because a rank was too low.
  • Authority is per row, so a guardian of one child sees nothing of another's.
  • The organization-wide deny channel is untouched: a guardianship row granting write can still be refused by a deny, because deny is absolute and scope-independent (D-032). What was lost is a narrow deny — "not medical" — not the ability to say no.

If the split turns out to matter in operation it is a new decision, not a permission to be re-added quietly (E-7).

docs.title: Defaults still depend on how the guardianship arose
docs.text:
The value a guardianship starts at depends on how it arose (D-046):

source Starting right_level Why self — a parent registering their own child write They created the record and are asserting the relationship. There is nobody better placed to hold authority over it staff, import — recorded by someone else view, chosen at creation and raisable A person who did not assert the relationship is not handed authority by a default court_order view, and raised only by the person who filed the order The document says what the authority is; the system should not guess above it

Applied by the code that creates the row, at creation — and this is the correct layer, not a compromise. A default depends on why the row is being created, which is a fact about the user's intent that no database rule can inspect. What must not happen is the default being applied only by a form: an import that omits it produces a view guardian where the person meant full rights, and nothing objects. And nothing in §6 catches this either, which is worth being plain about: a default that was never applied leaves no inconsistent row behind — only a quiet view where a write was intended, indistinguishable from a deliberate restriction. That gap is a consequence of §2's collapse: an omitted set of grants was visible as an empty set, and an empty set is reportable where view is not. What closes it is not a report but the shape of the write path: one place creates guardianships, it reads source, and it does not accept a right_level from a caller who is not entitled to choose one. The staff and court_order paths need a human choosing a value, and a default that fires before anybody is asked is not a default, it is a decision made on someone's behalf — the same refusal D-069 and D-076 make elsewhere.

Why source and changed_reason are both kept. The same word — "guardian" — now means two different starting scopes depending on paperwork, and the record has to say which was chosen and why. A guardian with read-only access and a guardian with full access are indistinguishable in the domain language and must not be in the data.

docs.title: 3. There is no household table
docs.text: Removed (D-057). An address is a person_contact row of type postal (01a-accounts-and-contacts.md §6), which already exists, already keeps history (valid_from / valid_to), and already carries a purpose — 'billing' for the address an invoice goes to. A separate household table was duplicating it under a different key, and the duplication had gone stale: its postal_address column was documented as denormalised from the billing contact's postal contact, with nothing keeping the copy true.

docs.title: Shared address still grants no access
docs.text:
Living at the same address does not grant any permission over another person at that address. A stepparent with no guardianship row has no access to the children's records. A grandparent at the address has no access. This is deliberate and it is a safeguarding property, not an oversight.

This was true when household existed (D-019) and it is true now, for a simple reason worth stating so nobody re-derives it: the access never came from the household tables. All authority over a child's records comes from guardianship (§1–2). Removing a table that granted nothing cannot grant anything.

docs.title: What replaced it
docs.text:
Household feature Now Billing address person_contact of type postal with purpose billing "Which children lived at this address in 2003?" A query over the temporal person_contact history (domain/03 §4) One invoice for three siblings The fee is flat and per person (D-037); there is no family price to invoice fee_obligation.household_id Column and its index removed (07-finance.md §2)

What was genuinely lost, recorded rather than glossed: a household was a group with a name and its own lifetime. Two people at one address are now related by a query, not by a row, so there is nowhere to hang "the Novák family" as a first-class thing and no valid_from for the grouping itself. Accepted, because nothing was using it — no code set fee_obligation.household_id, and household.name had no consumer. If family-level communication or a family discount is ever wanted, this is the decision to revisit, and the shape to bring back is a group with a period, not a fake person.

docs.title: Why not a family person row
docs.text: Some systems model a household as a fake person so that memberships and payments can attach to it. Do not. It creates rows in person that are not people, which breaks identity matching, produces nonsense in name searches, and — because it is a person — can receive a membership, an account, and eventually permissions.

docs.title: 4. How the resolver uses these tables
docs.text:
The guardianship channel is step 4 of the resolver (../domain/06-authorization-model.md).

How the channel is selected: a fact about the request, never a name. It applies when the person the action is about is not the person performing it. Nobody picks a channel and no caller gets to choose which one applies, which is what stops one authorization rule being implemented twice, once wrong (D-079); and a shape has none of the blind spots a name had, so a parent editing their child's address under a person.* code routes through guardianship too.

Asked about another person, it resolves in this fixed order, and it produces one of two outcomes: an allow, or no answer at all. It never answers "no".

  1. Is there a current guardianship row between this actor and this subject, at the date being asked about? If not, this step is not the channel's business and says nothing — the resolver continues to the actor's own roles and grants. Silence, not refusal (D-079).
  2. Is there an explicit deny covering this check? Deny wins here as everywhere else, and independently of how broad the underlying grant is (D-032) — but note that this deny is found by channel 0 of the resolver, before this step runs, so nothing in this list can override it. It is listed second only because it is the other reason a guardian with a sufficient right_level still gets nothing.
  3. Read the row's right_level: none, view or write.
  4. Compare it against what the action needs, which is a column on the permission rather than a number on the guardian: permission.right_kind is read or write, view covers read, write covers both, and none covers nothing (D-099). Covered → allow. Not covered, or none → no answer, and the actor's own roles are tried.

Why step 1 and step 4 fall through instead of refusing. This channel is entered by ordinary codes that a role may also carry, so a final refusal here produces an absurd result the moment one person wears two hats: the parent who is also the event registrar, holding view over their own child, refused the right to mark attendance. The relationship should not be able to revoke a job. What is not given up: none still grants nothing (that is what D-074 promised, not a power to block other bases), and an organization that genuinely must stop a specific person touching a specific child's records uses an explicit deny, which runs first, everywhere, at any scope. The prohibition survives; it simply lives in the channel D-032 built for it rather than in a capability level.

Two further properties:

  • An ended guardianship never opens this channel again. For every question, forever, the row is not current, so step 1 does not fire and no guardian authority flows. What a former guardian may still do is what any other member may do — through their own assignment, on its own scope, with the guardianship row doing nothing at all. That distinction did not exist while the channel was the only road to a child's records, and it is the honest version now.
  • The date is a parameter of the question, not read from the clock. So "could this parent have seen this record on the day they did it?" stays answerable, which is what auditing a past action requires. As-of must be threaded into every step above, including the deny lookup — a check that reads today's denies against a 2024 action invents history.

Asked about the guardianship row itself rather than through it, the same channel answers for a party to it, and only for the three acts in §1's table. That branch is not a fifth channel; it is this one, pointed the other way.

docs.title: 5. Acting on behalf — recording it
docs.text:
Every operation performed for a dependent must record both parties. This is not optional: without it, the audit trail attributes the parent's actions to the child.

Every access-log row for an act-on-behalf carries, together:

Field Records actor_person_id the guardian who acted subject_person_id the child whose record was affected on_behalf true, explicitly — not inferred from the two ids differing authorization_channel guardianship guardianship_id which row authorized it result allowed or refused

Concretely, when a parent registers their child for an event, the record must answer:

  • Who did it? The parent.
  • For whom? The child.
  • By what authority? A specific guardianship row, and the right_level it held at the time.
  • Is that authority still valid? Re-checkable from the row's dates.

A row that records only "the child registered" is not merely incomplete — it is wrong, and it is the kind of wrong that matters when someone later asks whether a parent consented to something.

docs.title: 6. Invariants to verify
docs.text:
These were executable queries. They are now requirements stated in prose, and nothing runs them (D-072).

  1. Adults still listed under a guardian. Every open guardianship whose subject is past majority by person.birth_date. Expected in the ordinary case and not an error — this is the periodic human review D-069 names as the entire control, and it exists precisely because no job acts on that date. Run it deliberately, never nightly: a report nobody reads is a queue, and the queue was withdrawn.
  2. Rights outliving the relationship. A guardianship_permission history row still open while its guardianship has ended. This is the exact failure that scoping to the row was meant to prevent; worth verifying because an application bug or a hand-edit can still create it.
  3. A dependent with no primary contact. A current guardianship set in which nobody is flagged as the emergency contact.
  4. A minor member or participant whom no guardian can see. Two shapes, one report, because they are the same gap arriving by different routes: no guardianship row at all, and a full set of guardians with every one of them at right_level = none. Age comes from person.birth_date — there is no membership category to read it from, because membership is ageless (D-038), and a birth date cannot go stale the way a category recorded when a row was opened would. This is a safeguarding gap, not a data-quality nit: the organization holds a member it cannot contact in an emergency and cannot obtain consent from. It is the finding here that most demands a reader, and nothing sends it to one (D-164). This check is one of the reasons guardianship is a required part of the model rather than an optional convenience.

The second half was added by D-082, and it is not a hypothetical refinement. A direct message to a minor is mirrored to the guardians at view or write — deliberately not to a guardian at none, because none means the organization already decided that party sees nothing about the child. Without this half of the check, a child whose guardians are all none would look, in every report, like a child with guardians, while in fact nobody outside the child receives a copy of anything sent to them. A right level that silently removes the only safeguarding net is a right level nobody understands anymore, and this report is what keeps none meaning what it says. 5. A guardian younger than the dependent, where both birth dates are known. Almost always a data-entry error, and detectable only when both dates survived the import. 6. guardianship.right_level disagrees with its own open history row. A new invariant created by D-074's current-value-plus-history shape. If it is ever non-empty, the copy is wrong and the row is right. 7. Two guardianship rows for one pair covering the same day. Zero is the expected answer, and the exclusion constraint in §1 is the thing that keeps it zero; this row exists because that constraint is hand-written, and a migration somebody forgot to run is a rule that quietly stopped. Which of two disagreeing right_level values the resolver answered with is a query-order accident, which is what this reports.

The nearest surviving signal of the old "households with no address" report is a live billing purpose with no postal address behind it, which is a finance problem (07-finance.md §2).

docs.title: 7. Open issues
docs.text:
• A guardian may appoint a guardian, with no approval from the organization. — settled: attributed, and nothing more. Audited, notified to nobody, not prevented; the recommendation this page made for a notice to a safeguarding contact is deleted with the question, for the reason D-137 gives (D-137, E-6). §1 states what that costs, and the cost is not closed by the decision.
  • One right level cannot separate the health facts from the rest of the record — the arrangement the per-code model existed for. E-7, and §2 states what it costs.
  • Whether a guardian may act for a dependent who is also a member in their own right — e.g. can a parent register their adult child for an event, if the child consents? Recommend an explicit consent-based delegation rather than a guardianship, since the legal basis differs. The group version of this is now answered by audiences (D-042).
  • Whether custody_arrangement free text should be structured. Recommend not — custody orders vary too much to model, and a wrong model is worse than honest prose.
  • Confirm that the membership gate's guardianship carve-out is intended. A lapsed parent keeps their right_level (D-039), which means an unpaid parent and a paid one are indistinguishable inside that namespace. It is almost certainly right — guardianship comes from a legal relationship, not a membership — but it should be a stated choice, not a side effect of where the gate was placed.

What this page once wondered about and no longer does — the default right level at creation, what happens at majority, whether an adult ends their own guardianship, the household grouping, background checks — is registered in ../open-questions.md with the decision that settled each.

docs.title: Data Model — Authorization: permissions, offices, grants
docs.text:
permission, role, role_holder and access_grant — the four tables an answer is made of — and the shape of the check they add up to. Design rationale, in plain language: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md.

Section numbers are shared across the six parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues), and 05e §14–§17 (a key, and what it may hold).

docs.title: 1. The shape of the answer
docs.text:
permission ─────────────── the atomic capability.       'membership.request.approve'
                            + where it may be granted:  applies_to  unit | unit_and_item
                            + read or write:            right_kind

access_grant ───────────── THE ONE TABLE THAT GRANTS.   grantee (person | audience | api_key),
                                                       scope ('unit' | exactly one item),
                                                       one code, effect (allow | deny),
                                                       period

role ───────────────────── an office, conferring nothing.     'treasurers'
role_holder ────────────── who holds it, for a period.        person X, 'treasurers',
                                                              2026-03-01 → open

selector_type ──────────── the language: every operand that   'ROLE', 'MEMBERS', 'PLACED',
                          may appear in an expression.          'AUDIENCE'
                          Shipped, written only by migrations.

audience ───────────────── a set a grant aims at, nameable     MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)
                          by code from another audience.
audience_operand ───────── one node of that expression        (a tree, not a string; an
                          — an AUDIENCE leaf doubles as       AUDIENCE leaf is also the
                          the reference edge to another tree)  edge to another audience)

guardianship ───────────── authority over one PERSON: right_level   (04-relationships.md)
api_key ────────────────── a caller that is nobody: a third grantee   (05e-keys-and-callers.md §14)
access_log ─────────────── what was decided, and by what authority.

One table grants. access_grant is the only place authority is written (D-005), plus the guardianship channel over one person, whose authority is guardianship.right_level (data-model/04, §10). Everything else here decides whom a grant reaches, which is not the same question — a role holder, a group member and an audience operand are all sets of people, and being in one is worth exactly what the grant aimed at it says (D-100). A hand-written set of people is written in the expression too, as PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), where every other set is written (D-105).

And the rule that answers every check (D-099):

allowed when some live allow applies, and no live deny applies.

That is the entire precedence rule. "Live" means the row has started as of the checked date, has not ended on it, and has not been revoked; "applies" is decided per channel in §10. There is no level to reach, no rank to compare, and no nearer grant that beats a further one; a deny is absolute (D-032, D-099). Why there is no ordering: an ordering could only ever rank one allow against another, and a boolean answer has nothing to rank.

Authority is written at exactly two sizes — the unit, or one item — because there is one unit and it is not a row (D-097), and the widest read permission in the system reaches every member from the unit. What that costs is stated once, in domain/04 §1.

role_holder and access_grant are different mechanisms, and only one of them grants. What they have in common is the temporal pattern every dated row in this system uses:

role_holder access_grant Says this person holds this office in this period this grantee may, or may not, do this one thing here Who the row can name A person, always A person, a set of people, or a registered integration (§14) Carries authority No — confers nothing (§3) Yes; it is the only thing that does Scope None. A role is held at the unit, because there is nowhere else The unit, or exactly one item Decides Whom a grant naming ROLE(x) reaches Everything, for one code Typical row "is the treasurer, from March" "may read this event's answers" Rows per broad capability One One per code — a broad office is a couple of dozen of them

The row count is the price, and it was paid deliberately (D-099). One grant per code is what buys "what exactly does this person have?" answered by reading rows — the same answer for a set of people, and the same answer for an integration (§15) — and it costs the question "what does manage give me on this event?", which has no answer because there is no such word.

The grantee column grew a third kind in the same table and role_holder did not, and the asymmetry is the model rather than an oversight: an office is held by a person because holding one is a thing a human does, and an office confers nothing anyway (§3).
