A key holds no office, appears in no role_holder row, and is in no set that ROLE(x) could reach. Its whole authority is the grant rows naming it, which is why auditing an integration means reading one list rather than reconstructing one (D-116).

docs.title: 2. permission
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. code text, required, unique The stable identifier — membership.request.approve. The code never changes; display_name can. resource text, required What the permission is about — membership_request. action text, required What may be done to it — approve. applies_to enum: unit, unit_and_item Where this code may be granted at all: at the unit only, or at the unit and on an item. Checked when the grant is saved, never at check time — see applies_to below. right_kind enum: read, write Exists for exactly one customer: the guardianship channel's none / view / write (D-074). Say the one customer out loud — see right_kind below. namespace text, optional system, or absent. What the column does is its own subsection below. description text, required What it means, for whoever has to read it. display_name text, required Human label for the permission editor. is_assignable boolean Default true. False: a permission no grant may name directly — a deprecated code kept only so historical audit rows still resolve to something readable. created_at timestamp, audit time

The one question this table does not answer is "may this code be granted on an event at all?" — that is applies_to, and it is answered on the save rather than in the resolver. Nothing else in the row constrains where a grant may sit.

No column marks these rows as the platform's, because every row of this table is the platform's. There is no permission.create and no permission.delete in the catalog: permission.view reads the register and permission.edit 🔒🔒 reaches the labels, which is all of it that a screen may touch, while a new code is a migration that also adds a resolver arm. Each half of what a protection flag used to promise is already carried somewhere else — no row may be deleted, because no code authorizes deleting one; the code never changes, because every grant row names a code by value and shape 4 says what that means; and the display_name is the one field the flag never protected either (D-142 found the check that watches it drift). A flag that is true on every row of a table nothing may add to is not a flag; it is a sentence about the table, and the sentence is this paragraph (D-152 deletes the four columns of this kind the design carried — on permission, selector_type, role and audience — because one argument covered all four).

Rules

  • code is well-formed: two or more dot-separated segments of lowercase letters and underscores.
  • resource equals the first dot-separated segment of code, so the code's prefix is never a second, drifting copy of the resource column. One exemption, deliberate: codes beginning system., whose resource is the thing being administered rather than the word system. It is the only one, and a code under any other namespace prefix with two meaningful segments (dependent.medical.view is the shape) means reopening this rule.
  • code is unique.
  • applies_to and right_kind are both required. A required enum with two values is cheap; a nullable one whose null-ness silently means something is how the guardianship channel would have acquired an answer that depends on a value nobody typed.
  • A code seeded as system. is seeded applies_to = unit. This is not decoration; see What namespace does.

docs.title: There is no wildcard permission
docs.text:
A check for X.y is satisfied by an exact allow of X.y, or by system.admin, which is checked outright and is the only permission meaning everything — every code, whatever its namespace, the system namespace's own nine rows included. What keeps it off an item is not a branch in the resolver but the value it is seeded with: applies_to = unit, refused at the save (What namespace does, and integrity check 3). A rule that qualified this one by namespace would be a rule about a namespace, which the section below forbids for every namespace (D-124).

A check for permission 'X.y' is satisfied by:
    - an exact allow of 'X.y', OR
    - an allow of 'system.admin'

There are no <resource>.admin codes — no prefix matching in the resolver, and none to come by (D-068). "Can do everything about events" is an office composed from the thirteen event.* codes — which is to say, a role some grants name, each grant naming one code (D-052) — because that composition is runtime data the organization edits, and a wildcard was the code guessing at it instead.

The cost is accepted: a new narrow permission is not automatically covered by the offices that should imply it. Integrity check 13 (permissions no live grant names) is the net, and it fails closed (D-007, reversed by D-068).

is_assignable = false exists for permissions that only make sense as part of a bundle — a deprecated narrow permission kept for historical audit readability, for instance. A bundle is a role's set of grants, and nothing else bundles.

docs.title: applies_to: where a code may be granted, and when that is asked
docs.text:
What the column encodes: event.create and membership.terminate are nonsense on an event. unit means the code may be granted at the unit and nowhere else; unit_and_item means it may be granted at the unit or on one item of a registered type.

It is checked when the grant is saved, not when a permission is checked (D-099). A grant of event.create written on one event is refused, with the reason in the error: an event cannot be created twice, so a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question — and a refusal at save time is one human conversation, where the same shape discovered at check time is a rule inside the resolver that every future reader has to re-derive.

What enforces it is the write path, and the direction of its failure is worth knowing. No database rule spans permission and access_grant columns, so integrity check 3 (§11) reports any row that got through — a row there means the check was skipped, not that a constraint was disabled. And because the rule sits on the save, a check that names an item for a unit-only code is not refused by it: the mismatched shape cannot be stored, so the check simply gets the unit's answer. That is a caller bug rather than a data bug, and §13 registers the question of whether the API should refuse it out loud.

docs.title: right_kind: a column with exactly one customer
docs.text:
Saying so is cheaper than discovering it later (D-099). D-074 fixes a guardian's rights at three values — none, view, write — and the guardianship channel has to compare a checked permission against something. This column is that thing, and it has no other consumer anywhere in the design:

Guardian's right_level Covers none Nothing. view Codes marked read. write Codes marked read and codes marked write.

The alternative was to store permission codes on the guardianship row, and D-074 refused it on the grounds that a volunteer cannot maintain a 74-code checklist per child. A two-valued column on the catalog side keeps that refusal intact: the organization grades each code once, when it is written, rather than per child, forever.

A new code is seeded write unless someone marks it read, because write is the narrower guardian reach: an unconsidered new code is then unreachable by a guardian with view, which is the direction this model fails in everywhere else. This is a seeding convention derived from D-074's fail-closed posture rather than a ruling in D-099, and §11 has no check for it — a code mis-marked read is visible to a human reading the catalog and invisible to the database, which is worth knowing before trusting it.

Of round 16's four new codes, api_key.view is the one marked read — it is the read of a list. The three writes are write, as any code that lets its bearer mint a caller is. The marking changes no answer, in either direction: this column is consulted only by the guardianship channel, which asks about one child's record, and these four codes exist only at the unit — so a key never reaches the column, and neither does anything else. It is filled in because the column is required of every code, two values above (§2, Rules).

docs.title: What namespace does
docs.text:
namespace What it means Example absent An ordinary code. membership.request.approve system A code about the system itself. It is seeded applies_to = unit, so no grant on an item can carry it, and the resolver no longer branches on the prefix. permission.edit

The namespace selects no channel, for any namespace — and the guardianship channel is chosen by what a prefix could never express: whether the action is about a different person from the one performing it. A parent editing their child's address is checked under person.contact.edit — an ordinary, un-prefixed code — and reaches the guardianship channel anyway, because the subject of the act is not the actor. See §10. A rule that routed on a namespace would miss exactly this case, since a guardian acting under a person.* code looks like a person acting on themselves; that routing is what D-074 removed, and the dependent. codes it dispatched on are indexed in removed-concepts.md.

What stops someone handing another person authority over the permission system by sharing an item with them. The guarantee is a seeding rule plus integrity check 3: every system. code is seeded applies_to = unit, and the save-time refusal rejects any item grant carrying it. The guarantee is not structural — there is no resolver branch on a prefix to fall back on — and naming the layer matters, because a system. code seeded unit_and_item by someone in a hurry reopens the hole with nothing in the schema to catch it, and that mis-seeding is what check 3 looks for. A new namespace remains a data change rather than a resolver branch; it just has one tenant and no routing left.

docs.title: 3. role — an office
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. code text, required, unique among roles, and unique across roles and groups registrar, treasurers, counselors. The cross-table half of the rule is §8's namespace rule; a single constraint cannot span two tables, so the write path carries it (§8, Names are one namespace). name text, required What the office is called on screen. description text, optional sort_order integer, required Default 0. created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person Who last changed it.

Deleted with their mechanisms, in one list, because D-081 requires each one to be answered:

Gone With it Who answers the question now scope_required "is this office held org-wide or at a unit?" Nobody — the question has no subject. There is one scope (D-097), so a role is always held at the unit (§4 has no scope columns). requires_membership the membership gate, default-on, enforced in the resolver (D-039) The expression, per grant: MEMBERS * ROLE(x) gates on a current membership, ROLE(x) alone does not (§8, §10). The posture is opt-in, and §11's report is the control. max_term_months the prefilled term, and with it the "expiry is the default" nudge Nothing. Nothing forces a holder row to end, and §11's report of offices held past their end date is the control (§4, D-071). is_delegatable the refusal to let an office's authority be delegated (domain/06 §9) Nothing about roles. Delegation of authority survives only on a grant row (is_delegated + delegated_from), where the grant's own expiry is the control (§6).

role is runtime data, not a fixed vocabulary, and it has no shipped rows at all. The organization creates offices, names them, fills them, and deletes the ones nobody ever held; the platform ships none, which is D-132 applied by D-150. The name this document still uses everywhere is counselors, and it is a worked example of an office somebody wrote — nothing more. D-100's reason for putting a permanent, organization-wide population in this table rather than in person_group stands exactly as it was, because it is an argument about which table a set may live in: such a population is the opposite of D-098's definition of a group, and the table decides the sensitivity that protects the set (D-100, D-154). §12 of 05d states what ships and what day one looks like.

role has no valid_from / valid_to, deliberately (D-053). A role is a definition — a named office — and a definition does not come into and out of force. It is valid all the time, for as long as the row exists.

The period belongs on the holder row. role_holder.valid_from / valid_to is where "this person holds this office from March until December" lives (§4). The distinction is between what the office is and who holds it: the first is not a historical fact, the second is.

There is no retirement mechanism. No role.retire permission, no resolver check on a role's period. A role the organization no longer uses is one nobody holds any more, and §11 reports the offices still held past their holder row's end date.

docs.title: An office confers nothing
docs.text:
The codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x) (D-100). That is not a relabelling: an office's power lives in grant rows that are individually visible, individually dated, individually auditable and individually revocable. "What may a treasurer do?" is therefore a query over rows a screen can show. Roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is (D-068, D-100).

Three rules this table has to get right:

  • role.edit edits a name, a description and a sort order. The sharp edge is role.assign. Adding one person to treasurers inherits every grant that names ROLE(treasurers), including ones written later, by other people, for reasons whoever is doing the assigning has never seen. That is the invisibility §8 records for composition, arriving through the office door instead of the expression door — which is why role.* is the most sensitive code family in the catalog (🔒🔒) and why §11's report of ROLE(...) grants written without MEMBERS is worth reading.
  • A role that has ever been held cannot be deleted, for two reasons: role_holder.role_id is a foreign key and D-003 forbids taking the history with the row; "what authority did this person have in 2019?" must survive the office being abolished, which is exactly when someone asks. The guard runs row by row and the refusal is absolute:
  • any role_holder row references the role — refuse, with a message in terms the operator can act on: this office has holders, end the holder rows instead, so the history survives. A role that clears it was created by mistake and never held, and deleting it is legitimate. What used to stand here was a second refusal, for rows the platform had shipped — an is_system role was refused outright, "because deleting a row some grants name would silently widen or narrow whatever they aim at". The reason is true and the refusal covered one row, which is the wrong shape for a true reason (D-152). What reaches every office is the report instead: an office that is gone leaves every ROLE(x) leaf that named it a failed operand, and the two reports of §11 check 7 — the narrowing and the widening, in that order, because a wide failure is only better than a narrow one when somebody is reading — are the control that covers an office somebody deleted and an office that was never written in the first place (D-106).
  • There is no permission inheritance between roles. A unit_leader does not get the assistant_leader permissions by being implicitly senior: inheritance chains produce authorization answers nobody can predict by reading the configuration, which is what makes such systems undebuggable. Composition is available and visible instead — an expression says ROLE(x) + ROLE(y), in the grant, where whoever reads the grant sees it (§8).

role is registered in grant_scope_type, so an office is an item (D-100): "these two people may manage the counselors roster" is a grant of role.assign on one role, which is D-098's move applied to an office as well as a group. Without it the only way to say that is a grant at the unit, which reaches every office — the exact over-reach this table's sensitivity exists to avoid.

Why a role and a group are two tables when they are technically the same shape is answered where the difference bites — D-100 puts it in one line: the difference decides who may edit the membership, and one table would merge those two permissions into one. role.* is the most sensitive family in the catalog (🔒🔒); writing a group's roster is person_group.member.manage (⚠). One table with a kind column gives a single code that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into the office whose grants reach everything. The groups themselves are person_group, in 02-organization.md — this document describes only the selector that reads them.

docs.title: 4. role_holder — who holds an office
docs.text:
A role_holder row is an office, a person, and a period (D-100). It carries no scope columns and no resolver channel: a holder row grants nothing by existing, and what it changes is whom a grant naming ROLE(x) reaches (§10).

Fields

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. person_id reference to person, required Who holds the office. One person, never a rule — F-12 is closed by D-100 and its answer is no, for the reason the register always gave: a derived holder list cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023", and an office record that cannot answer that is not an office record. role_id reference to role, required valid_from date, required Default today. valid_to date, optional Absent = open-ended. Nothing forces it to end — see below. granted_by reference to person, required Who appointed this person. Kept, and not the provenance column this section deletes elsewhere — see What granted_by records and what audit_log records, immediately below. The arrow of this column goes to person and never to audit_log: it is a fact about the holder row, readable by anyone who may read the office, and reconstructing it from the trail would put the answer behind audit.view. granted_at timestamp, audit time Set when the row was written. Redundant with created_at in the ordinary case and kept because an appointment can be entered retrospectively, which is the only case where the two differ and the one where the distinction matters. note text, optional Why, in the writer's words. The only place the reason survives the audit trail's payload window (D-088). created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person

This table has no scope columns (D-097: a role is always held at the unit, and there is nothing else to hold it at), and no columns recording who ended a row. Who ended one, and when, is the audit trail's answer; the why is note, on the row that opens. The one thing with no answer is a reason for ending a holding that anyone can count. A reason here would be free text (D-128), and free text is counted only when people happen to type the same words — which is the same ground D-098 refused it one table over, now with the cost stated instead of the column.

A holder row holds a person, not a mandate (D-136). No column records — and none will record — whether an office was won by a vote or given by whoever could assign it: the organization runs elections outside this system and imports the outcome as a row. That is why granted_by below is who wrote the fact rather than whose authority made it so, and why note is the only place "elected, 2026–2028" can appear. The argument and the cost of refusing are in ../domain/04-organization-structure.md §6.

What granted_by records, and what audit_log records. The two look like duplicates and answer different questions, so the line is worth drawing properly. audit_log records an act: that a particular person, in a particular session, from a particular address, asked to appoint someone, and whether they were allowed to. It is the record of the writing. granted_by records a fact about the row: who appointed this person, which is a property of the office holding in the same way valid_from is. Who is entitled to say is the audit's question; who said it is the row's.

Two reasons the fact cannot live only in the trail, and the first is decisive.

  • The trail's payloads do not last (D-088); the before-and-after images are emptied after 24 months. "Who put her in charge of the money?" has to be answerable in year five, from the same screen that shows when the appointment started, and an answer that requires audit.view, a date range and an intact payload is not an answer to a question about the current officer.
  • The row's readers are not the trail's readers. role_holder is read by whoever administers offices; the trail is read by whoever holds audit.view 🔒🔒, and D-086 graded that deliberately. Making the ordinary screen reach into the audit trail to show an ordinary field either widens audit.view or leaves the field blank, and neither is acceptable.

The same argument decides access_grant.granted_by, and what separates the columns that stay from the ones that go is whether the value is a property of the row that still exists. An ending describes a row nobody is looking at, and "who closed this" is a question about an act — the trail's subject. An appointment describes a holding somebody is looking at now.

One diagram rule follows from it. The relationship drawn from granted_by points at person. There is no edge from role_holder to audit_log and there must never be one: the trail is written about the act, by the same transaction, and the holder row neither refers to it nor depends on it.

Rules

  • valid_to is either absent or strictly after valid_from.
  • At most one open holder row for a given person and role. There is no scope term left to distinguish two concurrent holdings, because there is no second scope. A person may have been treasurer three times, and be treasurer once.
  • Rows for the same person and role may not overlap, counted over all rows and not only the open ones, half-open so a row ending on a day and one beginning that same day do not collide. Dating rows imports this invariant set whether the author wants it or not — it is D-098's argument for the identical rule on person_group_member, D-002, and shape 1, which says a hand-written migration must emit it and the ORM will not.
  • A person who left the office in 2020 and returned in 2024 is two rows, never one row edited in place, because the edit destroys the answer to "was she treasurer in 2019?" — and that is the question this table exists to answer. Moving from one office to another closes one row and opens another.

Indexes

  • over open rows only, by role — the read that answers "who is in ROLE(treasurers) today", which is now an operand of a grant rather than a tier of the resolver, and runs on every check that names the office;
  • over open rows only, by person — the read that answers "what offices does this person hold", for the screen where someone is about to be given one more.

docs.title: Nothing forces a holder row to end, and the report is the control
docs.text:
This is D-071's posture, and it is now load-bearing rather than backstopped: a membership lapse no longer silently withholds anything from a holder row. A holder row that nobody closes authorizes for as long as a grant naming the office lives, and the only things between an overdue treasurer and a written authority are:

  • the report — open holder rows, oldest first, with the grants each office is named by;
  • role_holder.valid_to where a human typed one, and §13 keeps the question of whether it should be mandatory for high-authority offices; and
  • the audience expression, which is where a lapse now matters: MEMBERS * ROLE(x) stops reaching a lapsed member the day the membership ends, and ROLE(x) never noticed.

The mirror-image failure is the more likely one. A holder row that outlives the person gives that person authority they should not have; a grant written as ROLE(x) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member silently, forever, and looks fail-closed so nobody notices. Integrity check 6 (§11) is the standing report of that shape, and it is now the only one of its kind: with no seeded grants there is no default that carries MEMBERS, so the safe path is no longer the path of least repetition — it is the one somebody writes on purpose, and the report is what notices when they forget (D-100, D-150).

docs.title: 5. scope_exposure — deleted by D-097
docs.text:
There is no such table, and this section exists because four pages link to its number. D-097 left one unit, and a unit is a scope rather than a row, so there is no boundary for authority to cross and nothing for an exposure row to sit on. D-031 was not weakened; it was deprived of its subject.

What is lost, stated once. Access to a body's children used to have to be granted by that body — by the people who recruited its leader, who can be asked, and who chose the person being let in. Nothing in this model reproduces that, and what stands instead — a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write — is missing exactly the half where the named adult was somebody the body chose. domain/04 §1 states the same cost where the unit is defined, and this document does not repeat the argument.

Who answers each deleted question now. scope.expose and scope.exposure.review are not in the catalog. The direction-of-authority check has no enforcer and needs none: a row has no direction when there is one unit. org_unit, unit_participation, unit_ancestors() and unit_descendants() are gone with the hierarchy, and with them every rule about paths, depths, nesting and reparenting — 02-organization.md describes groups. D-078's rule, that an exposure extends an assignment and never a grant, has no subject: a holder row has no scope to extend.

A caution that outlives the table. A write-path rule whose only guard is a report, and a report that stops running, is a rule that quietly stops existing: the nightly exposure report was that check's only detector, and nothing sent anybody when it stopped. Every rule in this document that has no enforcer says so, and §11 is where those reports are listed.

The way back is a decision, not a migration. The plausible reason is that the organization has outgrown one center's visibility, and taking it would mean re-arguing D-031 from its own premises — D-097 deleted the table that made the old rule work, so there is nothing to switch back on.

docs.title: 6. access_grant — the per-item layer
docs.text:
This is the "per-item permission" table. You specified it means a capability on that item: "person X may act on item Y". It is also the unit-level table, because the unit is one of the scope types rather than a different kind of thing, and there is no other grant table to hold the difference. The heading names only the first half of that and stays as it is: pages across the corpus and in the decision log link to this anchor, so the slug is the load-bearing part and it is not moving.

One grant is: a grantee, a scope, one permission code, an effect, and a period (D-099).

Fields (grant_scope_type)

Field Kind Notes code text, required, unique unit, event, person_group, role, document. The key a grant points at. name text, required item_table text, required The table scope_id references — event. For the unit, nothing: the row exists so the scope type has a name, and is_item_scoped is what says so. is_item_scoped boolean Default true. False for exactly one row: unit. A grant at a non-item scope has no scope_id, and that single fact is what "the unit is a scope, not a row" means in the schema (D-097). description text, optional

Seeded rows, and the list is short on purpose:

code Item-scoped Means unit No The organization. There is exactly one, and it is not a row anywhere else. event Yes One event. Nothing owns it (D-102); a unit grant reaches every event and an event grant reaches one. person_group Yes One group (D-098) — how "these two may work this group's roster" is said without inventing a scope. role Yes One office (D-100) — the same move applied symmetrically. document Yes Deferred; a document layer still to be designed. It stays in the registry because the registry's whole point is that a new grantable thing is a row here rather than a migration.

supports_levels is deleted with the ladder, and so are the organization and org_unit rows: the first is unit renamed (a scope with no item under it, which is all it ever was), the second is deleted with the hierarchy. membership is not in the seed. Nothing in this design writes a grant on an individual membership row — the thing a membership is protected by is membership.* codes held at the unit — and if that ever changes, adding it is one row here, which is what the registry is for. That the row is gone rather than merely unused is an inference from D-097's and D-099's lists of what is seeded, and §13 records it as one.

Rules (grant_scope_type)

  • Every access_grant.scope_type names a row here. This is the one piece of referential integrity the polymorphic scope does get.
  • Exactly one row — unit — has is_item_scoped false.

Fields (access_grant)

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. person_id reference to person, optional The grantee, when the grant names one person. audience_id reference to audience, optional The grantee, when the grant names a set (§8). Evaluated against the person being checked, per person, as a predicate — never as a list of ids. api_key_id reference to api_key, optional The grantee, when the grant names a caller that is nobody (§14). A key is in no set, so this row is read as written and never evaluated (D-117). scope_type reference to grant_scope_type, required unit, or an item type. scope_id integer, optional The concrete item id. Absent exactly when the scope type is not item-scoped — that is, exactly at unit. No foreign key: polymorphic by design. See the note below. permission_id reference to permission, required One code, not a bundle (D-099). What level used to stand in for, without the ladder. effect enum: allow, deny, required Allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies. D-013's deny survives as an effect on a row rather than as a level called revoked, and its reason for existing is unchanged: a court-ordered restriction must not be beatable by a broader grant. valid_from date, required Default today. valid_to date, optional Absent = open. Discouraged; see below. is_delegated boolean Default false. delegated_from reference to person, optional The person whose authority this delegation carries. granted_by reference to person, required granted_at timestamp, audit time grant_reason text, optional revoked_by reference to person, optional revoked_at timestamp, audit time, optional revoke_reason text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person

Rules

  • Exactly one of person_id, audience_id and api_key_id is set. A grant to none of them is meaningless; a grant to two would be ambiguous — any person in the audience, or only this one? A grant to both a person and a key would be a grant to a caller and a different caller at once, and there is no reading of it. The three are named together because a rule with an unnamed third case is how a model acquires an answer that depends on which column an implementation happened to look at first (D-116).
  • valid_to is either absent or strictly after valid_from.
  • scope_id is absent exactly at unit scope — and that is the whole of what the rule says. It constrains the absent case alone; grant_scope_type.item_table is what states which table an id belongs to.
  • effect is allow or deny. There is no third value and no ordering between them: deny is absolute and is checked first, which is D-032 entire surviving content.
  • permission_id names a permission whose applies_to permits this scope shape — a grant at an item requires unit_and_item. Refused at save with the reason (§2, applies_to).
  • is_delegated and delegated_from agree in both directions: the flag is true exactly when a delegating person is named.
  • A grant is never a delegation from the person it is granted to: delegated_from does not equal person_id.
  • A revocation names who made it: if revoked_at is set, revoked_by is set.
  • A delegation must expire: if is_delegated is true, valid_to is set. This expiry is the whole guard against a delegation outliving its reason: nothing about the person who lent it is re-validated when a check runs, so an open-ended delegation would go on working after the act that justified it was gone. Integrity check 11 (§11) reports one.
  • An audience grant cannot be delegated. is_delegated requires delegated_from, which is a person, and delegating "everyone" is not a coherent act: if audience_id is set, is_delegated is false.
  • A grant to an API key cannot be delegated either, on the same reasoning and with the same test: if api_key_id is set, is_delegated is false. Lending is one person's act towards another; a grant to an integration carries the authority of whoever installed it rather than anybody's, so the rule borrowed from the bullet above is not an extra burden here but the absence of a thing that was never present. The mandatory expiry is refused for a key too, for the same reason: that expiry exists to stop a loan outliving its reason, and there is no loan to expire (D-120). One rule over three grantees, not a third rule for the third grantee (D-116).

docs.title: Inheritance, stated once
docs.text:
A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. That is the whole of it (D-099), and it follows from two deletions rather than from a new rule: after D-097 there is no intermediate scope left between the unit and an item, and after D-102 there is no ownership relation to test.

This is D-006 with the unit tier left standing — per-item permissions are capabilities on the item — and it deletes can_event() outright, along with the unit-authority rule that nearly every event permission in this corpus was reached through. What that rule was doing, so that its absence is noted rather than assumed: it asked whether the actor had authority over the event's owning unit before honouring an event grant. There is no owning unit, so there is nothing to ask, and the question "who is connected to this event?" is answered by the operands of §8's language instead — ORGANIZERS, PLACED, CONFIRMED — each of which is a set the item itself defines.

A unit grant of system.admin therefore reaches everywhere on its own. The old resolver needed a special clause for that ("system.admin qualifies whatever the checked scope is"); it existed because organization scope and unit scope were different tiers. With one unit scope and plain inheritance, the clause has nothing to fix.

docs.title: The uniqueness rule has to be careful with grantees
docs.text:
The obvious index — one live grant per (grantee, scope) — never worked, because a person can legitimately hold a personal grant and be covered by an audience grant on the same item, and those are different rows with different lifetimes. A second reason it cannot work: one code per row, so one person legitimately holds a dozen live allows on one item. A broad office is a couple of dozen rows (D-099), each a different code, and a rule that permitted one live grant per grantee and item would refuse the second of them.

Rules

  • At most one live allow per (grantee, scope, permission) — counted over the rows that name a person and are open, unrevoked, and effect = allow.
  • At most one live allow per (audience, scope, permission), counted the same way over the rows that name an audience.
  • At most one live allow per (key, scope, permission), counted the same way over the rows that name an API key.
  • A person, an audience and a key are three different grantees, so the same code on the same item may exist once for the person, once for a set they are in, and once for an integration. It grants nothing extra and it is not an error; it is a decision about the same capability written more than once, which is what the grantee column has always meant. A key's row is not a second copy of a person's, and no row here is read as another one's duplicate (D-116).

Indexes

  • person, audience, key and scope lookups, each restricted to open rows;
  • a deny-only index over open rows with effect = deny, keyed by grantee, scope and permission — the deny lookup runs on every check, at every scope, and it is the first thing the resolver does.

Denies are excluded from all three unique indexes, so a deny may coexist with an allow on the same grantee, scope and code — which is exactly what makes an explicit deny meaningful. A personal deny beats an audience allow, because the deny check runs first and is scope-independent (§10). A deny aimed at a key defeats that key's allows and nobody else's, and a deny aimed at the person who installed a key does not touch the key at all: deny is absolute over the grantee it names, and these are different grantees (D-118).

docs.title: effect, and why a - in an expression is not a deny
docs.text:
Two mechanisms that both subtract, and are not interchangeable (D-099):

effect = deny - in an audience expression Narrows Every grant that applies to the person, including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else One grant's reach Says "she must not have this, whatever else she is given" "this grant is not for the people in that set" Beatable by Nothing. Checked first, absolute, scope-independent Yes — any other grant that reaches her Lives on A grant row An operand of the grant's audience (§8)

The first cannot be expressed by the second, which is why denies stay — that is D-013's whole reason for existing. And denies are legal at the unit as well as on an item, since "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone" is exactly the case an expression cannot serve: subtracting her from one grant leaves every other grant aimed at the same set intact.

A deny is a real row and can therefore be wrong in a way an allow cannot be. A live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow is dead weight, and a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason — integrity check 5 (§11) reports the shape, as D-099 requires.

docs.title: Live-grant uniqueness excludes denies — deliberately
docs.text:
A deny must be able to coexist with an allow on the same scope, because that is the only way to express "this person has access to the unit's events, except this one". So the rule that keeps one live grant per grantee, item and code — carried here as uq_access_grant_live — covers allows only; a deny row is outside it by design, and the resolver checks denies first.

This is the rule's shape, not an implementation detail of an index (D-072), and the distinction is load-bearing here rather than pedantic: "unique among live allowing grants" is a conditional rule, so the migration must emit a partial unique index whose predicate excludes deny. A plain unique constraint over the same columns is a different and wrong rule — it would refuse the deny beside the allow, which is precisely the pair the domain requires. See shape 2.

The condition also excludes revoked_at, which is easy to write wrongly in the other direction. A revoked grant must not occupy the unique slot — that is what lets a grant be revoked and re-made rather than edited. So the predicate is "open and unrevoked and allow", three tests, and a partial index that gets one of them wrong is invisible until the day someone cannot save a grant they should be able to.

docs.title: What is refused when a grant is saved
docs.text:
Seven checks, one transaction, each with the layer named — because none of them is a database rule, and D-081 forbids writing them as if one were:

  1. The code may be granted at this scope. permission.applies_to permits the scope shape (§2). Refused with the reason in the message, per D-099's example: a grant of event.create on one event is refused because an event cannot be created twice.
  2. The code is assignable. is_assignable is true (§2's deprecated-code case).
  3. Every bound operand in the grant's audience may bind here. An operand whose selector_type.binds_to_item is true is legal only on an item-scope grant, and only where selector_type.argument_type matches that grant's item type. PLACED on a person_group grant is refused because that item is not an event; ORGANIZERS on a unit grant is refused because at the unit there is nothing to bind it to, with the operand named in the message (D-102).
  4. The audience's expression is well-formed and acyclic (§8) — and "acyclic" is measured over the expanded tree, so this check follows the AUDIENCE leaves into the audiences this one names (D-103). Saving a grant is not where a cycle is created, but it is where a person is standing in front of the one screen that can refuse it, and a grant must never be saved pointing at an expression that cannot be evaluated. There is no depth bound to check here — D-105 left the tree unbounded — so this check carries no size rule at all, and the cycle walk is its only structural refusal.
  5. Every AUDIENCE leaf names an audience that exists and that has a code (D-103). Both halves read a second table, so neither is a constraint on this row: the dangling case is the orphan check of §11 item 2, and the null-code case is that item's neighbour in item 12. A leaf pointing at an unnamed audience is refused rather than resolved-at-read, because resolving it later would make a grant's reach depend on whether somebody had typed a code into a different screen.
  6. A code that a key may never hold is not granted to a key. system.admin and the four api_key.* codes are refused when api_key_id is set (D-122, §15). This is the sharpest refusal here, and the reason it is here rather than in a constraint is worth stating: the other five checks read columns — this one reads a list of five codes that is a column of nothing at all, an equality written against named rows precisely so that no rule can derive it and widen it. No database rule can span it, so integrity check 20 (§11) is the entire net for rows that were written before the rule existed or by a path that skipped the save.
  7. The writer holds what the row names. A write to access_grant may name only a permission that the person writing it holds, at a scope that reaches what they are writing — the granter's ceiling (D-163). access_grant.create has always said you may write grant rows; until this check it never said what they may say. The mechanism is free: it is the check the resolver already performs, pointed at the granter at save time, so a writer predicts may I grant this? from the question they already ask — can I do this myself? What it closes is what the catalog called the sharpest hole in its file: system.admin can now be handed out only by somebody who already holds it, and stated as an invariant — the set of privileges held by anybody in this system can only grow from a person who already holds what they are handing out. Three consequences belong beside the rule: a right held only through a delegation does not raise the ceiling — lending is not holding, and delegation is not obstructed, because a delegation's row is written by the delegator, who holds the right directly and passes this ceiling on exactly the occasion D-143 already validates at; the ceiling stops escalation, not spread — a person who holds person.view at the unit may hand it to twenty people, since they hold it, and no report covers that distribution and none was called for, because this design's answer to a widening nobody wrote is a report plus a written procedure rather than a mechanism. The entry a reader will find nearest to it, check 7's wide half (§11), is about something else: a grant that got wider because a set under a - stopped resolving, which is an expression changing shape under a row nobody edited; and granted_by becomes load-bearing in a new way — the ceiling is evaluated against a named person, so an authorless grant could not be checked at all, and D-125 records that a grant's granted_by names a person, so these rows have no empty to read. Day one is unaffected: D-150's single account holds system.admin at the unit, which satisfies every code — the origin of all authority is exempt by construction rather than by a special case. No integrity check stands behind this refusal, and none was called for: the ceiling lives at the save, and the two reports a reader will find nearby look at other things — check 9's holder list and check 7's wide half (§11) — and both are read, not sent (§11). Scope, so the ceiling is not over-read: this is a rule about writes to access_grant and nothing else. Editing an audience's expression or a role_holder row is a different code and is unchanged; whether those should carry an analogous ceiling is a question this round neither answers nor pretends is settled. One write to access_grant is outside this check, and it is exactly one: the twelve rows an event create writes beside the event (08a §8, D-151). The ceiling reads a writer who chose whom a grant names, and the create chose nobody — its audience is a fixed expression that resolves to nobody at that instant, and the writer gains none of the twelve (D-170). Rebuilding a missing bundle by hand is not that write: it is a person choosing rows, and it is checked.

Why the save path and not the check path, said once for all seven. A grant that cannot mean anything is a data-entry mistake, and a data-entry mistake is refused where the person making it is standing. The resolver's job in the same situation is the opposite and is already fixed: an operand that does not resolve is the empty set, so anything that slips past these checks denies rather than widens (§8, Evaluation) — except through -, where an empty operand widens, which is why these are refusals and not warnings. Checks 3 and 4 (§11) report what got through, and a row there means the write path was skipped — there is no constraint to have disabled.

An eighth refusal lives on the other screen. Ending or deleting an audience is refused while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names it (§8, Rules). It is listed here only so that a reader of this section does not conclude the grant save is the whole write path.

docs.title: No foreign key on scope_id — the accepted trade-off
docs.text:
scope_id has no FK because it is polymorphic. This is a deliberate choice, and D-101 extended it to audience_operand.selector_arg_id, which is polymorphic for the same reason and takes the same four mitigations:

Polymorphic scope_id grantable_item supertable Adding a grantable type One row in grant_scope_type New table + FK from supertable + migration Referential integrity None — can point at a deleted item Full Query cost Direct Requires a join Risk Orphaned grants after an item is deleted Migration churn on every new feature

Polymorphism is what makes a new grantable thing — an event, a group, an office, a document that does not exist yet — a configuration row rather than a schema change, which matters a great deal given how much of this system is not yet specified.

The mitigations are mandatory, not optional:

  1. grant_scope_type validates the scope_type value (FK above).
  2. Deleting an item must close its grants — an application obligation, and tested.
  3. A nightly orphan check per scope type, and the same scan over selector_arg_id (§11, check 2).
  4. scope_id is BIGINT and ids are never reused.

To overrule this, add a grantable_item(id, item_type) supertable and give every grantable entity an FK to it. Tracked in ../open-questions.md — it is a real fork and worth a deliberate decision.

docs.title: Why valid_to is discouraged here too
docs.text: An item grant is typically for one event, so an open-ended item grant is nearly always a mistake. Application validation should require valid_to for item-scoped grants, with access_grant.grant_reason explaining any exception. The sentence stays an application rule, because D-071's posture applies here too: nothing in the schema forces a grant to end, and the report of long-lived open grants is the control. Nothing backstops a forgotten grant. There is no prefilled term and no membership gate between a forgotten row and an answer, so a forgotten grant is simply live.

docs.title: 7. permission_level — deleted by D-099
docs.text:
There is no such table, and this section exists because one page links to its number (D-099). permission_level mapped (permission, scope kind) → the level a grant had to reach, so that one access_grant.level could serve many codes without a mapping hidden in application code. Its two surviving jobs sit on permission itself: applies_to (§2) says which scope kinds a code means anything at, checked on save, and right_kind (§2) is compared by exactly one channel — guardianship (§10). The third job, "how much of this permission does this grant carry", has no answer: a grant is one permission, and the row exists or it does not.

The table's job Where it is now Which scope kinds this permission means anything at permission.applies_to (§2), checked on save How much of this permission a given grant carries Nowhere — a grant is one permission The comparison the level made possible permission.right_kind, used by the guardianship channel alone (§10)

What is lost, said once. A level was a bundle with a name, and a named bundle is something you can ask about: the audit trail could say "she held contribute". The answer to "what did she have in 2024?" is now the set of grant rows that were live then — more precise, less quotable, and a broad office is a couple of dozen rows. That price was paid deliberately, and D-068 had already refused the same idea once. Roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is.

How an ordering could come back, and what it would cost. Names for sets of codes cost nothing — that is what a role already is. A real ordering means re-importing this table, the rank-comparison rule (D-012) and locality's tie-break (D-032's other half), all deleted with their only consumers. The door is wide on the naming side and narrow on the ordering side.

Decisions behind this page: D-002, D-003, D-005, D-006, D-007, D-012, D-013, D-031, D-032, D-039, D-052, D-053, D-068, D-071, D-072, D-074, D-078, D-081, D-086, D-088, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105.

docs.title: Data Model — Authorization: the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry
docs.text:
What an audience is as a row, how an expression is written and rendered, and which operands the language has.

Section numbers are shared across the six parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues), and 05e §14–§17 (a key, and what it may hold).

docs.title: 8. audience — grants that target a set of people
docs.text:
A grant can name a person, an audience or a registered key (D-042, widened by D-116). This section is the language of the middle one: a person is a reference and so is a key (05e §14), while an audience is a set, and a set needs a language. An audience is an expression over named sets, stored as a tree (D-101): MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers) - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) is one grant's grantee. One grant composes a rule and a roster — "the kitchen crew, plus whoever leads this pack" — in the same expression, and it intersects and differences as well as unions.

Fields (audience)

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. code text, optional, unique where set Two jobs. (1) A stable handle for reports — an audience is aimed at by a grant through access_grant.audience_id, a reference. (2) The only thing another audience can name: AUDIENCE(<code>) resolves through this column, so naming an audience is what makes it composable, and an unnamed audience is simply not one (D-103). Naming stays opt-in — there is no reason to force a handle onto a grant's private addressee list — and the leaf may not point at a null code, which is a check reading another table and therefore not a constraint (§11, check 12). code joins the shared namespace of roles, groups and reserved words; name does not, and the two are different columns serving different questions. name text, required What a human calls it in the editor. description text, optional Why it exists, for whoever finds it in three years. valid_from date, optional valid_to date, optional Absent = open. An ended audience reaches nobody, and that is the one test that gates the whole expression (§Evaluation). Ending one is therefore a save-time refusal once anything names it (rule below): under - an emptied operand makes the result wider, so "ended" would otherwise be a way to widen a grant by editing a different screen. created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person

Rules (audience)

  • The expression is the audience. An audience with no root operand row is an empty set, and a freshly created one is exactly that — not a misconfiguration, and how an expression gets built one node at a time. What is not legal is a grant aimed at one being reported as granting something, which is the editor's job (§The cost of composition) and integrity check 7 (§11).
  • An audience is aimed at by reference and named by code, and those are different relations. A grant points at audience.id; another audience points at audience.code. The name collision problem therefore does reach this table, and §Names are one namespace is where the rule lives (D-103).
  • Bare names do not resolve to audiences. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS names a role or a group, and the audience arm has to be written AUDIENCE(veterans). Why: letting a bare name reach a third table would silently change what stored expressions mean — D-103 keeps bare resolution at its two kinds.
  • code is unique among the rows that have one, and joins the shared namespace (§Names are one namespace).
  • An audience may not be ended or deleted while something live names it — a live grant aimed at it, or a live audience reachable from a live grant through any number of AUDIENCE leaves. Refused at save, and the reverse lookup is one indexed query over audience_operand rows whose selector_kind is AUDIENCE. Why: without this, "ended" is a way to empty an expression from a screen nobody associates with it, and under - an empty operand makes the answer wider, not narrower (D-103). No foreign key does this job: the reference is a code inside a polymorphic column, not a foreign key (§The expression tree).
  • Naming an audience requires the right to read it — audience.view over it, in the catalog's vocabulary — and grants nothing to the people it contains (../appendix/permission-catalog.md). Fail closed. Why: AUDIENCE(veterans) in a grant someone else saves is how one person's composition decision becomes another's authority, and the read permission is the only place that asymmetry is visible to the writer — see what you name is D-091's requirement.
  • The row carries no size rule. There is no depth limit, no width limit and no node budget on an audience, and nothing replaces them on this row (D-105) — the tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it. What a large expression costs is a report's job (§The cost of composition), and a report with nothing behind it is a convention and not a guard (D-081).
  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.

This table carries no rule key, no kind, no scope parameter and no configuration column: an audience has no kind and no rule key, only an expression. Which operands exist, whether they take an argument and what type it is live in the selector_type registry (§The selector registry), and no bound on an expression's size is configured anywhere (D-105).

docs.title: Author in sets. Evaluate per person.
docs.text:
p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is by definition (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C: the set notation and the per-person boolean test are the same function read from two ends. The choice decides what gets stored and what a writer is allowed to say, not what the machine computes:

  • Sets are the source language, and they are the closed one. - is complement against EVERYONE and * distributes over +, so the set form is no weaker than a boolean one — it buys zero expressive power and everything in the way of safety. The operators are +, - and *, one spelling each; there are no boolean spellings — no &, no |, no !, which were offered with the age operands and declined (D-107). D-060 refused a rule engine, and a per-person boolean language is the door to one.
  • An operand must be a named registry row — a row of §The selector registry — and a writer may compose seeded operands and nothing else. Every row denotes a set of people: MEMBERS denotes the people who pass is_current_member and stores nothing; OLDER(15) denotes the people who are fifteen or older on the checked date, the same shape of thing. What an operand requires is the name, not a table behind the set — an attribute may be an operand (D-107). OLDER(18) is a row, seeded, shipped with its evaluator arm like every other row; AGE >= 18 is not a row and cannot be, because the language has no >= to put anywhere.
  • Eligibility is capability (D-060): no eligibility rule table, no prerequisite system, nothing evaluated outside can(). There is no gate the system applies on its own, and the language holds a vocabulary a person may use to write one.
  • A check never materializes a set. The resolver compiles the expression down to a predicate for the person being checked. An implementation that evaluates MEMBERS as a list of ids and then tests for containment pays three thousand rows per request — the one way to get this wrong, and the reason the requirement is written here rather than left to whoever builds it. Integrity check 16 (§11) is the CI assertion of that sentence.
  • The workloads this corpus promises need sets, not predicates. "Who does this grant reach?" must be shown, expanded, in front of a human — a requirement on the screen (D-091), and a predicate can only report true while a set is the answer. "What may a treasurer do?" (D-100) needs the person→set index, and role_holder and person_group_member are it; an expression is unindexable. And naming an operand is what makes a compilation reusable: a compiled predicate is keyed by the expression it came from and the ruleset version, so one edit to a shared name refreshes every grant that embeds it (§10, D-114).

docs.title: Grammar, precedence, and the canonical rendering
docs.text:
expr    := term ( '+' term )*
term    := operand ( ( '*' | '-' ) operand )*
operand := EVERYONE | MEMBERS
         | OLDER '(' n ')' | YOUNGER '(' n ')'
         | ATTENDED | PLACED | CONFIRMED | ON_WAITLIST | ORGANIZERS
         | ROLE '(' name ')' | GROUP '(' name ')'
         | PERSON '(' person ')'
         | AUDIENCE '(' code ')'
         | '(' expr ')'

  OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) read person.birth_date AS OF THE DATE THE CHECK IS MADE,
  so `MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19)` reaches different people on different
  dates with no write, and can(..., on date) for a past date answers for that
  past date. Their argument is an INTEGER — the only operand argument in the
  registry that is not an entity reference (§*The selector registry*). There is
  no comparison operator anywhere in this grammar: no '>=', no '<', no bare AGE
  -- which is where D-060's refusal of a rule engine lives.  See the prose
  under this block, and D-107.

  '+', '-' and '*' are the whole operator set, each with one spelling. OLDER
  and YOUNGER are ordinary named operands, composed by the same three
  operators as every other row.

  Each of ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST and ORGANIZERS appears either
  bare — bound to the item the grant sits on — or written '(' event ')'.  A bare
  bound operand on a unit-scope grant is refused (§6, *What is refused when a
  grant is saved*).

  PERSON takes a person and names a set of one.  A hand-written set of people is
  therefore a sum, not a leaf: `PERSON(a) + PERSON(b)`
  ([D-105](../decisions/round-11-12.md#d-105--there-are-no-lists-a-hand-written-set-is-an-expression-like-any-other)).
  AUDIENCE names another saved audience by its
  `code`; an audience with no code cannot be named, and a bare name never
  resolves to one ([D-103](../decisions/round-10b.md#d-103--an-audience-may-name-another-audience)).
  • + union, * intersection, - difference — three operators, one spelling each. MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19) is an ordinary term.
  • There is no comparison operator in the language. No >=, no <, no bare AGE: an operand is a registry row and AGE >= 15 has no row to be, which is the whole of D-060's protection now (§Author in sets, and D-107).
  • * and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; brackets override.
  • The canonical rendering prints every bracket, always. The rendering is derived from the rows and is what every screen shows; if it is also kept as a column for search, it is a copy and the rows win (see §The expression tree).

Printing every bracket is not a courtesy, and the example is the proof. Under this precedence, the unbracketed MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS means "everyone except the counselors in that group", which is not what its author meant — they meant "all counselors not in that group", whose stored form is (MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS. The editor rewrites what is typed into canonical form before saving, so no expression in this system is ever read bare; and once everything is stored fully bracketed, changing what binds tighter later changes nothing already stored.

A hand-typed sum of twenty people is a left-to-right chain, so it prints as nineteen nested pairs of brackets. That is what "storage and display both say what was written" buys, and it is asked for. If it turns out unreadable, the answer is that a set of people big enough to be unreadable is a person_group — not a flattening rule invented in advance (D-105).

docs.title: The selector registry
docs.text:
selector_type is a seeded table, not an enum (D-101): the language becomes data. The parser reads its reserved words from it, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the write path checks arity against it. It is the shape grant_scope_type already has.

Fields (selector_type)

Field Kind Notes code text, required, unique The reserved word: MEMBERS, ROLE, PLACED. name text, required For the editor's dropdown. takes_argument boolean, required Whether the code may be written with an argument. The arity check reads this column and nothing else. binds_to_item boolean, required True exactly when the argument-less form means "relative to the item being checked" (D-102). argument_type text, optional Which table the argument names a row of — role, person_group, person, event, audience — or a scalar: integer, the argument kind OLDER and YOUNGER take (D-107). Six values, five of them entity kinds and one of them not an entity. Absent exactly when takes_argument is false. This is what the save path compares against the grant's item type, which is a reason the registry is doing real work and not merely tidying. It is not always a grant_scope_type: person never was and audience never will be, because a grant is never about an audience — it is aimed through one. The two coincide for exactly the item-scoped operands, which is the set the binding check reads. A scalar argument is never in that set, since OLDER binds to nothing. description text, optional The sentence a writer reads before using it. AUDIENCE carries its gloss here, because the name misleads without one.

Seeded selectors, in full, because this table is the language — thirteen rows, all of them shipped. The number is only the cheap form of the real check: this list is the language, so an operand appearing anywhere other than here — in a screen's dropdown, in a resolver's switch, in a decision entry that never reached this table — is a bug, and §13 keeps the document-level report that hunts exactly that. Every seeded row is either a rule about people or takes an argument, so the registry carries no special case left to explain; OLDER and YOUNGER are the only rows whose argument is not an entity reference.

code Argument Binds to item Means EVERYONE never no Any person, including those with no account and no membership. MEMBERS never no Holds a membership live on the checked date — the same predicate the membership gate applied (D-039). OLDER required (integer) no The people who are n years old or older on the date being checked, from person.birth_date — the only operand in the registry whose argument is a number rather than a row (D-107). It is a row here for the reason the whole table exists: it is a named operand, and it denotes a set of people — the same shape of thing MEMBERS denotes, which is a test over membership rows and stores nothing either. A person with no birth date is not in the set, as a person with no membership row is not in MEMBERS: that is an ordinary answer, not a resolution failure, and §11's report of unresolved leaves must not page about it (§Evaluation). Its membership moves at midnight with no write — see §The cost of composition. YOUNGER required (integer) no The people strictly younger than n on the date being checked — OLDER's mirror, n and up against under n. Each is the complement of the other, and the language has no complement a bare leaf can carry (only -, which needs something on its left), so both are seeded rather than one being spelled out of the other; that is the whole of their relationship, and it is why there is no AGE_BAND row and none is wanted — a band is composed out of the operators every other row is composed with, and OLDER(13) - OLDER(18) is thirteen to seventeen. Same argument kind, same date rule, same non-failure for a missing birth date. PERSON required (person) no One named person — a set of one, which is a set, so it is a named operand like every other row: the exception for a named individual lives inside the expression that granted the rule, next to the thing it exempts (D-100). A hand-written set of several people is written the same way, as a sum of these — PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) — because a set of one is a set, and a set of three is the same thing three times (D-105). There is no separate "hand-typed list" operand and no table behind one. ROLE required (role) no Holders of that office live on the checked date (role_holder). GROUP required (person_group) no Members of that group live on the checked date (person_group_member). AUDIENCE required (audience) no The value of another saved audience's expression, evaluated live on the checked date — the one operand whose argument is a decision about access rather than a roster, and so the one that makes a rule namable (D-103). ATTENDED optional (event) yes, event response = attending. PLACED optional (event) yes, event Attending and not waitlisted — the capacity set, the one the events module counts and the index already serves. CONFIRMED optional (event) yes, event PLACED and is_confirmed — holds a paid place. ON_WAITLIST optional (event) yes, event Attending and waitlisted. ORGANIZERS optional (event) yes, event Runs the event (event_organizer).

Two operands a reader might reach for are not in this table. LIST is not an operand: a hand-written set of people is a sum, PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), written inside the expression like every other set (D-105). GUARDIANS is not a selector either: guardianship is a channel carrying a right_level over a child on the guardianship row, not a set a grant may be aimed at, and an operand naming it would re-grant, one code at a time, what that channel grants whole (D-113).

Rules (selector_type)

  • Rows are platform-seeded. Adding an operand is a decision entry plus a seed row, never a row somebody types into a screen: each operand is a branch of the evaluator and a fact about stored data, and an editor that could invent one would produce an expression nothing evaluates — which then resolves to the empty set and denies quietly forever (§Evaluation).
  • The registry is organization-read-only, and saying that out loud is what makes "a closed language" true of a table rather than merely asserted. Every row ships with the platform, every row arrives with a release, no screen edits this table, and no organization adds to it (D-103). No row carries a flag saying so, because a flag true of every row of a table nothing may add to says nothing (D-152). What refuses an edit is that no code authorizes one and no screen offers one — there is no selector_type.edit anywhere in the catalog — which reaches further than a flag did, because it does not depend on which screen you arrived from, and an import that names this table has no row to write. The language becomes data means the parser and the editor read one place instead of three; it does not mean the language is extensible at runtime. A code in this table with no shipped resolver arm is a deployment bug, and it surfaces as an empty set — an operand that reaches nobody, an allow that allows nobody, and a deny that on the - side denies everybody. That is the whole hazard of calling a closed set "data", and it is why the seeding of this table is release engineering rather than configuration. There is no third kind of row — a row either ships with an evaluator arm that reads it or it does not ship, and "shipped as a row, not implemented in the evaluator" is not a category this model allows, however useful it would be as a roadmap marker.
  • Every code is a reserved name in the shared role / group / audience namespace (§Names are one namespace).
  • argument_type is absent exactly when takes_argument is false, and names a real table exactly when it is true — one exception: the scalar domain integer, which OLDER and YOUNGER take and which names no table because it names no row (D-107). Anything reading this column has to know the scalar case exists, and has to know what the scalar is not — it is not a reference. That is why §11's check 2 walks two keyless columns (access_grant.scope_id, audience_operand.selector_arg_id) and why the design's wider count of them — seven, kept in 00 §9 — never reaches an operand: an 18 sitting in selector_arg_id points at nothing, so there is nothing for a merge to repoint, nothing for a cascade to find, and nothing for the orphan scan to walk. The check counts references, and 18 is not one (§A hand-named person is now a keyless reference, where the argument kinds are enumerated).
  • The four attendance tiers name columns of event_registration and nothing else. That is the requirement that keeps the writer's choice honest — picking between tiers only means something if the choices are the stored facts.

Three operands are not in this table, and each absence is load-bearing.

  • PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is refused, and this paragraph is the whole reason. The reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register, so an operand built on it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. That column is a safeguarding signal, three-valued on purpose (D-067), and keeping it out of the selector language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things". It is refused because of what it would do on the - side of an expression when a volunteer forgets a tick box — not because of what it is: a predicate over a column is an ordinary kind of operand (D-107).
  • GRANTS is refused. It was wanted so that an expression could name "the people reached by these grants" — a bulk-editing affordance dressed as an operand. An operand must resolve to a set of people, and a set of grants is not one: the moment an expression can name the grant table, MEMBERS - GRANTS(...) is expressible, and a language in which a grant can subtract a grant is a language in which the answer to "who may do this?" requires evaluating the whole expression tree of every other grant to answer one check — the closure property of §Author in sets doing the job it exists for. The bulk edit it was asked for is real and is an editor affordance — select the grants, change their grantees, in one screen, which changes rows and leaves every stored expression meaning what it meant. Refusing it here is what keeps that screen a UI feature instead of a resolver feature.
  • WHITELISTED is not seeded, and the reason is that there is nothing to evaluate. The nearest facts are source = staff (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. Either it means one of those or it is a new column on event_registration, which is an events decision and not a selector decision, and the events decision has been made: refused (D-148), so this is no longer a question waiting on a word in a grammar. An operand that reads no state is not a vocabulary item but a syntax error wearing one's clothes. F-20 is a question about whether the feature is wanted, not about whether the language could hold the word.

PERSON(x) is a registry row, and a hand-named person is a set nobody maintains: PERSON(a) is created by being typed. That is tolerable for exactly one operand, at the size of one person, because the alternative — a second grant aimed at that person, which stays legal and is arguably clearer for a permanent exception — leaves the exception invisible next to the rule it exempts. A grant aimed at one person is the ordinary expression of a temporary exception, and its cost is not the typing: a typed person is a selector_arg_id with no foreign key behind it, and §A hand-named person is now a keyless reference is where the repointing requirement that hangs on that lives.

docs.title: What LIST is, said plainly — withdrawn by D-105
docs.text:
LIST is not an operand and audience_member is not a table. The answer to "plus Honza" is PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), written in the expression where every other set in this language is written (D-105).

Naming three people inside a grant must not mean making them members of a person_group. A group's members are true when no grant points at them (D-098), so editing a roster to move one grant's reach edits a set that other grants read — and it invents a group nobody talks about. The answer to "plus Honza" is PERSON(honza), and the answer is not a roster edit. An exception written this way is invisible to every other grant until somebody opens this one and has no name of its own, and AUDIENCE(x) still resolves to another audience's whole expression and nothing less, so nobody can reach into the middle of it from outside.

The limits of writing people in the expression. There are no per-person dates: audience_operand carries no period and gains none, so a June-to-August exception is its own grant with its own period (D-099) — where there is one audience and one grant there are now two grants, and a reviewer asking "what does Honza have?" must find both. There is no per-name provenance: created_by on a node answers "who last saved this tree" and not "who added Honza". "Who was on this audience in 2026" is a recomputation over audit payloads that expire after 24 months (D-088), so the question stops being answerable in 2028. And two writers can collide: a hand-written set is one expression edited as a whole, so whoever builds the editor owes this an optimistic-concurrency check or a queue — a silent lost update here quietly removes somebody's access, and nothing in the schema will notice.

Decisions behind this page: D-039, D-042, D-060, D-067, D-081, D-088, D-091, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-107, D-113, D-114.

docs.title: Data Model — Authorization: the expression tree and what each operand costs
docs.text:
The storage half of §8: the audience_operand tree itself, the namespace rule, what each operand costs, and how a tree is evaluated.

Section numbers are shared across the six parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 05-authorization.md holds §1–§7, 05a §8 (the audience table, the grammar, the selector registry), 05b §8 continued (the tree and what each operand costs), 05c §9–§10 (access_log and the resolver), and 05d §11–§13 (invariants, seed data, open issues), and 05e §14–§17 (a key, and what it may hold).

docs.title: The expression tree
docs.text:
Each row of audience_operand is one node — a binary tree: two operands and one operator per row. Why: one evaluator of about fifteen lines answers every operand, and the tree keeps the writer's brackets instead of silently rewriting them (D-101).

Fields (audience_operand)

Field Kind Notes id integer identity Surrogate key. audience_id reference to audience, required Denormalized onto every row so that the whole tree is one indexed fetch. The read path never walks a parent chain; it selects by audience_id and assembles in memory. One indexed read per audience in the closure, not one per check (D-103): an expression naming AUDIENCE(veterans) has to fetch that audience's rows as well. No transitive walk over audience_operand rows, and no recursive query. The closure's size is discovered by walking it at save, not bounded by a number — the walk that checks acyclicity has already counted the audiences, so the cost is known before the first check runs, and it is not known in advance of the expression (rule below, and §The cost of composition). Every row also carries its parent's audience_id, so a node never belongs to a different audience than the one above it (checked on save, asserted by check 10). parent_id reference to audience_operand, optional On the child, so a node belongs to exactly one expression. Absent on the root. operator enum: +, -, *, optional Set on a node, absent on a leaf. left_id reference to audience_operand, optional Set on a node. Left and right are not interchangeable: - is not commutative, and the pair is the expression's meaning. right_id reference to audience_operand, optional Set on a node. selector_kind reference to selector_type, optional Set on a leaf, absent on a node. selector_arg_id integer, optional Polymorphic, and deliberately without a foreign key — it points at role, person_group, person, event or audience depending on kind — or it points at nothing: OLDER and YOUNGER write their integer into this same column (D-107), because the column is an integer and the value is one. An integer in this column is not a reference: nothing to repoint on a merge, nothing for a cascade to find, nothing for the orphan scan to walk — which is precisely why that scan filters on the selector's kind and walks the five entity kinds rather than every row in this column (§A hand-named person is now a keyless reference).
