docs.text:
One resolver, and the key's entry point takes fewer arguments than the person's. §10 of 05c is the implementation and it is not duplicated here; what belongs here is the signature and the refusal inside it:

can_key(api_key, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at)   → allowed | denied

No owner_person_id, and no person of any kind (D-121). That is not an omission to be filled in later: the parameter is the impersonation vulnerability, because a claimed person would make the trail's word for who acted an input, and this design's on_behalf exists precisely to be "true, explicitly — not inferred from the two ids differing". A key has no channel to infer from, so a claimed person would be exactly that — claimed. A request authenticates as a person or as a key, never as both, and in both audit trails actor_person_id and api_key_id are mutually exclusive.

Channels are unchanged, and there is no seventh one. A check answered for a key records unit_grant or item_grant exactly as one for a person does, and authorization_ref_id still names an access_grant.id — so no new reference-less polymorphic key is introduced here, and the two this model already has stay the two. The channel enum's own note already says that system "was never a channel rather than a namespace"; a key is not a channel either. What the trail adds is who, not how.

Invariant 19 now reads "a caller". It forbade any row mapping a person — or a person and a code, or a person and an item — to a permission answer, and as written a table keyed by api_key_id and permission_code holding a boolean would not have been forbidden by it. "The integration's permissions" is the most natural cache in this system to write and it is precisely a current answer, so the invariant's subject is now a caller, a person or a key (D-123). last_used_at is not such a row and is named as permitted beside the three shapes §11 already permits: it is a timestamp about an event that happened, and nothing reads it to decide whether to allow something now. A column named api_key.last_checked_permission would be, and is the shape the review looks for.

Who enforces what — 00-conventions §6a, because a machine is exactly the writer that was never written:

Rule Layer secret_hash present, code and secret_hash each unique among live rows, valid_to after valid_from migration-level constraint — the invariant, and now naming both columns rather than the one D-130 found missing api_key_id set on a grant means is_delegated false; a grant never sets two grantees model validation at the save, and check 1's shape report is the net A grant of a refused code to a key the save path only — no constraint spans permission and access_grant, so check 20 is the entire net api_key_id and actor_person_id never both set on a trail row migration-level constraint on each trail A live key nobody has used, or whose owner has no live account nightly report — a convention, and §15's tabs are where it is read

docs.title: 17. What is not designed here
docs.text:
Stated because a reader will otherwise assume the nearest mechanism applies.

  • What this system does to itself is not a caller and has no row. The 1 January membership sweep, payload reduction, migrations and the bank statement pull write rows with an empty actor column, which is read as the system acting on its own and is a complete answer to who did this; where the audit trail keeps a label, it is one of six from a list rather than free text (00-conventions §7a, D-125). api_key was deliberately not stretched to cover them: a sweep is not a caller, and a table whose rows may or may not carry a secret is a table whose invariants become conditional.
  • Break-glass is a report and a procedure, not a mechanism (D-126). A key is not a person, carries nobody's authority and may never hold system.admin, so it cannot stand in for somebody who cannot log in; what it can do is nothing, which is why the answer is check 9's second column and a written procedure (domain/02 §3).
  • The outbound direction is F-27. Everything here is a caller arriving. Anything this system initiates — an accounting export, a refund, a webhook (a mechanism this corpus deleted rather than deferred) — has no design, and the one refusal that cited "a second integration with its own authorization" as a reason now has a mechanism to point at (07-finance.md §2b).
  • Nothing about the wire. How a secret is presented, what it looks like, how it is hashed, how a session is carried after a person logs in — API layer, and D-072 is the standing division. What is decided here is only what may be stored: a hash, and nothing else.
  • No rate limiting, no IP allowlist. Either would be a second, weaker authorization implementation, which domain/06 §10 rejects because "they diverge; the weaker one becomes the exploit". A rate limit is an availability measure and earns no permission code.
  • No anonymous caller. A public read of published facts is an integration with a key granted specifically those codes — there is no fourth kind of caller, and nothing in this design grants anything to a request that authenticated as nobody.

docs.title: Data Model — Audit and Import: the two audit trails, and audit_log
docs.text:
audit_log and its trigger, what is stripped before a row is written, and the history query. access_log (the authorization audit trail) is in 05c-access-log-and-resolver.md.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 06-audit-and-import.md holds §1–§2 (the two audit trails and the audit_log table), 06a §3 (the legacy import pipeline), and 06b §4–§6 (the redaction log, the integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 1. Two audit trails, and why both
docs.text:
access_log audit_log Records Who did what, and by what authority Which fields of a row changed, and their values before and after — including a person's descriptive values, which are in the entry deliberately (§2.2) Answers "Who accessed this child's record, and were they allowed to?" "When did this person's address change, and who changed it?" Volume Very high High Raised by Application code, on every permission check and action Every write to an audited table, on every path — §2.1 names who owes that write, since no trigger is defined anywhere

Keeping them separate is deliberate. They have different retention needs, different query patterns, and different access permissions. Merging them produces a table that is too large to query and too sensitive to expose to anyone who needs one half of it.

Both questions are asked about the whole record, and that wording is load-bearing. There is no medical record to ask about — D-083 removed the referent rather than building it — so there is one record about a person, and everything in it other than name, gender and age lives in person_attribute (09-attributes.md). "Who accessed this child's record, and were they allowed to?" is the question person.view really guards.

The same holds for what this trail's payloads hold. A person's descriptive values are in an audit entry deliberately (§2.2), and they are emptied once the entry passes the payload window (D-088). Both halves belong in this table's own summary, because a summary that contradicts the section underneath it is the more dangerous kind of stale, and a summary is what people read.

docs.title: 2. audit_log
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id occurred_at timestamp, audit time Default: now transaction_id integer, required Default: the id of the enclosing transaction. Groups all changes made in one transaction, so a multi-table operation (approve a request → create a membership) reads as one event rather than two unrelated ones. actor_person_id reference to person, optional Taken from the request context, not from the row. NULL when an integration made the call — api_key_id below carries the actor then — and NULL for the writers that have no request context at all: a migration, the yearly expiry sweep, a run of the import pipeline, whose person is in import_batch.created_by and not here. 00-conventions §7a reads that empty as this system acting on its own, which is an answer and not a missing one. A correction made by hand through the application is not one of those writers — somebody was in front of a screen, and their name goes in this column api_key_id reference to api_key, optional Which registered integration made the call, when the request authenticated as a caller rather than as a person (05e-keys-and-callers.md §14). Set together with actor_person_id never: a request is made by a person or by a key, and a row naming both answers who did this twice, which is the impersonation this design refuses at the resolver instead (D-121). It names the caller and nothing beside it — not the person who installed that key, whose column is attribution for an act and never an actor here actor_label text, optional Not free text: a value from the label list of 00-conventions §7a — system:renewal-sweep, system:payload-reduction, system:log-reduction, system:bank-pull, migration:0042, import_batch:17 are instances of its rows, and bare system is retired, because it means "one of the above, and I am not saying which" (D-125). It exists for the writers that have no row of their own, and a writer that is not on that list joins it there before it writes — the list is prose, so nothing in the database refuses a label outside it and check 4 of 06b §5 is what notices. A caller that is not a person is a row in api_key_id, not a label, so an integration's write never arrives here. A row naming none of the three is no longer this trail's gap, because §7a says what it means; what check 4 counts now is a label that is not on the list, and a write path that owed a person and named none operation text, required One of: insert, update, delete table_name text, required record_id surrogate id, required The row that changed. No reference: the table is named per row, so it points at any table in the database changed_fields list of text Which columns changed. Enables targeted history queries without parsing JSON old_values free-form jsonb, optional Redacted before insert, and emptied once the row passes the payload window. See §2.2 for all three operations and why they are not one new_values free-form jsonb, optional Redacted before insert, and emptied once the row passes the payload window. See §2.2 on_behalf_of reference to person, optional Set when the actor was acting for another person. Mirrors access_log.on_behalf (04-relationships.md §5) session_id text, optional ip_address network address, optional request_id text, optional

Indexes

  • One row's history: table name and record_id, newest occurred_at first.
  • One actor's actions, newest first — two of these, not one, because an actor is a person in one column and a key in another: rows naming a person, and rows naming a key. The review that asks what an integration wrote is asked by key.
  • Everything in one transaction, by transaction_id.
  • By time alone, newest first.
  • Rows by a member of changed_fields. The targeted history queries ask "which rows changed this column", so the list has to be searchable element-wise rather than as a whole value.

docs.title: 2.1 The trigger
docs.text:
Nothing in this repository defines a trigger, so this section's guarantee is a rule and not a mechanism (D-072): every insert and every update to an audited table writes exactly one audit_log row, and the change and its audit row stand or fail together. "The audit trail usually has it" is not a version of this rule — the trail is how the organization answers "who changed this child's address, and when?", and an answer that depends on which code path made the change is not an answer. The layer that owes it is the write itself, on every path: the screens, the legacy import, the yearly expiry sweep, a bulk reorganisation, a call made with a key — which names its key — and a row somebody corrects by hand through the application, which names that person. The paths with nobody in front of a screen and no key behind them are the scheduled writers and the migrations, and an empty actor column is their name, with actor_label saying which of them (00-conventions §7a). Model-layer validation logs the intended path, which is the only path that was never at risk; check 5 in §5 is the net under the rest, and it is a report, not a guard. The one thing this rule cannot reach is a change made from outside the application altogether — it writes no audit row because there is no write to attach one to, and §5's report of a change the trail never saw is what notices afterwards, not before.

The steps below are what is owed, in the order that makes it safe. The order is a rule, not a detail: the redaction step has to run before the write, and the "nothing changed" test has to run before anything is spent on a row that would log noise.

  1. Read the acting person, the acting key where the request authenticated as one, and the on-behalf-of person from the request context (app.current_person_id, app.on_behalf_of); an unset or empty value means no person actor, not an error — 00-conventions §7a reads it as this system acting on its own, and step 7 is where that gets its name. A context naming a key has an actor and is not that case: the key goes in api_key_id, and a row whose actor is a key never sets on_behalf_of, because a key acts for itself (D-121).
  2. On an insert, take the new row as the after-image.
  3. On an update, take both the old and the new row, and work out the changed fields: the keys present in both images whose values differ, named in key order.
  4. If that comparison found nothing, stop and write nothing — a no-op update must not log noise.
  5. On a delete, take the old row as the before-image; there is no after-image.
  6. Redact both images (§2.2): the credential values that must never be logged at all, and — where the row belongs to a redacted person — the personal data erasure has already removed from the business tables. Everything else is stored as it stands, including a person's descriptive values, which are guarded by §8 item 7 rather than stripped here.
  7. Write one audit row carrying: the actor — actor_person_id or api_key_id, never both — and, where the write had no actor of either kind, the actor_label naming which of this system's own writers it was, taken from the list in 00-conventions §7a: the renewal sweep, payload reduction, the bank statement pull, a named migration, or a named batch. The label is not a fallback for a writer that could have named someone — a person who corrects a row by hand through the application is actor_person_id, and a call that authenticated is api_key_id — so a row arriving here with none of the three has not joined the list, and check 4 of 06b §5 reports it. Then the on-behalf-of person, the operation as lower-cased insert, update or delete, the table name, the record id taken from the new row and falling back to the old one, the changed fields, both redacted images, and the session id, ip address and request id from the request context.
  8. Change nothing about the row being written. The audit row describes the change and never amends it — and it commits in the same transaction as the change. That togetherness is what a trigger gave for free and what a logging step written beside the write must supply deliberately: one transaction, so there is no moment in which the change exists and its audit entry does not.

The obligation covers inserts and updates on person, membership, guardianship, role_assignment and access_grant; on role and role_permission — the role tables, not just the assignments, because a role is runtime data the organization edits (D-052) and editing one changes effective permissions for every holder at once with no assignment written, so without these two tables the single largest privilege change available in the system leaves no trace on any other audited row; and on every remaining business table — the exact set is still open in §6, and the recommendation there is all of them. There is nothing left to attach this to, which changes what the sentence is and not what it covers. It is the list of tables for which a write path owes an audit row; a business table created next year is inside it from the day it exists; and check 5 in §5 is what notices when the list and the write paths drift apart.

person_attribute is inside that obligation on exactly the same terms as any other business table, and the sentence is worth writing down because this document asked for an exception here and was refused. A write to a descriptive value owes its audit row like any write, and it carries its before and after images like any write (00-conventions §8 item 7). The reason no exception survives is that both halves of the design collapse without one: D-085 chose overwrite-in-place on the strength of this trail being the only history a value has, so a trail recording a value changed without recording which one would be a history of nothing; and D-083 says a diagnosis is not a different kind of fact from a shoe size, so excluding attribute values from the payload while person_contact changes are logged with their values would be a sensitive subset of the person record re-enacted inside the logging rules — the privileged corner arriving as a list of table names after it was deleted as a list of permission names.

Therefore this table holds a child's allergy list in the clear, in a table designed to be read by auditors and kept longer than the record it describes — which since D-088 is true of the payloads for 24 months and is untrue afterwards (§2.2). That is the design, not an accident of it, and what it means is that the guard on audit_log is now load-bearing in a way it was not: an audit entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it quotes, which is stated as a requirement on audit.view's sensitivity mark in appendix/permission-catalog-a-codes.md §8 and argued in 05c-access-log-and-resolver.md §9 — where the case against copying data into a less-guarded place applies to this table directly, since this table is the copy. The failure mode inverts, and it is worth naming because the shape is unfamiliar: everywhere else the worry is a table nobody audits, and here it is a table whose payloads outrank its own permission. No check in §5 can see that — a sensitivity mark is a line in a document, not a row in the database — so it is a review item with exactly one place it is written down, and that is the fragility.

What the payload window does to that paragraph, and what it conspicuously does not. The window does not repair the grading; it shortens the period during which a wrong grading is a leak, which for an organization of this size is the only control that will ever actually be in place (D-086 is the decision that named the exposure, and the strongest argument AT-4 ever put up for it is that the payload is temporary rather than that the guard is good — an argument that outlived the question it was made against, since D-138 settled that one code is the gate and a window can only bound how long it reads for, never how far). It does not retire the mark either. A reduced row about a person_attribute change still names the table, the record id, the field that changed, the actor and the moment — which is to say it still says this child had a value of this kind recorded, here, by this person, and that is a statement about a child even with the value gone. So the mark stays where D-088 leaves it, at the top tier, and the window is a bound on the damage rather than a discount on the permission.

role and role_permission are audited for a reason the other tables do not share. Everywhere else, the audit log answers "who changed this record?". Here it answers the harder question the next incident will ask: "what did role X grant on the date this decision was made?" Because a role edit rewrites the meaning of every assignment that points at it, in place, there is no way to answer that from the assignments — the assignments did not change. The log is the only record of what the role said at the time.

DELETE is intentionally outside the audited operations on business tables, because nothing in this data model is hard-deleted (see 00-conventions.md). Staging tables do get deleted; they are not audited. The absence is a consequence of the deletion policy rather than a gap in the obligation above. It is true of ordinary operation and false of exactly two moments.

The first is §3's import revert, which does hard-delete business rows — the person, membership, event_registration and event rows a batch created — which of them depends on which kind of batch it was, and §3's Reversibility is the list — and those rows were live, referenced and visible to real users before they went. So a revert writes audit entries for its deletes, naming the batch and the row it removed.

The second is §4's erasure, which deletes the person_attribute rows of the person being anonymised (00-conventions §4 records why that one table is erased by deletion rather than by overwriting, and the condition on which that stays safe — nothing may reference an attribute row). It is recorded once, in redaction_log, naming person_attribute in redacted_tables — and not as one audit_log row per erased value. That is a consequence of §2.2 rather than an exception to the revert rule, and the difference is worth seeing: revert deletes rows whose contents are safe to quote and whose existence is what someone will ask about, while erasure deletes rows whose contents must not be quotable afterwards and whose existence is the only fact that may survive. Note what this argument is, because §2.1's argument is the opposite one and both have to be true at once: per-value audit entries here would either write the erased value into a row that outlives the erasure — which is a redaction that failed, and precisely the copy §2.2 exists to destroy — or accumulate hundreds of identical rows whose entire content is "something was erased", which is exactly what §4's log is for. So values are quoted in the trail as a rule, and the rule stops at the moment the person they describe asks not to be described any more.

DELETE is outside the audited operations everywhere else only because there is no third path that reaches a business row with a delete. That makes revert the one place the list in §5 check 5 cannot be derived from table names alone: an audited operation rather than an audited table, which is why check 5's replacement assertion enumerates the paths that may delete, not just the tables that may be written. Erasure is the second such path and belongs on that enumerated list too; it audits nothing per row, so the assertion has to know it exists rather than infer it.

docs.title: 2.2 Redaction before logging
docs.text:
Three operations act on this table's payloads, and they are told apart by two questions: when does it run, and whose interest does it serve. A fourth is tempting and is refused below, where the refusal carries the reasons. The three are not variations on one idea and must not be implemented as one job. Two of them run on the way in or on request, on the strength of a person's right or a credential's nature; the third runs on a calendar, on the strength of nobody's right at all. Collapsing the third into the second is the easy mistake available here — both empty the same two columns — and §5 carries a separate check for each because they fail in opposite directions.

An audit log that stores the data it audits is a second copy of that data, with weaker access controls and a longer retention period. This is true of audit_log, which holds the whole person record in its payloads, and the answer is not an empty payload. The copy's access controls and its retention are what is wrong about it; emptying the payload fixes neither while destroying the table's reason for existing. So each half is answered with what it is: the guard is audit.view at the top tier of the catalog, and the retention is a 24-month window on the payloads (mechanism three). See 00-conventions.md §8 item 7 and 05c-access-log-and-resolver.md §9, which argues against copying data into a less-guarded place and, read against this table, names the copy in question.

Mechanism one is a small set of values that must never enter the trail at all. Credentials, tokens, the secret half of an integration: for these, being in a log is the harm, and no guard is wide enough to make them safe there. This is the only job the key-name list below has.

Mechanism two is erasure reaching payloads that were written lawfully at the time. Redacting a person removes their values from images already in the trail (§4, and check 6 in §5); nothing here prevents those values from having been written, and the erasure is what unmakes them.

Mechanism three is the calendar doing the same thing to everybody: payload reduction. A row older than the retention window has old_values and new_values emptied and every other field left exactly as it was. It is a scheduled job, it is owed to no one, and it applies whether or not the person whose data the row quotes has asked for anything. D-088 is where the window was set and why; the argument that it is not a second species of redaction — and the reason the sentence further down about never in a cleanup job does not forbid it — is stated under The third operation, in full further below. That is out of order on purpose: the sentence about cleanup jobs belongs with the steps it governs, and this operation has to survive it before it can be used.

The redactor takes one table name and one row image and does this:

  1. If there is no image at all, there is nothing to redact — return no value.
  2. For each key in the credential list — secret_hash and the integration secrets beside it — if the image carries that key, replace its value with the marker «redacted». Keys the image does not have are left alone. The list is applied wherever a listed key turns up, in any table.
  3. Return the image.

That is the whole mechanism, and the list is short on purpose. It is keyed on field names, which is the right shape for it: a name-based rule is the only kind that reaches a credential hidden in an unexpected column, and a credential is safe behind no guard, so the rule has to fire on sight.

The fourth operation, refused here because somebody will propose it. It reduces a person_attribute image to its two references — person_id and attribute_definition_id — saying whose fact and which fact and nothing of its content, with no «redacted» marker either, on the grounds that a log read by more people than the record should not hold what the record holds. It is refused for two reasons, both of them this section's own decisions:

  • It re-creates, inside the logging rules, the sensitive subset that D-083 deleted (D-083). A rule that strips attribute values while person_contact changes are logged with their values is a list of more-sensitive-than fields wearing a table name instead of a permission name.
  • It leaves D-085's history empty. Overwrite-in-place was chosen because the trail is the history; an entry that records a value changed without recording which one is a history of nothing, and the question this table's history is actually asked for — what did we believe about this child in March? — would be unanswerable by design rather than by accident.

What is right about the proposal is kept as the guard instead: the copy is as sensitive as what it quotes, so the permission that reads it belongs at the top of the catalog (appendix/permission-catalog-a-codes.md §8), and that is a line in a document rather than a mechanism, which is the weakness to keep in view.

What the credential list is not, stated where a reviewer will read it. It is not the thing protecting personal data, and it cannot become that, because a list of names is only as good as somebody having predicted the name of every field that would ever matter — and this system generates those names at runtime, one per code the organization invents. allergy is not on the list and never will be, which is now the correct state of affairs rather than a hole: an allergy is a value in person_attribute, it is logged, and it is protected by who may read the table it was logged into.

The requirement is an ordering, not a database feature, and it applies to mechanism one alone: credential stripping runs on the way in, never in a cleanup job that might not run. A trigger was one way to guarantee that ordering and this repository defines none (D-072), so what guarantees it is the shape of the write — redact, then write. A path that writes and repairs afterwards does not satisfy it, because for one transaction the secret is in the log and readable, and because the repair is the cleanup job being forbidden here. Nothing stops that third option except whoever writes it, which is exactly why the sentence is about ordering. Mechanism two runs in the opposite direction — it reaches rows already written, which is the only way an erasure can affect a trail that must not be rewritten — and the two are not in tension because one is about a value that should never have been written and the other is about a value that was. See 00-conventions.md §8 for what else the move to generated schema took out of this section's defence in depth.

The third operation, in full: payload reduction, and the paragraph above is the first thing it has to survive. D-088 set two clocks for this system and they point in opposite directions. The accounting skeleton — membership, fee_obligation, payment, and the anonymised person row they hang from — has no clock at all (§4, and 00-conventions §8 item 3). This table has two clocks in one row: the rows live as long as the system does, and the payloads live 24 months. After the window a row is reduced — old_values and new_values emptied, everything else left untouched: actor person, actor key, on-behalf-of, operation, table name, record id, changed fields, transaction, session, channel. The trail goes on answering "who changed this row, when, and were they allowed to" for the life of the system, and stops answering "and to what" after two years. Twelve months is the floor a window may be set to, not a stylistic preference: anything shorter stops covering a full year of a child's activities, and a year is the unit an incident is asked in.

Why the cleanup-job sentence does not forbid this, which matters because the two rules are one word apart. Read literally, "never in a cleanup job that might not run" describes reduction exactly: it is late, it is a job, and it unwrites content from rows already committed. It is still not the same rule, because these two are distinguished by what their failure costs and not by what their mechanism looks like. The credential rule forbids the late unwriting of a secret, and its failure mode is lateness — write first and repair afterwards and the secret sits in a table that audit.view reaches for one whole transaction, which is the harm arriving before the repair can. Reduction requires the late unwriting of history, and its failure mode is not lateness but absence: a job that stopped running, an over-age row still holding a child's allergy list because nobody looked. A rule whose failure mode is lateness has to be pinned to the write, because the write is the only moment at which it can still be obeyed. A rule whose failure mode is absence cannot be pinned to the write at all — carrying out reduction at the moment of writing is not obeying it, it is refusing it, because the window is the entire content of the rule and at write time there is no window to have passed. So reduction is a scheduled job with a check underneath it, and the check is the rule rather than a reassurance about it: check 7 in §5 counts rows older than the window that still carry a payload, and nothing about that count is sent anywhere (D-164). The sentence above forbids late unwriting of a credential; this paragraph requires late unwriting of history; both are true at once and neither is an exception to the other.

Reduction is not redaction, and it is not revert, and the three are worth setting side by side because only one of them is anybody's right.

Runs On whose behalf What disappears Row survives? Caught by Stripping — mechanism one Before the insert, on every write path No one; the value should never have been in the table The listed credential keys, replaced by the marker Yes — it is written once, already clean Nothing; it is an ordering rule, and its breach is one readable transaction Redaction — mechanism two When a person asks, immediately The person the row is about That person's values, from rows of any age, permanently Yes, with the values gone Check 6: a redacted person's payload still holding content Reduction — mechanism three On a schedule, once a row passes the window No one; it is policy Both payloads of every over-age row, indiscriminately Yes, standing empty Check 7: an over-age row still carrying content

What none of the three ever does is delete an audit_log row. The rows are the permanent half; a reduction that pruned rows would quietly delete the answer to "who changed this, and when", which is the half D-088 chose to keep. Every delete near this table is on some other table: a revert (§3) hard-deletes business rows a batch created and writes audit entries for having done so; an erasure (§4) deletes person_attribute rows and records that in redaction_log rather than one entry per value; and since round 20 a scheduled job deletes access_log rows whole at 24 months — a delete on the other trail, which is precisely the distinction the two clocks were drawn to make.

All three operations are updates, and an append-only guard has to be written knowing that. Nothing in this repository defines an append-only trigger (D-072), but the property is still asserted in prose, and the neighbouring trail states it as a literal refusal of updates (05c-access-log-and-resolver.md §9). A blanket refusal of updates blocks the erasure scrub and the reduction job alike, quietly, from the side of the rule that looks safest. What is worth keeping is not nothing changes but nothing is corrected: no write may alter what a row says about who did what, to which row, when; the only writes permitted after the fact are the two that remove content and never add or amend any.

Erasure is untouched by all of this and still immediate. A redaction scrubs that person's values from payloads whatever their age, including rows written yesterday and rows two days from reduction; the window is a ceiling on how long anything may be in there, not a waiting period anything has to serve. This is the sentence to keep if only one is kept: reduction never satisfies an erasure request, and an erasure never waits for reduction. Check 6 and check 7 exist separately because a system can pass one and fail the other, and the two failures mean opposite things — check 6 firing means a person's right was not honoured, check 7 firing means a policy was not applied.

What it costs. The window is the cheapest thing this design will ever do about the exposure D-086 accepts, and it bounds that exposure without repairing it (above, after §2's paragraph on the guard). What it spends is the past: D-085 was justified by the trail being the history, and now that history's values expire, so "what did we believe about this child's allergy list in 2019" is unanswerable twice over — the value was never kept in the business row, and the copy of it is gone. The honest name for that trade is no long history, not no temporal columns, and it is drawn out next to the values in 09-attributes.md §6. If a case ever needs the long version, the fix is temporal columns on the value — D-085 reversed — and not a longer window, because stretching the window stretches precisely the guard D-086 graded and re-creates the second copy D-083 refuses to keep.

The half of this that is not settled, and is not pretending to be. Indefinite retention of named membership and fee rows is a claim that needs a legal basis and a decision log cannot grant one. What the corpus now states, as an assumption pending review rather than as settled law, is organizational history plus accounting obligations, held up by a redacted person row that keeps the skeleton non-identifying — and the review is the one B-3 already asked for, now with a concrete policy in front of it instead of a blank (§6).

The neighbouring trail takes the same window and the opposite shape. access_log sits at the same 24 months, and it was decided there by round 20: its rows are deleted rather than emptied (05c-access-log-and-resolver.md §9). Same clock, different kind. The reduction above may never touch a row, because what changed is the half D-088 chose to keep forever; on the read trail nobody needs the row at year three, the payloads of reads are not held there anyway, and a row that answers nothing identifiable is not worth the exception. This is the third named exception to 00 §4's "nothing is hard-deleted", and the only one driven by a clock — the other two exceptions that page names are a staging truncate between batches and a delete a person asked for. Mechanism three above is a job too, and the difference between them is the difference the corpus keeps insisting on: mechanism three empties a row that stays, this one deletes the row.

No free-text field about a person is on the credential list, and none is being added to it. The list once carried notes, custody_arrangement, termination_note, rejection_note and status_note beside secret_hash, on the theory that free text is where a diagnosis hides. All of them are logged with their values now, for the two reasons this section has already given: person data is one class (D-083), and a scrubbed history is a history that did not happen. A name-based rule cannot tell sensitive free text from sensitive structured text anyway, which is why the list is keyed on credentials only. The residual risk is stated rather than left implicit: an audit table holding a child's descriptive values is a wider surface than any single screen, and what stands between it and a volunteer with an interest is one sensitivity mark plus whoever implements it.

What still argues against person.notes, and it is not this. Consider whether person.notes should exist at all: it is the last free text about a person outside the attribute vocabulary, the vocabulary is where such a sentence is visible to a report and to a curator rather than only to whoever next opens the record, and the open question is argued there in 01-identity.md §2 as well as here.

docs.title: 2.3 History query
docs.text:
The full change history of one row is found by taking the audit_log rows for its table name and record id, newest occurred_at first, and reading out when it happened, the operation, which fields changed, the old and new values, and who did it. That last one has three answers, not two: the actor's person name where the row names a person, the integration's code where it names a key — never anything derived from its secret, which this table does not hold in the first place — and actor_label where it names neither (D-121). The third answer is a label from 00-conventions §7a's list and not a string somebody typed, so it names a writer rather than marking an absence — which is what lets the history view print it as an answer.

For a person_attribute row this query is the history, not a shadow of it. Values are overwritten in place (D-085), so every value a child's allergy list ever held sits under one record_id, and this is where the question "what did we believe about this child in March, and who wrote it down?" gets answered — for a March inside the payload window. After the window the same query returns the same rows and a different kind of answer: who, when, which row, which field, and no value (§2.2, mechanism three). That is not a degradation to be smoothed over on the screen. An entry with a reduced payload and an entry that genuinely recorded no value are two different facts, and a history view that renders both as an empty cell tells a reader the organization never knew something it has since stopped holding — so the reduced state has to be said, the way a key's code or an actor_label is said when the row names no person. The date the row crossed the window is not stored anywhere and should not be: it is the row's own occurred_at plus the window, which is configuration a reader of the screen may not have, so the honest label is that the values are no longer retained rather than a date of when they went.

The consequence is the one §2.2 spends its length on, restated where it bites: a history screen over this table is a person-data surface. It is reached through audit.view, and it deserves to be reached through person.view too — a reader who may see that an allergy was recorded in 2019 but may not see the allergy is holding the second question and will ask it out loud. The guard on the trail is what is relied on; a per-entry "could this reader see this field" check inside the history view was considered and left unimplemented, because it would mean running the resolver per audit row against a value that no longer exists anywhere as a row to resolve against. It is a registered question rather than an omission now: AT-4.

docs.title: Data Model — Audit and Import: the legacy import pipeline
docs.text:
import_batch, the staging tables, the six stages, the field→code mapping, reversibility, idempotency, and what a source row actually evidences. The trail these stages write to is §2.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 06-audit-and-import.md holds §1–§2 (the two audit trails and the audit_log table), 06a §3 (the legacy import pipeline), and 06b §4–§6 (the redaction log, the integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 3. Import pipeline
docs.text:
Six stages, from ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md. The guiding requirements: idempotent, reversible per batch, never overwrites self-registered data, preserves provenance.

What arrives is two exports, and each is evidence of a different thing. D-090 recorded the corpus as roster rows — people attending units — and nearly everything below was built on that word, including the section that policed what a roster may be read as proving. D-092 corrected the description from the source itself: a membership export and an attendance export.

Half What one source row says What the pipeline writes People name, birth date, member of the organization for a period a person, and a bounded membership (D-093), which brings its root participation row with it Events an event, and who attended it an event that belongs to nobody (D-102) and one event_registration per listed attendee

Neither half names a unit, and unit assignment is out of scope by instruction — a consequence, not an omission. parsed_unit_code and parsed_unit_name stay in the parser (§3's staged-row table says what reads them now, which is nothing), no batch creates a body of any kind, and no belonging row is ever imported for one. The consequence in one sentence: the system's historical record contains no sub-unit participation, so "who was in pack X in 2011?" has no answer on day one and gets one only from live data forward. The model has always been able to hold that history; the source cannot say it, and the sentence is here so that the first person to ask the question finds the sentence instead of the absence.

import_batch — one run of the pipeline, and the unit revert works on.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id name text, required batch_kind text, required One of: people, events. A batch types itself, and it does so because it has to rather than because it is tidy: one field_mapping cannot serve both halves of the corpus, so the kind is what decides which mapping shape, which parse rules, which source_row_hash definition (Idempotency below) and which of staging_import_row's created ids get read. There is no default — a batch that does not say which it is does not leave staging. Recorded as a consequence of the answer that split the corpus in two (D-092), not as an open question, because the same answer decided this about it description text, optional source_type text, required One of: csv, xlsx, json, sql_dump, manual_entry, other source_reference text, optional Where the file lives, or what it is. Enough to find the original again source_hash text, optional SHA-256 of the source file. Detects re-importing the same file under a new name row_count integer, optional status text, required One of: staging, parsed, matching, review, applying, applied, reverted, failed. Default staging dry_run boolean, required Default false. A dry run parses and matches but writes nothing to business tables created_by reference to person, required Required, and it is the reason no import is anonymous. The pipeline's own writes name themselves import_batch:<id> (00-conventions §7a), and that label leads here — to the person who uploaded the file — so an imported row is attributed twice over, once to the batch and once through it to somebody created_at timestamp, audit time applied_at timestamp, audit time, optional applied_by reference to person, optional reverted_at timestamp, audit time, optional reverted_by reference to person, optional revert_note text, optional field_mapping free-form jsonb, optional This batch's raw-column → attribute-code map: one entry per raw column in the source, each naming one code or discard with a reason. Fixed for the batch, reviewed as a unit, editable only as a new decision — see The legacy field→code mapping below, which explains why the grain is a column and not a row. On an events batch this map is mostly discard, and that is its honest shape rather than a smell: event title and date become parsed_event_* values, not attribute codes, and the only columns on such a file worth a code are the descriptive ones riding along on the attendee error_summary text, optional notes text, optional

Indexes

  • Batches by status — the queue of runs that are not finished.

staging_import — one source row, kept exactly as it arrived.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id batch_id reference to import batch, required source_row_number integer, optional raw_data free-form jsonb, required The row VERBATIM. Never modified. This is the evidence source_row_hash text, required Deterministic hash of the meaningful fields. The idempotency key: re-importing a file matches on this and skips already-applied rows

Rules

  • (batch_id, source_row_hash) is unique — one staged row per batch per source row. It covers all rows, not only unapplied ones.

Indexes

  • The staged rows of one batch.

staging_import_row — what the parser made of that source row, and what became of it. One staged row is one person, on both halves of the corpus: a person's membership period on a people batch, a person's attendance at one event on an events batch. That is a decision rather than an observation, because an attendance export arrives most often as one row per event with the attendees packed into a cell, and unpacking it there would put the idempotency key and the review queue at the wrong grain — a batch that resolves half an event's attendee list would have nothing to skip on the re-run. So the parser unpacks a packed attendee list into one staged row per attendee before this table, and the event's own columns repeat down those rows, which is what the matching rule below is for.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id staging_id reference to staging row, required parsed_given_name text, optional parsed_family_name text, optional parsed_name_normalised text, optional Diacritics stripped, casefolded parsed_birth_date date, optional parsed_birth_precision text, optional Reuses the person.birth_date_precision values parsed_unit_code text, optional Parsed, and read by nobody. Kept deliberately: an export that surprises whoever runs it with a unit column is exactly what this field and the unit_not_found warning are for, and keeping them costs nothing. Nothing resolves them, no batch creates an org_unit, and no imported sub-unit participation row can appear as a result (D-092, §3). An earlier draft had these two columns driving unit creation and the identity of a historical unit; that machinery is gone, the columns are not parsed_unit_name text, optional As parsed_unit_code parsed_period_from date, optional A people batch. The start of the membership period the export states parsed_period_to date, optional A people batch. Often NULL in the source; see the inference rules below. An imported membership is never left open-ended (§3.1) parsed_event_title text, optional An events batch. The occasion as the export states it. Normalised at match time rather than stored twice; the verbatim value is in staging_import.raw_data parsed_event_date date, optional An events batch. With the title, what an attendee row is matched against, so that ten thousand attendees produce the events that happened rather than a copy each — the rule is below parse_status text, required One of: ok, warning, error. Default ok parse_warnings list of text For example birth_date_year_only, unit_not_found, ambiguous_name. Warnings do not block; errors do. unit_not_found still fires on a file that carries a unit column and still changes nothing, because nothing reads the parsed unit resolution text, optional One of: link_existing, create_new, discard, deferred resolved_person_id reference to person, optional resolved_by reference to person, optional resolved_at timestamp, audit time, optional resolution_note text, optional applied boolean, required Default false applied_person_id reference to person, optional What this row created applied_membership_id reference to membership, optional What this row created — set on every row of a people batch whose source states a membership period, because the export does state periods and importing one is not inference (§3.1, D-093). Empty on every row of an events batch, and a set value on an events row is §3.1 having been broken: membership may be imported from a period the source states, never from an attendance list applied_event_id reference to event, optional An events batch. The event this attendee row was matched to, or created by it. Shared across rows, which is the difference from the four ids above: a hundred attendees of one camp name one event, and revert has to know that (§Reversibility) applied_registration_id reference to event registration, optional An events batch. What this row created — one per attendee, and the only row an attendee who was not listed gets, which is none (§3.1, D-059) created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • One event per (title, date), not one per attendee. uq_staging_event_match is this rule's name. Enforced inside the transaction that applies a staged row, in this order: 1. normalise the title and take the date; 2. look for an event this batch has already created with that pair, then for an event already in the system with it; 3. reuse what was found, otherwise create it and record it on this row;
  • write the registration. Application layer, deliberately — the pair spans rows of one batch rather than columns of one row, and a uniqueness claim across a batch describes how the file is read, not what the data holds (00-conventions.md §6a is the register for that kind of answer). The failure it prevents is the loud kind run quietly: ten thousand attendee rows becoming ten thousand events, none of them deletable except by revert.
  • Which created ids a row may carry is decided by import_batch.batch_kind, not by the row. A people batch fills applied_person_id and applied_membership_id; an events batch fills applied_person_id — an attendee who had to be created is still a person created — plus applied_event_id and applied_registration_id. A row carrying one from each group is a batch that was typed wrongly, and revert reads this rule to know what it is about to delete.

Indexes

  • The staged rows of one parsed row.
  • The review queue: parse status and resolution, restricted to rows with no resolution or a deferred one. Decided rows are not in it.
  • Applied rows only.

docs.title: The legacy field→code mapping
docs.text:
Any legacy column that is not identity machinery becomes an attribute code, and this is where the vocabulary comes from: most of the first two hundred definitions arrive here rather than from a deliberate act of design (09-attributes.md §7 owns the rule, and states why; what follows is only what the pipeline has to obey).

  • Every raw field name in a batch maps to a code, or is mapped to discard with a reason, or the batch stops. An unmapped column is an error at apply time: the batch refuses and names the column (D-141). It does not invent a code named from the raw column header, and it is never mapped to an existing code picked by similarity — an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable, and a human makes that judgement afterwards with both codes in front of them. What changed is which side of the batch the refusal lands on: a column that maps to nothing used to arrive as a definition waiting for curation, which meant a person at a desk could grow the vocabulary by typing a header, and an import could land several hundred codes nobody had read. Creating a code is the act of whoever holds attribute.define, and the batch has nobody holding anything (09-attributes.md §7).
  • The mapping is recorded on the batch, in import_batch.field_mapping, so a mapping later found wrong can be re-run rather than reverse-engineered from the damage it did. The mapping is not the schema: changing it is an act of curation with an audit entry, not a migration.
  • Which table it is not on, because the wrong one is plausible. An earlier draft of this subsection said the mapping sat "on staging_import_row alongside the raw value", and that is the wrong grain twice over: staging_import_row is one row per person and holds a fixed set of parsed_* columns, so a per-column fact has nowhere to sit there, and anything per-row would be a mapping that can differ between two people in the same batch — which is precisely how one legacy column ends up as two codes, quietly, with nothing to review. The raw values themselves stay where they always were, verbatim in staging_import.raw_data; the map is one table up.

What this costs is a stage that is allowed to fail loudly. A batch with unmapped columns does not apply, and somebody has to say what those columns were — friction at the worst possible moment, since imports are always late. It is the cheaper failure. The alternative is a silent drop, which is the same loss as deleting the column and the same one §3's guiding requirements were written against: in 2031 someone asks what the old system's POZNAMKA column held, and the answer is that a script nobody still works with decided it was not interesting.

docs.title: Reversibility
docs.text:
staging_import_row holding the created ids is what makes per-batch revert possible, and the two batch kinds leave different ids behind — which is why the order below is one list rather than one per kind. Revert removes only what this batch created, and it runs in this order:

  1. Take every staged row of the batch being reverted.
  2. Undo what they created, dependents first, in this dependency order: the event_registration rows, then the event rows those registrations pointed at, then the membership rows, then the person rows — and a row the batch created outright is removed rather than merely amended. A people batch leaves the first two arms empty and an events batch leaves the membership arm empty (§3.1); both arms exist, and neither may be skipped in the general implementation just because the batch in hand does not use it. Four arms, and the implementation walks all four.
  3. Finally mark the staged rows themselves unapplied.

An event is deleted at most once, which is the one place revert is not row-local. applied_event_id is shared across the attendee rows of one occasion, so step 2 must collect the distinct events the batch created and delete each after the last registration pointing at it is gone. An event the batch created that anything outside the batch now references is the refusal below, not a delete — and the pre-flight check has to look for that reference specifically, because a row referencing an event does not reference the staged row that made it, so the ordinary reference scan cannot see it.

Revert is only safe before live data references the imported rows. Once a real person has been linked, or an attendance recorded against an imported person, or a live registration attached to an imported event, deleting the row breaks it. Therefore:

  • Revert is allowed only while import_batch.status = 'applied' and no row created by the batch has been referenced by a later live record.
  • Detecting that requires checking for references — implement as a pre-flight check that reports which rows cannot be reverted, and refuse rather than partially applying.
  • After that window, corrections are made by editing the data, not by reverting. This is the honest behaviour; a "revert" that silently orphans references is worse than refusing.
  • Step 2's removals are audited like any other write, one entry per row deleted, each naming the batch — and the batch is not an anonymous name: its label under 00-conventions §7a is import_batch:<id>, and that row's created_by is required, so the entry leads to a person whoever read it. Where a person pressed the revert themselves, actor_person_id names them and no label is involved at all. This is the only hard delete a business row can meet, and it is precisely the case where someone will later ask "this person existed in March and is gone now — what happened?" An undo that erases the rows and leaves no trace of having erased them is not a rollback but a cover-up, and it is the same undo a reviewer is trusting when they agree to revert at all. 00-conventions.md §4 is why no other path is allowed to do this.

Bias toward import in small batches and review before applying. Reversibility is a safety net, not a workflow.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
The (batch_id, source_row_hash) uniqueness above makes re-staging cheap. Idempotency across batches needs the hash to be computed from the row's semantic content, not its position — and since D-092 the corpus has two semantic contents, so batch_kind selects which of the two definitions below runs. A people row and an events row about the same person must not look like the same row, and they cannot: their last two inputs come from different halves of the world.

A people batch, one row per membership period — unchanged from the previous round, and unchanged on purpose:

source_row_hash = sha256(
    normalise(given_name) || '|' ||
    normalise(family_name) || '|' ||
    coalesce(birth_date::text,'') || '|' ||
    coalesce(unit_code,'') || '|' ||
    coalesce(period_from::text,'')
)

An events batch, one row per attendee at one occasion:

source_row_hash = sha256(
    normalise(given_name) || '|' ||
    normalise(family_name) || '|' ||
    coalesce(birth_date::text,'') || '|' ||
    normalise(event_title) || '|' ||
    coalesce(event_date::text,'')
)

Read unit_code in the first definition honestly: for this corpus it is empty on every row, since the export names no units, so it is a constant input doing nothing. It stays, because removing it is a version change that buys nothing and the rule under this block is the one that matters — the hash function must be stable, changing it invalidates every previously staged row, and version it if it must change rather than editing it in place. Two definitions where one was expected is the same rule applied to a corpus that turned out to be two files: nothing staged under the people definition is disturbed by the events one, and both are versioned from here.

Then a re-import of an overlapping export produces rows that match already-applied ones, and the pipeline can skip them. Note what the two hashes are keyed on, since the events one is the weaker instrument: it keys on a title and a date, which is the most the export states, so a source that spells one camp two ways is two rows, and two sources that spell two camps one way on one day is one row. The matching rule above inherits both, and neither is fixable in the pipeline — the fix is a human in the review queue.

docs.title: End-date inference
docs.text:
A membership export rarely states when a period ended, and since D-093 it is allowed to answer: an imported row is now a real membership, so what its end date is inferred from is a live question again rather than a question about a participation row. Three defensible options:

Rule Effect Risk Leave valid_to NULL Person appears to be current Wrong and dangerous — inflates the member count, and an open row reads as present-tense belonging. And it is dangerous in the loaded sense again: an open imported membership satisfies is_current_member(), so it passes the permission gate (D-039). The row above this one said, one round ago, that "a roster batch can no longer take" that route because a roster batch makes no membership — D-093 withdrew the premise, and with it the only reason this option had stopped being a live hazard. It is a hazard again, which is why Never NULL below is a rule and not a preference End at the end of the organizational year of the last period the person appears in Defensible, documented May truncate a period that continued End at the last date the person appears in any export Best fidelity, needs all exports Requires the complete dataset

The rule: end at the end of the organizational year of the last period in which the person appears, marked data_confidence = 'low' and with a parse warning (D-169). The table above was written with its middle row's hinge left blank — which day is the end of the organizational year — and the blank was answerable from two pages away: the organizational year runs with the calendar (D-047), so the person's last day as a member is 31 December. Read valid_to as the column actually is, though. Every period here is half-open and is_current_member requires valid_to to be after today, so the value written is 1 January of the following year; a literal 31 December ends the row on the thirtieth, which is one day short in every imported record and invisible in every report that does not name the day. The boundary is read from expiry_month and expiry_day on the membership_type row and never compiled in as a literal, for the only reason those two columns exist — a job containing 1 and 1 is the one way to lose the property that the date may be moved.

The other two rows are refused, and not for the same reason. Leaving valid_to NULL stays banned outright: an open imported row satisfies is_current_member() and so walks through the permission gate (D-039). Ending at the last date the person appears in any export is refused on feasibility rather than on principle — it is the highest-fidelity option in the table and it requires the complete dataset, which the corpus is not: two exports with gaps (D-090, D-092). What the chosen rule buys that the third would not is that an imported period ends on the boundary a live membership's period ends on, so the yearly sweep and the member-count-per-year report read one calendar.

Never NULL — and read that as the surviving half of the ban D-090 left standing: never an open-ended membership, and never one inferred from an attendance row (§3.1). Both ends of the period are what makes an imported membership safe; the import itself is not. The cost of this rule is stated in its own table: a period that really did continue into the next year is truncated. That is the direction of error this design takes — short by a year, which surfaces as a person who cannot sign in, rather than open forever, which surfaces as a person who can.

docs.title: 3.1 What a source row actually evidences
docs.text:
The question is what a source row may be read as proving, and the answer has two halves that are not the same answer, because the corpus is two exports and not one roster: between them they evidence presence at an occasion and membership of the organization, and evidence no unit at all (D-090, D-092).

A people row evidences a bounded membership, and the import writes one. The source states a name, a birth date and the period during which this person was a member of the organization — which is a membership claim made by the source rather than inferred by the reader, and that distinction is the whole of what D-093 changed. So a people batch writes a membership with both valid_from and valid_to set, data_confidence = 'low', the batch id on it — and nothing else in the temporal layer: one row in the transaction, and no second row to keep it company (03-membership.md §5). One row per period the source states, not one per calendar year: an export of consecutive years is a period, and the renewed_from_membership_id chain is left to whoever reconstructs it by hand, because a renewal chain asserted by a parser is a lineage nobody chose and it is the kind of derived history D-096 refuses to infer about units for the same reason.

An events row evidences presence at one occasion, and nothing beyond it. It writes an event_registration for the listed attendee with was_present = true, against an event that belongs to nobody (D-102), so the import owes no owner choice at all — and no row at all for anybody who is not listed: inventing not_attending from silence would put words in a source that said nothing (D-059). Neither half of the import writes a belonging row for a body. A people row produces a membership and an events row a registration; D-041's second species of belonging is not a thing either half could write (D-041, D-097). What an imported event does owe, since D-102, is the bundle its create would have written — twelve item-scope grants beside the event row, in the same transaction, aimed at ORGANIZERS, or the imported event has nobody who can read its answers (08a §8, D-151).

Never an open-ended membership, and never one inferred from an attendance row. The reason is D-039 and it has not moved — an open membership satisfies is_current_member(), so an inferred 1998 row hands whoever signs up under that name authority in the present, through every gated role, decades after the file that mentioned them was last opened. The end-date rule above is what stops an imported period from reading as current; this sentence is what stops the class, and check 1 in §4 is what catches a batch that did it anyway. What changed is how much of the class the rule has to cover, not whether it covers it. D-090 banned the row outright because the input looked like a roster and any membership in it would have been an inference; D-093 withdrew the ban because the input states periods, and because the hazard the ban was sized for was a standing one — an import that infers, run by whoever holds the file, repeatedly, for years — whereas what is being decided is one reviewed batch, mapping read before it applies, on a corpus that will never arrive twice. A rule sized for a recurring process is too strict for a one-time one, and the safety that mattered was never the ban, it was the review. The stakes were named in D-041 and D-039 before they were resolved, and they are why what remains is a rule rather than a preference.

Both failure modes stay on the record, because the next import will be a third shape. The rule once hedged — import a participation, unless there is evidence of payment, in which case a membership may be inferred — and was then stated as its opposite: "a roster row makes a participation and nothing else; membership rows come only from the current register." Both were arguing against something real. The hedge was a rule waiting to be misapplied by whoever found a dues column in a later file and read it as permission. The flat ban was correct about rosters and wrong about the corpus: it generalised from this file has no money in it to no membership may arrive from a file, and the corpus arrived with membership periods in it.

What this gives up, since it gives up something. "Did they pay?" has no answer for any imported period — no money arrives in either export, so there is no fee_obligation and no balance on these rows at all (07-finance.md §2), and every cross-decade member count is a mix of an export and a register distinguished only by data_confidence and import_batch_id. *What remains given up is that the imported membership is the source's claim about a status rather than a record of the act: nobody paid a fee in this system for 1998, and the row says the organization's export said so, which is the most the evidence supports.

docs.title: 4. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify. This section arrived late and by decision (D-135); every other data-model page had one and this page argued its way out of having one, on the grounds that the pipeline is correct by construction. That argument is about the write path, and these three are about the data afterwards — which is the half the argument never covered. Check 1 is the one §3.1 has been pointing at ever since it wrote "check 1 in §5", citing a section this page did not have.

  1. An imported membership that should not exist. Two ways in, both stated above as rules: an imported membership with valid_to absent, and a staging_import_row on an events batch carrying an applied_membership_id. Either one means an imported period reads as present-tense belonging, and this is the only check on this page that reaches the permission gate: an open membership satisfies is_current_member() (D-039), so a row the end-date inference left open, or a membership written from an attendance list, hands authority in the present to whoever signs up under that name decades after the file was last read (§3.1). Non-zero here is not untidy data; it is authority — the same shape as 09's erasure check, in that a single row is the finding, and the same shape as that one in that nothing sends this finding to anyone: since D-169 supplies the missing date at parse time, a non-zero result here means the inference did not run, which is a bug in a path rather than a question for a person.
  2. One event per (title, date), and one registration per attendee row. uq_staging_event_match (§3) is enforced inside the transaction that applies a staged row, deliberately at the application layer, because the pair spans rows of a batch rather than columns of a row. That is exactly why the report exists: an application-layer rule has nothing beneath it, so this count is not a net under a constraint but the whole of the backstop, and the failure it is sized for is the loud one run quietly — ten thousand attendee rows becoming ten thousand events, none deletable except by revert. The mirror half catches a staged attendee row that produced more than one registration.
  3. A batch whose own accounting does not close. Four readings of one promise — that a batch can always say what it did, which is what makes revert possible at all: an applied batch still holding staged rows that are neither applied nor discarded nor deferred; a staged row marked applied carrying no created id; a staged row carrying ids from the other half of the corpus (a people row with an applied_event_id, an events row with an applied_membership_id) where §3 says batch_kind decides which ids a row may hold; and a batch marked reverted whose created ids still resolve to live rows. Read the last of the four against the trail rather than only the count: revert writes one audit entry per row it deletes, each naming the batch (§Reversibility), so a batch that left rows behind also left an entry for each deletion that did not happen — and a live row with no matching entry is the difference between an undo that was refused and an undo that lied.

Check 1 is the one that matters, and it matters for a reason the other two do not share: the other two find bad data, and this one finds data that grants permission. Checks 2 and 3 are what a pipeline with an application-layer rule and a hard delete owes the people who inherit its output — cheap to run, and only interesting when they are non-empty.

docs.title: Data Model — Audit and Import: the redaction log, the integrity checks, open issues
docs.text:
redaction_log, the checks that run over both trails, and what is still outstanding. The trail the redaction writes into is §2; the batches the checks watch are §3.

Section numbers are shared across the three parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 06-audit-and-import.md holds §1–§2 (the two audit trails and the audit_log table), 06a §3 (the legacy import pipeline), and 06b §4–§6 (the redaction log, the integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 4. Redaction log
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required The row is NOT deleted. The id survives so historical references resolve requested_at timestamp, audit time Default: now requested_by reference to person, optional legal_basis text, optional gdpr_art17, court_order, internal_policy — required for accountability performed_at timestamp, audit time, optional performed_by reference to person, optional redacted_tables list of text Which tables had values overwritten — and which had rows deleted. person_attribute is erased by deletion rather than by overwriting (00-conventions §4), so naming it here is what records that the erasure reached the person's descriptive data, and omitting it is indistinguishable from not having reached it retained_reason text, optional Why some data was kept. It has a standing answer to hold now. Membership periods, fee obligations, payments and this anonymised person row are kept with no end date because they are the organization's own history, which is the judgement this field was built to carry and which, until D-088, nothing in these documents had actually made. What the field adds per case is that this erasure made it knowingly, and the reason for anything retained beyond the skeleton. The basis underneath the standing answer is an assumption pending legal review (§6), not settled law note text, optional

Rules

  • A redaction cannot record when it was performed without recording who performed it: performed_at without performed_by is illegal.
  • An erasure must also rewrite the expressions that named the person, and say what it changed. Since D-105 a hand-named person is a PERSON(x) leaf of audience_operand, and selector_arg_id carries no foreign key, so nothing refuses the deletion underneath it. The failure is not a dangling row, it is an inverted grant: a leaf that resolves to nobody is the empty set, and the empty set subtracts nothing, so an expression reading EVERYONE - PERSON(x) begins denying everybody the moment x is erased. So the erasure walks audience_operand for leaves naming that person, removes or rewrites them under the same access_grant guard that covers any other change to reach, prints the resolved set before and after for every expression it touched — the same report D-104 adopted — and names audience_operand in redacted_tables, because a field that lists which tables the erasure reached is worth nothing if the one table where the person still appears is left off it. The nightly orphan scan in 05d-invariants-and-seed.md §11 is the backstop for this, and is not the control: the control is the erasure path itself, because a scan that reports a grant denying everybody every night is a report somebody stops reading.

Indexes

  • A person's redaction history.

This log is the answer to "prove you honoured the erasure request". It records what was removed, when, on what legal basis, and — importantly — what was deliberately retained and why. A redaction performed without a record is indistinguishable from a data loss incident.

Two clocks, and this log is where the permanent one gets written down. An erasure now performs three acts with three different lifetimes. It overwrites the person row's names and contact points, immediately and irreversibly; it deletes the person_attribute rows, so that redacted_tables naming that table is the only sentence left saying they existed; and it scrubs that person's values out of the trail's payloads — out of rows which, since D-088, are scheduled to lose their payloads anyway (§2.2). What an erasure does not do is touch membership, fee_obligation, payment, or this row's person_id — and the reason is now a stated justification rather than nobody having decided when those rows end. That difference, between a rule nobody defended and a rule with a reason attached, is exactly what retained_reason carries.

This log is not subject to payload reduction, and that is a decision rather than an oversight. Reduction empties the payloads of rows past the window. A redaction_log row holds no values to empty — a person id, a legal basis, a list of table names, and the reasoning — and it is the evidence that a person's request was honoured, which is the class of statement D-088 chose to keep for the life of the system when it chose to keep the skeleton. Reaching this table with reduction would delete the proof of an erasure in order to apply a policy about history, and those are not the same act.

For the descriptive part of a person's record this log is the only surviving record, by design. The attribute rows are deleted; the audit entries that quoted their values are scrubbed by the same act (§2.2's mechanism two, which is the only direction in which a trail that must not be rewritten can still be erased); and the codes they pointed at stay live because a code belongs to the organization and not to the erased person (09-attributes.md §6 draws the two directions: retiring a code is an act about the vocabulary and keeps values, erasing a person is an act about the person and removes them). So redacted_tables naming person_attribute is the whole of what the system can honestly say — this person had descriptive data and it is gone — and it is enough, because the sentence the organization is entitled to keep is that it held a record and removed it, not what the record said.

docs.title: 5. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  • Imported memberships with no end date. Count membership rows that carry an import_batch_id and have no valid_to. Zero is the only acceptable answer: these are the rows that silently satisfy the permission gate, so this is a security check as much as a data-quality one (§3). Do not read this as a data-quality report any more, because since D-093 it is the only thing standing between an imported row and the membership gate. While imports made participations this check was theoretical — there were no imported memberships to find — and it is now the load-bearing one, since the corpus is expected to create thousands of rows that would each satisfy is_current_member() if their end date were missing. And the zero has a route to it now: since D-169 a rule supplies the date, so a non-zero result means the inference did not run — it no longer means nobody knew what belonged in the column, which is the finding this check used to be the only record of. Its sibling is re-pointed rather than removed.
