The previous round's version, from D-090, read "an imported membership from a batch whose source is a roster, whatever its dates say", and that finding no longer exists as a finding — imported memberships are expected now. What replaces it is the surviving half of the same ban (§3.1): count a membership carrying an import_batch_id whose batch_kind is events. An attendance export states presence, and a membership drawn from one is the inference somebody re-enabled because they found a column that looked like dues. Run both halves on the same report: the first catches a missing end date, the second catches the wrong kind of source.
  • Imported people who were later merged away. Count people whose record_origin is legacy_import and whose merge pointer is set. Non-zero is probably fine and worth an eye.
  • Batches left in a non-terminal state for a long time. Count import_batch rows whose status is none of applied, reverted, failed and which were created more than 30 days ago; non-zero means a run somebody stopped steering.
  • Audit rows whose actor names nothing. The trail has three ways to say who did this: a person, a registered integration (05e-keys-and-callers.md §14), and — for the writers that have no row of their own — a label from the list in 00-conventions §7a. The report runs over all three columns, because a version of it that looked only at actor_person_id and actor_label would count every integration write as a finding until whoever reads it stopped reading. What it no longer counts as a gap is the shape it was built to count. A row naming no person and no key is not a row that failed to answer who did this: §7a reads it as this system acting on its own, and the renewal sweep, payload reduction, the bank statement pull and a named migration write rows in exactly that shape, correctly and by design (00-conventions §7). Two things are reported instead. (a) A row whose actor_label is not one of the labels §7a lists, including a row naming no person, no key and no label at all — the vocabulary is a documented list and not a table, so nothing in the database refuses a label from outside it and this count is the only thing that ever notices (D-125). A row that reaches the trail with nobody and nothing in it has not joined that list, which is the failure the list exists to catch. (b) A row on a write path that owed a person and named none, in the two shapes a reader can actually test: a transaction whose request context carried a current_person_id (06 §2.1 step 1) while actor_person_id stayed empty, and any audit row about one of the rows §7a names as having no empty to interpret — import_batch.created_by and api_key.created_by are required and a grant's granted_by names a person, so a business row that cannot lawfully be authorless cannot have been written by a writer that is. What this check cannot catch, said because two rows a reader would want are not among them. A row naming a key and a person — the row a forensic reader most wants flagged — is never reported here. It is illegal, and the rule carried by the two columns is what refuses it (05e-keys-and-callers.md §16, D-121); a count over empty columns cannot see a row whose columns are full. A row naming a key that no longer exists is stopped before any count runs: audit_log.api_key_id is an ordinary reference and not one of the two reference-less keys, and no key row is hard-deleted (00-conventions §4). What stays uncounted, and uncounted everywhere in this section, is the pair no rule compares — a write audited against a key whose valid_to or revoked_at fell before the row's occurred_at, which leaves every column filled and this check, which reads emptiness rather than dates, silent.

That silence is now a ruling rather than an oversight, and the reason matters more than the ruling (D-133). The window is not the obstacle and it was never honest to say it was: the three columns such a check would compare are api_key.valid_to, api_key.revoked_at and this table's own occurred_at, every one of them accounting skeleton, every one outliving the payload by decades. A report could be written over them tomorrow and would work in year thirty. What was decided is that it will not be written, which leaves the design without a guarantee it had been reading as though it had: nobody will be able to demonstrate that no write was ever audited against a key that had already ended, and no count anywhere will ever answer that question — not after 24 months, and not before them either. What this section does hold, and what the sentence above should never be read as replacing, is narrower and worth restating while it is being narrowed: every audited write left a row; that row's envelope — actor, table, record, moment — is intact for as long as the row exists; and the payload is emptied on schedule rather than lingering. Those three are checked. The fourth was wanted by nobody who read it, so it is stated as a rule with no report beneath it, which is the only remaining honest state — and 00a now says so in the same words this page does, because a register row claiming a report that no page has is the defect D-129 exists to catch. A reader who needs the fourth guarantee needs a different instrument than this table: the trail is a record of what happened to people, and what an ended key did after it ended is tracked on the key's own page (05e-keys-and-callers.md). - Tables whose write path does not audit. Compare the business tables this system has — staging tables excluded — against the maintained list of audited ones. Non-zero means a table is writing history that is never recorded. Read this one carefully, because its meaning got worse rather than weaker. While a trigger existed, a table was audited by being named in a trigger definition, and forgetting one was a decision somebody made in a migration and could see. Now a table is audited because the code that writes it calls the audit entry point, so the list and the code are two artifacts that must agree and nothing forces them to — which makes this report the entire control over the completeness of the audit trail, and the one check here whose finding must not wait for the monthly run. If it ever reports a table, the finding is not "some history is missing"; it is "every change to that table since it was added is unrecorded, and that period cannot be reconstructed later." - Redacted people with surviving personal data. Count redacted people whose names are not the redaction marker and who still have a current contact point whose value is not redacted; non-zero means an erasure was left half done. The count now reaches three more places, and the three fail in two different shapes. First, person_attribute: a redacted person with any attribute row is an erasure that did not happen, since those rows are deleted rather than overwritten (00-conventions §4). That is check 5 of 09-attributes.md §8 read from this side — the same assertion, not a second one. Second, and its shape is the opposite on purpose: event_answer. A redacted person with an answer row still carrying a value is an erasure that stopped short of the event tables. Those rows are not deleted — nothing about an event goes on a schedule, and an answer outlives its event indefinitely — so erasure overwrites: value emptied, and answered_at, answered_by and the row itself kept, because they were asked and they answered is the event's fact while this is what they said is the person's (D-140). value is the whole of the content here, since an answer is one typed value rather than a column per type (08-events.md §7) — there is no second field that survives an emptied value by holding the answer in another shape, which is the trap a check like this would otherwise set for itself. event_registration is counted by nothing here, and that is not an oversight: whether a person came is organizational history rather than something to withdraw, 00 §8's item 2 says so by name, and a check that reported surviving registrations would be reporting the design working. Third, and a different assertion, which only exists because values are logged on purpose: for a redacted person, no audit_log row about one of their person_attribute changes may still carry content. Content means value, value_option_id or recorded_note inside old_values or new_values; person_id, attribute_definition_id and source are not content and survive the scrub deliberately, because they are the only way this check can still find the rows after the erasure deleted the business ones — an audit row keeps its table_name and record_id when the row they named is gone, and its person_id is what ties it back to the person who asked to be forgotten. Read this check correctly and it has exactly one meaning: the scrub did not run. Before an erasure, a payload full of descriptive values is the design working (§2.2); afterwards it is the thing the person asked for the system to stop having. Note what the check structurally cannot see — a copy that is present, readable, and perfectly legal, held by somebody whose permission is graded below its contents — because that failure leaves no rows to count; it is the guard, and the guard is reviewed by a person. This check, check 5, check 7 and check 8 are the four here whose findings cannot wait for the monthly run — three because a value that outlives the rule about it is not something a schedule notices, and check 8 because it is the same failure wearing the other trail's clothes. Nothing in this design sends any of them to anybody, so "cannot wait" names a duty to open these four rather than a message that arrives on its own (D-164). A redaction property that is reported once a month is a redaction property that fails between the reports, and unlike a missing audit row, a value that outlives its erasure is not something anyone notices until a regulator asks what the table holds. - An audit row past the payload window that still carries a payload. Count audit_log rows whose occurred_at is older than the retention window and whose old_values or new_values still holds anything. This is check 6's mirror, and merging the two is the way to lose both. Check 6 asks whether an erasure ran, fires on one person's rows, and fails as a right not honoured; this one asks whether the calendar ran, fires on everybody's rows alike, and fails as a policy not applied (§2.2's three operations, which fail in different directions). A system passes one while failing the other in both directions, so they are two queries, not one query with two clauses. Its finding cannot wait for the monthly run, and the reason is the one §2.2 gives: reduction's failure mode is not running. Nothing about the trail looks wrong from inside it — a reduced row and a row that escaped reduction both still answer who, what, when, which is the half that was supposed to survive — so the only difference between them is a payload nobody looks at until somebody with audit.view opens a history screen and finds a child's allergy list still sitting there past the window it was meant to have left. Count the rows, do not sample them: a job that stopped after the newest partition keeps the oldest rows full and looks entirely healthy to a sample. And read the window from the same place the job does, because a check holding one value and a job holding another reports clean forever, which is the exact failure this check exists to prevent and the one it can cause by itself.

  • An access_log row older than the window that is still there. Count rows whose occurred_at predates the window and which still exist. This is check 7's sibling and deliberately not its copy. Check 7 counts payloads that should have been emptied out of rows that stay; this one counts rows that should be gone, on the other trail. Same clock, opposite operation — and merging them into one "anything past 24 months" report is how both are lost, because the two findings are repaired by two different jobs, one of which is an update and the other a delete, and because a single count cannot say which half of the retention policy stopped. The direction of failure is the same, and it is the reason this finding cannot wait for the monthly run: a job that stopped leaves a trail that looks entirely sound from inside it, since nothing about a growing table reads as a promise broken. The only difference between it and a healthy one is rows accumulating past the date the design said they would not exist, and the person who notices is the one asked what the system holds about them. Count, do not sample, for exactly the reason check 7 gives: a job that stopped after the newest partition keeps the oldest rows and passes any sample drawn from the top. And read the window from the same configuration the job reads — this is the second check that can be permanently satisfied by a disagreement between two copies of one number, and it is the failure mode each of them would cause alone. What it cannot do is demonstrate that anything was ever deleted. It counts what remains, which is the only thing a count over a table can see, so a job that deletes from the wrong table passes it; the standing guarantee here is not this report but the one on the other side of it, that the change trail is never pruned (05c §9). This delete is the third named exception to 00 §4, and the only one driven by a calendar rather than by a person asking or a batch being reverted.

  • A change the trail never saw: an audited row whose newest audit row predates its own updated_at. For every table 06 §2.1 obligates, take each row's updated_at and the newest occurred_at among the audit rows naming that table and record_id, and report the rows where the change is newer than the trail's knowledge of it. It exists because of the one write this design performs outside the application: the recovery in the break-glass procedure un-suspends an account or re-issues a credential by hand, produces no audit row, and leaves a row that is live, referenced and invisible to every other check in this section (domain/02-actors.md §3, D-126). It can see the recovery at all because account is a business table, and a business table owes an audit row on every insert and update (06 §2.1); which tables those are is a recommendation awaiting confirmation (§6), and that is this report's real ceiling — a table nobody confirmed is a table this check reads as never changing. Nothing in the schema distinguishes a legitimate recovery from somebody editing a row they had no business editing, so this is a report and not a guard, like every item above it. What it cannot catch. An edit that also inserts its own audit row by hand — the trail is append-only to the application, not to whoever holds the database. And an edit that leaves updated_at alone, which is the quieter half of the blind spot: 00-conventions §7 is explicit that nothing maintains updated_at unless somebody says so, so this report is exactly as wide as whatever maintains that column, and an application that sets it only on its own screens narrows it to those screens. What it does not lose to payload reduction: reduction empties old_values and new_values and keeps the row (D-088), and a reduced row keeps its occurred_at — so 24 months after the values went, this check still has both timestamps to compare. Coverage outlives content by design, which is the one part of this list that gets no worse with age.

Check 5 is worth automating as a test, not just a nightly query — a test that reads the table list in these documents and asserts every business table on it appears on the audited list, since that is the nearest thing left to what asking the database used to answer. A new table added without being put on that list is a silent, permanent hole in the audit trail — and it will be discovered only when someone needs the history that was never recorded.

docs.title: 6. Open issues
docs.text:
• Which tables must be audited. Recommend: all business tables. The cost is storage; the cost of a gap is unbounded. Still open as a decision, closed as a recommendation — §2.1 already obligates every business table, so what is actually outstanding is somebody confirming the list rather than deriving it.
  • Retention period for audit_log — decided as policy, still open as law (D-088). It used to read "retention period before archival to cold storage; legal input required", which got the question wrong in two ways at once: it assumed the answer was a storage tier rather than a shape, and it assumed one clock rather than two. The policy is now rows forever, payloads 24 months, 12 months as the floor a window may be set to, enforced by the job and the check in §2.2 and §5 rather than by an archive nobody queries. What remains open is the half a decision log cannot settle: whether the indefinite retention of named membership and fee_obligation rows has a lawful basis. That is recorded as an assumption with a name attached (../open-questions.md), not as settled law, and the review now has a concrete policy in front of it instead of a blank. It has four policies in front of it now, not three: these rows kept with no end date, the audit payloads emptied at 24 months, the access_log rows deleted at 24 months (D-145), and — added by D-166 — whether a child may hold an account with no guardian's consent recorded anywhere (domain/02 §2). The second and third are this system's own clocks; the first and fourth are the two a data subject asks about, and the fourth is the only one of the four that this design answers by not holding a record at all.
  • Whether audit_log should be partitioned by month from the start. Recommend yes, and the reasons changed when the payload window arrived. The old reason was "the write volume and the multi-decade horizon", which is still true of the rows — they are the permanent half — but the bulk of a row is its payloads, and those are now on a 24-month clock. Monthly partitions serve the reduction job too: a partition entirely past the window can be reduced as one unit rather than as a sweep across a table that grows for the life of the system. The open part is which the deployment does first, not whether the horizon justifies it.
  • ✅ Closed — the end-date inference rule for imported membership periods (§3.1). An imported membership ends with the calendar year of the last period in which the person appears: their last day as a member is 31 December, and the value written into valid_to is 1 January of the following year, because every period here is half-open and current membership is read as valid_to after today — a literal 31 December in that column would end every imported row one day early and look correct in every report that does not name the day (D-169). The boundary was never missing, and that is the part worth keeping: D-047 put it in membership_type as expiry_month and expiry_day, and that row's own note says the organizational year runs with the calendar — the four words this bullet asked for were sitting in the row the date is read from, which is also why the day is read from those two columns rather than compiled into a job as a literal. Sharper, not smaller, since D-093 put memberships back on the receiving end of it: the inferred end date is not the end of a record nobody reads, it is the valid_to of a row that gates authority, so the year boundary is the value standing between the import and the permission gate. (When this bullet was written the row in question was a unit_participation; D-097 removed that table, which sharpens the point rather than softening it — there is now exactly one period an inferred date can be ending, and it is the consequential one.)
  • ✅ Resolved — whether the import should create a membership at all for a historical period, or only a unit_participation (§3.1). Settled by D-090 on the shape of the corpus rather than on the merits of the two options — the corpus carried no payment data, so the exception arm of "participation unless there is payment evidence" had an empty set to fire on — and then narrowed by D-093, which is what this bullet now records: the corpus turned out to state membership periods, so a bounded membership may be imported, both ends dated, data_confidence = 'low'. What the resolution actually settled was never "no imported memberships" but "no inferred ones", and that half still holds in both directions: never open-ended, never from an attendance row. Superseded here and kept visible: this bullet used to end "participation only, always; membership rows come only from the current register."
  • Not a question, because the answer that split the corpus already answered it: a batch types itself (import_batch.batch_kind, §3). Two halves of corpus mean two shapes of row, and one field_mapping cannot serve both — an events export has no column that maps to an attribute code and a people export has nothing to map to a registration. Recording it as an open question would invite somebody to answer it with the larger alternative (one batch, two mappers that can never both apply), which the answer in D-092 explicitly passed over as the bigger change.
  • Exact redaction scope: which fields are personal data vs. organizational history (§4). Requires legal review — much narrower than it was, and still not closed. D-083 removed the category question (there is no specially-graded subset of the person record), and D-088 has since drawn the line: identity and descriptive values are erased, the accounting skeleton is retained, and the trail's payloads expire. What the review is asked about is therefore no longer "which fields" but "on what basis does the retained half survive indefinitely" — one question about one list, which is the item above.
  • Whether person.notes should exist at all, given the redaction burden it creates.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Fees and Payments
⚠ PROVISIONAL ON POLICY, SETTLED ON ARCHITECTURE
docs.text:
How money moves is now decided. Money arrives from a bank API and is requested by a variable symbol and a QR code (D-075); money that cannot be matched waits for a person (D-076). There is no card gateway, no checkout and no dispute handling, and §2a is the consequence.

What the money is for is answered. The fee is priced in koruna (D-155), it buys membership and nothing else (D-156), there is one live price edited in place, and the number on an obligation is the number a person wrote there (D-161, D-160). Nobody waives a fee and nothing refunds one inside the system (D-157, D-158).

Five questions are open, listed and numbered in §5: discounts, invoices, the accounting export, jurisdiction, and what gets a variable symbol. Those are policy questions this document cannot answer, and each needs somebody in the organization to be asked.

This document exists because membership activation depends on payment (../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md), and because the yearly expiry and renewal window (D-040) need somewhere to read a due date from.

docs.title: 1. What the domain requires
docs.text:
Settled:

  • There is a yearly fee, flat, per person — it does not vary by age, by household, or by membership type, because there is one membership type (D-037).
  • Becoming a member requires paying it; the membership activates on payment (D-040).
  • The fee expires on a fixed organizational date, typically January. At that date the membership lapses — the person is not a member — and a renewal window follows during which they may renew without re-applying. A payment inside the window opens the new period at the expiry date, so the record shows no gap.
  • There is no grace status. The window is tracked as dates, and the resolver does not know it exists.
  • The fee is charged in koruna. One currency, and a second one is refused rather than deferred; the column stays because the refusal is cheap to reverse with it (D-155).
  • The fee buys membership — no insurance is bought with it, sold with it, or implied by it, so no date in this system is evidence of cover (D-156).
  • There is one live price, edited in place when a billing year is reopened, because what a person owed was never stored in the price list anyway (§2) (D-161).
  • What a person owes is whatever their obligation says. No proration rule and no waiver mechanism decide it: a reduced fee is an obligation written with a smaller amount_due, the same act that writes any other amount (D-160, D-157).
  • Money out is recorded exactly like money in — a refund is a payment in the opposite direction, and nobody initiates one inside this system (D-158).

Unspecified — family or sibling discounts beyond a per-person amount_discount, whether the organization owes people invoices, whether anything is exported to an accounting system, what the law of this country requires of a fee, and what gets a variable symbol. Each is in §5.

Settled, and the big one — the organization collects, but not through a card gateway: money is requested by variable symbol + QR code and arrives from the bank API already tagged (§2a, D-075).

docs.title: 2. Minimal provisional shape
docs.text:
Four tables, deliberately small and easy to replace.

fee_schedule — a price. One is live at a time, and it is edited in place when a billing year is reopened; there is no price history, and none is needed, because what a person owed was never in here.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id code text, required name text, required description text, optional membership_type_id reference to membership type, optional NULL = applies to any type, e.g. an organization-wide surcharge period_months integer, required Default 12 amount money, required Zero or more currency three-letter currency code, required CZK, and the only value this organization writes. Required and explicit anyway: a second currency is refused for now, and the column is what makes that refusal cheap to reverse (D-155) is_active boolean, required Default true created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Nothing on a schedule is scoped to a body. A fee_schedule is scoped to a membership type — one row, so nothing in practice — and to nothing else at all: it is the price, current until somebody writes a different one into the same row. A fee is what it has always been charged as: flat, per person, at the unit (D-037). Why nothing narrower: D-095 had already ruled that entry below the membership carries no money — into the sub-units, there is no fee — so a supplementary fee for one body was a possibility no answer ever took. If a group ever needs a charge of its own, that is a policy question for §5 and a new shape of obligation, not a column to hold in reserve.

Rules

  • code is unique. It covers all rows, not only active ones.
  • amount is zero or more.

Indexes

  • The one lookup that matters is the live schedule for one membership type: the type and is_active together, which are expected to return one row.

One live price, and why editing it in place is safe. fee_obligation snapshots fee_schedule_id "so the amount is reproducible even if the schedule is edited", and it copies amount_due beside the reference — so the record of what a person owed was never in the schedule at all. Only the price list was, and a price list is not a record (D-161). What is given up is the price list's own history: nobody can ask this system what a membership cost in 2027. The answer available is an aggregate over the obligations of 2027, which reports what people were actually asked rather than what a list said. No code is named for editing the price row, and the gap is named rather than filled: on the reading this design carries, opening a billing year is reached by whatever grant already lets a person write a fee at that scope, which is this corpus's inference from D-161 and not a ruling inside it.

fee_obligation — one thing someone owes.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required The person the fee is for. Not the payer — see paid_by_person_id on payment membership_id reference to membership, optional One of the three target columns; exactly one is set membership_request_id reference to membership request, optional One of the three target columns event_registration_id reference to event registration, optional One of the three target columns. The event arm is real, not a hedge: an event with a fee_schedule creates one obligation per registration (D-066), and payment confirms the place. fee_schedule_id reference to fee schedule, required Snapshotted so the amount is reproducible even if the schedule is edited description text, required period_from date, required period_to date, required amount_due money, required amount_discount money, required Default 0 amount_paid money, required Default 0 currency three-letter currency code, required CZK, as on the schedule it came from status text, required Default unpaid. One of: unpaid, partially_paid, paid — and nothing else. The three values say how much of this obligation has arrived, and nothing more: lateness is read from due_date, and a fee nobody is going to pay is a row with a smaller amount_due (D-159) due_date date, required The yearly fee expires on a fixed organizational date (D-040); this obligation's due_date is what the lapse sweep compares against (§4). The renewal window that follows is carried as dates, not as a status (§1). This is also the only place lateness lives: an obligation past this date and not paid is overdue, and no status value says so (D-159) created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows

Rules

  • period_to is later than period_from.
  • amount_due, amount_discount and amount_paid are each zero or more.
  • Exactly one of membership_id, membership_request_id and event_registration_id is set — one, not zero and not two. Every obligation is for exactly one thing: a membership period, a membership request, or one person's place at one event. The per-person choice for events is deliberate: the fee is flat and per person (D-037), and a per-family price would need the household grouping designed again first (D-057).
  • status is arithmetic, not a decision. It reports how much of amount_due has arrived, so there is no value to set for a fee that will not be collected and no value to set because due_date has passed. A fee nobody is going to pay is an obligation written with a smaller amount_due; being late is a report over a date (D-157, D-159).

Indexes

  • One person's obligations, by status.
  • Obligations ordered by due_date, restricted to the rows still open — unpaid or partially_paid. Closed rows are not in it. Read down this index past today's date and it is the overdue list: one fact stored once, with no status value to keep in step with the calendar.
  • Obligations carrying the event arm, and obligations carrying the membership arm — each restricted to the rows where that column is set.
  • Obligations within a period_from / period_to range.

The event arm is the third target that is genuinely used. D-037 settled the fee as flat and per person, so an event carrying a fee_schedule has one obligation per registration, created by the code that places the registration and paid to confirm the place (D-066). Nothing creates it if that code is not written: no trigger writes it, and a trigger could not have been forgotten — the trade is stated in 00-conventions §6a. An event with a fee and no obligation is invisible until someone reconciles money against the roster.

Exactly one, never zero and never two — and unlike most rules in these documents this one can still be stated declaratively, so a migration should state it. Three columns, exactly one set: count how many are present and require that count to be one, which is a condition on the row and nothing else. No subquery, no other table, and therefore emittable by any migration that can put a condition on a row at all — the case where the ORM argument simply does not apply. It is worth naming explicitly, because it is the counterexample to the general worry — most of what D-072 deleted genuinely cannot be restated declaratively (shape 3), and this is not one of them.

If a fourth target is ever proposed, ask whether it is used, and expect the answer to be no. "At most two of three," with one arm kept against a hypothetical, is not the same domain as exactly one over three real targets, and the difference only shows up when somebody adds the fourth.

If a family discount is ever wanted, the row is still the right shape — one obligation covering several people — but it now needs the grouping to be re-introduced first, as a group with a period rather than a fake person (04 §3).

payment — money that moved, as one recorded act.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id public_id external identifier, required Unique. Appears in URLs and exports; id stays internal (00-conventions §3) amount money, required Never zero. A negative amount is money going out — a refund, a correction, or a reversal. This is the only way money leaves: there is no refund state anywhere for a row like this to point at, so a refund is written as one of these and the person who recorded it is in the row (D-158) currency three-letter currency code, required CZK, on money going out exactly as on money coming in paid_at timestamp, required When the payment occurred, which may differ from when it was recorded — a bank transfer recorded a week later. Both matter recorded_at timestamp, audit time Default: now method text, required One of: bank_transfer, cash, voucher, credit_note, other. card and direct_debit removed — there is no card gateway and no mandate system (D-075) variable_symbol text, optional The symbol the money arrived under, copied verbatim from the bank statement. Set on every row the import created; the join back to payment_request. Never typed by hand reference text, optional Bank reference, transaction id, receipt number paid_by_person_id reference to person, optional Who actually paid. May differ from the person the fee is for — a parent paying for a child, a grandparent paying for a grandchild, a sponsor. This is the act-on-behalf record for money on_behalf_of reference to person, optional status text, required Default confirmed. confirmed or reversed, and nothing else. A bank transfer the bank has reported does not later fail, expire, or get reversed by a card network, so the two values describe whether we still stand behind the row. There is no pending and no failed: a promised transfer is not a state (D-075) confirmed_by reference to person, optional notes text, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • amount is never zero; zero is meaningless. Negative amounts are reversals.
  • public_id is unique.

Indexes

  • A payer's payments, newest paid_at first.
  • Payments by date, newest first.
  • Lookup by reference, restricted to rows that have one.

payment_allocation — which payments satisfy which obligations. It is many-to-many in both directions: one payment may cover several obligations, and one obligation may be paid in instalments.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id payment_id reference to payment, required fee_obligation_id reference to fee obligation, required amount money, required Never zero allocated_at timestamp, audit time Default: now allocated_by reference to person, optional note text, optional

Rules

  • A given payment is allocated to a given obligation at most once — one row per pair, over all rows.
  • amount is never zero.

Indexes

  • Allocations of one payment, and allocations of one obligation — both directions are asked.

The allocation table is the part most likely to be right. A payment and an obligation are genuinely many-to-many, and any design that puts payment_id on the obligation (or vice versa) breaks the first time a parent pays for three children in one transfer. That is the common case in this organization, not an edge case.

docs.title: 2a. How money actually arrives
docs.text:
D-075. The system requests a payment and then reads one. It never touches the money.

The flow, in order:

  1. A liability exists — a membership period, a membership request, a place at an event.
  2. The system issues a payment_request carrying a variable symbol and an amount.
  3. The payer is shown the symbol, the amount, and a QR code that encodes all three.
  4. The payer's own bank moves the money. The system is not involved and learns nothing yet.
  5. A bank import reads the account statement and produces a bank_transaction for each incoming transfer, with the variable symbol still attached.
  6. The symbol resolves to a live request. The import creates a payment, links it, and the obligation's balance falls.
  7. If the symbol resolves to nothing live, the row goes to the queue (§2b).

payment_request — the liability rendered payable.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id variable_symbol text, required Unique across all rows, forever, including cancelled and long-settled ones. Eleven digits from a sequence fee_obligation_id reference to fee obligation, required What is owed. The request never invents an amount of its own amount money, required Copied from the obligation at issue time, so a later price change cannot rewrite what someone was asked for currency three-letter currency code, required CZK, copied alongside the amount for the same reason recipient_account text, required The account the QR code tells people to pay into issued_at timestamp, audit time expires_at date, optional When the request stops being payable — the close of a renewal window, or the day before an event voided_at timestamp, optional Set by a person, or by cancelling the event the request was for (§2b) voided_reason text, optional

Rules

  • variable_symbol is unique over every row that ever existed, not over live rows. A symbol issued in 2019 must never resolve to a 2026 obligation, because bank statements get re-imported and late payments are the entire reason the renewal window exists.
  • The symbol comes from a sequence. It is never derived from a birth date, a membership id, a member number, or anything else a person can guess or work out. Anyone can type eleven digits into a payment form at their bank; a guessable symbol means a stranger's money lands in a child's record, and the damage is not cosmetic — it reads as a paid fee and an active membership that nobody earned, in the one part of this database that is kept with no end date (D-088). A fee row is the organization's own history from the moment it is written, not a draft somebody confirms later. That is also the ceiling on the damage: since the fee buys membership and nothing else (D-156), no date here can be read as anything more than that.
  • amount is a copy, not a live reference. What a person was asked to pay is a historical fact about the ask, and recomputing it from the current schedule would make every price change rewrite history.
  • One obligation may have several requests over time — a first request expires, or the amount is corrected — but at most one live request per obligation.
  • A request is not an invoice. Nothing is delivered, nothing is numbered for a tax authority, and whether the organization also owes people invoices is still an open question (§5).

bank_transaction — one incoming transfer as the bank reported it.

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id bank_account text, required bank_reference text, required Unique per bank account. This is the idempotency key: the same statement imported twice must create nothing the second time arrived_at date, required The bank's date, not the import's — this is the date D-040's renewal window is measured against amount money, required variable_symbol text, optional As reported. Can be absent, wrong, or a stranger's payer_description text, optional Whatever the bank gives: a name, sometimes an address matched_payment_request_id reference to payment request, optional NULL means unmatched, which is the queue imported_at timestamp, audit time import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional

Rules

  • bank_reference is unique within a bank account. Re-importing a statement is safe and must be.
  • A transaction is immutable once imported. Corrections are new rows or a re-import, never an edit — this is the organization's copy of somebody else's ledger, and the only version of it that will ever agree with the bank.

The renewal window stops being a promise. D-040 backdates a renewal to the expiry date when payment lands inside the window, and its own note said that rule was only as good as the reliability of payment dates. Until now they arrived when somebody noticed a transfer. They now arrive from the bank, dated by the bank. The sweep in §4 can run unattended because the thing it depends on is no longer a person remembering in February.

What this deletes from the design. No checkout, no card tokens, no PCI surface, no webhook endpoint to authenticate, no dispute or chargeback state, no reconciliation report against a processor's payout. payment.status loses pending and failed: a bank transfer the bank has reported is confirmed on arrival, and there is no in-between state to model. What remains in status is whether we still stand behind the row — confirmed or reversed.

docs.title: 2b. Money that cannot be matched
docs.text:
D-076.

An unmatched transaction is a fact with no subject, so the absence gets stored rather than guessed at — the same discipline as "unanswered is the absence of a row" (D-059). matched_payment_request_id IS NULL is the queue; there is no separate worklist table to fall out of sync with the rows it describes.

How a transaction ends up there: the symbol matches no request. The symbol matches a request that has been voided. The request is already settled. The amount is less than asked, or more. There is no symbol at all — cash-basis donors and people who type their own name in the wrong field.

What the system does with any of those: nothing. It records the money and waits.

A person decides, and there are exactly four outcomes:

Outcome When Attach it to a different request The symbol was mistyped; the real obligation is obvious from the payer Split it across requests One transfer, three siblings — the ordinary shape of family payment here Record as a donation Money with no obligation behind it, which is not the same as money that is missing one Refund it, by hand Nothing was meant to be owed. A second payment in the opposite direction (D-075): the transfer goes out at the bank, and what arrives here is a payment naming whoever recorded it (D-158)

Why the tempting shortcut is refused. Falling back to the payer's identity when the symbol fails looks like it removes most of the queue. It removes most of the queue's accuracy instead: a parent with two children pays one amount against one symbol is the normal case, not the edge case, and an identity fallback resolves it to whichever child the query reaches first. A fee recorded against the wrong child is a finance error and a membership that appears paid when it is not, both at once — and the sibling it was meant for stays the one who looks unpaid. Both halves sit in rows that are kept with no end date. A fallback is not allowed to be wrong on the common path, and this is the common path.

Auto-refunding is refused for two reasons: it needs the bank integration to work outbound as well as inbound, which is a second integration with its own authorization; and it returns the grandparent's attempt at a camp contribution. The first of those has changed kind while the refusal stands. Calls coming in are a designed thing now — a registered key, granted like any other caller (05e) — so "outbound is a second integration with its own authorization" is no longer an absence but a decision with a shape to copy, and the outbound direction itself is F-27. The second reason was never a mechanism, and stands alone.

Cancellation is where most of the volume comes from, and it is decided now rather than later. D-064 made cancellation a recorded fact rather than a state, so the event survives, the registrations survive — and so would an outstanding request against an occasion that is not going to happen. So:

  • Cancelling an event voids its outstanding payment requests, recording why.
  • Money already received for a cancelled event becomes a queue item, for a person to refund or to carry forward to a later event. It is not auto-refunded, for the reasons above.

This is EV-3's answer, which is why it is closed here rather than left parked in the events module. Nothing about the queue's shape changes, and nothing about its end does either: the queue is where the system stops and a person begins, and that person's next act is at the organization's bank, not on a screen in this design (D-158).

The queue is not allowed to be silently ignored. It is a count on a dashboard, not a page nobody navigates to, and its oldest item is a number someone sees monthly. Unmatched money is the one finance backlog that gets worse by itself: the payer believes they have paid, and the organization believes they have not.

docs.title: 3. Keeping membership.outstanding_balance honest
docs.text:
03-membership.md has a denormalised outstanding_balance. If it stays, it must be maintained in the same transaction as any allocation change, or it will drift. Two options:

Option Pros Cons Maintain it inside the transaction that writes payment_allocation Always current, no recompute Every path that writes an allocation has to do it — the trigger that used to do it for all of them at once is gone — and the arithmetic is easy to get subtly wrong Drop the column, compute on demand Cannot drift Slower worklist queries Keep as a materialized view Cannot drift, fast Refresh lag

Recommendation: drop the column and use a view. The "approved but unpaid" worklist is not a hot path, and a wrong balance produces either a wrongly-suspended member or a wrongly-chased family. A wrong number here has a human consequence.

The definition, stated once, wherever it is implemented:

balance = amount_due − amount_discount − the sum of allocations whose payment is confirmed

Only confirmed payments count. An obligation is not settled by money that has been promised, intended, described in an email, or reported by a payer who believes they sent it. There is no state for a transfer that is on its way (D-075): either the bank has reported it and it is confirmed, or the system has not heard of it. A member is activated by the first, never by the second.

docs.title: 4. How this connects to membership
docs.text: The activation gate. A membership's fee is settled when no obligation attached to it has a positive balance after discounts, and that is the whole test with no status excepted from it — a fee nobody is going to collect is an obligation written with a smaller amount_due, so it never presents itself as a balance to work around (D-157, D-159). This test used to exclude obligations carrying waived, written_off or refunded outright, and every one of those values is gone, so the exclusion would now exclude nothing — which is the way you see it was a repair and not a rule. "Settled" is the only thing money says about membership; it does not grant permissions by itself (D-005). The route from a settled fee to anything a person may do goes through a set: the fee makes is_current_member() true, is_current_member() is what MEMBERS evaluates, and only a grant whose expression names MEMBERS cares (D-100) — which is why money cannot become authority by itself.

docs.title: The yearly expiry sweep
docs.text:
Run on 1 January (D-047). This is the one automatic membership transition in the system, and the only thing in this document that changes a person's status.

For every membership that is active, has an obligation with a positive balance, and whose due date has passed:

  1. Mark it lapsed, ending it at the expiry date — not at today. The period ended on that date whether or not anyone noticed.
  2. Open the renewal window as a date, never as a status. The resolver does not know windows exist.

Nothing has to be told afterwards. MEMBERS is evaluated live on the checked date (D-100), so the two facts step 1 writes — the period ending and the lapsed status — are visible to the next check, with no job in between and no stored answer to invalidate (D-114, domain/06 §8). What the sweep costs is stated where cost belongs: on 1 January the answer moves for every member at once, and a screen opened that day computes it rather than reading it (D-112).

Note the personnel consequence, which is easy to miss and fatal to get wrong. This runs for everyone at once, including the person who runs it, and nothing waives the membership test for a named person: D-100 deleted system.gate_exempt, person_holds_gate_exempt and the resolver clause behind them. The answer is the grant text. A grant written MEMBERS * ROLE(it) stops applying to its holder at the sweep; a grant written ROLE(it) keeps applying, because the set test is simply not in it. Assumption: which offices are written that way is not settled by D-100, and getting it wrong fails in the direction that locks a person out with no permission left with which to undo it — the standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand without MEMBERS is what makes each such choice visible before 1 January rather than on it (03-membership.md §6).

The expiry is the one automatic transition in this design, and what makes it allowable is that it is not a decision (D-023, D-040): the fee covers a fixed period and the period ends, and the renewal window absorbs the late-transfer case, because a payment inside it backdates the new period to the expiry date and the record shows no gap.

What the window cannot absorb is a payment that arrived before the expiry but was recorded after it. That is a data-entry lag, not a non-payment, and it is corrected with membership.backdate rather than left as a real gap. Worth a report: members who lapsed and then paid within a few days.

docs.title: 4a. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify. This section arrived late and by decision (D-135); what it does is not new to this folder, it is what every other page here already had. The rules below are all stated somewhere above this heading — §2, §2a and §3 each state one and then said nothing about what would notice a breach.

  1. The balance the system shows, recomputed from §3's definition. amount_due − amount_discount − the sum of allocations whose payment is confirmed, per obligation, and the same sum rolled up wherever a membership's balance is displayed. Two states put a row on this list: an allocation whose payment has since been reversed still sitting in the total, and a discount recorded on the obligation but not carried into the roll-up. What it cannot catch is the definition being wrong on both sides — a screen and a report that each recompute amount_due − amount_paid agree perfectly and are both counting money that was only promised. If §3's recommendation is taken and the column becomes a view, this check does not retire. It moves from "the copy agrees with the sum" to "the view implements the sum", which is the same query and the same failure list, and D-075's rule that only confirmed payments count is what it is checking either way.
  2. A payment whose allocations do not account for its amount, and an obligation allocated past what it owes. payment_allocation is many-to-many in both directions and §2's rules constrain the pair and the sign of each amount, never the sums. So a payment with unallocated remainder is money that moved and was never attributed to anything, and an obligation allocated beyond amount_due − amount_discount is an overpayment that nobody has refunded. The layer here is the write path, and there is no constraint to sit beneath it: the sums span rows of two tables, which is shape 3, so this report is not a net under a rule — it is the whole of the backstop. §2 called this table "the part most likely to be right", and that is an argument about the shape, not about the data ten years in.
  3. Money nobody ever asked for. Two readings of one failure, cheapest first: an obligation still at unpaid or partially_paid whose due_date has passed with no live payment_request pointing at it, so nothing has ever carried a variable symbol to anybody. The two conditions are read together and neither is stored twice: due_date past plus a status that is not paid is overdue, which is why no status value carries it (§2) (D-159); and upstream of that, an event_registration for an event carrying a fee_schedule with no fee_obligation behind it, which §2 already warned of in one sentence — an event with a fee and no obligation is invisible until someone reconciles money against the roster, because nothing creates the obligation and no trigger could have been forgotten. Do not read this list as the queue. An unmatched bank_transaction is money with no subject, and D-076 rules that it waits for a person, which is a correct state with a page of its own (§2b). This is the opposite case: a liability with no ask attached, which is silent in both directions — nobody is chased and nobody pays.

Checks 1 and 2 are the two that matter, and §3 says why in one line: a wrong number here has a human consequence — either a wrongly-suspended member or a wrongly-chased family. Check 3 is the one that finds a whole class of missing money rather than a wrong row, and it is the only one of the three that can be non-empty because a feature was never written rather than because a row is wrong.

docs.title: 5. Open issues — the whole of this document, essentially
docs.text:
Five questions are open, and they are the five below. What this section used to ask that it no longer does, and the arithmetic of the list, are at the end of the page rather than inside the list.

  1. Are there family/sibling discounts? amount_discount exists but the rules are unspecified. With a flat per-person fee (D-037), this is the only remaining fee variation, so it is worth a deliberate yes or no. A per-family discount needs a grouping to be designed first — there is none (D-057) — so it is not a constraint change but a shape. A per-person discount is unaffected and is just amount_discount.
  2. Invoicing: does the organization issue invoices (legal requirement in some jurisdictions)? If so, an invoice entity and a numbering sequence are needed. Sharper now: a payment_request looks like an invoice, prints like one, and is not one — it has no tax identity, no sequence required by law, and no delivery record. If invoices are legally required, the honest answer is a second document over the same obligation, not a renaming of this one.
  3. Accounting integration: does anything need to be exported to an accounting system? What is open here is the direction. Who may call this system is designed (05e); this system calling anyone else is F-27.
  4. Jurisdiction. This is the half of an item that used to read "currency and jurisdiction", and only the currency half was answerable: the currency is koruna, on all four tables that carry one (§2) (D-155). What is left is what the law of this country asks of a fee, which this design does not know and has no column for: whether invoices of item 2's kind are compulsory rather than chosen, and whether the organization owes anything about its money to anybody outside itself. This is the finance module's share of the same sitting that already holds the four data policies in front of a legal review (00-conventions §8, 06b §6).

  5. What gets a variable symbol, and one per what? — raised by D-075 rather than left over. That decision fixed how money arrives and named the payment_request that carries it, but not the two choices the module is actually built from.

    • Scope. Do event fees get a symbol, or only membership fees? A camp fee is the same mechanism, and a symbol is what lets a family pay for it at their own bank without staff involvement. Recommendation: every payable, because the alternative is a second, hand-recorded money path sitting beside an automatic one — and hand-recorded is what D-040's renewal window just escaped.
    • Granularity. One live request per liability, matching the fee_obligation row exactly — which is what §2a already assumes. Not per person, because a parent paying for two children in one transfer is the ordinary case and per-person symbols make that impossible to match. Not per person-year either: a camp is a separate liability from a fee and must never share a symbol with one.
    • The amount mismatch, which D-076 defers and this question cannot. 500 sent against a 550 request goes to the queue, which is correct as a mechanism and silent as a policy. Whether partial payment settles anything, whether 4.90 vs 5.00 is a shortfall, and whether the payer finds out at all when their money lands and does not fit — nothing here sends anything to anyone (D-137), so finds out means a person telephoning them or a module that is not designed yet — those are undecided, and the queue will show them at volume the first spring the import runs.

    Why this is not a footnote: it decides whether the module has one money path or two.

What this section used to ask, and where each answer lives. The list ran to eleven items; four are closed and one is narrowed to what is left of it. They are kept here in one line each, because for most of them this page is the only place the question was ever written:

  • The fee amount — the question this page asserted twice and never filed, which is why nothing could ever have closed it. Filed now as item 12 of the old numbering and answered in the same act: one live price, edited in place, and the amount a person owes is the number written on their obligation (D-161).
  • Is the fee prorated for mid-year joins — no rule. Someone joining in October gets an amount_due of whatever the person opening it writes, and the renewal twelve months later is written by the same kind of act. Nobody will be able to point at a rule and say this organization prorates, or refuses to (D-160).
  • Who may authorize a refund — nobody, because nothing is initiated here. The transfer goes out at the bank; what arrives here is a payment naming whoever recorded it (D-158).
  • Does the fee cover insurance — it does not. No date in this system is evidence of cover, so the retention question that would have followed from one never arrives, and the softer "still covered during grace" reading D-040 rejected was about a thing that does not exist (D-156).
  • Scholarships and hardship waivers — no mechanism, at any level of granularity. What this item used to be hard about was that a waiver had to be visible to few people and invisible to the rest, with only which codes exist standing between the two; the problem is dissolved rather than solved, because there is nothing to see (D-157).
  • Payment methods, and collecting rather than recording — both closed earlier by D-075. bank_transfer arrives by import and cash is recorded by hand; voucher and credit_note stay in the enum until somebody says otherwise; there is no card and no direct debit (§2). What remained in those two items was maintenance, not a decision.

The count, recounted. Five questions are open: discounts, invoices, the accounting export, jurisdiction, and what gets a variable symbol — the last still three questions in a trenchcoat, because it decides whether the module has one money path or two. The number this section printed was nine remaining open, and nine was right, while the list printed underneath it named seven of those nine and counted the variable-symbol item twice — eight printed, with who may authorize a refund and currency missing, which are the two this round closed. A summary that is right above a list that is wrong is worse than a wrong summary: the summary is what a reader quotes, and the list is what a reader answers from. The claim at the top of this document, repeated in §1, that the fee amount is unanswered named a question that was not on the list either, so it had to be filed before anything could answer it. A count next to a sentence is a claim, and the count was the part nobody had checked.

None of the five is architectural. The architecture is why they can be left open: how money arrives, how it is requested, and what happens to money that does not match are all decided, so what remains is policy that requires somebody in the organization to be asked — discounts, invoices, the accounting export, jurisdiction, and the choices item 5 names. This document does not need a rewrite; it needs answers.

None of the five is registered in the open-questions register, and this page is why: the register's finance row reports a number of open questions and names none of them, so a reader who never opens this document finds no finance question at all. The questions settled along the way — activation on payment, the flat per-person fee, the absence of a household grouping, collecting rather than recording — are registered there with the decision that settled each, and nothing else on this page is. The five above are the finance module's own open issues until somebody registers them or says here why not.

docs.title: Data Model — Events
docs.text:
event, event_organizer, event_registration, event_question, event_answer.

Domain rationale: ../domain/07-events.md.

Nothing here is provisional. Every hook this module uses — access_grant scoped to an item, grant_scope_type, audiences and their selectors — is in place, and the two vocabularies among them ship with the platform. The tables below fill those hooks; they do not extend the model.

An event has no owner. No column of event names a unit or a group, and there is no event-shaped check: every event permission goes through the ordinary can(), with nothing event-shaped in it (§8). The people connected to an event are named by selectors that bind to the event being checked (§8).

Section numbers are shared across the two parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 08-events.md holds §1–§7, 08a §8–§11 (projections and guards, the three queries that matter, integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 1. Why these five tables, and no event_series
docs.text:
Table What it is event The occasion. A date, a registration window, an optional capacity — and no owner (§2) event_organizer Who is running it — an appointment on the event, not a grant (§3) event_registration One person's answer: attending, or not attending. Unanswered is the absence of a row event_question What this event asks registrants event_answer What one person said to one question

No recurrence. A weekly meeting is a group — a person_group with dated member rows (D-098) — not an event (../domain/07-events.md §1). Adding event_series would mean every downstream table — registrations, capacity, presence, organizers, questions — needs a second possible home, and the feature that needed recurrence is already modelled.

No event_status column. Visibility is the permission model; cancellation is a fact (../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §10).

docs.title: 2. event
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only public_id external identifier, required Unique. Generated when the event is created title text, required description text, optional The committee's own notes — internal public_note text, optional Shown to registrants. Separate from description, which is internal: "bring a sleeping bag and a torch" vs. the committee's own notes location text, optional Free text: a camp site, an address, "the usual place" location_detail free-form jsonb, optional {lat, lon, meeting_point, …} when known starts_at instant in time, required An instant, not a date. A Thursday group meets at 5pm; a camp starts on Saturday morning. The instant carries a timezone, and the timezone is the organization's, recorded rather than assumed ends_at instant in time, required An instant, not a date, for the same reason all_day boolean, required Default false. Display only — an all-day camp still has instants underneath registration_opens_at instant in time, optional NULL = open as soon as the event is visible. The event is visible to whoever holds event.view, which normally includes everyone holding it at the unit — see ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §10 for what that does to the private-by-default draft. So NULL is a reasonable default and wrong for a jamboree whose sign-up should not open before the dates are fixed registration_closes_at instant in time, optional NULL = when the event starts. This is the "unlimited" case: registration stays open until the thing happens capacity integer, optional NULL = unlimited. Bed count, bus seats, fire-safety limit. Enforced as a WAITLIST threshold, not a block, and a staff registration may exceed it (../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §8) waitlist_deadline instant in time, optional When an unpaid registration at a full event releases its place to the waitlist (§6). NULL = never releases. Only meaningful when the event has a fee AND a capacity; ignored otherwise. This is the ONE automatic transition in this module — see §6 for why it is accepted and what it costs fee_schedule_id reference to fee schedule, optional NULL = this event is free, which most are. Set = a fee applies; registering creates a fee_obligation (§6). The amount and currency live in fee_schedule, not here — events do not price themselves cancelled_at instant in time, optional Cancellation is a FACT, not a status: revoking grants would hide the cancellation from the registrants, who are exactly the people who must be able to see it. A cancelled event stops accepting registrations and KEEPS every registration row — those rows are the record that the camp was planned and who was coming cancelled_by reference to person, optional Who cancelled. Set exactly when cancelled_at is set cancel_reason text, optional Free text, and it may be absent ("cancelled — see email") created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional Who created the row. Not an owner — created_by is attribution, and a permission is never derived from an identity (D-005) updated_at timestamp, audit time, optional updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows

Rules

  • ends_at is later than starts_at.
  • capacity is either absent or greater than zero.
  • When both registration_opens_at and registration_closes_at are set, the close is later than the open. When either one is absent nothing is required of the other — each is independently meaningful on its own.
  • cancelled_at and cancelled_by are set together or not at all. A cancellation has a who and a when, or neither. The reason is free text and may be absent ("cancelled — see email").
  • waitlist_deadline may be set only when both capacity and fee_schedule_id are set. A waitlist deadline is meaningless without a capacity to fill or a fee to pay, and stating this prevents a column that silently does nothing.
  • public_id is unique.
  • No column of event names a scope. There is no owner, no holding group, no creating unit, and no rule anywhere in this module that reads one (§8).

Indexes

  • Upcoming events by starts_at, and events by registration_closes_at — both restricted to rows that are not cancelled. Every "what is happening" and "what is still open" list excludes cancelled events, so the cancelled ones are simply not in the index.

docs.title: There is no owner column
docs.text:
No column of event names a unit — there is no org_unit_id to fill, no holding group, no creating unit, and no rule anywhere in this module that reads one (§8). Why: an event is an item in grant_scope_type under the code event, and nothing more. A grant at the unit reaches every event; a grant on one event reaches that event and nothing else (D-102).

event.create has applies_to = unit, so writing it on an event is refused when the grant is saved, with the reason in the message (D-099).

Nothing in this module reads an owner. There is no index on one (the index list above is the whole set), no check in §10 that reads one, no cascade running through one, and no rule in §5 or §8 that compares one. The people connected to an event are reached through event_organizer and event_registration, which point at the event directly.

Import consequence. The one-off import owes event rows and event_registration rows and it owes no owner column — one less thing to invent a value for (D-090). It does owe the twelve per-event grants of §8, one bundle for every event row it writes.

docs.title: No status column, and why that is not an omission
docs.text:
Nothing is stored that can be derived. "Is this event over?" is ends_at in the past. "Is it cancelled?" is cancelled_at set. "Needs attention now" — the list an admin screen runs — is every event with cancelled_at absent and ends_at not yet past, ordered by starts_at.

completed is derived, never stored, so there is no state to keep consistent and no job to move rows between states. Draft is not a state either: publishing is an access_grant, not an UPDATE. A status column and a permission system that both claim to answer "who may see this?" will eventually disagree, and the one that gets enforced is whoever wrote the last IF.

A new event is visible to everybody already holding event.view at the unit — there is no owner-only draft state behind it, and nothing to withdraw to make one. Privacy is therefore an act rather than a default; see ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §10.

docs.title: Why fee_schedule_id and not an event_fee table
docs.text:
The fee amount and currency already live in fee_schedule (07-finance.md §2), and an event points at the schedule that prices it. An event_fee table would duplicate that and immediately drift.

What the pointer no longer buys, and this is where D-161 actually lands. D-161 deleted fee_schedule.valid_from and valid_to: there is one live price, edited in place when a billing year is reopened, and no price history — so a 1998 camp's fee does not recompute from the 1998 schedule, and no page here may claim it does. The record of what a person owed was never on the schedule anyway: §6's create copies the schedule's amount and currency onto the fee_obligation beside its snapshot of fee_schedule_id, and that row is where the answer lives. Membership states it the same way — "what did we charge in 1998?" is answered from the obligation, not the price list (../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md §3). What the deletion costs is one question: what did the price list say a 1998 camp cost? The closest answer this system holds is an aggregate over the obligations of 1998, which reports what people were actually asked rather than what a list said.

docs.title: 3. event_organizer
docs.text:
The absence of a valid_to is deliberate. This is a roster, not a period: you are on the list, or you are not. An organizer who drops out is removed (recorded in audit_log), because "was Jan an organizer of that camp?" must have one answer, not a set of intervals.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only event_id reference to event, required The event this person is on. Deleting the event removes its organizer rows — the one cascade in this design, and guard 2 in §8 is what makes it safe person_id reference to person, required organizer_role text, optional lead, assistant, cook, driver, medic, quartermaster — free text. NOT a controlled vocabulary: every organization labels these differently, and a closed list here would be a guess of the kind D-095 refused for reason codes. The system does not ship somebody's vocabulary. is_primary boolean, required Default false. The person the parents are told to call. At most one per event — a uniqueness rule the schema can express, so it is a constraint and not a report (Rules, below) sort_order integer, required Default 0. Display order for the list. Cooks before drivers is a real preference and not something to derive note text, optional added_by reference to person, optional Who put them on the roster created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • One row per person per event — the (event_id, person_id) pair is unique, over all rows.
  • At most one organizer of an event has is_primary set. The rule covers every row of the event; rows where the flag is not set are unrestricted, so an event may have any number of ordinary organizers and exactly one primary.
  • Removing an organizer is a removal of the row, not the ending of a period, and audit_log is where the history of it lives. There is nothing to overlap, so there is no no-overlap rule here.

Cascade on delete here, and nowhere else in this data model. It is justified because event_organizer is a roster of assignments on the event, not a business record: a deleted event has no organizers in the domain sense either. In practice nothing deletes an event — the deletion policy is temporal closure, and cancellation sets cancelled_at. The cascade exists so that a mistaken INSERT into a draft event can be cleaned up without leaving orphan rows, and it is the only cascade in the design. Deleting an event that has registrations is refused outright (§8, Guard 2), and the refusal belongs in the database rather than in the delete path: the reference from event_registration to event carries no cascade, so an import or a hand-written fix meets the same wall the screens do. A refusal only the screens knew about would delete the record of who was coming.

docs.title: Organizers are appointments, not grants
docs.text:
event_organizer is the domain answer to "who is running this camp?" — the labelled, ordered list that parents see. It is deliberately not an access_grant (D-062; ../domain/07-events.md §5):

  • A grant has no room for organizer_role = 'cook'.
  • "Who is running this camp?" should not be answered by reading the permission table.
  • Revoking a grant to remove a cook would also revoke their ability to see the event at all, which is not what "they are no longer cooking" means.

Authority to act on the event does not come from this table. It comes from a live allow — at the unit, which reaches this event, or on this event — and never from a role or an appointment conferring anything by itself (D-005).

What this table is aimed at. It is the extension of the selector ORGANIZERS, so a grant can name the people running an event without any of them being granted anything by being listed (D-102). An operand is a set, not a grant — the same sentence data-model/05 §8 repeats for named sets generally. See §8 for the twelve grants that aim at this table.

docs.title: 4. event_registration
docs.text:
One row per person per event. Two stored values; "unanswered" is the absence of a row.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only event_id reference to event, required person_id reference to person, required person_id, NOT membership_id. An event's roster must survive independently of how membership is recorded, and imported historical attendance has no membership row to point at. A 1998 camp roster is participation, and an inferred open-ended membership would put every one of those children inside MEMBERS today — see the note below response enum: attending / not_attending, required TWO values. unanswered is written NOWHERE. It is the absence of a row, so "who has not replied yet?" is a subtraction, not a stored state (../domain/07-events.md §3). Returning someone to unanswered deletes the row, which audit_log records — the honest act, and the one that leaves least behind responded_at timestamp, required Default now. When the ANSWER was given, which may differ from when it was recorded. A phone call on Tuesday entered on Thursday has two dates and both matter source enum: self / staff / guardian / import, required Default self. How this person got here, and the audit answer to "how did they get in?". staff is written by a person holding event.register_other, and it bypasses the registration window and the waitlist deliberately (§5, Guard 1): whoever has the permission may register anyone. guardian is acting-under-guardianship; the acting person is in access_log registered_by reference to person, optional NULL when source is self. Set otherwise: which organizer, or which guardian is_waitlisted boolean, required Default false waitlist_position integer, optional Order within the waitlist. Assigned on insert when the event is at capacity, and rewritten on promotion. See §5 is_confirmed boolean, required Default false. Registration is not the same as a held place. An event with NO fee confirms immediately on registration; an event WITH a fee confirms on payment (§6). This is the "payment confirms the place" rule, and it is the only place in this module where money changes a registration's meaning confirmed_at instant in time, optional Set exactly when is_confirmed is true was_present boolean, three-valued NULL = not yet marked — no register was taken. true = turned up. false = marked absent. THREE-VALUED ON PURPOSE: "we did not take a register" and "we took one and they were not there" are different facts, and only one is a safeguarding signal. For a camp this is the record of who was actually in the organization's care, and it cannot be reconstructed afterwards (§9). It is deliberately not the basis of any selector — PRESENT(<event>) is refused, and why is in §8 presence_marked_by reference to person, optional The person who took the register. Held by whoever has been allowed event.presence.mark — deliberately a separate code from event.manage_participants, not a rung beneath it: there is no ladder for one permission to sit below another (D-099), and that is the stronger form of the same protection. The volunteer at the door is not also the person who can delete a child from the roster, because they were granted one code and not the other presence_marked_at instant in time, optional When the register was taken fee_obligation_id reference to fee obligation, optional Set when the event has a fee_schedule and this registration created an obligation. The reverse pointer from fee_obligation.event_registration_id also exists (§6) — both directions, because each is asked a different question: "what does this person owe for this camp?" and "what is this obligation for?" created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time, optional updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows

Rules

  • One row per person per event, full stop — the (event_id, person_id) pair is unique over all rows. This is what makes "unanswered = absence" work: there is exactly one place an answer could live.
  • A not_attending row has is_waitlisted false and is_confirmed false. A decline is not waitlisted and not confirmed; otherwise a "no" could hold a place on the waitlist, which is nonsense.
  • is_confirmed is true exactly when confirmed_at is set.
  • is_waitlisted is true exactly when waitlist_position is set.
  • Presence is marked all together or not at all: was_present, presence_marked_by and presence_marked_at are either all present or all absent, and was_present absent is the same condition as the other two absent. A partially-set trio is a bug, not a state.

Nothing in this table ages out.
