A registration is a fact about a dated occasion and the row is kept: no expiry when the event ends, no clock on it, and no job that forgets people — the rule the accounting skeleton already follows, for the same reason (D-140, D-088). A cancelled event keeps every registration (guard 2 in §8), and a cancelled event with no registrations would be an event that demonstrably never happened.

was_present inherits that retention rather than getting one of its own — no retention shorter than the event's, no permission narrower than the roster's, no presence_record table, no safeguarding register behind it. The mark is read with the codes that already reach the event and written by whoever holds event.presence.mark, which is all the protection a column can be given that is also a fact an organizer needs (D-147). Erasure reaches a registration the way it reaches organizational history: the person stops being identifiable, the row stays, and the mark on it stays (00-conventions §8). What that costs is stated rather than left to be found: a 1998 camp roster holds a mark of who was in the organization's care for as long as the database exists, readable by whoever reaches that event. The alternative was a column with a clock of its own and a permission of its own, which is the first wall of an archive this design has refused four times and would record a fact this system does not keep — there are no background checks here (D-043) and no medical record (D-083).

Indexes

  • The set the capacity test counts — an event's registrations whose response is attending and which are not waitlisted. Capacity is compared against exactly this set (§5), and the other registrations of an event must not slow it down. This index is also exactly the extension of the PLACED selector (§8), so the audience the capacity rule counts and the audience a grant may name are the same rows, served by the same index — no second index and no second definition.
  • An event's waitlist in waitlist_position order, restricted to waitlisted rows — which is the extension of ON_WAITLIST (§8).
  • An event's registrations by was_present, restricted to rows where presence has been marked at all. Note that this index serves a report (§9) and no selector: the rows it is missing are precisely the unmarked ones, and that is the reason PRESENT is refused.

docs.title: Why person_id, not membership_id
docs.text:
An imported 1998 camp roster names children who have no membership row to point at. With the corpus large and number-bearing (D-056), linking registration rows to membership would make those rows unrepresentable. D-098 applies the same reasoning to person_group_member; the argument is stronger here.

An inferred open-ended membership is the dangerous object. MEMBERS is evaluated live on the checked date, so one open-ended row makes a 1998 camper a member today, and every live grant whose expression contains MEMBERS reaches them. Recording past attendance as a membership writes exactly that row, which is why the registration names the person and not a membership.

The trade-off, stated: no database constraint can enforce "only members may register", and none is wanted — eligibility is capability (../domain/07-events.md §4), and capability is a grant, not a membership row.

docs.title: 5. Capacity and the waitlist
docs.text:
Capacity is a threshold, not a block. Registering for a full event succeeds and produces a waitlisted row.

Is this event at capacity? The question is asked of one event and answered only from the registrations it has: count its attending, non-waitlisted registrations — its PLACED set (§8) — and compare that count with its capacity. An event with no capacity is never full — with no capacity set there is nothing to reach, and the answer is no.

The placing rule runs before the row is written, once per row, on every insert, so that EVERY insert path obeys it — self-service, staff, guardian and import alike. Application-level placement would let one of the four paths forget, and the forgotten one would be the one that matters. The order of these steps is a rule: the decline branch settles all four flags and ends the rule, and the capacity test is counted before confirmation is decided, because confirmation is a property of the place the earlier steps gave the row.

  1. Read the event the registration names.
  2. A decline never occupies a place. If response is not attending, set is_waitlisted false and waitlist_position absent, set is_confirmed false and confirmed_at absent, and stop here — none of what follows applies to a "no".
  3. Waitlisting is a SELF-SERVICE outcome. Waitlist the row when all three of these hold: source is self; the event has a capacity; and the event's attending, non-waitlisted registrations already number at least that capacity. Then set is_waitlisted true and waitlist_position to one past the highest position already on that event's waitlist — 1 when the waitlist is empty. If any of the three fails, set is_waitlisted false and waitlist_position absent. A staff registration is admitted even past capacity: the organizer who knows there are two spare tents is not to be blocked by a number they cannot edit mid-camp (../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §8, D-065). The overrun is permitted, attributed, and REPORTED (§10, check 5).
  4. Confirmation: immediate when there is no fee to wait for. If the event has no fee_schedule_id, set is_confirmed true and confirmed_at to now. Otherwise set is_confirmed false and confirmed_at absent — §6, payment confirms the place.
  5. Write the row carrying those flags.

The rule runs on insert only; a later edit of the row does not re-run it. Promotion and the release below write the same flags deliberately.

The source = 'self' disjunct is the whole of "organizers may register anyone", made mechanical. Without it every staff registration is waitlisted behind self-service ones, and the leader adding a child on the day is told the camp is full when they can see two spare beds. Note what this rule does not consult: not a level, not a role, not an owning unit. source is a stored fact written by whoever holds event.register_other, and the capacity rule reads the fact.

docs.title: Promotion, which is a deliberate act
docs.text:
Promotion is not automatic — no trigger, no job. An organizer picks someone from the waitlist:

  1. Take the one registration this person holds at this event — the pair names exactly one row (§4).
  2. Clear the waitlist on it: is_waitlisted false, waitlist_position absent.
  3. Set is_confirmed and confirmed_at by exactly the test the placing rule uses: confirmed now when the event has no fee_schedule_id, unconfirmed with no confirmed_at when it has one.

The promotion deliberately bypasses the capacity test: the whole point of promoting is that a place has freed up, and re-testing would just fail again.

Promotion writes the same two flags the placing rule would have, so a promoted registration and an admitted one are indistinguishable afterwards — which is correct, because the difference between them is when, not what.

docs.title: When an unpaid registration releases its place
docs.text:
If waitlist_deadline is set, an unpaid registration at a full event releases its place to the waitlist at that moment. This is the one automatic transition in this module, and it is recorded as such. The release is scoped as narrowly as the rule can be: only at a full event, only with a fee configured, only past the deadline, only unpaid, and never a staff registration (which is admitted by hand and by a human who can see the roster).

  1. Take every registration that is attending, not already waitlisted, source self, and not confirmed.
  2. Keep only those whose event has a fee_schedule_id, has a waitlist_deadline, has that deadline already past, and is not cancelled.
  3. Move each one onto the waitlist: is_waitlisted true, waitlist_position one past the highest position already on that event's waitlist — 1 when the waitlist is empty.
  4. Take the place back: is_confirmed false, confirmed_at absent.

Why this is accepted despite the design's refusal of automatic transitions (D-023). It is a deadline, not a sweep: it applies to a narrow conjunction, it is opt-in per event (waitlist_deadline is NULL by default, so most events never run it), and the state it produces is visible — the person is on the waitlist, not silently deleted. The alternative, no deadline at all, means a place is held forever by someone who never paid, which is worse.

docs.title: 6. Payments and confirmation
docs.text:
Registering creates a fee obligation; payment confirms the place.

Creating the obligation runs after the registration row is written, so that the registration has an id to be pointed at. The order is a rule: the obligation cannot be created before the registration it belongs to exists, and the registration's fee_obligation_id cannot be written before the obligation does.

  1. Read the event the registration is for.
  2. If the event has no fee_schedule_id, or the registration is not attending, stop — a free event owes nothing, and a place someone declined owes nothing.
  3. Read the fee schedule the event points at.
  4. Create one fee_obligation for this registration, carrying: person_id taken from the registration; event_registration_id set to the registration; the event's fee_schedule_id; the event's title as the description; the event's start and end as the obligation's period; the schedule's amount and currency; and a due date of the event's waitlist_deadline, falling back to the event's starts_at when it has none.
  5. Write the new obligation's id into the registration's fee_obligation_id.

Exactly one arm of fee_obligation names what the fee is for. The rule lives in fee_obligation and is stated there in full (07-finance.md §2): exactly one of membership_id, membership_request_id and event_registration_id is set on every obligation — exactly one, not "at most three". Every obligation is for exactly one thing: a membership period, a membership request, or one person's place at one event, and an event fee uses the third arm. The per-person choice is deliberate, because the fee is flat and per person (D-037) and a family price would need people grouped into households first, and the model has no such grouping (D-057). Obligations carrying the event arm are indexed on event_registration_id, restricted to the rows where it is set.

docs.title: Confirming on payment
docs.text:
confirm_event_place(obligation) is called by the payment flow. It is not a rule on fee_obligation's status — the payment module owns that transition, and a rule there would make every fee, membership or event alike, confirm an event place.

  1. Take the obligation the call names.
  2. Follow its event_registration_id to the registration it pays for.
  3. Confirm that registration only when it is attending and not waitlisted — in the selector vocabulary, only when it is PLACED (§8); a waitlisted person stays waiting until promoted (§5), so paying does not by itself place them.
  4. Confirming means setting is_confirmed true and confirmed_at to now.

confirm_event_place is deliberately an operation the finance module calls, not a rule hanging off fee_obligation's status change. The argument is about ownership and does not depend on where the code lives: anything that fires because a fee became paid fires for membership fees and event fees alike, and "the fee is paid" means something different in each case: a membership activates (D-040), an event place confirms. Two transitions, two owners.

Free events confirm immediately — see the placing rule in §5. An event with no fee_schedule_id has nothing to wait for, and requiring "confirmation" for a free hike would be a state with no meaning.

docs.title: 7. event_question and event_answer
docs.text:
Fields — event_question

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only event_id reference to event, required The event that asks it. A question is defined per event, never shared (§7) label text, required Tent preference, Dietary requirements help_text text, optional position integer, required Default 0. Display order data_type enum: text / long_text / integer / decimal / bool / date / choice / multichoice, required choices list of text, optional For choice and multichoice only. An ordered list on the question rather than a child table: the options are a property of the question, they are ordered, and they are never referenced by anything else is_required boolean, required Default false. The person REGISTERING must answer. Not a gate on registration itself: a form that blocks sign-up is a form nobody completes, and the organizer would rather have the registration and chase the answer applies_to enum: attendee / organizer / all, required Default attendee. Who is asked. Organizers may be asked things attendees are not (T-shirt size for the leaders' shirts) and vice versa bound_attribute_code reference to attribute definition, optional NULL = an ordinary question, which most are. Set = this question asks about the fact stored under that definition code: the form prefills from the person's current value as a suggestion the answerer confirms or edits, and submitting writes a fresh value back to the person record dated today. It names attribute_definition.code and never a person_attribute row id — that distinction is what keeps erasure's one hard delete invisible (D-139, 00-conventions §4). See A question bound to a stored value below valid_from date, required Default today valid_to date, optional NULL = still asked. A question can be retired after people have answered it. Answers survive (an answer is never removed with its question), because "what did they say?" must outlive "do we still ask this?" created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules — event_question

  • choices is present exactly when data_type is choice or multichoice, and never otherwise. Stated as an equivalence rather than a one-way requirement so that a text question cannot carry a stray choices list that the UI might honour.
  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.

Fields — event_answer

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only question_id reference to event question, required person_id reference to person, required Who ANSWERED — for a child, the child. The person who submitted on their behalf is in access_log and in registered_by, not here. Answers are about the person the question concerns value free-form jsonb, required Typed by question.data_type. One loose value rather than a column per type: the alternative is eight nullable columns only one of which is ever set, which is the shape 01a-accounts-and-contacts.md §6 rejected for person_contact answered_at timestamp, audit time Default now answered_by reference to person, optional

Rules — event_answer

  • One answer per question per person — the (question_id, person_id) pair is unique over all rows.
  • An answer is not removed when its question is retired: there is no delete rule from event_question to event_answer.

docs.title: Answers as rows, not JSONB on the registration
docs.text:
This is the choice that makes the feature worth having. The whole reason to collect "dietary requirements" is to be able to answer "who needs a gluten-free meal, and how many?" — and that is a question the data must answer directly: for one event and one question, take every answer given to it, group the answers by the value given, and count each group, largest group first.

With answers stored as a JSONB blob on the registration, that becomes JSON traversal, an index that does not help, and a report nobody writes. The cost is one row per answer — which is exactly the number of things the organization must act on.

docs.title: Reusable question libraries were considered and rejected
docs.text: There is no shared pool of question definitions: no question_code, no library a question is copied from, nothing that has to mean the same thing at two events. A pool earns its keep only when the same question must mean one thing everywhere, and tent preference does not — what one camp asks and what another needs are allowed to differ, and defining a question per event keeps them from having to agree. This is the shape D-044 refused for membership requirements, and it is refused here for the same reason.

docs.title: A question bound to a stored value
docs.text:
One nullable column, bound_attribute_code, and it points at the vocabulary. Set, it says this question asks about the fact stored under that code — nothing more. It never names whose value, and it never names a row. The code has to be one the vocabulary holds, checked on the save path like any other reference by value, and because a definition is retired rather than deleted, the refusal this column can ever need is for a code nobody ever wrote — a typo, or a name invented at a desk. A retired code is legal to bind and binding it is not an error: the questions that were asked under it stay asked, which is what retirement has always meant here.

It prefills as a suggestion. The form shows the person's current value inside the question, and the answerer sees that they are being shown it: they confirm it or they change it, and either way they are the one answering. Nothing is hidden from them and nothing is copied silently, which is the half of the design that makes a stale fact safe to display at all — a value that arrives unasked-for and looks authoritative is worse data than a question, and a value that arrives labelled "this is what we have, is it still right?" is the same value doing good (D-139).

Submitting writes back, as a second act. A confirmed or edited answer writes a fresh person_attribute value dated today, recorded as written by the person who submitted the form, through the same person.edit the answering channel already uses, and audited with that person as its actor (09-attributes §4). The answer itself stays a row of the event either way: the write-back is a second act, not the same row twice, and what lands in the person record is a fresh statement, not a second home for the stored value. Where that write is not permitted it is refused and the answer still saves — a form never half-writes a person.

Which one wins: neither, and that is the shape. The person record wins as of today, because the write-back is dated today and the attribute's history is the record of what was believed when. An answer is not corrected when the record later changes, and the record is not corrected because an old answer said otherwise — they are two dated statements of one fact at two moments, which is how this corpus already treats a name. Where the answer contradicts the stored value the difference is on the screen, in the prefill, and a person who edits the prefill is editing the record: that is the repair route, and it is why the binding is not the silent disagreement the question feared.

What the binding may never become. Not a reference to a person_attribute row id — 00-conventions §4 forbids one from any table, and this binding stays legal precisely because attribute_definition.code is never deleted, is retired instead, and so outlives the person whose values sit under it; a value's key would have made erasure's one hard delete visible. Not a copy in either direction without a person in the loop: no write-back the answerer did not see, and no back-filling of an old answer when the record moves. And not a link that survives a change of mind unnoticed: re-pointing a bound question at a different code is an act somebody must take deliberately, because the answers already given belong to the old code and stay exactly what they were. What this costs is a new path into person_attribute — the first place outside a person's own editing where an attribute value arrives with no staff member in the middle of it — which is why the column is per question, per event, and NULL by default.

docs.title: Health facts, and the discipline this requires
docs.text:
An event form is how the people running an event find out what they need to know about the people who came. Anything a form asks is read by whoever runs that event, and the number of such people is decided by whoever creates the event (D-061, ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §12). "Read by whoever runs that event" is a grant the create writes — event.answer.view on the event, aimed at ORGANIZERS, one of the twelve of §8 — which makes this a checkable warning rather than a nicety: the number of people who can read an event's answers is a grant plus the roster in §3, and both are readable.

The form is not the ceiling on what an organizer may know. There is no medical record: the facts that would have been in one are attributes on the person, and a person holding person.view at the unit can read them — the unit is the only scope there is, so that grant reads everyone's (09-attributes §4). An organizer who holds person.view may already have read the allergy, and any document implying the contrary is making a privacy promise the model does not keep (D-083).

What the form is for: it asks now, about this event, of a person who may not be in the system at all, and its answer carries a date. That is a genuine property the record does not have — a recorded attribute says what somebody believed, once, at no particular time. The two do meet, and they meet by code, not by copy: a question may be bound to an attribute definition, and the meeting is the confirmation pass — a prefill the answerer sees and may change, and a write-back dated today — never a silent prefill (AT-1, D-139). Bound or not, the answer stays the dated statement, and that is what the record cannot be.

Nothing in the data model distinguishes a preference from a condition, and nothing could: D-083 refused the category. "Vegetarian" and "coeliac" are both data_type = 'text' in event_answer.value, so the line is what an organizer types into label — form design guidance, not an enforced constraint:

Belongs on an event form Belongs on the person, as an attribute What the organizers need on the day, for this event Diagnoses, medication, allergies, conditions What a visitor who is not in the system must supply Anything already recorded, curable and audited on the record T-shirt size for a camp that is ordering shirts now Anything whose value outlives the event that asked

Asking a returning camper to restate a recorded allergy at every event is not a privacy measure; it is the same fact, fresher in one table and unmanaged in it. The event answer is where a health fact lands when the organization has not collected it properly — and the fix is the record plus a confirmation pass, not a cleverer form, which is what a bound question is: the record shown so it can be corrected, by the person who owns it.

Nothing about an answer expires. No expiry when the event ends, and no clock on it: the row is a fact about a dated occasion and it is kept, exactly as the registration beside it is (§4) and exactly as a cancelled event keeps its registrations (guard 2 in §8). Erasure reaches it, and empties it rather than deleting it — a redacted person's event_answer.value is set to empty and the row survives, because "they answered that question" and "this is what they said" are two different facts and only the second one is theirs to withdraw (D-140, 00-conventions §8). So the asymmetry is gone: a dietary answer naming a condition and the same sentence recorded as a person_attribute are data of one class — there is no specially-sensitive category, which is not the same as this data being insignificant (D-083) — and they now follow one rule, so the copy a camp leader actually reads is no longer the weakest-protected one. What it costs: an emptied answer still says something — that a question was asked and answered, by whom, on what date — and that residue is deliberate, the same residue D-088 leaves in an audit payload; and it is a rule the store implements rather than one the schema enforces, which is why the erasure check in 06b §5 counts emptied-value answers the way it counts surviving names (EV-2).

Decisions behind this page: D-005, D-023, D-037, D-040, D-043, D-044, D-056, D-057, D-061, D-062, D-065, D-083, D-088, D-090, D-095, D-098, D-099, D-102, D-139, D-140, D-147.

docs.title: Data Model — Events: guards, the three queries, integrity checks
docs.text:
How authority reaches an event, what the module may assume, the three questions a screen asks it, and the checks that hold it together.

Section numbers are shared across the two parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 08-events.md holds §1–§7, 08a §8–§11 (projections and guards, the three queries that matter, integrity checks, open issues).

docs.title: 8. Projections and guards
The unit-authority rule, and can_event() — both deleted
docs.text:
Every event check goes through the ordinary can() and nothing else — or through can_key(), which is that same function's other door and takes no person (05c §10); an integration's call at ('event', 42) is matched exactly the same way, by an allow at the unit or on that event. There is no can_event(person, permission_code, event, at) wrapper and no unit-authority rule for events: an event is an item like any other, and the resolver matches scope exactly. The person whose job is to run the organization's camps passes a check at ('event', 42) because their allow is at the unit, not because anything tested the event.

Who enforces it — can(), with no event-shaped clause in it. The only non-item scope is the unit, and a grant at the unit reaches every item of every type (D-099), so there is no gap between a unit grant and one of that unit's events for anything to close. Why nothing closes one: there is no scope between the unit and an event — nothing to inherit through and nothing to test on the way. Authority reaches an event the same way it reaches any other item, and an event carries no authority of its own (D-102).

docs.title: Selectors that bind to an event
docs.text:
Five sets describe the people connected to an event, and each is a selector that binds to the item being checked — written with no argument inside an item-scope grant, and with an explicit event in every other context. They are seeded rows of selector_type, the registry of data-model/05 §8, and that registry is what makes the two write-path rules below checkable rather than a matter of tact (D-101, D-102).

The four attendance tiers, defined over event_registration columns and nothing else:

Operand Definition Read it as ATTENDED response is attending said yes to this event PLACED response is attending and is_waitlisted is false holds a place — the capacity set (§5) CONFIRMED PLACED and is_confirmed is true the place is paid for, or the event was free ON_WAITLIST response is attending and is_waitlisted is true waiting for a place

These are definitions, not four new ideas, and their shape is arithmetic on two existing columns: CONFIRMED ⊆ PLACED, PLACED and ON_WAITLIST partition ATTENDED, and a not_attending row is in none of them. Nothing is a level and nothing orders anything else; CONFIRMED is not "more" than ON_WAITLIST, it is a different conjunction. The extension of PLACED is the set §5 counts against capacity, and the same partial index serves both (§4).

ORGANIZERS is the fifth, and its definition is the roster in §3 — the labelled, ordered, domain answer to "who runs this", evaluated over event_organizer rows for the event checked. There is no sixth operand, and nothing guardian-shaped can become one. A guardian's authority is a right_level ∈ none | view | write held over a child, read off the guardianship row when the check is about someone other than the actor; it is not a set that the expression language resolves, and GUARDIANS is not a row of selector_type in either spelling (D-113, D-074).

PRESENT(<event>) is refused. An operand over was_present is the obvious sixth attendance tier and it is not available, and the reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register, so a grant aimed at PRESENT would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. The column is a safeguarding signal and is three-valued on purpose (D-067); keeping it out of the selector language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things". Where presence is needed it is needed as a report (§9), and the report is honest about the rows it does not have.

WHITELISTED does not exist, and nothing reserves the name. There is no stored state to name: the nearest facts are source = 'staff' (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. A tier is a state of a registration, and an invitation is not about a registration at all — invited is a grant aimed at that person, a person who never registered is described by the absence of a row (D-059), and one who registers onto a full event is already ON_WAITLIST. So the need is met by rows that exist and this is settled rather than pending: no is_whitelisted column, no fifth tier, no operand, and anyone adding is_whitelisted is reimplementing grants badly. The sentence belongs where the tiers are listed, beside the PRESENT refusal, and it stands there in ../domain/07a §9 (D-148). The count of operands refused here does not move: WHITELISTED was already one of the operands this table does not hold.

Two binding rules, both refused when the grant is saved, both naming the operand in the message:

  1. A bound (argument-less) operand is legal only on an item-scope grant. At the unit there is no item for it to bind to, so a grant at the unit whose expression names PLACED, ATTENDED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST or ORGANIZERS is refused. The explicit form (PLACED(<event>)) remains legal at the unit, and it means the same words with the event written down — which is the difference between the two, not an accident of parsing.
  2. A bound operand is legal only on a matching item type. PLACED on a person_group grant is refused, because that item is not an event. This is selector_type.argument_type checked against grant_scope_type at the write — which is the reason D-101's registry is doing real work and not merely tidying a table.

A consequence of rule 1 worth naming for whoever builds the editor: an audience is a stored row and a grant is a different stored row, so an audience whose expression contains a bound operand is perfectly storable and simply cannot be aimed at a unit-scope grant. The refusal lands on the grant, where D-102 puts it, and the audience browser should show which scopes an expression is usable at rather than letting the save discover it (../domain/07-events.md §7).

The twelve grants an event arrives with, one of which is event.answer.view on ORGANIZERS. "Answers are read by that event's organizers" (D-061) is a row in access_grant, not a clause in the resolver: authority over an event lives in grant rows, and so does this. It is aimed at a set, so it does not contradict D-062 and does not make event_organizer a grant table: adding a cook to the roster changes a set, and the grant keeps pointing at the set. The registered spelling is the catalog's event.answer.view, singular answer; event.answers.view is that one code misspelled, not a second code. It is not alone and it is not shipped: the act that creates an event writes one item-scope allow per event code beside the event row, in the same transaction, each aimed at an audience whose expression is the bare operand ORGANIZERS — every event.* code whose applies_to admits an event, which is all thirteen of them but event.create, held at the unit because nothing owns an event. Twelve rows, derived rather than curated, so the list cannot drift from the catalog the way a hand-written one does (D-151).

Who writes them, which is the question D-102 left open and this section used to hedge. The person creating the event, through the create; the import, once per event it writes, or an imported camp's organizers cannot read that camp's answers. Nothing ships either row, so the module no longer reads a "seed template" — the row-count question that made a template necessary was that a bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant, so one row could never cover every event, and per-event rows are what the check has always counted. That is also the correction this round owed 05d §12, which claimed the opposite in as many words. What the bundle contains besides the answer row is the part to read twice: event.grant_access is in it, so whoever runs an event may grant access to that event without holding access_grant.create at the unit, and event.organizer.manage is in it, so an organizer may add an organizer and widen all eleven others. The ceiling on both was the scope and applies_to, and since D-163 it is those two plus the granter's own twelve — an organizer may hand out what they hold at that one event and nothing wider, which binds nobody in practice because the twelve are exactly what an organizer has, and stops only the grant that reaches past their own event. system.admin is unit-only and cannot be written onto an item at all, which is the guarantee D-099 left behind when it deleted the levels; and the create that wrote these twelve is the one write D-170 exempts from the granter's ceiling, which is why the next sentence matters as much as this one. Integrity check 2 in §10 is the net for a missing bundle, and check 1 for a grant saved at a scope that cannot bind it.

The preview requirement this creates. "Who does this grant reach?" is not a property of a grant row once an operand binds: PLACED is different people on different events. The editor must therefore compute the expansion for an item and name the item it computed against. The same bound holds inside a check: the item is bound at resolution, so nothing expanded while computing one item may be reused for another. Stated as a requirement in ../domain/07-events.md §7. That expansion is not capped or deferred: a few dozen registrants on a typical event and a big camp on the order of two hundred is a preview nobody feels — a size stated, not measured, with a named trigger to reopen it (D-112).

There is no permission cache. A check resolves; a request memoizes; the only cached thing is a compilation — an expression root plus ruleset_version, holding no person and no item (D-114). ruleset_version keys that compilation, not an answer, and it is bumped by audience_operand and selector_type alone: a write to event_registration changes no rule's text and is not a ruleset write.

So a registration write is visible on the next check. Marking a register, confirming a place, flipping is_confirmed or promoting somebody off the waitlist changes who is in ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED and ON_WAITLIST, and the change is visible on the check immediately after the write, with no job in between, because a check resolves the expression against live rows. The same is true of ORGANIZERS, which reads the organizer rows and not the registration table at all: five bound operands, five live reads, and a birthday crossing OLDER(n) moves an answer on exactly the same footing as a registration write does. This immediacy is by construction, not by policy: no row anywhere in the schema maps a person to an answer (invariant 19), so no answer can lag the rows it is computed from.

Who enforces "a registration change reaches an answer" — nobody, because there is nothing left to invalidate (D-081). The read path does it, and a page cannot opt out of a read path the way it can forget to add a row to a list.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
Guard 1 — the registration window. No registration row may be created for an event whose window does not admit it. The guard runs inside the transaction that inserts the row, on every insert path — which makes that coverage a requirement on the paths, not a property the database supplies for them. Steps 4 and 5 read the event's own dates and step 2 exempts a source value, so no constraint states this rule and no report would catch a violation the way a window violation should be caught: at the write. The order is a rule: "there is no such event" must be settled before anything reads the event's dates, and the staff carve-out must be answered before the checks it overrides.

  1. Read the event the registration names. If there is no such event, refuse the row — a registration cannot name an event that does not exist.
  2. If source is staff, admit the row and stop here. Staff may always register, including at a cancelled event (to record who had been coming) — they are acting deliberately and are attributed.
  3. Otherwise refuse the row if the event is cancelled (cancelled_at is set).
  4. Refuse it if registration_opens_at is set and has not yet arrived.
  5. Refuse it if the effective close has passed — registration_closes_at, or starts_at when registration_closes_at is absent. This is where "NULL = open until the event starts" is enforced.
  6. Admit the row.

Guard 2 — an event with registrations cannot be deleted. Deleting an event is refused as soon as the event has any registration row at all, and the refusal says what to do instead: cancel it (set cancelled_at) so the record of who was coming survives. Cancellation is the mechanism.

Guard 2 is what makes the cascade in §3 safe. Organizers cascade when an event is deleted — but an event that anyone registered for cannot be deleted at all. So the cascade can only ever fire on a draft with no registrations, which is the only case where losing the roster is harmless.

docs.title: 9. The three queries that matter
Who has not replied yet?
docs.text:
"Unanswered" is a subtraction (../domain/07-events.md §3). The subtrahend is who the event is open to — which, for an open event, is an audience.

The question asked of one camp is: every person who may register for it and has not answered. The audience is the eligible set, the registration table is the answered set, and the answer is the difference between them, listed by preferred name. What makes the question answerable at all:

  • The eligible set is evaluated, not stored: it is the people named by the live allow grants of event.register_self — at the unit, which reaches this event, or on this event — through their audiences, assessed as of the day the question is asked, not as of the day the grant was written. A child who joined a group last week is on this list; a child who has left is not.
  • Only live allows count, and a person against whom a live deny of the same code applies is not eligible however many allows reach them — deny is absolute, and an eligibility list that ignored it would chase people who were deliberately excluded (D-013).
  • Where the grant's expression contains a bound operand, the eligible set is computed against this event, which is the only thing it can mean (§8).
  • The answered set is one row per person at most (§4), so the subtraction cannot leave the same person on the list twice.
  • People who have been merged away are excluded, so a tombstone never turns up on a list somebody is being asked to chase.

This is the query that would be impossible if unanswered were a stored value, because the eligible set — an audience, evaluated as a rule — is what defines the question. Storing "unanswered" rows would mean enumerating an audience into rows, and re-enumerating whenever a child joins a group.

docs.title: Who is actually coming?
docs.text:
Four numbers an organizer needs about one event, in one row, all counted over that event's attending registrations: how many are not waitlisted (coming), how many are waitlisted (waiting), how many are unconfirmed and not waitlisted (holding a place without having paid), and the event's capacity — the limit. An event with no registrations still has to produce the row, with zeros. attending > capacity is the overrun, and it is visible here rather than prevented (§10 check 5).

The first two of the four are PLACED and ON_WAITLIST counted rather than listed, and the third is PLACED minus CONFIRMED. The selector definitions in §8 and the counts here are one set of facts stated twice on purpose: the screen and the grant must not be able to disagree about who "coming" means.

docs.title: Who was actually there?
docs.text:
For one camp, the attending registrations listed with each person's preferred name, birth date and was_present, with the unmarked listed first — the unmarked sort ahead of both a mark and an absence recorded as false, because the unmarked are the work remaining. This is the camp roster as a safeguarding record, not a plan.

NULLS FIRST puts the unmarked at the top, which is the work remaining. Once every row is true or false, this is the answer to "who was in the organization's care at that camp" — and it is the reason was_present is three-valued rather than a boolean defaulting to false.

This report has no selector twin, and that is the point. Nothing in the selector language computes over was_present, so no grant can reach fewer people because the register was never taken. §8 states the refusal; this query is the reason it matters.

Nor does the column have a clock of its own or a permission of its own, and that is a ruling. Presence is a column of a registration and inherits everything a registration is: the retention registrations have, which is no expiry and no clock, and the codes that already reach the roster and the mark (D-147). A presence.retention shorter than the event's was refused because it would delete the answer to this query on somebody's number, and a presence.view narrower than the roster's was refused because it would be a permission whose whole purpose is to hide a fact from the people who are asking because they were there. There is no presence_record table and nothing behind this roster is a register: this system keeps no safeguarding register — no background checks are recorded (D-043) and there is no medical record (D-083) — and a column with a special clock and a special permission would have been the first wall of an archive this design has refused four times. What protects the column is that it is boring: the index behind this query (§4) serves a report and no operand, the rows are readable with the codes that reach the event, and erasure reaches them the way it reaches organizational history — the person stops being identifiable and the mark stays (00-conventions §8).

docs.title: 10. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. A bound selector on a grant that cannot bind it. Counts live grants whose expression contains ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, ON_WAITLIST or ORGANIZERS in argument-less form and whose scope is the unit, or whose scope is an item of a type other than the operand's argument_type. Both rules are refused on the write path (§8), so a non-zero result is evidence about the code, not the data: somebody added a path that saves a grant without going through the check, and a grant like this resolves to the empty set and silently authorizes nobody.
  2. An event whose organizers do not hold the twelve. Counts non-cancelled events for which any of the twelve is missing — a live allow, on that event, of each event.* code except event.create, aimed at an audience whose expression is the bare operand ORGANIZERS (§8). Every event is counted, not only events that already have an organizer row: the twelve are written at the create, while that set is still empty, so an event nobody has staffed yet is owed all twelve already. The report names which of the twelve are missing, because eleven of a bundle is the same defect wearing different clothes — a missing event.answer.view means the organizers cannot read the answers of the camp they are running (⚠⚠, and the row this report was originally written for), a missing event.manage_participants means they cannot fix the roster at the gate. The failure shape is the one check 10 knows well: an event imported or created by a path that forgot, where every row it left behind is individually correct. Since D-151 this report has an author to name: an event arrived without its bundle through some one create or some one batch, which makes it a bug report about a path rather than about a missing migration. The count is the same either way, and so is the camp whose organizers cannot read anything.
  3. An event with no organizer. Counts events that are neither cancelled nor already begun and have no event_organizer row at all — an event nobody is running: either abandoned mid-setup, or a data-entry error. Not a rule on write, because an event is legitimately created before its organizers are named.
  4. A registration held by a person who has been merged away. Counts registrations whose person carries a merge pointer. The merge should have repointed them; a non-zero result catches the ones it missed.
  5. An event running over its stated capacity. Counts, for each non-cancelled event that has a capacity, its PLACED registrations, and reports the events where that count exceeds the capacity. PERMITTED — a staff registration may exceed deliberately (../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §8) — so this is a report, not an error. A pattern of overruns means the capacity numbers are wrong, not that the rule is.
  6. An unpaid registration holding a place past the waitlist deadline. Counts attending, non-waitlisted registrations on a non-cancelled event whose waitlist_deadline has passed and whose fee obligation is not yet paid — unpaid or partially_paid, which is the whole enum since D-159 deleted overdue along with written_off: lateness lives only in the obligation's due_date, so a status that is not paid and a due_date in the past is overdue (07-finance.md §2). A predicate still naming overdue would match nothing at all and print a clean result. It should be empty once the release in §5 has run — a non-empty result means the job is not running.
  7. An answer to a question the person was never registered for. Counts answers whose person has no registration for the event that owns the question. Either the registration was deleted, or the answer was written against the wrong person.

  8. Presence marked on a registration that declined. Counts not_attending registrations whose was_present is not absent. Contradictory: you cannot have been present at a thing you said you were not attending. Nothing above forbids the combination, so this is a written prohibition and a check rather than a guard — a prohibition nobody runs is a convention, not a guarantee.

  9. A registration outside its event's registration window. Counts registrations whose created_at — the moment the row was written, which is the moment Guard 1 governs, and not responded_at, which is when the answer was given — falls before the window opens or after it closes, excluding the ones an organizer recorded deliberately (source = 'staff', whose window is the event's own period). Guard 1 in §8 is supposed to make the first two shapes impossible, and there is no constraint behind that guard — a window spans two columns of two tables, so the check runs inside the writing transaction or nowhere (shape 3). A non-zero result is therefore evidence about the code, not the data: someone added a second path that places a registration.

  10. A fee-bearing event with registrations and no obligations. Counts non-cancelled events that require a fee and have at least one registration, where no fee_obligation exists for some of those registrations. The obligation is created by the code that places the registration (§6); there is no rule attached to the registration row that would create it, so a path that forgets produces a person with a confirmed place and no bill — invisible to every check here, because every row it left behind is individually correct. Money-versus-roster reconciliation (07-finance.md §2) is the same discovery arriving later and more expensively; this is the version worth running nightly.

Checks 1, 2 and 10 are the same shape and should be read as one warning. Each tests whether a piece of code that nothing else depends on actually ran: the grant save, the event creation, the placing rule. Each will read empty on correct data and each is the kind of bug that a schema change never surfaces, because every row a forgotten step leaves behind is individually valid.

Check 5 is the important one to read correctly. It will produce rows, and that is not a failure — exceeding capacity is a permitted, attributed act (../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §8). What the report is for is the pattern: an event that overruns every year has a capacity number that is wrong, and the fix is to change the number rather than to start refusing people.

Numbering: the numbers of checks 1–10 are cited from other files; they are not reassigned.

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
Tracked in ../open-questions.md under G. Events.

  • The age ceiling on an open event: there is none (D-070). No min_age/max_age on event, no age branch anywhere in the registration path. If it is ever revisited the shape is a new seeded selector operand, not a column on the row.
  • event.manage_participants and event.presence.mark are two codes. Marking a register is a separate code, not a level below the roster — there are no levels — which is the same protection stated in the only vocabulary D-099 leaves (D-099; §4, EV-5).
  • What else an organizer should hold — settled: everything the event has, on that event. The question was asked because D-102 shipped event.answer.view alone, leaving an organizer who held no unit-scope grant able to read the answers of a camp and able to do nothing else at it, which read as an omission and was not resolved by this module adding rows on its own initiative. It is resolved by not seeding anything: the create writes one allow per event code whose applies_to admits an event, so the answer to "what may an organizer do?" is twelve rows anyone can list, and the answer to "what may an organizer do elsewhere?" is nothing, which is the shape D-100 says an office has anyway (§3, §8, D-151).
  • Who writes the per-event grant — settled: the create, and the import. This used to be answered as "a template the creation path and the import both instantiate", with the observation that D-102 does not say (§8, check 2). There is no template, because there is no seed — the rows are ordinary grants written in the event's own transaction by whoever holds event.create, and the import owes twelve of them for every event row it writes (D-151).
  • Retention of event_answer — settled: nothing expires, and erasure empties the value. Neither a registration nor an answer ends with its event, and neither ends on a clock; what reaches an answer is erasure, which sets value to empty and leaves the row (§7, 00-conventions §8). The asymmetry this question rested on — the same fact kept indefinitely as a person_attribute and quietly discarded as the answer a camp leader reads — is closed by making the two rules agree, which is the stronger answer than the clock it replaces (D-083, D-140; EV-2).
  • Cancelled events and fees. Cancelling keeps the registrations. What it does to the obligations is the finance module's (§6), and for events it has an answer (D-076): cancelling voids the outstanding requests, and money that already arrived waits in the unmatched queue (07-finance.md §2b).
  • was_present as a safeguarding record — settled: it stays a column of the registration. No retention of its own and no permission of its own: it inherits both from the registration, and the codes that already reach the roster are the codes that read it (§9). PRESENT stays refused, so presence governs nothing about access, and no presence_record table is coming either, because this system keeps no safeguarding register — no background checks are recorded (D-043), no medical record exists (D-083) — and a clock plus a permission would have been the first wall of one (D-147; EV-4).
  • Whether organizers should be access_grants after all. The mechanism is settled — a set named by a selector, aimed at by grants — and D-062's answer stands: the roster is not itself a grant. What used to hang off that question — whether more codes should reach ORGANIZERS — is settled beside it, by the create writing the event's whole code family onto the event (../domain/07-events.md §5).
  • Waitlist notification. Promotion is deliberate; telling the promoted person is not designed. It belongs to the communication module.

Decisions behind this page: D-013, D-043, D-059, D-061, D-062, D-067, D-070, D-074, D-076, D-081, D-083, D-099, D-101, D-102, D-112, D-113, D-114, D-140, D-147, D-148.

docs.title: Data Model — Personal Attributes
docs.text:
The layer every fact about a person lives in, once you subtract what they are called and counted as. Written because D-083 removed the category this file might otherwise have been built around — a privileged medical record — and D-084 put an organization-maintained vocabulary in its place.

Read domain/08-person-data.md first if the word "attribute" makes this look like a dumping ground. It is the opposite: a layer with a defined boundary, a curated vocabulary, and an explicit list of what it cannot do.

docs.title: 1. The sentence, and the boundary it draws
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is descriptive data of one class, held in fields, whose meaning the organization defines at runtime. Not files. Not a per-domain table each with its own permission codes. One kind of data, one kind of access, one vocabulary.

That sentence is a scope claim inherited almost verbatim from the answer that produced D-083, and it is deliberately wider than "health data". A drug dosage and a shoe size are the same kind of object: something the organization recorded about a person, which will be wrong in three years, which nobody can enumerate in advance.

The boundary is drawn by rules, not by sensitivity.

Stays structured, in its own table Becomes an attribute person_name history, gender, birth_date + birth_date_precision — 01-identity §2–3 Health: allergies, medication, conditions, instructions, checkups person_contact — purpose, primary flag, validity — 01a §6 Education, occupations, qualifications, languages person_identifier — per-scheme uniqueness — 01a §7 Insurance numbers, membership numbers of other bodies, measurements, clothing sizes account, account_credential — 01a §4–5 Dietary habits, transport preferences, notes, anything collected this season

The test for the left column: does a rule exist that this layer physically cannot hold? "Exactly one primary postal contact among the open rows", "a school id may repeat, a birth number may not", "one current name per person" — each is a constraint over a known set of columns. A key/value table has no known set of columns; that is its entire purpose. Folding those four tables in would have relocated working constraints into application code and been called uniformity, which is shape 3 built on purpose. Identity is closed because it was enumerated years ago and has not changed since. Description is open because nobody can enumerate it. That is the whole boundary, and it is worth restating in review whenever a new table tempts someone to put it in either column.

What is not here either, because it is not data about a person: relationships (04-relationships), belonging (03-membership), money (07-finance), event registrations and their answers (08-events), authority (05-authorization).

docs.title: 2. attribute_definition — the vocabulary
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id code text, required The stable handle. Stored as typed, compared normalized — see the rules below. label text, required What a human sees. One language, and see the note on the vocabulary below (D-149). description free text, optional What belongs in this field and what does not. Cheap to write, and the only defence against a code meaning four things to four people. value_type text, required One of: text, long_text, number, date, yes_no, one_of, date_year. Governs the input drawn and the warning given — not what may be saved (§4 of this file's rules, D-084). value_unit text, optional Display suffix — kg, cm. Rendering only. allow_multiple boolean, required, default false Whether more than one value may be current at once. Allergies: yes. Blood type: no. status text, required One of: live, retired. Two values, no third (D-084, D-141) — a definition is live at its save and retired is the only other thing it can be. See the status rules. category text, optional Display grouping — health, contact-admin, program. Grouping only: it grants nothing and restricts nothing, and any sentence that says otherwise is reintroducing the sub-resource D-083 removed. sort_order integer, optional retired_at, retired_reason timestamp, free text Retiring is an administrative act and is explained. Standard columns 00-conventions §7.

Allowed values for one_of live in a small child table, attribute_option: definition, code, label, sort_order, status. It is a table rather than a comma-separated string because options are renamed, retired and re-ordered, and a retired option must keep meaning what it meant on the day it was chosen — a value stored against it is a historical fact.

Words are stored in one language: the one the organization writes in (D-149). No label_cs/label_en pair, no translation table, no per-language row, no locale column in either table above. The refusal is about what a label is: label is what a human sees, and a label is not a rendering of something more authoritative underneath it — a row holding two labels would have to be asked which of the two the record is, and whichever answer was chosen would demote the other to a translation of it. The families who read another language are served by whoever reads the question aloud or writes it down, and by an event form's own question text, which is free text typed in whichever language the event is run in and is not a vocabulary item: the vocabulary is for the record, the form is for the conversation, and only one of the two has to be stable enough to query. What it costs: an imported label arrives in whatever language the paper form was in and stays there, so correcting it is a curation act under attribute.define and not a locale switch — and an organization that genuinely runs in two languages will hold two codes for one fact, a misery this design does not prevent and does not pretend to.

Rules

  • Codes are unique in normalized form. Before comparison a code is trimmed, case-folded and has internal whitespace collapsed. Allergy, allergy and allergy are one code, and the second one is refused on write. This is the only anti-duplication rule the database can still enforce here, which is exactly why it is stated as a rule and not as a convention.
  • A definition is live at the save. attribute.define is the curating permission, and the same person's write that names a code publishes it — no review list, no waiting, no age-out, and no curator role: the permission is the curator (D-141), because a role is an office that confers nothing (D-100) and the only thing here that curates is a permission. A value may not invent a code: a value recorded for a code that does not exist is an error at the write, not a definition waiting for somebody. What this costs is stated rather than smoothed over — a bad code is live the moment it is saved, and every value recorded against it, a real value on a real person, inherits it from that moment. The defence is three things and there is no fourth: the save needs a permission, the trail records every save, and the code can be retired — which keeps its values and stops new ones (D-109).
  • Retiring keeps the values. A retired code leaves data entry and stays readable, reportable and revivable. Deleting the label must never delete the fact underneath it: a code discovered to have been named badly is an administrative event, and if retiring it destroyed nine years of records it will never be retired, and the vocabulary accretes instead of being curated — the slow failure this whole table is arranged to avoid.
  • A definition with values may not be deleted, only retired (00-conventions §9 — references restrict, none cascade). A definition with no values ever recorded may be deleted, and that is the only delete this table offers.
  • Changing value_type does not rewrite values. Existing values are kept as they were written; the new type governs what is typed from then on. A type change is a display decision, and the history is not the display's to correct.
  • allow_multiple may go false → true freely, and true → false only with a report. Turning it off does not merge existing multiples; it leaves the database holding a shape the definition forbids, which §8 check 3 will then report forever. Ask first whether the multiples are real.

Permission. Creating, renaming, merging or retiring a definition needs attribute.define (permission catalog). Recording a value needs no new permission — see §4. One of those four acts stopped being freely available in round 20, and it is the rename: a definition whose code an event question is bound to is now a code something references, and a code that is referenced may not be renamed — a rename would silently re-answer every form that was asked under the old name, leaving no row in the wrong state for a report to find, which is the shape this rule exists for (D-139). A merge is still a merge, and it is the deliberate half: merging two codes carries the questions bound to the disappearing one over to the surviving one as part of the act, because an answer recorded under a code has to keep meaning what it meant when it was given. Retiring was never affected: a retired definition keeps its code, and a bound question asked against a retired code is the design working, not a dangling reference.

docs.title: 3. person_attribute — a value one person has
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required attribute_definition_id reference to attribute_definition, required Points at the vocabulary, live or retired; never at nothing. A value with no code is a note, and notes are their own code. value text, required One column, always text. Not a jsonb, not parallel typed columns. See the note below. value_option_id reference to attribute_option, optional Set when the type is one_of; the value text is then a denormalisation kept for display, and the option reference is the truth. recorded_note free text, optional "the doctor said this may change in spring". Kept beside the value rather than inside it, so the value stays comparable. source text, optional self, guardian, staff, legacy_import. Standard columns created_at / created_by double as recorded at / recorded by.

There are no valid_from / valid_to columns, and that is a decision rather than an omission. A row here is the current belief, overwritten in place; the sequence of beliefs is in audit_log (D-085), which holds those values and is therefore the table §6 is about — this document's history is a permission mark away from being an empty list, and saying the two are connected is the most this section can honestly do about it. The corpus gives periods to things that are true over an interval — a membership, a contact address, an assignment — and a descriptive value is not that: it is a statement whose truth is asserted now about whatever it is about, with a timestamp on the assertion. Putting periods here would invite a UI that asks when an allergy began, which is a medical question the organization is not competent to record and has no rule that could use.

value is one text column, and there are no typed siblings. A value_number and a value_date beside it would let the database do something useful with a date — and would then make 2019, recorded as a year for a checkup, unsavable, which is the failure D-084 refuses: an empty field behind a validation error is a worse record than an imprecise one. The type belongs to the definition and to the form renderer; the storage stays uniform. What that costs is listed in §5 rather than discovered later.

Rules

  • A value may not be blank. Absence is the absence of a row (D-059); an empty string is a lie that looks like an answer.
  • At most one current value per (person, definition) unless the definition allows multiple. One row per pair, because there is no history — so the rule is a plain uniqueness rule except that whether it applies depends on a column in another table, which no constraint can express: shape 3. Check inside the writing transaction, and report the survivors (§8 check 3). A partial unique index would be the right tool for the single-valued definitions and the wrong tool for the rest; choosing per definition is how this rule becomes a report instead of a guarantee.
  • Overwriting is an update, not a delete-and-insert. The row keeps its created_at — that is when this fact first entered the system, which is a question someone asks — and the changed value with its author lands in the audit trail.

A bound event question may prefill from this table and write back into it. The binding lives on the question, not here: event_question.bound_attribute_code, nullable, pointing at a definition code and never at a person_attribute row (D-139). The form prefills the person's current value as a suggestion the answerer confirms or edits — nothing is hidden from them and nothing is silently copied — and submitting performs a second act: a new value in this table, dated today, recorded as written by the person who answered, while the answer itself stays a row of the event. The binding survives everything it could be accused of because of what it names: a definition code is never deleted and is retired instead, so it outlives the person whose values sit under it, and 00-conventions §4's rule that nothing may reference a person_attribute row — the condition on which erasure's one hard delete stays invisible — is untouched. What the binding may never become: a reference to a row id, which stays exactly as forbidden as §4 says it is, and a second home for the value, which it is not — prefill is a suggestion, the write-back is a fresh value, and a form answer and a stored value are two dated statements of one fact at two moments, the same shape this corpus already uses for a name.

Indexes — on person_id (every read is per person), on attribute_definition_id (every report is per code), and the per-(person, definition) rule above.

docs.title: 4. Who may read, and who may write
docs.text:
Read: person.view, and nothing else. No attribute.* read permission exists, because there is nothing to gate that person.view does not already gate (D-083). The three channels behave normally:

  • A unit leader holding person.view scoped to their own unit reads their own members' descriptive data, including an allergy list.
  • A guardian at view or write reads the child's whole record; at none, none of it.
  • A person reads their own.

This makes person.view the widest read permission in the system, and the catalog marks it accordingly rather than leaving it at the level it had when the record was smaller than the person. Any future narrowing — "read everything except…" — is a decision entry about a second grant scope, not a new code with a suggestive name (E-7 is closed for exactly this reason).

Write: person.edit for values, attribute.define for the vocabulary. That split is the design: data entry is open to anyone who can already edit the person, because the alternative is the fact never getting recorded; the vocabulary is narrow, because the vocabulary is what makes the data queryable. What the split no longer offers is an escape valve. A value arriving for a code that does not exist is an error at the write, not a proposal waiting for somebody (D-141): the leader with a drug name at 23:00 either types it under a code that exists or says nothing, and that failure — the fact buried in a notes value, or the fact absent — is the price the strict rule pays on purpose, because a vocabulary is the one registry where an unreviewed addition is permanent in effect even where it is deletable in principle. The write-back of a bound form question is not a third path either: it goes through the same person.edit the answering channel already uses, is audited with the answerer as its actor, and is refused — the form still saving its answer — where the write is not permitted, so a form never half-writes a person (D-139).

docs.title: 5. What this design cannot do
docs.text:
Stated here because an open key/value layer is repeatedly described as flexible by people who have not yet needed any of these, and because D-084 was taken with them in view rather than in the abstract.

Cannot Why What is done instead Constrain a value No constraint can reference the contents of a row chosen at runtime The definition's type drives a warning; a human may always save Type-check at the database Values are one text column ISO-format by convention, and §8 check 6 reports a type that is wrong for the whole definition Compare or aggregate safely 12 and 12 kg and twelve are three strings Report on the one_of codes; treat free text as a list to read, not a number Express the one-value rule as a constraint The rule reads another table (shape 3) Enforced in the writing transaction (§3), which is a guard and not a constraint; §8 check 3 reports what got past it. The two are not alternatives — one stops it, the other notices it did not Answer "what did we believe in 2019" from business data Rows hold the current belief only audit_log, which holds the values themselves (§6) and which D-081 records as the corpus's weakest control. This is the accepted risk, not a footnote: the history is real and nothing but an omitted line of code stands between it and being empty — and since D-088, nothing at all stands between it and being empty after the payload window closes (§6) Restrict one field to some readers D-083 refused a privileged subset One scope over one record; a court-ordered exception is a decision entry, not a code Trust that a code means one thing Codes are typed by humans Normalized uniqueness, description on every definition, §8 check 1, and a save that needs attribute.define — the permission is the curator (D-141) Keep a bound form's answer and the stored value equal A bound question prefills from the value and writes a new one back (D-139); the two are one fact stated at two dated moments, and nothing reconciles them The value wins as of today, because it is the row dated today; the prefill is where a disagreement shows itself, and neither row is rewritten when the other changes

docs.title: 6. Erasure, retirement, and the audit payload
docs.text:
Two opposite operations, and confusing them is the obvious mistake.

  • Retiring a code is administrative and keeps values. The label leaves service; the facts stay.
  • Redacting a person is legal and erases values. When a person is anonymised (00-conventions §8), every row in this table belonging to them is deleted. A redacted person with attribute values attached is a redaction that did not happen — §8 check 5, the one check here whose non-zero result is a breach rather than a report.

The trail holds these values, and that is the load-bearing consequence of the whole module. An audit entry about a person_attribute carries the before and after images, as it does for a contact point or an assignment. Three things had to be true for that to be the right call, and it is worth reading them as a dependency rather than as reassurance:

  • D-083 says a diagnosis is not a different kind of fact from a shoe size, so a rule that stripped attribute values out of the payload while logging a change of address with its value would be a sensitive subset of the person record, reintroduced as a list of table names after it was deleted as a list of permission names.
  • D-085 overwrites values in place because the trail is their history, so a payload without values is not a conservative trail, it is no trail: the question in §5's table becomes unanswerable by design, and the reason overwrite was cheap enough to choose disappears with it.
  • Therefore the guard on audit_log carries person data now. An audit entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it quotes, which is written as a requirement on audit.view in appendix/permission-catalog-a-codes.md §8 and argued in 05-authorization §9 — where the case against copying data into a less-guarded place is, in this table, a description of the table itself. That single guard is a decision, not an omission: audit.view is the whole gate — one permission, one check, no per-entry filter (D-138). The alternative was a per-entry check inside the history view asking whether this reader could see this field; it would have been correct, and it would have made what an officer can read about 2019 depend on an audience expression changed last week — and the trail's value is that it is legible without re-resolving the past, which is exactly what such a check spends. The widening is therefore a stated property of the code rather than something left to be discovered: it opens the entire trail, it is granted rarely, and it is marked.

Those payloads now expire, which is a consequence of D-088 and not a detail of it. Audit rows live as long as the system; their old_values/new_values are emptied 24 months after they are written. Read that against the paragraph above and both halves are true at once: the trail is the only history this table has, and it stops being a history after two years. The honest description of what §5's row costs is therefore not "no temporal columns" but no long history — three decisions stacked, none of them wrong on its own: values live in one row that is overwritten, the copy of them depends on a write path remembering to log, and the copy ages out.

The window is not a mitigation of that property, and it is not the guard either. It bounds how long a value sits where a holder of audit.view can read it, not who can read it while it sits. If the long history is ever actually needed — by a safeguarding review, or by a dispute about what was known and when — the fix is temporal columns on the value, which reverses D-085. It is not a longer payload window, because stretching the window stretches exactly the guard D-086 graded, and D-083 refuses to keep a second copy somewhere safer.

What is left of the redactor is small, and says so. It scrubs the values that must never be logged at all — credentials, tokens, integration secrets — and it stopped carrying the personal-data case when the sensitive subset went: a key-name list cannot protect a table whose column names this organization invents at runtime, and allergy is not on it and never will be. 00-conventions §8 states that once for the whole schema, and 06-audit §2.2 keeps the withdrawn rule visible so nobody reinstates it by inference.

Erasure is the one thing here that is absolute. Erasing a person deletes their rows and removes their values from payloads already written, however lawfully (06-audit §4); a trail that keeps what the person asked to have forgotten is not a history, it is the thing they asked to be rid of, filed where it reads well.

docs.title: 7. The legacy import, which is where the vocabulary comes from
docs.text:
The old system's columns become codes, and this is the largest single event in the life of the attribute layer — most of the first few hundred definitions arrive here rather than from a deliberate act of design, because the corpus you have is thousands of roster rows with free-text columns beside them. That is one file arriving with the organization's descriptive vocabulary in it, and it changes how the mapping has to be reviewed.

  • Every raw field name in a batch must map to a code, be mapped to discarded with a reason, or stop the batch. Silently dropping an unmapped column is how a decade of a fact the organization collected disappears on a Tuesday.
  • An unmapped column is an error at apply time. The batch refuses and names the column; a value may not invent a code, and a column may not borrow one by similarity either. Nothing guesses at import time, because an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable — merging near-duplicates is a curation act afterwards, by a human holding attribute.define, where the trail can see it (D-141).
  • The map is authored against a vocabulary that already exists. The import does not bootstrap the vocabulary, it fills it in: every code the map names must be defined and live before the batch applies, or the batch refuses. This is not a trap but the shape the largest single event in this layer's life actually has — the map is authored and read before the batch applies, as one artefact, top to bottom, so whoever wrote the map wrote the vocabulary first, and the codes arrive live because they were live before the batch was ever typed. The cost is stated plainly: the first few hundred definitions are a writing job under attribute.define that must happen before the import that seemingly produces them, and a batch held at the door for an undefined column is this design working, not failing.
  • The mapping is recorded on the batch, in import_batch.field_mapping, one entry per raw column (06-audit §3 explains why the grain is a column and not a staged row, which is the plausible wrong answer). The mapping is not the schema; changing it is an act of curation with an audit entry, not a migration.

docs.title: 8. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. Codes close enough to be the same thing — same normalized form after stripping punctuation and collapsing plural forms, or the same label. A list to read, not a failure, and the continuous cost of an open vocabulary.
  2. A live definition with no values ever recorded. Retirable. Worth knowing: a dead code in a picker is a small tax paid by everyone who opens the form.
  3. More than one current value for a definition that forbids multiples. The bypass of §3's cross-table rule — an import, a hand-fix, a path that skipped the check. Non-zero means the guard is missing, not that the data is odd.
  4. A value that is blank, whitespace, or longer than the type could have produced. A yes_no code with a three-sentence value is a definition being used as a note field, and the report is a conversation about which one it should have been.
  5. A redacted person with attribute rows, or with attribute values still present in audit_log. Should never be non-empty; this is the erasure guarantee.
  6. A definition whose values contradict its declared type wholesale — a date code where nothing parses as a date. The type is advisory for one value and a signal for all of them: at that point the definition is wrong, not the data.

Check 5 is the one to open the day it is non-empty: a person's data outliving their erasure, and nothing in this design tells anyone that it has — reading this report is the whole control there is (D-164). Check 3 is the one that indicts the code rather than the data: non-zero there means some write path skipped §3's guard, and the fix is the path, not the rows. Check 1 is the vocabulary talking — never a failure, only the permanent cost of an open vocabulary, and the list worth reading before saving a near-duplicate. Everything else on this list is housekeeping.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text: None registered.
