If a role has a period and an assignment does not, then an assignment from 2019 rests on a role that is "not in force" — so was that person a leader in 2019? The honest answers are either "yes, and the role's period is irrelevant" (in which case the role's period never did anything) or "who knows" (in which case the design has damaged its own history). Making the role permanently valid avoids the question entirely.

What this removes. The whole retirement mechanism D-052 introduced:

Removed Replaced by role.valid_from, role.valid_to, ck_role_period, ix_role_current nothing — the columns are gone role.retire permission role.unassign, per assignment. A role nobody holds is unused, not retired The resolver's check on the role's period (channel 4) nothing. Channel 4 already checks the assignment's period, which was always the load-bearing one uq_role_code_current (partial unique, so retired codes could be reused) code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE — plain, because codes are never in competition Integrity check 17 (roles expiring while held) Reformulated as check 17 (unused roles) — a glance, not a warning

What this keeps from D-052. Roles are still runtime data: created, edited, assigned and — if never assigned — deleted. is_system still guard-rails deletion. role and role_permission are still audited, because role.edit still changes effective permissions for every holder at once. The BEFORE DELETE trigger stays.

The consequence worth carrying forward. Because a role never expires, the only thing that ends authority is the assignment ending. That puts the entire weight on role_assignment.valid_to, which is exactly where the design already wanted it — and it is why the open-ended assignment is called the classic access failure (data-model/05 §4). A role-based permission now has no expiry of its own; it is the assignment or nothing.

See: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3, ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §7.

docs.title: D-054 — The sub-unit vocabulary is not seeded; the organization defines its own types
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4

Superseded by D-097: there is no unit-type vocabulary left to seed or to withhold. 'The organization defines its own labels and the platform ships none' transfers intact to person_group and role, where it remains the rule.

Amends: D-008 in spirit; the self-referencing table is untouched

Decision. The unit-type seed data contains exactly one row: the root. No sub-unit types are seeded at all. org_unit_type is runtime data, like role (D-052): the organization creates the types it uses, renames them, and adds new ones as its structure changes.

Why. Your answer: "Seed only the root."

pack/group/team was a placeholder, and it was the last thing in the schema that was comfortably wrong — three invented words that would have read as a specification to anyone implementing the system. The deeper reason to remove rather than correct it: the organization's own vocabulary is not knowable at specification time, and guessing it badly is worse than not guessing. This is the same argument as D-052 applied to units. The retired national/region/district ladder (D-035) was a guess; so was its replacement.

Consequence: nesting is entirely permissive. org_unit_type_rule exists and is seeded with nothing, so any type may sit under any other — including under the root — until the organization states a rule. This was already true with the placeholder (data-model/02 §10); it is now true with no ambiguity about which types the permissiveness applies to. A new type is usable the moment it is created.

Consequence: the root type is special and must be seeded. The organization row stays, because exactly one unit must have parent_unit_id IS NULL (D-035) and that unit needs a type. It also carries the property that matters: allows_minors = false on the root type, since no minor belongs to "The Organization" as a unit — minors hold memberships and sub-unit participation.

What this means for every example in these docs. The words pack, troop, section and group still appear throughout the documentation as illustration — "a pack has its own roster" is how the prose explains a self-governing sub-unit. They are not types the system ships with. Read them as "some sub-unit type the organization has defined", the same way unit_leader in §11 of the permission catalog is a role the organization may not have.

What this removes. The three placeholder rows (pack, group, team) and the "PLACEHOLDER" note that graded them. Nothing else: no columns, no constraints, no checks. The change is confined to data-model/02 §10.

See: ../data-model/02-organization.md §10, ../domain/04-organization-structure.md §1–2.

docs.title: D-055 — The permission catalog is deliberately comprehensive and granular
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Amends: D-030

Decision. The permission catalog is large and granular on purpose, and it stays that way. It is a menu from which administrators assign people only what they actually need — not a checklist every deployment is expected to use in full. Adding a permission remains one row plus its permission_level rows (D-007), and further permissions will arrive with the modules not yet specified (events, documents, communication, reporting).

Why. Your answer, in full: "The permissions will be added by the additional modules I am yet to specify. It is good, that the list is large and granular so that the admins can assign people only the permissions they actually need."

This settles F-1, and it settles it in the opposite direction from the roles question. The two are not symmetrical and it is worth saying why, because the asymmetry looks like an inconsistency:

Roles Permissions What it is A grouping an organization invents A capability the code implements Who defines it The organization, at runtime The system, at build time Why Nobody can guess your vocabulary You cannot assign a power that is not expressible

A permission is not a preference. membership.terminate exists because the code has a terminate operation; an organization that never expels anyone simply never grants it. A role is the opposite: unit_leader is only meaningful because someone in this organization chose that word. So a comprehensive permission catalog costs nothing but rows, while a comprehensive role list would be a specification pretending to be data.

The sharp edge. Granularity is what makes least-privilege possible, so it is load-bearing rather than decorative — but .admin subsumption means a new permission is retroactively held by everyone with the namespace's .admin. Split a broad permission in two and an existing holder of the .admin gains both halves without an assignment being written. That is the intended behaviour (D-007), and it is also why role.edit is marked 🔒🔒: the catalog's granularity only helps if the grants are actually narrow.

What this does not settle. The catalog's contents remain open to revision as the unbuilt modules land — this decision fixes the disposition (comprehensive, granular, menu-like), not the exact 90 rows. permission.edit exists for later pruning, and appendix/permission-catalog.md §12 tracks what is still being decided.

See: ../appendix/permission-catalog.md, ../open-questions.md F-1.

docs.title: D-056 — The legacy import expects a large corpus with legacy member numbers
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4

Decision. The import is designed for a substantial historical corpus — thousands of records, not hundreds — and the old records carry a legacy member number. That number is imported into person_identifier with scheme = 'legacy' (data-model/01a §7).

Why. Your answer: "Large, with legacy member numbers."

This is the favourable case for D-004, and it materially changes what the import has to be:

If there were no numbers With legacy numbers Matching Name + birth date + address, probabilistic, review-heavy Exact key when the number is present; heuristics only for backfilling it Review burden Every match needs a human (D-004 assumed this) Only the unmatched remainder does Confidence "Probably the same person" "Same number, same person"

The consequence for the review design. D-004's "no automatic merging, ever" was costed on the assumption that review was the bottleneck and the corpus was small enough to review by hand. With thousands of rows,"review everything" is no longer feasible, and the honest position is that the number-bearing rows are the trustworthy set and the rest is a work queue. The number does the work the human would have done; the human handles the rows the number cannot resolve. This is a strengthening of D-004, not a weakening — the rule is unchanged, but the input is better, so the rule is cheaper to obey.

What must hold for this to work. The legacy number must be imported verbatim and never reissued. person_identifier is already the right home: it records a scheme and a value with a period, so a second numbering era can coexist with the first. The check that matters is that no legacy number is ever assigned to two people — worth an integrity check on the (scheme, value) uniqueness, which the table's index already provides.

The part that gets harder, not easier. Volume and numbers make identity resolution reliable, but they do nothing for the membership-vs-participation question raised by D-041. At this scale, a 1998 roster almost certainly records which unit someone attended and not whether their fee was paid, and the import must decide per row which of the two it becomes. The safe default — participation, unless there is payment evidence — matters more at thousands of rows than at hundreds, because the failure mode compounds: an inferred open-ended membership would make every 2003 roster member a current member today through the gate (D-039).

Not settled here: the exact volume, the format, and the year range — those are operational inputs the import batch will carry. B-1 stays open for the sample, but the shape of the answer is now known.

See: ../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md, ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md, ../open-questions.md B-1.

docs.title: D-057 — household is removed
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Supersedes: D-019 — the table it described is gone, but the principle it stated is not, and that is deliberate. Amends: D-037

Decision. The household and household_member tables are removed, along with fee_obligation.household_id, its CHECK arm, and ix_obligation_household. A person's address is a person_contact row of type postal — data-model/01a §6 — which already exists, already keeps history, and already carries a purpose ('billing') that the permission model can distinguish. Same-address matching for the legacy import becomes a query over person_contact, not a maintained table.

Why. Your answer: "Drop household entirely."

D-037 had already removed the load-bearing half: the fee is flat and per person, so there is no per-family price for a household to hold. What remained was two conveniences — "one invoice per household" and "which children lived at this address in 2003?" — and both are served by tables that must exist anyway:

  • The invoice. person_contact with purpose = 'billing' is where a billing address belongs. A household table was duplicating it under a different key, and the duplication had already gone stale: household.postal_address was documented as "denormalised from the billing contact's primary postal contact", which is a copy with no trigger keeping it true.
  • The 2003 address question. person_contact is temporal (valid_from / valid_to, "Addresses change; history is required"). So "who lived at this address in 2003?" is answered from the contacts table directly — and more honestly, because it asks about the address a person had, rather than requiring that someone first grouped those people into a household row that has itself since been renamed or split.

The one thing genuinely lost. A household is a group with a name and its own lifetime, and person_contact records addresses per person. Two people at one address are related by a query, not by a row — so there is nowhere to hang "the Novák family" as a first-class thing, and no valid_from for the grouping. Accepted, because no feature was using it: nothing set fee_obligation.household_id, and the display-name use (household.name) has no consumer in the design.

What this does not change. The safeguarding property D-019 was written to protect survives intact, and this is the point worth checking before deleting anything: being at the same address still grants no access. It never came from the household table in the first place — all access comes from guardianship + guardianship_permission (D-020). Removing a table that granted nothing cannot grant anything. The old D-019 entry stays in the log, marked superseded, because "why does living together not imply access?" is a question that will be asked again.

Also removed with it: integrity check 7 (households with no address and no billing contact), which has nothing left to check; the household bullet in data-model/04 §7; and D-9 in open-questions.md.

See: ../data-model/04-relationships.md, ../data-model/07-finance.md §2.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 5 — the events module (D-058 … D-071)
docs.text:
Events designed end to end, plus the withdrawal of per-resource admin permissions and of anything that forced an assignment to end.

Refinement round 4 (D-047 … D-057) ← | All decisions | Refinement round 6 — the no-SQL round (D-072 … D-081) →

docs.title: D-058 — An event is a dated occasion owned by exactly one unit
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Ownership reversed by D-102; the dated-occasion half stands. An event is still an occasion with dates rather than a recurring template, and still has exactly one set of dates. There is simply no unit for it to belong to, and the people connected to it are named by selectors that bind to it.

Decision. event.org_unit_id is NOT NULL — exactly one owning unit. A weekly meeting group is not an event; it is unit_participation. Events are the things people register for: camps, trips, hikes, jamborees.

Why. Two answers, and the second is the structural one.

  • On ownership: "One owning unit." A joint camp between two packs is Pack A's event that Pack B's children register for. Pack B is a guest, and its access is written explicitly — an audience grant, a named person, at the level that fits. Nobody arbitrates "whose event is this?", and one unit remains the author of the record.
  • On recurrence: "No recurrence — meetings are participation." A Thursday group meeting forty times a year is already recorded as "this child takes part in this Thursday group." Forty event rows would say what one participation row says, with forty capacities, forty organizer rosters, and forty chances to be wrong.

The ownership rule is forced by D-049, not merely preferred by it. If an event could belong to two units, the root's inability to read a sub-unit's events would have an exception shaped exactly like a joint camp, with no principled place to stop. One owner keeps the rule total.

What this forecloses. There is no event_series, no RFC 5545 rule, no occurrence table, and no event_unit join table. Each would require every downstream table — registrations, capacity, presence, organizers, questions — to carry a second possible home.

Consequence worth stating. "Was Jan at the meeting on 14 March?" is not answerable from the events module. That is presence tracking for a standing group, which is a different feature. The boundary is deliberate; the confusion between the two is the thing to watch for.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §1–2, ../data-model/08-events.md §2.

docs.title: D-059 — "Unanswered" is the absence of a row; a registration stores two values
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. event_registration.response has two values — 'attending' and 'not_attending'. 'unanswered' is written nowhere. It is the absence of a registration row. "Who has not replied yet?" is a subtraction: (people who could contribute to this event) MINUS (people with a registration).

Why. Your answer: "Absent row — two stored values."

The framing that settled it was your own correction: registration is "positive with additional fields, or negative (or none)". "None" is not a third stored value — it is the lack of a record, and storing it would mean writing rows for people who have not acted.

Three reasons absence beats a stored value, and the third is decisive:

Absent row Stored 'unanswered' Rows written before anyone acts None One per person asked "Asked and silent" vs "never asked" Distinguishable — the eligible set is a query Indistinguishable without an invite table "Who has not replied?" A subtraction against an audience Requires enumerating the audience into rows

The third is the real argument. The eligible set is an audience — a rule the resolver evaluates (D-042) such as unit:7:participants or all_members. Enumerating it into 'unanswered' rows would mean re-enumerating every time a child joins the pack, and the stored rows would drift out of agreement with the rule that generated them.

Returning someone to unanswered removes the row (DELETE, recorded in audit_log). That is the honest act — it leaves the least behind, and "no row" then means the same thing whether the person never answered or their answer was withdrawn.

Consequence. unit_participation uses the same reasoning for the same reason, and this decision makes the pattern explicit: where a state is the absence of a fact, store the absence. Compare D-002 for the temporal case and D-053 for the definitional one.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §4, ../domain/07-events.md §3.

docs.title: D-060 — Eligibility is capability; there is no separate rule engine
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5 Resolves: the deferral in D-006

Decision. Registration requires contribute capability on that event. Nothing else. There is no eligibility rule table, no age gate, no prerequisite system. event.register_self is already mapped to contribute in permission_level.

Amended by D-107 in round 12, in the direction of this entry's purpose rather than of its letter. The words "no age gate" were doing two jobs in that paragraph. As "the system applies no eligibility test of its own; there is no rule table; nothing is evaluated outside can()" — they stand, and that is the decision this entry was recording. As "nobody may write an age test in this model" — they are now false, and were only ever true because of a sentence in domain/06 §6 that round 12 deleted: "an attribute is not a set of people … age is not." OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are seeded operands now, so event.register_self may be granted to MEMBERS * YOUNGER(15), and the age ceiling this entry explicitly declined to enforce — the one EV-1 went on to record as unenforced — is statable. What has not moved is who decides. A gate is a grant somebody wrote, shown by the preview, attributed in the audit trail; it is not a conclusion the system draws from a birth date. This entry's real subject was always that, and it is why the entry is amended rather than superseded.

Why. Your answer: "I feel like the people with 'contribute' permissions (capabilities) on that item should be allowed to register."

This dissolves D-006's deferral rather than satisfying it. D-006 said "eligibility ... will be a separate concept when events are specified." Your answer says the separate concept was never needed: the capability ladder already is one.

view        may SEE the event
contribute  may REGISTER for it
manage      may ORGANIZE it
admin       may control it

Why audiences make this sufficient rather than merely simple. Registering 200 children individually is 200 grant rows — but opening an event to members is one, which the shape of the row made visible at the time:

INSERT INTO access_grant (scope_type, scope_id, audience_id, level)
VALUES ('event', :camp_id,
        (SELECT id FROM audience WHERE code = 'all_members'), 'contribute');

The requirement now, without the statement: an access_grant may address an audience instead of a person, so "everyone who is a current member may take part in this event" is one row rather than one per member — 05-authorization §8.

An age-gated camp is a camp opened to unit:<id>:participants for a unit whose participants are that age. This is the case audiences (D-042) were built for, and events are where the investment pays off.

What this does not do, stated plainly. (Round 12: this paragraph describes a choice now, not a limitation — YOUNGER(n) is seeded, so an organizer who wants a ceiling grants event.register_self to MEMBERS * YOUNGER(15) and sees whom it reaches before saving. What still does not exist is a test the system runs by itself. D-107.) It does not enforce an age ceiling on an open event. If a nine-year-old holds contribute on a camp for teenagers, they can register. The design decides eligibility by who may register, not by inspecting the person — the check is the grant. Whether that is sufficient is carried in ../open-questions.md rather than hidden.

Organizers are not bound by it. Anyone holding event.manage_participants may register anyone, and the registration records source = 'staff'. That is the permission's purpose: the leader who knows there is a spare bed is trusted, and the act is attributed.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §4, data-model/05 §7.

docs.title: D-061 — Event answers are read by that event's organizers
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. Answers to event_question are readable by the organizers of that event, with no additional permission. You confirmed the consequence explicitly: the event form is the route by which a camp leader learns a child has a nut allergy.

Why, and the part that must be recorded. This is only coherent — and only defensible — because the dependent.* namespace is unreachable by unit leaders. The permission catalog states it outright:

"Resolved only against guardianship_permission, never against roles. A unit leader does not get these by virtue of leading the unit — that is a safeguarding property."

So a camp leader cannot reach dependent.medical.* at all. Not by leading the pack, not by running the camp, not by being an organizer. There is no permission that changes it. Which means an allergy recorded on a camp form is the only way the people running the camp will know.

This is a widening, and it is recorded as one. Access to a child's health information moves from "few people, via a guardianship-scoped permission granted by the guardian" to "every organizer of any event the child registers for." That is a coherent position — the parent tells the people present, per event, and the medical file stays closed — but it is not an accident of where the gate was placed, and it must not be "fixed" later by tightening the wrong thing.

Two consequences that follow.

  1. Only preference-level detail belongs on a form. Nothing in the schema distinguishes "vegetarian" from "coeliac" — both are data_type = 'text' in event_answer.value. The discipline is in the form label, so it is guidance, not a constraint. A CHECK cannot tell them apart, and a keyword list would fail on the first unusual phrasing.
  2. Event answers are not a medical record. They are operational detail for one event, read by that event's organizers, and ending with the event. The two stores are not duplicates of each other and should not be merged or synchronised.

Open: the retention policy. A dietary answer citing a medical condition is health data with a retention obligation, and there is no policy yet.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §7, ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §12, appendix/permission-catalog.md §9.

docs.title: D-062 — Organizers are appointed on the event, not granted
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. Events have an event_organizer roster, and it is the domain answer to "who is running this?" — labelled, ordered, attributed. It is not an access_grant, and it does not by itself confer authority to act on the event.

Why. Your answer: "Roster only; grants stay separate."

The tempting alternative, and why it fails. Write an access_grant at manage whenever an organizer is added, so "the organizers" is a query over grants and the two can never disagree. It fails on three counts:

Grant at manage event_organizer A cook's label No room for organizer_role = 'cook' organizer_role, free text Display order Not expressible sort_order, is_primary "Who is running this camp?" Read the permission table Read the roster Removing the cook Revokes their ability to see the event Removes them from the list

That last row is the practical one: "they are no longer cooking" does not mean "they may no longer see the camp."

event_organizer is the event-scoped analogue of position_assignment — an appointment on the thing being run. Like a position it may carry a label and an order; like a position it is not a permission bundle. organizer_role is free text, not a CHECK: every organization labels these differently, and a controlled vocabulary here would be a guess of the kind D-054 removed for unit types.

It has no valid_to, deliberately. A roster is not a period: you are on the list or you are not. An organizer who drops out is removed (audited), because "was Jan an organizer of that camp?" must have one answer, not a set of intervals.

How authority actually reaches an organizer is D-063 — the unit's roles reach its events.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §3, ../domain/07-events.md §5.

docs.title: D-063 — An event is an ARTIFACT of its unit, not a child of it
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer, as a consequence you did not have to state) Date: refinement round 5

Superseded by D-102. The argument's shape survives — an item's people are named, never inherited from a container — but with no unit and no owner the question 'whose event is this?' has no column left to answer it from.

Amends: nothing. Extends: D-031

The problem. The resolver matches scope exactly. There is therefore no path from a unit_leader role held at ('org_unit', 7) to a check made at ('event', 42) — even when unit 7 owns event 42:

unit_leader ── holds role at ──► org_unit 7 (the pack)
                                     │
                                     │  ✗ NO PATH
                                     ▼
event 42 "Summer camp" ◄─ owned by ──┘    resolver checks scope exactly

The pack's leader — the person whose job is running the pack's camp — does not pass can(leader, 'event.view', 'event', 42). Nothing is broken; the answer is simply no. But the module cannot ship with that gap, because it would mean the leader must be granted every event their own unit creates.

Decision. A permission is satisfied at ('event', E) if it is satisfied at the event's owning unit, ('org_unit', E.org_unit_id), and that unit is the event's owner. One wrapper function, can_event(), calling can() twice.

Why this is not inheritance downward, and why that distinction is the whole point.

Inheritance (rejected, D-015/D-031) Artifact rule (chosen) What a leader gains Authority in the unit's sub-units too Authority over the unit's own events Blast radius Grows on every restructure Fixed — one owner, pinned by D-049 Reverses D-015, D-031 Nothing

An event is not a child of its unit; it is a thing the unit made. The unit's authority already covers the unit. Asking "may this person do this in Pack 7?" is asking the right question about the right scope — and it is a question the resolver already answers correctly.

Restructuring the hierarchy still changes nothing about who may do what. Adding a sub-unit still grants nobody anything. D-015 and D-031 stand untouched, and the rule is exactly as narrow as the case requires.

Why a wrapper function rather than a change inside can(). Putting this clause inside the resolver would make every permission check — on people, memberships, units, fees — evaluate an event-shaped rule. Keeping it in can_event() means the exception is visible, named, and confined to the module that needs it.

And it is a two-way door. can_event() calls can() twice and adds no authority of its own; nothing is written to access_grant to make it work. If the organization decides that leaders should not automatically run every event their unit creates, deleting the second can() call is the entire change, and it needs no data migration.

The root is unaffected. An organization-scoped registrar still cannot see a pack's camp — events are precisely the sub-unit records D-049 protects. The fix, if the root wants it, is one scope_exposure row naming one assignment.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §6, ../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §8.

docs.title: D-064 — There is no event status; visibility is the permission model
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. event has no status column. Draft is not a state: a new event has no grants beyond its organizers' own authority, so nobody else can see it, and publishing is an access_grant, not an UPDATE. completed is derived (ends_at < now()). Cancellation is a recorded fact — cancelled_at, cancelled_by, cancel_reason.

Why. Your answer, which is the right instinct: "Isn't the draft solved by not giving anyone else permissions, but the organizer?" It is, and it is better than a status enum for a reason worth stating:

A status column and a permission system that both claim to answer "who may see this?" will eventually disagree — and the one that gets enforced is whoever wrote the last IF.

With no status column there is nothing to disagree. The questions a draft flag would answer are all answered by grants:

Question Answer "Is this ready to be seen?" Has anyone been granted view? "Who can see it before it is announced?" Its organizers, and anyone already granted "How do I hide it again?" Revoke the grant — revoked_at set, the row kept

Where the logic deliberately diverges: cancellation. If cancelling were done by revoking grants, the event would vanish for exactly the people who need to know it is off — the registrants. They would see nothing at all: not "cancelled", just gone. So cancellation is a fact, the event stays visible, and it is marked.

Draft and cancellation therefore use different mechanisms on purpose, because they have different audiences: draft is about who may discover an event, cancellation is about who must be told.

A cancelled event stops accepting registrations (the window closes implicitly) and keeps every registration row — those rows are the record that the camp was planned and who was coming, which is precisely what is needed to notify and refund.

See: ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §10, ../data-model/08-events.md §2.

docs.title: D-065 — Capacity is a waitlist threshold, and organizers may exceed it
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. Registering for a full event succeeds and produces a waitlisted row — it is never refused. Organizers may register past capacity outright, and the overrun is permitted, attributed and reported rather than prevented. Promotion from the waitlist is a deliberate act by an organizer, never automatic.

Why. Two answers, and they only look contradictory:

  • "Waitlist" — the thirteenth caller for a twelve-bed camp is not turned away, they are written down.
  • "Organizers might exceed, also they might choose to include people from the waiting list" — a leader who knows there are two spare tents should not be blocked by a number they cannot edit mid-camp.

The two coexist because the waitlist is a SELF-SERVICE outcome. The trigger applies it only when source = 'self'. A staff registration is admitted regardless. So:

Path At a full event Self-service Waitlisted, ordered Staff / organizer Admitted, the overrun reported Promotion Deliberate — an organizer picks who comes off the waitlist Capacity change An UPDATE — visible and attributed

Capacity is therefore three things at once, on purpose: a rule for self-service, a number organizers can exceed, and a report. data-model/08 §10 check 5 produces rows and that is not a failure — an event that overruns every year has a wrong capacity number, and the fix is the number, not refusing people.

Promotion is not automatic because a place freeing up is not the same as it being right to give it to the next person — the organizer may know the next child cannot come on those dates. What is automatic is one narrow release rule, recorded as such in D-066.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §5, ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §8.

docs.title: D-066 — Payment confirms the place, and the release deadline is the one automatic transition
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. An event may have a fee (event.fee_schedule_id), and payment confirms the place. Registering creates a fee_obligation; a paid obligation sets is_confirmed = true via confirm_event_place(). Events without a fee confirm immediately, and most events have no fee — you were explicit that payment "does not have to be at all events."

Why. Your answer: "Payment confirms the place, also the payment does not have to be at all events."

The second half is the part that shapes the schema: fee_schedule_id is nullable, and NULL is the common case. A free hike confirms on registration, and there is no "confirmation" state with no meaning.

The accepted cost, recorded rather than hidden. This design has spent real effort avoiding automatic state changes (D-023, D-040), and payment-confirms-the-place reintroduces one: an unpaid registration at a full event releases its place to the waitlist at waitlist_deadline. It is accepted because it is a deadline, not a sweep — narrowly scoped, opt-in per event, and visible in what it produces. The predicate as decided:

-- Only at a full event, only with a fee configured, only past the deadline,
-- only unpaid, only self-service, never a cancelled event.
e.fee_schedule_id IS NOT NULL
AND e.waitlist_deadline IS NOT NULL
AND e.waitlist_deadline < now()
AND r.source = 'self' AND r.is_confirmed = false
AND e.cancelled_at IS NULL

The requirement now, in words: release happens only at a full event that has a fee, a deadline that has passed, an unpaid self-service registration, and is not cancelled — six conditions, each of which is load-bearing, and the list is the rule rather than an illustration of it. Stated in 08-events §5.

waitlist_deadline is NULL by default, so an event that does not opt in never runs this rule at all. The alternative — no deadline — means a place is held forever by someone who never paid, which is worse.

A function, not a trigger. confirm_event_place() is called by the finance module and is not a trigger on fee_obligation.status, because a trigger would fire for membership fees and event fees alike and "the fee is paid" means something different in each case: a membership activates (D-040), an event place confirms. Two transitions, two owners.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §6, ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §11.

docs.title: D-067 — Presence is a three-valued fact on the registration
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. event_registration.was_present is a nullable boolean, marked by an organizer with presence_marked_by / presence_marked_at.

Value Meaning NULL Not yet marked — no register was taken true Turned up false Marked absent — a register was taken and they were not there

Why three-valued rather than a boolean defaulting to false. "We did not take a register" and "we took a register and they were not there" are different facts, and only the second is a safeguarding signal. A boolean defaulting to false would assert absence where the organization only failed to look.

Why it matters more than it looks. For a camp, the end-of-week presence record is the record of who was actually in the organization's care. That is the row that matters if the fee buys insurance (finance question 9 — "member on the date of the incident"), and it is the row that cannot be reconstructed afterwards from registrations.

Presence is not registration, and the distinction is enforced: a not_attending registration with was_present set is contradictory and reported (data-model/08 §10 check 8).

A walk-in is not representable, deliberately. A sibling who turns up on the day was not in the organization's care — no guardian recorded, no name on the roster — and must not silently appear to have been. Recording them means registering them, which means the organizers have a name and a guardian. That is the correct friction.

Note the contrast with D-059. There, absence of a row was the right encoding for unanswered. Here, a stored NULL is the right encoding for not marked. The difference: "unanswered" is the absence of a fact about the person, while "not marked" is a fact about the organization's incomplete work — and the work being incomplete is itself worth recording, because it is a task still outstanding.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §4, ../domain/07a-capacity-presence-and-forms.md §9.

docs.title: D-068 — There are no per-resource admin permissions; roles are the bundle
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — reverses D-007 Date: refinement round 5

Your answer. Asked whether person.admin should subsume person.merge and person.redact — the standing case against prefix subsumption, since both are irreversible and both are privacy incidents if granted wrongly — you answered: "Only the system should have admin permissions, not the individual items."

The phrase needed disambiguating, because "individual items" names two different things in this schema: the per-resource permission (person.admin, over the whole resource) and the item-scoped grant (access_grant over one event). You confirmed the first reading.

Decision. The sixteen <resource>.admin permission codes are deleted — the ten documented ones (person.admin, account.admin, membership.admin, unit_participation.admin, org_unit.admin, position.admin, guardianship.admin, audit.admin, event.admin, audience.admin) and the six sitting in deferred namespaces (document, fee, payment, report, consent, message). So is the resolver's prefix-match branch. What remains:

  • system.admin is the only permission in the system that means everything, and it is reached only through a role assignment (system namespace — never an item grant, never guardianship). Unchanged.
  • "Someone who can do everything about events" is a role the organization composes, bundling the thirteen event.* codes. Not a permission the code invents for them.
  • access_level.admin (rank 40) is untouched. This is a different thing that shares a name, and the collision is the most likely place for a later reader to go wrong. The level answers "how much authority does this grant carry" — view < contribute < manage < admin, used by permission_level to decide whether a contribute-level grant satisfies event.register_self. The permission code answered "does this capability imply that one". The ladder survives; only the wildcard code dies.

Why this is coherent with the rest of the design rather than an exception to it. D-052 already settled that roles are runtime data and the seed set is not a specification — the organization composes permission groups at runtime. A per-resource admin code is the code composing a permission group on the organization's behalf, in advance, for a bundle nobody asked for. Deleting it makes the two mechanisms agree: the code implements capabilities, the organization groups them. It is the same division D-055 drew when it refused to prune the catalog — a large menu of narrow things, composed by whoever needs them.

The cost is real, and it is the cost D-007 existed to prevent. Stated in D-007's own words: without the wildcard, every new narrow permission requires updating every role that should already have implied it — and someone will miss one, producing a permission that silently is not granted. That failure mode is back. It is accepted because it fails closed: someone cannot do a thing they were arguably meant to be able to do, and they say so, rather than doing a thing nobody meant them to be able to do. D-007 traded a loud inconvenience for a quiet hazard. The reversal takes the opposite side of the same trade.

What replaces the protection — since the wildcard is gone, reachability needs a check of its own. Integrity check 18 lists permissions that no role grants, which is the query that surfaces a permission silently orphaned by the absence of a wildcard (numbering follows the existing list in ../data-model/05 §11. It was written as an executable query, and this is it as decided:

-- 18. ORPHANED PERMISSIONS — granted by no role at all. With no .admin wildcard
--     (D-068), a new permission nobody bundles is silently unusable. This report is
--     the safety net the wildcard used to be.
SELECT p.code, p.resource
  FROM permission p
 WHERE p.is_assignable
   AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM role_permission rp WHERE rp.permission_id = p.id)
 ORDER BY p.resource, p.code;

The requirement now: every assignable permission that no role bundles is reported, which is the net the .admin wildcard used to be; the check is item 18 of 05-authorization §11, and like the other eighteen it is now something to be verified rather than something that runs.

What happens to the F-4 question that prompted this. It does not dissolve — it moves, and becomes visible. A role bundling all eleven person.* permissions still reaches person.merge and person.redact, because those are ordinary codes in the bundle. The difference is where the decision lives: previously a resolver rule made the implication, invisible in every role editor and true for every resource whether or not anyone wanted it. Now the implication appears as the contents of a role the organization wrote, reviewable line by line in role_permission, dated, and alarmable. role.edit on that role is already audited for exactly this reason (D-052). The guidance therefore moves from the schema to the seed: a role bundling a resource including its irreversible codes should be named for what it is, and the seed roles in §11 are written so that no seeded role mixes person.merge/person.redact with routine person.edit. That is now expressible as a report rather than a caveat.

Two survivors, and why neither is an exception. Both look like wildcards and neither is the thing being deleted:

  • dependent.admin stays. It is not a prefix-match artefact — it is a code a staff member chooses and stores, one row in guardianship_permission, granting the full set for one child. A wildcard that must be deliberately written is what this decision endorses, not what it removes. It also has a property no role wildcard can have: an explicit is_granted = false row overrides it, so a court-ordered restriction survives a broad grant. Deleting dependent.admin would make the common restriction easier to express, not harder — listing nineteen narrow rows per child where a court case needs two. The distinction to keep: person.admin implied capabilities nobody wrote down; dependent.admin is a shorthand for capabilities somebody did write down, in a specific row, about a specific child.
  • system.admin stays, for the reasons already in §7 — it is the break-glass capability, concentrating the most dangerous thing in one alarmable holder rather than scattering equivalents. It was never a prefix-match beneficiary; it is checked outright.

A third thing called "admin", which also stays. dependent.profile.admin, dependent.medical.admin, dependent.consent.admin are not wildcards at all — they are actions meaning "edit" inside a sub-resource, paired against .view. Nothing is implied by them. Three unrelated meanings now share one word in this schema — the access level (rank 40), the deleted resource wildcard, and an edit action — and any of the three may be what a reader means. When one of them comes up in conversation, say which.

Migration. Deleting role_permission rows for the sixteen codes; no other data moves. Any role that held only person.admin becomes an empty role, which is correct and visible rather than quietly over-privileged — and role.delete still refuses to remove a role that was ever assigned (D-052), so the empty shell survives as evidence of what someone once meant. Re-deriving it means naming the bundle, which is the point.

Two-way door? No. Re-adding a wildcard later is mechanically cheap and semantically loud — it re-creates the implication silently for resources added after the day you added it. Treat it as a fresh decision, not a revert.

See: ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §1, ../data-model/05-authorization.md §2, ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §4.

docs.title: D-069 — Guardianship ends when a person ends it; the system takes no position on majority
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — reverses D-024 Date: refinement round 5

Your answer. Asked what the system does when a guarded child turns 18 — review queue, auto-expire, or nothing — you answered "Nothing at all."

Decision. No job, no review queue, no computed candidate date, no flag. A guardianship row is ended by a person ending it (guardianship.end), or by import, and the system does not notice birthdays in this connection at all.

Why this is better than the queue D-024 proposed, and where D-024 went wrong. D-024 reasoned from "fail open rather than silently strip access" and picked the gentler of two automatic behaviours. Both were automatic. The queue was not a refusal to act; it was a deferral of the action, and it smuggled in a claim the system cannot support: that majority is a date the system knows. It is not. D-024's own rationale said thresholds vary by jurisdiction — and then computed a date anyway. A review queue is not a neutral container for a wrong date; it is a worklist of cases staff are told to decide, and the item on it asserts something the organization has not decided.

The deeper problem with the queue: it inverts who decides. Under D-024 the system raises the question at 18 whether or not anyone wanted it asked, in every case, for every family — including the ones where the adult child asks their parent to keep handling their medical correspondence. The queue's default is that the arrangement is suspect. That is the wrong default for a relationship the organization did not create.

What "nothing" costs, stated honestly. Nothing is tracked, so "who is still listed as my guardian, and since when?" has no automatic answer. It has a manual one: guardianship carries valid_from/valid_to, so the question is a query on a person's rows and the answer includes the date each was ended. What is lost is a prompt, not a record — which is the same trade the module makes everywhere. See the pattern below.

This is the latest in a consistent line of refusals, and the reasoning is identical each time. Across five rounds the design has allowed itself exactly two automatic transitions — the yearly fee sweep (D-040) and the event waitlist release (D-066) — and has refused, among others, automatic membership lapse states (D-023), event status (D-064), and recurrence (D-058). Guardianship expiry is the next one refused. The pattern: an automatic transition is cheap to design and expensive to defend, because it acts on every case including the ones it was not designed for. A nightly job that ends guardianships at 18 fails closed and strips a legally valid arrangement overnight; a queue fails open and adds a standing assertion the org never made. The third option — a person who knows the family ends the row — is the only one that can also decide not to.

Consequence to carry: nothing here weakens the exit path, so the exit path must exist. With no automatic end, guardianship.end is the only door, and it must be reachable by someone. Two things follow, both worth stating because they are now load-bearing in a way they were not when a job existed to help:

  1. The adult child must be able to end it about themselves. They are the subject of the row and currently hold no permission over it — they are not a guardian of themselves. This needs a route, and it is now the module's sharpest open item.
  2. A stale row is invisible by design, so the query, not the job, is the control. A periodic human review is a good idea and is explicitly not a scheduled system behaviour.

Follow-up raised: E-2 is closed and replaced by E-5 — "how does an adult end a guardianship over themselves?" That question existed before this decision and was masked by a review queue that would have surfaced it. It is now unavoidable.

See: ../data-model/04-relationships.md §2, ../domain/02-actors.md §5.

docs.title: D-070 — An event has no age ceiling; the grant is the rule
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Your answer. Asked about the one gap in eligibility is capability (D-060) — an event opened to all_members can be registered for by a nine-year-old even if the camp was planned for teenagers — you answered "Leave it — the grant is the rule."

Decision. No min_age/max_age on event. No age check in place_event_registration(). Age restriction is expressed entirely by choosing the audience the event is opened to.

Why the option was tempting, and why refusing it is right. The offered design was the cheap one: a column pair plus one branch, reported rather than blocking, matching position.min_age. It would have cost little and reversed nothing. It is refused on consistency grounds, which are the only grounds worth having here. A condition evaluated at registration time that the capability model does not know about is the first rule-engine rule. Not because age is special — because the moment one exists, the second is cheap, and within two years the honest answer to "who can register for this?" is "check the grants, and also the age columns, and also whatever else we added there." D-060 dissolved a deferred question by noticing the capability model already answered it; a condition living beside it reopens the question by insisting the capability model is not enough.

The residual risk, stated rather than waved away. A leader registers a child for an event the child is too young for, and nothing in the system objects. Accepted, on three conditions that are all already true in the schema:

  1. It is attributable. Staff-driven registrations carry source = 'staff' and a created_by, so the judgement is recorded as belonging to a named person.
  2. It is visible. §9's roster query lists registrants with birth dates, so age is on the page a leader looks at while confirming.
  3. It is the normal case correctly handled already. A genuinely age-bounded event is opened to the unit whose members are that age, and that is how a section-based organization works today. What is not covered is one narrow shape — an event open to everyone that should be restricted — and it is narrow enough that a column pair would be a permanent mechanism serving an exception.

If it is ever revisited, the trigger is specific: the shape recurring often enough that leaders routinely open the wrong event to the wrong people. Then the right answer is probably still not columns on event but an audience that encodes the age band — all_members is a rule the resolver evaluates, and so could members_aged_13_plus be. That keeps eligibility in one place, which is the property being protected here. Do not reach for a condition on the row when the mechanism for evaluating membership of a set already exists.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §4, ../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §9.

docs.title: D-071 — Nothing forces a role assignment to end; the gate and the report are the control
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — overrides the recommendation in F-3 Date: refinement round 5

Your answer. Asked whether valid_to should be mandatory on high-authority role assignments — the classic volunteer who was never removed — you answered "Nothing — rely on the gate."

The docs had recommended the other way. F-3 said yes, at the application layer, and argued the membership gate made an open-ended assignment more dangerous, not less. You disagree, and the disagreement is worth recording because the recommendation was not obviously wrong.

Decision. role_assignment.valid_to stays nullable with no application-layer requirement and no per-role policy. The controls are the membership gate (D-039) and a report. No new constraint anywhere.

Why the recommendation was wrong, in one place. F-3 said the gate makes open-ended assignments more dangerous. It is the other way round: the gate already does what an expiry date would do, for exactly the population an expiry date would target, and it does it without inventing a date nobody chose. A forced valid_to is an guess about when authority should lapse, written by whoever made the assignment — usually inherited from a form default. The gate instead ties expiry to a fact the organization already maintains and renews on purpose: whether this person is a member. When the fee lapses, gated roles stop granting. The expiry date was always going to be a worse approximation of that.

What the gate does not cover — the honest residue. unit_leader and assistant_leader have requires_membership = false by explicit decision (a volunteer whose own fee lapses still runs the Thursday meeting), so a lapsed leader keeps leading. Also any role held by a non-member, and anything carrying system.gate_exempt. For those, the answer is a periodic human review over open-ended assignments, and D-068 now makes that query sharper, since a role's full reach is visible in role_permission with no wildcard hiding implications in the resolver.

Note the dependency this decision creates. D-053 put all the weight on role_assignment.valid_to as the only thing that ends authority, and warned that the open-ended assignment is the classic access failure. This decision declines to add a guard rail at precisely that point, so the two together should be read as one load-bearing pair: authority ends only when somebody ends it, and the only defence left is that somebody looks. The report is not a nice-to-have here; it is the entire control.

See: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §4, F-3.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 6 — the no-SQL round (D-072 … D-081)
docs.text:
4,689 lines of DDL deleted and every rule it carried restated as a requirement. The round that made the prose the specification.

Refinement round 5 — the events module (D-058 … D-071) ← | All decisions | Refinement rounds 7 and 8 (D-082 … D-090) →

docs.title: D-072 — The documentation carries no SQL; the schema is the ORM's job
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — closes F-4a Date: refinement round 6

Your answer. Asked whether the permission catalog should be generated from the seed data rather than maintained beside it, you answered "Delete the schema, I will use ORM anyway."

The question was a symptom. F-4a was about two lists disagreeing. The real cause is that the documentation was asserting a deployment. It carried 4,689 lines of PostgreSQL across 19 files — 31% of the repository: every CREATE TABLE, a can() function, trigger bodies, 91 INSERT INTO permission rows whose only purpose was to make a list executable, and one integrity check whose entire job was to read pg_proc and grep a function definition for a string. Under an ORM, not one of those lines would ever be run as written. Hand-written migrations and ORM-generated migrations disagree about who owns the schema, and the docs asserting DDL was the losing side of that argument before it started.

Decision. No SQL in the documentation. Field lists, types at the level of what kind of thing this is (a period, an amount, an identifier), nullability, uniqueness, no-overlap rules, temporality, indexes that exist for a reason, and derived facts are all stated as requirements, in the document that owns the entity.

The deletion is a translation, and this is the part that matters. The DDL was not illustration; in most places it was the only precise statement of a rule, and prose beside it was the argument. Deleting the block and keeping the argument would silently drop the rule. What must survive as written requirements, at minimum:

  • the no-overlap rules — one open participation per person per unit, one open guardianship per pair, one open role assignment per person-role-scope, no two overlapping current contact points of one purpose. The rule is the design; the GiST index that PostgreSQL happens to use for it is not
  • the resolver's channels and their order (D-010)
  • three-valued was_present, where NULL means "no register was taken" and not "absent" (D-067)
  • birth_date_precision, because an imported 1990-01-01 often means year 1990
  • tombstone and redaction both survive on person, with the two partial indexes that exist because every ordinary listing excludes both
  • a person may not be merged into themselves, and merged_into / merged_at are set together or not at all

A rule for writing the docs from here. Where a rule can only be stated precisely enough to be checked, state it that precisely. "A guardianship may not overlap another guardianship for the same pair" is a requirement. EXCLUDE USING gist (guardian_id WITH =, dependent_id WITH =, period WITH &&) was that same requirement wearing an implementation's clothes.

What got genuinely weaker, which should not be written as though it were free. The 19 integrity checks were executable. They are now invariants to be verified by something — listed in the document that owns them, with no query attached. The one that suffers most is the time-bomb added in the last round, which failed the build if .admin prefix-matching ever reappeared in the resolver (D-068). It is now a sentence in a Markdown file. A prohibition nobody runs is a convention, not a guard. It stays, because the alternative is silently forgetting it existed; it should not be described as equivalent.

Seed data goes with it. There is no seed INSERT set, so there is no seeded role list and no seeded permission list in the docs. This is what D-052 already argued — roles are runtime data and the seed set is not a specification — and D-072 removes the one place the docs kept pretending otherwise. Starter roles and starter permissions are described as what the organization begins with, not as rows.

F-4a closes by dissolution. With no seed block there is exactly one list of permissions, which is the catalog. Two artifacts cannot drift when only one of them exists.

Two-way door? No. Re-deriving 4,689 lines of DDL from prose is a redesign, not a restoration — the constraints encode decisions the prose does not always restate. Git has them.

See: ../data-model/00-conventions.md, F-4a.

docs.title: D-073 — Guardianship is administered by its own parties, not by staff
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — closes E-5 Date: refinement round 6

Your answer. "The guardian has the same rights as the user, so they can modify their own guardians as well as the guardians with the write permissions. There is no need to take this through the management team." and, when asked how far that reaches, "Guardian can be assigned by other guardian."

Decision. The parties to a guardianship are principals on that row, not third parties holding a grant on it. A guardian may end the arrangement, may add another guardian to the same child, and may change the permission level of the row they are a party to. The adult who is the subject of a guardianship may end it over themselves. None of these routes through staff. A staff member remains a way for it to happen and is never the way.

This is the founding principle, applied one level down. The rule this system was built on is that authority over a nested thing originates at that thing and cannot be claimed from outside it; the organization itself may not decide permissions over a sub-unit, and only the system administrator is exempt. D-031 applied that to units. A guardianship is a nested thing, and its "unit" is the people in it. A staff role reaching in to decide who is responsible for a child is exactly the move the authorization model refuses everywhere else.

E-5 closes, and it closes differently from every option on offer. E-5 asked how an adult ends a guardianship over themselves and offered three shapes — support request, ownership channel, request object — all of which assumed the answer must come from somewhere other than the people involved. It does not. Note also that the answer is not the ownership channel: ownership is your own record, and a guardianship row is not the subject's record any more than it is the guardian's. It is a record of a relationship between them, and both parties hold it.

Mechanically this is a direction, not a fifth channel. The resolver has four channels and D-010 keeps them at four. The guardianship channel already asks "may guardian G act on D's records?"; D-073 gives it a second question, "may a party act on the guardianship row itself?", answered for exactly three acts — end the row, add another guardian, change the permission level. Adding a channel would have been the same capability at the price of touching every document that enumerates them, and enumeration is how the order stays a rule.

Read D-069 and D-073 as one decision in two halves. D-069 refused to let a birthday end a guardianship and deleted the review queue, on the grounds that a person decides. It left the question of which person, using what open — the exit it assumed had no door. D-073 is the door. Without it D-069 was a refusal with no alternative; with it the pair says something quite coherent: a legal relationship between two people ends when one of those people says so, and the organization's job is to be told, not to permit it.

The asymmetry, stated plainly, because it is real. A guardian may appoint a guardian. So anyone with authority over a child can give a second person that same authority with no approval from the organization — the ordinary case being a mother adding the father, and the case that is not being everything else. The design accepts this and holds one line instead: the act is attributed. Who added whom, when, from which account, is audited, and the other party is notified. That is a deterrent and an evidence trail, not a prevention.

Not decided: whether adding a guardian over a minor should notify anyone at the organization beyond the audit log, and whether a subject may refuse a guardian appointed over them. See E-6.

See: ../data-model/04-relationships.md, E-5.

docs.title: D-074 — A guardian's rights are none, view, or write. Nothing more granular
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — supersedes the mechanism of D-020; deletes dependent.* Date: refinement round 6

Your answer. "Guardian rights should be only 'none', 'view', or 'write', nothing more granular."

The docs had it the other way round, deliberately. guardianship_permission was a table of per-capability grants — dependent.profile.view, dependent.medical.admin, dependent.consent.admin, dependent.event.register, dependent.fee.pay — and the glossary asserted "Being a guardian grants nothing by itself. Every capability is a separate, revocable, audited row." That was drawn as a consequence of the standing instruction that both read and write permissions be explicit. It went further than that instruction said: explicit and granular are not the same property. Explicit means nothing is implied by identity. That is fully preserved here — a guardianship row with level none grants nothing at all.

Decision. One value per guardianship row, from exactly three: none, view, write. Not a capability list. A guardian either cannot see the child's records, can see them, or can change them.

It is the same ladder, not a new one — which is the part that keeps the model honest. The design already ranks authority as revoked(0) < view(10) < contribute(20) < manage(30) < admin(40) and compares by integer, never by string (D-012). The three guardian rights map onto it: none → 0, view → 10, write → 20. Guardian authority is therefore a range of an existing ladder, not a parallel enum, and the resolver compares it with the machinery it already uses for grants. A fourth guardian value would have been the beginning of a second authorization model.

Amended by D-099, which deleted the ladder this paragraph leans on. The three values and everything they mean stand — the decision was never the numbers — but there is no rank left to map onto. The comparison now runs against a column on the permission: permission.right_kind ∈ read | write, where none covers nothing, view covers the codes marked read, and write covers both (data-model/05-authorization.md §1). That column has exactly one customer, and this entry is who it was added for. The paragraph's real work was never the shared arithmetic: a guardian not being staff is carried by the channel's shape test (D-079) — a check that is not about this child never reaches the guardianship channel, whatever its right level. And the closing warning survives intact, only cheaper to honour: a fourth value would still be the start of a second authorization model, and three values against two kinds is a lookup rather than a scale to keep in step.

What this deletes. Every dependent.* permission code, including dependent.admin and the three sub-resource .admin codes that D-068 deliberately exempted. The consequence is worth noticing: after D-068 deleted admin as a wildcard and D-074 deletes it as an action, the only things in the entire system still spelled admin are access_level.admin (a rank) and system.admin (the one wildcard permission). The word is no longer ambiguous three ways; it is ambiguous two ways, and the third is recorded as deleted.

And since D-099 deleted the ladder, it is ambiguous one way. access_level.admin was a rank in a table that no longer exists; system.admin is now the only live permission code in the system whose last segment is not an action, and it is allowed to be one for the two reasons D-104 records: its meaning is defined by the resolver rather than read off the name, and D-068 exempted it explicitly rather than by silence.

What it gives up, written down rather than discovered later. It is no longer expressible that this guardian may register the child for events but may not read the medical record, or that a grandmother may see the roster but nothing else. Under D-074 she either can see everything about her grandchild or nothing. The rescue is that write is not manage: a guardian at write still cannot do organization-wide things, cannot see a different dependent's records, and cannot reach beyond the records the dependent's own record contains. If the split turns out to be needed in real operation it is a new decision (E-7), and it should not be reintroduced as a permission nobody argued for.

D-046 survives, simplified. Defaults still differ by how the guardianship came into being — a parent recorded at creation starts at write; a court-appointed guardian and a grandmother-added emergency contact start elsewhere. What differs is now one value instead of a set.

See: ../data-model/04-relationships.md, ../appendix/permission-catalog.md, E-7.

docs.title: D-075 — Money arrives from a bank API; a payment is requested by variable symbol and QR code
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — closes finance questions 3, 5 and 6 Date: refinement round 6

Your answer. "Collection via gateway is the closest. It will be collected from the bank API and payments will be requested through variable symbol + a QR code."

This is not the gateway the finance document was braced for. Its question 6 anticipated a card gateway and listed what that drags in: checkout, webhooks, disputes, chargebacks, reconciliation, PCI. What you describe is the bank-account model, and it is a different animal: nobody pays by card through this system. The system issues a payment request carrying a variable symbol; the payer is shown that symbol and a QR code containing it; their own bank moves the money; the bank API reports the incoming transfer with the symbol still attached. The system never touches the payment — it reads a statement.

Four consequences, in descending order of how much they change the schema.

  1. The variable symbol is the design, so it must be unique forever. It is the only correlation key between "we expect money for this membership" and "money arrived at this account", which makes the payment request — not the payment — the entity the finance module is built around. Uniqueness is not per year, not per membership, not per unit: a symbol issued in 2019 must never resolve to a 2026 obligation, because bank statements are replayed and late payments are the entire reason the renewal window exists.
  2. A symbol is a sequence, never a derivation. Anyone can type eleven digits into a payment form. A symbol derived from a birth date, a membership id or a member number is guessable, and guessing one redirects a stranger's money into a child's financial record — a wrong fee balance, a membership that appears paid, a child recorded as covered who is not. Unguessable is not a privacy preference here; it is the integrity of the ledger.
  3. There are no reversals, so there is almost no status column. Bank transfers do not bounce, are not disputed by the payer's bank and do not expire. payment.status needs nothing resembling pending, failed, declined or disputed. A refund is a second payment in the opposite direction, not a transition of the first. The status enum that question 3 asked about collapses, and refunds — a policy question with no answer for six rounds — mostly answer themselves.
  4. A QR code is a rendering, not data. It encodes the symbol, amount and recipient that already exist. No stored image, no re-generation job, nothing to invalidate.

The consequence for D-040 is the one that matters operationally. The renewal window opens a new membership period at the expiry date when payment lands inside the window, and D-040's own note said the reliability of that rule depended on payment dates arriving reliably. Until now they arrived when somebody noticed a transfer. They now arrive from the bank. The backdating rule stops being a promise about someone's February and becomes a property of the import.

What is not decided, and is now the interesting part of the module. Whether event fees get a symbol as well as membership fees; whether a symbol is issued per person, per membership period, or per individual liability (a camp is a separate payable from a fee); and what the amount mismatch means when a payer enters 500 for a 550 request. See F-10.

See: ../data-model/07-finance.md, D-040.

docs.title: D-076 — Money that cannot be matched waits for a person
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — closes EV-3 and finance question 1's sibling Date: refinement round 6

Decision. A bank transfer that resolves to no live payment request — unknown symbol, the symbol of a cancelled event, an already-satisfied request, an amount that does not match, more than the request asked for — is recorded as an incoming transaction and enters a queue. The system neither applies it nor returns it.

The queue's outcomes, all chosen by a human: attach it to a different request; split it across several; record it as a donation with no obligation behind it; or refund it by hand.

Why not auto-apply by payer identity, which is the tempting answer. Because the case it gets wrong is not the edge case. A parent with two children pays one amount against one symbol is the ordinary shape of family payment in a youth organization, and an identity-based fallback resolves it to whichever child the query reaches first. A fee recorded against the wrong child is simultaneously a finance error, a membership that appears paid when it is not, and — where the fee buys insurance — a coverage record that is untrue. The fallback would be wrong on the common path, which is the one place a fallback is never allowed to be wrong.

Why not auto-refund. It requires the bank integration to work outbound as well as inbound — a second integration, with its own authorization. And it returns the grandparent's attempt at a camp contribution.

Where most of the queue's volume will actually come from: cancellation. D-064 made cancellation a recorded fact rather than a state, which means the event survives, the registrations survive, and so does an outstanding payment request against an occasion that is not going to happen. So: cancelling voids the outstanding requests, and money that had already arrived becomes a queue item for a person to refund or carry forward. This is EV-3's answer, which is why EV-3 is closed rather than deferred to finance.

The pattern, third occurrence. Across six rounds the design has permitted exactly two automatic state changes — the fee sweep (D-040) and the waitlist release (D-066) — and refused every other offer to act on a person's behalf. D-076 is the third refusal, and the first in the opposite direction: the earlier two released a person from something they owed; this one declines to release money from the person it belongs to. Unmatched money is a fact with no subject, and per D-059's discipline the absence gets stored rather than inferred.

See: ../data-model/07-finance.md, EV-3.

docs.title: D-077 — Messaging is direct by default, broadcast is an ordinary scoped permission, and the recipient chooses the channel
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) — first decision of the communication module (amended by D-082, which supplied the thing this entry declined and left unprovided: a rule for the private message to a child)

Date: refinement round 6

Your answer. "There will be internal messaging through the system. Personnel with 'broadcast' permissions are able to send messages to everyone, other users only to direct persons. The messages get then directed to email, push notifications or IM depending on the user's choices." — and, asked about the unit leader left out by that split, you chose a scoped permission.

Three decisions in one sentence, and the first is structural.

  1. The system is the medium; email, push and IM are delivery. A message is written once, internally, and then distributed. This is the load-bearing choice, because the alternative — the system as a mail relay — has no record of what anyone was told.
  2. Two sender tiers. Everyone may write direct messages. Broadcast is a permission.
  3. The recipient chooses the channel. The sender chooses who; the recipient chooses how it reaches them.

Therefore: one message, one recipient row each, and the medium resolved at delivery. A message plus a message_recipient per addressee carrying read state; the channel is selected per recipient against their own contact points. A bounced email is a failed delivery on one channel, not a lost message. person_contact.purpose gains a messaging purpose and each contact point carries its own opt-in, which is the existing contact-point model doing work rather than a new subsystem beside it.

broadcast is granted at a scope, which is the whole authorization model speaking again. Granted organization-wide it reaches everyone; granted on a unit it reaches that unit's people. No new mechanism — role assignments already carry a scope. A single global broadcast flag would have made a pack leader announcing a 9 a.m. start either the holder of an organization-wide power or the author of twelve identical messages, and the first of those is precisely the arrangement every other part of this design exists to prevent. Note that this lands on scope authority rather than on audiences: who may address a set is authority over that set, and authority over a set originates inside it.

Age is not a sender concept, and that is a decision, not an omission. The question asked whether staff may address a child directly or only their guardians; the answer replaced it with a sender-tier model that has no age in it. Consistent with D-070, there is no age branch in the resolver. The residue is stated rather than hidden: any account in the system may send a direct message to any other account, including a child's. The rule the communication section had promised — "a rule against contacting minors directly" — is not implemented as a restriction on senders. See MSG-1 for the recommendation, which is to restrict visibility rather than permission: direct messages reaching a minor mirrored to their guardians, so nothing is blocked, nothing is secretly unread, and the resolver still has no age branch.

Two-way door? The delivery half yes — adding a channel is a new contact purpose. The sender tiers no: once people can message each other, retracting that is a feature removal, and any later safeguarding rule has to be written as surveillance over a channel that already exists.

See: ../domain/02-actors.md, ../appendix/permission-catalog.md, ../open-questions.md § Communication.

docs.title: D-078 — An exposure extends an assignment, never a direct grant
docs.text:
Status: decided — found by deleting the SQL, not by running it Date: refinement round 6

Superseded by D-097 with the exposure table itself. Its distinction, that widening an inherited reach is a different act from writing a grant, has no subject after D-099: a grant has exactly one shape, and there is nothing to extend it.

What happened. Translating the resolver out of SQL for D-072 meant reading each branch for what it decides rather than what it says. The unit-grant tier had two branches, and the second one consulted scope_exposure. It joined the direct grant to se.org_unit_id while also requiring se.org_unit_id = the unit being checked. Both conditions pin the grant to the checked unit — which the first branch had already tested. The branch could never succeed where the first one failed.

It was not a vulnerability. A branch that can only ever return true where another branch already returned true grants nothing. The damage is to the reader: a tier that appears to widen direct grants through exposures is a tier that will be trusted, reviewed and extended on that basis. It survived every review of the SQL precisely because it reads correctly.

The rule, now stated. scope_exposure.role_assignment_id points at a specific person's assignment. The unit is agreeing that this person, in this role, for this period may act here — which is what makes the exposure legible as an act of the unit rather than a grant to a whoever-holds. A direct access_grant contains no assignment for an exposure to attach to, and a grant already at the checked unit needs no extension to work there. So the role channel is the table's only consumer, and the unit-grant tier matches exactly.

Why the tempting repair must be refused. "Exposures don't extend my direct grant — that looks like an oversight, let's add it back" produces a system where a unit that exposed a treasurer role assignment has also, silently, exposed itself to every direct grant held by every person who happens to hold some other assignment there. The repair would widen an exposure to cover people the exposing unit never approved, in the one direction the founding principle forbids. Anyone reaching for it should read this entry first, which is why it is a decision and not a comment.
