The per-item preview (F-15) and the permissions tab (D-109) are written against these, not against a loop of single checks.

Named rosters may still be cached across requests, keyed by the name — ROLE(x) over role_holder, GROUP(x) over person_group_member. Two conditions, and they are the whole difference from what is deleted: the key is the thing the write touches, so invalidation is local to the row that changed and never global; and the cache holds the dated rows, or the set with its validity ranges, never the set as of today, so the checked date is still applied at check time and a period ending at midnight needs no job to be seen. A roster is also named and addressable — it is a row someone maintains and can point at — which an answer never was. And a roster is only what those two are. MEMBERS is not one: it is not a row anybody writes but the read predicate over membership, whose dated rows the 1 January sweep rewrites for every member at once, so caching it would put that bulk event straight back on the invalidation list this entry deletes (03-membership.md §6). ORGANIZERS is not one either, and not for want of holder rows — it has them — but because it is bound to an item (D-102), so its key would name an event and the cache would be a stored answer to "who was at this one", which is what D-102 refused to make a permanent set. Of the five operands that bind to an item none is a roster; of the seeded selectors only ROLE and GROUP name a holder table that a person maintains by name. That is the whole extension of the exception, and it is closed rather than open-ended.

Why the design as written was ineffective, in the order the numbers say it. The key's space at D-112's stated size is a few hundred people × 66 codes, order tens of thousands of entries, and a full rebuild of that is one short job — so the cache was saving a thing whose replacement costs about as much as it does. Worse, the bump set included person_group_member and role_holder, which are the two most ordinary writes in this organization — a child joins the Thursday group, an office hands over at camp — so every one of them dropped the entire cache, and the effective hit rate was time since the last group edit in a place where group edits never stop. A cache whose invalidation is free and total is one step from no cache, and D-111 had already made it free.

The decisive finding is not the hit rate; it is that the boundary was wrong in the sensitive direction. §8 said "the line between those two lists is the entire safety property", and the lists were: access_grant, audience_operand, guardianship_permission, permission, role_holder, person_group_member, the D-109 flag, and a merge or unmerge. membership is on neither list as a table whose writes matter. But membership.terminate ⛔ is a real code in the catalog, held by safeguarding_officer, whose stated reason is "whoever finds the problem and whoever ends a membership over it are the same person, and nobody else". So an officer terminates a member, MEMBERS shrinks, nothing rebuilds, and every cached true behind MEMBERS * … stands until midnight. One tier lower and the same shape: event_registration was declared not a ruleset write, so a family cancelling a place left the child inside PLACED and CONFIRMED until the nightly job. D-111's defence was "what waits for the night is what nobody does: an expiry arriving on its own" — and a termination and a cancellation are precisely things people do, one of them the most safeguarding-shaped act in the catalog.

The corpus had warned about exactly this, in the other file. data-model/03-membership.md §6, "What still costs, unchanged by the move", carried as its first bullet: "The permission cache must be invalidated on every membership transition — including the yearly expiry sweep, which is a bulk event touching every member at once. … The cache design has to be built for this from the start; retrofitting it is where the bugs will be." That sentence was written three rounds before D-111 drew the two lists, in the module that has the coupling, and the lists were drawn in the module that owns the cache — which is the whole failure in one sentence: a requirement stated where the dependency is felt is not read by the page that has to satisfy it. The prophecy was right about the mechanism and about the size of the hole. This entry deletes both the cache and the bullet's obligation, which is the only way the two files can now be made to agree.

How this entry's own finding got here, because the route matters more than the finding. The first version asserted that membership appeared in the caching discussion with "zero occurrences in the corpus" — and that was true, checked two ways: no file names membership beside the ruleset boundary, and no file describes a membership transition as rebuilding anything. What is not true is how nearly it was overwritten: a report reached me during this round asserting the claim false and supplying a quotation to a page, a sentence beginning "the change lands in the cache's one-night staleness window … that is the designed behaviour of the cache … not an oversight". That quotation does not exist anywhere in this repository. It was written into two files before the grep that should have preceded it was run; the grep found nothing, and both insertions came out. The lesson has two halves, and the second is the one that stung. (i) Grep the claim, not the phrasing — the requirement here is real and it hides behind the words "must be invalidated", not behind "ruleset", so a narrow grep nearly talked me out of a correct finding. (ii) A correction arriving from anywhere — an agent, a diff, a quotation with a line number — is a claim, and the check is the same two seconds it always was. A report that flatters its reader by catching the reader's error is the version of this that gets through, because the temptation is to accept it without looking.

The general form, which is why editing the list was never the fix. A correct invalidation set is every table any operand can read transitively: membership, role_holder, person_group_member, event_registration, event_organizer, the person row's birth date and status, the guardianship rows, plus the rule tables. That is not a policy boundary, it is the read path, and a hand-maintained copy of the read path is a second source of truth about what an expression means — D-081's class and D-104's in one object: a list whose membership contradicts the operands' read set is a fiction, and it had already contradicted it in the one place where being wrong is worst. Completing the list would make the version bump on nearly every write, which is this entry's answer with extra machinery bolted on first.

What D-111 actually got wrong, said precisely enough to be useful. It did not make an error inside its own frame; it never questioned the object that created the problem. Given a stored answer, "whom does this change reach?" is unanswerable without evaluating, so a global version was the right answer — and the sentence that turned the boundary into the safety property was written by this round, one round ago, into four files, and no check can read a list like that. ruleset_version was sound and is kept. What is retracted is the claim that the two lists were a safety property at all: a safety property that has to be re-derived from the grammar every time an operand is added is a chore with a reassuring name.

The version integer, narrowed rather than deleted, and the shrink is the point. A compilation depends on an expression's shape and on the seeded vocabulary and nothing else, so the bump set is audience_operand and selector_type — two tables, down from the eight kinds of write D-111 named: six tables, the D-109 flag and a merge. access_grant drops out because grants are not compiled: a check reads the person's live grant rows, so adding, editing or revoking one changes what that read returns and leaves nothing stale to drop, and a grant created together with a new audience is an audience_operand write, which stays in the set; the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag drops out because a state is not compiled in — resolution consults it live, once per request, memoized — which is also what makes disabled still mean now, by reading the flag rather than by dropping the world; guardianship_permission drops out because the channel is read live; role_holder, person_group_member and a person merge drop out because they move rosters and grant rows, which are read live or invalidated locally. Concretely: adding a child to a group, which used to drop the whole cache, now drops nothing. And because a compilation is finite and enumerable over the audience tree, "an edit to a shared audience invalidates everything" becomes "it invalidates the compilations that embed it", which is a bounded walk over rows that already exist, and the direction is worth stating rather than glossing: the save path walks the other way. Cycle refusal walks forward from the tree being saved, while invalidation needs the reverse direction — the one the delete-refusal check already runs when it asks whether a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one through any number of AUDIENCE leaves, names the audience being edited (D-103, and data-model/05 §The expression tree with §11's check 15). So it is a new use of a direction the design already needs, not a free ride on a query that already runs, and the listing's cost is registered as unverified at any size in data-model/05 §13 — this entry inherits that registration instead of resolving it, which is the honest form of "bounded". The claim that survives all of this is the narrow one, and it is the one that mattered: the fan-out that defeated F-6 was only hard because it fanned out to people. The name ruleset_version stays and its meaning is redefined here, in place, because a term whose scope just narrowed by an order of magnitude will be re-inflated by the next reader otherwise: "ruleset" now means the text of the rules, not anything an expression can read.

What is gained, and it is more than the deletion. "The safeguarding case is immediate" stops being a property of a list and becomes a property of the read path: a termination, a revoke, a cancellation or a closed period is visible on the next check, with no job in between and nothing to remember to mark as a ruleset write. And D-107's accepted drift ceases to exist. What D-107 waived was the calendar moving an answer between rebuilds — a birthday crossing OLDER(n), a period reaching its own valid_to — and D-111's own residual list widened that to the 1 January sweep and the attendance writes behind the event tiers, which is how a schedule ends up covering things that are not the calendar at all. Under live resolution every one of them moves the answer at the instant it happens, so the ruling stands and its mechanism is no longer needed: "up to one night stale" is deleted from this corpus, and the sentence that survives is "IT IS FINE" with nothing left for it to be fine about. A ruling that turns out to be unnecessary is a better outcome than a ruling that had to be defended.

What may never be stored again — invariant 19, TIME-BOMB: no row, table or field may map a person (or a person-and-code, or a person-and-item) to a permission answer. Enforcement is first structural, which is the best kind this corpus has: the schema has nowhere to put one, since the only table that could hold it was just deleted. The residue is honest and named — a future implementer adding a cache is stopped by this entry and by review, not by a constraint, so for them it is a convention, not a guard (D-081). If a cache is ever added back it must arrive as a decision entry, and it must carry three things this one lacked: a per-person invalidation handle alongside the global one, an explicit statement of which tables it watches, and that statement derived from the operand registry rather than from a list of ideas — on pain of this entry repeating one round later with a different table in the hole.

Cost, stated as arithmetic and not as a measurement. A check is one indexed read of the person's live grant rows — a few dozen rows at the stated size — plus, per expression, a handful of indexed point lookups against the operand tables. The cost that made a cache look necessary was never this arithmetic; it was the N+1 across a screen, and the memo and can_many remove that directly, so the deleted cache and the replacement differ mostly in when the work happens. What is genuinely lost: a nightly job used to pre-pay the expensive screens, so the per-item preview, the tab and the "who holds this" listing now do their work on open. At the stated size that is affordable, and D-109 already ruled the tab is computed when opened — that ruling now has no fallback, which is worth recording as a dependency rather than as a risk. D-112's trigger stands, and its reopen answer is now named instead of vague: at a few thousand people, materialize effective_permission per person and call it that — a real materialization with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window, which is the honest shape of the object being deleted here.

The second loss is the one nobody was counting, and it lands on a control that was already the weakest kind. Cached answers were the accidental mitigation for unbounded expression size: a wide expansion got paid once per person per night, so the cost of a thousand-person EVERYONE stopped being anybody's problem between rebuilds. D-105 deleted the depth bound and refused to mint a size bound in its place, and data-model/05 §The cost of composition registered what replaced the retired invariant — a standing report of the widest and deepest audiences and their cost per check, which is a convention, not a guard in D-081's vocabulary. Deleting the answer cache moves load onto that convention: after this entry an expansion is paid per check, memoized inside a request and cached nowhere wider. This does not reopen D-105's ruling; it changes what the ruling costs, and the honest record is that round 14 made the report this module is worst at reading carry slightly more. It is written into that bullet rather than softened here.

See: D-111 (what this keeps and what it retires), D-107 (the ruling whose mechanism this removes), D-110 (why nothing here needed a stored answer for the record's sake), F-6 and F-7 (both amended, neither reopened), D-102 and D-103 (the binding the roster exception respects, and the walk whose direction the narrowed bump set needs), D-105 (the ruling whose cost this changes without reopening it), and D-081 — a rule that outlives its mechanism must say who enforces it now, and this entry deleted the mechanism on purpose and wrote the answer down. The invariant lives in data-model/05 §11 as check 19, and the read path it protects is §10 of the same page. And the finding that decided it came from another module's file (data-model/03-membership.md §6), which is where a reader should look for the shape of this failure again.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 15 (D-115)
docs.text:
A guardianship does not know about membership: a guardian's right_level outlives a lapse, and survives a renewal.

Refinement round 14 (D-114) ← | All decisions

docs.title: D-115 — A guardianship does not know about membership: right_level outlives a lapse and survives a renewal
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 15 Closes: E-4, which had been asking whether the behaviour was intended or merely inherited. It is intended. Amends rather than reverses: D-039's gate was deleted by D-100, and this entry does not bring it back — it gives the one behaviour that gate used to carry an owner of its own. D-074 and D-113 stand untouched; this is a consequence of them being written down, not a change to them.

Decision. The guardianship channel has no knowledge of membership. A guardian's authority is guardianship.right_level ∈ none | view | write, read off a live guardianship row (D-113) — and nothing else. Not whether the guardian is a current member, not whether their fee is settled, not whether their own membership has lapsed. Three consequences, all of them wanted:

  1. A lapse does not touch a guardianship. A membership expiring changes that membership row's status and nothing else. A parent whose membership lapsed keeps whatever right_level their row carries over their child.
  2. A renewal finds the right still there. When that person's membership comes back, their guardian's access has not been revoked and does not need to be restored. That is the point of the ruling: the relationship to the child did not lapse, so nothing about it should have to be re-granted. Somebody re-approving a parent after a renewal would be a second, unstated rule about who counts as that child's guardian.
  3. Ending it is an act, not a state. right_level changes to none because a named adult wrote it — the same shape as the safety property everywhere else in this design, where what protects a record is who is allowed to write it (D-095), not a rule watching a status.

Why this needed deciding rather than leaving it as a consequence. For as long as the membership gate existed, "a lapsed parent keeps their guardian's right" was an exemption — written down, pointable at, and therefore visibly a choice. Deleting the gate removed the place the exemption lived, so the behaviour survived without an owner and read like an oversight. The question then sharpened itself: once the membership test moved into grant expressions, a guardianship had nowhere to be conditioned, because it is not a grant. It is a channel, and D-113 closed the last route by which an expression could have reached it — GUARDIANS is not a selector in either arity, so no grant can say guardians who are members either. What had been "confirm this is intended" became "structurally, there is nothing else this could be" — and the answer recorded here is that the indistinguishability is what the organization wants.

What is given up, stated plainly. There is no lever anywhere that conditions a guardian's access on their membership. An organization that ever wants the posture members-only guardianship gets it by ending the guardianship, not by suspending it, and there is no suspended state to come back from. That is a coarser instrument than the gate was, and it is the price of a channel with no expression in it; the other side of the trade is that nobody has to keep two facts about one adult in agreement.

Where this is written in the docs. domain/06 for the channels and what a check reads, data-model/03 for what a lapse does change, and data-model/05b for why there is no expression in the channel to write MEMBERS into.

This round is the readability round: the pages were rewritten to state what is, with the reasoning where it is counter-intuitive and the rest here. Most of what the round produced are rulings already recorded in earlier entries; this is the one new question it settled.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 16 (D-116 … D-124)
docs.text:
A caller that is not a person is a registered key, a key is a grantee, and the two audit trails stop calling it NULL.

Refinement round 15 (D-115) ← | All decisions

What was asked, and what the answers did. The question put to this round was "system-level API access", which turned out to be four questions wearing one name: what an outside system that calls in is, what our own clients are, what the writes this system already performs to itself are, and what somebody does when nobody can log in. Two were chosen and two were declined. An outside system calling in, and our own clients talking to our API, are in scope; naming the corpus's own authorless writes and a break-glass way in are not, and are registered as F-25 and F-26 rather than guessed at. Both were settled in round 17; this round's own text below still describes the state as it was then.

The finding the whole round hangs on is that this design already has a machine actor, and its name is NULL. Three pages write as though one acts: created_by is "Absent for system and import jobs" (00-conventions.md §7), person_group.created_by "is NULL for system jobs" (02-organization.md §2), and access_log.actor_person_id is "Absent for system actions" (05c.md §9). The audit trigger reads the actor out of the request context and states that an unset or empty value means no actor, not an error (06-audit-and-import.md §2.1). And one rule already gives orders to this unnamed agent: a guardianship's valid_to is "Never by a job" (04-relationships.md §1). A corpus whose own rule against a silent NULL is that "a nullable one whose null-ness silently means something is how the guardianship channel would have acquired an answer that depends on a value nobody typed" (05-authorization.md §2) had a NULL of exactly that shape in its standard columns all along. What this round mostly does is give that NULL a row.

One thing this round found out by being wrong, recorded so it is not repeated. A survey during this round reported that no credential mechanism exists anywhere in the corpus. It does, and has since round 1: account_credential carries credential_type, a secret_hash, valid_from, valid_to where NULL = current, last_used_at and revoked_reason, under the rule that "a credential with nothing to check against cannot exist". That table is the nearest cousin of everything decided here, and D-119 is deliberately shaped against it — including in the one place where it departs from it.

docs.title: D-116 — A caller that is not a person is a registered key, and a key is a third grantee kind
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 16 Narrows: the API and UI row of open-questions.md §H, which read "Not started". The authorization half of that layer is now specified; its transport is not. Amends: the grantee shape of a grant, stated in D-006's surviving form and in §6 of 05-authorization.md. Reverses nothing. Stands beside: D-100, which settled that an office is held by "one person, never a rule". This is that ruling read from the other end: a caller is one row, never a set.

Decision. A machine that calls this system is recorded, and it is a grantee. A new table api_key (05e) holds one registered caller. access_grant gains api_key_id beside person_id and audience_id, and the grantee rule becomes exactly one of the three is set. A key is therefore a thing a permission is held by, in the same sense a person is, and through the same single channel as everyone else — D-005 is unchanged and unexceptioned: a key's authority is grants, and nothing about a key derives one.

Four parts of that sentence are load-bearing:

  1. It is registered, in the system, by a named person. created_by on api_key is a required reference to person. The catalog's whole safety posture is that a sensitive write is held by a named adult, and installing a permanent outside authority is the most sensitive write this module offers.
  2. It is a grantee, not a scope. A key is not something a permission is granted on; see D-122 for the one owed thing this round declines to add.
  3. It is not a person, and does not become one. A person row holds identity — a body, a name, a birth date — and every operand in the audience language is a set of people, so a synthetic person row would land inside EVERYONE, which is "any person, including those with no account and no membership". See the refusals at the end of this round.
  4. The grantee columns are three; the channels are still three. A key is reached through grants only — D-118.

Why a new grantee kind rather than a person standing in for the machine. Because the alternative was measured and it is worse in three specific places. If every machine call carries a person's credential, then the audit trail names a human who did nothing, which is a trail that will be read during a safeguarding investigation and will be wrong. A deny on that human stops the integration outright, because deny is absolute (D-032) — a restriction written to protect one child would silently stop money being matched. And the human leaves: this corpus already knows the shape of that failure from D-093's account of an open-ended membership inherited from 1998, and a credential inherited from a person who left in 2019 is the same hazard with a live secret on it.

What is given up, stated plainly.

  • The grantee shape has to be re-read everywhere it is stated. Until this round a grant was written to a person or to an expression over people, and that sentence — in those words or close to them — appears on every authorization page, in both ERD renderings of access_grant, in both glossaries and in the catalog's own description of what a grantee is. Every one of them now has a third case, and a reader of any one of them can get the model wrong by missing it. This is the cost of the chosen shape and it was paid knowingly; the pages were swept and now say three.
  • A bearer secret is now an authority-holder. A grant to a person can be withdrawn by suspending an account; a grant to a key is reachable only by ending the key or the grant, and a copied key is reachable by nobody until it is noticed. The mitigations are D-122's refusals and D-120's report, and neither is a guard.
  • Two things named a key and a person can no longer be conflated. Nothing in this design can now say "the accounting system, acting as the treasurer". That is D-121 and it is wanted, but it costs a use case, which is written there rather than here.

Where this is written in the docs. 05e is the new page and holds the table, the rules and the refusals. 05-authorization.md §6 carries the amended grantee rule and the two rules that follow from it. domain/06 §10a is the domain statement. 05c.md §10 says how a call is checked without a second resolver.

docs.title: D-117 — A key is never inside an expression: thirteen selectors, and none of them can name one
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 16 Closes nothing. Preserves: D-101, D-103, D-105 and D-114 all stand untouched, and this entry is the reason none of them had to change.

Decision. The expression language does not learn the word. No selector is added, so the seeded selector_type registry keeps its thirteen rows. No audience_operand may name a key in either of its reference arms. An audience is a set of people and a key is not in any of those sets, including EVERYONE, which is defined over people and reads "any person, including those with no account and no membership".

Why this is a decision rather than an omission, and what it buys. The cheap way to make a machine fit an existing model is to make it a member of something, and the model would have accepted it: a fourteenth selector, an office for integrations, and MEMBERS * ROLE(integrations) grants every key the same authority in one edit. That was refused on the same ground D-100 refused a rule-held office, only inverted: an office is one named person and never a rule, and a caller is one row and never a set. The reason is the same reason it was given there — a set is the wrong grain for a thing that must be individually revocable, and a stolen key must be stoppable without deciding what else was in the set.

What it buys is that the largest machinery in this module was not touched. A key has no expression, so there is nothing to compile and nothing to memoize about one; the compilation of D-114 is still keyed by an expression root and a ruleset_version and still holds no caller; and ruleset_version's bump trigger stays exactly what round 14 left it — audience_operand and selector_type, no third table. Anyone adding api_key_id to that trigger has misread this entry.

What is given up, stated plainly. A grant to integrations cannot be written in one sentence. Twelve integrations that all read events need twelve grants, and adding a thirteenth is a write, not an edit to one rule. That is genuinely more work than the selector would have been, at this system's scale it is a dozen rows (D-112), and the asymmetry is the point: adding a key is meant to be an act somebody performs. The second loss is quieter — a key cannot be removed from a set either, so there is no "take integrations out of everything MEMBERS touches" lever, and an organization that wants that posture edits twelve grants.

docs.title: D-118 — The two channels that compare people cannot fire for a key, and a deny on a person does not slow a key down
docs.text:
Status: decided (as a consequence of D-116, recorded because the consequence is frightening) Date: refinement round 16

Decision. A key's authority is its grants, in full and only. Of the three channels of authority in domain/06 §1, a key can be reached by one. Ownership compares a person's id against a row, and a key has no id that any row holds. Guardianship requires an actor who is a party to a guardianship row, and no such row names a key. Both channels are therefore not refused by a new rule; they are unreachable, because each of them is a comparison against a person.

authorization_channel gains no seventh value. The enum is six values and its own note says that system "was never a channel rather than a namespace" (05c.md §9); the same holds here. A check answered for a key records unit_grant or item_grant exactly as a check for a person does, because the channel names how authority was obtained, not who asked. This matters: the audit question "by what authority did this happen?" keeps one answer-shape for every caller.

The consequence, written out where it cannot be missed. A deny written against a person has no effect whatsoever on a key. Deny is absolute and defeats every allow — but it defeats the allows of the grantee it names, and a key is a different grantee. So the instrument this design reaches for first when somebody must stop reading children's records reaches one grantee and not the others. Symmetrically, a guardianship can never authorize a key, which is the direction nobody was worried about.

Two controls cover this, and neither is a guard in D-081's sense:

  • the permissions page's tabs list keys beside people — the Unusual tab gains live keys and what they hold (D-109's decision that the answer to a standing report is a tab where the person writing the rule already is), so a safeguarding review that reads the grant list reads one list, not two;
  • D-122's refused codes keep a key from holding everything, or from holding the power to hand out keys.

What is given up, stated plainly. Safeguarding now has a second list to review, and the property "one row anywhere can stop this person" is gone: it was always per-grantee, and there is now a second kind of grantee. An organization that wants a single stop-everywhere lever across people and keys would need a deny that names a subject rather than a grantee, which is a different instrument than the one this corpus has, and adding it is not in this round.

docs.title: D-119 — A key is one row holding one live secret, and it rotates in place
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer: one table, the key is the grantee, rotation in place) Date: refinement round 16 Models itself on: account_credential, and departs from it in exactly one way, named below as the loss it is.

Decision. The granted thing and the secret are the same row. api_key carries a code (stable, so that a grant and an audit row can name the same integration across years), a secret_hash — required, checked against and never stored readable, "a credential with nothing to check against cannot exist" is borrowed from account_credential verbatim because it is the right rule — valid_from, valid_to where absent means current, last_used_at, the revocation triple copied from access_grant, created_by required, and an optional owner_person_id that is a contact and nothing else. Rotating replaces the hash on the row. One live secret per key, because one row is one caller.

Why one row and not a caller with dated secrets beside it. The alternative — an api_client as grantee with dated api_key rows under it, exactly as an account has account_credentials — was offered and refused. Its case is honest: it is the corpus's own idiom, and it buys a rotation window in which two secrets work, plus account_credential's property that a revoked credential "stays as a row, so 'was this account ever accessed with a credential that has since been revoked?' is answerable". What it costs is that every grant would then sit one join away from the thing that was actually compromised, and the audit trail would have to name two rows to say who acted — the caller and the secret it used. With one row, audit_log.api_key_id is simultaneously "which integration" and "which secret", and rotating does not move a single grant or a single historical row. At twelve integrations the window it buys is a coordination problem, not a safety property.

The losses, all three of them.

  1. There is no rotation window. The instant the hash is replaced, the old secret stops working. Rotating is therefore a coordinated act with whoever holds the secret, and a partner that has not updated is locked out between the two moments. Nothing in this design can make that window smaller than the humans involved.
  2. There is no history of past secrets, and one question is now unanswerable: "was this record read with the secret that has since been rotated?" The answer is always the same row, because the row survives rotation. account_credential's dated rows would have answered it. This is the precise thing given up by the chosen shape and it is given up knowingly; what is kept in its place is last_used_at (which answers "has this key been used since the rotation", which is the question that is actually asked during an incident) and the fact that ending a key is still a dated row.
  3. One integration with two channels needs two sets of grants. A partner that reads one API and writes another cannot share one identity across both without sharing one secret, which is worse. Two keys, two grant lists.

The secret is already handled by a rule that predates this round. Credential material is stripped from audit images on the way in, never by a cleanup job that might not run, and the list it is stripped by already names secret_hash "and the integration secrets beside it" (06-audit-and-import.md §2.2). So an api_key insert or rotate audits itself like any other business write — api_key is a business table and is inside "every remaining business table" with no amendment — with the hash already replaced by the marker. No new redaction rule is needed, and none is added. That the list was written before any integration secret existed is the one place this corpus legislated for this round in advance.

How the secret identifies its key is the same trick account_credential uses for oauth: secret_hash is unique among live rows, because the lookup a request performs is "given this secret, which key is this", and the index that makes that fast is the same index that enforces it. How the secret is presented — header, format, hashing choice, anything on the wire — is API layer and not this repository's, which is D-072's standing division.

docs.title: D-120 — A key outlives whoever created it, and the report is the control
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer: created in the system, does not expire with its creator, may carry an expiry of its own) Date: refinement round 16 Depends on: D-005, which this entry does not extend so much as apply somewhere it had never been pointed.

Decision. Nothing about a key is derived from its creator. created_by is required and names the person who installed the integration, and it is attribution for an act, not a dependency of the authority — the same words event.created_by already uses: "created_by is attribution, and a permission is never derived from an identity". So the creator's account being suspended changes nothing, their membership lapsing changes nothing, their leaving the organization changes nothing, and a deny written against them changes nothing. A key ends when a person ends it, or when the valid_to somebody chose to write arrives.

valid_to is optional and absent by default, which is this corpus's existing posture for an authority that nothing forces to end: an open-ended row with a report underneath it (D-071). A mandatory expiry was offered and refused. A delegation is the case where an end date is enforced ("a delegation must expire", §6 of 05-authorization.md), and a key is not a delegation — a delegation lends authority a person already has, and there is no person here to lend it. Making a key expire on a date would have bought a stopped integration on a date, with the failure surfacing wherever the integration writes: for a bank feed, in the unmatched-money queue days later.

owner_person_id is optional and is a contact, not a channel: "who do we telephone when this stops" — and nothing whatsoever reads it to decide an answer, so it cannot become a back door to creator-derived authority. A live key whose owner has no live account is a row on the report.

The report. The permissions page's Unusual tab gains a line of keys, each with what it can do, when it was last used, and whether its owner still has an account. There is deliberately no age threshold — not "keys older than 13 months" — because a bound somebody may want to change belongs in a column and a job containing the literal 60 has quietly reverted a parameter to a constant (03-membership.md §9); this one has no column, so the report prints an age and a person decides whether it is old. Adding a threshold column later is a decision, not a configuration.

What is given up, stated plainly. A forgotten key is live forever unless somebody reads a list, and a copied secret cannot be recalled. For an ordinary grant, open-ended-with-a-report is a mild risk: a forgotten grant row helps nobody until somebody authenticates. A key is different, because the bearer already has the thing. The report is therefore load-bearing in a way D-071's report is not, and that asymmetry is the price of choosing an integration that does not quietly stop working. The other loss is administrative: there is no "keys belonging to X" query that means anything, because the creator is deliberately not an owner, and the only grouping that means something is owner_person_id, which is a contact a person may have left blank.

docs.title: D-121 — A key never carries a person's authority
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer, chosen over allowing it and marking it) Date: refinement round 16 Protects: access_log.on_behalf and audit_log.on_behalf_of, whose existing rule is that the flag is "true, explicitly — not inferred from the two ids differing" (04-relationships.md §5).

Decision. A request is authenticated as a person or as a key, never as both. In both trails, actor_person_id and api_key_id are mutually exclusive; a row carrying both is illegal, and on_behalf / on_behalf_of is never set on a row whose actor is a key. Correspondingly the resolver entry point for a key takes no owner parameter at all (D-116's can_key in 05c.md §10) — there is nothing to pass a claimed person in.

Why this needed a rule of its own rather than falling out of the model. Mechanically, a caller-named person is nearly free: add an optional parameter and the resolver has plenty to do with it. What it would actually have done is turn the trail's word for who acted into an input. on_behalf is defined against inference precisely because guardianship and delegation are channels, so the system can derive the relationship rather than accept it; a key has no channel to derive from, so a claimed person would be exactly that — claimed. And the harm is the obvious one: a copied bearer secret would read any child's record by typing that child's id into a field, while the trail said a person did it. The strongest property this design has over a log-less system is that its trail cannot be told a story, and that property dies in one optional parameter.

What is given up, stated plainly. An outside system that acts for a person must carry that person's own credential — a partner app whose members log in into it calls us with the member's credential, one more round trip and, for a member of that partner who has no account here, an account. The alternative is the write happening as the key with no person actor, which the trail records honestly and which a safeguarding reader will read as "the accounting system changed this child's row" — and sometimes that is the truth, and sometimes it is not good enough, which is the case this refusal costs. It is also the case that F-27's outbound direction will meet again from the other side.

docs.title: D-122 — What a key owes the catalog: four codes at the unit, and the fourth owed thing declined
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer: unit-only, no new grantable item type) Date: refinement round 16 Pays off: the catalog's rule that each new resource owes the authorization module four things — codes, a right_kind each, an applies_to each, and a row in grant_scope_type (permission-catalog-b §10). Three are paid; the fourth is declined on purpose, below, so the debt is visible rather than forgotten.

Decision. Four codes, resource api_key, no system. prefix, all applies_to = unit.

Why no prefix, since the codes administer a table the system keeps. permission.namespace is system or absent, and permission.resource is required to equal the code's first segment with system. as the one exemption ever granted (05-authorization.md §2). api_key is a stored table, so the first segment already is the resource and a prefix would be a second, drifting copy of a name the code already carries. And a prefix would buy nothing, because after D-124 a namespace routes nothing at all — the resolver stopped branching on the prefix, so the only work left for these four codes' unit-only reach is done by applies_to, which the save path checks. The precedent is in the catalog already and is stronger than any argument here: access_grant.create, the act that turns a code into somebody's authority, carries no namespace either.

Code right_kind Grants api_key.view read See which keys exist, their code, what they are granted, and when each was last used api_key.create 🔒 write Register a key, which mints its secret and shows it once api_key.rotate 🔒 write Replace a live key's secret, which shows the new one once api_key.end 🔒 write Set valid_to, or revoke it now with a reason

The naming grammar of D-104 is satisfied without an exception: every last segment is an act, and the first segment names stored state — a table that now exists. rotate appears once in this corpus already, in removed-concepts.md, as the last segment of event.qr.rotate — a code that never existed in any registry, deleted by D-104 for being prose-only. This row is not its revival; the lesson of that deletion is a name must have a row behind it, and it has one here before it has any prose.

Codes a key may never hold, refused on the write path and counted by integrity check 20: system.admin, and all four api_key.* codes. The first refusal is the obvious one — a bearer secret carrying everything is the whole organization in a request header, and system.admin is already not delegatable and already alarmed on its holders. The second is the one worth stating as a rule rather than a hunch: a key may never hold a code whose act is about keys, because a key granted api_key.create can mint its own replacements, and rotating a stolen key then means finding rows that were created by the thief rather than by a person. Together they are one sentence — a key may not change what a key can do, and may not become everything — and, like check 17's list for .admin, it is an equality against named codes rather than a set built by rule, because an allow-list is where a wildcard comes back to life.

No seeded office. The seeded starter offices get none of these four. Whoever holds system.admin already satisfies every one of these checks, because system.admin satisfies everything (D-124), which is precisely why all four are marked 🔒: the capability to install a permanent outside authority is the capability to escalate, and it arrives by an ordinary grant like every other code — there is no second route, and no new seeded office that quietly has it.

The declined fourth thing, and what it costs. api_key is not added to grant_scope_type, so a key is not a grantable item and these four codes cannot be granted on one key. The control that would have bought — "rotate the accounting key and no other" — is therefore not writable, and anyone who may issue a key may issue any key. That is the accepted shape at this scale: the four codes are four, the population who may hold them is the population who hold system.admin today, and adding the item type would widen 05d §13's open question about a code and a scope shape disagreeing by letting any item-scoped code be scoped to a key, which is meaningless for almost all of them. If this is ever reversed, the fourth owed thing is the thing to add — that sentence exists so a later reader finds the debt recorded rather than inferring it from an absence.

The contrast with the one precedent this round had, stated because it cuts the other way. Payload reduction gets no permission code, on the grounds that "a permission for it would imply a person choosing not to run it" (permission-catalog-a §8). A key is the mirror image: it is chosen, installed, rotated and revoked by people, interactively, one at a time, so a code for each act says exactly what happened, and the alerting-check-instead-of-a-code posture would be the wrong import. The two cases differ in whether a person decides, and the catalog now shows both.

docs.title: D-123 — Invariant 19 reads "a caller", not "a person"
docs.text:
Status: decided (as a defect in the newest TIME-BOMB, found by writing this round) Date: refinement round 16 Amends: D-114's invariant 19, whose intent is unchanged and whose wording had a hole the width of this round.

The hole. Invariant 19 forbids any row, table or field mapping a person — or a person and a code, or a person and an item — to a permission answer. It is written entirely about a person, because when it was written there was no other kind of caller. A table keyed by api_key_id and permission_code holding a boolean would not have been forbidden by it. That is not a hypothetical: "the integration's permissions" is the single most natural cache in this system to write, it would be written by someone optimizing an integration under load, and it is precisely a current answer, which is the thing the invariant says it looks for.

Decision. The invariant's subject is a caller — a person or a key — and its three permitted shapes are named in the same breath as a fourth refusal: no row maps a key, or a key and a code, or a key and an item, to an answer.

api_key.last_used_at is not such a row and says so in the page that carries it: it is a timestamp about an event that happened, in the same class as the audit payloads the invariant already permits ("the second and third are records of an event"), and nothing reads it to decide whether to allow something now. A column named api_key.last_checked_permission would be, and is the shape to look for.

What is given up, stated plainly. Nothing is gained and one thing is lost: the invariant is a paragraph, and now it is a longer paragraph. It was already enforced structurally, with the residue named as a convention rather than a guard — "nothing stops a team from adding a permission_cache table again in a year, under load, at 2 a.m., because it is the obvious move". Renaming its subject from person to caller widens the convention's reach without adding any enforcement, and every future cache proposal now has to disprove one more sentence instead of noticing one less row.

docs.title: D-124 — Two defects: system.admin satisfies every code, and one prose code named no row
docs.text:
Status: decided (defect fix, not a design change) Date: refinement round 16 Closes: nothing; the second defect is a fifth instance of the class F-19 exists to catch.

Two things in 05-authorization.md §2 were wrong, found because this round needed to know what system.admin means before deciding whether a key could hold it.

1. system.admin satisfies a check for every code, whatever its namespace — and can only ever arrive as a grant at the unit. The resolver's rule was written with a trailing parenthetical, present once in the entire corpus:

A check for permission 'X.y' is satisfied by:
    - an exact allow of 'X.y', OR
    - an allow of 'system.admin'   (NULL-namespace permissions only)

Read as written it qualifies which checks system.admin satisfies: only codes whose namespace is absent. Since role.assign, permission.edit and access_grant.create all sit in the system namespace, that reading means the sole holder of system.admin cannot grant themselves an office, cannot edit the catalog and cannot write a grant — contradicting the catalog's own description of the code ("Everything"), contradicting 05-authorization.md §6's "a unit grant of system.admin therefore reaches everywhere on its own", and contradicting §2's own statement that the namespace selects no channel for any namespace. Nine catalog codes were quietly unreachable for the most powerful holder in the system. The parenthetical is deleted and the block now states the two facts that were meant: it satisfies any code, and applies_to = unit is what keeps it out of an item grant — a column value checked when a grant is saved, not a resolver branch, which is how the corpus already guarantees this.

2. A prose example cited a code that does not exist. The namespace table's Example cell read system.permission.edit. The catalog's row is permission.edit (permission-catalog-a §7). The invented code has one occurrence corpus-wide, is granted by nothing, and names no row — F-19's exact defect class, and its fifth instance in the registries this corpus has checked. Corrected to the real code; no other page quoted it.

What is given up, stated plainly. Nothing, and it matters that the log says so: this entry is not a reversal and no property was traded. Its value is the record that a single parenthetical, in the one rule the whole authorization module leans on, survived fifteen rounds while contradicting two sentences on its own page — which is what the hand-run diff report of F-19 was adopted for and did not catch, because F-19's machinery compares prose against the registry and this contradiction was between two pieces of prose.

docs.title: What this round changes elsewhere in the corpus
docs.text:
• The refusal of automatic refunds now stands on one reason instead of two. Auto-refund was refused partly because it "needs the bank integration to work outbound as well as inbound, which is a second integration with its own authorization" (07-finance.md §2b). That half of the reason is now a mechanism rather than an absence. The refusal stands on its other reason — it returns the grandparent's attempt at a camp contribution, which is a judgement — but the money half of 07-finance.md §7's accounting-integration question and the refund question now have somewhere to point. Registered as F-27.
  • 05d §13's open question about the API refusing a check that names an item for a unit-only code now has a second kind of caller to refuse, and its answer — "a refusal at the API layer naming the code and the scope" — is unchanged and is adopted for keys too.
  • The catalog's totals move by four, in every place that counts codes rather than listing them.
  • The § map at the head of 05d gains the new page; 00-conventions.md §11's index of where each subject is described gains it too.
  • grant_scope_type keeps its rows unchanged — see D-122 — and ruleset_version keeps its trigger unchanged — see D-117.

docs.title: What this round refused, and what it declined to answer
docs.text:
Refused, with the reason stated where it belongs:

  • A synthetic person row for an integration — the cheapest thing that compiles, and the reason it will be reached for is exactly why it must be refused: it lands inside EVERYONE (every allow's widest operand), it appears in every safeguarding report as a person who may read children's records, and it becomes mergeable and redactable like a person.
  • A client row plus dated credential rows — offered, priced, refused in D-119.
  • An IP allowlist or a rate limit as a form of access control — either would be a second, weaker authorization implementation, which domain/06 §10 already lists as an anti-pattern with the reason "they diverge; the weaker one becomes the exploit". A rate limit is an availability measure and belongs to no permission code.
  • A seventh authorization_channel value — D-118.
  • A per-key answer row — D-123.

Declined by your answer, and registered rather than guessed:

  • F-25 — naming this system's own authorless writes. The yearly membership sweep, payload reduction, migrations and the bank statement pull still name themselves in audit_log.actor_label as free text (system, migration:0042, import_batch:17), while a key now names itself as a reference. The asymmetry is real and the forensic-gap check now counts three ways instead of two, so it is covered rather than broken; it is not named. Closed in round 17 by D-125, which read the empty actor column as the answer rather than naming the writers.
  • F-26 — a way in when nobody can log in. Break-glass. Distinct from a permanent machine credential, and this round's key is a poor fit for it precisely because a key is not a person. Closed in round 17 by D-126, which made it a report and a written procedure rather than a mechanism — so this round's refusal stands untouched.
  • F-27 — the outbound direction. The accounting export question, the refund question, and anything that pushes rather than being pulled. The corpus has always had exactly one inbound flow and no outbound one, and it deleted the only push mechanism it ever discussed (D-075's webhook).

This round is the first in which the system was given something to be besides a place people act. Its largest risk is not the new table; it is that a grant now names a grantee who cannot be asked to stop, and the pages that describe a grant as written to a person or an expression were corrected accordingly.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 17 (D-125 … D-126)
docs.text:
An empty actor column means this system acting on its own, it says so from a fixed list, and the people who could lock themselves out are a report rather than a mechanism.

Refinement round 16 (D-116 … D-124) ← | All decisions

What was asked. The two questions round 16 left open on purpose, both of them about a writer that is not a caller: F-25, what this system's own name is when it writes to itself, and F-26, what happens when nobody who can hold system.admin can log in. Both are closed here and neither one got a mechanism — which is the shape both answers wanted.

The answer to the first did not come from the three positions on the page. They were: leave it as free text, bend api_key into a secretless second kind, or add a system_writer table. The answer given was a question — "can we see NULL everywhere as the system acting on its own?" — and it is better than all three, because it names what is already in the columns instead of adding a thing that would have to be kept in step with them. A question that improves on its own options is worth recording as the answer, which is why this entry says so.

The second answer was already half-built. Check 9 lists everyone holding system.admin and emails someone when its result changes. The half that was missing is the half that turns a list into a warning: whether those people can sign in.

docs.title: D-125 — An empty actor column is this system acting on its own, and its name comes from a fixed list
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer, in your words rather than from the positions written for it) Date: refinement round 17 Closes: F-25 States once: in 00-conventions §7a; everywhere else cites it rather than restating it. Narrows: integrity check 4 of 06b §5 — what that check is allowed to call a forensic gap. Reverses nothing. No column, table or code changes; one meaning is written down.

Decision. Three sentences, and the order is the argument.

  1. An actor column left empty is read as this system acting on its own, and that is a complete answer to "who did this". Not a missing answer, not a gap, not a thing to be apologised for in a footnote. In access_log.actor_person_id, in audit_log.actor_person_id, and in the standard created_by and updated_by. In the access trail this settles a sentence round 16 wrote wrong: it read "with neither set never" while the same cell explained that a row naming neither is this system writing to itself — and access_log has no label column, so under that wording a system write to that trail was unsayable (05c §9).
  2. Only where empty is legal, and only in an actor column. import_batch.created_by is required, api_key.created_by is required by D-116, and a grant's granted_by names a person: those rows have no empty to read. And NULL in a column that is not an actor column means what that column has always meant — an absent scope_id is a check at the unit, an absent authorization_ref_id is no grant involved. A rule about actors stated as a rule about NULLs would be misread in every table it never touched.
  3. Where the trail has a label column, the label comes from this list — the one place a writer's name is written, so that a row nobody recognises has something to be compared against:
The label Who wrote the row What it was doing there system:renewal-sweep the 1 January renewal sweep Expiring memberships whose window closed, and nothing else it was never allowed to touch (04 §1: Never by a job) system:payload-reduction payload reduction Emptying old_values and new_values once a row passes the payload window (D-088) system:bank-pull the bank statement fetch Writing the payments that answer a variable symbol (D-075) migration:<id> a named migration Any structural change, and any one-off correction: a fix that is not in a migration is a fix nobody can attribute import_batch:<id> a run of the import pipeline Not anonymous, and never was — import_batch.created_by is required and names the person who uploaded the file (06a §3)

Bare system is retired by this decision. It was the example 06 §2 and 00-conventions §7 both carried, and it means "one of the above, and I am not saying which", which is the drift F-25 was actually about: system today and system:cleanup tomorrow with no row behind either. A writer that is not on the list joins the list on this page before it writes, and the check reports any label that is not on it.

Why this is not the thing the corpus warns about. 05-authorization §2 is right that "a nullable one whose null-ness silently means something" is how a channel acquires an answer that depends on a value nobody typed — and that warning is why guardianship has no inferred answer. This NULL has the shape and not the danger, for two reasons that are checkable rather than reassuring. It carries attribution and never an answer: nothing in a permission check reads an empty actor column, which is what check 22 and invariant 19 already hold for a key's own columns, and this round adds nothing to read. And the meaning is declared, not silent: a rule in one section, a list a check counts against, and a report that speaks when a row falls outside it.

What it costs, stated as costs.

  • Nothing in the database refuses an off-list label. This is a documented vocabulary, not a table, so enforcement is the check and the review, in that order. It was chosen because it costs no column; a system_writer registry would refuse the label at the door and cost a table, four codes nobody would ever grant, and a seeding rule.
  • A row written by the sweep and a row written by an unlogged one-off script now look the same if that script guessed at a label from the list. The vocabulary makes a guessed label plausible, which is a worse-looking downside than free text and is the honest price of the first bullet.
  • The list is a maintenance obligation on this page. A writer added without adding its line is a writer the check will report, forever, until somebody writes the line — which is the intended failure direction: the report complains rather than the row lying quiet.

docs.title: D-126 — Break-glass is a report and a written procedure, not a mechanism
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 17 Closes: F-26 Widens: check 9 gains its second column — who can sign in, not only who could hold it. Adds a home, not a feature: the procedure lives in domain/02-actors §3, beside the state machine it operates on. Reverses nothing.

Decision. Three parts, none of them a mechanism.

  1. The report. Check 9 already lists everyone with a live allow of system.admin, however they came by it, and already emails someone when its result changes. It gains a second column: for each of them, is account.status active, and is their credential live (account_credential.valid_to unset or in the future, not revoked — the table is 01a §5). The alert is the new half: an empty result — a world where somebody could hold the capability and nobody can reach a screen — goes to the same place check 9 already goes, within the hour.
  2. The procedure. Written where account state is described, and it says what to do before it says how to recover: who is the person who can be telephoned, who may ask them, and what gets written afterwards. The recovery is performed on an account, never on a grant — an un-suspended account, a re-issued credential, and then the ordinary screens, so every authority change that follows is an application write with granted_by and an audit row like anybody's. D-120's owner_person_id is explicitly not the person to telephone; that column answers whose integration is this, not who fixes it.
  3. What the model still refuses. A sealed recovery key holding system.admin stays refused, and the refusal is unchanged from D-121 and D-122: a key carries nobody's authority and may not hold that code, so it cannot be the thing that walks in when a person cannot. A time-boxed self-service path stays out too — it is a request, an approver, an expiry and a family of codes, which is a module, and this design has no self-service anywhere: nobody joins, appoints or un-suspends themselves, and an emergency path that lets somebody do that would be the second and weaker authorization this corpus rejects by name.

The honest limit, which is the reason the report is the answer and not the escape hatch. The recovery edit is made outside the application, so it writes no audit row, and nothing in the schema distinguishes a legitimate recovery from a hand-edited account. This corpus's habit when it refuses to design a bypass is to name the gap in a check, so that gap gets one: a row in an audited table whose newest audit row predates its updated_at — a change the trail never saw. It is a bullet in 06b §5, appended rather than inserted so no existing check changes number, and it is a report rather than a guard, like the two beside it. What it cannot catch: an edit that also inserts its own audit row by hand — the trail is append-only to the application, not to whoever holds the database — and, after twenty-four months, nothing: payload reduction empties the values and keeps the row, so coverage outlives content by design (D-088).

What it costs, stated as costs. The report is somebody's job and says so in the domain page; an empty result may be entirely ordinary in an organization where the treasurer does everything, so the alert reads as a question rather than an incident; and the new check is one more line that will be mostly empty and has to be read anyway, because it is exactly the line that is quiet until the day it is not.

docs.title: What this round changes elsewhere in the corpus
docs.text:
• A new section, 00-conventions §7a, is where the meaning lives. 05c §9, 06 §2, 06b §5 and 05e §17 cite it instead of each carrying their own sentence about NULL — which is how the four of them came to disagree in round 16.
  • actor_label is no longer free text where the trail has one: its examples become the five labels above, and bare system is retired. The forensic-gap check's "gap" narrows to a write path that owed a person and named none, or a label outside the list.
  • Check 9 gains a column and an empty-result alert; 05d §11 says what the second column is read from.
  • One check appended to 06b §5: an audited row whose newest audit row predates its updated_at.
  • domain/02-actors §3 gains the procedure — the first place in the documentation where something is written down as something a person does rather than a state the system holds.
  • Both questions leave open-questions.md with one row each in § R, so every link written against F-25 and F-26 this month still lands somewhere true.

docs.title: What this round refused, and what it still declines
docs.text:
• A system_writer registry, and a secretless kind of api_key. Both were on F-25's page and both are declined for the reason on that page: a table whose rows may or may not carry a secret is a table whose invariants become conditional, and a job is not a caller and should not have to authenticate. The vocabulary buys the same report for no column. If a fourth writer arrives whose name cannot be fixed this way, that is the moment to reopen this, not before.
  • A fourth kind of caller. This system is not a caller: it holds no grants, appears in no role_holder row, and cannot be aimed at by a grant. Reading an empty actor column as "the system" is a rule about attribution, and it changes nothing about who may hold what — the reason api_key stayed at three grantee kinds and thirteen selectors stayed at thirteen.
  • A recovery mechanism of any kind — sealed credential, emergency grant template, break-glass screen. The refusal is the decision. What is designed is the visibility, and the writing.
  • Whether system.admin should be held by more than one person as a rule. F-26 asked whether a minimum should be seeded. It is not, because the report makes a single-holder world visible and a seeded minimum would only make it quieter — and D-120's posture is the report, again. It stays a decision the organization makes, and the alert is what makes it an informed one.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 18 (D-127 … D-132)
docs.text:
A round is closed by a script now, not by a reader who happened to look; one page answers who enforces each invariant; a reason is something somebody typed; and a name that other rows are written against may not be renamed.

Refinement round 17 (D-125 … D-126) ← | All decisions

What was asked. F-10 was the last item on the "answer next" list that no answer could settle, because it is not one question. It asks, of every invariant in this schema, which layer carries it — and it had been open for eleven rounds because the honest answer is per-rule, not per-shape. Round 18 was scoped, when you picked it, to four things: make the registry diff an executable that gates a round; answer F-10 per instance rather than per shape; decide what shape 4 actually contains; and make a referenced code immutable by rule. Everything else on this page was found by doing those.

What the round found, which is why it is longer than it was scoped to be. The gate ran before the answers were written, and the answers were written against what it said. Its first report was 281 findings; its last is twenty. Nothing was silenced to get there: the difference is a rule set that stopped holding opinions, where every exemption comes from a page in this corpus rather than a line in a script. What those twenty are is recorded in scripts/registry-baseline.txt with a reason beside each. In the course of writing the register that closes F-10, eight places were found where this corpus disagreed with itself — a count that counted only what somebody had looked at, a check reading a column no table has, a rule two pages stated and nothing enforced. Those eight are D-129, and they are the round's real output: the gate is machinery, the disagreement was the defect.

One decision on this page is not yet in the model. D-132 was ruled here and is applied in round 19; it says so in its own status line, because a decided change that the documents have not caught up with is exactly the state D-129 exists to make visible.

docs.title: D-127 — The registry diff is a committed script, and it gates a round
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer, including that this repository stops being markdown-only) Date: refinement round 18 Amends: D-104's machinery — what it adopted was "a hand-run diff report", which is a habit, and habits do not survive a round that finds nothing. Enables: F-10's closure rests on it, because a register of 69 rows is a claim about 20 pages. Costs this repository: its first file that is not markdown (scripts/check-registries.py, plus scripts/registry-baseline.txt).

Decision. Four parts.

  1. The diff is scripts/check-registries.py, committed. Python, no dependencies, reads markdown and nothing else, writes nothing except with --update-baseline. It exits non-zero on a finding that is not in the baseline, so "the round is finished" is a thing a reader can be shown rather than a thing the writer says.
  2. The registries are the documents, never a list beside them. Each register the script reads is a section of a page that already holds it: the catalog's code rows (70), catalog-b §10's deferred namespaces (19) and §9's headings, which declare a whole namespace absent, removed-concepts.md's first column (24 dead names), 05a's selector registry (13), 05's grant_scope_type seed (5), and 00 §7a's label table (5). Three of those counts are stated in prose elsewhere — thirteen selectors, five labels, five scope types — and the script reads thirteen, five and five out of the tables, which is the only agreement between the documents and the script that means anything. A vocabulary §11 calls seeded and no page enumerates is reported rather than skipped, and the claim of which vocabularies are seeded is read from §11 on every run: that is how reason_code was reported all round and why the finding disappeared by itself when D-128 deleted the table.
  3. A register that stops parsing is a finding, not an empty set. no-registry is the loudest kind the script emits, because an unparsed registry makes every token in the corpus a finding for about one second and then, once silenced, no finding at all — which is the failure mode worth spending a finding kind on.
  4. A round is not closed while a finding is unbaselined. The baseline is a file, not a setting: every line is a finding somebody read and decided to keep, and the text after the # is the record of why. Two kinds of thing live in it now. Five names the corpus uses in order to refuse them — person.admin, event.admin, event.answers.view, membership.manage, GUARDIANS — where the fix the script wants would delete the refusal. And ten registered permission codes that no page names outside the catalog, which the finding correctly calls a question rather than a defect, and which were each asked and answered.

Why "code-shaped" is a rule the corpus already had. Most dotted tokens in these files are table.column, and treating them as codes produced the first run's four hundred-odd noise findings. The script does not decide what a code looks like; it reads the catalog's own §1 grammar back at the prose — a code's last segment is an act, its first segment names stored state, and both vocabularies come from the registered codes. So an invented act is caught by the registry's vocabulary, not by a guess about English, and a column named person.contact is a column because a **Fields** (person) block says so. An ALL-CAPS word counts as an operand only inside a backtick span containing an expression operator, since in these files the same shape also carries SQL keywords, column types and one group's name.

What the first run actually found, since a gate nobody believes is decoration. Two names prose used as if they were granted. membership.manage was the example of a save-time refusal in five places — three of which were refusing to save a grant of a code that has never existed, which refuses nothing — and catalog-b §12 had already asked for it to be re-pointed at membership.terminate and had been left open; the diff is what closed it. person.address.edit was named twice, in 05 and 05c, for an edit whose real code is person.contact.edit. Both are fixed here. It also found that decisions/ must be exempt outright, that the corpus's own §9 and §10 are the right source for the namespaces that are absent or deferred on purpose, and that a finding's identity must not contain a line number, or moving a sentence re-opens a finding somebody already read.

What it cannot see, stated because a gate that overstates itself is worse than none.

  • A name that is nowhere. A word the prose never uses cannot be missing from it; this checks prose against registries and registries for readers, not for coverage of the world.
  • Both sides wrong at once, which is the failure D-104 recorded five times and the one this script is weakest against: if a registry row and the sentence quoting it were invented together, the diff is green. GUARDIANS was exactly that — a name in six pages and a row that should never have been minted.
  • Whether a write path still contains its rule. This repository has no code, so 43 of the register's 69 rows rest on it. That limit is not new and is not this script's to close; it is why 00a says so in its own last section.

What it costs, stated as costs. A script is a second thing to maintain, and its registers are the sections it parses, so a page that renames "The selector registry" produces a no-registry finding rather than a silently narrower check. The baseline can hide things, which is why a line without a reason after the # is a defect in the baseline itself. And there is no CI: this repository has no build step, so the gate runs when somebody runs it, and what changed is that finishing a round now means running it.

docs.title: D-128 — A reason is text; the reason_code table is deleted
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer — "write it as a string everywhere") Date: refinement round 18 Deletes: the reason_code table and the claim that its contents are a seeded vocabulary. Renames: status_reason_code, rejection_reason_code, termination_reason_code and ended_reason_code to status_reason, rejection_reason, termination_reason and ended_reason — 01a §2, 01 §3, 03 §4 and §6, 04 §1, and the naming row in 00 §2. Amends: erd-b's reference vocabularies, five down to four. Reverses: nothing — the table had no decision entry of its own, which is the second half of why it went.

Decision. Every <verb>_reason is a text column, required where the act needs a why and free text where it does, and a value somebody types rather than a row of a table. 08-events already made this argument for organizer_role and cited D-095 for refusing a closed list of reason codes; round 18 applies the refusal corpus-wide instead of in one column. Where a reason is also a permission question the answer is unchanged: a rejection requires a reason (03 §4), a termination records one, and what the words were is audited, not which bucket they came from.

Why this was the right shape rather than the cheap one. The table was the corpus's only no-registry vocabulary: 00 §10 promised it as seed data and no page anywhere enumerated a row of it. A vocabulary that nobody lists cannot be granted, cannot be checked, and cannot be translated — it can only be copied by an implementation that has to guess, which is how environments disagree. The second reason is the design's own: a reason code becomes a statistic, and a statistic somebody maintains by hand is a report that silently under-counts every reason that was typed differently. Free text is counted only when people happen to write the same words, and 05's note on why a grant has no reason column now says exactly that rather than implying a tidy vocabulary was waiting somewhere.

What it costs, stated as costs. No grouping without a vocabulary: "why do memberships end?" is a text search, and the answer will be a list of near-duplicates rather than a bar chart. Four renames across five tables are a migration, and a rename is the one change 00 §10 treats a rename as a data migration rather than a schema one. And one sentence stays deliberately stale: 02 §1's "Not present" table still names join_reason_code and closed_reason_code, because those are columns this design refuses outright and never had under either spelling — the argument for their absence is about the absence, not the suffix.

docs.title: D-129 — Where the register and the page disagree, the page is wrong
docs.text:
Status: decided (needed in order to write D-130, and then used eight times in one pass) Date: refinement round 18 States once: as consequence 4 of 00 §6a; everywhere else it is applied, not restated. Direction, not a new rule: this is D-104's "prose contradicts a registry" moved from names to claims. Reverses nothing.

Decision. Two halves, and the second is the load-bearing one.

  1. 00a holds no rule. Every row links to the page that owns the rule and adds only the three facts that page is allowed to leave implicit: which layer carries it, which report would see a breach, what a breach looks like. Where a register row and the page it cites disagree, the page is wrong and is edited in the round that noticed; the register row is never softened to match a page's error, because a register that restates rules is a fourth copy of them and this corpus keeps getting copies wrong.
  2. A register row is a claim about a page and is verified against it, never asserted. Every quotation in the register was grepped out of the file it cites before it was written down. This is not a style rule. Two of the eight disagreements below were found by an agent's report that was confidently wrong, one "correction" of an earlier draft arrived with a sentence and a line number that did not exist, and a register whose rows are remembered rather than re-derived decays into the thing it replaced — a page that says who enforces a rule, with the same authority and less evidence.

The eight, in the order they were found. Each was a place where two documents disagreed, not a place where one document was silent.

What the corpus said What the other page said What changed 00 §9: "exactly two reference-less keys" Five more polymorphic columns are read by no orphan scan at all — access_log.scope_id, .authorization_ref_id, .entity_id, field_conflict.entity_id, audit_log.record_id The row says two validated, five not, and names all five.
