The old count was the count of the ones somebody looked at; the five are F-30 05d §11 check on group names, reading person_group.code person_group has no code; §1's naming rule refuses one, and the section's own head promises no check reads a column the schema lacks The check reads person_group.name 05e §14's layer row: secret_hash unique among live rows The same page's §17 report needs code unique too, or two keys share a name and the trail of who called is ambiguous The row names both columns 01 §3's name table: an ordering rule only 01b §10 needed a "current name" to check against, which requires at most one person_name row per (person, name_type) with valid_to absent The rule is stated where the table is, which is where the write path reads it from 00 §6a's consequence 2, exemplified by "one live exposure per unit and assignment" scope_exposure was deleted by D-097 The example is now access_grant's one live allow per grantee, scope and permission — the partial index that is still there the same paragraph, promising a report "where uniqueness is decided by data" no page contained such a report, in any round 01b §10 gains the duplicate-identifier count the paragraph had promised since it was written 04 §1: one guardianship per pair, "enforced by the write path" every other shape-1 rule in the corpus names a hand-written exclusion constraint, and shape 1's layer row in 00a says the write path is never the answer A hand-written exclusion constraint over all rows, plus 04 §6 check 7 appended 03 §4: the circular pair is broken with an optional column 00 §9 is the rule that says so, and the page did not cite it, so the choice read as local The row cites it

Why the tie-break points that way and not the other. The alternative — the register is the summary and the page is the detail, so a conflict means the summary is stale — is normally right and is wrong here, because the register's three columns are exactly the things a page states once, in passing, three sections away from where the enforcement is decided. It is a lookup, and a lookup that has to be believed more than the page it points at has stopped being a lookup.

docs.title: D-130 — One register answers who enforces an invariant, and F-10 closes
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: refinement round 18 Closes: F-10, open since round 3 and last argued in round 10. Adds: data-model/00a, one page, 69 rows. Amends: 00 §6a, which stops answering "which layer for which rule" by example and points at the register instead. Adds questions: F-28–F-31, which are the register's blanks, kept as questions because a blank filled with an invented check is worse than a blank.

F-10's answer, in one line per shape, and then the part that is not one line. Shape 1 is a hand-written PostgreSQL exclusion constraint emitted by a migration. Shape 2 is a partial unique index, where the predicate is the rule. Shape 3 is the write path, inside the transaction. Shape 4 is D-131. That half was already the recommendation in §6a and was never the hard part; the hard part was that "shape 3 is the write path" answers a question nobody was asking, because every reader wants to know about their rule. So the decision is not the four lines, it is the 69 rows: 4 shape 1, 15 shape 2, 43 shape 3, 7 in shape 4's section, each naming the page that owns the rule, the layer, the report that would notice, and what a breach looks like afterwards.

Why the answer is a page and not a decision entry. A migration is written by somebody reading one data-model page at a time, and the question "is this rule guarded?" arises at the row, not at the summary. An answer that lives in a decision log is invisible at exactly the moment it is needed, which is how F-10 stayed open for eleven rounds while its four shapes were cited by name from every module of the data model.

What listing them found, which is why the listing is the decision.

  • Eleven of the 69 rows name no report at all, and every one of them is a shape-3 row. That is the finding, and its shape is the argument: a shape-1 or shape-2 rule with no backstop still sits under a constraint, which is the strong case, while a shape-3 rule with no report is a rule whose only enforcement is a line of code and whose only evidence is silence. Eleven is a number the corpus did not have before this round, and one of them — per-scheme identifier uniqueness, which §6a's own sentence has promised a report for since round 6 — is the row round 18 filled.
  • Two modules have no check list at all. 07-finance.md and 06a-import.md state rules and carry no "Invariants to verify" section, so every rule they state is unassigned by construction rather than by oversight — which is where most of the nineteen live, and is F-31.
  • Nine numbered checks are assertions about the code, not reports over data — the six TIME-BOMB checks of 05d §11 (15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22), 02 §6 check 4, and 08a §10 checks 1 and 9. They verify that a guard still exists; they never verify that the data is clean, and a check whose result is "evidence about the code" was being cited as a backstop before anyone counted. Filing one as a backstop overstates coverage in exactly the direction that matters, so 00a cites them as save-refusal and never as a report — which is also why this register's coverage claims are narrower than a reader might expect.
  • A report beneath a real constraint is a courtesy, not a control. Most of the nineteen are already caught below the application, and saying so is the difference between a register and a list of worries.

What closing F-10 cost, honestly. F-10's page described "four shapes, each appearing dozens of times" and named about fifteen instances between its bullets. Listing them took an inventory of every Rules block and every Invariants to verify section in 21 data-model pages — nine pages have such a section — and came back with 69 rows, nine checks that were assertions, and eleven blanks. The count, not the colour, is what was wrong about the question. And the page has a maintenance obligation that the decision cannot discharge: its rows are quotations of other pages, its value decays the moment those pages move, and the registry diff cannot see any of it — check-registries.py checks names, not claims. Re-deriving the rows belongs to any round that changes which layer carries something.

docs.title: D-131 — Shape 4 is not empty, and a code that is referenced may not be renamed
docs.text:
Status: decided (found by writing the register, in the section F-10 had called empty) Date: refinement round 18 Corrects: the candidate list F-10 carried, which named two members and got one of them wrong in each direction. States: in 00a §4, and in the three pages that own the three values. Reverses nothing — it declines a shape-4 membership that was never granted.

The test, taken from the deleted instance rather than invented. org_unit.parent_unit_id was shape 4's only member and died with the hierarchy (D-036 reversed by D-097), which left the shape "currently empty" on the strength of one column. The reason a reparent was shape 4 at all is the test: every row stays individually valid while the meaning of what references it moves under it, and nothing left behind is a row a report could find. Run that test against the corpus and the shape has six members, four of which were already stated somewhere and two of which nobody had thought to ask.

The value A rename rewrites Verdict permission.code every access_grant row, which holds the code by value, and every role definition listing it immutable, and the catalog's own "adding one is free, renaming one is a migration" was a wish with no rule behind it selector_type.code every stored expression, through selector_kind immutable, and the truest instance in the shape: it is the word the language is written in, and F-10 did not carry it api_key.code the grants issued to it, the audit rows, and the report of who called immutable, for the reason 05e §17 already needed the uniqueness for person_group_member's group_id/person_id, an imported bank transaction, person.merged_into_person_id their own meaning; each page already forbids the edit immutable, already stated, now in the register audience.code nothing not immutable, and this is the correction

Why an audience's code is not in the shape, which is the part that was wrong rather than missing. AUDIENCE(code) is resolved once, at save, into selector_arg_id on the leaf (05b §5); the stored tree holds the audience's identity, not its name, so "renaming the audience afterwards rewrites nothing" — which is not a discovery about immutability but rule 5 of the name namespace, stated out loud on the page that owns it, being contradicted by a candidate list eleven rounds old. F-10's shape-4 candidate was the defect D-129 is about, wearing a question entry's clothes. audience.code keeps its partial unique index (one code per audience, among the ones that have a code — shape 2) and loses its claim to immutability, and a rename of a named audience is an ordinary audited edit.

What carries the rule, and what that is worth. Not a trigger. The referrer listing that D-103 already requires before an audience may be renamed, extended to the three codes: the editor shows, before it lets the name change, every grant holding that permission code, every expression using that selector, every grant and audit row naming that key. Behind it, the prose that was always the real rule — 00 §10's prohibition on rewriting a historical row's meaning — and in front of it, the retirement path, which is the only sanctioned rename: mint the new code, migrate the grants, end the old row, and let both appear in the trail.

The honest limit. The listing reaches rows, not sentences. A renamed permission.code also rewrites every page that named it, and no query lists prose — that is D-127's half, and the two half-diffs together are the whole guarantee, which is weaker than a constraint and is what D-072 traded away on purpose. 00a's shape-4 rows carry the word nothing in their layer column and this entry is where nothing is explained rather than apologised for.

docs.title: D-132 — Day one is one account holding system.admin, and every role after it is written by the organization
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer), applied two rounds later by round 21 — D-150 for day one, D-151 for the event's own grants, D-152 for the flag columns, D-153 and D-154 for the two named audiences and counselors. The seed this entry left standing is gone from 05d §12, which is now titled for what it actually lists. It is recorded here because it was ruled here, and because a ruling that lives only in a conversation is a ruling that gets re-litigated.

What round 21 corrected in this entry, and added to it. Three things, and they are listed rather than quietly folded in because this page is the record of the ruling. The numbering moved: the sweep this entry calls round 19 is round 21, because round 19 was spent on other questions and round 20 on thirteen of them. Part 3's list of ten is not ten ungranted codes — four of them are event.* codes, and since D-151 every event's organizers hold them on that event from the moment it is created, so the correct reading is "ungranted at the unit, held on every item by the people who run it". And the consequence this entry says it has to say out loud is wrong in its arithmetic: the organization does not write that answer grant "once" — D-132 said once where the design needed once per event, because a bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant. What it did not list and round 21 deleted anyway: permission.is_system and selector_type.is_system, on the argument that a column whose content is "a migration wrote this row" is not a protection of anything (D-152), and role.delete's refusal that read that column. Deletes (in round 19): the seeded roles, the two seeded audiences, the seeded event.answer.view grant, the worked-example offices that 05d §12 presents as seed, role.is_system and audience.is_system. Confirms: permission, grant_scope_type and selector_type do ship as seed data. Reverses: D-068's habit of shipping a starter bundle — not its rule, which stands and is the reason this is affordable.

Decision. Four parts.

  1. Day one is one account holding system.admin, and nothing else. No role, no audience, no grant. The person who sets the system up holds the only capability that ships, and every authority after that is a role they write, aimed at an audience they wrote, granted with codes from the catalog. The requirement was one system administrator, and they will set everything up — which is the same position D-068 already takes about per-resource admin codes: the bundle is not the design's job.
  2. Three vocabularies still ship: permission, grant_scope_type, selector_type. They are not configuration, they are the language — a grant naming a code that does not exist is not a narrow permission but a save-time refusal, and a selector added at runtime is a word no resolver knows. That distinction is exactly 00 §10's argument for putting them in migrations, and it survives the seed deletion untouched.
  3. Ten catalog codes are granted by nobody at first — event.cancel, event.delete, event.organizer.manage, event.question.manage, the four guardianship.*, person_group.edit, person_group.end. They stay registered, they keep their right_kind and their applies_to, and they are grantable from day one by whoever holds system.admin. A permission the catalog carries and no seeded role happens to hold is not dead weight; it is the list the organization reads in order to decide what to grant, which is the second half of why the catalog exists at all.
  4. role.is_system and audience.is_system go with the seed they flagged. A column saying this row came from the migration is a flag whose only function is to protect rows the design has just stopped shipping, and system.admin needs no protection because it is a permission, not a role.

The consequence the round has to say out loud: event answers. D-102 made creating an event oblige an event.answer.view grant aimed at ORGANIZERS, and 08a §10 check 2 reports the events that arrived without one. With the seed gone, the organization writes that grant itself, once, as an ordinary grant — there is no exception carved for event-answer privacy and none is needed, because the check that catches a missing one does not care who wrote it. The failure shape is unchanged and now has one more way to happen: an organizer is a person with a title and no permissions, and it reads as a bug report rather than a constraint violation.

What it costs, stated as costs. A first run of the system has no useful permissions until somebody writes them, which is a real onboarding cost and the reason this was worth deciding rather than discovering; the honest mitigation is that the catalog is written to be read as a checklist. Every worked example that used a seeded role becomes an example of writing one, so round 19 is a sweep of twenty-five pages rather than a deletion — and ORGANIZERS, which appears most of those twenty-five times, is a selector and stays. And nothing refuses the setup account a bad day: one account holding everything is the shape with the least ceremony and the most blast radius, and D-126's check 9 is already the report that watches whether that account can still sign in.

See also 00a — who enforces each invariant, data-model/00 §6a, D-104 for the diff this round made executable, and D-072 for why the answer to "who writes the constraint?" is a document.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 19 (D-133 … D-136)
docs.text:
Two trail rules are unchecked and now say so; four of seven polymorphic columns get an orphan scan and the audit row deliberately does not; the two modules with no check list get one; and an election is not recorded, because a role holds only the people.

Refinement round 18 (D-127 … D-132) ← | All decisions

What was asked. Round 18 had just emptied the top of the "answer next" list and filled it again with six questions of its own making, all of them found the same way: write down who enforces each invariant and count the blanks. This round was asked to put questions, not to change the model, and it did: four were put, four were answered, and none of the four changed a table. That is the shape this corpus is in — the remaining questions are about what a report is able to see and what a piece of prose is worth when nothing runs it.

What the round found while answering, which is the part worth reading. Three of the four questions arrived with a premise that did not survive being checked against the page that owns the rule.

  • F-29 blamed the payload window for a gap the window does not cause. The check it was debating would compare a key's valid_to, its revoked_at and an audit row's occurred_at — three columns of the accounting skeleton, all permanent. The report could be written and would work in thirty years. So the answer "no report" is not a limit the design is under, it is a guarantee the design declines, and the documents now say that instead of implying the opposite.
  • The register row minted beside that question described a rule no page states. 00a carried "which audit views a holder may open follows the payload window, not the table" against a citation to 06 §2. No page in the corpus says any such thing; 06 §2.3 says close to the opposite — a per-entry check inside the history view was considered and left unimplemented — and that question is AT-4, already open. Under D-129 a register row is a claim about a page and is verified against it, never asserted, so the row is withdrawn. It got into the register in round 18 by the route D-129 warns about: the inventory was written from the pages, and this row was written beside the inventory.
  • F-30's own positions could not count. They offered to "scan the two a person can cause" and then named four columns. The seven columns were re-counted from the field tables before anything was decided, which is also what turned up a second, quieter defect: erd-b still said "there are exactly two reference-less keys" after round 18 had corrected that exact sentence in 00 §9. The register and the appendix had drifted apart by one round.
  • Round 18 had fixed one page of that count and left four. Checking the drift meant grepping the sentence, and the grep found the same claim in 05b twice, 05a and erd-a twice — "exactly two polymorphic keys in this design go without a foreign key", where the design has seven, every one of them with a sibling column naming what it points at (grant_scope_type, argument_type, scope_type, authorization_channel, entity_type, entity_table, table_name). Three of the five cite §11 for the assertion, and §11 never makes it — which is D-129's defect again, a claim about a page that the page does not make, stated five times and verified zero times. All five now say two of seven and point at the page that keeps the count. A count that was taken by looking is a count of what somebody looked at, and one round is long enough for the corpus to believe it.

One decision from round 18 is still not in the model. D-132 was ruled last round and is applied by a sweep this round owes and has not yet run: the seeded roles, the seeded audiences, the seeded event.answer.view grant, the worked-example offices presented as seed, role.is_system, audience.is_system. F-18 below is the second decision this round closed that had been arguing, in the present tense, from is_system.

docs.title: D-133 — Two trail rules stay unchecked, and say so out loud
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-29 asked what a report may be asked to see about an audit row whose payload has been emptied on schedule. Two rules had no report beneath them: that no write is ever audited against an api_key that had already ended, and — as the register had recorded it — that which audit views a holder may open follows the payload window. Both were listed as blocked by D-088's 24-month window, which empties the payload and is the part a check would have to read.

Answer. No check is written for either rule, and the page that states the first one now says the guarantee is not offered. Of the three positions on the page — check the envelope rather than the payload, accept the blindness and say so, or widen the window for the columns these checks need — the second was chosen, and chosen with its reason corrected first.

Why not the cheap-sounding one. "Check the envelope" is genuinely cheap: the columns involved are a key's valid_to, its revoked_at, and the audit row's occurred_at, none of which is a payload. Writing it was declined, not impeded, and the decision records what that costs rather than dressing it up: nobody will ever be able to demonstrate that no write was audited against a key that had already ended. A report nobody reads is not a control either, and this corpus has already decided — nine times over, in checks that exist only to re-ask whether a guard is still there — that the number of reports is not what makes a rule true. Widening the window was refused for the reason the question itself named: a privacy answer dressed as an integrity one.

What was actually wrong in the question, and what was wrong in the register. The window was never the obstacle — see the lede. And the register's second row for this question described a rule that exists nowhere. Both halves are repaired: 06b §5 now carries the ruling beside the sentence that admits the gap, and the phantom row is deleted from 00a rather than re-worded, because there is nothing to re-word it into. The nearest real rule — a history screen over the trail is a person-data surface, and a per-entry "could this reader see this field" check was considered and left unimplemented — is stated where it lives, in 06 §2.3, and its open question is AT-4. This decision does not answer AT-4 and does not close it.

Deletes: one row of 00a, and with it the eleventh none. Changes no table, no column, no code.

See: 06b §5, 00a, D-088, D-129, and F-29 in § R.

docs.title: D-134 — Four more polymorphic columns get an orphan scan, and the audit row never
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-30. Seven columns hold an id with no foreign key behind it and a sibling column saying what kind of thing it points at. Two were followed by an orphan scan (05d §11 check 2); five were not scanned anywhere: access_log.scope_id, access_log.authorization_ref_id, access_log.entity_id, field_conflict.entity_id and audit_log.record_id. The question said explicitly that these are not one decision, and it was right, because the answer for the trail is the opposite of the answer for a conflict row.

Answer. Four get a scan; audit_log.record_id never does, and the pages say why in those words.

  • field_conflict.entity_id, scanned outright. A conflict recorded against a row that is not there is a broken import. There was no sentence anywhere saying so, which is the reason this one was the cheapest of the four.
  • access_log's three, scanned with the legal-absence rule written beside them. A reference that no longer resolves because a person was erased at their own request is not an integrity failure, and a scan that cannot tell that apart reports the erasure path's own correct output as a breach.
  • audit_log.record_id, deliberately not scanned. An audit row that outlives the row it described is what a redaction looks like afterwards. Counting those as orphans would train the reader to ignore the report — the first false alarm is the expensive one — and the alternative, a legality rule over the whole trail, is a rule about absences so broad it would be read once and never again. The column is not an oversight any more; it is the one place this design states that the trail is allowed to point at nothing.

What this corrected as it went. 00 §9 and erd-b both counted reference-less keys, and after round 18 fixed the sentence in one of them the two disagreed by a round; both are now correct and say which columns are scanned, which are scanned-with-an-exception, and which is exempt. 00a's row for this rule cited only the appendix, which is the inventory rather than the rule's home, and under D-129 it now cites 00 §9.

Adds: one numbered check in 05d §11, beside check 2 and cross-referenced with it, and no TIME-BOMB label — this one is a report over data, which is what the label is for keeping apart. Changes no table and no column. Whether an orphan in access_log after an erasure is legal is a rule about which rows survive erasure, and the check inherits whatever 00 §4 and 06b already say.

See: 00 §9, 05d §11, erd-b, and F-30 in § R.

docs.title: D-135 — The two modules with no check list get one each
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-31. Every data-model page states its rules and then lists what would notice a breach — except 07-finance and 06a-import, which state rules and stop. That is why most of the register's blanks sit in those two modules: their rules were unassigned by construction, not by oversight, because there was no section for an assignment to live in. It was the only yes-or-no on the page.

Answer. Yes: three checks on each page, in a new 07 §4a and a new 06a §4.

The check What a row means Finance 1 — the balance, recomputed from §3's definition A member wrongly suspended, or a family wrongly chased. Survives §3's own recommendation to drop the column, because then it checks the view against the definition instead of the copy against the sum Finance 2 — a payment whose allocations do not account for its amount Money that moved and was never attributed, or an overpayment nobody refunded. No constraint can span the two tables, so this report is the backstop Finance 3 — money nobody ever asked for An open obligation with no live request, or a paid-for event with no obligation behind the registration. Silent in both directions: nobody is chased, nobody pays Import 1 — an imported membership that should not exist An unbounded period, or a membership written from an attendance list. The one row in the register that reaches the permission gate: an open membership satisfies is_current_member() (D-039) Import 2 — one event per (title, date), one registration per attendee row The application-layer rule uq_staging_event_match has been lost, and ten thousand attendees have become ten thousand events Import 3 — a batch whose own accounting does not close Rows neither applied nor discarded, a row that created nothing, ids from the wrong half of the corpus, or a reverted batch that left rows behind — read against the audit entries the revert wrote

What the round noticed while writing them. The import page had been citing, for two rounds, "check 1 in §5" — a section that page does not have. The citation was correct in intent and wrong in fact, and §3.1 now points at §4, where check 1 is the one it meant. The strongest of the six import checks was therefore already in the corpus as a promise about a section that did not exist, which is the same failure as a register row with no report beneath it, one level up.

Adds: two sections, six checks, and three rows in 00a for rules both pages had stated and never registered — the bounded imported membership, a batch's own accounting, and a payment's allocations. The register is 71 rows where it was 69, and its none column is seven where it was eleven. It also costs the register its excuse: What the register cannot say had been explaining the concentration of blanks by pointing at these two pages, and can no longer.

See: 07 §4a, 06a §4, 00a, and F-31 in § R.

docs.title: D-136 — An election is not recorded; a role holds only the people
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-18, open since D-100 deleted position with its is_leadership, min_age and max_holders: does a role say elected or appointed, and if so what does an election write? The page's own framing was fair to both sides — role_holder has valid_from, valid_to, granted_by and note, which is nearly enough to describe an election, and granted_by names the secretary rather than a mandate.

Answer. Neither. The organization manages elections outside this system, and a role holds only the people who hold it. No column for term kind, no table of elections, no record of how a person came to fill an office. What arrives is the outcome: one role_holder row, a period, and note for whoever wants the reason written beside the fact rather than buried in the trail. Stated where a reader will meet it, in domain/04 §6, with a pointer from 05 §4.

The refusals, each with the reason it was refused.

  • A boolean on role — elected or appointed — would make the distinction queryable and would guard nothing. A field that looks like a control in a place where no control is wanted is worse than the absence of one, because someone starts relying on it, and the first exception teaches them not to. The question itself noticed this: it observed that a flag "invites a check which D-100's posture would refuse to enforce".
  • A table of elections would describe a process this system does not run. There is no ballot, no candidate list, no quorum rule anywhere in these documents, and D-043 already settled that this is not the registry of everything true about a volunteer.
  • The distinction has nowhere to bite. An office confers nothing by being held (D-100), so there is no dangerous thing an election could confer and no answer anywhere in the resolver that would move if a row knew how its holder arrived. This is the fact that makes the answer cheap, and it is worth naming before anyone offers to make the answer expensive again.

The cost, stated because the page says it out loud rather than leaving it to be discovered: nothing in this system will ever refuse to appoint someone to an office the bylaws reserve for a vote. That rule lives in the bylaws and in the people reading them.

Two of the question's load-bearing facts had already gone while it sat open: role.max_term_months is deleted (05 §3 lists it among the columns deleted with their mechanisms), and role.is_system — which the question cited as what keeps seeded offices distinct — is deleted by D-132, whose sweep is still owed. A question that has been open long enough to lose its premises should be re-read before it is answered, and this one was.

Changes no table and no column. Three pages that had been calling this an open question now say it is closed: glossary, catalog-a §5, and domain/06 §5.

See: domain/04 §6, 05 §4, D-100, D-043, and F-18 in § R.

docs.title: What the round did not do
docs.text:
• It did not run D-132's sweep. The seed still ships in the pages: 05d §12, catalog-b §11, and role.is_system in 05-authorization.md. That is a cleanup with a decision already written, and it is the next thing this repository owes itself.
  • It did not answer AT-4, which D-133's repair brushed against and explicitly left where it was.
  • It added no check that it could not point at a page. That rule held even where it was inconvenient: the register still says none seven times, and three of those seven are open questions rather than chores.

The gate ran. scripts/check-registries.py reports no unbaselined finding at the end of this round, and mkdocs build --strict is clean. D-127 says a round does not close on an unbaselined finding; nothing here needed a new baseline line, which is the quiet way for a round to go.

What the link pass swept up on the way. Five links still pointed at F-8 by its heading slug, which stopped resolving the round an explicit <a id="f-8"> was put inside that heading; the target was fine and the address was not, which is the one kind of breakage a reader never sees coming because the question is still there, one click away from nowhere. A slug is derived, and a derived thing has to be recomputed, not remembered — which is why every anchor touched this round was recomputed rather than typed.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 20 (D-137 … D-149)
docs.text:
Thirteen open questions answered in one sitting: the attribute vocabulary loses its proposal stage and its queue, access_log rows are deleted at 24 months while the audit trail keeps its shape, a delegation is validated once and stands, a display name's drift gets the check it already had, and four words — WHITELISTED, a translated label, an expired registration, a notification nobody receives — are refused in writing. Four questions survive the round untouched and a fifth arrives with it; not one of the five is 🟡.

Refinement round 19 (D-133 … D-136) ← | All decisions

What was asked. Put the open questions, in batches, and write down what came back. Seventeen were on the page; thirteen were put and answered, and four were left where they are (A-4's remainder, E-3, F-9, F-11) because answering them needs a document or a lawyer rather than a ruling. Every 🟡 on that page was answered this round — all six of them — which is why the page now reads as a list of things that can be deferred, and why § J emptied itself and was deleted the way sections B, C and D were.

What the round found while answering, which is again the part worth reading. Four of the thirteen questions arrived with a premise the corpus had already invalidated, and in one case the premise and the answer were on opposite sides of a contradiction the corpus was living inside.

  • F-32 was not a choice between two policies; it was a contradiction with one side already implemented. The question asked whether a stale delegation should be reported or left invisible, presuming the design re-checks it. domain/06 §9 does promise that — "validate at grant time and re-check at use time" — and 05 §6 says flatly the opposite: "nothing about the person who lent it is re-validated when a check runs". removed-concepts records why: the column that made a use-time re-check possible was deleted, "and with it the second half of the guard — there is no source row left to re-validate". So two pages promised a thing two other pages say cannot happen, and the invariant register said the rule was enforced twice, once of them silently. The ruling picked the side the data model was already on, which makes this entry a repair with a reason attached rather than a change of behaviour.
  • F-28's register row claimed a rule had no report beneath it. The report was already written. 01b §10 counts persons whose given_name/family_name differ from the open person_name row — the exact check the open question offered as "cheap to write" — and closes by saying the check exists and that what is undecided is whether a report is the right thing or the copy is the wrong one. Round 18 minted that row beside the inventory, and its **none** was wrong in the understating direction: the table said nothing watches a rule that something watches. Round 19 found a register row claiming more than its page said; this round found the mirror image, and D-129 catches both — a register row is a claim about a page, and none is as much a claim as a citation.
  • AT-2's proposal stage was a third status no decision had granted. D-084 settled the vocabulary in one sentence — "a status of live or retired" — and the pages and the inventory carried proposed anyway, complete with a proposed_by, a proposed_at, an import fallback that writes it, and an integrity check whose whole job is to age it out. A mechanism was built for a status that arrived by transcription.
  • E-6's answer had no addressee. The question's own recommendation asked for a "safeguarding contact" to be notified, and no such office exists: safeguarding_officer is listed among the worked examples the catalog marks as not shipping, and D-132 is about to delete the seed that would have offered one. A question that asks "who should be told" cannot be answered by naming a person the design does not have, so the answer is the one that needs nobody: the trail is the control.
  • One deletion moved ten citations, all of them ordinals. Deleting 09 §8's first check renumbers the six that follow it, and ten sentences cite those checks by number: six inside the page that owns them, two in the invariant register, one in 01b and one in 06b §5. Two more citations died with the thing they pointed at — both were the curation queue reaching for the age-out check that is now gone. All ten were rewritten, and all ten were found by grepping the number rather than by remembering to look: a checker aimed at the target of §8 check 4 keeps passing after the list above it shrinks, because the target still exists and still says check 4. An ordinal is a pointer that moves when the list above it changes, which is the same failure this corpus keeps hitting from the other end: a checker verifies a target and never a claim, and nothing at all verifies a number beside a sentence. This round counted this list wrong while writing it — it said seven sentences and then named eight — which is why the count here is stated as grepped, not as remembered.

docs.title: D-137 — A guardian may appoint a guardian, and nobody at the organization is told
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. E-6 asked what happens when a guardian adds a second guardian over a child. Guardianship is a channel with a right_level (D-113), so the act is inside the model already: a person with guardianship.assign writes a row. What was undecided was whether the organization should hear about it — the page offered a notification to a safeguarding contact, a review queue, or silence, and it recommended the notification.

Answer. Attribution is enough. No notification, no queue, no addressee. The act is a write, the write is audited with the actor who made it and the person it was about, and that trail is the whole control. There is no office to notify and nothing in this design that would receive a notification at all.

Why the recommended option was the wrong one, not merely the expensive one. The recommendation named a "safeguarding contact" as if the design had one. It does not, and it cannot offer one without a grant aimed at a person or an office somebody writes — which is exactly the machinery D-132 is going to delete from the seed. A notification whose recipient is a row somebody must remember to create is a control that is off by default and silent about being off, which is worse than the trail, because the trail is on whether or not anyone configured it. This is the same reasoning that refused a report for F-29: a guard nobody reads is not a control, and a guard nobody configures is not one either.

What this costs, said plainly. Nothing will ever tell a parent, a second guardian, or an officer that a third adult was given authority over a child. The answer to "who added this person, and when" is excellent and the answer to "did anyone think about it" is the person who did it, alone, at the moment they did it. The mitigation that does exist is that guardianship.assign is one of the codes this corpus marks ⚠⚠ — the grant is the rare thing, not the act.

Changes no table and no column. The open question's recommendation is deleted with the question; the guardianship.assign row in catalog-a §5 is unchanged.

See: domain/06 §1, 04 §Guardianship, and E-6 in § R.

docs.title: D-138 — One permission guards the whole audit trail, and the widening is on the record
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. AT-4 asked whether audit.view is enough to guard a trail that holds person data. The trail's payloads are values a person wrote — an old address, an allergy, a diagnosis — emptied 24 months later (D-088) but readable in full until then, and they are readable whether or not the reader may read the person they describe. 06 §2.3 records that a per-entry "could this reader see this field" check was considered and left unimplemented; D-133 declined to stretch the trail for a report and explicitly did not answer this.

Answer. audit.view is the whole gate. One permission, one check, no per-entry filter, now decided rather than merely unbuilt. The history view is a person-data surface and is treated as one: the code is granted rarely, it is marked, and what it opens is the entire trail.

What was refused, and what the refusal is really buying. The alternative was a check inside the history view comparing each entry's subject against the reader's own reach. It would have been correct and it would have been slow in the way D-114 says this system accepts — a check that resolves rather than caches — but it would also have made the trail's readability depend on the same audience expressions it exists to explain, so that a rule changed last week would silently rewrite what an officer can read about 2019. The trail's value is that it is legible without re-resolving history, and a per-entry check spends exactly that. The widening is therefore accepted as a property, stated in the pages that grant the code instead of being left to be discovered by whoever first opens the screen.

What this does not do. It does not widen anything. No behaviour changes: nothing in the corpus has ever implemented the per-entry check, so this decision turns an omission into a position and pays for it in a sentence. It is also not the same question as F-17 — whether "who could read this in 2023" is reconstructable at all — which stays open.

Changes no table and no column.

See: 06 §2.3, 05c §9, D-114, D-133, and AT-4 in § R.

docs.title: D-139 — An event question may bind to a stored value: it prefills as a suggestion and writes back as an answer
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. AT-1 asked whether an event_question may be tied to an attribute_definition code, so that a camp form asking "do you take any medication" and the person's stored attribute are the same fact twice, or one fact asked twice. Two reasons had kept it open: the form's answer and the record's value would disagree with no rule saying which wins, and 00 §4's erasure exception had a condition on its face: "This exception is safe only while nothing references an attribute row, and nothing does today", naming this very binding as the thing that would break it.

Answer. The binding is allowed, in one direction, with both ends named. A question may hold a bound_attribute_code — nullable, pointing at the definition, never at a value row. The form prefills from the person's current value as a suggestion, which the answerer sees and may change; nothing is hidden from them and nothing is silently copied. On submit, the answer writes back to person_attribute as a new value, dated today, recorded as written by the person who submitted the form. The answer stays a row of the event either way; the write-back is a second act, not the same row twice.

Why the binding does not detonate the rule it was fenced off by. The condition in §4 protects erasure's one hard delete: redaction deletes person_attribute rows outright, and that delete is invisible only for as long as nothing points at those rows. A bound question points at the vocabulary, not at a value — at attribute_definition.code, which is never deleted, is retired instead, and survives the person entirely. So the reference edge §9 would have to walk does not exist: the question names a code, the value rows under it come and go with the person, and erasure's delete stays invisible. This is recorded here rather than left as a lucky consequence, because the next person to design a binding will reach for a value's key; a reference from an event row to a person_attribute row id remains exactly as forbidden as §4 says it is.

Which one wins, and when neither does. The person record wins as of today, because the write-back is dated today and the attribute's history is the record of what was believed when. An answer is not corrected when the record later changes, and the record is not corrected when an old answer said otherwise — they are two dated statements of the same fact at two moments, which is the shape this corpus already uses for a name. Where the answer contradicts the stored value, the difference is visible on the form (the prefill shows the stored value) and that is the intended repair route: a person who edits the prefill is editing the record.

What this costs. A form can now write to the person record, which is a new path into person_attribute and the first place outside the person's own editing where an attribute value arrives without a staff member in the middle of it. The write goes through the same person.edit permission the answering channel already uses, is audited with the answerer as its actor, and is refused — with the form still saving its answer — when that write is not permitted, so a form never half-writes a person. And a bound question now cannot be re-pointed at a different code without noticing that its past answers belong to the old one; they stay what they were.

Adds: one nullable column, event_question.bound_attribute_code, holding an attribute_definition.code by value and not a row id — which is what keeps 00 §4's ban on row references intact, and what makes this decision answer a question shape 4 had never been asked. Because a code is now referenced, D-131's test reaches a vocabulary code for the first time: attribute_definition.code joins shape 4. A definition may still be retired, and may still be merged — the merge of two codes is exactly the deliberate re-point this entry already demands, and it carries the bound questions with it rather than orphaning them — but a code with a question bound to it may no longer be renamed, because a rename would silently re-answer every form that was asked under the old name. The register carries the row (00a §4), and the register grew from six members to seven the day a form was allowed to point at a word. Retires: assumption 58's half that a form answer never reaches the person record.

See: 09 §3, 09 §4, 08 §7, 00 §4, domain/07a §12, and AT-1 in § R.

docs.title: D-140 — Nothing about an event is deleted on a schedule, and erasure empties an answer without deleting it
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. EV-2 asked how long an event_answer survives its event. Three pages said answers "end with the event" and none said when, what happens to them, or who does it; the same question noted that the identical fact recorded as a person_attribute is not deleted on a schedule at all, so the freshest copy of a health fact was the weakest-protected one.

Answer. There is no expiry for registrations or answers. Neither ends with its event, and neither ends on a clock. They follow the rule the accounting skeleton already follows: the row is a fact about a dated occasion, and it is kept. Erasure does reach them, and it empties them: a redacted person's event_answer.value is set to empty and the row survives, because "they answered that question" and "this is what they said" are two different facts and only the second one is theirs to withdraw. The rows of event_registration are kept as they are today; a cancelled event already keeps every registration (08a §8, guard 2), and a cancelled event with no registrations would be an event that demonstrably never happened.

Why this direction and not a schedule. The question's own sharpest point was the asymmetry: the same sentence of personal data, kept forever in one table and quietly discarded in another, with the discarded one being the copy a camp leader actually reads. A schedule would have had to be justified to the person it deletes from, and "we forget it after N years because that number is defensible" is a weaker answer than "we keep what happened and we erase what you ask us to". It also would have been the third retention clock in a system that has deliberately managed with two (D-088).

What "empty the value, keep the row" costs. An emptied answer still says something — that a question was asked and answered, by whom, on what date — and that residue is deliberate, the same residue D-088 leaves in an audit payload. It is also a rule that store has to implement rather than one the schema enforces: 00 §8 now lists event_answer beside person_attribute among the places erasure has to reach, and 06b §5's erasure check counts emptied-value answers the way it counts surviving names, so an erasure that forgot the event tables stops passing a check.

Deletes: the phrase "answers end with the event" wherever it stands as a policy, and event_answer's open retention item from two open-issue lists. Changes no table and no column.

See: 08 §7, 08a §11, 07a §12, 00 §8, D-083, and EV-2 in § R.

docs.title: D-141 — A definition is live at the save; the proposal stage, its queue and its check are deleted
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. AT-2 asked who curates the attribute vocabulary and how long a proposed definition may sit before somebody rules on it. The pages described a two-stage life: an attribute_definition could be proposed, carrying proposed_by and proposed_at, waiting in a curation queue for a curator to make it live — and an import column nobody had mapped arrived there by itself, so the corpus could acquire vocabulary through nobody deciding anything.

Answer. There is no proposal, and every field must be defined beforehand. attribute.define is the curating permission and a definition is live at the save: the same person's write that names a code publishes it. status keeps the two values D-084 granted it — live and retired — and nothing else. proposed_by and proposed_at are deleted, there is no review list, no waiting, no age-out, and no curator role: the permission is the curator.

Refused: a value inventing a code. A person recording a value under person.edit cannot create vocabulary by typing something adjacent to it, and the mechanism that made that possible — writing the unknown as a proposed definition and letting it wait — is gone. An import column that maps to no defined attribute is an error at apply time, not a proposal. A row that would need a new code either has one already written by someone holding attribute.define, or it does not import and the batch says so. That is the strictest of the options on the question's page and it was chosen for the reason the answer gave: a vocabulary is the one registry where an unreviewed addition is permanent in effect even if it is deletable in principle, because every value recorded against a bad code inherits it.

What this exposes, stated rather than smoothed over. attribute.define is held by nothing at day one — the seed that would have held it is deleted by D-132, and the vocabulary therefore starts empty and stays empty until a person with the code writes it. Day one has exactly one account, holding system.admin, so day one's vocabulary is written by that account; after that, whoever the organization aims the code at. Two pages had been asserting a "named curator" as a role that reads what it is given; both are corrected, because a role is an office that confers nothing (D-100) and the only thing here that curates is a permission.

What a bad code costs now. It is live the moment it is saved, with no gate in front of it, and the values recorded against it are real values on real people from that moment. The defence is three things and no more: saving a definition needs a permission, the trail records every save, and a code can be retired — which keeps its values and stops new ones (D-109's rule for anything a rule names).

Deletes: the proposed status, proposed_by, proposed_at, the curation queue, the "Proposed code" glossary entry, the import's unmapped-column fallback, and 09 §8 check 1 — which ages out a status that no longer exists. Renumbering §8's remaining six checks moves six ordinal citations in other pages and four more in the same page; all ten are recomputed, not remembered. Changes one table (attribute_definition: one status value and two columns gone; event_question gains D-139's column in the same round, so the vocabulary and its first consumer move together).

See: 09 §2, 09 §7, 06a, 08a §11, catalog-b §12, D-084, and AT-2 in § R.

docs.title: D-142 — The displayed name stays a copy, and the check that counts its drift is named at last
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-28 asked whether the denormalised given_name/family_name on person is a copy to keep in step with person_name, or a field to delete so that the displayed name is always read from the history. The register carried the rule "the denormalised name agrees with the name history" with no report beneath it at all.

Answer. The copy stays, and the drift is reported. person.given_name/family_name remain, written in the same transaction that writes the name history, and the check that counts the persons where they have driven apart is named as the rule's backstop: 01b §10 counts persons whose two columns differ from the person_name row with no valid_to. That check already existed — see the lede — so what this decision changes is which page admits it.

Why keep a denormalised copy at all, in a corpus that has deleted several. Because the name a reader must be able to print for a person who has never been opened as a record — a roster printed at a door, a label, a search hit — should not depend on walking a history table to find the open row. The alternative was a view, and a view is what this design already has: the copy is the materialised half of it, and the drift check is the price of materialising anything, paid in the open. The display rule is unchanged — preferred_name ?? given_name, from 01 §2.

What it costs: a name can be wrong in one place while right in another, and only a report will notice. That is what a denormalised column is; the design declines to be surprised by it.

Deletes: nothing but a sentence in 01b §10 that was still asking the question the check beside it had answered, and one **none** in 00a — the second of the seven to go, and the first that was wrong because it understated what the design already does.

Changes no table and no column.

See: 01 §2, 01b §10, 00a, D-129, and F-28 in § R.

docs.title: D-143 — A delegation is validated once, when it is written, and stands to its own end date
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-32 asked whether a delegation whose delegator has lost the code should be reported or left invisible, on the understanding that the design re-checks the delegator at use time, so that a loan stops working the instant it goes stale and the delegatee gets an ordinary denial that explains nothing.

Answer. The delegator is checked once, at grant time, and never again. No report is written, nothing cascades, and the delegation stands until its own valid_to or a revocation. "You may not lend more than you hold" is a set-membership test on the person writing the grant (domain/06 §9); it is true of the moment it is checked and it is not a promise about the term. The check was simplified as well as scoped: the register's layer column no longer claims the rule is enforced twice a day, once of them silently.

Why this is a repair and not a policy choice. Because the design was already this way and one page had not noticed — see the lede. 05 §6 states that nothing about the lender is re-validated when a check runs and draws the consequence itself: that is why a delegation must expire. removed-concepts records that the column which made the re-check possible is gone with the table it named. Keeping domain/06's promise would have been a design change; deleting it is the cheapest correct answer available, and the user's ruling said to simplify the check rather than to build it.

The two bounds that survive, which are what makes this tolerable rather than merely cheap. A delegation must expire — valid_to is required on a delegated grant and integrity check 11 reports one that does not — and system.admin may not be delegated at all. So the failure this ruling permits has a shape: a person keeps an authority their lender no longer holds, for a term somebody fixed in advance and cannot exceed, and the trail says who lent it to whom. What it does not permit is a permanent loan of the only code that can restructure the system.

What it costs. A delegate may be doing something they should no longer be able to do, and nothing will tell anybody until the loan's own date arrives or someone notices and revokes it. The corpus previously promised the opposite and promised it silently — a stale loan would stop with an ordinary denial, indistinguishable from never having had it, which is the kind of guarantee that reads as safety and is actually a person wondering why their tool broke. A bound that is visible and ends is a better object than an invisible one that might never end.

Deletes: the use-time half of the delegation rule in domain/06 §9, the register's second enforcement point for that row, and F-32's report option. Changes no table and no column — and no code, since the resolver never had the second check to remove.

See: domain/06 §9, 05 §6, 05d §11 check 11, removed-concepts, and F-32 in § R.

docs.title: D-144 — right_kind is a note: required by the schema, checked against nothing, and no longer claiming to be checked
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-33 asked whether a permission's right_kind has to agree with what the code says — event.answer.view being view — or whether it is a description that the row keeps for its reader. The register carried "a code's right_kind matches what the code says" against the save path, with no report beneath it.

Answer. It stays required and it agrees with nothing. No constraint, no check, no report. The column is required because a row in permission is read by a person deciding what to grant, and a code whose declared kind reads oddly is worth noticing while reading; not because anything will ever tell anybody. It is admitted as a note, which is what catalog-a §8b has been saying all along with its sentence that the marking changes no answer and is filled in because the column is required.

Why keep a required column that nothing checks, when deletion was on the table. Deleting it was the tidy answer and it was refused, for a reason worth keeping: the code's naming grammar (D-104) is enforced by a hand-run diff, and a second, independently written word for the same fact is where that kind of drift surfaces in a human reading rather than in a script. The column's whole job is to be legible. The cost is symmetrical and is now stated in the page rather than hidden in a column comment: a right_kind can contradict its code forever, and only a reader will notice.

What this corrected as it went. The register row is withdrawn, not repaired — D-129 again, the third row this register has had to lose. No page enforces the match; no page claims to; the row was a claim about a save path that has no such rule. This is the third of the register's eleven none rows to be resolved, and the only one resolved by deletion.

Deletes: one row of 00a and one shape-3 rule from its count. Changes no table and no column — permission.right_kind remains required exactly as it was.

See: 05 §2, catalog-a §8b, 00a, D-129, and F-33 in § R.

docs.title: D-145 — access_log rows are deleted at 24 months, and the job that does it has a name
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-8 asked whether the access trail is bounded at all. The page that owns the table had already reversed its own original "never deletion" and put forward the same 24 months audit_log's payloads get — as a proposal awaiting a person, saying so in as many words, with rows kept and their state columns emptied. Assumption 50 registered the legal premise under it.

Answer. Confirmed, with the rows going rather than the contents: an access_log row older than 24 months is deleted. audit_log is untouched and keeps D-088's opposite shape — rows for the life of the system, payloads emptied at 24 months. The two clocks now differ in kind as well as in length: one trail shrinks and stays, the other disappears. Monthly partitioning survives as the mechanism, because dropping a partition is how a row deletion of this size is done without locking the table.

The corpus-wide consequence, which is the reason this entry is long. 00 §4 says "Nothing is hard-deleted. There is no deleted_at and no delete for business data," and then names two exceptions — a staging truncate and the delete erasure has to make. This is the third, and it is named in §4 rather than excepted in a corner, because a page that quietly deletes rows while the conventions page promises none is the kind of page that gets "fixed" back. The exception is narrow in exactly the way §4 wants its exceptions narrow: it reaches no business row, it deletes only access_log, only by age, only forward from the write, and it is the third writer the append-only guard must let through beside erasure and payload reduction. "Append-only" continues to mean no application writes or removes these rows, which is what it always protected.

What dies with a row. Everything the row could answer after its 24th month: that a person opened a record, that a screen was reached, which channel and which grant answered it. audit_log answers what was changed, and answers it forever; nothing answers what was read beyond two years. The register and the inventory say so plainly instead of letting the reader infer permanence from the word "trail", and 05d §11 check 23 — which walks this table's three keyless columns, with the legal-absence rule beside them — keeps working unchanged, because a deleted row cannot be an orphan. It also gains nothing: the age-out gets its own check, the sibling of the one that counts audit rows past their window still holding a payload, because D-133's reasoning cuts both ways — a reduction nobody verifies is a reduction that quietly stops happening, and here the failure direction is data kept too long, which is the failure the window exists to prevent.

Adds: a sixth actor label, system:log-reduction, to the fixed vocabulary in 00 §7a. A job that deletes rows must be nameable, and an empty actor column that could mean the renewal sweep, the bank pull, the payload reduction or a migration is not an answer to "who deleted my access history". Every sentence in the corpus stating that the list has five labels is corrected to six — five pages, one of them the register row for F-25, which is the live record of that decision and is amended rather than left to be contradicted.

Refused: emptying the rows instead, which the proposal on the page preferred. It is the weaker rule with the better story — it keeps "the table never loses a row" — and it was declined because a row that says this record was read on this date by this person is itself the personal data the window was asked about, not a skeleton worth keeping.

Changes no table and no column. Deletes: the "rows are never deleted" position in three pages, the proposal framing in two, and assumption 50, which is now a decision.

See: 05c §9, 00 §4, 00 §7a, 06b §5, 05d §11, D-088, D-125, D-134, and F-8 in § R.

docs.title: D-146 — An outbound call is a person's act or a job, and nothing about it is designed yet
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. F-27 asked what happens when this system calls out — everything designed so far is a person calling in, or one of two inbound jobs pulling data — so who is the actor of an outbound write, and against what is it authorized?

Answer. No outbound integration is designed, and no third kind of actor will be invented when one is. An outbound call is either a person acting — the actor column holds them, their permission is checked, and the trail shows them the way every other act shows them — or this system acting on its own, which is the empty actor column and a label from the fixed vocabulary (D-125). There is no service identity, no key acting as a person, no "the integration did it". If a future integration needs a caller that is not a person and is not this system, that is D-132's successor conversation, not a column added in passing.

What was refused with it. An api_key acting as its own actor for outbound calls. Keys were given a careful, narrow shape last round (D-116): a key is a caller into this system, is never inside an expression, and is refused five codes by equality. Making the same object mean "the thing we call out to" as well would put the accountability of an outbound write on a secret instead of on a person or a job, and a secret is exactly the thing that leaks.

What this costs. A real integration, when it comes, will have to make one of the two choices explicitly and will probably find the choice uncomfortable: a person acting means their permission gates a third party's system, and a job means an empty actor column on a write the organization cannot pin on anybody. Both are answerable; neither is answered here, and the point of deciding now is that the answer must be one of the two, so the vocabulary of five labels becoming six (D-145) is the only growth this axis gets by accident.

Changes no table, no column, no code.

See: 00 §7a, 05e §A key, D-125, D-116, and F-27 in § R.

docs.title: D-147 — Presence stays on the registration: no clock of its own, no permission of its own
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. EV-4 asked whether was_present — the three-valued mark of who actually turned up (D-067) — needs its own retention rule or its own permission, because "who was in our care on that day" is the sentence a safeguarding question would be asked with.

Answer. Neither. Presence is a column of a registration and inherits everything a registration is: the same retention D-140 just settled for registrations, and the same two codes that already reach the roster and the mark. It is not a record class and this system does not keep a safeguarding register. There are no background checks here (D-043) and no medical record (D-083); a column with a special clock and a special permission would be the first wall of an archive this design has refused four times.

What stands in its place, since the need is real. The question "who was there on 14 March" is answered by a report over registrations — which is why the index behind it exists and why it serves a report and no selector — and the answer is legible for as long as the registrations are, which is now indefinitely rather than until somebody's retention number. The protection this column has is that it is boring: readable only with the codes that reach the event, erased by nothing except the person's own erasure, which reaches a registration the way it reaches an answer.

Refused both halves — a presence.retention shorter than the event's, and a presence.view narrower than the roster's. The second would have been a permission whose whole purpose is to hide a fact from the people who are asking because they were there.

Changes no table and no column.

See: 07a §9, 08a §11, D-067, D-140, and EV-4 in § R.

docs.title: D-148 — There is no WHITELISTED, and the refusal is written where the tiers are
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. EV-6 named the word people reach for: an audience for "the ones we invited". The language has four attendance tiers and ORGANIZERS, and refuses PRESENT(<event>) outright because was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register — a volunteer's forgotten tick would revoke a child's own photos. WHITELISTED was never seeded, was described as having no stored state to evaluate, and was asked about in the open questions because the word kept coming up in the corpus as a refusal without a home: the question's own instruction was that "no WHITELISTED" is a sentence that has to exist somewhere, in the same paragraph that refuses PRESENT.

Answer. Refused, in writing, where the tiers are listed. No is_whitelisted column, no fifth tier, no operand, and no reserved name. Anyone adding is_whitelisted is reimplementing grants badly, and the sentence now appears beside the presence refusal in the one place that named a PRESENT refusal without it (domain/07a §9).

Why the answer is free here, which is worth noticing. The refusal already existed four times over — 08a §8, domain/07, domain/06a §Event sets, 05a and the catalog all state it, and three of those passages already pair it with the presence refusal. The count of refused operands does not move: WHITELISTED is already one of "three operands not in this table" and of the two event sets refused in domain/06a. What was missing was a sentence with the word in it in the presence section, and that is a paragraph, not a design.

The need underneath, which is not denied. An invited person who has not registered is, at capacity, ON_WAITLIST if they register onto a full event and described by the absence of a row if they never register (D-059) — and they are invited by a grant aimed at them, which is a row that exists and says who. A tier is a state of a registration; an invitation is not about a registration at all. That is the argument the refusal rests on, and it is why the fifth tier would have cost the meaning of the four that exist: PLACED is the capacity set, so an invited person who registers onto a full event is already misdescribed the moment a whitelist set is added beside it.

What this costs: the same thing every prose refusal costs — nothing in the database refuses a future WHITELISTED row in selector_type, so an operand with no state behind it is a deployment bug rather than a type error, exactly as an off-list actor label is. That is D-125's cost again, on the vocabulary side.

Changes no table and no column.

See: domain/06a §Event sets, 05a, 08a §8, 07a §9, D-102, F-20, and EV-6 in § R.

docs.title: D-149 — Words are stored in one language, and a label is not translated
docs.text:
Status: applied.

Question. AT-3 asked whether attribute_definition and attribute_option labels need a second language, because a form that asks a question in a language the family reads is the whole point of a form.

Answer. One language: the one the organization writes in. No label_cs/label_en pair, no translation table, no per-language row, no locale column anywhere in the attribute vocabulary. The vocabulary is the organization's own words, written at runtime by whoever it hands the curating permission to (D-084), and the page that owns the table describes a label in four words: what a human sees (09 §2). A label is not a rendering of something more authoritative underneath it — and a second language would need one, because a row holding label_cs and label_en has to be asked which of the two the record is, and whichever answer is chosen demotes the other to a translation of it.

What happens to a translated form, since the need is real. The people who need another language are served by the person reading the question aloud or writing it down, which is how a Scout organisation has always done it, and by an event form's own question text — a question's text is free text somebody types in whichever language the event is run in, and it is not a vocabulary item. The vocabulary is for the record; the form is for the conversation, and only one of the two has to be stable enough to query.

What this costs: an imported label arrives in whatever language the paper form was in and stays there, which makes correcting it a curation act under attribute.define — live at the save, per D-141 — and means an organisation that genuinely runs in two languages will have two codes for one fact, which is a misery the design does not prevent and does not pretend to.

Changes no table and no column.

See: 09 §2, 09 §5, D-084, and AT-3 in § R.

docs.title: What the round did not do
docs.text:
• It did not apply D-132. That sweep — the seeded roles, the seeded audiences, the seeded event.answer.view grant, the worked-example offices presented as seed, role.is_system, audience.is_system — is a cleanup with its decision already written, and it was deliberately kept out of this round so that thirteen answers and one twenty-five-page sweep would not be committed together. It is round 21 and it is the next thing this repository owes itself. D-141 and D-143 both reach across to it, and both are written so that the sweep has to read them rather than the other way round.
  • It did not answer the four that survive, and did not manufacture answers for them: F-9 and F-11 turn on a decision about what a membership type is for, E-3 turns on how this organisation reads its own civil code, and A-4's remainder is the calendar. None is 🟡.
  • It did not answer the question it raised — F-34. D-141 deleted the proposal stage without noticing that it was also the answer to a scheduling question: the vocabulary the legacy import needs has to exist before the import applies, because an unmapped column is now an error at apply time rather than a row that arrives proposed and waits. So several hundred definitions must be authored by holders of attribute.define in advance, while D-132 is about to delete the seed that hands that code to anybody. Who writes them, when, and who holds the code afterwards is a real hole with no answer in it yet, and answering it here would have been a ruling wearing a question's clothes — the same mistake this round refused to make about a safeguarding contact. It is recorded in domain/03 §9 and in the catalog's open issues, and it is 🟢 only because the first import is not next week.
  • It did not touch the legal review, which is the largest unowned risk in this corpus and now has a third policy in front of it: named membership and fee rows kept indefinitely, audit payloads emptied at 24 months, and access rows deleted at 24 months (assumption 49; D-145). That review is the organisation's job, not a question this register can close.
  • It added no check it could not point at a page. The check this round adopted — the age-out count over access_log — is named in 05c §9 and given to 06b §5, where the audit sibling already lives. The register's **none** count goes from seven to five, and every one of the five is a rule whose answer is "nothing, by decision".

The gate ran, and it was not free. scripts/check-registries.py finishes this round at no unbaselined finding, and mkdocs build --clean --strict is clean with no link reported. Two of this round's edits touch pages the checker reads — the attribute statuses in erd-b and the label vocabulary in 00 §7a — so the run was made after them, not before. Three findings had to be met, and each was met on the page rather than in the baseline: 04 §1 had stopped naming guardianship.assign when this round deleted the notification sentence that named it, so the page now names the code itself, which is the stronger sentence and clears the finding (D-137 is an argument about that one permission); presence.view, spelled twice in order to say it does not exist, is the one line this round added to scripts/registry-baseline.txt with its reason beside it; and the third was the same presence.view from the other file. The habit worth keeping from this: a refusal is a sentence the checker cannot tell from a mistake, so the baseline is where a round writes down that it read the sentence and meant it — and a baseline line without a reason after the # is that mechanism failing quietly, not a formality.

What the link pass swept up on the way, counted as grepped rather than as remembered. Six of the thirteen closed questions were cited from elsewhere by their heading slug rather than by the short id § R would later carry, and deleting an entry deletes the slug it derived. Twenty-six links had to move: AT-4 ten, AT-2 four, AT-1 four, E-6 three, EV-2 three, EV-6 two. All twenty-six now point at the short anchors § R carries, which is what they should have pointed at when the convention was written. Two lessons, and the second is about this paragraph. First: a derived slug has to be recomputed, not remembered — the old EV-2 heading was ### EV-2 🟡 Retention of \event_answer`and its slug wasev-2--retention-of-event_answer, with the emoji gone, the backticks gone and the **underscore kept**, which is three rules in one string and none of them obvious. This entry stated the slug asev-2--retention-of-event, cut off at the code span, and that was wrong; round 19 wrote the sentence abouttags and this round needed it about inline code. Second: **the first pass said twenty-two and named six questions whose counts did not add up, and it missed three live links** — [round-07-08](round-07-08.md), [round-19](round-19.md) and § R's ownF-29row all still pointed atAT-4's dead slug, and nothing I ran told me so untilmkdocs build --strict` printed it as an INFO line beneath a successful build. A link that resolves to nothing is reported at the same volume as a file being copied, and the count that was wrong was the one I had written down instead of the one I had grepped.

docs.title: Decision Log — Refinement round 21 (D-150 … D-154)
docs.text:
D-132 was decided in round 18 and never applied: the seed was still described on the page that owns the seed, deferred to a round that went off to do something else twice. This round applies it. The roles, the two named audiences, the shipped answer-view grant and every is_system column in the design go, and applying a decision that had been settled for three rounds turned out to need three rulings the decision did not contain: where the first system.admin comes from when nobody yet may write a grant, who writes the per-event answer-view grant once nobody ships one, and what protects a vocabulary once the flag on its rows is gone.

Refinement round 20 (D-137 … D-149) ← | All decisions

What was asked. Round 20 was split on purpose: thirteen answers in one file, the twenty-five-page sweep in the next (D-132's sweep, deferred since the round that decided it). This file is the second half of that split, and it was under way before it stopped being mechanical. A deletion is only a deletion if nothing was relying on the thing deleted, and three things were: the first account's authority, every event's answer privacy, and the four vocabulary columns that told a screen not to edit a row. Each became a question, the questions were asked, and the answers are D-150 to D-152. D-153 and D-154 are the two named things the sweep swept up.

What the round found while applying it, which is again the part worth reading. A deferred decision is not a decision that stopped costing anything: while it sat unapplied, pages kept being written against the seed as if it were shipped, and two of them disagreed about what the seed was.

  • D-132 said day one has "no role, no audience, no grant", and day one needs one grant. Every authority in this design arrives through access_grant (the catalog says so in as many words: every code, system.admin included), so an account that holds system.admin holds a grant row. And on day one nobody holds access_grant.create, because the seed that would have carried an office holding it is the seed being deleted here. The round asked where that first row comes from and the answer was flat, and right: from the same place every other authority comes from — it is a permission, and it is the one that means everything. Nothing bootstraps anything; there is no fourth kind of actor, no bootstrap_person_id column, no CLI-only back door into the resolver. The account holds one code and that code satisfies every check, so access_grant.create, role.create and audience.manage are all available in the same instant the account is. D-132's "no grant" was a sentence about bundles — no starter set, no office, no audience — and this round says so instead of leaving a decision to be re-litigated by a reader who takes it literally.
