What this round did instead is make the invisibility sayable — the page names what is registered there (the closed items, with their decisions) and what is not (the five), so the next round that touches money inherits a sentence to correct rather than a silence to rediscover.

Not one of the register's five survivors was answered, and nine new questions were filed there. A-4's remainder, E-3, F-9, F-11 and F-34 are questions about the core design, and sixteen answers touched the core design exactly twice — at the ceiling on a grant (D-163) and at the account of a child (D-166) — neither of which was on the list. D-169 looks like it closes A-4 and does not: the calendar question was answered in round 4, and what D-169 closed was a module page's bullet that had not noticed. What did move is the page's total, from five to fourteen: the nine questions this round found and verified but did not ask are now § K, each naming the page that holds it, because the alternative was to leave them in a decision entry where only a reader of decision logs would find them. That is the whole repair this round could make for its own finding: an answer on a page is not a registered question, and neither is a question written up in the log that found it.

Questions found, verified and deliberately not asked this time, so that they are not rediscovered as findings: whether a person_group_member row must lie inside its group's own period (data-model/02 §8, "nowhere ruled", and the register records the containment as enforced by nothing); whether an ended group is hidden from pickers and whether it may be reopened, which collides with §1's rule that a returning name is a new group; where a claimed group continuity is recorded, since D-098 refuses group-to-group edges and nothing replaced what D-096 gave units; whether person.gender is needed and with what value set; whether there is or will be a national SSO identity provider, which decides how much of account_credential is ever built; whether person.notes should exist given the redaction burden it creates; which tables the audit obligation covers, where the page asks for confirmation rather than derivation; who reads the unpaid-money queue monthly, since four pages say someone; and whether staff may create accounts for children, which D-166 keeps open. None of these is closed. All of them are one sentence long.

And the legal review now has four policies in front of it, not three: named membership and fee rows kept indefinitely, audit payloads emptied at 24 months, access_log rows deleted at 24 months, and — added by D-166 — whether a child may hold an account with no guardian's consent recorded anywhere. The second and third are this system's own clocks; the first and fourth are the two a data subject asks about.

docs.title: Domain Overview
docs.text: What the organization is, who interacts with the system, and how the core lifecycles flow. Read ../glossary.md first — this document uses its terms strictly.

docs.title: 1. The organization
docs.text:
A youth organization (Scout-like: uniformed groups, trained adult leadership, camps and weekly meetings) with:

  • Child members — youth participants, who join one another in groups.
  • Adult members — counselors and leaders who run the programs, hold offices, and put people into groups.
  • Caretakers — parents and legal guardians of child members. They may or may not be members themselves.
  • Non-member supporters — people who interact with the organization (donors, volunteers, alumni) without holding a membership.

"Child" and "adult" are how the organization talks about people. They are not two kinds of membership: there is one membership type and it is ageless, so "is this person a child?" is a question about person.birth_date and the date being asked about (§2). Only three things downstream key off the difference: guardianship, eligibility an organizer writes for one event, and the mirroring rule for messages.

The system models no internal structure of the organization. There is one unit, it is a scope rather than a row, and the nested bodies the organization has been reorganized into over four decades are not stored, not versioned and not imported — an absence decided on purpose, whose cost is written down in D-097. What remains of "the inside of the organization" is groups: named sets of people with a lifetime, in 04-organization-structure.md. A reader arriving expecting a hierarchy should learn that here, on the first page, because the absence changes every later answer about scope.

docs.title: 2. Actors
docs.text:
The system distinguishes actors by what they can do, not by what they are. The full treatment is in 02-actors.md; the summary:

Actor Has account? Has membership? Can do Anonymous visitor no no see public info, submit a registration or a membership request Registered person yes no maintain own profile, submit/renew a request, view own history Member yes yes own profile, event signups, own history Caretaker yes maybe view and act on their dependents — only as the guardianship row allows Staff / registrar yes maybe organization-wide administrative permissions Historical record no a bounded period, if the export states one nothing. Data only, never a login.

A minor is not an actor row. One row above is a member, and whether that member is a minor today is person.birth_date against the date of the check — a fact about a person that changes on its own, never a kind of account. What a minor genuinely cannot do alone is a guardianship question (02-actors.md).

Imported rows create person rows with no account, and import must never be blocked by a "users must have email addresses" rule. They also create membership rows: bounded ones, both ends dated, only for the periods the people export states, data_confidence = 'low', marked with the batch that wrote them (D-093). An imported period is never open-ended and never inferred from presence — an open membership satisfies is_current_member(), so inferring one would make every 1998 attendee a current member today. No sub-unit row is ever imported, because neither export names a sub-unit (03-identity-and-legacy.md §7).

docs.title: 3. The three lifecycles
docs.text: Almost everything in the system is one of three multi-step processes. They are separate because they succeed and fail independently: you can register without applying, apply without being accepted, be accepted without paying, and pay without ever joining a group.

docs.title: 3.1 Account lifecycle
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │                                             │
 (none) ──register──> pending_verification ──verify──> active ──┴──> suspended
                                                            │              │
                                                            └──> closed <──┘

An account is about authentication only. It says "this person can log in". It says nothing about membership. A person can hold a verified, active account for years and never become a member — a parent who only ever manages their child is exactly this case.

One gate the arrows do not draw: an account may not reach active while an unresolved identity_hypothesis names its person, which is what a sign-up that strong-matches someone who already exists runs into (D-089). Verification is necessary and not sufficient; a human decision is the second condition. Because that makes a stalled queue a person who cannot log in, a hypothesis that blocks activation is age-checked, and somebody reads the count. One live account per person is the rule doing the underlying work (02-actors.md §3).

docs.title: 3.2 Membership lifecycle
docs.text:
(none)
   │
   ├─ request submitted ──> under_review ──accept──> approved ──payment confirmed──> active member
   │                             │                                                    │
   │                             └──reject──> rejected                                 │
   │                                                                                   │
   │                                     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │                                     ├──> lapsed (fee expired at the yearly date)   │
   │                                     ├──> terminated (cause, with reason)          │
   │                                     └──> suspended (temporary hold)               │
   │                                                                                   │
   │      ┌──────────────── renewal (no new application) ────────────────────────────┘
   │      │        inside the renewal window → the new period opens at the expiry date
   │      │        after it                  → the new period opens at the payment date
   │      ▼
   │   active member again
   │
   └──────────────────────── re-apply ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every transition creates or closes a row; nothing is overwritten. A person who was a member 1990–2010 and again from 2024 has two membership rows, and the gap is visible as data rather than inferred from a date.

Two properties of the lapse are worth naming before the detail. There is no completed status: nothing ages out of a membership, so there is no state for having finished one. And the lapse happens to everyone at once, on a fixed date — the yearly expiry — which is why the renewal path matters more than the word "grace" suggests (D-040).

Detailed in 05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: 3.3 Authorization lifecycle
docs.text:
(none) ──grant──> active ──end date reached / period closed──> inactive
                     │
                     └──delegate──> delegated grant (with end date, provenance recorded)

Every grant has a start, an end, a granter, and a reason. Nothing is permanent by default and nothing is revoked by deletion — closing a period is the act, and the row stays. Detailed in 06-authorization-model.md.

docs.title: 4. The relationships between people
docs.text:
Four relationships, deliberately not merged:

Relationship Direction Example Grants access? Guardianship guardian → dependent parent → child No by itself — only the right_level (none / view / write) carried on the live guardianship row is authority, and that row is the whole of it (D-074). Membership member → the organization anyone → the unit No. Being in a group person → group child → the Thursday group No — a person_group_member row is a dated roster entry. Holding an office person → role adult → counselors No — a role_holder row says who holds it, and an office confers nothing by being held.

Being a member and being in a group are two rows, not one. A person is a member of the organization and on a group's roster: different facts, different lifetimes, and different guards on who may change them — which is why someone who stops attending on Thursdays is still a paid-up member, and someone who is paid up may turn up to nothing. The two rows are edited by different people for different reasons, which is the whole case for keeping them apart.

The recurring theme: participation is not authority. A person can be deeply involved — a parent of three members, a twenty-year veteran, the founder of a group — and still have no administrative access. Access comes only from an explicit grant. This separation is what makes the permission system auditable, and what prevents the classic failure where a relationship ends (custody changes, a leader steps down) and access silently persists.

docs.title: The counselor who is also a parent
docs.text:
This case is not special:

  • One person row.
  • One open membership, of the one membership type, member — the same shape as the child they lead.
  • One role_holder row: they hold the office counselors over a dated period.
  • A person_group_member row or two, dated, for the groups they actually turn up to.
  • Two guardianship rows (to their own children), each carrying its own right level.
  • Whatever access_grant rows somebody wrote whose grantee names them — as ROLE(counselors), or MEMBERS * ROLE(counselors) where membership is required of the holder.
  • No row of its own for "is a counselor". The role_holder row is all of it.

There is no counselor membership type, and being a counselor is an office held for a period — not a kind of membership, and not a grade of person. Nor is it a shipped office: no role ships, so the counselors role of this example is one the organization wrote, and day one is one account holding system.admin (D-150, D-154). This person's membership is identical to that of the child they lead, which is exactly the point.

Their grants reach the unit's members, which is the whole organization: there is no smaller body to scope inside, so a unit-scope grant is the broadest thing a person can hold. Their guardianship reaches their own children through a different channel entirely — entered by the shape of the request (subject ≠ actor) rather than by any permission they were given (D-079), and capped by the right level that row records. Being a leader does not give them access to other people's children's records, and the reason is mechanical: no rule could imply it, so the access exists as rows or not at all.

That is a safety property, not a convenience. Child-protection practice requires that a leader's access to minors' personal data be bounded by their function, and two properties carry it here: an office, a roster, a membership and a guardianship each confer nothing by being what they are (D-100), and a grant is one code, one scope, one effect per row (D-099), so "what exactly does this person have over minors?" is answered by reading rows rather than by evaluating a rank. What the design does not do is guarantee that the reach was written by the body it governs — see rule 5 in the overview. The boundary is enforceable and reportable; who is obliged to read the report is a convention, not a guard.

docs.title: 5. Multiplicity, in both directions
docs.text:
Specified directly: one parent can manage multiple children; multiple children can be managed by the same parent. The model generalizes both:

  • One guardian → many dependents (many guardianship rows).
  • Many guardians → one dependent (both parents, stepparents, legal guardians — no assumption that a child has exactly two, or exactly one).
  • A guardian's authority is per-dependent, so a parent can hold write for one child and view only for another — a realistic custody arrangement.

The same person can be a guardian of someone and a dependent of someone else: the relation is a general graph, not a two-level hierarchy. This costs nothing to allow and avoids a rewrite when a member's sibling needs a guardian and the member is the one who has them.

docs.title: 6. The four decades of history
docs.text:
This is the constraint that most shapes the schema.

The system must answer, correctly and indefinitely:

  • "Was this person a member when they attended that camp in 2003?"
  • "This person registered in 2026 claiming they were a member in the 90s — is that true?"
  • "Who was on this group's roster on 1 June 1998?" — if somebody recorded the roster; the import supplies no group history.

It must not answer, and does not try to:

  • "Who was in Pack 12 on 1 June 1998?" and "what was that unit called in 2001, and what is its successor today?" There are no units, no nesting and no successor relations to traverse.

Consequences, which the data model implements:

  1. Everything temporal is a period, never a boolean or a single date.
  2. Nothing is hard-deleted, except by three named acts, each somebody's decision rather than a cleanup job. Erasing a person redacts their values wherever they were copied, including in the audit payload, immediately and at any age. Payload reduction empties an audit row's values 24 months after they were written and leaves the row standing, so the trail keeps answering who changed this, when, and were they allowed to and stops answering and to what (D-088). Reverting an import batch removes the rows that batch created. Reduction is not redaction: one answers to a person and is absolute, the other answers to a calendar and is bounded. The accounting skeleton — membership, fees, payments — is deliberately outside all three and kept indefinitely as the organization's own history. Assumption: that this "forever" has a legal basis is exactly what this document cannot establish for itself; the claim is recorded as an assumption awaiting review, not as settled law.
  3. People's names change, so a name is a child-table row with a validity period and never a column that gets overwritten. A group's name is a column, and nothing replaces the deleted name-history table: a rename edits it and the old name is gone. What survives a rename is the identity beneath it, because grants and expressions store a kind and an id, never a name.
  4. Imported data is low-confidence. The people export carries a name, a birth date, and the period each person was a member of the organization. Where an export also carries the organization's legacy member number — the number its paper records are keyed on — that number is imported verbatim into person_identifier under the legacy scheme, is never reissued, and makes a match exact rather than probable: same number, same person. Every other identity claim the import makes is a proposal a human confirms. See 03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: 7. What this design does not decide yet
docs.text:
Referenced by the schema but not designed, pending your specification:

  • Fees and payments — a provisional shape exists in ../data-model/07-finance.md because membership activation depends on it. Expect to rewrite it.
  • Communication — its shape is decided (direct by default, broadcast an ordinary scoped permission, the recipient chooses the channel, a minor's guardians get a mirror of a direct message), and its codes are in the catalog. There is no message or message_recipient table yet, and no design for templates, opt-out granularity, retention or moderation.
  • Notifications — nothing in this design sends anything to anybody today (D-164), and what is deferred is a module nobody has designed: the renewal window made notifications dated rather than status-driven, which is a design note, not a design.
  • Documents, reporting, API and UI.

docs.title: 8. Next
docs.text:
• Terminology → ../glossary.md
  • Accounts and registration → 02-actors.md
  • Historical data → 03-identity-and-legacy.md
  • What the system knows about a person → 08-person-data.md
  • Groups, offices and the unit → 04-organization-structure.md
  • Membership → 05-membership-lifecycle.md
  • Permissions → 06-authorization-model.md
  • Events → 07-events.md

Decisions behind this page: D-037, D-038, D-040, D-041, D-074, D-079, D-088, D-089, D-093, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-114.

docs.title: Actors, Accounts, and Self-Registration
docs.text: How a human being gets into the system, what an account is (and is not), and why registration is deliberately separate from membership.

docs.title: 1. The core separation
docs.text:
person ─────────── the human being. Exists even with no account and no membership.
     │
     ├── account ──── the ability to log in. Optional. Zero or more per person over time, one live.
     │
     └── membership ─ the state of being a member. Optional. Zero or more periods.

These are three independent things. Any combination is legal:

State Example person, no account, no membership 1994 roster entry imported from paper. person, account, no membership A parent who registered to manage their child. person, account, membership An active member. person, no account, membership An adult member who never uses the system; staff manage them. person, account, lapsed membership Someone who let their membership lapse but still logs in.

The schema must not reject any of these. In particular there must be no requirement that a person has an email address, or that a member has an account — otherwise the historical import is impossible.

docs.title: 2. Who registers, and why
docs.text:
People register on their own to get access to the system; a person becomes a member only by requesting a membership, being accepted, and paying the yearly fee. So registration produces an account, not a membership. The person is then a registered non-member — able to log in, maintain their profile, view their own history, and submit a membership request.

The split gives the system a clean place to hang capabilities that must work before membership exists:

  • A caretaker registering to manage a child before deciding whether to join themselves.
  • An adult applying to become a counselor, who needs to fill in an application first.
  • A returning member from the 90s reconnecting to their history.

docs.title: Registration paths
docs.text: Path Actor Result Self-registration an adult, or a minor — the path does not branch on age person + account Registration on behalf caretaker registers a minor who has no account person (child) + guardianship Staff-created account registrar creates one for an adult who is not self-sufficient with computers person + account, flagged created_by_staff Legacy import no account created person only, record_origin = 'legacy_import' Self-registration claiming history adult registers and asserts a past membership person + account + identity_hypothesis Sign-up colliding with an existing person adult signs up again through an address the system did not know, and strong-matches someone who already exists person + account, both held at pending_verification, + identity_hypothesis — and no merge, no link, no activation. The address typed survives as the credential it was offered as, and the hypothesis is what holds the account out of active (§3)

docs.title: Minor registration
docs.text: A minor may create an account unattended and nothing in the model objects, because an account is a login and authority reaches nothing except through grants (D-100, D-166). No minimum age, no consent step, no branch in the sign-up path. A new account holds no grants, and a new account is a person-shaped hole in the database until somebody writes a row about its person — a grant, a guardianship, a membership — which is what every new account is, not a safeguard designed for this case. If the organization wants a guardian's answer on record, it goes on the guardianship relationship, which already carries right_level and its own dates (../data-model/04-relationships.md §2); no column returns for it. What this page does not decide is whether the law of this country demands a consent step regardless — a policy in front of the legal review beside the four data policies, and stated there (06b §6).

docs.title: 3. Account state machine
docs.text:
Status Meaning pending_verification Registered; email/phone not yet confirmed. Minimal capabilities. active Normal. suspended Temporarily blocked (security, disciplinary). Membership unaffected. closed Voluntarily or administratively closed. Retained for audit; login refused.

Two deliberate choices:

  • Suspending an account does not suspend a membership. They are separate lifecycles; a person can be an active member with a suspended account (they'd interact by phone).
  • Closing an account does not delete the person or their history. The account row is closed and retained. person and all membership rows are untouched.

And a gate this table cannot express. active has a second condition beyond verification: an account may not reach it while an unresolved identity_hypothesis names its person. One live account per person is the rule doing the underlying work — uniqueness says a person may not hold two live accounts, and the gate says the second arrival waits for a human rather than being merged into the first or quietly linked to it.

Why a human, and not an automatic link: a merge made by machine turns one person's false positive into one person's record becoming another's. Making a queue state block a login buys two obligations, and both are checks rather than intentions:

  • A hypothesis that is blocking an account is age-checked. A queue that stalls is not a data-quality problem with no victim you can name: it is a specific person who cannot log in, whose only remaining channel is to telephone someone. Nothing here will tell anyone the queue has stalled — no message is sent, and the age on a row is the whole of the warning (D-164), which is why the block carries a number rather than sitting in a list.
  • The message the person sees confirms nothing. Not that the name matched, not that the birth date did, not that anyone by that name exists — because a sign-up form that can answer "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle, and this system's roster is children.

The trigger is a strong match only — exact legacy member number, or exact birth date together with a normalised name. The scored band below that raises nothing at sign-up: blocking a stranger's registration on a fuzzy score is the failure this rule would most deserve (03-identity-and-legacy.md §4).

Why: D-089.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
account holds authentication material. Two rules worth fixing now:

  1. The password hash lives in account_credential, not in account. This leaves room for multiple authentication methods (password, passkey, OAuth via a national Scout identity provider, staff-issued one-time links) without restructuring.
  2. Never share an account between a parent and a child. The temptation is real — "the parent will just log in as the kid" — but it destroys attributability. The correct mechanism is acting on behalf, which records who acted and as whom. An account shared between people makes every audit entry worthless, and in a youth organization the audit trail is the point.

docs.title: When nobody who can hold system.admin can sign in
docs.text:
system.admin is the capability this system has no substitute for: it is what rotates or ends an integration that is writing right now, what releases a data subject's erasure, and the only code that satisfies every other check (D-068). A key cannot be the way back in — it is not a person, carries nobody's authority, and may never be granted that code (D-122) — and no self-service path exists anywhere here: nobody joins, appoints or un-suspends themselves, so an emergency door would be the second, weaker authorization this design rejects by name. What exists instead is a report and this procedure (D-126).

  1. Read the report before acting from memory. Integrity check 9 lists everyone with a live allow of system.admin, however they came by it, and says for each of them whether they can sign in: account.status is active and their credential is live (account_credential.valid_to unset or in the future, not revoked). An empty second column is the alert, and the alert is a report somebody opens rather than a message somebody receives: nobody is told when that column empties, which is precisely why step 1 says to read the report instead of acting from memory and step 2 names a person long before one is needed (D-164, 05d §11).
  2. One named person is written down before it is needed, and someone knows their telephone number. api_key.owner_person_id is not that person — it answers whose integration is this, not who fixes it (D-120).
  3. The recovery is performed on an account, never on a grant. Un-suspend the account, or re-issue the credential, whichever is the actual obstacle. This is the one write in this design made outside the application, and it stays that way: it produces no audit row, and nothing in the schema distinguishes it from somebody editing a row they had no business editing.
  4. Everything after it is ordinary. The recovered person acts through the screens, so every authority change that follows carries granted_by, an authorization_channel and an audit row like anybody else's. The recovery restores a person's access; it does not hand out authority, which is the difference between this and the sealed emergency credential that was refused.

What catches the edit afterwards is one line of the integrity-check list: an audited row whose newest audit row predates its updated_at is a change the trail never saw (06b §5). It is a report rather than a guard, and it is honest about its own limit — whoever can make the edit can also write an audit row by hand, because the trail is append-only to the application and not to whoever holds the database. That is the residual risk this procedure accepts, stated here so that nobody discovers it during the incident.

docs.title: 4. Contact points and identifiers
docs.text:
A person's email, phone and address are rows, not columns. Each row carries its type, its purpose, its value, whether it is the primary one for that type and purpose, when it was verified, and the period it applied for.

Why not just person.email:

  • People have several emails (personal, school, work) and which one is primary changes.
  • A caretaker's contact details are often the effective contact for a child; the system needs both the child's own contact and the adult's.
  • Addresses change, and history is kept: an address row with a validity period answers "where did this member live in 2003?", which a column cannot.
  • Changing an email must not lose the old one, because historical records may reference it.

Purpose is the field that makes this useful operationally: login, membership, emergency, billing, guardian_contact. A person can have one address for billing and another for emergency contact, and the permission system can treat them differently — emergency contacts are visible to whoever holds the roster read on that camp; billing details are not.

docs.title: External identifiers
docs.text:
One row per identifier held against a person: a scheme, a value, and when it was verified if it ever was. (scheme, value) is unique among the identifiers that are still current — a superseded number may be reused, a current one may not be shared.

Identifiers issued outside the system belong here: a national Scout registration number, a government ID, an old membership card number from a previous system, a school ID. Keeping these separate from contact points is what gives the legacy import somewhere to put the old system's member numbers — which is precisely what makes reconnecting 1990–2010 members possible. See 03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: 5. Acting on behalf
docs.text:
Both read and write access for a caretaker are explicit:

  • A guardianship row establishes the relationship.
  • That row carries one right — none, view, or write. Being the parent implies nothing; a row at none grants literally nothing.

The right is one value, not a capability list, compared against permission.right_kind ∈ read | write: none covers nothing, view covers the codes marked read, write covers both. A court order that lets one parent register the child for events but not read the rest of the record cannot be written, and neither can "roster visibility and nothing else": a guardian at view reads the child's record whole, because the record has no compartment inside it to be excepted from (D-074, D-083). What the right is, and keeps: explicit, dated, revocable, audited — one deliberate value per row rather than an inference from who someone is.

write is not a license over the organization. The ceiling is the channel, not a rank: the guardianship channel is entered only when the check is about somebody other than the actor, so the widest right in the system reaches this child's record and cannot reach a roster, a fee schedule or another family — those checks are not about the child and the channel is never asked (D-079). Authority is per row, so a guardian of one child sees nothing of another's. A deny still refuses a guardian holding write, absolutely and regardless of scope — what is unavailable is a narrow deny, not the ability to say no. There is no per-resource admin wildcard either; a role that needs broad reach lists what it grants (D-068).

History is kept: every change of the value is a new guardianship_permission row, and the value on the guardianship row is always the open one's.

How a check resolves. A check about a dependent is evaluated against the guardianship row for the (guardian, dependent) pair and the right level it holds, not against roles. This keeps the two authority channels distinct:

  • Grants answer "what may this person do in the organization?"
  • Guardianship answers "what may this person do regarding this child?"

An office confers nothing by being held (D-100), so holding one gives nobody a guardian's right over a child and leadership has no channel of its own: a leader reaches data the way every other non-guardian does, through grants. If the organization needs its leaders to see a camper's emergency contacts, that is said, as a grant of person.view, and the scope chosen is the entire decision — every member of the organization or the people on one event, with nothing between them (D-097), and person.view has no narrower cousin to reach for if the first one turns out to feel like what it is (08-person-data.md). Audited either way; never through a fictional guardianship.

docs.title: Recording acts on behalf
docs.text:
Every operation performed on behalf of another person writes to access_log with both parties: actor_person_id is the parent, subject_person_id is the child, and on_behalf records that the actor acted for the subject rather than as themselves.

This is not optional bookkeeping. When a parent changes a child's address or registers them for a camp, the record must show that the parent did it, not the child. Without this, the audit trail falsely attributes the parent's actions to the child.

docs.title: 6. Effective contact for a minor
docs.text:
A recurring operational need: "who do we call about this child?" The answer is usually a guardian, but not always the same one, and not always the one with the most permissions.

Resolve it as three conditions on guardianship, applied in this order: the row's dependent is this child; the row is still open today, meaning valid_to is absent or later than today — a guardianship that has ended is not an answer, so the date is checked on the row rather than assumed; and is_primary_contact is set. The answer is the contact points of those guardians whose purpose is emergency.

is_primary_contact on guardianship is separate from the guardian's right level on purpose: a guardian with no system access at all can still be the emergency contact. Do not require login capability to be reachable in an emergency.

docs.title: 7. Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether staff-created accounts are allowed for children, or only adults. Still open, and untouched by the fact that the sign-up path has no age gate: D-166 removes a gate on a path, not a policy about who may open an account on somebody else's behalf, so a reader who takes "no gate" to mean "staff may create a child's account" has read further than the answer goes. The created_by_staff flag on account (01a §4) stays whichever way this is settled.

Not registered in ../open-questions.md, and a reader of the register alone would not find it: this page is the only place the question is written down.

Decisions behind this page: D-068, D-074, D-079, D-083, D-089, D-097, D-099, D-100, D-164, D-166.

docs.title: Identity Resolution and Legacy Data
docs.text:
How the system decides that two records describe the same human, and how four decades of paper and spreadsheet history gets brought in without corrupting live data.

This is the highest-risk area of the project. Get it wrong and either the history is unusable, or worse, two people's records get merged and you leak one member's data to another. The design below is deliberately conservative.

docs.title: 1. Why this is hard
docs.text:
A 1994 row has: a name, maybe a birth date, the period that person was a member, and, on most rows, a legacy member number (D-090), with free text — an address, remarks — in columns beside it. None of it can log in: the number keys the organization's paper, not a session, and it is missing from precisely the rows that most need the heuristics below — those predating the numbering, and those where it was written illegibly. Meanwhile:

  • Names change (marriage, adoption, correction of a misspelling).
  • Names repeat. In a youth organization spanning decades, "Jan Novák" is many people.
  • Diacritics and transliterations vary across decades of manual entry (Novák / Novak).
  • Birth dates are often wrong by a digit, or recorded as year-only.
  • The same human appears in multiple rosters under slightly different spellings.

So: automatic matching will produce both false positives and false negatives. False positive (two people merged) is a privacy incident. False negative (one person split) is a data-quality annoyance. The design must therefore bias hard toward false negatives — never merge on a guess.

This document is about one half of a person. Everything it resolves is identity: the fields that make a row a particular human — names, birth date, the account, contact points, issued identifiers. Everything the organization records about that human beyond those is descriptive data, and it is deliberately absent from every table below: no descriptive value is a match signal, and none may become one. A clothing size or a dietary habit identifies nobody, and making matching depend on one would make the reliability of a person's history depend on what the organization happened to collect about them (08-person-data.md, D-085). The line between the two halves is drawn by what a machine may act on without a human, not by how delicate a fact feels; the test is stated in 08-person-data.md.

docs.title: 2. The three record classes
docs.text:
Every person row carries record_origin:

Origin Meaning Confidence Has account? self_registered A human created this by registering high yes staff_created A registrar entered this person high maybe legacy_import Imported from historical records low no

Legacy-imported people are provisional. They are fully queryable — a member who left in 1998 is findable by name and birth date — but they are marked as unverified, they cannot be logged into, and they are the only rows eligible to be absorbed by a merge.

Rule: a merge always absorbs the lower-confidence row into the higher-confidence one. An import can never overwrite a self-registered person's data.

docs.title: 3. Identity hypotheses, not merges
docs.text:
The core mechanism. An identity hypothesis is a proposal that two person rows are the same human. It is a first-class table row, with a confidence score, evidence, a status, and a human decision.

The row holds the pair as person_a_id and person_b_id, stored in one order: person_a_id names the lower id, and the two are never the same person — a pair has one canonical spelling rather than two.

confidence is the matcher's score between 0 and 1; match_signals records which fields agreed and how strongly, which is what a reviewer reads to see why it was proposed. status is one of proposed, needs_review, confirmed, rejected, superseded. proposed_by says where the proposal came from — import_job, match_job (the nightly batch matcher), person or staff — and proposed_at when. reviewed_by, reviewed_at and review_note are the human part, and a hypothesis may not reach confirmed or rejected without a reviewed_at. At most one live hypothesis exists per pair — live means proposed, needs_review or confirmed.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
matcher proposes ──> proposed ──┬── staff confirms ──> confirmed ──> [merge executed]
                                  ├── staff rejects  ──> rejected (the pair becomes
                                  │                       proposable again — see §4)
                                  └── person asserts ──> needs_review → staff confirms/rejects

Three entry points:

  1. Import or background matching proposes hypotheses automatically at low confidence.
  2. A registering person asserts their own history — "I was a member 1990–2010" — which creates a hypothesis against the candidate rows, usually with proposed_by = 'person'.
  3. A sign-up that strong-matches a person who already exists raises one by itself, without anyone asserting anything, and that hypothesis holds the new account out of active (§4, D-089). The queue is the same queue and the review is the same review; what a person at a registration form adds is the ability to put a row in it.

A person's own assertion is evidence, not proof. It must still be reviewed, because claiming someone else's history is the obvious attack on an import-based system — and the prize is that person's data. Never auto-confirm a self-asserted link.

docs.title: 4. Match signals
docs.text:
The matcher scores candidate pairs on independent signals. Recorded in match_signals so a reviewer sees why the system proposed a match:

Signal Strength Notes Exact legacy member number decisive The corpus carries these (D-056). Same number, same person — matched, not scored. Exact birth date + exact normalised name strong Still not automatic — twins with similar names exist. Birth date within ±1 day or year-only match + name moderate Common with hand-written records. Name match after normalisation (diacritics, case, spacing) moderate Necessary but weak alone; "Jan Novák" is not unique. Same postal address at the same time moderate Strong if the address is distinctive. Read from person_contact history — there is no household table (D-057). Guardian name match weak Useful for minors in old records. Name-only fuzzy match weak — never sufficient alone

The decisive row changes the matcher's job. With a number on the record, the question is not "are these two the same person?" but "does this number already point somewhere?" — a lookup. The scored signals below are then for the rows the number cannot resolve: legacy records predating the numbering, records where the number is illegible, and people who were never issued one. At thousands of rows (D-056) this split is what makes D-004 affordable: the numbered rows are the trustworthy set and the rest is a work queue.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Applied before comparison, and the normalised form is stored so matching is reproducible:

  • Unicode NFKD, strip diacritics, casefold, collapse whitespace.
  • Common nickname/legal-name equivalences (configurable per locale — Jan/Jano, Josef/Josip).
  • Typo distance (Levenshtein/Jaro-Winkler) above a threshold counts as a partial match, never a full one.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
• confidence < 0.60 — not surfaced. Stored only for diagnostics.
  • 0.60 ≤ confidence < 0.90 — proposed, queued for human review.
  • confidence ≥ 0.90 — still requires human confirmation, but flagged as high priority. There is no auto-merge threshold.

No automatic merging at all, even for a near-certain match (D-004), and the rule does not need the premise that a merge cannot be undone — it can (§6). It rests on what the reversal cannot reach: the merged window stays one row's history, and the union of permissions is exercised from the moment the merge commits, whatever is discovered afterwards. A privacy incident from a bad merge is worse than any amount of manual review. The volume of the corpus — thousands of rows in two exports (D-092), most people rows carrying a number that makes the match a lookup rather than a judgement — is known, so no auto-merge tier is needed and none is reserved.

docs.title: The same signals at sign-up, split at the top of the band
docs.text:
A registration form collides with these signals too. A sign-up that strong-matches an existing person raises an identity_hypothesis and is then held out of active by it — an account may not reach active while an unresolved hypothesis names its person (D-089). The sign-up's own rows are created exactly as any sign-up creates them and stay pending_verification; what "creates nothing" rules out is the outcome — nothing is merged, nothing is linked, nothing is activated. The address the person typed stays on the pending account as the credential it was offered as, which matters because the reviewer's other answer is "this is a different person", and that answer should leave the applicant finishing the sign-up they started rather than starting it again (01a-accounts-and-contacts.md §4, 02-actors.md §3). Confirming the hypothesis merges the two rows under §5 and the pending account goes with the row that was absorbed; rejecting it lifts the gate and the account activates.

Here the threshold is not a tuning parameter, it is the entire answer. The band is split at its top, and only the top reaches the gate:

Signal at sign-up Raises a blocking hypothesis? Exact legacy member number yes Exact birth date and exact normalised name yes Birth date ±1 day, or year-only + name no Name-only fuzzy match, shared address, guardian name no

The soft band raises nothing at sign-up; the nightly matcher may still propose the pair for review, at a confidence that queues it rather than blocking anybody. The tempting rule, "raise one whenever the score is high", produces the failure this design would most deserve: a stranger's registration blocked by a fuzzy score. The cost of the version chosen is bounded and self-correcting (a true duplicate slips through, is matched nightly, and is reviewed); the cost of the tempting version is a child who cannot sign up for a camp on the day the form closes, which is not self-correcting at all.

Two obligations come with the gate, and neither is a queue-management nicety:

  • A hypothesis that is blocking an account gets an age check, and somebody reads it. Its victim is a specific person who cannot log in and whose only remaining channel is to telephone someone. The check is shaped like field_conflict's thirty days (08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §10); that a person opens it is the whole point of having it.
  • The holding message confirms nothing. It says the request was received and will be checked. It says nothing about whether the name, the birth date or the number matched anything, because a sign-up form that can answer "yes, that person exists" is an existence oracle, and this system's roster is children.

"I have a new e-mail address" is not this case and must not be routed through it: account_credential holds many credentials for one account, so a new address is an addition to the login a person already has. The collision case is narrower than signing up twice — it is a person arriving through a door the system did not know they had. Resolving the claim is confirming or rejecting a hypothesis, so it is person.merge, held by identity_reviewer (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §2); there is deliberately no account.link code, because an automatic link would be D-004 under another name.

docs.title: 5. The merge operation
docs.text:
Merging is a soft merge: the absorbed row survives as a tombstone.

person (surviving, id=100)          person (absorbed, id=847, tombstoned)
        ▲                                     │
        │                                     ▼
        └────────── person_merge ────► merged_into_person_id = 100
                 (id, surviving_person_id, merged_person_id,
                  merged_at, merged_by, hypothesis_id, reason)

docs.title: What moves
docs.text: Table Action person_contact Reassigned to survivor. Conflicts (two is_primary of the same type) resolved by review, not by rule. person_identifier Reassigned. Duplicate scheme+value collapses to one. person_attribute Reassigned. Two current values for one code is a review item, never a choice made by rule — this table holds one value per person and code with no validity period to keep both, so unlike two past addresses a merge cannot leave the pair standing: the pair is raised as a field_conflict and a human decides, exactly as two is_primary contacts of one type are decided. Where the definition allows several values (allow_multiple), the two rows simply coexist and nothing is decided (../data-model/09-attributes.md §3). person_name Reassigned, keeping validity periods — this is how a maiden name survives. account Reassigned to survivor. If the survivor already has an account, the absorbed account is closed, not deleted. membership Reassigned. Overlapping periods flagged for review — with one type (D-037) and a person-level no-overlap rule, an overlap here means a bad merge. An imported period can produce one too: the source states its own periods and nothing in the file knows that one human appears on two rows. Two imported periods covering the same date are outside the exclusion constraint — it watches the live statuses only — so the merge review is where they surface, and the honest reading of a pair is "the source said this", not "somebody decided this". person_group_member Reassigned, with the same overlap check. Two rows for one person in one group over overlapping dates is a review item and not a dedupe: two people who turn out to be one may genuinely have been put in the group twice, on different evidence, and the honest repair is one row whose dates a person chose. role_holder Reassigned. An office held twice by one person over overlapping periods is the same review case, with the same refusal to guess silently — and it is read out loud rather than filed quietly, because this table's rows are exactly what ROLE(x) reaches, so a duplicate holder row is a duplicate audience member. guardianship (as dependent) Reassigned. guardianship (as guardian) Reassigned. access_grant Reassigned. Union of permissions results — this is the security-critical step. Merging two people silently merges two sets of authority, and since D-099 that union is literally the rows both people leave behind: no rank resolves a collision, so a deny on the absorbed row survives alongside the survivor's allows rather than being deduplicated away, which is the outcome to read out loud at review. audience_operand, where selector_kind is PERSON Repointed, not reassigned. Every hand-named person in the system is a selector_arg_id — a column with deliberately no foreign key (D-011), which is why this row is a requirement on the merge and not something the database notices (D-105). The failure is asymmetric and it is the loud one: a leaf that resolves to nobody is the empty set, so a grant reading EVERYONE - PERSON(x) where x was merged away stops subtracting anybody and denies everybody. An orphan scan is the backstop; the merge is the mechanism. The same walk covers the other four argument kinds — an absorbed person_group, a deleted role, an event, a nested audience — because none of them has a key either person_merge Row inserted here. field_conflict Populated for anything that could not be resolved automatically.

docs.title: What does not happen
docs.text:
• Nothing is deleted. The absorbed person row keeps its id and gains merged_into_person_id. All historical foreign keys pointing at it still resolve, so a question about who belonged to something in 1998 keeps working.
  • Overlapping memberships are never silently deduplicated. Two overlapping memberships after a merge is suspicious — it may mean the merge was wrong. It becomes a review item.

docs.title: The cycle is refused here, not at the read
docs.text:
Chains are permanent (§6): merged_into_person_id is never rewritten forward, so A→B→C stays a chain and resolve_person() walks it. A chain that loops would make that walk never end, so a merge is refused when the person chosen as survivor resolves — by walking the chain — to the person being absorbed (D-087). That subsumes the case already ruled out, nobody merges into themselves, and catches the one that actually happens: absorbing B into A when A has already been absorbed into B.

Checking on the way in is the whole guard, and a read-side step limit is not an acceptable substitute. A hop bound does not prevent the cycle; its only achievement is deciding which of two wrong answers to return, and the wrong answer it returns is a tombstoned id — the exact failure resolve_person() exists to prevent.

The other half of the same rule is softer and needs a net under it. "Every place that accepts a person id from outside must call resolve_person()" is a rule application code can forget, and the schema carries no way to catch it (D-072). What catches it is a report of live rows that reference a tombstoned person, which is the only form of this failure that is visible after the fact (../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §10).

docs.title: The security rule that must not be skipped
docs.text:
Merging unions the two people's permissions. If a bad merge is performed, the survivor gains the absorbed person's access. Therefore:

  1. A merge is always performed by a human with person.merge permission.
  2. The merged result's effective permissions are re-displayed for confirmation before the merge commits.
  3. A merge can be undone (§6). The merged period cannot: access_grant rows created during it cannot be attributed to either human. Hence rule 2 — an unmerge repairs the record afterwards and does not repair this.
  4. Nothing is invalidated by a merge, because nothing is stored that a merge could invalidate: no row maps a person to an answer (D-114), and a merge is not a write that bumps the ruleset version. What the merge does to an answer is what the next check computes, from the survivor's grant rows and the PERSON(x) leaves the merge repointed. That is the same fact that makes rule 2 load-bearing rather than courteous: with nothing stored, the re-displayed effective permissions are the only place the merged answer is computed before the merge commits. See 06-authorization-model.md §8.

docs.title: 6. Reversing a merge
docs.text:
Unmerge is a required operation, not a courtesy for mistakes an organization hopes it will not make (D-087). It is also why merge chains exist: over a chain a reversal is a replay of pointers, while over a flattened pointer it would be a reconstruction of facts nobody recorded. Flattening is therefore closed off, not merely slower — it is a trade against a named feature, not against tidiness.

A permanent chain needs two rules, and neither is enforced on the read:

  • No cycle, checked at the merge (§5). Resolution deliberately has no hop limit.
  • Chain length is a signal, not an error. Resolution is unbounded; a chain longer than three hops is reported. Four merges in a row on one line of people does not mean the row is odd — it means the matcher is producing duplicates faster than a human can settle them, which is a statement about the queue and not about the row. A survivor that has itself been absorbed is normal; only the length means anything (../data-model/08a-event-guards-and-checks.md §10).

The reversal is four steps, and they restore the row split:

  1. Clear person.merged_into_person_id on the absorbed row. The tombstone comes off.
  2. Reassign rows created before merged_at back to the absorbed person.
  3. Flag rows created after merged_at for human review. Those are the ambiguous ones, and they are reviewed rather than split by a rule.
  4. Record the unmerge on the person_merge row as reversed_at, reversed_by and reversal_note. person_merge is append-only, so an unmerge records that a merge was undone rather than erasing the record of the mistake.

The access_grant rows are the specific hazard. Any grant created during the merged window might belong to either human. Flag every one of them; do not guess.

The asymmetry, stated plainly: the merge is reversible and the merged window is not. Steps 1, 2 and 4 repair the record. Step 3 is an admission. Whatever those two humans did while they were one row stays one row's history, because the grants exercised in that window were really exercised by somebody the record can no longer separate — which is precisely why the confirmation-before-commit rule in §5 is not made redundant by the existence of a reversal.

Unmerge needs no permission code of its own. Undoing an identity correction is the same act as making one, performed by a named human, so it is person.merge (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §2). A person.unmerge code would grade undoing a mistake as safer than making one. Like the merge, the reversal splits a person's permissions back in two, and there is nothing to invalidate: the split is simply visible on the next check.

docs.title: 7. Legacy import pipeline
docs.text:
Staged, reviewed, idempotent. Never a direct write into live tables.

What is arriving is two exports, and neither is a roster (D-092). A roster is evidence of presence in a unit, which is not what the source says. The source says two things:

Half What a row says What the batch writes The membership export a name, a birth date, and when that person was a member of the organization a person, and a bounded membership — both ends dated, data_confidence = 'low', batch id on it (D-093) The attendance export an event, and who came to it an event, and one event_registration per attendee at attending / was_present = true (D-094)

Neither names a sub-unit, and nothing is assigned to one. The parser keeps its parsed unit code — an export that surprises whoever runs it with a unit column is exactly what that field and its unit_not_found warning are for, and keeping them costs nothing — but nothing reads them, no org_unit is created by any batch, and no sub-unit participation row is ever imported. Two halves also means two shapes of batch on one import_batch: a people batch and an events batch, each carrying the field map and the checks that fit its half, rather than one batch holding two mappers that can never both apply.

Say where it hurts, because somebody will ask this question. The historical record this import leaves behind contains no sub-units. "Who was in Pack 12 in 2011?" has no answer at go-live — not a wrong one, none — and the first answer anyone reads will be a roster somebody typed in by hand. Nothing in the model is missing: it is what the source can say, and it is written here so that the first person to ask finds the sentence rather than the absence.

  source file(s)
       │
       ▼
  [1] staging_import          ── raw rows, verbatim, with the source file + line ref
       │
       ▼
  [2] staging_import_row      ── parsed: normalised name, parsed birth date,
       │                          detected unit, parse warnings
       ▼
  [3] matching                ── for each row, find candidate person rows and score them
       │
       ▼
  [4] review queue            ── human confirms: link to existing | create new | discard
       │
       ▼
  [5] apply                   ── a people batch writes person + bounded membership; an events
       │                          batch writes event + event_registration. Never an org_unit,
       │                          never a sub-unit participation row, never an open-ended
       │                          membership
       │
       ▼
  [6] import_log              ── what was applied, by whom, when; reversal instructions

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Idempotent. Re-running the same import must not duplicate people. Each staged row carries a deterministic source_row_hash; re-import matches on it.
  • Reversible per batch. import_log records every row created or modified in a batch, so a bad batch can be rolled back without touching other data.
  • Never overwrites self-registered data. If a legacy row matches a self_registered person, the import may add what the export evidences — a bounded historical membership period, a registration on an imported event — but never alters names, contacts, identifiers, or descriptive values the person maintains themselves. An added closed period contradicts nothing the person typed: it is a dated claim about the past, sitting beside their live row rather than over it. An open-ended period would be a different thing entirely, which is why the surviving ban is exactly that one.
  • Preserves provenance. Every imported row records import_batch_id and source_reference (file + line), so any value can be traced back to the paper it came from. When someone disputes a historical record, you can show them where it came from.
  • Records uncertainty rather than guessing. A row that cannot be parsed cleanly goes to the review queue with the raw value intact — it does not get a best-effort guess written as if it were fact.

docs.title: Raw columns become codes
docs.text:
Old rosters carry columns about the person — a remarks column, a "medical" column, a list of shirt sizes — and each of those arrives at step [5] as a value against a code, not as a blob beside the record (D-084). Those columns are in the membership export; the attendance export brings nothing that maps to an attribute code (D-090). The map therefore belongs to the people batch and a code-to-registration map to the events batch: one batch, one map. That makes the first import the single largest event in the life of this vocabulary — several hundred codes out of one file. The rest of the rules live in staging (../data-model/09-attributes.md §7); three consequences follow from arriving all at once.

  • The map is authored and read before the batch applies, not after. The mapping is recorded on the batch as one object rather than per staged row because it is one artefact a person reads once, top to bottom, and the reading is what makes the codes it names trustworthy. Reading it afterwards would put the live vocabulary at the mercy of whatever the batch had already written. Changing an applied map is curation with an audit entry, not a migration.
  • A raw column that maps to no code stops the batch, unless someone maps it or marks it discarded with a reason. An unmapped column is a decade of something the organization used to collect vanishing quietly.
  • A column nobody recognises stops the batch, and it never becomes a code named from the column header either. A value may not invent a code, and a column may not borrow one by similarity: an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable, and the review queue above is for people, not for vocabulary (D-141). Every code the map names is already defined and live before the batch applies, or the batch refuses — which is not a trap but the actual shape of this event: the map is authored and read top to bottom as one artefact, so whoever wrote the map wrote the vocabulary first, and the endorsement the old proposed status was invented to express is now simply having held the permission while reading the list. The cost is the first few hundred definitions being a writing job under attribute.define that must happen before the import that looks like it produces them. Who holds attribute.define day to day, and who writes that vocabulary before the first batch, is open and is the shape the answer has to take — a permission and a named person, not a queue (AT-2, and the new F-34).

docs.title: What each source row lands on
docs.text:
What the source says It becomes Why "Jan Novák, born 1962, member 1990–1995" a person with record_origin = 'legacy_import', and one membership per period the source states — valid_from and valid_to set, data_confidence = 'low', import_batch_id set, the renewal chain left to whoever reconstructs it A stated period is evidence of membership and infers nothing; a closed period cannot gate anything (D-093) the same, with the year repeated in the file a second membership only if the source states a second period; consecutive stated years stretch to one row, a gap in the source opens another One row per stated period keeps one row per membership, and a lapse stays visible in the one table that means it an event, and who came to it an event with no owner column at all, one event_registration per attendee at attending with was_present = true, and the twelve per-event grants an event create would have written Nothing owns an event: its people are named by selectors that bind to it (D-102) a person who might have come and did not nothing An export lists who came. Writing not_attending from silence puts words in a source that said nothing (D-059) a sub-unit nothing, ever — and there is now nothing that could be one The corpus names none (§7) and there is no structure to attach a name to. The row stays because it is the one a reader holding a 1998 spreadsheet will ask, and the answer has to be written down rather than inferred from absence money nothing — and no fee_obligation The corpus has no money in it (D-090)

The ban is one sentence, and it is the whole point: never an open-ended membership, and never one inferred from an attendance row. is_current_member() and the permission gate (D-039) both read membership, so a row running to no valid_to hands whoever signs up under that name authority in the present. The ban is sized for what it now guards: one reviewed batch whose map is read before it applies, on a corpus that will never arrive twice.

The line the whole design turns on is evidence against inference. A row that says member 1990–1995 is evidence of a membership; a row that says in Pack 12 in 1998 is evidence of presence and nothing more. Generating a membership for every historical row because the old data model implied it, and then marking it inferred, is the refusal that stands. A related observation worth keeping in front of anybody implementing this: a conditional with one live arm is not a safe default — wording of the form "X unless there is payment evidence", on a corpus that carries no payment data at all, leaves an arm with an empty set to fire on while still inviting somebody to build it.

Four consequences that arrive with the memberships.

  • No obligation, no payment, no balance. An imported membership creates no fee_obligation, and that has to be a rule rather than an accident: an obligation per historical year would land as unpaid and turn a decade of members into a wall of debt with a 1999 due_date for the lapse sweep to choke on. Related, and load-bearing rather than incidental: outstanding_balance is null on these rows — a zero would be a claim of settled that no export supports.
  • The person-level no-overlap rule is in the import's path. One row per period the source states, not one per calendar year, is a rule with a consequence: two stated periods covering one date violate it and reach the review queue (§5).
  • These rows are the oldest layer of the skeleton D-088 keeps forever (D-088): thousands of named people with birth dates who were never asked and never used the system, held on an unverified legal basis. Same judgement as for live rows, much larger population.
  • Every cross-decade member count is a mixture of an export and a register, distinguished only by data_confidence and import_batch_id. A membership-rate chart spanning the import boundary compares a source that states membership with a system that records it, and nothing in the query knows the difference.

A historical membership is also obtainable as a human act. Where the organization has a period the export does not state — a ledger found later, a written confirmation, a person who was a member in a year the file lost — the period is entered by hand under membership.backdate (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §4). The pipeline carries the stated ones; this is the route for the unstated: deliberate, attributed, outside the batch.

End dates are still often unknown, and this is the sharpest case of it. A period the export leaves open — someone last seen in a 2003 row with no end stated — cannot be written open: that is the one shape refused outright, and an unbounded historical record is the same hazard wearing a different name. Convention: end it at the end of the school/organizational year of the last row they appear in, marked as inferred. That is the only date the import infers — the periods themselves are stated — and it is precisely what the organizational year boundary is needed for, which is still open (A-4). With attendance and no money in the corpus, it is the sharpest remaining import question. Document the rule you choose; it will be questioned.

docs.title: 8. The returning-member case
docs.text:
The scenario member 1990–2010, returns 2024, should be the smooth path, because it is a common and important one (returning alumni become adult leaders and donors).

Flow:

  1. Person registers in 2024, self-asserting past membership.
  2. The system matches them against legacy rows and proposes hypotheses.
  3. A registrar reviews and confirms.
  4. The historical membership (1990–2010) and the current membership (2024–present) now sit under one person row, as two membership rows.
  5. Their profile shows their full history; the gap is explicit data.
  6. Any seniority or "years of service" calculation reads across both.

A 1990–2010 membership appears only where the source states the period or somebody records it by hand on evidence (membership.backdate, §7). The smooth path restores a person's member history without a human typing it, and what makes that safe is that the source states the period rather than the import guessing one.

Steps 2–3 can be streamlined when the match is strong (exact old membership number), but the confirmation step remains, for the reason in §3.

What the activation gate costs this path. The gate does not distinguish why a hypothesis exists: an account may not reach active while an unresolved hypothesis names its person, and a self-asserted claim names that person exactly as a collision does. So the smooth path has a human between registration and login, where the review could otherwise happen after the person was already using the system. The mitigation is the age check that gets read (§4), plus the fact that with a legacy number in hand step 2 is a lookup a registrar settles in seconds. What is not settled is whether a hypothesis the person raised about themselves should hold their account out of active at all, as against a hypothesis the system raised about a stranger who happened to match. Recorded in §9.

docs.title: Self-service without weakening the guarantee
docs.text: Rather than auto-linking, give the person a claim flow: they assert a past membership, staff confirm. Record the assertion on the hypothesis row, so that if the claim later proves false, you can see it was self-asserted rather than discovered.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
Still open, and tracked in ../open-questions.md:

  • Whether twins/siblings with similar names and the same birth date need a documented disambiguation procedure (recommend: yes, and never merge them automatically). The sign-up gate in §4 sharpens this: same birth date plus a normalised name is exactly the collision pair, and a collision now stops a registration instead of merely queueing a card.
  • Whether a hypothesis a person raised about themselves should hold their account out of active, as against one the system raised because a stranger's sign-up strong-matched them (§8).
  • The organizational year boundary that historical end dates get inferred from (A-4). With stated membership periods, attendance, and no money (§7) it is load-bearing by itself, and the inferred date closes a membership row, so the number of rows it touches is large.
  • Whether indefinite retention of named membership and fee rows has a legal basis. The design keeps that skeleton indefinitely as the organization's own history while audit payloads are emptied after 24 months (D-088); a decision log cannot grant the basis, so it is recorded as an assumption awaiting review.

Decisions behind this page: D-004, D-011, D-037, D-038, D-039, D-056, D-057, D-059, D-072, D-084, D-085, D-087, D-088, D-089, D-090, D-092, D-093, D-094, D-097, D-099, D-102, D-105, D-114.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
One organization, and the named sets of people inside it.

The vocabulary, first, because everything here leans on it.

Word Means Stored as unit the organization itself. There is exactly one. It is a scope, never a row nothing — a code in grant_scope_type group a named set of people with explicitly dated members and a lifetime. A set, not a body person_group + person_group_member role an office: a small, visible set of holders — leaders, finance, IT role + role_holder audience an expression over named sets, which a grant is aimed at audience selector one operand of that expression: MEMBERS, GROUP(x), ROLE(x), … selector_type, audience_operand

Roles and audiences belong to the authorization model (06-authorization-model.md, ../data-model/05-authorization.md) and are not re-specified here. This page owns the unit and the group.

docs.title: 1. The organization is one unit, and the unit is a scope
docs.text:
There is one unit and it is the organization. It has no parent, no children, no type, no code, no path, no depth, and no row. It is the non-item scope that grant_scope_type already carries — code unit, is_item_scoped = false — and a grant written at it has no scope_id. Nothing in the schema represents it, because there is nothing to represent: a second unit cannot appear, for the same reason a second answer to a question cannot appear in a field that does not exist.

Membership is unchanged and is not a group. One membership per person, at the unit, paid for yearly:

  • "everyone in the organization" is one query against membership;
  • "everyone in the Thursday group" is one query against person_group_member.

Two shapes, and neither one borrows the other's table. Renewal opens a new membership row rather than extending the old one (D-016).

A grant at the unit reaches everything — every item of every type — because nothing stands between the unit and an item and there is no ownership relation to test. That is a sentence about the permission system; it is stated here only because it is what "scope" means now that "row" does not.

Why the design carries no hierarchy: the legacy corpus names no units at all — two exports, people with their membership period and events with attendance, no unit column anywhere (D-092) — and a structure that describes nothing imported and restricts nothing carries no information (D-097).

docs.title: What that costs, said once
docs.text:
These are properties the hierarchy was carrying, listed here rather than distributed through the page. They are not argued away.

  1. The unit is not a locus of accountability for a child's records. This is the one that matters. Nothing in the model reproduces "access to a body's children was granted by that body" — by the people who know them, who recruited its leader, and who can be asked. With one unit there is no "outside it" to be stopped from, so the rule has no subject rather than a weaker form. A permission held at the unit reaches every member, and person.view is the widest read permission in the system (D-083, D-086). What stands between a child and a stranger's read is a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write.
  2. There is no subtree question. "Who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" stays answerable, because group member rows are dated (§5). "And everything nested under it" has no subject: a set of people has no sub-sets stored inside it.
  3. Restructuring is not a recorded event. A group that splits is an old group that ended and two that began, with no edge between them — and no table where such an edge could go (§4).
  4. Unit-scoped reports have nothing to report on. "A pack's roster", "a pack's events", "which units exist" are not hard questions, they are questions with no subject. The organizational-year reports that matter — membership and fees — live at the unit and are untouched.

One invariant class lost its only named instance here: shape 4 of the invariant register — a column that may not change once set, whose violation leaves every row individually valid — and parent_unit_id was the only member anybody had pointed at. Empty and unnamed are two different claims, and D-131 found the shape had six members, and round 20 made it seven: this deletion removed one of them, not the class.

It is not a two-way door. This is the deletion of a dimension, not a flag. Adding structure back is a decision with a reason attached — most plausibly "the organization has outgrown one center's visibility" — and it would have to argue the accountability rule from its own premises, because the mechanism that made it work — a scope written by the body it covered — does not exist.

docs.title: 2. What a group is, and everything a group is not
docs.text:
A group is a person_group: a name, a description, its own lifetime, and explicitly dated members. It is a set of people, not a body. Somebody names it, somebody puts people in it, somebody ends it, and the record of who was in it when is the roster's own (§5). A weekly meeting group, a project crew, a trainers' pool, schuzka2026-1 — all the same kind of thing, and the system has no opinion about which ones deserve to exist. A person may be on several rosters at once; none of them is marked as the one to show first.

Everything a body would have had, a group does not have.

A group has Because no parent and no children there are no sub-units, and groups do not nest no type, and no vocabulary of types a group needs no word for what kind of set it is no code, no path, no depth a label carries no identity (§4); a set has no position to sit at no nesting rules there is nothing to nest no rename history the name is a column, and the old name is not kept (§4) no split, merger or succession edge restructuring is not an event (§1, cost 3) no leadership of its own see §6 no roles an office is a role and a role is held at the unit; a group has none of its own, and no leadership column will be added to make one look derivable no fee membership is at the unit and is the only thing that costs money no permissions over its members see immediately below

Membership of a group confers nothing, and tidier storage does not quietly change that. A member of a group cannot do anything: participation is not authority, and it stays not-authority when it moves into a table with better columns. Authority arrives only through a grant that names the group, which is §4 of ../data-model/02-organization.md.

Where the line against an audience is drawn — the two are one row apart in shape and a mile apart in meaning: a group states its members, a selector picks them. A group's members are a list of people that is true whether or not any permission points at it. A leaf in an audience — a PERSON(y) row (D-105) — is an addition to an expression, meaningful only inside the expression it completes. A group exists to be talked about; a selector exists to be aimed at something. Merging them would make the permission table the system's roster.

Where the line against a role is drawn, in one sentence, because it decides who may edit the list. A role is an office with a small, visible set of holders and is written by the most sensitive code family in the catalog (role.*, 🔒🔒); a group is company, and its roster is written by person_group.member.manage (⚠). One table with a kind column would give a single permission that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder among the administrators (D-100). GROUP(x) and ROLE(x) stay distinct in the grant text so the distinction is visible to whoever reads the grant.

docs.title: 3. Joining a group is somebody else's act
docs.text:
Nobody writes themselves onto a roster.
