The gate is person_group.member.manage, held at the unit — which reaches every group, because nothing stands between a unit-scope grant and an item — or granted on one group as an item, which is how "these two people may work this roster" is said without inventing a scope (D-098, D-099). There is no self-scoped variant and none will be added.

Who enforces "do not place a child where nobody is responsible for them": whoever may write the member row in person_group_member, audited and naming who wrote it. A permission refuses every write by the wrong person regardless of the child's age (D-081).

What that costs. The system cannot say which groups are for children. Nothing on a person_group answers that question and, consistent with "no special features", nothing will: no allows_minors, no is_children, no type to hang it on. Combined with no recorded background checks (D-043) and with cost 1 above, the safeguarding story of this module is a permission held by named adults, an audit trail that forgets values after two years, and a report. If that turns out to be too little — after an incident, or an insurer's question — the route back is a rule about who may be placed where, argued once as a decision with its enforcement layer named in D-081's terms, and not a resurrected column whose name implies it enforces something.

A membership request is a request for membership of the unit, and carries no group. There is no requested_unit_id on a request: which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request. The request flow in 05-membership-lifecycle.md ends at the unit; a roster is somebody else's decision afterwards.

docs.title: 4. A name carries no identity
docs.text:
A group name is a label, and a label is not the group: a group name that comes back after a decade is a new group, unless somebody records that it is not.

Why the default matters: continuity is not a property of a label, it is a claim about the world, and only a human knows whether the crew refounded in 2026 is the crew of 2016. Left unstated, the question is answered anyway — by whoever writes the matching screen, who will match on name and let a thirty-year gap sit inside one group's life. So the default points at a new person_group row. A rename is an edit to one column and the previous name is not kept (§2).

The continuity claim has nowhere to live. Groups keep no group-to-group edges — no split, no merger, no succession — so an assertion of continuity has no field to hold it (D-098). What the method guarantees is therefore the direction of the default, which is the half that was ever enforceable: a returning name is a new group, and two groups that are really one look like two unless a person writes that down somewhere. Where that sentence goes is not decided. The cheapest true answer available today is a note on the second group's member rows and on the group's description, which nothing reads and nothing links; the honest alternative is to accept that the organization's memory of its own continuity is prose. Status: assumption — this page does not choose, and the question is recorded in ../open-questions.md.

Names are one namespace with roles and audiences. Because ROLE(x) and GROUP(x) do not have to disambiguate, a bare COUNSELORS resolves against roles and groups together, so names are unique across the tables, case/whitespace/separators are folded on write, and every selector_type.code is a reserved name — a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system (D-101). audience.code is in the namespace too (D-103), and the pair of rules is worth holding apart: a bare name never resolves to an audience — the arm must be written AUDIENCE(veterans) — yet a group still may not borrow an audience's code, because a name that resolves two ways is a silent grant whatever the resolution rules say. No single constraint spans the three tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts that it does. What a grant stores is kind + id, never a name, so renaming a group never rewrites a grant. Mechanics: ../data-model/02-organization.md §1.

docs.title: 5. A roster is history
docs.text:
Member rows are dated, and that is what makes the roster answerable. person_group_member carries valid_from and valid_to per person, so joining, leaving and coming back are all periods on the same pair, and the roster has a history of its own instead of borrowing the audit trail's. "Who was in schuzka2026-1 on 14 March 2026?" is a point-in-time read over those rows. It survives the audit trail's 24-month payload expiry (D-088) because it does not depend on the trail — which is the entire reason the rows are dated rather than a live flag, and the reason a naming habit like schuzka2026-1 is a habit an organization may or may not keep rather than the mechanism history rests on.

This is where a group is ahead of the operand that looks most like it. An audience named as an operand evaluates live, so its past shape survives only in the audit trail and stops surviving when the payloads expire; a group's set is its dated rows, so it keeps a past the audit trail cannot take away. "Who could see this child's data in 2024?" is answerable when the grant pointed at a group and is not answerable when it pointed at a nested audience (D-103). That asymmetry is a fact about which of the two is a roster, and it is the strongest reason the pair stays two tables.

Two facts, both kept, and not to be conflated. The group's valid_from/valid_to says the group existed over that span; the member rows' periods say who was in it. An open group with dated members answers the historical question perfectly well, and an ended group's rows are not tidied up. Ending the group is not an edit anyone makes on their own: setting that end date is refused while a live grant, or a live audience reachable from one, names the group, because an empty set inside a subtraction widens a deny that the person ending the group did not write and would not look at again (the write path and the checks that watch it are ../data-model/02-organization.md §3).

A person who left in 2020 and came back in 2024 is two rows, never one row edited in place, because the edit destroys the answer to "was she in the group in 2019?" (D-016, D-002).

Moving from one group to another closes one row and opens another: never rewrite a member row to point at a different group. Rewriting destroys "where was this child in 2003?", and unlike most tempting edits this one leaves no evidence that anything happened. Mechanics: ../data-model/02-organization.md §4.

No member row is ever inferred. The corpus names no groups any more than it names units (D-092), so the one-off import owes no group rows and no member rows at all: every person_group_member row in this system is typed by a person, which is also the only way one could be true.

docs.title: 6. Appointments
docs.text:
An appointment is a role_holder row: a role, a person, a period, who granted it, a note. Written by role.assign and removed by role.unassign, always held at the unit, because there is one scope and nowhere else to hold an office. The role it names is one the organization wrote — no office ships, and day one is one account holding system.admin (D-150). It confers nothing by itself: the codes an office carries are the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) (../data-model/05-authorization.md §3–§4). "That these two may manage the counselors roster" is a grant on the role, the same move a group gets. There is no position, no slot, no max_holders, and no is_leadership flag: nothing in the system records a seat that exists unfilled.

And nothing records how the person came to hold it (D-136). Elected at an AGM for a two-year term, handed over by the departing treasurer, filled by whoever the committee asked: the row says none of this, and no column will be added to make it say so. An election is an event in the world that this organization runs somewhere else — nominations, a ballot, a quorum, minutes — and what arrives here is the outcome: one holder row, two dates, and note for whoever wants the reason beside the fact. granted_by does not settle the question and never claimed to; it names the person who wrote the row, which for an election is a secretary recording a result rather than a mandate.

Why the obvious additions were refused. A flag — elected or appointed — would make the distinction queryable and would guard nothing, and a field that looks like a control where none is wanted is worse than the absence, because it invites someone to rely on it. A table of elections would describe a process this system does not run and does not hold, on the same ground D-043 refused to be a registry of everything true about a volunteer. And the distinction has nowhere to bite anyway: an office confers nothing by being held, as this section's first paragraph says, so there is no dangerous thing for an election to confer and no answer anywhere in the resolver that would change if a row knew how its holder arrived.

The cost, stated plainly because it is real: nothing here will ever refuse to appoint someone to an office the bylaws reserve for a vote. That rule lives in the bylaws and in the people reading them, and it is one of this module's standing conventions rather than a gap it means to close.

This module holds no eligibility rule of any kind. There is no requires_membership and no min_age on an office, and no gate in the resolver: membership is an operand, written into the grant.

The expression that says each thing, in the form D-101's canonical rendering stores it — every compound operand bracketed, a leaf left bare:

The rule to express The expression the office applies only to current members (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) the office applies whether or not the holder is a member ROLE(x), written without MEMBERS one named person is exempt from the membership requirement (MEMBERS * ROLE(x)) + PERSON(y)

PERSON(y) is the only way to name a human being in an expression. A set of named people is written PERSON(a) + PERSON(b), and there is no second spelling of it (D-105). A person who must be excepted is subtracted as themselves, and the exemption belongs + PERSON(y) inside the very grant that carries the rule, so the exception is read next to the thing it exempts. The registry of named operands lives in one table — the selector registry — and this page does not recite its row count.

The posture is opt-in per grant, so a grant written as ROLE(TREASURERS) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member silently and forever. The controls are a standing report of live grants that name a ROLE(...) operand without MEMBERS, and an import count — not the resolver. The only grants this system writes for itself are the twelve beside an event, they name ORGANIZERS rather than a ROLE(...), and they carry no MEMBERS on purpose (D-151). Nothing forces a holder row to end either; the report is the control (D-071). All of that belongs to the authorization model and is named here only because these were this module's workflows: 06-authorization-model.md.

Three consequences, stated plainly.

  • "The leader of the Thursday group" has no referent. A group has no leadership and no roles (§2), so the sentence means a person on that roster who also holds some office, and nothing links the two. The office is ROLE(leaders) and means what its name says.
  • Elected versus appointed is not stored data. It survives only as roles the organization invents (elected_council beside appointed_it) — or not at all.
  • A vacancy is not a reportable state. "This seat has been empty since March" needs a slot that exists unfilled. An empty office is the absence of rows in role_holder, and absence has no start date on the office. A rule-filled role stays refused: F-12's answer is no, role_holder names one person, because an office record that cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023" is not an office record (F-12).

docs.title: 7. The module and the permission system, in one table
docs.text:
Stated once here so that nothing below the line is re-specified in this page's voice. Full detail: 06-authorization-model.md and ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

Question Answer Owner Where is authority held? at the unit, or on exactly one item — nothing in between D-097, D-099 What is a group to the resolver? an item in grant_scope_type, and a GROUP(x) leaf in an expression D-098, D-101 Does being in a group grant anything? no. A set is not a grant D-005, D-098, D-102 for ORGANIZERS What may a role do? read the live grants whose expression names ROLE(x) — a role confers nothing D-100 How is precedence decided? allowed iff some live allow applies and no live deny applies. There is no level and no locality D-099 Does a unit-scope grant reach an item? yes, every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item only D-099, D-102 Is there a membership gate in the resolver? no. MEMBERS is an operand, evaluated live on the checked date D-100 Can the center be locked out of a body's data? the question has no subject: there is one body and its people are the only people there are D-097

There is no ancestor walk, because there is no tree: no unit_ancestors(), no unit_descendants(), no path-consistency check. The permission check matches scope exactly — the unit, or the item.

docs.title: 8. Open issues
docs.text:
Open, and tracked in ../open-questions.md:

  • Where a claimed group continuity is recorded. The method says continuity is asserted, never matched (§4); no table accepts the assertion. Until somebody rules, the default is the whole rule: a returning name is a new group.
  • Whether a group's previous name should be kept at all. It is not, deliberately, as part of "no special features". If the organization turns out to rename groups often, the answer is a decision and not a column someone adds quietly.
  • Whether an ended group should be hidden from pickers. A person_group with valid_to set has no stated behaviour either way yet.

Decisions behind this page: D-002, D-005, D-016, D-043, D-081, D-083, D-086, D-088, D-092, D-096, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-136, D-071.

docs.title: Membership Lifecycle
docs.text: Register → request → accept → pay → member. Plus the parts that are usually forgotten: gaps, returns, multiple periods, and renewal.

docs.title: 1. The flow you described
docs.text:
"The people can register on their own to get access to the system, however they become member only if they request a membership, they get accepted and pay a yearly fee."

Four distinct stages, each a separate record, because each can independently fail, stall, or be reversed:

Stage Record Can be reversed? What it means 1. Register person + account account can be closed "This person can log in." 2. Request membership_request yes — reject/withdraw "This person applied." 3. Accept membership_request.status = 'approved' yes — revoke before activation "The organization said yes." 4. Pay fee_obligation + payment refund "The obligation is met." 5. Activate membership opened yes — lapse/terminate "This person is a member."

Why stage 5 is separate from stage 3. Approval and activation are distinct because payment sits between them. A person can be approved and never pay; the organization needs to see that state ("approved, awaiting payment") to chase it, and it must not appear as a member.

Decided: membership activates on payment (D-040). membership opens at stage 5, and pending_payment is a real membership status so that "approved, awaiting payment" is a visible worklist rather than an invisible backlog.

docs.title: Two doors, one gate each
docs.text:
The flow above is one of two ways a person ends up in the organization's records, and for eight rounds this document wrote as if it were the only one. There are two entry paths and each has exactly one gate, with no third control anywhere (D-095, whose reasoning D-098 transfers to groups intact — joining one is still somebody else's act):

Membership of the unit A group How you get in You pay. Stages 1–5 above are this door, and it is the only self-service entry in the system — it opens a membership and nothing beside it Somebody else writes a person_group_member row What stops you The fee person_group.member.manage, held at the unit — which reaches every group — or granted on one group as an item Money The yearly fee Nothing

Nobody writes themselves into a group. The people who run a group add people to it; that is the whole of the rule, and it is carried by a permission rather than by a workflow. person_group.member.manage has no self-scoped variant and none will be added — a grant is always "over this group's roster", never "over my own", so the shape of request that would let a person place themselves is not refused by a check, it is not expressible. The same holds for offices: nobody appoints themselves, and the catalog holds no code that could say otherwise (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §5).

No fee below the membership, and no model wants one. The fee is the organization's; joining a group carries no money — "into the sub-units, there is no fee, it is entirely managed by the organization, including adding more members." That was said about units and it transfers unchanged, a group being among the things listed as having no fee (D-098). Putting a fee on a member row would immediately ask who sets the amount, who chases it, and what happens to a child whose family cannot pay a group's arrears, and none of those questions exist in the corpus or in any answer given. That is a refused model, not an unasked one.

What the asymmetry costs. The group door has no membership check behind it — a counselor may add somebody who is not a member, and nothing in the write stops them, because D-095 refuses a third gate as firmly as it refuses the first two. What keeps that person from reading anything is MEMBERS in the grants that matter — the test D-039 was, now carried in the grant text rather than the resolver (D-100) — which is what that test was always for. A group membership is a fact about belonging, not a credential: a member of a group can do nothing by being one, and the tidier table does not quietly promote it (D-098). The other cost is directional and appears in the other direction at import: the membership door is the only place a person's own initiative can produce a record, which is why the legacy corpus could be matched against people and never against groups (domain/03 §7).

And one cost is new, named where D-097 names it. Under the deleted hierarchy, access to a body's children had to be granted by that body, by people who recruited its leader and can be asked. A group's roster write is the same shape of permission and may be held at the unit, where it reaches every group in the organization, so what is left of the safeguarding story is a permission held by a named adult, an audit trail whose recorded values expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write — minus the part where the named adult was somebody the body chose. Nothing in the remaining model reproduces that property, and this document says so rather than letting the reader infer it.

docs.title: 2. Membership request
docs.text:
A request records the person it is for and the membership type asked for, and nothing else. status is one of draft, submitted, under_review, approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired, and submitted_at says when it went in. The review is carried on the same row: who took it up, when they decided, and on a rejection a rejection_reason with a free-text rejection_note beside it. An approved request points at the membership it produced; the link is not optional once the approval exists.

A request asks for membership of the unit, and it names no group (D-098): there is no unit column on the request, because there is one unit and it is not a row (D-097). The want behind such a column is genuine — a reviewer would like to know where the applicant hopes to turn up — and it is served by the notes the row already carries: a sentence, carrying no authority. Which group a new member lands in is a write on the group, not a preference on the request: one person_group_member row, written by somebody holding person_group.member.manage (§1), in a separate act with its own permission and its own audit entry. An approved request that produced no group row is a complete, ordinary outcome.

docs.title: Why a request is not a membership with a status
docs.text:
Tempting to collapse them, but:

  • A request can be rejected, producing no membership at all. A membership row with status rejected would pollute every "list members" query forever.
  • A person may submit several requests over time (rejected in 2024, approved in 2025). One table for both would need a request-version column and every query would need to filter it.
  • Requests carry review data (who reviewed, why, what was checked) that has no meaning on a membership.
  • Requests have different permissions: submitting is self-service; reviewing is a staff capability.

docs.title: There are no request requirements
docs.text:
Removed entirely (D-044). A request is accepted on identity and payment alone: no blocking checklist, no evidence collection, no waiver workflow, no requirement_code and no membership_request_requirement table.

Your answer, asked what a request must contain to be accepted: "Just identity and the fee — nothing to verify." The option to keep the mechanism as empty infrastructure for later was offered and not taken, which is the right call — a checklist that is always empty is a checklist nobody maintains, and it would have implied a gate that does not exist.

What this does not weaken. Two things that look like requirements are unaffected, because neither was a membership requirement to begin with:

  • Guardian consent for a minor's account is a fact about the guardianship relation, held in guardianship_permission, not a box ticked during an application (data-model/04).
  • Who may hold an office — a scoutmaster must be an adult — was never a property of membership, and after D-100 it is not a stored property of the office either: position.min_age is deleted with positions and role carries no age column, so what remains is is_minor() in a report (§7). Membership is ageless (D-038).

And background checks do not exist in this system at all (D-043). If the organization introduces them, the home is a dated record with an expiry, and it belongs with the office rather than the membership gate — a lapsed check is a reason someone may not hold a role, not a reason they stop being a member. Which layer would hold it is unresolved: an office carries no eligibility fields at all (D-100), so nothing in the model holds that kind of rule today (§7 and §9).

docs.title: 3. Membership
docs.text: A membership row belongs to one person and one membership type, and carries a status of pending_payment, active, lapsed, terminated, completed or suspended — always chosen deliberately, never defaulted. The period is valid_from and valid_to, and an absent valid_to means the period is still open: it is the current membership, not a row someone forgot to close. joined_via_request_id records the request it came out of, termination_reason the reason it was ended, data_confidence is high, medium or low, and import_batch_id is set on imported rows and on nothing else. Both of those columns have a live writer: the legacy import writes membership rows. The export states a membership period directly rather than only attendance, so the batch writes one row per stated period — data_confidence = 'low', import_batch_id set, both ends dated (D-093, domain/03 §7), and status = 'completed', the value an imported closed period carries: none of the six means a source stated this and nobody in the system decided it, and completed is the second-worst of the two available readings, taken knowingly (D-162). An imported membership never runs open-ended to today, and none is inferred from an attendance row — the part carrying the weight, because an open membership satisfies is_current_member(), so an inferred one would make every 1998 roster a current member today. So data_confidence on this table has two live sources and they mean different things: on a backdated row it is a human's judgement (membership.backdate, attributed to whoever typed it), on an imported row it is the batch speaking for itself.

docs.title: Overlap rules — the invariant that matters
docs.text:
A person must not hold two open memberships at the same time, and the rule is enforced by the database rather than by application code. Its precise statement is in data-model/03-membership.md §3; what it says, in words:

  • Two membership periods of one person may not cover the same date while either of them is pending_payment, active or suspended. Those three statuses are the whole of the rule's reach — a lapsed row, a terminated one and a completed one are outside it, which is why an ending period and a later beginning one sit beside each other without complaint.
  • Periods are half-open, so a membership ending on 30 June and another opening on 30 June do not collide.

The constraint is scoped to the person, not to the person-and-type, because there is one membership type (D-037): the invariant is one person, one open membership, ever, and "am I a paid-up member?" is one row, one status, one date. It belongs to the person alone, not to any structure above them — the unit is a scope and not a row (D-097), so there is no per-body membership to add up.

This is the invariant the import writes against. Say exactly what fires, because the rule's reach is narrow: it watches the three live statuses, so what the exclusion constraint refuses at apply time is an imported period colliding with a live membership — an export period that runs into or past the person's current one, which an open-ended imported row would produce for thousands of people in one transaction. What it does not refuse is an overlap between two closed imported periods: the statuses are outside its reach by design, so a source file that double-books somebody across 1993 lands quietly, marked only as data_confidence = 'low'. That is the honest cost of the same decision that keeps a returning member's old period from gating anything today, and it is why the batch is reviewed before it applies rather than after.

Assumption: btree_gist is available (PostgreSQL), because a temporal overlap is the one rule that can only be refused during the write that would create it. If the target database cannot express exclusion constraints, the fallback is a check inside the writing transaction plus the nightly consistency report — one of the strongest guarantees in the model degrading into the weakest class (data-model/00 §6a, shape 1): an application-level count is wrong exactly when two writers run at once, which is when an overlap is actually created, and the report finds it a day later in a form nobody can attribute. So it is not merely "weaker" and must be recorded as an accepted risk, chosen deliberately, rather than discovered in a migration tool's limitations.

docs.title: There is one membership type, and membership is ageless
docs.text:
A type row is a code and a name, four calendar values, and a sort_order. The calendar values start at twelve months' duration, expiry_month 1 and expiry_day 1 — the fee expires on 1 January (D-047) — and renewal_grace_days 60, which is the renewal window and not a status (D-048).

Seeded with exactly one row, member (D-037). A type carries no eligibility rule of any kind — no age floor, no age ceiling, no consent flag, no background check, no fee of its own; the columns that once said those things are listed with their reasons in data-model/03 §1. What is left is the two parameters a period needs: how long it lasts, and how long after it the person may renew without re-applying. The fee itself is not a property of the type at all: it is a flat per-person amount that lives on fee_schedule and is snapshotted onto each obligation, so "what did we charge in 1998?" is answered from the obligation, not the type.

Membership is ageless (D-038). No age floor, no age ceiling, no age-out, no child→adult transition. Age survives as a fact about a person (person.birth_date) and matters where the law makes it matter: guardianship and safeguarding (§7). Being a counselor or a leader is a role, never a membership type (D-100).

docs.title: 4. Multiple memberships over a lifetime
docs.text:
This is your 1990–2010 / 2024–present case. It is not an edge case; it is the normal shape of a long-lived organization's data.

person 100 — Jan Novák
  ├── membership #1   member   1990-09-01 → 2010-06-30   terminated  (left)
  │     └── (nothing here: the corpus names no groups, so nobody's data says where he was)
  ├── (gap 2010 → 2024 — 14 years, no membership rows)
  └── membership #2   member   2024-10-01 → NULL          active
        └── person_group_member  Thursday group  2024-10-01 → NULL
        └── role_holder          counselors      2025-01-01 → NULL

Note what the two membership rows now share: the same type. They differ only in their period and their end reason. In the original framing this person was a child member and then an adult member; in this one they were a member, twice, and were a child and then an adult the whole time. The second framing is the true one, and it is why the memorable case still works: the person never changed, and neither did the type — only the period did.

Half of this picture is reachable without a human, and the other half is not. Membership #1 and its dates are exactly what the membership export states, so the one-off import writes them — bounded, data_confidence = 'low', batch id set (D-093). The group row is the other half: the corpus names no groups either, so a 1990s roster exists only because somebody who remembers typed it, and the import owes no belonging rows of any kind (D-097, D-098). A membership is one period, not a period plus a body. There is one unit and it is not a row (D-097), so nothing sits beside a membership saying which pack it belonged to. What is lost is a place a 1990s belonging could have been written down, not a fact that was stored and then thrown away: the corpus names no units at all (D-092).

An office is held of nothing, and that is a fact about roles rather than a gap in this picture. role_holder names an office, a person and a period, and nothing else: there is exactly one scope, so a role is always held at the unit. "He was scoutmaster of that group" is therefore not a stored pair — the office and the group are two rows about the same person, and the link between them is somebody's reading of them. The neighbouring loss, recorded with the offices themselves, is that an elected-versus-appointed distinction survives only as a role the organization invents (D-100). Neither is a hole this module can fill.

Everything the system needs follows from this:

  • "Is this person a member?" → is there a membership with valid_to IS NULL (or covering today) and status = 'active'?
  • "How long have they been a member?" → sum of membership period lengths, not today − first join date. The gap must not count.
  • "How old were they when they joined?" → membership #2.valid_from − person.birth_date.
  • "Are they an adult?" → is_minor(person_id), computed from person.birth_date. In 2005 the same query said yes. The membership row is identical either way; only the person's birth date and today's date moved.

Never store is_member, member_since, member_type, or is_child on person. Every one of those is derivable, and every one of them will be wrong the moment history is corrected or a person returns.

docs.title: 5. Transitions and who can perform them
docs.text:
From To Trigger Permission required — draft person starts an application own draft submitted person submits membership.request.create (own, or the guardianship channel at write for a guardian — D-074) submitted under_review reviewer picks it up membership.request.review under_review approved reviewer approves membership.request.approve under_review rejected reviewer rejects membership.request.approve any withdrawn applicant withdraws own, or guardian with permission approved membership pending_payment approval processed system pending_payment active payment confirmed system (or fee.record for manual) active lapsed fee unpaid past the organization's expiry date membership.lapse or the yearly sweep active terminated disciplinary / cause membership.terminate — separate, more restricted permission active suspended temporary hold membership.suspend

No transition above writes completed, and none will. The value existed only for ageing out, and ageing out no longer exists (D-038). The one writer completed has is not a transition: the legacy import writes it on the row it inserts, so the status appears in the data with no live path leading to it (D-162, §3) — and §9 keeps the warning about what such a row reads as. terminated stays exactly what this table says it is for, untouched by the import.

Termination must not be the same permission as lapsing. A lapse is administrative (nobody paid). A termination is a decision about a person's standing in a youth organization, often with safeguarding implications. Conflating them means every volunteer who chases unpaid fees can also expel a member.

A lapse has two faces, and only one of them is a human decision. A lapse triggered by non-payment is the yearly sweep doing its job — nobody decided anything, and "why did I lose access?" has a date for an answer rather than a person. A lapse triggered by a staff decision is a deliberate act with a permission behind it. Both land in the same status; access_log is what distinguishes them, which is another reason the lapse is recorded as an event and not just a column change.

docs.title: 6. Renewal and the yearly fee
docs.text: The fee is flat, per person, yearly, and it expires on a fixed date — typically January (D-040). The membership-relevant part, in full:

docs.title: Renewal opens a new period, not an extended one
docs.text: Shape A, decided (D-016). The previous row closes and a new one opens, linked by membership.renewed_from_membership_id. Extending valid_to in place would be fewer rows and would silently lose the most commonly asked question about renewals — did they renew every year, or skip one and come back?

docs.title: The renewal window replaces the grace status
docs.text:
The old design had a grace status: during it the person was still a member. That is gone. What replaces it is a window tracked as dates, not as a status (D-040):

When What is true On 1 January The membership lapses. They are not a member, and member permissions stop. Inside the window (60 days after expiry) Still not a member — but they may renew without re-applying, and a payment now opens the new period at the expiry date, so the record shows no gap. After 2 March A payment opens a new membership at the payment date. The gap is real. Still no new application required.

The 1 January date has a consequence that reaches past the membership table. The yearly sweep is the only bulk event in a system carefully built to have none: on a single day, every membership in the organization lapses at once. That makes it the day every answer to a MEMBERS-carrying grant moves at once, and the day renewal traffic peaks. Nothing is invalidated, because nothing is stored: a period ending and a lapsed status are the whole of the change, and each member's next check resolves against them (D-114).

It is also the day a system administrator can lose the system they administer — the hazard D-051 was written against, and it is answered in grant text rather than by an exemption list (D-100): there is no gate-exempt permission, and no resolver clause holding a door open. A grant written MEMBERS * ROLE(it) stops applying to its holder at the sweep; a grant written ROLE(it) does not, because MEMBERS is simply not in it — which is exactly how D-100 says a whole office is made exempt, and the same sentence that makes the administrator survivable is the one that makes a lapsed treasurer dangerous. Assumption: which offices are written without MEMBERS, and who decides, is not settled by D-100 — the standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand without MEMBERS is what makes each choice visible to a human (data-model/03 §6), and §9 lists the undecided half as a question.

All four calendar values are columns — duration_months, expiry_month, expiry_day, renewal_grace_days — and that is a requirement rather than a convenience. The organizational year runs with the calendar, and 60 days was chosen for the window on the explicit condition that it stays easy to change (D-048): "Make it 60 days, but it should not be hard to modify." Because the window and the date live in a row rather than in a scheduled job, moving them is an UPDATE. The failure this prevents is a job that contains the literal 60 — invisible, and wrong the first time the organization changes its mind.

Why dates rather than a status. Your own answers pointed two ways on this, and it is worth being honest about that: you described the window as existing "for them to pay to stay members" — which implies still being a member — and separately confirmed they are "expired now, but they can rejoin without re-applying." D-040 resolves it as not a member during the window, but the record shows no gap once they pay, because the alternative puts a third state into every permission check and makes a lapse undetectable until the window closes. If the softer reading is what the organization actually wants, it is a change to the renewal rule, not a rewrite.

The backdating is the load-bearing detail. Without it, someone who pays in February for a January expiry is recorded as having a one-month gap and is misclassified as a returning member — which would pollute the returning-member query and, worse, is_current_member() would have said "no" for a month when the person considers themselves continuously paid up.

So the rule to implement is one decision, not a formula on dates alone: the renewal period starts at the old expiry, not at the payment date, whenever the payment lands inside the window. Landing inside the window is what selects the expiry date, and it is what produces no gap; landing after it selects the payment date, and the gap stands.

The bulk shape of the lapse is a computation cost, and it is paid on open. The lapse happens to everyone at once, on the same date, in a bulk sweep (D-039), and nothing is invalidated, because no answer is stored (D-114): a write that shrinks an audience shrinks it live, so every grant written MEMBERS * … stops reaching a lapsed member on their next check, and the sweep is the only job in the sequence. What the bulk shape costs is therefore computation at the moment somebody looks — the tab on the permissions page, the per-item preview and the who holds this listing each evaluate a changed answer for every one of those people when they are opened — affordable at the size D-112 states, and precisely what that entry's trigger reopens, with D-114 naming the reopen answer: materialize effective_permission per person and call it that. See data-model/05 §10.

docs.title: 7. There are no age transitions
docs.text:
No birthday changes a membership. There is one membership type and it is ageless, so a person's membership does not change when they turn 18, because it was never about their age (D-038).

What a system built around this must still handle — none of it a membership transition:

Concern Where it lives now A guardian's authority at majority Guardianship — and the system does not notice the birthday. No auto-expiry and no review queue; a person ends the row (D-069) Who may be added to a group Nowhere in the data: no column says which group takes children, and none will (D-095, and D-097 took the bodies such a column would have sat on). The control is person_group.member.manage, held at the unit or on one group, in the hands of the people who run it (D-098 transfers D-095 intact), and domain/04-organization-structure.md owns it Whether a person may hold an office Nowhere either: role carries no age column and no eligibility fields at all (D-100), so what remains is is_minor() in a report over role_holder — a report, not a check, since nothing refuses an office to a minor — and that is now the ruling rather than the gap: the age is reported and nothing is ever refused on it (§9, D-168) Consent for a minor's own account guardianship_permission, not a membership requirement Planning around age groups A query over person.birth_date. It is a report, not a state change.

One row of that table is emptier than it looks, and a membership document should say so out loud. Nothing here answers "which bodies take minors?": no column says it and none will, so what this module has to offer on safeguarding is a permission held by named adults, an audit trail whose recorded values expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write. The argument that this is a stronger control than a boolean, and the plain statement of what it cannot answer, belong to the groups module (domain/04-organization-structure.md); what belongs here is the observation that the fee gate protects nobody's childhood either — it protects the organization's membership roll, and it is not load bearing for placement. What D-097 additionally takes is the part where the adult holding that write was somebody the body itself chose; it is recorded as a loss there and not argued away here.

One edge case does not arise. A person finishing one membership while starting another at 18, and whether the overlap rule would block it, is a case an age-bracketed design had to decide. Here it cannot: there is one membership type, a person holds at most one open membership at a time, and turning 18 is an event in the person's life that the membership does not notice.

docs.title: 8. Back to the paper — the ten queries this design must answer
docs.text:
Stated explicitly so they can be tested. All are point-in-time queries and all must remain answerable indefinitely — with two exceptions carried openly rather than quietly dropped: query 3 has no answer for any group before go-live, because the corpus names no groups, and query 8 has no answer at all, because nothing in the model states which bodies accept minors. A list of ten that quietly became eight is how a specification loses a requirement:

  1. Who is an active member today?
  2. Who was a member on any given date in the past?
  3. Who was in group G on date D? — a point-in-time read over person_group_member, whose rows are dated at both ends for exactly this question (D-098); the group's own lifetime is a second, different fact and both are kept. "Who was in the organization on date D?" is a membership read with no belonging row involved: two queries, two shapes, and no "and everything nested under it" left to ask about (D-097). For a group this stops at go-live, and the stop is the corpus's, not the query's: the import names no groups either, so "who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" has no answer at all rather than a wrong one, and every group row from before launch is somebody's typed recollection (domain/03 §7, D-092)
  4. What is the full membership history of person P, including gaps?
  5. Who is inside the renewal window right now? (a case needing follow-up — the worklist that replaced "who is in grace")
  6. Who was approved but never paid? (a case needing follow-up)
  7. Which members are under 18 and have no guardian recorded? (a safeguarding gap, not a membership one — nothing in this system records background checks (D-043), so this is the safeguarding question that is computable)
  8. Which minors are in groups that do not accept them? — unanswerable, and left numbered rather than renumbered away, so that the gap sits on the list instead of off it. Nothing states which bodies accept minors: no column does (D-095, D-097), and a group is explicitly listed as carrying no such rule (D-098). So there is nothing to check a placement against, in either vocabulary, and no plan for there to be one — and that is a ruling now rather than a hole: the age is reported and nothing is enforced on it (D-168). What stands in its place is upstream — nobody is added to a group by somebody who does not hold that group's roster write — plus a report of who holds that write, which is a question about grants, not about people (§7)
  9. Who are the returning members — more than one membership with a gap between?
  10. How many members did the organization have in each year since the records begin? (historical reporting — must include closed memberships and must not double-count)

Four of these — 2, 4, 9 and 10 — reach back into the legacy corpus, and what they return there is a period a source stated, not a period this system recorded (D-090, D-093). The people export states membership periods, so the import writes bounded membership rows and those four queries do reach through the decades — over an export, though, not over a register, and the only thing telling the two kinds of row apart is data_confidence = 'low' and a batch id, which no report is obliged to notice (domain/03 §7). So query 10 is answerable in a form that should be labelled on the way out of the chart: a member count where the source states a period, and nothing where it does not. How far back that reaches is not a design fact: D-090 records the record count and the year range as inputs the batch itself carries.

The wrong answer is exactly one decision away, and the ban that stops it is one sentence. Generate a membership per attendance row and every historical query instantly returns a confident number built on nothing, while is_current_member() quietly hands today's authority to people last seen in 2003 (D-039). What stops that is not the column set but the rule: never an open-ended imported membership, never one inferred from attendance. The distinction underneath is the one worth keeping in words: evidence and inference are different rows, and a file that says member 1990–1995 is the first kind while a line-up of names at an event is the second.

Query 3 is the one with a hole in it: everything before go-live. Importing membership rows says nothing about which group a person was in, because a membership is not a placement; the group answer stays empty until somebody types a roster in by hand — which is the only way a group row can be written at all, the corpus naming no groups (D-092, D-098) — and the honest reading of a pre-go-live roster is that it is somebody's recollection. What the answer keeps is its shape: roster rows are dated at both ends precisely so that "who was in the Thursday group in 2011?" stays a point-in-time read, one that does not depend on the audit trail's recorded values still being there.

These stay on the list because they are answerable, indefinitely, for everything this system registers itself — and that indefinite half is itself a decision: the accounting skeleton is kept as the organization's history, while what the audit trail recorded inside it expires after two years (D-088). For the corpus, print which of the two answers a number came from.

Query 10 is the one that fails in most systems, and it fails specifically because someone made membership a boolean.

Query 1 is slightly harder than it looks, and deliberately: it is not status = 'active' alone, because a membership also stops being current at valid_to. is_current_member() is the single place that decision lives, and every caller should use it rather than re-deriving the predicate — otherwise the queries disagree with the permission resolver, which is the worst kind of bug to find.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
• The organizational calendar: which date the fee expires on, and how long the renewal window is (§6). The mechanism is settled; the two numbers are a guess.
  • Which offices are written without MEMBERS is ruled: per office, by whoever writes the grant, no default either way — not into the expression and not out of it. Which offices carry the term (D-165) is therefore nobody's standing decision: an office inherits no entitlement from a template and inherits no lockout either, no screen fills the term in and no screen strips it. The gate left the resolver for the grant text (§6, D-100), so the decision is made one grant at a time and nothing records the why — only whether the word is in the expression. And a grant written without the term needs no reason field: grant_reason is an optional column and stays optional, because a mandatory reason would turn the absence of a default into a small approval process. Day one's grant carries no MEMBERS term at all — it names one person, and a grant aimed at one person has no expression to carry one, and a grant with no expression to carry one cannot be read as having declined one — so the lockout D-051 was written against is answered by D-150 and not by an exemption. The report makes the outcome visible; it was never going to make the choice. Two clauses here are this round's reading of the ruling rather than the ruling's own words: that the standing report lists every such grant rather than the offices somebody marks sensitive, and the day-one clause above. Carried also at data-model/03 §6.
  • Whether an age rule has any home at all is answered, and the answer is a report. Nothing carries one: a role has no eligibility fields (D-100) and a person_group is refused one (D-098), so "a scoutmaster must be an adult" survives as a report over role_holder and is_minor() (§7) — and that is the ruling now, not the shape of the gap: age is reported and never enforced (D-168). Enforcement is therefore declined rather than deferred. What that buys, and what it costs: nothing refuses an office to a minor and nothing refuses a placement either, so the safeguarding answer stays a human reading a list; in exchange no rule silently excludes a person on a birthday, in a system with no level ladder and no eligibility column to hold one. Historical query 8 — which minors are in groups that do not accept them — stays unanswerable and stays numbered for exactly this reason (§8).
  • What status an imported closed membership carries is answered: completed, and the warning stays on the page (§3). The enum offers pending_payment, active, suspended, lapsed, terminated, completed, and none of them says a source stated this period and nobody in the system decided anything: terminated claims an end reason the export does not give, completed claims a lifecycle this model does not have. The answer takes the second-worst of the two lies, knowingly, and what makes it survivable is that the row does not stand alone: every imported membership is data_confidence = 'low' and both of its dates came from a source row (D-093), so the honest answer to did anybody decide this sits two fields away from the field that reads as a decision (D-162). A seventh value named imported was the alternative and it is refused: the other six say what happened to the membership, imported would say how the row arrived, and every historical query would then have to choose between an event and a provenance inside one column — where the corpus's whole answer to what did this import assert is already data_confidence, sitting beside status for exactly that reason. §5 produces no completed row on the live path, so the import is the value's only writer. The reporting consequence is kept, not resolved: a status that reads as a decision will be reported as one, and historical query 10 counts these rows as completed memberships — which is what the acceptance test wants, and the reason this sentence is here rather than in a footnote.

What this page no longer asks, so that a reader does not go looking for it: activation on payment or approval (it is on payment, §1); per person or per household (per person and flat, §6); renewal shape A or B (A, §6); age-out timing and the child→adult transition (neither exists, §7); background checks as a requirement (§2); simultaneous memberships of different types (impossible — one type, one open membership, §3); whether a body may refuse a minor, and who may add a person to one (nobody is added by somebody who does not hold that group's roster write, §7); and whether the one-off import may create memberships (it may, for the periods the source states, and never open-ended, §3). Each is settled, and the argument for each one is in the decision log rather than here.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

Decisions behind this page: D-016, D-037, D-038, D-039, D-040, D-043, D-044, D-047, D-048, D-051, D-069, D-074, D-088, D-090, D-092, D-093, D-095, D-097, D-098, D-100, D-112, D-114.

docs.title: Authorization Model
docs.text:
The permission system end to end. This is the document to read if you read only one.

The whole model, stated once.

Scopes. There are two. The unit — the organization, of which there is exactly one, and which is a scope and never a row — and one item: an event, a group, a role, later a document. A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type; a grant on an item reaches that item and nothing else. There is no tier between them and nothing to test.

A grant is: a grantee (a person, an audience or a registered key — exactly one of the three) + a scope + one permission code + an effect of allow or deny + a period.

The answer. Allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. There is no level, nothing is inherited downward, and no nearer grant beats a further one — because once the answer is boolean, there is nothing left to order.

Roles and groups are not sources of authority. They are named sets of people that a grant aims at.

A caller is a person or a registered key. A key is one row naming one integration that calls this system from outside it, installed by a named person. It is a third kind of grantee, reached by the grant channel and by nothing else, and it is in none of the sets above (§10a).

docs.title: 1. The three channels of authority
docs.text:
Every question of the form "may this caller do X?" — a person, or a registered key — is answered by consulting three mechanisms. They are separate because they have different lifetimes, different granters, and different revocation semantics. Only the first of the three reaches a key (§10a).

# Channel Question it answers Where the answer comes from Reaches 1 Grants What has this person, this set of people, or this registered key been given? access_grant, aimed at a person, an audience or an api_key The unit, or one item 2 Guardianship What may this person do regarding this child? guardianship.right_level compared with permission.right_kind One dependent 3 Resource ownership Is this their own data? (derived) The row's owner

Channel 3 is not a table. It is the rule that a person may always act on their own profile, their own requests, their own memberships. It is resolved by comparing person_id before the other channels are consulted.

What a channel reaches once one of them says yes. Each of the three answers whether, never how much of a person: there is one read rule and one write rule over a person's record, and no narrower tier standing beside them, so a grant that reaches the record reaches all of it. What that consists of, and why there is no sensitive corner left inside it to withhold, is 08-person-data.md — worth reading before proposing a fourth channel that reaches "only" one kind of fact.

Why the channels stay apart rather than one unified grants table. They differ in ways that matter:

  • Channel 2 has a legal character — guardianship is a fact about the world, often court-ordered, and the organization records what it was told rather than deciding it. It does not expire by itself. A guardianship ends when a party to it says so, and nobody else — not a job, not a birthday. Why: a parent's authority over health and school records does not end at 18 in many jurisdictions, and in some it ends at a different age, so any date the system computed would be a claim it cannot support (D-069).
  • Channel 1 is the only channel that can name a set rather than a person (D-042) — and it is the only channel that reaches a key, which is neither a set nor a person (§10a, D-116). A guardianship is between two named people and an owner is one person. That is a boundary, not an oversight — it is why an office can be aimed at but never held by a rule (§4, F-12).
  • A deny lives in channel 1 and defeats all three (§7.1). Nowhere else can one be written, and nowhere else can one be argued with.

Ownership and guardianship carry no scope, no membership condition, and no level. Nothing in §2 or §6 changes either channel.

docs.title: Roles and groups are not channels
docs.text:
A role confers nothing by itself: it is a named set of people that a grant aims at, in the same sentence as a group, an event's attendees, and "everyone". The codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x). Authority therefore has exactly one source besides ownership and guardianship, and it is D-005 said one level down: being something is not being able to do something.

Whether a person's membership counts is not a channel either. It is a term inside a grant's expression — MEMBERS, evaluated live on the checked date (§6.1) — and never a clause the resolver adds on its own.

docs.title: 2. Scopes — the unit and the item
docs.text:
There are exactly two scopes.

The unit is the organization. There is one. It is not a row, not a table, and not the top of a structure: it is the non-item scope that grant_scope_type already carries, whose code is unit, whose is_item_scoped is false, and at which a grant simply has no item to name.

An item is exactly one thing: one event, one group, one role, and later one document. A grant on it names it.

Reach is one-directional and there is nothing to test. A grant at the unit reaches every item of every type. A grant on one item reaches that item and nothing else. No item reaches another item, and no item reaches the unit.

That is the complete theory of scope. There is no nesting, no path, no depth, no tier between the unit and the item, and no relation on the item — no owner, no parent, no covering body — that a check consults. A point-in-time question about people — who was in the Thursday group in 2011? — is a point-in-time read over person_group_member, whose rows are dated (D-098).

Which codes may be granted where is data, not prose. permission.applies_to is unit or unit_and_item (D-099): event.create and membership.terminate are nonsense on an event, and the column says so instead of hoping a reader agrees. It is checked when the grant is saved, not at check time. Why: a grant of event.create written on one event is refused with the reason in the error, because an event cannot be created twice and a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question. The system namespace is unit-only for the same reason, which makes this column who enforces now the rule that system.admin can never arrive through an item grant (D-081).

Nothing in the model reproduces "access was granted by the body itself". There is one unit, so a person.view grant at unit scope reaches every member's whole record — and person.view is the widest read permission in the system (D-083, D-086). What stands between a person and that read is a person.view grant held by a named adult, an audit trail whose payloads expire after two years (D-088), and a report of who holds the write.

Every grant is attributable to one locus of accountability. "Who gave this person access to this record?" is always answered by a named person at the unit, on a date. It is not necessarily a nearby name: nobody's authority is derived from the body a piece of data belongs to, because there is one body. There is likewise nothing to restructure, so a grant's blast radius cannot grow by reorganization.

Nobody enforces a direction of authority, because there is no direction. The question "may the center read what happens inside a body?" cannot be asked — not "the application instead of the database", but unaskable (D-081; the rule it enforced was D-031). The real requirement behind that machinery was "tell everyone about this event", and it is one grant aimed at EVERYONE or MEMBERS (§6.2).

docs.title: 2.1 system.admin
docs.text:
system.admin is the one wildcard permission: a check for X.y is satisfied by an exact grant of X.y or by system.admin and nothing else (D-068). It crosses no boundary, because there is no boundary for it to cross.

Three properties keep a wildcard from being the hole in the design, and each stands on its own:

  1. It can be handed out only by somebody who already holds it — the ceiling is §5's, and what it buys here is that this code changes hands only through hands that already hold it (D-163; the refusal is 05 §6). A right held through a delegation raises no ceiling (§9), so that path opens no gap here either.
  2. Its holders are on a list, and the list is read. It is what tells a planned change from an incident; what it does not do is reach anybody by itself, because nothing in this design sends a message when the set changes, so the hour a new holder is noticed in is the hour somebody opens the report (D-164). One thing this does not sweep away: D-126's break-glass procedure names one recovery person in advance, and that name stays — a procedure needs a person where a notification needs none, and nothing here is a notification.
  3. It is not delegatable (§9), and it is applies_to = unit, so it cannot arrive on an item.

Day one is one account holding this code, and nothing else. An installation ships no roles, no audiences and no grants: setting it up writes one ordinary access_grant row granting system.admin at the unit to one account, with an ordinary audit row beside it, and nothing in the model can tell that row apart from a grant written a year later — which is the point. There is no bootstrap mechanism, no special column and no fourth kind of actor. Because the code satisfies every check, that account writes the first role, the first audience and the first grant immediately, with no second step (D-150). Why: a bootstrap mechanism would have put D-068's deleted starter bundle back through a door with migration on it. The cost is a first run with no useful permissions until somebody writes them, and the checklist is the catalog read as one (05d §12).

If system.admin becomes the mechanism by which ordinary organization-wide work is done, that is a signal about the catalog rather than about a boundary rule: the work is telling you it needs a permission that does not exist. Record it in the decision log instead of working around it.

docs.title: 3. Permissions — the atomic unit
docs.text:
A permission is a coded capability. It is the only thing the check function ever looks at.

A permission row carries its code, the resource and action it decomposes into, a description, and two more columns: applies_to (unit or unit_and_item, above) and right_kind (read or write). right_kind exists for exactly one customer: guardianship (§1, channel 2) grades a guardian at none / view / write, and that channel needs something to compare a permission against. none covers nothing, view covers read codes, write covers both. It is a column whose only job is one other mechanism, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it later (D-074).

Every code in this table ships with the software, and no row carries a flag saying so. There is no permission.create and no permission.delete code anywhere in the catalog, and the one write a screen does offer — permission.edit, 🔒🔒 — reaches a code's labels and never its code or its existence, so this is a property of the table and the sentence about it lives here: what protects a vocabulary is its table, not a boolean on its rows. A flag reaches only the deletions that pause to read it, and an import, a manual fix and a second client do not (D-152).

Codes are resource.action and are stable identifiers, never display strings. The UI shows a human label; the code never changes. Renaming a permission code is a breaking change and must be avoided.

docs.title: Naming convention
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning Example <resource>.view Read person.view <resource>.create Create (always applies_to = unit) event.create <resource>.<field>.edit Edit a field subset person.contact.edit <resource>.delete Delete (soft, and audited) document.delete <resource>.member.manage Write one set's membership person_group.member.manage

There is no row here for acting on a supervised person, because there is no dependent.* namespace to name (D-074). A guardian's act is checked under the ordinary code for the thing being touched — person.view, person.contact.edit — and reaches the guardianship channel by the shape of the request, not by its name (D-079).

Every capability is narrow and explicit. A check for X.y needs an exact grant of X.y, or system.admin. There is no <resource>.admin wildcard and no prefix match in the resolver (D-068).

An office is a stack of rows, not one word. The catalog holds seventy codes — the sixty-six this page counted, plus the four api_key.* rows (catalog §8b) — and a broad office is a couple of dozen rows (catalog §11). Why: that is the price of "what exactly does this person have?" being answerable by reading rows, and the reason there is no word like manage whose contents a reader would have to look up. Roles and audiences are the bundle, and nothing else is (D-099).

docs.title: 4. Roles are offices; groups are company
docs.text:
Two tables of the same shape, and the difference between them decides who may edit the membership.

Role (role, role_holder) Group (person_group, person_group_member) What it is An office: leader, finance, IT. Small, visible holders, expected to be seen Company: the Thursday group, the kitchen crew, this year's camp staff. People who do something together Holder row role_holder(role, person, valid_from, valid_to, granted_by, note) person_group_member(group, person, valid_from, valid_to, added_by, note) Held where At the unit, always. There is one scope, so there is nothing else to hold it at The group is its own item, and a grant can be written on it Permission that writes its membership role.assign, role.unassign — 🔒🔒, the most sensitive family in the catalog person_group.member.manage — ⚠ In an expression ROLE(x), or bare x GROUP(x), or bare x Authority by being in it None None

role carries code, name, description, sort_order — and no scope column, no membership flag, no term, and no delegation flag. Lending is said on the grant, not on the role (§9).

Why two tables when they are technically the same shape — and they are the same shape, which is exactly what D-080 teaches a reader to distrust. The answer is the permission consequence: one table would merge those two codes into one. A single membership table with a kind column gives you a single permission that both adds a child to the Thursday group and puts the holder into SYSTEM_ADMINS. That is the merge to refuse. Same columns, different codes, and ROLE(x) / GROUP(x) distinct in the grant text so the distinction is visible to whoever reads the grant.

A role confers nothing. The codes an office carries are the live grants whose audience names ROLE(x). That is what makes "what may a treasurer do?" a question with an answer: it is a query over visible grant rows, not a walk through a bundle table nobody reads. What "the treasurer's permissions" consists of:

role         code = treasurer                (a row the organization wrote, like every other)
role_holder  treasurer ← Ana, 2026-01-01 → open
access_grant audience = MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)   scope = unit
             permission = fee.view            effect = allow
access_grant audience = MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)   scope = unit
             permission = payment.record      effect = allow
access_grant audience = MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers)   scope = unit
             permission = report.finance.view effect = allow
  … one row per code, and the list is the office

Neither a role nor a group authorizes anything by existing, which is D-005 and D-019 restated one level down: participation is not authority, and storing the participation in a tidier table does not quietly promote it. A group additionally has no parent and no children, no type vocabulary, no code, no path, no nesting rules, no rename history, no split or merger edge, no leadership of its own, no roles, and no fee (D-098).

Both are items. person_group and role are registered in grant_scope_type, so "these two may work this group's roster" and "these two may manage the counselors roster" are grants on one item — reachable only by someone who already holds the corresponding code at the unit (§2).

Roles are runtime data (D-052, D-053) — and nothing is left to soften that: no role ships (D-150). The organization creates roles, composes them from grants, and deletes the unused ones, and the first of each is an ordinary write by the account described in §2.1. The worked examples of writing one live in appendix/permission-catalog.md §11. The office this page keeps reaching for as its example is counselors, chosen because it is the case that decided the table: a permanent, organization-wide population is the opposite of the organization's own definition of a group ("a temporary set of members that do events together"), and the table decides the sensitivity that protects the set every safeguarding convention hangs from. That argument is about which table a population lives in, never about who writes the row (D-154). An office is still only a set — being in it confers nothing until a grant names it (§6.2).

An elected leader is a holder of a role, and the audience that names them is ROLE(leaders), meaning what its name says. What is genuinely not stored is the elected-versus-appointed distinction, and D-136 settled that it will not be: an election is run outside this system and the outcome arrives as a holder row. The distinction survives only as roles the organization invents (elected_council next to appointed_it) or not at all — F-18 is closed on exactly that answer. Where the appointment workflows end is 04-organization-structure.md §6.

A role is held by exactly one person per row. A role cannot be held by a rule the way a group is: an office record that cannot answer "who was treasurer in 2023" is not an office record, and a derived holder list cannot answer that (F-12). Grants aim at roles rather than roles being filled by grants, which is the same fact seen from the other side.

docs.title: The holder period matters
docs.text:
valid_from / valid_to on role_holder means an office ends on a date even if nobody remembers to revoke it. Leavers are the classic audit failure: the volunteer who stepped down in 2019 still has an active account with treasurer access in 2026.

Nothing forces a holder row to end, and the report is the control (D-071). No other mechanism stands behind it: the report is carrying the whole weight of expiring authority (§6.1, §11).

docs.title: 5. The grant — one permission, one effect
docs.text:
A grant is the whole of channel 1, and its shape is the whole of this section:

grantee + scope + one permission_id + effect + period.

Grantee: a person, an audience or a registered key — exactly one of the three, never two and never none. Scope: the unit, or exactly one item. Effect: allow or deny. Period: valid_from, valid_to, live on the checked date.

Plus provenance: granted_by, granted_at, grant_reason, and for a lent authority is_delegated with delegated_from naming who it came from (§9).

One code per grant, not a set. That is what makes the answer readable: "what exactly does this person have?" is a list of rows, and "who else can do this?" is the same list read the other way. The list is the same shape for every grantee — what a set of people holds and what a key holds are read off these same rows, which is why auditing an integration is reading one list rather than reconstructing a second one (§10a).

Writing a grant is itself an authorized act: creating one requires access_grant.create at the matching scope. Composing an expression grants nothing (§6.2). There is one item-facing door, and it is a second code for the same write: every event carries event.grant_access among the twelve grants its creation wrote for ORGANIZERS, so whoever runs a camp can give the nurse, the cook and the two assistant leaders access to it without holding access_grant.create at the unit and without asking anyone (D-151). Two questions, two codes, one table. Three things bound them: the scope they can name — their own event, so nothing they write reaches another event, a group, or the unit — applies_to, which refuses system.admin on an item because that code is applies_to = unit (§2), and the granter's ceiling, which refuses a row naming a permission its writer does not hold, at a scope that reaches what they are writing — the check the resolver already performs, pointed at the granter at save time (D-163). The second and third are different kinds of bound and worth keeping apart: applies_to says where a code may ever be granted, the ceiling says who may grant it. So the item-facing door is wide but not open: an organizer hands out what they hold, at a scope that reaches the event in front of them, and no code they do not hold.

docs.title: Allow and deny are not symmetrical
docs.text:
Allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies. Everything else in this document is elaboration.

A deny is legal at either scope. A deny at the unit is precisely the case an expression cannot serve: "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone."

- in an expression is not a deny, and the two are not interchangeable. Subtracting a set narrows one grant's reach. A deny defeats every grant that applies to the grantee it names — a person, a set, or a key — including ones written elsewhere, later, or by somebody else. The first cannot express "she must not have this, whatever else she is given", which is D-013's whole reason for existing: a court-ordered restriction must not be beatable by a broader grant someone forgot about (D-099).

One report comes with this, and it is the whole hygiene of the thing. A live deny whose grantee, scope and code match no live allow is dead weight, and it should be reported — a deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason. Nothing enforces it; the report is the mechanism (§11).

docs.title: Why scope_type/scope_id and not one column per item type
docs.text:
scope_id has no foreign key — it is a polymorphic reference, and this is a deliberate, accepted trade-off (D-011):

  • Cost: no referential integrity. A grant can point at a deleted event.
  • Benefit: the permission system does not need a schema change every time a new grantable thing is invented, which — since documents and everything else are still deferred — will happen repeatedly.

Mitigations, all of which are required: the grant_scope_type registry validates scope types; deleting an item of a granted type must close its grants (an application-level obligation, tested); a nightly job reports orphaned grants; ids are never reused. The heavier alternative — a grantable_item supertable every grantable entity references — is declined for flexibility, and is ../open-questions.md if anyone wants to overrule it (F-2).

docs.title: 6. The resolver
docs.text:
One function answers every authorization question. Written once, used everywhere — an authorization rule that exists in two places will diverge.

The call names a person, a permission code, a scope, and a date. The scope is the unit or exactly one item: asking at the unit is how "may this person create an event?" is asked, and asking at an item is how "may this person edit event 1204?" is asked. at defaults to now. Where the thing being touched has an owner, the caller passes the owner too, because one step below needs to know whose record this is. The answer is allowed or denied; the function has no other output, and no part of it is stored. (Field names and the exact signature are in data-model/05 §10.)

Two doors, and the same function behind both. That call is can(person, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at, owner_person_id). A caller that is not a person enters through can_key(api_key, permission_code, scope_type, scope_id, at), which takes one fewer argument, and the missing parameter is the design (D-121): no owner, and no person of any kind, so nothing can be passed in that claims to be somebody. It is not an omission to be filled in later. A claimed person would turn the trail's word for who acted into an input, and on_behalf is defined against inference precisely because the relationships it records can be derived from a channel — which a key has none of. So there is no request "made by the accounting system, acting as the treasurer", and a copied secret cannot reach a child's record by typing that child's id into a field while the trail says a person did it. A request authenticates as a person or as a key, never as both, and in both audit trails actor_person_id and api_key_id are mutually exclusive.

The steps run in this order:

  1. Deny — absolute, at any scope. If any live deny applies — its scope is the unit or the exact item being checked, its code is the code being checked, its grantee is this person or an audience whose expression contains them on the checked date — the answer is no. No scope outranks a deny, and neither does a channel: a per-event allow cannot restore what a unit-scope suspension removed (§7.1).
  2. Ownership. If the target resource's owner is this person → yes for the read, edit and self-service actions. Never conditioned on anything (§6.1): a lapsed person must still be able to reach the screen they renew on.

  3. Guardianship — entered by the shape of the request, and it answers with allows only. Compare the actor with the owner of the thing being touched. Same person, and this channel is not in play at all. Different people, and the question is whether the actor holds a live guardianship over that subject as of at whose right level covers the checked permission's right_kind — view covers read, write covers both, none covers nothing (D-074). Covered → yes. Every other outcome — no row, none, a level too low — is not a refusal: the channel says nothing and the resolver continues, where the person's own grants are tried exactly as they always were (D-079). A parent who is also the event registrar holds view over their own child and must not be refused the roster by their own guardianship.

  4. Nothing escapes by naming. The act that routes here is chosen by whose record it touches, so a permission written next year for a field a guardian must edit is covered the day the field exists. Dispatch never reads a code's prefix: an ordinary person.contact.edit must reach this step like any other act.

  5. An ended guardianship never opens this channel again. What a former guardian may still do is what any other person may do, through their own grants.

  6. The row is the whole test. The guard must not be rewritten as "the subject is a minor": the resolver contains no age branch. It contains an OLDER(n) operand, which is a set a grant has to name before anything is looked at, and the difference is the point: nothing consults a birth date unless somebody wrote a rule that needed it, and no rule is inferred — and D-070 and D-077 keep it that way.
