  7. Allow — does any live grant apply? Two shapes, both boolean, neither ranked against the other:

  8. a unit grant of this code, to this person directly or to an audience whose expression contains them on at. It reaches this item because a unit grant reaches every item (§2) — there is no tier to walk and no relation on the item to test.
  9. an item grant of this code on exactly this item, to a person or an audience — event.view on event 1204 is how a helper sees one event and no other.

Either → yes. 4. Otherwise → no.

Steps 1–3 are not a precedence. With a boolean answer, two allows that both apply produce one answer, so there is nothing to order and renumbering steps 1–3 changes nothing about who can do what. Their order stands for two reasons that are not precedence — cheap checks before expensive ones, and step 2's "says nothing" fall-through — and neither order is load-bearing for the answer. What is ordered, and must stay so, is step 0: the deny is asked first and can defeat every allow below it (D-032).

A key walks these same five steps, and two of them can never answer. Step 0 counts only when the deny names this key; a deny aimed at a person, or at a set a person is in, is not consulted at all, because a key is in no set and is not that person (§10a). Step 3 reads the live rows naming the key instead of the rows naming a person or a set containing them, and step 4 is the answer for an integration holding nothing — the same default deny everyone else gets, and the whole reason a key's authority is its grants in full and only. Steps 1 and 2 are not reached rather than refused: ownership asks whether the owner is the actor and guardianship asks whether the actor is a party to a guardianship row, and neither question can be evaluated with a key in the actor's place. Nothing was added to refuse them. And a check for a key that does reach yes records unit_grant or item_grant exactly as a person's does, with the grant row for its reference — what the trail gains is who, not how, and there is no seventh channel (D-118).

Points worth stressing:

  • Default deny. Step 4. Any new resource starts with nobody able to touch it.
  • Fail closed, in every direction — and closed is a direction here, not a safe place to stand. An operand that does not resolve is the empty set; an expression that cannot be evaluated reaches nobody; a scope type nobody registered grants nothing. This is the same posture as step 4 and step 0, and it is the direction every uncertainty in this model resolves in. Why: an empty set narrows an allow and widens a deny, so fail-closed arithmetic is what the expression says, not what safety wants — which is why the answer to a failing operand is a report and not a refusal (D-106).
  • A grant may name an audience instead of a person, or a key instead of either. An audience is resolved by the expression in §6.2; a key names itself, so there is nothing to resolve. Either way the scope and the code are resolved exactly as for a personal grant.
  • Effective permissions are never stored. They are computed per request. A stored permission snapshot will drift from the grants that produced it — the only question is how long before anyone notices. There is a second reason to keep that question open: the snapshot is also the only artefact that could ever answer who could read this in 2023, since set membership is recomputed from state that keeps moving and the audit payload that recorded the change expires (§6.2, F-7).
  • Time is a parameter. at defaults to now, but the resolver accepts a historical time. This enables "could this person have done this on that date?" — needed for auditing past actions, and free if built in from the start. The dated rows behind MEMBERS, GROUP(x), ROLE(x) and the attendance selectors are all periods (§4, §6.2), so the recomputation has something honest to read.

docs.title: 6.1 MEMBERS — the membership test, moved into the expression
docs.text:
Whether a person's membership counts is a selector term, not a clause of the resolver. MEMBERS is evaluated live on the checked date like any other operand, and writing it or leaving it out is the grant writer's act (§6.2). The resolver has no membership branch and carries no exemption for one.

The four things a writer needs to be able to say:

To Write gate an office on a current membership MEMBERS * ROLE(x) leave a whole office ungated ROLE(x) — the same expression without MEMBERS waive it for one named person inside a gated rule MEMBERS * ROLE(x) + PERSON(y) apply it to nobody: ownership, guardianship, and any grant aimed at a person or a key nothing — a channel has no expression, and a grant aimed at one person or one key has none (§5)

The third row is also writable without a selector: "and also him" is a second grant aimed at that person, which is how the waiver looks when the writer would rather not touch the expression everyone else reads.

The test is opt-in per grant, and the failure mode must be named rather than buried. A grant written as ROLE(treasurers) with no MEMBERS authorizes a lapsed member, silently, forever. Nothing errors, nothing reports itself when it happens, and nothing about the grant looks wrong — a lapsed treasurer is still a treasurer. Three controls, none of which is the resolver:

  1. A standing report of live grants naming a ROLE(...) operand whose expression does not contain MEMBERS — every one of them, since nothing marks which offices should have carried the term (D-165). An office held by a non-member is the case worth a human eye, and the report is narrow enough to actually be read.
  2. The grants this system writes for itself are named, and the omission inside them is deliberate. Creating an event writes twelve item-scope allows beside the event row, every one aimed at the bare operand ORGANIZERS, and not one of them carries MEMBERS — an organizer appointed for one weekend is not required to be a paying member (D-151). They name no ROLE(...) operand, so control 1 does not look at them; every other grant row in the database arrives through a screen, and each of those is fair game for it.
  3. Import completeness. MEMBERS * COUNSELORS is only as correct as the counselor roster: an import that misses 300 counselors silently un-gates them. It fails closed — nothing breaks, which is exactly why nobody notices. The import reconciliation report of D-090 must count people marked as counselors in the corpus against role_holder rows written.

Who the test should spare is a decision the organization has already made, and it is a judgment about each grant rather than a default the design carries: "everything except guardianship and adult volunteers." A volunteer whose own fee is unpaid still runs the Thursday meeting, and losing the roster on the night the fee lapses is the failure to prevent. So leaving MEMBERS out is the normal shape of a grant to a contractor, a photographer or a parent helper, not an exemption somebody must be granted. And the ruling is that there is no default either way — not into the expression and not out of it: per office, by whoever writes the grant, with no screen filling the term in and no screen stripping it, and a grant written without the term needs no reason field — grant_reason stays the optional column it is (D-165). The line that judgment draws holds, and it holds hardest where only a report stands behind it: the report is how the organization notices; the resolver is not how it punishes.

Why the test sits in the expression. A resolver clause applies to everything or nothing, and so has to carry its own exemptions; an expression says which grants are gated, in the text of the grant, where the person writing it can see it and a report can read it. A clause cannot answer "is this particular permission meant to require membership?", because it records the answer nowhere. Nothing enforces MEMBERS being present: a convention, not a guard (D-081).

Who is gated:

Channel Gated? Why, and how it is written Ownership (step 1) No Otherwise a lapse locks a person out of the screen they renew on. Not expressible in an expression at all Guardianship (step 2) No A legal relationship, not a membership Grants (step 3) Only if the expression says so MEMBERS * …. A grant to a contractor, a photographer or a parent helper who was never a member is written without MEMBERS A deny (step 0) Never, in either direction §7.1

docs.title: 6.2 Audiences — an expression over named sets
docs.text: A grant aimed at a set of people names an expression over named sets — MEMBERS * ROLE(treasurers), EVERYONE - GROUP(x), PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) — stored as a tree of binary nodes, evaluated live on the checked date, and never materialized. The language and its operators, precedence and canonical rendering, the thirteen seeded selectors and the argument each takes, the rules that make the tree safe (cycles, the three states, keyless leaves, the editor's preview), and what a grant's reach is recorded in are a self-contained subject and live on their own page: 06a-audiences-and-selectors.md. What the resolver does with an audience is §6 above; what a grant is, and how allow and deny interact, is §5 and §7.

docs.title: 7. Precedence
7.1 Who decides — deny is absolute
docs.text:
1. Deny          (a live deny applies at ANY scope)   ← WINS OVER EVERYTHING
2. Ownership     (it's your own row)
3. Guardianship  (the act is about someone else — allows only)
4. Any live allow (unit grant or item grant — §6 step 3)
5. Deny          (nothing matched)

A deny is checked before anything else and is never subject to any ordering. A deny at the unit blocks access to one event even if a grant on that event explicitly allows it. There is no scope local enough to override a suspension (D-013; D-032's first half, which is the whole of its surviving content).

Absolute over the grantee it names, and over no other. A deny on a person leaves a key standing, and a deny on a key leaves the person who installed it standing, because a key is a different grantee and a deny defeats the allows of the grantee it names (§10a, D-118). Absoluteness is undiminished, and the reach of one deny row is per grantee: the instrument this design reaches for first when somebody must stop reading children's records reaches one grantee and not the others. Safeguarding review therefore reads one grant list holding three kinds of grantee, which is why the permissions page lists keys beside people (§10a).

A deny is also never subject to the membership test, in either direction. A deny blocks someone who is not a member, which is obvious. What is worth stating: a deny to an audience blocks the people in that audience whether or not they are current members, because the deny is evaluated against who the expression matches, not against whether they are paid up. Suspensions are absolute; MEMBERS is a condition on a grant of authority, and there is no authority here to condition.

A deny is legal at the unit as well as on an item, and "exclude her from what the unit grants everyone" is the case only a deny can serve (§5).

Nothing else orders. Two allows that both apply produce one answer, so there is no tie-break, no tier ladder, and no "is this amount high enough" question anywhere in the resolver: a grant says yes-or-no about one code. So a grant on an item applies at full force whatever the person holds at the unit, a unit grant keeps working for the unit's other items, and no grant can retract another — only a deny can (D-099).

docs.title: 8. There is no permission cache, and what replaces it
docs.text:
There is no permission cache. A check resolves; a request memoizes; the only cached thing is a compilation. Nothing in this system stores a permission answer, and no part of can() is written to a table (D-114).

What a check costs. One indexed read fetches the checked person's live grant rows — a few dozen rows at the size D-112 states — and each candidate grant's expression is evaluated against a handful of indexed point lookups in membership, role_holder, person_group_member, event_registration and the guardianship rows. The arithmetic is not the problem; the N+1 across one screen is: a 50-row list asking four codes per row is two hundred checks, and two hundred checks doing the same person's grant read two hundred times is the shape that makes a cache look necessary. The three mechanisms below fix that shape directly.

  1. A compiled expression is cached — parsed once, operand kinds resolved once, the parameterized predicate emitted once, keyed by the expression's root and ruleset_version. It holds no person and no item, because both arrive as parameters, and that is precisely why it survives across everyone in the organization while an answer never could: nothing in a compilation depends on whom or where it is being asked about.
  2. A request memoizes. The checked person's grant rows are read once and every code, item and date in that request is answered from them in memory; a named operand that recurs in one request (ROLE(leader), GROUP(cubs)) is resolved once. Its lifetime is the request, so it has no invalidation policy and no staleness window — there is nothing to invalidate.
  3. The bulk screens batch. can_many(person, codes[], item?) answers a screen's affordances from one resolution; which_of(people[], code, item) answers a list's from one pass. The per-item preview (06a §6.2, F-15) and the permissions tab (D-109) are written against these, not against a loop of single checks.

The one thing cached across requests besides a compilation is a named roster: ROLE(x) over role_holder, GROUP(x) over person_group_member, keyed by x. Two conditions, and together they are the whole of the exception. The key is the thing a write touches, so invalidation is local to the row that changed and never global — the property an answer cache could never have, because an answer's key names a person and the write that changes it usually names nobody. And the cache holds the dated rows, or the set with its validity ranges, never the set as of today, so the checked date is still applied at check time and a period ending at midnight needs no job to be seen. A roster is also something a person maintains and can point at; an answer never was. The exception is exactly two selectors wide. MEMBERS is not a roster — nobody writes its rows, and the 1 January sweep rewrites the membership dates it reads for everybody at once. ORGANIZERS is not one either: it has holder rows, but it is bound to an item (D-102), so a cache keyed by it would be a stored answer to "who was at this event", which is the set D-102 declined to make permanent.

What may never be stored again is invariant 19 (§11 of data-model/05d-invariants-and-seed.md): no row, table or field may map a caller — a person, or a key — or a caller and a code, or a caller and an item, to a permission answer (D-123). The subject is a caller rather than a person because "the integration's permissions" is the most natural such table in this system to write, it reads like configuration rather than like a cache, and a table keyed by api_key_id and permission_code holding a boolean is precisely a current answer. api_key.last_used_at is not one — it says an event happened, and nothing reads it to decide whether to allow something now. Its enforcement is structural, which is the best kind this corpus has: the schema has nowhere to put one. The residue is named rather than glossed — an implementer who wants a cache back is stopped by this page and by review, not by a constraint, so for them it is a convention, not a guard (D-081), and D-114 lists the three things a returning cache must carry: a per-person invalidation handle next to the global one, an explicit statement of which tables it watches, and that statement derived from the operand registry rather than from a list of ideas.

What live resolution buys.

  • "The safeguarding case is immediate" is true by construction. A revoke, a deny, a closed period, an ended guardianship, a membership.terminate ⛔ — safeguarding_officer, the most safeguarding-shaped write in the catalog — or a cancelled registration — all visible on the next check, with no job in between and no list to remember to include them in. A terminated member stops satisfying MEMBERS at the instant the row closes: data-model/03-membership.md §6 asks for exactly that, and asks it of nothing, because MEMBERS reads membership live (§6.1).
  • The calendar cannot drift an answer. A birthday crossing OLDER(n), a period reaching its own valid_to, the 1 January sweep — each moves the answer at the instant it happens. D-107's ruling stands — "IT IS FINE" — and needs no mechanism to hold it.
  • ruleset_version is bumped by a write to audience_operand or selector_type only. A compilation depends on an expression's shape and the seeded vocabulary and on nothing else. access_grant is not in that set because grants are not compiled: a check reads the person's live grant rows, so a new, edited or revoked grant changes what that read returns and leaves nothing stale to drop; the deprecated | hidden | disabled flag is not in it because a state is not compiled in — resolution reads it live, once per request, memoized, which is also why disabled still means now (D-109); role_holder, person_group_member, guardianship_permission and a person merge are not in it because they move rosters and rows that are read live or invalidated locally. Concretely: adding a child to a group drops nothing.
  • "Whom does this change reach?" is answerable. A compilation is finite and enumerable over the audience tree, so "an edit to a shared audience invalidates everything" becomes "it invalidates the compilations that embed it" — a bounded walk over rows that already exist. One qualification, stated in the direction and not the spirit: it is not the walk the save path performs for cycles, which runs forward from the tree being saved. Invalidation needs the reverse direction, the one the delete-refusal check already runs. Same forest, same rows, opposite way — and the cost of listing that forest is registered as unverified at any size in data-model/05 §13, so what is claimed here is bounded, not cheap (D-103).

A compiled form is bound to its item. Since a bound operand means the same expression yields different people on different items, a compiled form computed while checking one item may never be served for another: the item is a parameter of a predicate, and a predicate bound to event 1204 is not the predicate for event 1205 (F-6).

What is given up. Nothing pre-pays the expensive screens. The per-item preview, the permissions tab and the "who holds this" listing do their work when somebody opens them, which is affordable at the stated size — but D-109's ruling has no fallback, and that is a dependency, not a comfort. At D-112's trigger the reopen answer is named rather than vague: materialize effective_permission per person, and call it that — a real materialization with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window.

What is not given up is the rule stated in 06a §6.2, and it is the whole cost model of this page: inside a check, an expression is compiled to a predicate on the person being asked, never materialized as a set. No job anywhere is permitted to do the opposite.

docs.title: 9. Delegation
docs.text:
A leader going on leave, a treasurer handing over during an audit — the common need to lend authority temporarily.

A delegation is an ordinary grant with its provenance set: is_delegated, delegated_from naming the person whose authority is being lent, grant_reason, and a valid_to. Because a grant is one permission code, "do not lend more than you hold" is a set-membership test (D-099).

Rules:

  • A delegation always has an end date. Enforced on the write path.
  • A delegation cannot exceed the delegator's own authority, and it is checked once: when it is written. The save resolves the delegator and refuses a code they do not hold at that moment (05 §6). Nothing re-checks it at use time, and the page that carries this rule used to promise that it did (D-143). That was not a gap waiting for an implementation but a second rule the data model denies: a grant row records who lent it and never what the lender can currently do, so a use-time check would have had to resolve a person who is not party to the check, and it would have made a delegatee's access depend on somebody else's history. A delegation therefore stands to its own valid_to, or to a revocation — the delegator losing the code mid-delegation changes nothing, which is the cost of this rule and is said out loud rather than left to be discovered. Two bounds remain: a delegation must carry an end date (the check above), and system.admin cannot be delegated at all.
  • Lending is not holding: the ceiling (§5) reads the writer's own grants, so a permission held only through a delegation cannot be lent on, while the delegation already written stands to its own valid_to (D-143 above) (D-163).
  • The provenance is recorded, so an audit can answer "who really had this authority on that date?" — it lists both the holder and the delegator.
  • A deny cannot be lent and cannot be lent around. A delegation is an allow; the delegatee's answer is computed from their own rows plus the lent one, and their own denies still apply.
  • Delegation of system.admin is prohibited outright.

Lending is said on the grant, not on the role: role has no is_delegatable column, and nothing about an office says whether its authority may be lent.

Assumption: D-100 names is_delegatable in neither its deleted nor its kept list of role's columns. Recorded in ../open-questions.md; the open list carries it as item 55.

docs.title: 10. Anti-patterns this design rejects
docs.text:
Stated explicitly, because each is a common and expensive mistake:

Rejected Why Instead person.is_admin boolean Cannot scope, cannot date, cannot audit, cannot delegate A grant at the unit, aimed at a role Role on person (person.role = 'leader') One role per person, no history role_holder, many per person Checking membership type in code (if type == 'adult') Rules change; the check is invisible and untestable A permission, granted deliberately. There is one membership type now, so this is doubly wrong Deriving access from holding a role or being in a group Being something is not being able to do something (D-005), and a role confers nothing by itself A live grant whose audience names ROLE(x) or GROUP(x) — §4 A grant written as ROLE(x) when it meant MEMBERS * ROLE(x) It is a term the writer must type, and forgetting it silently authorizes a lapsed member The standing report of role grants without MEMBERS, and the import count — §6.1 An access_level, or any comparison of "how much" a grant gives A level is a bundle of permissions under one word, and it re-imports the rank rule and a tie-break that have no consumers Roles and audiences as the bundle — what D-068 already said — and one row per code when you need it in writing. §3, D-099 - in an expression used instead of a deny Subtracting narrows one grant's reach; it cannot say "whatever else she is given" A deny, which defeats every grant — §5, §7.1 An expression whose reach nobody saw EVERYONE is a legal operand, and a bound operand means different people on different items The editor expands the set for an item at the moment of granting — 06a §6.2 PRESENT(e) over was_present NULL until someone takes a register: a volunteer's forgotten tick would revoke a child's own photos The four attendance tiers, and presence stays a safeguarding signal — 06a §Event sets A GUARDIANS operand Guardianship is a channel with its own right_level over a child, reaching every action about that child; an operand would offer a subset of what they hold The guardianship channel (§1, §6 step 2); for a kept list of contact adults, a person_group — D-113 A LIST operand, or a table of an audience's own names A hand-written set is not a different kind of thing from a named one PERSON(a) + PERSON(b) inside the expression — §Grammar, D-105 Downward inheritance of authority through a unit tree, and scope_exposure rows Both need a hierarchy, and there is one unit A grant at the unit, which reaches every item — §2, D-097 "Most specific scope always wins", including against a deny Only allows could ever be ordered, and allows are not ordered Deny absolute, and no ordering at all — §7, D-099 A bulk "expose this body's scope" tool There is one unit and nothing to expose One grant at the unit, or one grant aimed at EVERYONE / MEMBERS — §2, D-045 Treating an organization-scoped role as universal "so the registrar can work" Everything is unit data; there is no second side of that distinction If a permission is missing, add the permission — §2.1 Role → permission mapping hardcoded in the app Cannot be reviewed by the organization, cannot change without deployment Grant rows naming ROLE(x) — readable, and the answer to "what may a treasurer do?" Deriving access from guardianship without a right Authorization by identity is unauditable and unsafe The explicit right level on the guardianship row, compared against right_kind A key acting as a person — "the accounting system, acting as the treasurer" It turns the trail's word for who acted into an input, and a copied secret would read any child's record while the trail named a person who did nothing can_key takes no person — §6, §10a; a system acting for a person carries that person's own credential. D-121 A synthetic person row for an integration, or an office for "the integrations" It lands inside EVERYONE, shows up in every safeguarding report as a person who may read children's records, and makes a stolen key a set rather than one revocable row One registered key, one set of grants per caller — §10a, D-117 Deleting a grant to revoke it Loses the record of what was revoked when valid_to, and a deny when the fact of the restriction matters A live deny that matches no allow A deny that denies nothing is how a stale restriction survives its reason The dead-weight-deny report — §5 Two authorization implementations They diverge; the weaker one becomes the exploit One resolver, §6 Unit leader sees all member data by default Fails safeguarding review Scoped grants, resolved per operation — and §2 on the protection that is not in the model

docs.title: 10a. A key — a caller that is not a person
docs.text:
An integration that calls this system from outside it is not a person with an account. It is a registered key: one row naming one caller, carrying a stable code so that a grant and an audit row name the same integration years later, and holding one live secret that is shown once and kept only as a hash. Rotating replaces that hash on the same row, so there is no window in which two secrets work, and rotating is therefore a coordinated act with whoever holds the secret (D-119). It is the third kind of grantee (§5), it rides the grant channel (§1, channel 1) and no other, and it is in none of the sets of people the language names (§6.2).

Registered, by a named person. Installing a permanent outside authority is the most sensitive write this module offers, so the act has to be somebody's. Nothing else about a key is a new kind of thing: it holds grants the way a person holds grants, it is checked by the same resolver, and a check answered for it records the same channels (D-116).

What a key is not. Not a channel — there are still three, and a key's allowed check names unit_grant or item_grant. Not a scope: a key is not a grantable item, so no grant is ever written on one, only by one. Not a set's member — nothing in §6.2 can name one, EVERYONE least of all. And not a person, which is what the four consequences below repeat from four directions.

Four consequences carry the design, and each of them refuses something that would have been cheaper:

  1. A key is never inside an expression. No selector names one and the registry keeps its thirteen rows; EVERYONE is any person, including those with no account and no membership, so a key is in nobody's set, its own included. A key has no expression, so there is nothing to compile and nothing to memoize about one, and §8's compilation — keyed by an expression root and ruleset_version, whose trigger stays audience_operand plus selector_type — is untouched by everything in this section (D-117). What that costs is that "grant this to the integrations" is not writable in one sentence: twelve integrations are twelve grants, and a thirteenth is a write somebody performs rather than an edit to one rule. There is no "take integrations out of everything MEMBERS touches" lever either, and a grant to a key cannot carry MEMBERS, because it has no expression to carry it in (§6.1).
  2. Two of the three channels cannot fire for a key. Ownership compares a person's id against a row; guardianship needs an actor who is a party to a guardianship row. Neither is refused by a rule — neither is reachable, because each is a comparison against a person. A key's authority is its grants, in full and only (D-118).
  3. A deny is absolute over the grantee it names, and over no other (§7.1): a deny on a person leaves a key standing, and a deny on a key leaves the person who installed it standing.
  4. A key never carries a person's authority (§6). can_key has no person parameter, so impersonation is refused by the shape of the call rather than by a check inside it, and in both trails actor_person_id and api_key_id are mutually exclusive (D-121). A grant to a key is never a delegation either — is_delegated needs delegated_from, which is a person, and there is no person here to lend anything (§9).

What a key may be granted, and the five codes it may never be granted. Four codes exist to administer keys, all unit-scoped and none of them under a system. prefix: api_key.view (read), and api_key.create, api_key.rotate, api_key.end (write, each 🔒) — the rows and their reasoning are in the catalog. No office holds any of the four — no office ships — and whoever holds system.admin already satisfies every one of these checks, because system.admin satisfies every code (D-124): the capability to install a permanent outside authority is the capability to escalate, and it arrives through the one grant channel like every other code — there is no second route and no office that quietly has it. Five codes may never be granted to a key: system.admin and those four, refused when the grant is saved and counted by integrity check 20 afterwards, since no database rule spans a permission and a grant. A bearer secret holding everything is the whole organization in a request header, and a key holding api_key.create mints its own replacements, so rotating a stolen key means looking for the rows a thief installed. One sentence covers both halves — a key may not change what a key can do, and may not become everything — and, like every other list of refused codes in this design, it is an equality against named codes rather than a rule that generates a set (D-122). A key is not itself a grantable item, so "rotate the accounting key and no other" is not writable: anyone who may issue a key may issue any key, which is the accepted shape at this scale and is recorded as an unpaid debt rather than as a feature.

A key outlives whoever installed it, and a report is the control. created_by is required and is attribution for an act, not a dependency of the authority: the installer's account being suspended, their membership lapsing, a deny written against them and their leaving all change nothing about the row (D-120). owner_person_id is optional and is a contact, not a channel — whose number to look up if this row needs asking about — nothing reads it to decide an answer, and nothing in this design telephones that person when a key goes quiet: the name is there for whoever is reading the tab valid_to is optional and absent means current: a mandatory expiry was offered and refused, because a key is not a delegation (§9) and an expiry would buy a stopped integration on a date, with the failure surfacing wherever that integration writes. The control is a line on the permissions page's Unusual tab — every live key, what it holds, when it was last used, and whether its owner still has an account, keys listed beside people so a safeguarding review reads one list — and there is deliberately no age threshold: the report prints an age and a person decides whether it is old. What that costs is stated as plainly as it should be: a forgotten key is live forever unless somebody reads a list, and a copied secret cannot be recalled.

What sits outside this design. Two of these were open last round and are settled elsewhere; they are listed here because a reader of this page needs to know where the edge is, not because they are unresolved.

  • What this system does to itself is not a caller, and no longer apologises for it. The 1 January sweep, payload reduction, migrations and the bank pull hold no grants and have no row: their write is the row with an empty actor column, which is a complete answer to who did this, and where the audit trail keeps a label that label comes from a fixed list rather than from whoever ran the job (00-conventions §7a, D-125). A key stayed the wrong shape for them on purpose: a sweep is not a caller and should not have to authenticate, which is why a secretless kind of api_key was refused rather than built.
  • A way in when nobody who could hold system.admin can log in is a report and a written procedure, not a mechanism. Integrity check 9 lists who could hold it and now also says whether they can sign in, and the recovery itself is written beside the account state machine (domain/02 §3, D-126). What is refused is the mechanism: a key is not a person, carries nobody's authority, and may never hold that code, so it cannot be the thing that walks in when a person cannot.
  • The outbound direction. Everything above is a caller arriving. An export, a refund, anything this system pushes rather than is asked for has no design (F-27).
  • Nothing about the wire — how a secret is presented, what it looks like, how a session survives a login. D-072 is the standing division, and what is decided here is only what may be stored: a hash, and nothing else.
  • No rate limiting, no IP allowlist. Either would be a second, weaker authorization implementation, which §10 rejects because they diverge; the weaker one becomes the exploit. A rate limit is an availability measure and earns no permission code.

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
• Who opens the Unusual section of the tab. §6.1 rules the MEMBERS question itself, including that the section lists every live grant naming a ROLE(…) operand whose expression carries no MEMBERS; what remains is F-21's older question, whether a tab gets opened at all (F-13, F-21).
  • The holder period. Nothing forces a role_holder row to end, and the report stands alone (§4, D-071).
  • Who may compose an expression? audience.manage covers creating and editing a set, and the catalog is silent on the edit that puts EVERYONE into a grant's audience (appendix/permission-catalog.md §12). No new code was invented for this — the gap is the finding.
  • What reopens the settled answers on this page. Two named conditions, both carried so nobody has to rediscover them: a materialized effective_permission table becomes worth building at D-112's size trigger, and then only as a performance structure with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window — never as a record of whom a rule reached (§8); and a historical check is answered by the same evaluator running over history as it is written, which is not a promise for the operands whose set is a current fact (06a, F-7, F-17).
  • The integration this system calls. Everything §10a designs is a caller arriving; who authorizes an export, a refund or a pull — and whether a permission code and an actor are even the right shape for what is a job — is open (F-27).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

Decisions behind this page: D-005, D-011, D-013, D-019, D-031, D-032, D-042, D-045, D-052, D-053, D-068, D-069, D-070, D-071, D-072, D-074, D-077, D-079, D-080, D-081, D-083, D-086, D-088, D-090, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-102, D-103, D-105, D-106, D-107, D-109, D-112, D-113, D-114, D-116, D-117, D-118, D-119, D-120, D-121, D-122, D-123, D-124, D-125, D-126.

docs.title: Audiences and Selectors
docs.text: The language a grant is aimed at a set of people in: the expression grammar, the seeded selector registry, the rules that keep the tree safe, and what a grant's reach is recorded in. Every set this language names is a set of people, and a grant may instead name one person or one registered key — and a key is inside no set this language can name (06 §10a). This is the audience half of 06-authorization-model.md and continues its numbering at §6.2 — read that page first for scopes, channels, grants, the resolver and precedence.

docs.title: 6.2 Audiences — an expression over named sets
docs.text:
A grant names a person, an audience or a registered key — exactly one of the three, never two (D-042, D-116). An audience is an expression over named sets of people, stored as a tree of binary nodes and aimed at by a grant (D-101). Fields, storage rules and the write-path checks are in data-model/05 §8; what belongs here is the language, and why it is shaped like this.

Author in sets. Evaluate per person.

A check asks about one person, so the resolver compiles the expression down to a predicate and never materializes a set. An implementation that evaluates MEMBERS as a list of ids and then tests for containment pays a row per member, per request — at the size D-112 states, a few hundred rows, and every one of them is a row the answer never needed. That is the one way to get this wrong, which is why it is a requirement rather than an implementation note, and it has no exception: nothing in this design expands a set in order to warm a store, because no store of answers exists (06 §8).

What the rule does not forbid, because the batch API would otherwise violate it: which_of(people[], code, item) evaluates the predicate for the people already in hand — the rows of the page being drawn — and is therefore a batched predicate, not an expansion. What stays forbidden is deriving a set in order to answer a question about one person, which is the direction that costs a row per member and returns an answer about one of them. The test is which side you started from: the person, or the set.

The two notations this language could have used — set algebra, and a per-person boolean formula — describe the same function: p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is by definition (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C. The choice therefore never decided what the machine computes; it decided what gets stored and what a writer is allowed to say. The set form won, and D-060 is the reason: a per-person boolean language is the door to a rule engine, because once &, | and ! exist, the next operand anybody wants is AGE >= 15 or FEE_PAID, and there is a parser standing there to accept it.

Why a set language closes that by rule instead of by discipline: an operand must be a named operand — a row of the registry (D-107). OLDER(18) is a row, and it denotes a set: the people who are eighteen or older on the date being checked. AGE >= 15 is not a row and cannot be one, because the language has nowhere to put >=. Every operand in the registry is a test with a set on the other side of it, so reading one column against one date (MEMBERS) is not a different kind of thing from joining one table against one period (GROUP(x)) — nothing in the model stores the list of members either. That is what keeps the rule engine out, and it does not depend on which predicates a reader happens to grant the status of "set".

So: the vocabulary is open and the grammar is closed. More attribute operands will arrive, as rows and by decision; the three operators stay the three operators; and D-060's decision stands untouched: no eligibility rule table, no prerequisite system, nothing evaluated anywhere but in can(). A person may write an age gate out of the vocabulary; the system applies none of its own accord. The premise behind opening the vocabulary is quoted in D-107: the people writing these rules know what they are writing — a claim about the authors and not about the people a rule reaches, so the two limits drawn there are this page's business too.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text:
expr     := term ( '+' term )*
term     := operand ( ( '*' | '-' ) operand )*
operand  := EVERYONE | MEMBERS
          | ROLE '(' name ')' | GROUP '(' name ')' | name
          | PERSON '(' person ')'
          | AUDIENCE '(' code ')'
          | OLDER '(' n ')' | YOUNGER '(' n ')'
          | ATTENDED | PLACED | CONFIRMED | ON_WAITLIST | ORGANIZERS
          | ATTENDED '(' event ')' | PLACED '(' event ')' | CONFIRMED '(' event ')'
          | ON_WAITLIST '(' event ')' | ORGANIZERS '(' event ')'
          | PRESENT '(' event ')'   ← considered and refused; never in the registry. See §Event sets
          | '(' expr ')'

OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are ordinary named operands — n a whole number of years, read against the birth date on the date being checked, which is why they sit in the column of the table below headed "the set, on the checked date" rather than anywhere in a section about conditions. MEMBERS * OLDER(13) * YOUNGER(19) — thirteen to eighteen, a band from two operands — is a set expression in exactly the sense MEMBERS * GROUP(cubs) * PERSON(a) is, and it parses under the rules below with nothing added to them.

This block and §The selectors are copies of the registry in data-model/05 §8, which is the registry — the seeded rows, not the prose. An operand that is not a seeded row does not exist however natural it looks in a grammar, and copies of a table drift from it (F-5); nothing checks a copy, so treat the registry as the source and re-copy rather than re-derive.

Boolean spellings are offered for this language and declined. p ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ C is (p ∈ A ∧ p ∈ B) ∨ p ∈ C, so &, | and ! would name three operators this grammar already has, and !A is already written EVERYONE - A at the same cost once brackets are printed the way the canonical form requires. A notation that expresses nothing new is not free: two spellings of one operator means the canonical rendering has to pick one, the editor has to accept both, the write-path checks have to reason about both, and two people's identical rules stop being textually comparable — which is the property the canonical rendering exists to buy. + - * are the only operators, and negation is a subtraction from EVERYONE, which has the extra merit of printing the universe it negates against instead of hiding it behind one character.

There is no comparison operator, and that is where the safety of this language lives. No >=, no <, no bare AGE, no FEE_PAID unless FEE_PAID is a row of the registry with an evaluator behind it. A writer composes named operands; the vocabulary grows by decision, not by typing.

A hand-written set of people is a sum, not an arm: PERSON(a) + PERSON(b). There is no operand for "the names somebody typed into this audience" and no table behind one (D-105); a set of one is a set, and a set of three is the same thing three times.

Merging the hand-written names into GROUP(x) is refused, and the refusal is why the replacement is a sum of PERSON() leaves rather than a group. Naming three people in one grant would create a row in the group browser that is not a group anybody talks about, and a group's members are the organization's record of who is in it, true when no grant points at it (D-098) — so editing a roster to move one grant's reach edits a fact that other grants read. PERSON(a) is the answer that respects that rule, and GROUP(kitchen) += Honza is not. person_group_member is the only dated set of people the system stores.

Widening everything a named set is used for is not a single edit. "add the kitchen crew to everything the troop-staff group is used in" is one edit per rule that names it. Named sets are the composition mechanism: GROUP(kitchen) + ROLE(troop_staff) composes as much as a naming edge ever did, in one grant, and a composite used more than once is named once as a saved audience and aimed at (D-091). The language has intersection and difference as well as union, which is why the counselor example below is writable at all.

Operators: + union, - difference, * intersection.

Precedence: * and - bind tighter than +; * and - bind equally, left to right; brackets override.

The canonical stored rendering prints every bracket, always. The alternative is a grant whose meaning is recoverable only by someone who memorized that table, and the reason this is a requirement rather than a courtesy is the worked example below: the same string means different things under different precedence, and a stored grant is read by people years later who did not write it. Because canonicalization happens on save, changing the precedence rule later changes nothing already stored — a nice property, and the second reason the rendering is a requirement.

Assumption: a bare name operand is legal. It is not in D-101's printed grammar and is required by its prose twice over — without it, MEMBERS * COUNSELORS, which D-100 writes as an import control, does not parse. Recorded in ../open-questions.md.

Names are one namespace, and that is a dependency. A bare name resolves against role and person_group together, since ROLE() and GROUP() do not have to disambiguate. So names are unique across both tables — and no single constraint spans two tables, so the write path carries the rule and an integrity check asserts that it does (D-081) — with case, whitespace and separators folded on write. Every selector_type.code is a reserved name, so a group called MEMBERS is refused at the save rather than silently rewriting every expression in the system. What is stored is always kind + id, so a rename never rewrites a grant.

docs.title: The selectors
docs.text:
Selector The set, on the checked date Argument Notes EVERYONE Any person, including non-members and the public none Legal — and the reason the editor must show its reach (§The cost lands on the editor) MEMBERS Anyone who passes is_current_member, on the checked date none Evaluated live. 06 §6.1 OLDER(n) Anyone whose birth date makes them n or more years old on the checked date a whole number of years D-107. The only operand in the registry whose argument is not a thing — an integer, so it references nothing: nothing to repoint on a merge, nothing for a cascade YOUNGER(n) Anyone strictly under n years old on the checked date a whole number of years The pair exists so the complement is not written EVERYONE - OLDER(n), which is correct and unreadable. The two partition the population among people who have a birth date: someone without one is in neither, and that is not a failure — see §The rules that make the tree safe PERSON(p) Just that person a person How a named individual's exception lives inside the expression that granted the rule; since D-105 also how several named people are written — summed ROLE(x) / x Holders of role x (role_holder) a role name GROUP(x) / x Members of group x (person_group_member) a group name AUDIENCE(code) Another saved audience's set, evaluated live an audience code D-103; the one operand whose argument is a decision about access rather than a roster, so the one that can name another audience (§6.2) ATTENDED / ATTENDED(e) Said yes to this event / to e optional event response = attending PLACED / PLACED(e) Said yes and is not waitlisted — the capacity set optional event The set the events module counts CONFIRMED / CONFIRMED(e) Holds a paid place: PLACED and is_confirmed optional event ON_WAITLIST / ON_WAITLIST(e) Attending and waitlisted optional event ORGANIZERS / ORGANIZERS(e) Runs this event optional event Appointed on the event, and still grants nothing by itself (§Event sets) PRESENT(e) — not seeded §Event sets. Refused by decision — nothing in the language could refuse it as a kind, so the refusal is a rule about the failure direction

Guardianship is not a selector, in either spelling — GUARDIANS and GUARDIANS(p) are not rows of the registry and were never seeded (D-113). Guardianship is a channel carrying a right_level of none/view/write on the live guardianship row, reaching any action about that child — wider than any grant an operand could have assembled, and narrower in the only way that matters (06 §1, D-074). An operand aimed at a child's guardians would therefore offer, one code at a time, a subset of what those people already hold. A kept list of a child's contact adults is a person_group.

Thirteen selectors, and this table is a copy of data-model/05a-audience-and-grammar.md §8, which is the registry. Which selectors ship is settled: these thirteen, seeded, organization-read-only, and a fourteenth is a decision entry plus a seed row (F-5). A count printed in prose is a count somebody has to reprint when the table changes, and no check prints it, so the registry row set is the number.

A key can never be one of them. No selector names a registered caller, no operand may hold one in either of its reference arms, and a fourteenth row for "the integrations" was offered and refused: a caller is one row and never a set, for the same reason an office is one person and never a rule — a set is the wrong grain for a thing that must be individually revocable. So a grant aimed at integrations is one grant per caller, and there is no set they are all in, EVERYONE included, since that operand reads any person. The registry stays at thirteen, and the module's largest machinery is untouched: nothing about a key is compiled, and ruleset_version still bumps on audience_operand plus selector_type and on nothing else (D-117, 06 §10a).

Bound operands — the argument-less forms — are the important half, and they exist to kill a specific flaw. ATTENDED(<event 1204>) written on event 1204 is one grant per event with the event's own id typed into it, so "every participant may see the other participants" is a thing you do 400 times and forget on the 401st. Bound, it is one expression written the same way every time. Two rules make that safe, and both are enforced when the grant is saved, refused with the operand named in the message:

  • A bound operand is legal only on an item-scope grant. At the unit there is nothing to bind it to.
  • A bound operand is legal only on a matching item type. PLACED on a group grant is refused, because that item is not an event. This is selector_type.argument_type checked against grant_scope_type.

selector_type is a seeded registry, not an enum — code, takes_argument, binds_to_item, argument_type. Which operands take an argument, which may bind to the item, and what type their argument is are columns of this table, not lists in code: the parser reads its reserved words from it, the editor builds its dropdown from it, and the write path checks arity against it. The language is data.

docs.title: The example, worked
docs.text:
The organization wrote:

MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS

meaning "all counselors that are not part of the group schuzka2026-1". Under the fixed precedence — - and * equal, left to right — it parses as:

(MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS

which is what its author meant, and that is the string that gets stored, brackets and all: the canonical rendering of what was typed.

The hazard is real even though this string lands safely, and that is exactly why the rendering is a requirement. Read with * taking the tighter binding — the other natural choice, and the one a writer who thinks of - as "everything except" will assume — the identical text means:

MEMBERS - (GROUP(schuzka2026-1) * COUNSELORS)

"everyone except the counselors in that group": a different set of people, and a far wider grant — nearly the whole membership instead of a handful of counselors. The corrected bracketed form is (MEMBERS - GROUP(schuzka2026-1)) * COUNSELORS, and that is what the editor writes to storage whichever way the typed string parses, so no stored expression is ever ambiguous and none is ever read bare. What canonicalization does not do is tell the writer, after the fact, that the expression they typed meant the wide thing. That is the editor's preview, and it is the same requirement as §The cost lands on the editor. The bare form does not mean the wide thing under this design; a parser with the wrong table would compute it, and then the stored brackets would disagree with the answer.

docs.title: Event sets, and the two sets that are refused
docs.text:
Nothing owns an event. There is no event.org_unit_id and no unit-authority test standing behind an event permission: an event is an item like any other, event.create is held at the unit and creates one, and a unit grant reaches every event because there is no tier between the unit and the item and no owner to test (D-102). The people connected to an event are named by selectors that bind to it.

ORGANIZERS is how the people running an event are named, and it is not a contradiction of D-062: an event_organizer row grants nothing stands, because an operand is a set, not a grant. An appointment is aimed at by grants; it is not special-cased inside the resolver. So the rule that answers are read by that event's organizers (D-061) is said where permissions are said: one item-scope allow of event.answer.view on the event, aimed at the bare operand ORGANIZERS, written in the same transaction as the event row. It is one of the twelve grants the act of creating an event writes for that event (D-151), and it is written without MEMBERS: an organizer appointed for one weekend is not required to be a paying member.

Presence is refused, and saying so here is the point. PRESENT(<event>) over was_present is not a selector, and the reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until someone takes a register, so an operand built on it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. That column is a safeguarding signal, three-valued on purpose (D-067), and keeping it out of this language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things." Wherever presence tempts a reader, that is the answer.

WHITELISTED does not exist — there is no stored state to name. The nearest facts are source = staff (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. Either it means one of those or it is a new column on event_registration, which is an events decision and not a selector decision — and that decision is made: refused, with no reserved name (D-148). It stays unseeded rather than being implied by a word in a grammar, and the refusal lives where the presence tiers are listed (07a §9).

docs.title: The rules that make the tree safe
docs.text:
The expression is stored as a tree: one row per node, a node being operator + left_id + right_id, a leaf being selector_kind + selector_arg_id, with audience_id denormalized onto every row so the read path is one indexed fetch and never walks a parent chain. Nothing bounds how tall or how wide an expression may get: there is no depth or width limit on an expression, in the column or in the code, and nothing stands in for one (D-105). "A check costs a bounded amount" is therefore not a property of this system: an expansion is bounded only by acyclicity. The tree is stored exactly as the writer wrote it — one row per node, two operands and one operator, left to right, no rebalancing — because a rebalanced tree is a different expression from the one a person wrote, and storing that expression rather than a normalized equivalent is the entire reason the tree exists.

  • Exactly one shape per row. A node has an operator and children and no selector; a leaf has a selector and neither. Expressible, so it stays a constraint.
  • One parent, never a DAG. A side table letting two expressions share a node is refused: editing the shared node would silently widen every grant using it. Structure, plus a CI check that no such table exists.
  • Cycles are refused when the row is saved, and the two walks that look for them are the only structural guard this module has. Structurally hard to build, refused rather than trusted, for the reason D-091 gives for its own guard: a hand-fixed row, a restore from before the guard existed. 1. Inside one tree: walk the parent chain from the row upward and refuse a revisit. 2. Across audiences: follow every AUDIENCE leaf and refuse a cycle through them at any distance (D-103). A single tree cannot cycle; a forest of audiences naming each other is not a tree, so the walk over a graph is not dead code, and it must never be relaxed — an expansion that never terminates is the failure nothing else here is standing against. The read path gets neither a hop counter nor a cycle check, which is the whole design: a cap on the read path becomes the thing that decides who a grant reaches, in exactly the case where the data is already wrong. The listing of what a rule names is a tab on the permissions page, with a Broken and an Unusual section, computed when opened, with no cadence to record because nothing runs; it lists the rules that name something deprecated, hidden or disabled, or that fail to resolve at all (D-109). It is not a guard in D-081's sense — nothing is blocked, no write is refused — but a report has to be remembered and a tab is where the person already is, which is the difference between a convention and a decoration. Unbounded cost is accepted at the stated size, and nobody is expected to go looking for a report (F-21).
  • selector_arg_id has no foreign key — it points at role, person_group, person, event or audience, five kinds of entity, depending on kind, or at nothing at all, since OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) write their integer into the same column and an 18 is not a reference (D-107). It is D-011's already-accepted trade-off, with its compensating orphan check. Every hand-named person in the system is a value in this keyless column, so a person merge and a redaction must repoint every leaf naming the absorbed or erased person, in all five entity kinds. Retiring a role, a group or an audience is not part of that duty: it is one write to that row, never N writes to N expressions (D-109), so a leaf that names a retired thing is not possible. PERSON(x) names a person, and D-088 lets a redaction require the row to actually go. Erasure wins. The reason the duty cannot be expressed anywhere better is stated in shape 3 — the ORM has no key to follow. And the failure is not tidiness: a leaf naming nobody is the empty set, which is quiet on the allow side and loud on the deny side, so EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with an un-repointed x stops subtracting anybody and denies everybody.
  • An operand that does not resolve is the empty set, and an expression that cannot be evaluated reaches nobody. Fail closed, in every direction. In a lawful database this has exactly one cause — a redacted person — because nothing else a leaf can name is deletable any more. A hand-edited row can still produce one, and disabled deliberately produces the same answer by design (below), so the evaluator's behaviour must not change: the empty set, narrowing an allow and widening a deny, listed in the tab above.
  • Nothing a rule can name is deleted. It is given a state instead — and the three states must stay three different things or one of them will quietly become another (D-109):
State Still resolves? Offered when writing a rule? Flagged? deprecated yes, unchanged no — not addable to a new rule, not introduceable by editing one yes, highlighted wherever the editor shows it hidden yes, unchanged no no — it is not obsolete, it is not everybody's business disabled no — the empty set no yes, and it is the only state that changes an answer

The invariant that stops deprecated drifting into disabled is checkable and cheap: deprecating or hiding what an expression names must not change the set the expression resolves to. That is the precise failure this whole design exists to make impossible — a rule that quietly stops granting because somebody tidied a list — so it belongs beside the two cycle walks as something a reviewer checks, not as a convention (D-081). disabled is the loudest switch in this system: it stops every rule naming that role, group or audience, in every scope, at once, and re-enabling restores all of them — a widening in which nobody edited a grant. So the flag is an audited write that prints the rules it touches, resolved before and after, which is the report shape D-104 and D-105 adopted for their own migrations, and it is a ruleset write (D-111); it is also the answer to how do I turn off that whole naming without editing forty grants?, which otherwise has no answer except a deny per grant. A deprecated or disabled name stays reserved (D-101), so nothing new can claim the word and split its meaning in two.

The cost lands on the editor, not the resolver. A grant's reach is not visible in the row that grants it, and seeing it is a requirement on the screen rather than a nicety: the person saving the grant must see the people, not the audience's name, because nothing in the grammar stops an expression from containing EVERYONE, and because PLACED means different people on different events (D-091, D-102). So the preview is computed for an item and says so on screen. That is a real amount of work for the editor, and it is the only thing standing between a writer and a grant that reaches everybody the organization has. At the sizes stated in D-112 that is a few hundred people, which is not reassuring — it is the same warning with a number under it, and the number says the preview will not be slow (F-15, F-16).

docs.title: What a grant's reach is recorded in
docs.text:
"Who could read this in 2023?" is answered by the words, and that is the whole of the answer — "Words only — the expression is the record" (D-110). This page promises no other answer and stores no list that would be one.

  • The expression is the record of a grant's reach. The preview still prints a resolved set before a save, and the audit row logs that printing as a rendering on a date, not as a statement of who was in it. A row saying this grant reached these 214 people starts decaying the night somebody's birthday falls; a row saying this person wrote these words on this date about this item cannot go stale.
  • What is refused beside it: keeping the preview's list alongside the audit row. That is a roster table, and it would store — indefinitely, against D-088's window — a per-person record of people who were never granted anything, only covered. This module refuses that trade whenever it is offered in another shape.
  • Why words-only is sound: nothing a rule can name is deleted (§ above), so the nouns survive. A retired office still resolves; a deprecated group still resolves; a name stays reserved. Refuse to delete the nouns and keeping only the words is not an amputation: without that ruling this answer would mean "the past is usually unanswerable"; with it, the past is usually computable and what is left is honestly bounded (D-110).
  • Answerable for ROLE, GROUP and MEMBERS (all periods, all dated), unanswerable for bound event operands (event_registration records the current fact), and lost for the hand-typed names once their audit payloads expire — which is what F-17 states rather than solves.
  • The conceded part, named so nobody finds it later: editing a shared audience changes what every grant naming it has meant all along, because those grants hold a word and not a copy. An edit to a shared audience is a retrospective edit to every rule that names it, and a recomputation for May will use today's inner expression. D-103 accepted this as the price of reuse; D-110 records that it is also the reason a past-date answer can be wrong rather than merely missing. The control is D-103's — the editor prints the resolved set before an edit to a shared expression saves, so the person editing sees at least once the thing they are changing backwards in time. What is not kept is a history of inner expressions: the audit trail records the edit, not the meaning that existed before it.
  • There is no snapshot, and no route to one. A materialized table of whom a rule reached is the roster just refused, and F-7 is dissolved. What returns at D-112's trigger is a materialized table on its own merits — a performance structure with a per-person invalidation handle and a stated staleness window, not a way back into the past (06 §8).

Decisions behind this page: D-011, D-042, D-060, D-061, D-062, D-067, D-074, D-081, D-088, D-091, D-098, D-100, D-101, D-102, D-103, D-104, D-105, D-107, D-109, D-110, D-111, D-112, D-113, D-116, D-117.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Camps, trips, hikes, and the occasional jamboree: things that happen on a date, that people register for, and that somebody has to run.

An event is an item in the permission system: grant_scope_type carries a row for it, a grant may be scoped to one event and mean that event alone (D-006), and audiences exist partly to express "tell everyone about this event" (D-042). Nothing owns an event (D-102): authority reaches one from a grant at the unit or a grant on it and from nowhere else, and the people connected to it are named by selectors that bind to the event being checked.

Data model: data-model/08-events.md and data-model/08a (the bound selectors, the three queries, the integrity checks).

Section numbers are shared across the two parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 07-events.md holds §1–§7, 07a §8–§13 (capacity and the waitlist, presence, cancellation, payments, the forms, open issues).

docs.title: 1. What an event is, and what it is not
docs.text:
An event is a thing with a date that people sign up for.

A weekly meeting is not an event. It is a group — a person_group whose dated member rows already say "this child takes part in this Thursday group" (D-098). A Thursday group that meets forty times a year is already recorded, and making each meeting an event would create forty rows saying what one row says, with forty capacities, forty organizer rosters and forty chances to be wrong. Events are the things you register for: camps, trips, hikes, the summer jamboree.

The boundary has a cost, and it is worth knowing before asking the question. "Was Jan at the meeting on 14 March?" is not answerable from the events module. That is presence tracking for a standing group, which is a different feature; what is modelled here is presence at a dated occasion.

There is no recurrence. No event_series, no RFC 5545 rule, no occurrence table: a group that camps four weekends a year has four events. Recurrence is what makes event tables complicated, and the one thing that looked as though it needed it — meetings — is already modelled as a group.

docs.title: 2. Nothing owns an event
docs.text:
An event is an item, registered in grant_scope_type under the code event, like a group or a role is. It has no owner. There is no column on event naming a person, a group, or a unit, and nothing in the resolver tests one (D-102).

Two facts are the whole of how authority arrives:

A grant at the unit reaches every event there is, because after D-097 there is no scope between the unit and an item, and no ownership relation to test A grant on one event reaches that event and nothing else

A joint camp is an event. The second group's children reach it because a grant names them, exactly like every other reader, and nobody has to arbitrate "whose event is this?" — the question has no column to be asked of.

Creating one needs event.create, whose applies_to is unit: anybody holding it creates an event, and nobody else does. Writing event.create on an event is refused when the grant is saved, with the reason in the message — an event cannot be created twice, and a creation permission attached to a thing that already exists answers no question (D-099).

The anti-pattern, named once. An event does not belong to a unit, a group or a person: event.org_unit_id is not in the schema, can_event() is not in the resolver, and there is no unit-authority rule to reach across (appendix/removed-concepts.md). An event is one dated row, and the question "who may see this event?" has one home, which is the grant table.

docs.title: Writing an event on one event
docs.text:
Because a unit-scope grant reaches everything, an item grant is for the narrow case, and the two are not interchangeable. This is where the model refuses things at the save rather than discovering them at the check:

Written Result event.edit on one event Allowed. A capability on the item — D-006 unchanged event.create on one event Refused at save, with the reason: applies_to is unit membership.terminate on one event Refused at save, for the same reason — a membership is a fact about a person at the unit, which no event owns A grant naming PLACED at the unit Refused at save, naming the operand — there is no item for it to bind to (§7)

docs.title: 3. Registration: one record, two stored answers, and no "unanswered"
docs.text:
A person's relationship to an event is captured in one row — event_registration.

What you asked for How it is stored attending response = 'attending' not attending response = 'not_attending' unanswered no row at all

"Unanswered" is not a value, and that is deliberate. It is the absence of a registration. Writing a row that says "this person has not answered" means writing rows for people who have not acted, which then have to be cleaned up when the event ends and which cannot distinguish "asked and silent" from "never asked" without a third table.

Returning someone to unanswered means removing the row (DELETE, recorded in audit_log) — which is the honest act, and the one that leaves the least behind.

Who counts as unanswered? (the people a live grant reaches on this event) MINUS (people with a registration). The question "who hasn't replied yet?" is a subtraction, and it is a query — data-model/08a §9. The reachable side is a set of people named by grants, which is what makes the subtraction a query at all.

docs.title: The registration window
docs.text:
Registration is open inside a period and closed outside it, and the period is two columns on the event — registration_opens_at and registration_closes_at.

NULL on the close means until the event starts — the unlimited case. NULL on the open means the window opens as soon as the event is visible at all: appropriate for a hike, wrong for a jamboree whose sign-up should not open before the dates have been decided.

docs.title: 4. Who may register: capability, not a separate rule engine
docs.text:
Registering yourself requires one permission: event.register_self, held on that event — either by an allow on the event itself, or by an allow at the unit, which after D-097 reaches the event along with every other item. Nothing else.

Why there is no eligibility rule: the capability already is one. A person holding event.register_self on an event may register for it, and there is no second question behind that — no age table, no prerequisite, no eligibility row, nothing evaluated outside can() (D-060).

There is no level to compare. view, contribute, manage and admin as ranks name nothing: a grant allows or denies one code at one scope, and the answer to a check is allowed when some live allow applies and no live deny applies (D-099). Four questions, four codes, each answered by its own row of access_grant:

Question Code May they see it? event.view May they register for it? event.register_self May they run its roster? event.manage_participants May they mark the register? event.presence.mark

Two of those codes being held by one person is two rows, not a person who sits at some level — which is what makes "what exactly does this person have on this camp?" a question with an answer.

This is why audiences matter here. Registering 200 children one at a time is 200 grant rows — but opening the event to everybody who currently holds a membership is one: a grant whose scope is that event, whose grantee is an audience whose expression is MEMBERS, and whose effect is allow. That row is what D-042 was built for, and it is the normal way to run an open event. Per-person grants are for the exceptions.

docs.title: An age rule is an audience, not a rule
docs.text:
The obvious objection is a camp for 11–14 year-olds: how does a grant express "only 11-to-14s"? A named set. The organization keeps a group of the older section and opens the camp to GROUP(<that group>) (D-098). An age-gated camp is a camp opened to a set whose members are that age.

There is a second way to write that sentence, and it is the same kind of thing. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) are seeded operands of the registry (D-107): shipped rows of selector_type, alongside MEMBERS, whose predicate the resolver owns, read against person.birth_date on the date being checked and composed by + - * like every other operand. So the camp for 11-to-14s is also writable as (MEMBERS * OLDER(11)) - YOUNGER(15) — one grant, one expression, no roster to keep current. The group is still the better answer where the section is a real group with a real roster behind it, because a maintained group says who is in it and an age expression only says who qualifies; the two are not rivals and an organization will use both.

An age ceiling is writable, and it is not written. event.register_self on this event, aimed at MEMBERS * YOUNGER(15), is an ordinary grant that stops a 9-year-old registering for a camp for teenagers. Write no such grant and nothing in the system objects, because nothing in it could: an event has no age ceiling of its own. D-070 is therefore closed as a choice, not as a limit — the organization keeps the judgement in the roster a leader reads and in the attributed registration that records who let a child through. Read it as a decision every time the next restriction is requested.

There are no min_age/max_age columns on event, and there will not be some.

Why: a condition evaluated at registration time that the capability model does not know about is the first rule-engine rule, and the second is always cheaper than the first. Two years after that, the answer to "who can register for this?" stops being readable from access_grant. A ceiling written in a grant is readable there; a ceiling written on the event row is exactly the thing that is not.

What makes the residual risk survivable is three properties the schema already has. The registration is attributable — source = 'staff' with a named created_by, so the judgement belongs to somebody. Age is one join away — person.birth_date, which the roster query in data-model/08a §9 already selects, so any list a leader works from can carry it without a new column anywhere. And age is one operand away, which is what makes the ceiling above a writing choice rather than a feature request. The ordinary case — the age-bounded camp — is handled twice over: open the event to the set whose members are that age, by a group somebody maintains or by the age operands themselves.

A writer may not type AGE >= 13. The clause to quote is that an operand must be a named operand — a row of the registry — and this language has no comparison operator for AGE >= 13 to be assembled out of (D-107). OLDER(13) is a set of people: the ones who are thirteen or older on the date being checked, in the same way MEMBERS is the set of people who pass is_current_member and ROLE(x) is the set who hold that office. Every operand in the registry is a test with a set behind it (06a §6.2).

Guardianship is deliberately not a selector, in either spelling (GUARDIANS and GUARDIANS(x)) (D-113): "True, GUARDIANS should not be selectable in the audience, guardians can perform ANY action (their read/write perms grant) on behalf of the child." A check about a child asks whether a live guardianship row links the two people and reads right_level ∈ none | view | write off it — a lookup over a relationship, not a set the language resolves — so an aimed-at-guardians operand would hand those people, one code at a time, a subset of what the channel already gives them.

The registry is organization-read-only, so the next predicate anyone wants arrives as a deployment — a shipped row with its evaluator arm beside it — and not as a setting. Either way every answer to "who may register" keeps living in one table, which is the property worth defending.

docs.title: 5. Organizers are appointed, not granted
docs.text:
An event has a set of organizers — the people running it. That list is event_organizer, and it is the domain answer to "who is running this?", labelled, ordered, attributed.

An event_organizer row grants nothing. access_grant remains what it is good at — showing a treasurer the books, opening the page to an audience, naming a parent who may register their child — and organizers are a separate concept: who is running this (D-062). An operand is a set, not a grant, so naming ORGANIZERS in an expression says who is in the set and confers nothing, in exactly the way that naming ROLE(leaders) or any audience has never conferred anything (D-005, D-042).

The consequence worth understanding: an organizer is an appointment on the thing being run. It can carry a label ('lead', 'cook', 'driver') and an order, and it is not a permission bundle — it does not carry event.edit, it says who the organizers are. Like a role, an organizer is a person named against something, and the codes that follow from it are the live grants that aim at them (D-100).

Why the two do not drift. The tempting design writes an access_grant whenever an organizer is added, so "organizers" is just a query over grants. It fails on the label (a grant has no room for "cook"), on the ordering, and on the reverse question — "who is running this camp?" should not be answered by reading a permission table. Two concepts, each doing its own job.

What an organizer gets. Membership of event_organizer makes a person a member of the set ORGANIZERS. What that set may do is whatever a live grant aims at it, and the act that creates the event writes twelve of those grants in the same transaction as the event row — one item-scope allow per code whose applies_to admits an event, every one aimed at the bare operand ORGANIZERS, the set derived rather than hand-picked (D-151; §12). One of the twelve is event.grant_access: an organizer hands access to the event they run without holding access_grant.create at the unit, bounded by the scope they can name, by applies_to, and since D-163 by the twelve they already hold at that event — the last of those three binds nothing, because handing out what they hold is exactly what the bundle gave them, and it is the grant reaching past their own event that the ceiling now refuses. Everything outside those twelve reaches an organizer the way it reaches anybody else — through a grant that person holds.

docs.title: 6. How authority reaches an event
docs.text:
Through a grant, and through nothing else. A grant at the unit reaches every event; a grant on one event reaches that event (§2). The resolver matches scope exactly, so a check for event.view at ('event', 42) looks for a grant at that exact scope, and a person whose job is running the camp succeeds there only because their grant sits at the unit — the widest scope there is, with nothing between it and an item (D-097).

Nothing inherits, and nothing is bridged.
