There is no org_unit scope to hold a role at, no owner column for a check to read, and no wrapper adding a second can() call for events: can_event() is not in the resolver, and the artifact-and-unit distinction it existed to draw has no pair left to distinguish (D-102). The check is plain can(). What an organizer, an ORGANIZERS grant, and a unit-scope grant each mean is in §7 and in the table below.

Nothing in the model reproduces "access was granted by the body itself". With one unit there is no body that chooses which named adult may reach its children, and no scope between the unit and the item for such a choice to live at (D-097; the same loss, stated for a person's whole record, is at 06 §2).

docs.title: Organizers still matter, and here is how
docs.text:
Membership of event_organizer is what makes someone an organizer in the domain sense: the person on the list, with a label, whose name the parents see. Authority for acting on the event comes from grants, as it does everywhere else:

Who How they may manage it The person who runs the organization's camps event.manage_participants at the unit — the grant reaches every event Somebody trusted with one camp the same code on that event, as an item grant An organizer, as such only what a grant aims at ORGANIZERS — the twelve the event's creation wrote, answer-view among them Somebody the organization has excluded a deny on the event or at the unit; deny is absolute and beats every allow (D-013) system.admin Everything — the sole exception, as everywhere

The policy is stated positively and, where it must be, negatively. Positively: a person holds what the rows name, and there is no wider default to be exposed by and no narrow one to be trapped by. Negatively: where holding something must be impossible, a deny says so, and deny is absolute (D-013). A genuinely private event is therefore an act — an item grant, plus a deny at the unit when the audience is broad (§10).

docs.title: 7. The people connected to an event
docs.text:
Who is connected to this event? There is no question about which body may read a roster: with one unit and no exposure between bodies, the question has no subject (§6).

Five sets answer it, and each is a selector that binds to the event being checked — written with no argument when the grant is written on an event:

Operand On the event being checked means Explicit form ATTENDED said yes to this event ATTENDED(<event>) PLACED said yes and is not waitlisted — the capacity set PLACED(<event>) CONFIRMED holds a confirmed place CONFIRMED(<event>) ON_WAITLIST is waiting for a place ON_WAITLIST(<event>) ORGANIZERS runs this event ORGANIZERS(<event>)

The four attendance sets are not four ideas; each is a definition over two columns of event_registration, and the definitions are stated with the columns in data-model/08a §8. They are ordered by containment rather than by rank — CONFIRMED ⊆ PLACED, PLACED and ON_WAITLIST partition ATTENDED, and a person who declined is in none of them — and no level or ladder is involved in any of them (D-099).

The bound form is the important half, and it kills a specific flaw. ATTENDED(<event 1204>) written on event 1204 is one grant per event with the event's own id typed into it, so "every participant may see the other participants" is a thing you do 400 times and forget on the 401st. Bound, it is one expression written the same way every time. That is the whole reason the argument-less form exists, and the two rules that make it safe are write-path rules, stated as requirements in data-model/08a §8.

PRESENT(<event>) is refused, and this is where presence tempts a reader. The obvious sixth operand is "the ones who actually turned up", computed over was_present (§9). It is refused, and the reason is the failure direction: was_present is NULL until somebody takes a register, so an operand built on it would revoke a child's access to their own camp photos because a volunteer forgot to tick a box. was_present is three-valued on purpose as a safeguarding signal — keeping it out of the selector language is what keeps it meaning "a person recorded this" rather than "this is who may see things", and D-067's reasoning for the third value is the reasoning for the refusal. And this consequence is the whole of the refusal, which is worth saying out loud: OLDER(n) reads person.birth_date (D-107), so nothing structural stops anybody writing PRESENT — there is only ever going to be this argument standing in the way, and it holds on its own (06a).

WHITELISTED does not exist, and is not a selector. The nearest stored facts are source = 'staff' (an organizer entered them) and promotion off the waitlist. Either the word is to mean one of those or it names a new column on event_registration, which is an events decision and not a selector decision — and the events decision is now made: refused (D-148). Nothing here reserves the name, and the refusal is written where the presence tiers are listed (07a §9) rather than being implied by a word in a grammar.

docs.title: The screen must say which event it is talking about
docs.text:
The audience preview is a requirement rather than a nicety: "the person saving the grant is looking at one row that mentions no person at all", so the editor must show the expanded people a grant reaches (D-091).

The preview is computed for an item, and the screen says so. PLACED means different people on different events, so "who does this grant reach?" is not answerable from the grant row alone — for a grant whose expression contains a bound operand, it is answerable only as "on event 1204, these 84 people", and the screen must name the event it computed against rather than presenting the list as a property of the grant. The consequences are requirements on the editor and on the read path, not on the schema:

  • An expression containing a bound operand is previewed per item. Asking for a preview of such a grant at the unit is not a large computation, it is a refused one — the same refusal the save applies. The per-item preview carries no cap, no cache and no background job, on stated grounds: the system is specified against a few hundred people in the organization, a few dozen registrants on a typical event and a big camp on the order of two hundred, so previewing one item evaluates a couple of hundred predicates and nobody feels it (D-112). That size is stated, not measured — nothing in these documents has measured anything here — and the trigger for reopening it is a few thousand people, or a thousand registrants on one event. Nothing pre-pays this work: the preview computes it on open, still affordable, now with no fallback behind it (D-114).
  • Where no item is in hand, the editor says what the expression means, not who it reaches.
  • A compiled expression holds no item, precisely because the item arrives as a parameter, so the item is bound at resolution: nothing expanded or resolved while checking one event may be served for another, and any cache of a resolution rather than of a compilation is keyed by the item or it is wrong. The reason is the one behind the bound form — the same grant on two events has two answers (D-102, 06 §8).
  • A registration write is not a ruleset write, and that is a statement about compilations, not about answers: ruleset_version is bumped by a write to audience_operand or selector_type alone, and a compilation holds no person and no item, so being outside that set buys a check nothing. Marking a register, confirming a place, flipping is_confirmed or promoting somebody off the waitlist moves ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED and ON_WAITLIST, and the new state is visible on the next check, because resolution is live and there is no answer stored anywhere to be behind the roster; ORGANIZERS, the fifth bound operand, moves on its own rows with the same immediacy (D-114). And the D-081 answer to "who enforces this": nobody enforces "a registration change must reach an answer", because there is nothing left to invalidate (D-081) — the read path does it, and a read path cannot be forgotten.

Fail closed as everywhere else in the model, with the direction stated rather than implied: an operand that resolves to nothing contributes the empty set, which narrows what a + or a * reaches and widens what a - takes away — EVERYONE - PERSON(x) with a dead x denies everybody, lockout and fail-closed being the same event (D-106). A person with no birth date is not that kind of failure: the operand resolves perfectly well and they are simply not in OLDER(18), exactly as a person with no membership row is not in MEMBERS. A broken leaf is not silent and still stops nothing — it is listed on the tab on the permissions page, and no save is refused for it (D-109). And that tab is nearly empty by construction, which is the point of the ruling: nothing a rule names is ever deleted. A retired office, group or audience is flagged deprecated, hidden or disabled and keeps resolving — only disabled changes the answer, and it changes it to the empty set because somebody asked for exactly that. The one thing still able to break a leaf is a person, because D-088 lets a redaction require the row to actually go and erasure wins: a redacted person is the corpus's only remaining way to produce a broken leaf.

A preview is a statement about the day it was taken. OLDER(n) and YOUNGER(n) make that true of every age-bearing expression in the sharpest form there is: the 84 names on the screen are the people who qualify on that date, and a birthday moves the list with no write and no edit to the grant. Nothing is told about it and nothing needs to be: there is nothing to be stale, because every check resolves against live rows and a birthday moves the answer at the instant it happens (D-114). What the preview is a statement about is the date it was taken, and that is a fact about the calendar, not a lag to be closed.

The preview is a workbench, not a record — and the record is the expression (D-110). The audit row written when a grant is saved says this person wrote these words, about this item, on this date. What the preview printed alongside it is logged as a rendering on a date, never as a statement of who was in it: a stored list of everyone a rule happened to cover, kept after the rule was withdrawn, is the roster table this corpus has deleted twice. So "whom did this grant reach in May?" is answered, if at all, by evaluating the words against the data of May — and these documents do not promise the answer. Words-only is affordable rather than brave only because of D-109: since nothing a rule names is deleted, the words keep resolving long after their reason is gone. What that concedes, so nobody finds it later: a shared audience holds a word, not a copy, so an edit to a shared audience is a retrospective edit to every rule that names it, and a re-evaluation for May uses today's inner expression. The control is the preview this very section is about — the editor prints the resolved set before an edit to a shared expression saves, so the person editing sees at least once what they are changing backwards in time. And a preview that cannot be computed still shows that it could not be computed, rather than an empty list.

Decisions behind this page: D-005, D-006, D-013, D-042, D-060, D-062, D-067, D-070, D-081, D-088, D-091, D-097, D-098, D-099, D-100, D-102, D-106, D-107, D-109, D-110, D-112, D-113, D-114.

docs.title: Events: capacity, presence, payments and the forms
docs.text:
What happens between a filled capacity and a completed event: the waitlist, attendance, cancellation, the money, and the questions an organizer asks.

Section numbers are shared across the two parts and never renumbered, because other pages cite them by number and their anchors are built from them: 07-events.md holds §1–§7, 07a §8–§13 (capacity and the waitlist, presence, cancellation, payments, the forms, open issues).

docs.title: 8. Capacity and the waitlist
docs.text:
An event may have a capacity — beds, bus seats, a fire-safety limit. When it fills:

Registrations past capacity are accepted as waitlisted, not refused. A person who registers for a full camp appears on the list, ordered, marked as waiting, and an organizer promotes them when a place frees up.

This is a real feature rather than a flag, and it is the honest model of how a camp with twelve beds actually runs: the thirteenth caller is not turned away, they are written down. See data-model/08 §5 for the ordering and promotion mechanics.

And organizers may exceed capacity outright — deliberately, because a leader who knows there are two spare tents should not be blocked by a number they cannot edit mid-camp (D-065). The overrun is permitted, attributed, and reported (data-model/08a §10): an event running over its stated capacity is a fact the organization can see, not a state it cannot reach.

The way past the number is not the resolver: the waitlist fires only for source = 'self', and a registration written by a person holding event.register_other arrives as source = 'staff' and is admitted. event.register_other is a grant at the unit or on the event, like every other code (D-102).

So capacity is three things at once, and all three are intentional:

Behaviour Self-registration when full Waitlisted — never refused, never admitted A staff registration when full Admitted, the overrun reported Any capacity change An UPDATE, visible and attributed

The set capacity is compared against has a name: it is PLACED, the attending non-waitlisted registrations of an event (§7) — the same set PLACED selects and the same index the capacity test already uses.

docs.title: 9. Presence: what actually happened
docs.text:
The registration says what someone said. Presence says what happened.

event_registration.was_present is a nullable boolean: NULL = not yet marked, true = turned up, false = marked absent. The three-valued column is not sloppiness — it distinguishes "we did not take a register" from "we took a register and they were not there", which are different facts and only one of them is a safeguarding signal (D-067).

Why this matters more than it looks. For a camp, the end-of-week roster is the record of who was actually in the organization's care — the only "who was there" this design keeps, which is the reason it is marked deliberately rather than derived (D-156 removed the other reason anybody had to ask: the fee buys membership and nothing else, so no date in this system is evidence of cover, and the question "was this person a member on the date of the incident" is no longer a question this system is asked to answer). It is also the row that cannot be reconstructed afterwards from registrations. It is also why the column is marked by an organizer and recorded with who marked it and when.

Presence is not registration. A child who registered and did not come is a registration with was_present = false. A child who turned up without registering — a sibling along for the day — is not representable, deliberately: that child was not in the organization's care and must not silently appear to have been. Recording them means registering them, which means they have a guardian and the organizers have a name.

And presence is not a record class. It is a column of a registration and it inherits everything a registration is: the same retention — nothing about an event goes on a schedule, so this mark is readable for as long as the registration is (D-140) — and the same codes that already reach the roster and the mark (D-147). Refused on both halves: no presence_record table with a retention of its own, and no presence.view narrower than the roster's — the second would have been a permission whose whole purpose is to hide the fact of attendance from the people asking because they were there. This system keeps no safeguarding register: there are no background checks here (D-043) and no medical record (D-083), and a column with a special clock and a special permission would have been the first wall of an archive this design has refused four times. The protection this column has is that it is boring, and the question "who was there on 14 March" is answered by a report over registrations — which is why the index behind was_present serves a report and no selector.

And presence is not an audience. The temptation to build PRESENT(<event>) on this column — to let "everyone who came" be a set a grant names — is refused, and §7 states why: the column is NULL until somebody takes a register, so an operand over it makes access depend on a volunteer's diligence, and it would turn a safeguarding record into an access control. Attendance for the purposes of a grant stops at ATTENDED, PLACED, CONFIRMED and ON_WAITLIST.

And there is no WHITELISTED beside those four. No is_whitelisted column, no fifth tier, no operand of that name, no reserved selector code waiting for one (D-148). The word is what people reach for when they want an audience of the ones we invited, and anybody adding is_whitelisted is reimplementing grants badly: a tier is a state a registration is in, and an invitation is not about a registration at all — it is a grant aimed at a person, which is a row that already exists and says who aimed it at whom. The invited person who has not registered is described by the absence of a row until they do, and is ON_WAITLIST the moment they register onto a full event (D-059); that is not a gap a fifth value fills, because PLACED is the capacity set, so a whitelist set beside it misdescribes everybody in it. What this costs is what every prose refusal costs: nothing in the database refuses a future WHITELISTED row in selector_type, so an operand with no state behind it is a deployment bug and not a type error — the same exposure an off-list actor label carries.

docs.title: 10. Cancellation, and why there is no status column
docs.text:
There is no lifecycle status. An event is a row with dates and a set of grants.

Visibility is the permission model. A newly created event has no grants of its own, so whoever can see it can see it because of a grant they already hold — normally an event.view at the unit, which reaches every event and therefore every new one the moment it is created. Publishing is not a state change — it is granting someone access: an audience, a group, a role.

Why not a status enum: a status column and a permission system that both claim to say "who may see this" will eventually disagree, and the one that gets enforced is whoever wrote the last IF (D-064).

There is no narrow default, and that is the shape of the model. After D-097 the unit is the only scope there is, so a person holding event.view at the unit sees a half-typed event the instant it is committed, and there is no narrower scope a grant could have sat at instead. A genuinely private event is therefore an act — an item grant, plus a deny at the unit if the audience is broad — rather than the absence of one.

So the questions that a draft status would answer are answered by grants:

Question Answer "Is this ready to be seen?" Has anyone been granted event.view beyond the unit-scope holders? "Who can see it before it is announced?" Whoever a live allow names — including every unit-scope holder "How do I hide it again?" Revoke the grant — revoked_at set, row kept — or write a deny

Cancellation is a fact, not a status, and the logic diverges from visibility here because the audience is different: the people who need to find out are the people who registered, and they must be able to see the event to find out anything.

Three columns carry it: cancelled_at says when, cancelled_by says who — a person, so the decision has a name attached to it — and cancel_reason says why.

Cancelling by revoking grants would hide the cancellation from exactly the people who need it. The registrants are the ones who need to read that the camp is off; if the event is hidden by revoking their view, they see nothing at all — not "cancelled", just gone. So cancellation is recorded, and the event stays visible, marked.

A cancelled event stops accepting registrations (the registration window closes implicitly) and keeps every existing row: those registrations are the record that the camp was planned and who was coming. That record is exactly what is needed afterwards — to refund them, and to know whom a cancellation notice would have to reach, since nothing in this design sends one (D-164).

completed is derived, never set. cancelled_at IS NULL AND ends_at < now(). There is no state to keep consistent, and no job to move events between states.

One more thing, which is structural: there is no event.is_published and no cancelled status, but there is a cancelled_at. An event that is cancelled and an event that is merely past are distinguished by one NULL — and the "what needs attention?" query is WHERE cancelled_at IS NULL AND ends_at >= now(), ordering by start. That is the whole lifecycle.

docs.title: 11. Payments on events
docs.text:
An event may cost money, and payment confirms the place — but payment is never mandatory, because plenty of events are free.

The rule, stated once:

An event with a fee Registering creates an obligation; the place is confirmed on payment An event without a fee Registering confirms the place immediately An unpaid registration at capacity Holds a slot until the deadline, then releases to the waitlist Money The finance module's problem — events record that a fee applies and what it is

The only schema here is a pointer: fee_obligation.event_registration_id, one arm of fee_obligation's exactly-one rule — an arm with rows behind it, not a dormant hedge.

The is_confirmed / deadline interaction is the one automatic transition in this module, and it is worth flagging as such: the design avoids automatic state changes (D-023, D-040), and payment-confirms-the-place is the one it accepts. It is a deadline, not a sweep: it applies only to registrations at a full event with an unpaid fee, and only after the deadline the organizer set. data-model/08 §6 records it as an accepted cost with the reasoning, and open-questions carries it.

docs.title: 12. The forms: questions and answers
docs.text:
An event may ask registrants for details it needs — tent preference, dietary preference, T- shirt size, whether they are coming by bus.

Questions are defined per event, and answers are rows.

event_question          what this event asks
   │
   └── event_answer     what a person said    ──  one row per question per person

Answers as rows rather than JSONB is the choice that makes the feature work: "who needs a gluten-free meal, and how many?" is a GROUP BY, not a JSON traversal. The cost is a row per answer, which is correct — the number of answers is the number of things the organization must actually act on.

Questions may apply to attendees, organizers, or both, and may be required or optional. Required means the person registering must answer; it is not a global gate on registration, because a form that blocks sign-up is a form nobody completes.

Reusable question libraries are rejected. A shared pool of question definitions is structurally the requirement machinery removed in D-044, and it earns its keep only when the same question must mean the same thing across events. Tent preference does not: what one camp asks and what another needs are allowed to differ, and per-event definitions keep them from having to agree.

docs.title: Health data, and the widening this represents
docs.text:
Event answers are readable by that event's organizers, with no extra gate (D-061). The mechanism is a grant written by the act that creates the event: event.answer.view on that event, aimed at the bare operand ORGANIZERS, in the same transaction as the event row (D-102, D-151). It is one of the twelve the creation writes — every event.* code whose applies_to admits an event — and it is written without MEMBERS, because an organizer appointed for one weekend is not required to be a paying member. Three things follow:

  • "No extra gate" is literally true and visible. That grant is the whole mechanism; there is no clause special-casing organizers. Anyone who wants to see who may read an event's answers reads a grant row.
  • The reach of that grant is per-event. ORGANIZERS with no argument binds to the event the grant sits on, so the row cannot accidentally name the organizers of every camp at once.
  • A create is the author of an event's authority. Whoever holds event.create decides who will be able to read a future event's answers, and the widening is one code deep. What keeps it honest is that "who could read those answers?" stays a query over rows, and an event whose rows did not arrive is a countable failure rather than a rumour.

Two consequences of that reach follow, and the second is the significant one.

1. Only preference-level detail belongs on a form. A dietary preference ("vegetarian", "no pork") is an operational note for the cook. A condition ("coeliac", "nut allergy") is medical data, and nothing in the schema distinguishes them — the difference is what the organizer types into a label. So the discipline is in the form design, not the constraint: data-model/08 §7 states it, and it is guidance, not enforcement.

2. This is the route by which a leader learns a child has a nut allergy, and that is a deliberate widening. A guardian's reach over a child is one value on the guardianship row — none, view or write — read by a channel of its own, entered only when the act is about someone other than the actor and never answered by a role or a grant (D-074, D-079; appendix/permission-catalog.md §9). What a leader gets over a child's data is not of that kind:

"A person does not get these by virtue of leading — that is a safeguarding property."

There is no medical record to be unreachable. Personal data is one class (D-083), so a guarantee that a camp leader "cannot reach a child's medical record at all" describes a category the model does not have. What is true, in the two forms that matter:

  • No role gets it by leading. A leadership role written out of the worked examples is given its rosters and its events — and no read over a person's data (permission-catalog §11). Leadership is not guardianship, and the guardianship channel answers only for the person its row names.
  • It is one grant away. Whoever holds person.view at the unit reads every child's whole record, allergy list included, and a grant at the unit has no narrower reading available, because the unit is the only scope there is (D-097). Nothing in the resolver will stop that and nothing should — but the model does not promise it is impossible either, and a promise the model does not make is worse than none.

So the protection is a decision about a role, revisitable by whoever administers roles — not a wall.

Which means: under any office written the way those examples write one, an allergy recorded on a camp form is the only way the people running the camp will know. That is a coherent and defensible configuration — the parent tells the people present, per event, and nobody outside the family holds the fact — but it is a widening from "the few adults whose guardianship row names them, at one right_level" to "every organizer of any event the child registers for", and it is recorded as such in D-061, with the reasoning, so that nobody later "fixes" the apparent duplication between the two stores by tightening this one.

Event answers are not the person's record. They are operational detail for one event, read by that event's organizers — and they are kept: nothing about an event goes on a schedule, so an answer outlives its event, its organizers and the season that asked the question (D-140), while the same fact recorded on the person is audited, curable and erased with them. Those two copies are the same class of data (D-083), and the retention question that used to sit between them — the same sentence of personal data kept forever in one table and quietly discarded in another — is closed by the two rules agreeing, not by a schedule: an erasure reaches both, and the only difference left is the shape of the reaching, a delete where the row is the value and an emptying where the row is also a fact about the event. What still differs between the copies is who may read them, which is the widening the paragraphs above record. See AT-1 for the alternative this round took up instead of choosing between the two stores: collect the fact once and confirm it at the door — a bound question prefills from the stored value as a suggestion and writes back a fresh dated one (D-139).

docs.title: 13. Open issues
docs.text:
Tracked with the rest in ../open-questions.md: the answered ones under R. Resolved, each carrying the decision that answered it, and the live ones where the module map points. Five of the seven below are settled and say so rather than reading as still open — that is deliberate, because a list of open issues that keeps asking an answered question is how a design gets reopened by a newcomer who reads the list and not the log. The ones this module raises:

  • The age ceiling on an open event — settled: accepted as a risk. The grant is the rule, and a ceiling is writable today as event.register_self aimed at MEMBERS * YOUNGER(15) (§4, D-107). EV-1 stays closed as a choice the organization renews rather than a limit it inherits — nobody has to be told the ceiling cannot be stated, only whether it should be (§4, D-070).
  • What else an organizer should hold — settled: the bundle is derived, not curated. Creating an event writes one item-scope allow per code whose applies_to admits an event — twelve beside every event, event.answer.view among them — each aimed at ORGANIZERS (D-151). A code added to event.* is in the next event's bundle without anyone remembering a list. Everything outside those twelve reaches an organizer only through a unit-scope or item grant they happen to hold, and that is the intended shape: the creation act writes the set of people connected to the item, and writes nothing else (§5, §6).
  • Whether a bound selector makes its audience single-scope. An audience whose expression names PLACED cannot be aimed at a unit-scope grant, so a shared audience row can stop being reusable across scopes. The refusal lands on the grant, which is faithful to the rule as written; whether the editor should warn at the audience instead is unsettled (§7).
  • WHITELISTED — settled: refused. No stored state to name it, so it is not a selector, and there will be no fifth presence tier, no is_whitelisted column and no reserved name (D-148). It was a question about whether the feature is wanted rather than about whether the language could hold it — a predicate over a column is an ordinary operand now (D-107) — and the need it was reached for is met by rows that already exist, which §9 states.
  • Event answer retention — settled: nothing expires, and erasure empties rather than deletes (§12). A dietary answer naming a condition was data of exactly the same class as what the person record holds, held under weaker rules and fresher; the two rules now agree, so the asymmetry is gone rather than mitigated (D-140, EV-2).
  • Cancelled events and fees (§10–11). Cancelling keeps the registrations; whether it releases the obligations, refunds them, or neither is the finance module's call.
  • Presence for minors and the safeguarding record — settled: it stays a column of the registration (§9). No retention of its own, no permission of its own, no presence_record table, and no safeguarding register behind any of it (D-147, EV-4). §7's refusal of PRESENT is the surviving sharp edge, and it is the reason no permission of its own was needed: the column is a record of what happened, and not a set anybody is granted over.

Decisions behind this page: D-023, D-040, D-043, D-044, D-059, D-061, D-064, D-065, D-067, D-070, D-074, D-079, D-083, D-097, D-102, D-107, D-139, D-140, D-147, D-148.

docs.title: Domain — Personal Data
docs.text: What the system knows about a person, why it is all one kind of thing, and what that choice costs. The tables are in ../data-model/09-attributes.md; the reasoning is D-083, D-084 and D-085.

docs.title: 1. One class of data, and no privileged corner
docs.text:
Everything about a person apart from their name, their gender and their age is personal data, stored in fields rather than files — and it is not different in any way.

There is no special shelf inside the person record, no code list whose names begin with something clinical, no access path that exists only for the sensitive part. A drug dosage, a preferred contact language and a shoe size are the same kind of fact: something the organization wrote down about somebody, which will be out of date in three years, which nobody could have enumerated when the schema was designed.

The consequence is uncomfortable and intended: the permission that reads a person's record now reads everything in it. A volunteer with that permission sees the allergy list and the insurance number and the note about who in the family the child actually lives with. That is what "not different in any way" means, and it is why the catalog marks reading a person as one of the serious permissions in the system rather than an ordinary one.

docs.title: The three exceptions, and why they are exceptions
docs.text:
Name, gender and age stay structured, in the identity model (03-identity-and-legacy.md). Not because they are less sensitive — a name is the most persistent piece of data here — but because they answer a different question. They are what a person is called and counted as; everything else is what the organization happens to have noticed. The three are also the only descriptive facts that have been stable across every system this organization has used, which is the practical test for whether something earns a column.

The boundary between "identity machinery" and "descriptive data" is drawn by a harsher test than sensitivity: a fact keeps its own table when there is a rule about it that an open layer cannot express. "Exactly one primary postal contact", "a school id may repeat but a birth number may not", "one current name" — those rules need a known set of columns, and an open layer's whole value is that it has none.

docs.title: 2. The vocabulary is the system
docs.text:
If the organization decides at runtime what it collects, then the list of things it collects is the part of the design that matters. The tables are trivial; the vocabulary is not.

An open vocabulary left open decays the same way every open vocabulary does. Within months there will be allergy, Allergy, alergie, and allergies (2), each with some of the values, and after that the layer still stores everything and answers nothing. Three defences, none clever:

  • Codes are compared in normalized form, so the obvious duplicates are refused rather than filed.
  • Recording a value is open; naming a thing is not. Anyone who can edit a person can write down what the doctor said tonight. Creating a code — deciding that this is now a thing the organization knows about people — takes a permission and a person who reads what they are given.
  • An improvised need has somewhere to go, and it is not a queue. The failure this is aimed at is specific and familiar: at 23:00 on a Friday, there is no field for "carries an adrenaline auto-injector", so the leader types it into a notes box, and it is never read by anyone again. The answer is blunter than the proposal stage it replaced: naming the code is the act of whoever holds attribute.define, and it is live the moment they save it — the permission is the curator, and a person holding a permission is faster than a review list (D-141). The leader at 23:00 does not hold it, and this design no longer pretends otherwise; what it keeps is that a notes box is the worse of the two remaining options, and that a value recorded against a code does exist reaches the screen that gets read at 23:00 (../data-model/09-attributes.md §4).

Curation is a job, and the documents say so rather than assuming it happens. The queue that used to make the job visible is gone, and with it the age signal that said nobody had read the vocabulary in a month. What carries it now is narrower: attribute.define is held by few people, every definition they save is live at once with nobody between the save and the record, and the report that notices a vocabulary rotting is the one that lists a live code whose values contradict its type, a live code nobody ever used, and two codes close enough to be the same thing (../data-model/09-attributes.md §8).

docs.title: 3. Who needs to know what
docs.text:
Who What they need What the design gives them A leader The allergies and instructions for the children they lead, tonight, without asking permission Whatever the organization has granted them, and nothing more — with the cost attached: there is no scope smaller than the whole organization except a single item, so "the children in their unit" has no scope to be granted as such. A person.view at unit scope hands over every member's entire record, allergy lists included; the narrower thing a leader actually wanted is a group roster or an event. The starting grant set gives leadership rosters and events but not a read over the person record A guardian Everything about their child, or nothing, depending on what the organization decided The guardian right level — none, view, write — over the whole record (D-074) The person themselves Their own data Their own record, which is not a special case in the resolver — "about you" is already a channel An event organizer What matters on the day, for the people who registered The registration, and the event form that asks. Where the organization already recorded a fact, the form prefills it as a suggestion the answerer confirms or edits, and confirming writes a fresh value back dated today — the question binds to the definition and never to a stored row (D-139, AT-1) A first aider at a camp The short list: what is this child allergic to, what do they take, what should we do The values are fields, so a list can be produced — which is the argument for fields over documents

Read the leader row twice: it is the sharpest edge in this module. There is no privileged subset of the record to be kept away from anybody, so nothing in the model can promise that a leader cannot read a child's data. What carries the protection is that no leadership role written from the worked examples carries a read over the record, because leadership is not guardianship — and an office confers nothing at all (D-100), so the only thing that could give a leader that read is a grant, written somewhere, naming them. The organization may hand it over deliberately, in one grant, and see exactly what that exposes. (permission-catalog §11 note 3)

The last row is the one that justifies the whole shape. A scanned form in a drawer is a legally tidy answer and a useless one at 23:00 in a tent; the fact has to be something a screen can show somebody who is not thinking clearly.

docs.title: 4. What was refused, and what it cost
docs.text:
One level cannot separate the medical record from the profile. The design therefore cannot say "everything except the diagnoses", which is the shape an arrangement a court might order takes. It expresses such a case as a guardian who either has the record or does not, and somebody will have to explain the difference to a parent. The model fails visibly — one decision, in one place, audited — where a capability list fails quietly, because a list of eighteen ticks nobody read is not a safeguard, it is a receipt. If the case arrives in reality, the route back is one new grant scope over a defined set of data, argued once as a decision, and not a fresh namespace of suggestive permission names. Why: D-074, D-083.

There is no per-field type wall. A field declared as a date warns when someone types 2019, and lets them save it. A wall is the wrong tool precisely where the true value is imprecise and the imprecise answer beats none: probably allergic to wasp stings, mother thinks it was only once is a fact worth keeping, and a validation error would discard it in favor of an empty field.

No history on the row, and no long history anywhere. Values are overwritten and the audit trail holds the sequence — the values themselves, not a note that something changed, since a trail that will not say what changed cannot serve as a history. Elsewhere the model keeps history in business tables when "what was it on that date?" is routine; guardianship is the standing example. Here it is not routine, it is what someone asks during an incident. So the history of a child's allergy list lives in the one control these documents elsewhere admit is discipline rather than guarantee (D-081), in two dependencies, not one: somebody has to write the audit row, on every path including the ones nobody thinks of, and somebody has to keep the trail guarded as the copy of the whole person record that it is. On top of that, the trail's values are emptied 24 months after they were written, though the rows remain (D-088): two years of a child's changing facts are recoverable, and what the organization believed in 2019 is not recoverable at all. That is a real risk, accepted in the open; the entry to reverse if the long version is ever genuinely needed is D-085, not a longer trail.

docs.title: 5. Forgetting
docs.text:
Two operations that look alike and must not be confused.

  • Retiring a thing the organization collects keeps what was collected. The label leaves the form; the values stay readable and reportable, and the label can come back. Deleting a name must not delete nine years of facts, or nobody will ever retire a badly-named thing and the list will only ever grow.
  • Erasing a person deletes what was collected, everywhere, including in the trail's payloads. The organization keeps that it held a record and that it was removed — and not what the record said.

The audit trail carries these values, in the clear, because it is the only place they have a history. What changed is not what the trail holds but who may read it: an entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it quotes, so the permission that opens the trail sits with the serious permissions rather than among the administrative ones (permission-catalog §8). There is no list of sensitive field names the trail scrubs, and there must not be one: such a list is only as good as somebody having predicted the name of every field that would matter, and this organization invents those names at runtime. The protection is the guard — one line in one table of one appendix, and the documents say so where they describe it (../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

What erasure does is absolute in a way the guard is not. It deletes the values and reaches into the trail to delete them again from copies written years earlier, lawfully, when nobody was asking questions about them.

A third way values leave the trail, and it is a policy rather than a right. Every two years' worth of audit rows have their contents emptied whether anybody asked or not (D-088). The distinction from erasure is worth holding onto, because the two are easy to conflate and only one of them is a person's entitlement: erasure is requested and verifiable — the check is that nothing survives — while expiry is neither requested nor satisfied by nothing surviving, since the row itself remains and only its values go. So its failure mode is the opposite one: it fails by not happening. That is why it is a scheduled job with a check that reports an over-age row still holding content, and not a line in a policy document (data-model/06 §2.2 keeps that apart from redaction, which must never be deferred). It is also why the sentence the trail is a second copy of the person record — the sentence that decides who may read it — is true for two years and untrue afterwards.
